en: [Sūtrabhāṣya, page 53] Subhāṣita.
The Mīmāṃsā System of Philosophy.
Together with its commentary.
In the first chapter, the ninth quarter.
Now, therefore, begins the inquiry into Dharma. || 1 ||
Lo!

It should be understood that those words which are well-known in common usage for certain meanings should, where possible, be taken as having those very same meanings in the Sūtras; their meaning should not be imagined through the addition of missing words (*abhyāhāra*) and the like, nor should they be assigned technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*). In this way, the Vedic sentences themselves are explained by these [Sūtras]; otherwise, both the Vedic sentences and the meanings of their own constituent words would have to be explained [separately].

[The preceding words] must be explained, for otherwise an excessive burden of effort would result. Now, in common usage, this word *atha* is seen to signify the commencement of a topic immediately following what has preceded; yet here, no such preceding matter is perceived.
Nevertheless, there must be something by whose existence the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) is appropriately conceived as occurring immediately thereafter.

For it is thus that [the inquiry] becomes conceived as having its meaning established by well-known words; and that is the study of the Veda, for when that exists, [the inquiry] is made manifest. [Objection: "This is not so; for an inquiry into Dharma is appropriate even after other actions, and even prior to the study of the Veda. [Reply: It is said: the Teacher employed the word "atha" (now/then) with reference to such an inquiry into Dharma which is not possible without the study of the Veda. How so? Because here an investigation of various kinds regarding Vedic sentences will take place. Furthermore, we do not [mean] here...
The reading "yatre" (where) is likely intended; in the phrase "prabala," the Kāśmīra recension reads "sathana."
[Page 54] Bhāṣya:

We learn from the preceding part that there is a prohibition of the inquiry into Dharma prior to the study of the Veda, and from the subsequent part that there is immediate succession. It is not possible for this single sentence both to prohibit the inquiry into Dharma before the study of the Veda and to establish immediate succession after it; for in that case, the sentence would be split.

This is a single sentence; for the mode of expression here is different from that which precedes it, which prohibits the desire to investigate dharma after the study of the Veda, and different from that which follows it, which teaches immediate succession.

In the phrase "having studied the Vedas," in one [interpretation] the immediate succession is enjoined by restating [the study], while in the other it is the reverse; thus, because the purpose is one, it establishes the status of being a single sentence. Furthermore, once the Veda has been studied, this [duty] arises: one must return from the teacher's house, [and then consider] the Vedic sentences.

And [the Vedas] are to be investigated; in that regard, the instruction for these two [types of students] is: "Do not return from the teacher's house; how indeed could one investigate the Vedic sentences? If this is so, then the study of the Veda would not be understood as preceding [the investigation]; for thus they recite: "Having studied the Veda..."

"One should go home"—if one were to say this here, then having studied the Veda, one who desires to investigate Dharma would be transgressing this sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). And indeed, the sacred tradition is not to be transgressed.

To this it is replied: we shall indeed transgress this tradition; for by not transgressing it, we would be imagining the Veda—which actually possesses meaning—to be meaningless. For its purpose is seen to be the instruction regarding ritual action (*karman*). Nor do the venerable ritualists [attain that purpose] from the mere recitation of it.

"They declare a fruit, and even where they seem to declare one, in that case too—since substances, preparatory rites, and actions are for the sake of another—the mention of a fruit must be an *arthavāda* (a commendatory statement)," thus [the author] will state its status as an *arthavāda*. Nor is this "immediate succession" (*ānantarya*) enjoined for one who has merely studied the Veda. Furthermore, there is no word here that expresses immediate succession; rather, the suffix *-ktvā* is remembered to denote "prior time," not immediate succession. Moreover, the study of the Veda has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*), which would be contradicted if immediate succession were intended. This meaning [of immediate succession] could only be obtained through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and not from the direct sense of the word.

Bathing is enjoined for an invisible purpose; however, they say that its culmination—by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—is the observance of the rules regarding not loosening [the girdle] and so forth, occurring simultaneously with the study of the Veda.
This is precisely to avoid the charge of having an invisible purpose, as in the injunctions: "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe," and "One should return from the teacher's house."
"He will refute [it]," according to the Kāśmīra and Kīra recensions.
[Page 55]

Therefore, having first completed the study of the Veda, one should thereafter desire to know Dharma—this is the force of the word *atha*. Nor do we say that the inquiry into Dharma must not be undertaken after any other action; rather, [we mean] that after studying the Veda, one should not depart in haste.
Immediately thereafter, dharma is to be investigated; such is the meaning of the word "atha" (then/thereupon).

The word *ataḥ* indicates what has preceded and serves as a reason (*hetu*). For example: "There is safety for me from the mendicants; therefore, I dwell in this place. In the same way, it is understood that the fact that the Veda has been studied is the reason for the desire to know Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*); thus, immediately after [the study of the Veda], Dharma is to be investigated—this is the force of the word *ataḥ*. For one who has not studied the Veda would not be able to investigate the Vedic sentences concerning Dharma; therefore (for this reason), immediately after [the study of the Veda], Dharma [is to be investigated].
Therefore, the meaning of the word [in the sūtra] is "one should desire to know."

The desire to know Dharma is *dharmajijñāsā*; for that is the wish to know it. How is it to be desired to be known? [By asking: What is Dharma? What is its definition? What are its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)? What are the fallacious means of accomplishment (*sādhanābhāsa*)? And what is its ultimate purpose (*kiṃpara*)? Among these, "What is Dharma? What is its definition?"—this has been explained by a single sūtra: "Dharma is a beneficial matter characterized by Vedic injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo ’rtho dharmaḥ*). [As for] "What are its means of accomplishment? What are the fallacious means of accomplishment?"...

"What is its purpose?"—this has been explained by the definition of *śeṣa* (subservience). Wherein lies the supremacy of the *puruṣa*, or where is the *puruṣa* subordinate? This aphorism, "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*), is the summary of these propositions. Is Dharma well-known or unknown? If it is well-known, it need not be inquired into; if it is unknown, it is even less so. Thus, [the inquiry] would be useless.

Is the inquiry into Dharma purposeful? For many learned people are at variance regarding Dharma—some declare one thing to be Dharma, others another. One who proceeds without investigating that [Dharma] might adopt only something partial and be frustrated, and might even incur misfortune.
Therefore, Dharma is that which ought to be investigated; for we maintain that it is Dharma which unites a person with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). This is stated:
"Dharma is a purposeful matter characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*). (1.1.2)

"Codanā" refers to a statement that impels one toward action; for it is observed that when one is urged by a teacher, one thinks, "I shall do it. That by which something is characterized is its definition (lakṣaṇa), such as smoke [which characterizes fire].

For they say that "the characteristic [is] of fire. We maintain that whatever is characterized by that [characteristic], that object connects the person with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). For an injunction (*codanā*) [makes known] an object of such a kind as past, present, future, subtle, concealed, or remote.

Nothing other than the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is capable of making [the dharma] known; nor would such an injunction speak of an object in the same manner as any ordinary worldly statement—such as "There are fruits on the riverbank"—which may be true, yet may also be false. It is replied: this which you say, that "it speaks and yet is false," is a contradiction.

Thus he says; it is said that [the Vedic injunction] causes one to understand—it becomes the cause for one who is understanding—and when that which has become the cause exists, one understands, and thus it causes one to understand. And if, when the injunction exists, it is understood that "heaven results from the Agnihotra," how can it be said that "it is not so"? Or, if it is not so, [then the injunction is false].

How is it understood? To say that one understands a non-existent object is a contradiction. Furthermore, from the scriptural injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," nothing uncertain is understood—such as whether heaven exists or does not exist. Nor can this certain understanding be false; for a cognition is false only when, having arisen, it subsequently perishes with the realization, "This is not so. But this [knowledge] never undergoes sublation at another time, in another person, in another state, or in another place. Therefore, it is not untrue.
Know that the contract is there.

If that worldly statement comes from a trustworthy person or concerns an object of the senses, it is indeed non-false; however, if it comes from an untrustworthy person or concerns something beyond the range of the senses,
it is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*), as it originates from human intellect, for it is subject to error by a human being.

If it is argued that "it is understood from another human statement," then that too is equally [unreliable]. Human testimony does not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge regarding matters of this kind, just as the word of those born blind has no authority concerning specific colors. Nor is it the case that the instruction of the learned is untenable; for Manu and others did indeed provide such instructions, and therefore they must have been virtuous men.

And it has been understood that "form is perceived by the eye," which is known from perception itself. It is replied: for instructions may arise even from delusion; and when there is no delusion, they may arise even from the Veda.
Furthermore, from a human statement, it is thus: [Page 57] Bhāṣya. Delusion may arise even from the Veda. Moreover, from a human statement: "Thus..."
The cognition arises as "this person knows," not as "the object is thus";
for indeed, a cognition based on the word of a human being may sometimes be erroneous, but there is no evidence whatsoever for the falsity of the Vedic word. [Objection: "But surely..."

Having observed that human speech is false by means of the *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [inference], this [Vedic] speech is also understood to be false because of its similarity to speech. It is not so, because they are different; for when one thing is false, it does not follow that another must be false simply because of its difference from it—just as [the falsity of] Devadatta [does not imply the falsity of Yajñadatta].

If [the person] is dark-complexioned, then Yajñadatta must also be dark-complexioned. Furthermore, it is understood from the statement itself that the inference—"The Vedic word is false because it shares the same nature as human speech"—is set aside; for there is direct cognition (*pratyakṣa*) through the Vedic word, and inference cannot be an authoritative means of knowledge when it contradicts direct perception. Therefore, the object characterized by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is conducive to the highest good (*śreyaskara*). [Objection: "In that case, one should desire to know what is conducive to the highest good; what is the use of the inquiry into Dharma? It is replied: [The text continues with the response: ...[as follows]... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly after "uccarate," which is likely a scribal error for "ucyate. The translation reflects the available portion.)
—That alone which brings about the highest good is designated by the word *dharma*. How is this to be understood? For one who performs a sacrifice is called "righteous" (*dhārmika*);
and whoever is the agent of something is designated by that very thing, just as, for example, [one is called] a "cook" (*pāvaka*) or a "reaper" (*lāvaka*).

Therefore, that which unites a person with the supreme good is expressed by the word *dharma*. Not only in common worldly usage, but even in the Veda, it is taught that *dharma* belongs precisely to those things denoted by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), as in: "The gods sacrificed with the sacrifice; those were the first *dharmas*. Thus, they declare that *dharma* consists of the very acts signified by the term *yajati*.
In this context, both the beneficial (*artha*) and the harmful (*anartha*) are indicated by the injunction (*codanā*). What is the beneficial?

That which leads to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and others. What is the harmful? That which leads to transgression (*pratyavāya*), such as the *Śyena*, *Vajra*, and *Iṣu* sacrifices and so forth. In that regard, let it not be said that "the harmful has been declared to be *dharma*."

The word "bhūta" (being) is used here to signify "that which is already existent. But how, then, is this [the Śyena sacrifice] something undesirable? Because it is violence; and violence is prohibited. But how can that which is undesirable be taught as something to be performed? It is said in reply: the Śyena and other such sacrifices are not understood as being themselves to be performed. For their instruction is: "This is the means for one who desires to strike [an enemy]"—as they recite, "One practicing malevolent magic (abhicaraṇa) should sacrifice with the Śyena"—and not, "Malevolent magic ought to be practiced."

— thus [it is said]. Now, is it not the case that this sūtra, "Dharma is characterized by injunction (codanā)," was intended to express these two meanings: that dharma is characterized by injunction and not by the senses and so forth; and that dharma is a beneficial purpose (artha) and not a harmful one (anartha)?
"Thus, s· bhā.";
for this is a single sentence, and it would be split if that were the case. It is replied: where...

The meaning is understood from the sentence; in that case, it is thus. However, this applies to Vedic texts, not to the Sūtras, because when the meaning is already known from another source, it is understood as "this [Sūtra] is for this purpose. And by that, the Sūtra "A portion is recited" (Ekadeśaḥ srucyate) is indicated; and it should be understood that these two are portions of two distinct sentences. Alternatively, since the meaning already exists and is characterized by an injunction, its status as Dharma is stated; thus, it has a single purpose. Now follows the investigation of its cause: "tasya nimittaparīṣṭiḥ" (3).
We have stated that "the knowledge of Dharma has its source in Vedic injunction (codanā)";

this was stated as a mere proposition. Now we shall examine its source: whether it is the injunction alone, or something else as well? Therefore, it is not yet determined that "Dharma is an object characterized by injunction. To this, it is replied: when there is contact of a person's sense organs with an existing object, the arising of cognition is perception (pratyakṣa).
The signless [is not the ultimate] because it is an apprehension of what exists. || 4 ||

Commentary: This is now examined: first of all, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not a means [of knowing Dharma]. What is the reason? Because it is defined as such: "Perception is the arising of cognition in a person when there is contact with the sense organs" (*satsaṃprayoge puruṣasyendriyāṇāṃ buddhijanma*).
That is, perception is that cognition which arises for a person when there is a connection between the sense organ and its object.

And this [Dharma] is yet to come; it does not exist at the time of cognition. Furthermore, this is the apprehension of what exists, not of what does not exist. Therefore, perception is not a means [of knowing Dharma]. [The term] *buddhi* refers to cognition, and *janma* to its arising.
Or, whether it be "contact" (*sannikarṣa*), this sūtra does not intend to restrict any one of these [factors] exclusively;

rather, it is restricted only to the extent that [perception occurs] when there is contact between the sense organ and its object, and not when there is none. If more than one factor were to be restricted, the sentence would be split. Furthermore, because inference, comparison, and postulation are preceded by perception, they too are not the primary cause [of knowledge].
Even non-existence does not exist, because [of this],
Chapter 9, Section 1, Page 59.

But the relationship between a word and its meaning is innate; its cognition arises from instruction, which is non-deviating with respect to an object not perceived [by other means]. That is the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), according to Bādarāyaṇa, because it is independent. 5.

The Bhāṣya says: "Innate" (autpattika) means eternal; for "origination" (utpatti) is used here figuratively to mean "existence" (bhāva). The relationship between word and meaning is an existence that is inseparable, not one that occurs after they have already arisen.

Next is the relationship: the innate relationship between a word and its meaning, which is the means of knowing that dharma characterized by the Agnihotra and so forth, which is not apprehended through perception and other means.
How so? Because there is "instruction" (*upadeśa*); "instruction" is the utterance of a specific word. And there is no deviation in the cognition [it produces], for the cognition produced by it—

It is subject to error. And that which is called knowledge, if it were not subject to error, it could not be said of it, "This is not so. It would not be the case that it is as it is cognized, nor that it is as it is not cognized. If one thing were in his heart and another in his speech, this contradiction would be perceived from such a speaker: "Does it exist, or does it not exist? Therefore...

That [knowledge] is authoritative because it is independent; no other means of cognition or another person need be relied upon for this cognition. The mention of Bādarāyaṇa is to proclaim his view as such, in order to honor Bādarāyaṇa, not to set forth his own personal opinion.

The author of the *Vṛtti*, however, explained this passage beginning with "the investigation of its cause" (*tasya nimittaparīṣṭiḥ*) in a different manner: "The cause need not be investigated, for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception and the rest, are well-established; and since the former [the cause] is included within them, that too need not be investigated. To this, he replies: "It must be investigated because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). For instance, mother-of-pearl appears like silver; therefore, perception is subject to deviation."

And because inference and the other means of knowledge are rooted in that [perception], one who acts without having examined them therein might be frustrated and sometimes meet with misfortune. This is not so; for what is perception is that which is "not separated" from its definition (or, according to another reading, "distinct from its definition").
[Bhāṣya, p. 60]:
That which does not deviate [from the object] is perception; that which deviates is not perception.
What, then, is perception? "Perception is the arising of cognition in a person when there is contact with an existing object through the sense organs."

When there is contact of the sense organs with that very object which is the domain of the cognition, the arising of a person's awareness is true perception (*satpratyakṣa*). That cognition which arises from contact with one thing while having another thing as its object is not perception. But how is this understood—that "this [cognition] occurs when there is contact with that," and "this [cognition] occurs when there is contact with another"? That which does not occur when there is contact with another occurs when there is contact with that; the opposite of this is contact with another. How is this to be known? For instance, even when there is mother-of-pearl...

Thinking thus, one considers: "My eye is in contact with silver. For where a subverting cognition arises—such as "This is not so; it is a false cognition"—that occurs when there is contact with something else;
whereas the opposite occurs when there is contact with that [very thing]. How is this known prior to the arising of the subverting cognition?
At that time, there is no distinction whatsoever between right cognition and false cognition.

For when the mind is afflicted by the eyes and so forth, or when the sense organ is [afflicted] by cataracts and the like, or when the object of speech is [obscured] by subtlety and so forth, then there is false cognition; whereas when these are not so afflicted, there is right cognition. Indeed, the contact between the sense organ, the mind, and the object is the cause of right cognition; in its absence, there is false cognition, due to a defect residing in either of those two.

It is the cause of false cognition; for when the instruments [of knowledge] are defective, cognition becomes false. How is this understood? Because we observe correct apprehension (*saṃpratipatti*) when the defects have been removed. If it is asked, "How is the distinction between the defective and the non-defective known?", we reply: if we search with effort and do not perceive a defect, we shall consider it non-defective due to the absence of evidence [to the contrary]. Therefore, that cognition alone is incorrect in which the instrument is defective or where there is a conviction of falsity, and no other.

Now, is it not the case that "every cognition is indeed without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), like a dream-cognition; for the nature of a cognition's lack of an objective basis is observed in a dream, and even for one who is awake, there occurs only a cognition such as 'a pillar' or 'a wall'?"

Therefore, that too is without an objective basis. It is argued: "How could the well-ascertained cognition 'this is a pillar,' which arises from this [perception], be subverted? [We reply: In the case of a dream, it was likewise well-ascertained prior to waking; there is no difference [between the two]. No, for in a dream, a subversion is observed. [Page 61] It is not [subverted] when there is no subversion.

Due to the weakness of the mind when it is accompanied by sleep, sleep is the cause of false states, such as the perception of space and so forth, or of space within space. In deep sleep (*suṣupta*), there is simply an absence [of cognition]; for one is indeed called "deeply asleep" precisely because one is not conscious. Therefore, the cognition of one who is awake is not false. [Objection: But surely even for one who is awake, there may be a defect of the sense organs. [Response: If there were such a defect, it would be perceived. Even at the time of not seeing space [in a dream], [the waking cognition is not false].
If it is argued that [this] is not understood, [we reply]: in that state, one who has awakened understands, "My mind was in a state of sleep.
But [the world] is empty. How so? Because we do not perceive any difference in form between the object and the cognition thereof.

Furthermore, our cognition is devoid of form; therefore, we perceive that there is no such thing as an object-form distinct from it. This might be so, provided that cognition possessed the form of the object;
however, for us, cognition is formless, while the external object possesses form, for it is connected with external space.

It is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For perceptual cognition has an object as its domain, not another cognition as its domain; for it is momentary and will not persist until the time of another cognition.
As for the claim that "this [cognition], while being produced itself, is known and makes another object known, like a lamp"—that is not so. No one perceives a cognition once it has been known.

But when [the object] is known, one understands it through inference; in that case, simultaneity is untenable. Now, it might be argued: "It is said that 'the object is known' only when the cognition has already arisen, not when it has not arisen; therefore, the cognition arises first, and subsequently the object is known. True, the cognition arises first, but it does not follow that one perceives [the object] at that time—this is an additional point [in the Kāśikā commentary].
The reading in the Kāśikākośa is "pratyayāt";
the reading in the Prācīna [manuscript] is "viparyayavaśādāgataḥ".
"Because of the perception of the opposite at the beginning of waking and at the end of dreaming, there is indeed an absence of deep sleep," so says the *Kārikā-saṃgraha*.
[Page 62] But first, the cognition is known. For this sometimes occurs: that one who is already known as Pārtha is called "unknown.
And there is no apprehension of the form of the cognition without the designation of the object.
[Objection: There is apprehension [of the object]; therefore, cognition is not inexpressible (*avyapadeśya*), and that which is inexpressible is not non-perceptual.

Therefore, cognition is not perceptual. [Reply: Furthermore, even if cognition were of a single form, it would simply be the absence of cognition itself, not of the object which exists as something perceptual. Moreover, there is no single form, for [cognition] is indeed without a form (*anākārā*).

For we infer the existence of the Buddha, and we perceive the object with its specific form through direct perception itself; therefore, cognition has an objective basis. Furthermore, the cognition of a cloth occurs only when threads are specifically employed as its cause; otherwise, even when threads are being taken up, [the cognition might] occasionally [not arise].

The cognition of a jar would occur for one whose sense faculties are unimpaired; however, this is not the case, therefore cognition is not without an objective basis. Consequently, perception does not deviate from its object.

Inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition of an object not in contact [with the senses] based on the observation of one part by someone who knows the relationship [between the two parts]. It is of two kinds: that where the relationship is observed through perception (*pratyakṣatodṛṣṭasaṃbandha*), and that where the relationship is observed through generalization (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭasaṃbandha*). An example of inference where the relationship is observed through perception is the cognition of fire from the sight of smoke. An example of inference where the relationship is observed through generalization is the recollection of the sun’s motion after observing Devadatta’s arrival at another location preceded by his movement. [An example of the latter is] the cognition of the meaning from the knowledge of the word.
Cognition regarding an object not in close proximity [is perception]. Analogy (*upamāna*) also produces a cognition regarding an object not in close proximity, namely, similarity;

for example, the sight of a *gavaya* [produces] the recollection of a cow. Furthermore, presumption (*arthāpatti*) is the postulation of a fact because what is seen or heard cannot otherwise be accounted for;
for example, when Devadatta is known to be alive, the unseen fact of his being outside is inferred by observing his absence from the house.

Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Non-existence (*abhāva*) is also the absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*), regarding the object that is not in contact [with the senses], namely the fact that "it does not exist. Therefore, because it is well-established, its cause (*nimitta*) need not be examined.

Now, one might object: "Granted that perception and the others may indeed be other means of valid cognition, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not a means of valid cognition. Why? Because it is not a cause [of knowledge] since it apprehends what is already existent."

(19) The word "animittam" (without cause/sign) [is used] while [the author] is laboring; it is appropriate that the reading should be "yo 'supalambhanaviṣayaḥ yatra na pratyakṣam" (that which is not an object of perception, where there is no direct perception).
"Of the living Devadatta," according to the Kāśikā Saṃgraha.
This concludes the first five [sections]. 11 | 17 | In the row, [page 63], it is not perceived in the commentary;
that which is not perceived does not exist, just as the horn of a rabbit. Those things which are perceivable...

The sense organs of animals and the like do not exist [at the time of the sacrifice], nor are animals perceived immediately after one who desires cattle [performs the rite]. Therefore, the sacrifice does not have cattle as its fruit. Furthermore, the fruit must exist at the time of the action; for when there is exertion, there is pleasure at that same time. If it is argued that "it will grant the fruit at another time," we say no; we understand that "there is no fruit from the sacrifice at another time."
Why? Because when that [past action] existed, it did not then give its fruit;
and when the fruit arises, it no longer exists. How can that which is non-existent give [the fruit]?
Furthermore, we perceive another cause of the fruit directly before our eyes. And while a visible cause exists...

When something is already perceived, it is not possible to postulate an unseen [result], due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, we maintain that for the Veda, whose reliability is thus observed to be compromised, even results such as heaven cannot exist. Furthermore, there is certain scriptural statement that contradicts what is perceived; having prescribed the *pāśucayana* (the piling of bricks), it says: "This very sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes directly to the heavenly world"—yet this refers to the perceptible body.
"He points it out, yet he does not go to the heavenly world," for that is directly perceived by the giver;

thus, "he does not go" is a prescriptive statement. A statement of this kind, which contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is not authoritative—just as, for example, "gourds sink in water" or "stones float. Because of its similarity to such cases, there would be a lack of confidence even in the injunctions regarding the Agnihotra and other rites. Therefore, Dharma is not an object characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*).
"An injunction is the characteristic of dharma;

for the relationship between a word and its meaning is innate, and the knowledge of that [dharma]—which is characterized by the Agnihotra and so forth—is not apprehended through perception and other means. The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the opposing view. The relationship between a word and its meaning is non-human (*apauruṣeya*). The knowledge of that [dharma]—characterized by the Agnihotra and so forth—which is not understood through perception and the like, is thus correctly cognized through an injunction (*codanā*). [This is] in contrast to the human [source].
For if there were doubt regarding the cognition produced by the word "hi," one might suspect its falsity;
however, we understand that the cognition of another person is false when the result [of their action] turns out to be false at a later time—thus says the Kāśikā Saṃgraha.
Furthermore, it is heard that the fruit occurs at that very same time; this is understood from the statement "the sacrifice is the instrument" (*yāgaḥ karaṇam*).
And if the cause has arisen, the effect must necessarily follow—thus [it is stated] in the *Prāyaścittapradīpa*.
"For when there is a connection in the form of a tree, then [there is] its cognition"—thus [it is stated] in the Kāśikā-saṃgraha.

[Page 64] For it would be so then. But if the word itself speaks, how can it be false? For at that time, we do not seek comprehension from any other person. When it is said "it speaks," it means "it causes understanding."

[The opponent argues: "When one is perceiving, there is a cause [for that perception]; and when the word is the cause, one perceives it oneself. How could one say, being deceived, 'This is not so'? Nor does the injunction regarding this [perception] produce a doubtful cognition such as 'it may be so, or it may not. Nor does a subsequent non-designative cognition arise at another time, in another place, in another state, or with respect to another person, to the effect that 'this was false'? [The author replies: Having observed the absence of a connection between the object and the cognition of a competent person...

In this case as well, a cognition based on inference arises, thinking, "There will be a contrary [result]," and being contradicted by this perceptual cognition, it is sublated. Therefore, dharma is indeed characterized solely by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*).

"It may be so; however, there is no connection whatsoever between a word and its meaning. How then could it have either a human origin or a non-human origin? Why? If there were a connection with the meaning, then upon the utterance of the words 'razor' (*kṣura*) and 'sweetmeat' (*modaka*), one's mouth would be cut or filled. This is said with reference to a connection characterized by contact. As for [other types of relations] such as cause and effect, sign and that which is indicated, purpose and that which serves it, substratum and that which rests upon it, or conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and so forth..."
These [objections] regarding sound are simply untenable.
The relations are being stated.
That relation which is to be designated, that one you do not designate—namely, the relation characterized by the connection between the signifier and the signified. Thus it is said.

[Objection: "If a word is a communicator [of meaning], why does it not communicate when heard for the first time? [Reply: It is said: For us, perception is the authority in all cases. Indeed, having perceived the cognition [it produces], we understand that "it is a communicator"; but we do not understand "it is not heard for the first time" because we have not perceived the cognition at the first hearing. Rather, only after it has been heard a certain number of times is it determined: "this is the name (saṃjñā), this is the named object (saṃjñin)."

To whatever extent there is comprehension of the meaning from hearing, it occurs to that same extent. Just as the eye, having seen, does not illuminate without the aid of light, so too it does not become "seen" [without it].
If [it is argued that] "it is produced," [then the answer is as follows]. (Prāyaścitta-puṭa). [Regarding the phrase] "but those beginning with marriage" (Kārikā-saṃgraha).

13. Bhāṣya: First, it does not cause [the word] to convey [the meaning]. There is a connection between the word and the object through the power of convention (*saṃketa*).

Why? Because by their very nature these two—the word and the object—are unconnected. For we perceive the word in the mouth and the object on the ground. Furthermore, people designate them thus: "This is the word, not the object; this is the object, not the word. There is also a difference in form: they utter the word "cow," and they understand the object as possessing dewlaps and so forth. And since they are distinct entities...
Whatever relationship exists is seen to be produced, just as, for example, that between a rope and a jar.

Now, regarding the word "cow" (*go*), what is the word? The venerable Upavarṣa says: "It is the phonemes *g*, *au*, and the visarga (*ḥ*); for in common worldly usage, the term 'word' (*śabda*) is well-established as referring to that object which is apprehended by the sense of hearing."

And these [phonemes] are apprehended by the sense of hearing. If this is so, the cognition of meaning is not possible. How so? Meaning is not perceived from each individual phoneme; nor does there exist any other thing called a "collection" (samudāya) distinct from the phonemes, from which such a comprehension could arise. When...

When there is the sound *ga*, there are not the sounds *au* and the *visarjanīya*; when there are the sounds *au* and the *visarjanīya*, there is not the sound *ga*. Therefore, there exists no other word "go" distinct from the sounds *ga* and the rest, from which the comprehension of the meaning could arise. [Objection: When the word has disappeared, the comprehension of the meaning occurs through recollection.

If you say this, we reply: No, because memory itself is momentary; let those who are satisfied with mere appearances be so. There is no fault in the view that the final syllable, accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding syllables, is what conveys the meaning. [Objection: "But in that case, the common worldly expression, 'We understand the meaning from the word,' would be untenable.
[Response: It is said: If it is untenable, then let it be untenable. For it is not the case that... [the worldly expression is authoritative].

An object that is not apprehended through perception and other means of knowledge cannot be accepted merely on the grounds that a statement is "unreasonable. We observe that worldly statements are both reasonable in their meaning and unreasonable in their meaning; for example, such statements as "Devadatta!
Bring the cow," and so forth, and such statements as "Ten pomegranates, six cakes," and so forth.

But is it not the case that even the authors of the treatises have said this: "In this context, there is no negative particle (*na-kāra*) [denying] the verbal action (*ākhyāta*) which consists of a sequence of prior and posterior stages"? (Kāśikā on Pāṇini 3.4.69).
"There exists some aggregate distinct from the letter *ga* and so forth," as stated in the Prācīna-puṣpa manuscript.
"The skin of a spotted deer," this is an addition in the Kāśmīra manuscript;
it is found in the Prācīna-puṣpa manuscript on page 66.
It is not as in the case of [expressions] such as "he goes," "he cooks," or "he speaks," which refer to the entire duration from the commencement until the completion;
for even the statement of a treatise-author is not sufficient to establish this point, which lacks authoritative proof.

Nor is this argument untenable; for it is possible that "from the syllables arise the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), and from the mental impressions comes the comprehension of the meaning. Thus, in the comprehension of meaning, the syllables are the cause.

If it is argued that "the word is merely secondary (*gauṇa*) in the comprehension of meaning," we say no; the status of being a cause is not secondary in the case of the supreme [entities], because [the effect] exists when they exist, and does not exist when they do not.

Or perhaps [it might be argued that] "it would be figurative" (gauṇaḥ). No; for one cannot postulate a meaning that is not apprehended through perception and other means of knowledge simply so that "the word may not be figurative. Indeed, when it is said, "The boy is fire" (agnir māṇavakaḥ), the word "fire" does not—on the grounds that "it may not be figurative"—[imply actual burning].

Thus it is determined that "this is the young student. Nor is there a word "go" (cow) perceived as something other than the phonemes *ga*, etc., because no perception of difference occurs and there is indeed a perception of non-difference. For the phonemes *ga* and so forth are directly perceived. Therefore, the word "gauḥ," consisting of the phonemes beginning with *ga* and ending with the visarga (*visarjanīya*), is nothing but the phonemes themselves. Consequently, there is no word called a "pada" distinct from them. [Objection: But even in the hypothesis of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), there is the postulation of something unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*). [Reply: It is said: In the hypothesis of a [distinct] word, there would be both that [postulation of an impression] and the postulation of the word itself. Therefore, the phonemes alone constitute the word.

Now, what is the meaning of this word "cow"? We reply: it is the form (*ākṛti*) characterized by the dewlap and so forth. But is it not the case that "the form is yet to be proven, or does it not exist at all"? No; being perceptible, it cannot be something that requires proof, for it is seen directly as "a necklace," "a svastika," or "a vardhamānaka. [Objection: "It is an illusion."

If [it is argued]: No, for it cannot be said that there is no delusion when there is no perversion of the conditions (*pratyaya-viparyāsa*). If it is argued: "Even in the absence of an external object, such a cognition arises—just as in the cases of 'a row,' 'a herd,' or 'a forest,'" we say: No, this statement you have put forward is incoherent. Do you mean to say that a cognition of a "forest" occurs even when the forest does not exist? This is a direct denial of perception itself, implying that "even those [trees] do not exist. If that were so, then that [position] has already been refuted.
"This sound is indeed [the word] *go*," according to the Kāśikā Saṃgraha.
[Page 67] Chapter 1, Section 9.

15. Bhāṣya: This is a "grandiose" (*māhājānika*) argument. Now, [the opponent] says: "Is the proponent of the *alatisagāva* (non-existent cow) being censured? Your other tenet is being refuted. He then drinks from the forest. The cognition of "forest" (*vana*) follows—[so he argues]. Even so, one who is unable to refute the subject at hand falls into a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) by refuting another tenet of that [proponent], because it is not a proof (*asādhakatvāt*). For he...
He will say: "Let it be corrupted; if it is corrupted, what does that matter?
Whether it is corrupted or uncorrupted, has your position been established, or has my own argument been refuted?
Nor [is it the case that] because a forest distinct from the letter *ṭa* is not perceived, therefore there is no forest.

It is understood that "the forest does not exist. If, in the case of a forest, a cognition contrary to its actual existence were to arise due to some other cause, then one would conclude that the cognition of the forest is indeed false, and thereby understand that "the forest does not exist.
However, the cognition regarding cows and the like does not undergo such subversion. Therefore, there is a disparity between the two cases.

Furthermore, one does not have a misconception regarding forests and the like, nor does one think, "these do not exist. Therefore, the comparison with a row [of ants] and a forest is irrelevant. Consequently, Jaimini’s statement that "the genus (*ākṛti*) is the meaning of a word" is established. And how it is that the genus is the meaning of a word, we shall demonstrate more precisely later on (Book 9, Chapter 3).
Now, as for the question, "What is this relation?"—it is that when the word is cognized, the object is cognized;
however, it has been previously established (at 13.1) that this [relation] is artificial. Therefore, we consider that some person must have created the relation between words and their objects.

"It was composed for the sake of worldly transaction"—this is what is now being addressed: "Because the relationship [between word and meaning] is non-human (apauruṣeya), it is established. But how is this understood—that "this relationship is non-human"? Because there is no person who could be its creator. How is it that there is no creator? Because of the absence of perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because the other [means of knowledge] are preceded by that [perception]. [Objection: But might it not be the case that, due to having existed for a very long time, it has become beyond the range of perception?

[This refers] to those of the present day. For [if it were so], that which has existed for a long time would not be remembered. Nor could there be a lack of remembrance regarding [places like] the Himalayas and so forth, as there is in the case of wells, gardens, and the like. [The term] "Mahāyānika" appears in the manuscript as "Puruṣaviyoga."
Regarding the word "satī" here, the Prācīna-puṣpa reads "te hi."

For there occurs the destruction of those [traditions] through the destruction of a region or the destruction of a family. Yet, there is no separation of persons from the linguistic usage of words and their meanings. It might be argued: "Those who deal with the mere relationship [of word and meaning], disregarding the mention of an author as being purposeless, might forget it.
This is not so. For if a person were to create a relationship and then employ it in practice, at the time of that practice...

He must necessarily be remembered; for it is through agreement that the purpose of the author's usage is established, not through disagreement. For instance, by the word *vṛddhi*, the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* would not be understood from Pāṇini’s usage by one who does not accept Pāṇini’s composition.
Likewise, by the letter *m*, the *sarvaguru* (all-long) *cchaka* would not be understood by one who is not [a follower of] Piṅgala.

Or, for one who does not accept Piṅgala as the author [of the *Chandaḥsūtra*], by that very fact, both the author and the user are agreed upon. Therefore, those who employ the Veda must necessarily remember the author of its relationship [to its meaning], as well as the author of its usage. For it is not the case that, regarding the author of the rule "vṛddhir ādaic" (Pāṇini 1.1.1), there is [an expectation] such as "that whose initial vowel among the vowels is vṛddhi" (Pāṇini 1.1.73).
Thus, something might be perceived [as stated in] Pāda 1, Sūtra 32.

Therefore, we understand from this reason that the Vedas were not composed by anyone for the sake of worldly usage after having established a relationship [between words and their meanings]. And even if forgetfulness were possible,
nevertheless, we cannot accept an author of the relationship in the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just as...

It may be that there is non-perception even of something that exists; however, we do not accept the existence of a rabbit’s horn on the basis of this alone without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the relationship between a word and its meaning is non-human (*apauruṣeya*). Now, one might object: "We may indeed understand a creator of the relationship through inference (*arthāpatti*), yet we do not observe people understanding a meaning from a word for which a relationship has been newly created. If they were to understand it [newly], they would understand it even upon hearing it for the first time. Since we do not observe this, [it is understood that the relationship is eternal]."

If it is argued that [the relationship] must exist because of the connection [between word and meaning], we say no, because the instruction is given as something already established (*siddhavat*). For if, due to the absence of a creator of the relationship (*saṃbandhṛ*), the meanings were not necessarily perceived, then they would have to be conveyed by way of presumption (*arthāpatti*). (Kāśikā-kṛt, Kāśī edition).
The *Piṅgala-sūtra* states "mastrigurū," and Halāyudha’s commentary on it explains this as "a short [syllable] followed by three long [syllables]."
[Page 69] Bhāṣya:
We understand that there is a creator of the relationship [between word and meaning]. However, there is another way:
children are seen perceiving an object directly while listening to elders who are conversing for their own purposes. Those elders, when they were children, likewise [perceived it] from others.

"From those who are firm, and from others as well"—thus there would be no beginning—or alternatively: "Not even a single connection between a word and its meaning ever existed, and then connections were set in motion by someone. Regarding this, in the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*):

If [the creator] existed, he would not deserve to be the author of the relationship; for those who speak from the standpoint of worldly convention point to perception as their authority, whereas others merely postulate a creator. And when perception stands as the adversary, a mere postulation is not valid. Therefore, there is no creator of the relationship.

"And there is no exclusion" (7.2): just as in this region the word "cow" applies to that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, so it is in all inaccessible places as well; how could many makers of the relationship agree?
One person alone would not be able [to do so]; therefore, there is no maker of the relationship. (Another says:)

"And there is no non-distinction [of time]," for there is no time whatsoever distinct from the act of relation in which not even a single word was related to any meaning. How so? For the very act of establishing a relation is not possible; by whomsoever this relation is being made, it must necessarily be done by means of some word. By what means was that [word] by which it is performed itself established? Or was it established by yet another word? [And so on ad infinitum.]

Regarding the question "by what [is it known]?"—to the question "by what?", it does not remain [unanswered]. Therefore, one who necessarily establishes this relationship must admit that certain words whose relationships have not been established are nonetheless proven through linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). If there is such proof through usage, then a relationship is not strictly required.
Nor is there even a presumption (arthāpatti) that it must be so.

It might be argued: "How can children, for whom the relationship [between word and meaning] is not established, understand from the two [the speaker and the listener]? There is no such thing as what is seen being impossible; for we see children understanding from elders, and they do not understand by having previously grasped the relationship created by an author of the relationship.
Therefore, there is a discrepancy.

Regarding the phrase "in the unperceived" (7.2), it means that when an object such as Devadatta is not perceived, [one thinks] "I shall act toward him. (*This is the reading in the Prācīna-puṣpikā manuscript.)

[Page 70] Bhāṣya: The creation of a designation is impossible; for designations are made in order to comprehend specific particulars and with reference to those specific particulars. Since those specific particulars are not being cognized, both [the purpose and the means] are unfeasible.

Therefore, the relationship between a word and its meaning is non-human (apauruṣeya). And for this reason, it is a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), because it is independent (anapecatvāt). This being the case, it does not depend upon another person or another cognition. Therefore, the Vedic injunction (codanā) alone is the source of dharma.
It does not have another characteristic; the mention of Bādarāyaṇa has already been explained [in Sūtra 7.15].

Now, as for what was said [at 10.24]: "Verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because its result is not seen at the time of the action, and because the action no longer exists at a later time. To this it is replied: It would not be a means of valid cognition if there were only five means of valid cognition; for whatever is used to cognize something is a means of valid cognition, and by verbal testimony, too, something is cognized; therefore, verbal testimony is also a means of valid cognition, just like perception. Nor does something become "not cognized" merely because it has been cognized by one means of valid cognition but not yet by another. Furthermore, it is not heard [in scripture] that they...

The fruit arises from the action alone; however, as for the claim that "the fruit of the action is obtained" and that "there is another perceptible cause for the fruit at a later time," this is not a fault, for in that case both that [action] and the word [of scripture] are the cause.

As for the statement cited (11/11), which contradicts perception—"This very sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes by means of the self to the heavenly world"—and which, it is argued, designates the perceptible body as the "self," we reply: this is because of its connection with the body, [not because it is the body]. Of whom...

That body, because it possesses those sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*), is called "the possessor of sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudhī*). [Objection: Who is this other one? We do not perceive him. [Reply: We perceive him through the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth—he who breathes in, breathes out, exhales, blinks, and performs such activities; and he is the "possessor of sacrificial implements" within the body. [Objection: But is it not the case that the body itself...

"It breathes in and breathes out. No; for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth possess properties contrary to those of the body, because they do not persist as long as the body does. The qualities of this [body], such as color and so forth, exist for as long as the body exists;
however, the vital breaths and so forth do not exist even when the body is present. Thus ends the opinion of the author of the *Upavṛtti*.
[Page 71] Chapter 1, Section 1.

[They] are perceived, but unlike the qualities of the body such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, they are not perceived by another. Therefore, because of this difference from the qualities of the body, he who possesses the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudhin*) is other than the body. An objection is raised: "From what source does this conviction arise—that [the self] is distinct from pleasure and the rest? [The reply is: Because those [pleasures and so forth] are abandoned.
"It exists," [you may say]; for we do not perceive its essential nature apart from pleasure and the like.
Therefore, it does not exist here, just like a horn [on a rabbit]. If it is asked, "In whose absence would there be pleasure and the like? we shall reply: "In no one's absence at all. For indeed...

Whatever is perceived must have a correlate; and when a correlate is also perceived, it is understood that "this is the correlate of that. Indeed, having perceived the moon or the sun, one does not inquire after a correlate by asking, "To whom does this belong?
It is determined that it belongs to no one at all. Therefore, [the self] is distinct from the body and so forth.
Thus it exists. Now, whatever is perceived must necessarily have a related possessor.

Therefore, having perceived even the self in this manner, one should seek another related entity by asking, "To whom does this belong? Having postulated that as well, one should postulate yet another.

If one were to postulate another [relation], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Now, if you, having postulated one relation, do not postulate yet another relation, then you should rest with that much alone and be satisfied with that; therefore, you ought to be satisfied with cognition itself and rest with that much alone.

[The opponent] objects: "If there is nothing other than consciousness (*vijñāna*), how can it be said that 'the agent eats'? The designation of a knower as the agent is established by this word. Therefore, so that this word may not be meaningless, one must postulate a self (*ātman*) distinct from consciousness."
"We shall assume [the meaning].

Indeed, the Vedas will assume this word to be meaningful if they consider it necessary to do so. For many people here in this world who maintain that the self exists—proponents of the existence of the self—are the direct speakers of this very word.

* "yo'yam" (this one who... according to Kāśikā and Kīka; "yo ya" (whosoever... according to Prācīna-puṣpa. + "anvicchema" (let us seek) according to Kāśikā and Kīka. + "devā" (O gods) according to Kāśikā-saṃskaraṇa.

[Page 72] They exist; nevertheless, it is not tenable to postulate a self-series (*ātmasantāna*). How much less so, then, can one do so on the basis of observing words such as "he knows," which refer to something beyond the senses? Therefore, this is untenable.
It is said: We perceive the self through desire. How so?

For desire arises toward an intended object previously perceived; for example, we have no desire for those sweet fruits situated to the north of Mount Meru which have never been perceived by those of our own kind. This is not the case even when an object has been perceived by another person.

A desire arises in the perceiver with respect to objects. Furthermore, there is a desire on one day for that which was perceived on another day. Therefore, we understand that this desire has the same agent as the perception. If this perceiver were merely consciousness itself, once that [consciousness] had ceased, whose desire would there be on the following day? But if, indeed, the knower is eternal and distinct from consciousness, then he who was the perceiver on one day [is the same as the one desiring on the next].
"Tomorrow too he will surely come," [one might say]. Otherwise, this statement would not be logical.

To this it is replied: "What is our conviction that it is illogical? We have no cognition of anything through a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Since we do not perceive anything other than consciousness (*vijñāna*), and since we do not perceive it, we understand that it does not exist, just like the horn of a hare. And when that [external object] does not exist..."

The existence of consciousness is not untenable precisely because it is apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, its momentariness is established by that very same direct perception. Nor is it untenable that there is no "I" on another day, given that the knower is nothing other than consciousness and consciousness is impermanent; this too is due to the fact of its being apprehended through direct perception.
It is never observed that "he who was perceived on one day is the very same person who desires on another. However, this is observed: in some cases, one person desires what was seen by another;
in some cases, one within a particular continuum desires it, while another in a different continuum does not desire it.

"Therefore, there is no fire distinct from the fuel and so forth. To this it is replied: No, for it is not tenable that "those who have passed away desire [this]," nor does memory arise regarding what was never previously perceived. Therefore, memory is untenable within the mere aggregate of momentary consciousness.
