[Page 73] Bhāṣya: Here it is argued: "Memory, like desire, is a cognition similar to a previous cognition, or has as its object the domain of a previous cognition; this is what is called 'memory. And that is not untenable even when the seer has perished, because it is indeed apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). In this dense mass of aggregates (*skandhaghana*), whatever cognition was produced by one dense mass of aggregates is perceived by another born from that same continuum, but not by another not born from that continuum. Therefore, the dense masses of aggregates are distinct."

Thus, regarding this matter, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.12): "A mass of pure consciousness alone, having arisen from these elements, perishes after them; after death, there is no consciousness."

It is said: this is not so; for when something is seen on one day, there arises the cognition on the following day, "I saw this"—and this occurs with respect to the inner self (pratyagātman), not with respect to another, since that other is not oneself.
On another day he saw [it]; therefore, there exists a fire distinct from that, which is this word "I."
He said: "The word 'half' is also seen used figuratively in other contexts; for example: 'I myself am the son.'"

"I myself am Devadatta; I myself go. To this, it is replied: we do not designate the word "I" as being employed for some other referent as the cause [of our cognition]. Rather, we perceive a cognition distinct from the word, such that we say, "We ourselves perceived this object on another day; we ourselves remember it today. Therefore, we understand this matter thus: "We ourselves were yesterday; we ourselves are today. Those who... [1]

And today they have not perished. Furthermore, regarding this matter, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: beginning with "This, indeed, is the Self," it concludes, "He does not decay, for he is not subject to decay. Likewise [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1].

Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.14 states: "Verily, this Self is indestructible, O Maitreyī, its nature is such that it does not perish. And consciousness is perishable; therefore, he [the Self] is other than that which is perishable.
"In one [instance]," according to the Kāśikā-saṃgraha.
"He is the one who saw it on another day," according to the Prācīna-pustaka.
"And those who here... (Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, Kapiṣṭhala-Kaṭha Saṃhitā). Some also accept that the letter *ma* is the description (*varṇya*) of the word *bṛhat*.
[Page 74]
[Śabara: We say: let us go. It is not possible to understand that things exist in the manner in which they are perceived, rather than in the manner in which they are not perceived.
For if that were the case, it would be understood that there is no hare, yet the horn of a hare exists!

Nor can it be said that "the notion of 'I' is not an error," because there is no subverting cognition [to prove otherwise]. Therefore, there exists something distinct from pleasure and the other [mental states]. If this is so, then that very thing is designated as "possessing the sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudhī*).
He says: "If there is something other than consciousness (*vijñāna*), then having set aside consciousness..."
Regarding that illustration: "This is it, and it is like this"—yet that is not illustrated.
"Therefore, there is nothing other than that. To this it is replied: "That is self-cognizable;

it cannot be seen by another. How, then, can it be demonstrated? Just as someone with sight perceives form for himself, yet is unable to demonstrate it to another who is blind from birth, so too it is not the case that it cannot be demonstrated.

—By this much alone, it is understood that "it does not exist. In this way, this person perceives himself by himself, yet he is unable to show himself to another, because another perceiver lacks the power of vision directed toward that person; for even another person [is likewise].

One perceives one's own self, and not the self of another; therefore, all beings, perceiving themselves by their respective selves, exist [as such], even though they do not perceive the person of another. Regarding this point, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.7):

It is said: "When speech has become silent, what is there? This person is indeed light; he is the self-luminous light," so he replied. Regarding the point that "he is not perceived by another," there is also a Brāhmaṇa passage (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.6): "He is ungraspable, for he is not grasped. This means that he is not grasped by another. Why? Because of the statement regarding his being self-luminous. Furthermore, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage...
It occurs [in the text]: "In this state, this person becomes self-luminous.
But by what means is this explained to another? Regarding that means as well—143.
* There is a difference in the readings of those passages extracted from the printed edition.
[Page 75]
First Chapter, First Section.

The Brāhmaṇa (of the *Hṛdaya Upaniṣad*, Chapter 3, Brāhmaṇa) states: "He said, 'This Self is not "this," it is not "that. It is impossible to point out that this [Self] is of such a form. Whatever another perceives, that is what is negated for him."
The means of instruction is as follows: another person perceives the body; by means of that, the Self is taught—namely, "The body is not the Self;

there exists something other than the body, and that is the Self"—thus it is taught by way of the negation of the body. Likewise, the vital breaths and so forth are not the Self; by way of their negation, that which is other than them is taught. Similarly, pleasure and so forth residing in another are perceived by another through signs; [it is taught] "These too are not the Self"—by way of excluding those, that which is other is taught. "He who perceives for himself, there is no person other than him."

— This too is inferred from human activity: when a person exerts himself on the previous day toward the acquisition of goods such as sacrificial grass and the performance of remaining rites, his activity makes it understood that "surely he perceives the impermanent as permanent."
It is also taught by way of analogy: "Just as you yourself perceive your own self, understand it through this analogy: 'I also perceive it in exactly that same way.
It is like someone describing their own sensation to another, saying, "It is as if I am being crushed."
"It occurs to me as if I am being born; it occurs to me as if I am passing away; it occurs to me as if I am being obstructed.
Because this is heard and personally realized, there exists a person distinct from that [process].

As for what was said—"Setting aside consciousness, let that [object] be pointed out" (22.13)—if you negate the very means itself, it is impossible to attain the goal without the means; this indeed is the method for things to be known: "in whatever way something is perceived..."

"It is so. For example: what is that which is called "whiteness" (*śuklatva*)? It is that in which the state of being white (*yuktatva*) exists. What is that which is called "the property of being white" (*śuklatva*)? It is that wherein the application of the word "white" (*śukla-śabda*) occurs. Where does its application occur? It is that which is cognized when the word "white" is uttered.
It is not possible to point out the nature of anything by setting it aside [from its linguistic usage].
When the condition is understood, the meaning of the condition becomes understood;
therefore, it is not necessarily [the case that] consciousness [is the cause].

For even when the means of cognition (*pratyaya*) is not itself perceived, the object is indeed perceived. Indeed, it is not the case that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is perceptible; rather, the object to be qualified (*viśeṣya*) is perceptible. This has already been stated previously (9.15). Therefore, this must necessarily be done—[Page 76].

The Bhāṣya says: "One should understand that the agent is consciousness. This has already been stated [at 10.4]: "It is the Lord. Therefore, there exists a permanent Person (puruṣa) distinct from pleasure and the other qualities.
Sūtra: "Now, as for what was said [at 21.119]: 'A mass of consciousness alone [arises] from these elements...'"

"Having arisen, it perishes along with them; after death, there is no consciousness"—to this it is replied: "Right here, the Blessed One has led me to the very limit of delusion. Following this objection, [the Blessed One], having set aside the intention of [the opponent's] delusion, described it thus: "Indeed, I do not speak of delusion, O Maitreyī; for this Self is indestructible, possessing the nature of non-perishing; however, there is for it a contact with the elements" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 6.5.13).
Therefore, it is not mere consciousness; hence, there is a difference. As for what was said (11.14): "Nor is this..."

The word "goes" is an injunctive term. Even if it were not an injunctive term, it would merely restate what is already understood from another statement, namely, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice. Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Because it is seen [to be] produced by action. (Pūrvapakṣa 1) Bhāṣya:

It was stated (at 7.4) that "the relationship between word and meaning is eternal. That is untenable, because the word is non-eternal; the word perishes, and then this [same] word is produced again in relation to its meaning.

An uncreated relationship is not tenable; for no one understands any meaning from a word that has never been uttered before. "But how is sound impermanent? Because it is perceived at a time subsequent to effort, it is understood that "it is produced by that [effort]" due to its immediate succession to effort. But surely—

"Let it manifest him. We say: no. For there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever for its existence prior to manifestation. And that which exists is manifested, not that which does not exist (Pūrvapakṣa 1).
Sūtra:
Because of its non-abiding [nature]. (Pūrvapakṣa 2) Bhāṣya: No; for we perceive it even after it has been uttered for a moment. Therefore, it is not destroyed.
Thus we understand. Nor is it the case that "Being" (sat) is not perceived; for there are causes of non-perception [as stated in the Kāśikā:
*cāpīpipat* and *macainamucaritaṃ*].
[Page 77]

Because it is not perceived even when there is an absence of obstructions and the like; nor is it the case that this [hearing] does not reach its object, since its object is space and it is not perceived even within the cavity of the ear (Pūrvapakṣa-bhāṣya).
2) [The view that it is] from the word *karoti* (he does), [is stated in] Sūtra 8 (Pūrvapakṣa 3).
Moreover, speakers employ such expressions as "Make a sound" and "Do not make a sound," yet they certainly do not understand that "this very same sound [is being produced]."
And because [the word] is perceived simultaneously by different beings.

(Sūtra 8) Bhāṣya: Furthermore, we perceive the sound simultaneously in various locations; this is impossible for a single, eternal entity. Since there is no distinction [in the nature] of an eternal thing, it cannot possess multiplicity; however, this is possible for effects.
A simultaneous connection is not possible for many things being produced in various places;
therefore, for this reason as well, it is impermanent. (Pūrvapakṣa 4)
And [the rule] "pa.
prakṛtivikṛtyośca" (Pūrvapakṣa 5).
Furthermore, in the case of "dadhyatra," the letter *i* is the original form (*prakṛti*) and the letter *y* is the modification (*vikṛti*).

Thus they teach: whatever is produced is impermanent; and since the similarity of the sound *i* is perceived in the sound *ya*, by that too their relationship as original material (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikāra*) is indicated.
(Pūrva-pakṣa 5)
"And because of its increase through the multiplicity of agents" (Pūrvapakṣa 6).

Furthermore, a loud sound is heard when it is uttered by many people; if it were merely manifested [rather than produced], it would be perceived as being of the same magnitude whether uttered by many or by few. Therefore, we consider that surely some part of this [sound] is produced by each individual, such that through their accumulation, this [sound] [reaches its full magnitude].
The Great One is perceived. (Pūrvapakṣa)
[Page 78] But that view is equal [to the objection]. (Uddyota 1)

But [the word] *tu* (but/however) reverses the position. As was stated [in the prima facie view, sūtra 1]: "Because it is perceived at a time subsequent to effort, sound is produced. If we are able to state the eternity of sound through a clear reason, then—by the force of the cognition of its eternity—it will follow that "it is manifested by effort"; provided that it is unmanifested prior to utterance and is manifested by effort. Therefore, this point is equal for both positions [sūtra 2].
Furthermore, the non-perception of an existing thing is due to the non-arrival of its object. (Uddyota 2)
Bhāṣya: It was stated previously (pūrvapakṣa 2) that the cause [of sound] is something other [than conjunction and disjunction], namely, "perished as soon as uttered.

Here too, if we are able to clearly demonstrate its eternity, then—observing that it is sometimes perceived and sometimes not perceived—we shall postulate some cause for its perception based on the force of the cognition of its permanence; and that [cause] would be the presence of conjunction and disjunction.
We shall state that conjunction and disjunction alone are the manifestors [of sound], in the sense that "when they exist, [sound] comes to be.
If it is argued that "sound is heard even when conjunction and disjunction have ceased," this is not so; for conjunction and disjunction do not truly cease, since sound is perceived.
For they are not perceptible.
“If conjunctions and disjunctions only manifest sound and do not produce it—
since sound has space as its locus and space is one— then that very same [sound] which is here...”

The auditory space is one and the same even in different locations; therefore, if it were manifested by conjunctions and disjunctions residing in Śrughna, it would be perceived in Pāṭaliputra as well. For one who holds that [the conjunctions and disjunctions] produce [the sound], however, since those aerial conjunctions and disjunctions reside in air, they will produce [the sound] only in the air. Just as threads produce a cloth upon the threads, it is logical that there is no perception of it in Pāṭaliputra.

"Because they reside in the ear; for even one who holds that [the sounds] manifest [the word], this fault does not apply: the conjunctions and disjunctions do not assist the ear-cavity located at a distance, and therefore that which is covered by a parasol at a distance is not perceived. This is not so; for if they have not reached [the sense organ]...

[Page 79] Bhāṣya: Conjunctions and disjunctions might assist the auditory organ; in that case, two people situated in nearby and distant locations would perceive the sound simultaneously. Yet they do not perceive it simultaneously. Therefore, [the conjunctions and disjunctions] have not reached [the organ].
They assist [the perception]; if they did not assist, then conjunction and disjunction would not be the cause for the apprehension of sound.
Thus it is said.

This is not so; for when air-particles are impelled by a stroke, they strike against other stationary air-particles, thereby producing conjunctions and disjunctions in all directions as far as the space extends. And because air is imperceptible, these conjunctions and disjunctions are not perceived. Sound is perceived only while those [conjunctions and disjunctions] continue to proceed, not when they have ceased. Thus there is no fault. For this very reason, sound is perceived from a distance when carried along with the wind. (Uddyota 2)

The application [of the word] is the final [reason]. (Uddyota 3) Bhāṣya: Another reason has been stated [in the Pūrva-pakṣa 3]: "People employ [the word] in usage, saying, 'Make a sound,' or 'Do not make a sound. If sound were undoubtedly eternal, the employment of the word..."
"It shall be 'make'; just as from cow-dung [the word] 'make' [is derived] in the context of dissolution" (Upaniṣad 3).
"Like the sun, there is simultaneity" (Upaniṣad 4).
As for the objection (Pūrva-pakṣa 4): "It is impossible for that which exists in one place to be seen simultaneously in multiple places"—look at the sun, O beloved of the gods! It is one, yet...

It appears as if situated in many places. But how is it understood that "the sun is one"? It is said: Devadatta, facing east, sees the sun directly in front of him at this moment; another person standing to his south does not see it.
He perceives that, at present, there is no crookedness in himself, nor any straightness in Devadatta.
(Note: *saṃbā* according to Kā0 kī0; *devānāṃ priyo yaḥ* according to Kā0 saṃ0).
"And the present state of the self is transverse," according to the Kāśikā-saṃgraha; however, "and the present thought of the self is transverse," according to the Kāśikā-kīrti.
[Page 80]

Bhāṣya: Therefore, it is said that "the sun is one. Due to its distance, its location cannot be ascertained; hence, there is delusion. Similarly, in the case of sound as well, there is a failure to ascertain its location due to delusion. If the auditory organ were to go to the location of the conjunctions and disjunctions and grasp the sound, then perhaps its existence in multiple locations might sometimes be understood; however, it does not go to the location of those conjunctions.

For the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*) is indeed perceived directly as being located in that place; however, the conjunctions and disjunctions of the aerial elements (*vāyavīya*), which belong to the imperceptible air, are not apprehended even when they manifest in the region of the ear-cavity—thus there is no inconsistency. It is for this very reason that there is the delusion that "the sound is in various places," and that "sound is a location of space (*ākāśadeśa*)," and that it is one.

Furthermore, [the case of] space is also not [analogous], because [space] does not exist in multiple locations. Moreover, if there is a single form, then by virtue of the difference in location, it may well be that the locations themselves are distinct, but not the sound. Therefore, this too is not a fault. (Uddyota 4)
Sūtra Bhāṣya Hṛdaya (The Heart of the Commentary on the Sūtras)
The change of phoneme is not a modification [of the original].
(Uddyota 5) Furthermore, in the case of "dadhy atra," there is no relationship of original and modification (pūrva-pakṣa 5).

The letter *ya* is a different word from the letter *i*; for those employing the letter *ya* do not take up the letter *i*, just as those desiring to make a mat do not take up *vīraṇa* grass. Nor is something called the "original" (*prakṛti*) designated because of perceived similarity; for one does not call a lump of curd...

The relationship between the original state (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*) is understood from the growth of the *kunda* flower and the fruit; therefore, this too is not a fault. (Uddyota 5)
[The sūtra] "The increase of sound [is the reason]" (Uddyota 6).

Commentary: As for this [argument]: "When many people strike a drum and produce sound, a great sound is perceived; from this it is understood that there is an accumulation of parts of the sound for each person" (Pūrva-pakṣa 3).

It is not so; for sound is partless, since no distinction of parts is perceived. And because it is partless, magnitude is impossible; therefore, sound does not increase. [In the case of] "one *mṛdura*" (soft), it is "*kaṃbu*" according to the Kāśikā commentary.

[Page 81] No; for when they are uttered by many people, those very same syllables are repeatedly perceived due to the continuous conjunctions and disjunctions [of the air], which pervade the entire circumference of the ear-cavity.

It is perceived as if it were large, as if it possessed parts; conjunctions and disjunctions, being produced by the breath, manifest the sound (*dhvani*) while making the word (*śabda*) audible. Therefore, this increase belongs to the *nāda*, not to the *śabda*. (Uddyota 3)
But [the fire] must be permanent, because the act of seeing is for the sake of another. (Sūtra 18) (Siddhānta) Bhāṣya.
The word must be eternal. Why? "Because perception is for the sake of another.
Perception means utterance; that is for the sake of another (to convey meaning). For if a word were destroyed as soon as it was uttered, it could not convey meaning to others.

It would be possible [to perceive it]; therefore, it should not be uttered for the sake of another. If, on the other hand, it has not perished, then the comprehension of meaning is appropriate because it has been perceived many times. If it is argued that "the comprehension of meaning arises from seeing that which possesses meaning," [we reply: nothing possesses meaning, because all [sounds] are new. If it is argued that "there will be an artificial (kṛtrima) relationship for some prior [sound]," that has already been stated.

Furthermore, once it is understood that [the word] is "similar" [to the correct one], the cognition [of the incorrect form] would be set aside due to delusion, just as the cognition of a "mālā" [is set aside] upon hearing the word "mālā. If it is argued, "Just as there is no cessation of the cognition of an object possessing a dewlap and so forth from the word 'gāvī', so too will it be here," we say: no, for in that case there was no intention to utter the word "go"; here, however, there is no intention to employ another word. Moreover, it is not possible to establish both linguistic usage and the relationship between a word and its meaning by means of uttering only a single [corrupt] form. Therefore, because the perception [of the word] is for the sake of another, the word is eternal.
Because [the cognition] occurs simultaneously everywhere. || 18 ||
It has been established: when the word "cow" (go) is uttered, a cognition arises simultaneously with respect to all cows.
This is because the word denotes the universal form (ākṛti). Furthermore, it is not possible to establish a relationship between a word and a specific individual.

For one who intends to produce the form after having pointed it out, how will he teach that distinct form denoted by the word "cow" within a mass of cows, given that many individual *mālatī* flowers exist therein, without the use of the word? But if the word "cow" is eternal, [it is possible] because of its frequent repetition.
Furthermore, since it has been heard before in other individual cows and is understood through the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to denote the genus (*ākṛti*),
it must therefore also be eternal.
Because of the absence of number. || 20 ||

People say, "The word 'cow' has been uttered eight times," and not, "Eight words for 'cow' [have been uttered]. What follows from this? If it is so, then by this statement it is understood that they recognize [the same word]; we, at least, recognize it, and it is not due to any weakness of our sense organs.
In this way, others also recognize [it] as "this is that very same one. Recognizing it, they too—just like us—are entitled to say, "It is not another."
"It is your opinion that, while there is difference, those who are deluded by similarity will say, 'This is that.
That is not so; for they do not perceive it as 'similar,' but rather as 'this is that very same thing. And it is only when difference is clearly known that it can be understood as a delusion. Not so.
And there is no such perception as "this is that other," nor is there any other means of valid cognition [to establish it].

It might be argued: "Cognition and action are also recognized through recognition; therefore, they too must be eternal. This is not a fault. For those two are not objects of perception; if they were perceptible...

It is indeed eternal. If it is argued that "because the sound previously uttered has perished, there is a new production [of sound]," we reply: this [sound] has not perished, since we perceive it again.
For we do not fail to recognize, upon perceiving again, something previously seen by direct perception even after it was unseen for a moment.

They imagine [something] to be destroyed. While so imagining, they would not have confidence in their mother upon seeing her for a second time, nor in their wife, nor in their father. For one does not conclude "it is non-existent" merely by its non-perception, and thus imagine that it has been destroyed. It is only when the absence of a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatā*) is known that we understand "it does not exist. Indeed, [this is not the case] when there is a means of valid cognition.

If perception were present, there would be non-authoritativeness [of other means of knowledge]. However, when it is understood through non-delusion that "it exists," there is no absence whatsoever; nor is there delusion regarding an existence that is unestablished, nor is there an existence that is already established. Therefore, in the absence of delusion, there is no non-existence. Thus, [the phrase] "if they recognize it" (*pratyabhijānanti cet*) is an addition in the Kāśikā commentary.

[Page 83] Bhāṣya: Therefore, by this sequence, it is established. Consequently, even though one does not perceive the past conduct that preceded it, one ought to understand that it has not perished—just as, for example, those who have departed from a house.

Even those who do not see all the people in the house, yet perceive them upon re-entering, do not conclude that they were destroyed prior to their previous entry; likewise, they cannot say of this [sound] that it is "another" than the previous one. Even those who accept the destruction of all entities at every moment are unable to say so of sound, for in the end...

Because they observe accumulation, they think thus; yet there is no end to sound, nor is any victory perceived. The cognition "that" is perceptual (*pratyakṣa*), while "similar" is inferential (*ānumānika*);
and an inference that contradicts perception neither arises nor accomplishes its own purpose.
Therefore, it is eternal.
Because of independence. || 21 ||

Bhāṣya: Of those substances whose origin is not perceived and whose mere existence is observed, the impermanence of some is nevertheless understood—namely, those for which a cause of destruction is apprehended. For example, upon seeing a new cloth, even if one has not perceived it being made; then...

Or, one perceives impermanence even by seeing form alone—understanding that "this [object], produced by the conjunction of threads, perishes upon the destruction of the conjunction of threads or the destruction of the threads. But no such cause for sound is perceived, from whose destruction it might be understood to perish.
And because there is an absence of manifestation for yoga. || 22 ||
Bhāṣya: This sūtra follows after certain words [of the objection]: "But surely the air would be the cause;
thus the air, having risen up, becomes sound through conjunctions and disjunctions. And so the authors of the Śikṣā say: 'The air attains the state of being sound. This is not so.

If the body were composed of air, it would be a particular configuration of air. However, we do not recognize the constituent parts of air as existing within the body, in the way that we recognize the threads as the constituents of a cloth. And this is not the case! If it were so, then upon touching [the body]—
[Page 84] Bhāṣya:
We do not perceive them; nor do we touch the aerial atoms inherent in sound.
Therefore, it does not have air as its cause. Consequently, it is eternal.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark. || 23 ||

Furthermore, there is an indicative mark (liṅga) to this effect: "By speech, which is multiform and eternal. For this sentence, while having another purpose, restates the eternity of speech. Therefore, sound is eternal.
And [the mantras] would be non-expressive regarding the origin [of the ritual], because the meaning does not have that as its cause. (Pūrvapakṣa) [This is understood from the context].
Bhāṣya: Even though the relationship between the word and its meaning is innate (eternal), nevertheless, dharma is not characterized by *codanā*. For *codanā* is a sentence;

indeed, from any single word within the sentence "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," it is not understood that "Heaven results from the Agnihotra. Rather, it is understood from the three words [taken together].

When uttered, there is no fourth word here other than this [collection of words]. Nor does such a collection exist in the world from which meaning could be understood through linguistic usage. These words have been employed, and their meanings are eternal;
however, the collection is not employed [as a unit]. Therefore, the meaning of the collection must be either artificial or a delusion.
Furthermore, the meaning of a word is not itself the meaning of a sentence, for a word functions with respect to a universal (sāmānya).

The sentence refers to a particular, whereas the general is one thing and the particular is another. The understanding of the meaning of a sentence cannot arise from the meanings of the individual words because of the lack of a relationship between them. If there were no such relationship, then upon the understanding of any single word-meaning, another distinct meaning would have to be understood; indeed, upon the understanding of one, everything would be understood. But this is not the case. Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is something other [than the sum of the word-meanings].

It might be argued: "Even from a word that is not joined with [another], there is comprehension of meaning through its own inherent nature (svabhāva), provided there is no [other] connection. If this were maintained—that "a word would transcend its own property"—this is not the case; for it is not a property of words that meaning is cognized even from a word that is not joined [with another]. Indeed, it is not so.
Alternatively, there is a reading in some places: "vā'vacanāni.
And it is not the case that...
[Page 85]
First Chapter, First Section.

33. Bhāṣya: "Some people comprehend a certain meaning from a word heard for the first time. To this it is replied: "This is a property of the word (*pada*), not a property of the sentence (*vākya*); for we observe that even from a sentence heard for the first time, people do comprehend its meaning. This is not so; if they were to understand it from what was heard for the first time, [it would indeed be a property of the sentence].

In that case, everyone would understand [the sentence-meaning]. But others who do not know the word-meanings do not understand it; and this is precisely how it is for that [sentence]. Now, it might be argued:

"The connection with the sentence-meaning will certainly remain unimpaired even for those who know the word-meanings; for, refined by the knowledge of the word-meanings, they will understand it, just as one understands that very same word-meaning upon hearing it a second time or more."

We say: no. If it is held that at the end of the sentence, the final phoneme—accompanied by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes—conveys a meaning distinct from the meanings of the individual words, then the assistance [of those preceding phonemes] would at that time be derived solely from the knowledge of the word-meanings. Therefore, the cognition of the sentence-meaning is either artificial or a delusion; the knowledge of the sentence-meaning cannot occur through the medium of the word-meanings.

[Objection: "Surely it will be thus: when a word denoting a universal, such as 'cow' or 'horse', is followed by a proximate qualifying word such as 'yoked' or 'black', then the meaning of the sentence is understood. [Response: That is not so; for how indeed could it be that [the meaning is understood] from the words 'cow' or 'horse' alone?

Alternatively, the cognition produced by the hearing of words expressing a universal—which extends over all cows and all horses—might be restricted to some particular instance in accordance with the sentence. However, the exclusion of black and other colors from the word "white" and so forth is not the meaning of the word; nor is it possible to assume such a meaning merely to prevent the word from being meaningless.

Therefore, the meaning of a sentence is not produced by the meanings of the individual words; consequently, it is artificial (*kṛtrima*). These are indeed collections of words, and collections are seen to be the work of persons, as for example: "Now, moving through the groves of blue lotuses with beautiful cries, the blue geese, as if clothed in dark silk, seem to vanish. Therefore, even the Vedic [sentences] are created by persons. (Pūrvapakṣa)
The reading "rāmā" is found in the Prācīna-pāṭha; the reading "samāḥ" is found in the Kāśmīra-kṛta manuscript.
"praṇyantīva" according to the Kāṭhaka-saṃhitā.
In this very same way, the reading is everywhere.
[Page 86] b.
"The collection of existing things is for the sake of action, because the meaning is caused by that. (Sūtra 25) (Upanibandhana).
Commentary: Regarding those very same (word-meanings), the "existing" (bhūtānām)—that is, the present—(words) are [collected] for the sake of action.

[Objection: "There is the utterance [of the sentence]. [Reply: No, because a sentence that functions as a distinct meaning without depending on the word-meanings is not established. Why? Because there is a lack of proof; there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which we might cognize it. For indeed, there is no such thing as a sentence that proceeds without depending on word-meanings."

Thus, for one who possesses the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes, there exists a devotion [to the word] that functions as something distinct from the individual word-meanings.

Now, it might be argued: "Presumption (arthāpatti) exists, because we perceive a meaning that transcends the individual word-meanings, and that is not possible without an understanding [of a sentence]. To this, we reply: No, because of the [meaning of the] object...

Because it has that as its cause, there would be an *arthāpatti* (presumption) [of the sentence-meaning] only if no other cause were conceivable even when the word-potency (*śakti*) is absent; however, a cause is indeed apprehended. What is it? It is the word-meaning (*padārtha*).
For words, having denoted their respective word-meanings, have their function exhausted;
then, the word-meanings, once apprehended, bring about the understanding of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

This is established as the reason: "Therefore, silver must not be given on the sacrificial grass (barhis)"; thus all [the statements] are expectant [of further explanation]. How do they assist the injunction?
By means of figurative praise (guṇavāda): silver originates from weeping; for one who gives it upon the sacrificial grass, weeping follows.
The merit of that [prohibition] is this: that he did not weep. But how can it be said, "he did not weep," when he was actually weeping? Or how can there be silver when no tears have been produced?

It is said: [The Veda] is the narration of past events (*vṛttānta*), because praise is understood for the purpose of glorification (*stuti*). While this narration is occurring, two things are produced: (1) the knowledge of the event itself, and (2) either an inclination toward something or an aversion toward it. Among these, the narration of the event is neither a motivator nor a deterrent; thus, because it lacks a [practical] purpose, it is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*). However, one acts out of inclination and desists out of aversion; therefore, those two [inclination and aversion] are what are intended to be expressed. This holds true even in the case of the narration of past events.

If [the Veda] were being produced, the defect of having a beginning would follow for the Veda! "But how is it free from the horns of a hare?"—thus says Mādhava. "They have become [existent]"—thus in the Kāśikā-saṃhitā.

For instance, the form of the mantra "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*) has no application in the act of cutting the grass. (Pūrvapakṣa)

Because of the fixed order of the words. (Pūrvapakṣa 2) Bhāṣya: For mantras have a fixed sequence of words—as in "Agnirmūrdhā divaḥ"—and not in the reverse order. If they were for the purpose of conveying meaning, the meaning would be understood even from the reverse order.

Thus, the restriction would be purposeless. Alternatively, if it is for the sake of a specific pronunciation—meaning that in the opposite case there would be a different pronunciation—then this restriction is resorted to. Therefore, whichever position renders the restriction meaningful, that indeed must be the correct position. But surely, even if it is meaningful, the restriction [remains problematic].
It is observed, for example, in the expression "Indrāgnī. And that is appropriate, because there is no cognition of the meaning [of the compound] as being reversed. (Pūrvapakṣa 2)
[This is] from the teaching of the Buddha. (Pūrvapakṣa 3)

[Objection: Even when [the word] is already understood, because it is recited, it becomes capable of expressing that meaning, as in "O Agnīdh, distribute the fires. Because of the statement regarding that which does not exist. (Pūrvapakṣa 4)
In the sacrifice (*yajña*), that which serves as the means must be manifested; yet there is nothing of the kind!

There exists a certain sacrificial implement with four horns, three feet, two heads, seven hands; what could the word [denoting it] signify here? Sūtra: Because they are connected with a purpose in regard to an insentient object. (Pūrvapakṣa 5) Bhāṣya:
Indeed, they connect a purpose with an insentient object—as in: "O herb, protect him!"—thus [they are not for the sake of the object].

If words of this kind were to assist by means of denotation, they would have to convey the medicinal herb for the protection of the cattle; however, it is not possible to convey that which is insentient. But if their purpose is utterance, this fault does not arise. Therefore, [mantras] are for the purpose of utterance. "O, listen, O pressing-stones! is an example. (Pūrvapakṣa 5)
"Because of the contradiction in meaning. (Sūtra 36, Pūrvapakṣa 6).

Commentary: There is also a contradiction in meaning—for instance, [the text says], "Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the intermediate space"—yet who could ever determine that it is the very same heaven and that it is the very same intermediate space?

And if one does not ascertain [the meaning], how could a name be of any benefit? However, there is no contradiction in the case of mere utterance. Therefore, names are for the purpose of utterance. "One Rudra did not stand with a second; there are countless thousands of Rudras upon the earth."
— Thus is the illustrative example. (Pūrvapakṣa 6)

Because it is unintelligible. (pṛ0 8) Furthermore, the meaning of certain mantras is simply impossible to understand, such as:

Because of connection with impermanent things, mantras would be purposeless.

"They say thus: 'In the Kīkaṭas there are cows'—referring to the regions named Kīkaṭas;

Furthermore, there would be no benefit to the sacrifice from a conversation with insentient things that are merely parts of the sacrifice. If an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) were to be postulated, it ought to arise from the mere utterance itself. For whatever is to be performed, that—
The utterance must have a purpose, and it should not be performed in any way if it were not for the sake of the *apūrva*. If the *ai* were not made to convey the *au*, nothing would be meaningless;
however, if it were not employed [for that purpose], its inclusion in the sacred tradition (*samāmnāna*) would be purposeless. Therefore, the *apūrva* arises from the utterance, and thus...

The objection beginning with "tadarthaśāstrādi" (Pūrva-pakṣa) has been stated. To that it is replied: the recitation of mantras in a sacrifice is solely for the purpose of conveying meaning. As for what was said—"there is no purpose in conversing with deities or the constituents of the sacrifice"—the purpose in the sacrifice is indeed the illumination of the sacrificial constituents. How so?

For a sacrifice cannot be accomplished if the sacrifice and its constituents are not illuminated. Therefore, the illumination of the meaning for the sake of accomplishing that [sacrifice] is a great benefit to the ritual action.

And it is understood that one performs that [action]; therefore, this has a purpose. And since that purpose is perceived, it cannot be denied by saying, "The purpose is not the expression of meaning. But surely, if they assist through the expression of meaning, then statements such as "He takes it with four" would be meaningless. Let them be meaningless if they must; we do not at all deny it.
It has been observed that the mention of the purpose is helpful [to the understanding of the injunction]. (Siddhānta)
[Su]:

"But the repetition is for the sake of the quality.

(Sūtra 41; Uddyota 1). Commentary: As for what was stated [at 56.4], "He takes it up with four"—since there is no word expressing conjunction, it does not have the sense of a combination. Rather, it is understood from the sentence that "the taking up qualified by the number four must be performed"; thus, one should not perform it with a single mantra, contrary to the scriptural injunction. Exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) || 42 || (Uttara-pakṣa 2) Bhāṣya: [One might argue that] in the case of exclusion (*parisañcaccāṇe*), faults such as those mentioned in sūtra 56.4 would arise regarding the statement, "With the mantra *imāmagṛbhṇan*, he takes up the horse's halter. From the indicative mark (*liṅga*), there is application to the mere rope; from the direct statement (*śabda*), however, there is application to the specific one, namely the horse’s bridle.
And while the sentence (*vākya*) exists as the means of application, its indicative mark is that sentence inferred from its recitation within the context (*prakaraṇa*).

It does not exist. Which one is it? It would be that [rule] stating "one should perform the taking up with this mantra," (in the presence of which, by virtue of the indicative mark, it would apply even to the mere act of dyeing). Therefore, in the case of the donkey's halter, there is no application at all. (Uddyota 2)

Or it is an explanatory statement (arthavāda). (Uddyota 3) — "He spreads the sacrificial cake [puroḍāśa] with the words, 'O wide-spreading one, spread yourself wide! This repetition of the scriptural text is for the purpose of an explanatory statement, namely: "By that, he indeed causes the master of the sacrifice to expand. But surely...
"This is not a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) for the mantra, nor is there any purpose in praising what is already established.
True; this is neither an injunction (*vidhi*) for the mantra nor a praise (*saṃstava*).

Rather, it is the spreading (*prathana*) itself that is praised therein. Furthermore, the spreading, which is already established by its very nature, is here restated (*anūdyate*) in order to praise it—thus, the spreading [is praised].
When that which is being performed is done with such a mantra, it is praised. What is the benefit in that case?
It causes him to expand his progeny and cattle even unto the Lord of Death.

Is this alone its fruit? We say: no. [If so,] how will there be praise?—it is for this reason that it is stated. How can there be the word "he causes to expand" (*prathayati*) when there is no actual expanding?
Because of the mention of the mantra—the Adhvaryu priest says to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), "Expand yourself" (*prathasva*) by means of the mantra.
And he who says "make it known" makes it known; just as he who says "do it" causes it to be done. (Uddyota 3)
"The other [is] not contradictory" (Uttara-pakṣa 4).
Commentary: As it was stated [in the Pūrva-pakṣa 2]: "Because the restriction of words has a purpose, their meaning is not intended [to be expressed]."

Thus, while the restriction may indeed be purposeless, it is not the case that the perceived [utility] lacks authority. If it is argued that "the restricted recitation is for the sake of the unseen (adṛṣṭa)," we reply: the postulation of the perceived is not contradictory; even in our view, that which is accepted in this manner becomes conducive to prosperity (abhyudaya). (Uddyota 4)

She attains [the result]; therefore, it is an injunction for the purpose of restriction, stating that "it must be performed by this means," because it is a purificatory act (saṃskāra). (Uddyota 5) | Regarding the expression, it is an explanatory praise (arthavāda). (Uddyota 6)

In the statement "four are its limbs" (4.1.4), the word is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*), because there is a basis for such figurative interpretation; otherwise, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the mere utterance would lack a valid foundation. "Four are its *hotṛ*-priests" refers to the four officiating priests, while "four are its limbs" intends the four *savana* (pressings). "'Two are its heads' refers to the wife and the sacrificer. "'Seven are its hands'... [and so on].

With reference to the Vedic hymns (*chandāṃsi*): "Bound in three ways" means bound by the three Vedas. "The bull rains down desires, he roars"—this refers to the activity of sound—and "the great god has entered into men," which intends to refer to the qualification of human beings. For example, the praise of a river: "A river with cakravāka birds for breasts, rows of swans for ivory ornaments, kāśa grass for a garment, and moss for hair."

Desiring to establish the similarity of the sacrificial implements to sentient beings for the sake of the success of the sacrifice, [the author] indicates this by means of the words "exertion" (*śrama*) and "wound" (*vraṇa*): "O herb, protect him! (5.1.5), and "Listen, O pressing-stones! (5.1.6).

Following this, there will be the recitation of the *prātaranuvāka*, wherein even the insentient pressing-stones would listen; how much more so, then, learned Brāhmaṇas? And thus, even the insentient pressing-stones are addressed at the end of the *śrāma*. (Uttara-pakṣa 6)
There would be no contradiction on account of the secondary sense.

"It is not the father that grows, nor the mother"—from this it is understood that others do grow. Now begins the section concerning the authority of Smṛti.
Since dharma has the Veda as its source, that which is not based on the Veda would be unreliable. (Sūtra 1)
Bhāṣya (Pūrva-pakṣa): Thus far, the authority of the entire Veda has been stated; now, however, regarding that [portion] where...

We do not perceive any Vedic word [for these], yet people remember them, thinking, "In this manner this matter is to be performed," and "For this purpose"—is it indeed so, or not? For example, as in the cases: "The Aṣṭakā rites are to be performed" and "The teacher is to be followed."

"One should dig a pond," "One should establish a water-station (prapā)," "The tonsure ceremony (śikhākarma) should be performed"—such [injunctions] are examples. To this it is replied: "Since Dharma has its root in verbal testimony (śabda), that which lacks verbal authority should not be relied upon. It has been stated that "Dharma is characterized by verbal testimony" and "Dharma is an object characterized by an injunction (codanā). Therefore, because they lack a foundation, they are not to be relied upon. [Objection:

But how could those who know, "This thing must be done in such a way," ever say, "This must not be done"? [Response: This is not so, because the recollection [of such acts] would otherwise be impossible.

For indeed, an object that has not been experienced is not remembered; nor is the recollection of something non-Vedic and non-worldly possible, because of the absence of a prior cause for cognition. For if a barren woman were to remember her own son, thinking, "This was done by my son," she would never perceive it as a valid cognition, realizing, "I have no daughter. This [recollection] is therefore correct.

—Thus [it is argued]. "Even so, just as their Smṛti is authoritative because it is 'this Veda' through an unbroken tradition, so too will this [Smṛti] be authoritative. This is not so; for since the other [Veda] is perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa), its prior cognition is not untenable. However, in the case of the Aṣṭakā and other such rites whose objects are unseen (adṛṣṭārtha), because there is no cause for a prior cognition, it is understood to be merely a Smṛti based on delusion (vyāmoha). For example, suppose someone born blind were to say, "I remember the specific form of this object"—from where would his prior cognition have come?
— being thus questioned, he would point only to another person who is blind from birth; and of that [other person], too, [he would do the same].
[Page 117] Bhā. Why? From one who is blind from birth—thus, even if there were a succession of those blind from birth, the wise would never at any time recognize: "This is right vision. Therefore...
One should not pay heed to such a thing, lest it become independent [of other factors]. (Pūrvapakṣa)
Or rather, inference may be a means of valid cognition because of the identity of the agent. (Sūtra 2)
(Si0) Bhā.
Or rather—the alternative view is set aside. Smṛti is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for it is indeed a cognition;
why then should it be otherwise? Its preceding cognition...

If it is argued that [the cause] does not exist because there is no cause for it, we shall infer the cause of this very beginninglessness of memory; however, that cause is not experience, because it is untenable—
for humans are not capable of experiencing such a kind of object within a single lifetime!

Furthermore, that which was experienced in another birth is not remembered; however, the text [of the Smṛti] may be inferred [as being based on Vedic authority] because of the identity of the author [of both the Smṛti and the Veda]. Therefore, the connection of the three social classes with the Veda is established. But [it may be argued]: "They do not perceive such a text at all. Not perceiving it...

Even if one were to infer [the original text], forgetting is also possible; since it is possible for those of the three higher castes who remember it to have previously possessed that knowledge, and since forgetting is likewise possible,
the inference of the text is justified— thus, tradition (smṛti) is a valid means of knowledge.

Furthermore, mantras indicative of the Aṣṭakā rites are seen in the Veda, such as "The one whom people rejoice in," and so forth. Likewise, the authority of practices involving established rules (niyama) is due solely to their having a visible purpose—for instance, by following the teacher, the teacher will be pleased and will teach; and being satisfied, he will explain the logical principles that resolve the knots of the texts.

And thus it shows: "Therefore, the more sinful one follows behind the more virtuous one who goes ahead. Furthermore, it is understood that water-booths and ponds are for the benefit of others, not for the sake of religious merit (*dharma*). And thus there is the scriptural indication: "Like a water-booth in a desert..."
The ancient manuscript of the Kāśmīra recension reads "akārtha" instead of "kārtha."
[Page 118] For example:

"Thou art a sword," and likewise, "They carry water on their heads as if on dry land. There is also the rite of the crest-lock (*goṣūktika-śikhā-karman*) and the vision, namely: "Where the arrows fall together.
Therefore, those [Vedic injunctions] which have a visible purpose are authoritative for that reason alone; however, regarding those which have an invisible purpose, [the authority rests elsewhere].
"Inference from the word 'Vedika'. (Thus concludes the section on the authority of Smṛti, 1.3.12). Next is the section on the superiority of Śruti.
But in case of contradiction, it should be disregarded; for there is no inference when [the scripture] is absent.

Bhāṣya: Now, where there is a contradiction with Śruti, how is it to be treated? For example, the complete wrapping of the Audumbarī post contradicts the Śruti text, "One should chant the Udgītha while touching the Audumbarī. Likewise, [the rule regarding] practicing Vedic celibacy for forty-eight years [contradicts other texts].

(2) This contradicts the statement: "One who has a son and black hair should establish the sacred fires. (3) The rule that "the food of one whose king has been purchased is not to be eaten" contradicts the statement: "Therefore, when the Agniṣomīya sacrifice is concluded, one should eat in the house of the sacrificer. That [Smṛti] is authoritative because the agent is the same; thus [is the argument].

To this we reply: it is understood that this is a delusion because it is impossible. Why is it impossible? Because of the injunction regarding touch; it is not possible for everything to be covered, since the Udgātṛ must touch it while singing. Understanding that it must be touched by the Udgātṛ while he sings, how could one possibly cover it?
"Do we reject [the Smṛti] on the grounds of the recollection of the total covering?"—so we say.
How so? Because it is not without a root; that recollection will have a Vedic statement as its source. It would indeed have a Vedic statement as its source, if touching were...

It is a delusion; for if there were no delusion, it would be untenable due to its impossibility. Just as an experience that is impossible is not accepted, so too is a Vedic statement [that contradicts perception]. How then is the traditional recollection (*smaraṇa*) of "covering everything" explained? It is a delusion. How is the assumption of delusion established?

Because it contradicts the scriptural knowledge (*śrauta-vijñāna*). Now, for what purpose should these two injunctions be treated as optional alternatives (*vikalpa*), given that [the text] says, "Where the boys are like those without topknots" (*kumārā viśikhā iva*)? [This is] an addition found in the Kāṭhaka-saṃhitā manuscript.
[Page 119] Bhāṣya:
Is it like rice and barley, or like the *ṛk* and *sāman* chants? An option does not arise when there is no cognition of delusion;
if the cognition of wrapping all [the posts] were authoritative, then touching [them] would be...

There is confusion: if tactile perception (*sparśana*) were the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then the Smṛti would be confused. But by speaking of an alternative (*vikalpa*), he admits the validity of tactile perception as an option; and its source is Śruti. If that [Śruti] is admitted as a means of valid knowledge, it cannot be merely optional. And yet, the Smṛti regarding the "covering of everything" (*sarvaveṣṭana*) is indeed optional.

First, one is not able to postulate a *śruti* (Vedic text) [for the Smṛti], because it is sublated by direct perception (*sparśa*). Furthermore, only when that [perception] is free from delusion can a *śruti* be postulated. Nor can it be said that while there is no delusion in one case, there will be delusion in another; for whatever is the basis for that [Smṛti] in one case is the very same in the other. If it is not [deluded] in one case...

There is delusion [in one view]; yet, because [the opponent] is satisfied by the authority of scripture, there is no delusion regarding the other [view]. Furthermore, it cannot be said that "this scripture, whose syllables are fixed in one position, is not a faulty reading. Therefore, in this position, the cognition does not arise from delusion.

It is understood that [the rule] has been transferred to another context; therein, the fact that the practice of veiling everything is rooted in a cognition based on mishearing, lack of self-restraint, and so forth, leads to a contradiction, and thus it is set aside. For there is no authority whatsoever for accepting its validity when such a contradiction exists.
Therefore, just as in one case it is impossible to assume a scriptural basis (*śruti*), so too...

In the other case, it is because the cause is the same. Furthermore, because there would be a determination based on mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). What is this mutual dependence? If the memory is authoritative, then the tactile perception is an error; if the tactile perception is authoritative, then the memory is an error. This constitutes mutual dependence. In that regard, [regarding] the tactile perception...
