—O messenger! Why? Because "there is an absence of an injunction for usage.

That is to say, an injunction for usage is possible only if those very same words [are used] and those very same meanings [are understood]; otherwise, if the words were different, the meaning would not be cognized. Therefore, there is identity of the word. It is replied: "This is the purpose; let the reason be stated. Thereupon, the reason is stated: "Because of non-differentiation. We do not perceive any differentiation between those [words] and these [meanings].
For this very reason, there is identity of the word, and we comprehend both those words and those meanings; therefore, there is no difference.
We say: as it has been stated (78.22), "Those who carry on their backs are the divine cows;

that which is clarified butter is honey; that which has golden leaves is the lord of the forest"—there is no statement here which would assert that those carrying on their backs possess the nature of cows, such that "those which are cows... [would apply].

"They carry [the oblation] lying on their backs"—thus it is said; and if, by this statement, "cowness" (gotva) were being enjoined, then the phrase "they carry lying on their backs" would be a mere restatement (anuvāda), yet no such beings as "those who carry while lying on their backs" are well-known. Therefore, they must necessarily be enjoined.

While those [other qualities] are being enjoined, it is not possible to enjoin "cowness" (gotva), for in that case the sentence would be split. Furthermore, if the other [qualities] were Vedic, then the meaning of "lying on the back" (uttāna) and so forth would not be understood; in that case, "cowness," whose characteristic is already known, could certainly not be made known. Nor is the statement regarding "carrying on the back" meaningless; it will be purposeful as a means of praise (stuti). Thus...

The sweetness of clarified butter and the golden-leaved nature of the tree—therefore, those very same words and their meanings [are identical]. (Thus concludes the section on the identity of words in the world and the Veda. 1st Adhyāya, 3rd Pāda, 10th Adhikaraṇa.)

If the meaning [of words] is indeed worldly, then there arises a doubt: "Is the word's referent the form (*ākṛti*) or the individual (*vyakti*)? [And what, then, is the form, and what is the individual?
The form is the mere commonality (*sāmānyamātra*) of substances, qualities, and actions; the individual consists of the unique particularities (*asādhāraṇaviśeṣa*).
Sūtra-bhāṣya [Page 132]
Śrī Bhāgavata Rūpaḥ.

[The opponent says: "The individual [is the meaning]. Why is there doubt? Because when one says 'cow' (gauḥ), there arises a cognition of the universal, yet the connection with action occurs in the individual.
To this it is replied: "It is stated that the individual is the word-meaning. Why?"

"Because of the absence of an injunction [for the individual], the injunctions for the performance of acts such as seizing (*ālambhana*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and immolating (*viśasana*) would not be possible with respect to the class (*ākṛti*). If it is argued that 'where the utterance [of a word] would be purposeless, there it refers to the individual; therefore, elsewhere it is a term denoting the class'—to this it has been said (at 33): 'And it is improper for a word to have multiple meanings. If it is asked, 'How then is the comprehension of the class [attained]? "

The word will serve as an indicator (*anatiścibhūta*) of the individual entity (*vyaktipadārthaka*), in the sense that "whatever has such a form is a cow," just as "whoever possesses a staff is a staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*); yet the word *daṇḍin* does not denote the staff itself. The same applies here as well. (Pūrvapakṣa)
Because it is not a word denoting a substance.

(Sūtra 31) (Pūrvapakṣa 2) A "substance-word" is a word that denotes that which has a substance as its substrate; there would not be a word denoting that which has a substance as its substrate in that case, if the generic form (*ākṛti*) were the primary meaning—[as in the cases] "six [cows] are to be given," "twelve are to be given."

"Twenty-four [days] are for compassion"—this is not so; for a generic form (*ākṛti*) is not connected with numbers such as six and so forth. Therefore, it does not denote the generic form. (Pūrva-pakṣa 2)
And because of the mention of another [animal] (Sūtra 32). [The opponent argues:

"If the animal dedicated to Pūṣan should run away, one should sacrifice another animal of that same kind for that purpose. If the word were expressive of the class (*jāti*), the sacrifice of another would not be possible.
For even in the case of another animal substance, that very same class remains; therefore, the word is expressive of the individual (*vyakti*).
(Pūrvapakṣa 3) ||
The form [is the meaning of the word], because it serves the purpose of action. (Siddhānta 33).

The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position. The form (ākṛti) is the meaning of the word. Why? Because it serves the purpose of action; for the injunction, "One should pile the fire-altar with bricks," is possible only with reference to the form.

If the word ‘śyena’ has the sense of a genus (jāti), then, since it denotes an individual, it would be impossible to produce the individual śyena by means of piling (cayana); thus, because it would express an impossible meaning, it would be meaningless. Therefore—

It denotes the generic form (*ākṛti*). [Objection: "But surely the piling up will be performed by means of individual *śyena* birds. [Reply: The word *śyena* does not denote that which is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*); rather, it refers to that which is most desired to be attained (*īpsitatama*). Therefore, the *śyena* must be brought about through the act of piling; thus, it is accepted that the word denotes the generic form. [Objection:
"In both cases, the impossibility of the action itself is pointed out—the generic form cannot [perform the action]."

The meaning of the word [is the class], why? Because if the meaning of the word were the individual, the action would not be possible; for instance, in the case of "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*). Likewise, the individual is not the meaning of the word, because if the individual were the meaning of the word, the action would not be possible; for instance, in the case of "one should pile the *śyena*-altar" (*śyenacitaṃ cinvīta*). If it is argued that in the statement "he sprinkles the rice-grains," the class (*ākṛti*) has the individual as its secondary signified sense (*lakṣaṇārtha*), then it could equally be said elsewhere in the case of "one should pile the *śyena*-altar" that the individual has the class as its secondary signified sense. Which, then, is the better position here?

"The meaning of a word is the form (ākṛti). If the individual (vyakti) were the meaning of a word, it would not be applied to another individual. Yet, if it is applied to another individual, then the individual is not the meaning of the word, for an individual is indeed devoid of all generalities and particularities. To this, it is replied:

— This is not a fault; [the word] will function with respect to another individual (vyakti) that is indeed devoid of all generalities (sāmānya) and particulars (viśeṣa). If it functions with respect to another individual devoid of all generalities and particulars, then that [individual] is simply a generality. "No," it is said: for that object which is the substratum (āśraya) of both the generality and the particulars is the individual; and a word denoting an individual does not function with respect to the generality nor with respect to the particular. Rather, it denotes their very substratum; therefore...
"Functioning with respect to another individual is not a fault, for that [individual] is not the universal.

[Objection: If it also functions with respect to other individuals, why does the word "cow" not function with respect to an individual horse, which is devoid of all universals and particulars? [Reply: We say—only with respect to those...

The usage [of a word] is observed; it will apply to those [instances], but not everywhere. Furthermore, the usage of the word "cow" (*go*) is not observed in the case of a horse (*aśva*). Therefore, it will not apply there.
If, in whatever [case]...
• "If [it is] devoid of all generalities and particularities," thus it is in two places in the Kāśmīra manuscript (kā0 saṃ0 pu0).
[Page 134] Bhāṣya:

Usage is observed, and therein resides the function [of the word]. However, in the case of a cow born for the very first time, the initial usage would not be possible, because it has not been previously observed.
Furthermore, the cognition of the universal—namely, "this too is a cow," or "this too is a cow"—or "this is a cow"—would not be possible.

It might be argued that [the word] "cow" refers to this specific cow; however, a cognition of the universal (sāmānya) occurs even with respect to an individual cow never before seen. Therefore, one cannot maintain the position that "the word 'cow' denotes an individual based on usage. If that is so, then it is simply the nature of the capacity (śakti) that it applies to some individuals and not to others; just as fire is hot.
"The water is cold; thus it will be. This is not established, for it is not understood that it exists in some [cow] and does not exist in others.
"This is true; 'cowness' (gotva) will be the defining characteristic; in whatever possesses cowness, [it exists]."
"In the case of an individual" [is the objection]. "In that case, then, a qualified individual would be perceived!

And if it is qualified, the qualifier must be understood prior to it; for no one can perceive a qualified thing without having first perceived its qualifier."—[To this we reply: "Let it be that it expresses the *ākṛti* (form) as the qualifier and the individual as the qualificand; for one who takes *ākṛti* to be the meaning of the word..."
"The individual is not the word-meaning, nor is the configuration the word-meaning for one for whom the individual is the word-meaning. Both are the word-meaning of both;
however, for someone, one or the other is intended to be expressed as predominant.
Therefore, in some cases the configuration is intended to be expressed as subordinate, while the individual is intended to be expressed as predominant."

This is not so; for if both were being expressed, there would be a relationship of primary and subordinate status between them. Furthermore, if the class-form (*ākṛti*) is understood through the word, then it cannot be asserted that the individual (*vyakti*) is also the meaning of the word. Why? Because the class-form is eternally connected with the individual.

And when that [genus] has been understood through its connection [with the individual], another connection is understood; this is directly perceived by oneself—that when a word is uttered, the individual is cognized. As for the distinction as to whether it is from the word or from the genus, that is not perceptible; it is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): even without the word, one who has previously grasped the genus would indeed cognize that individual; whereas he who, even when the word is uttered, does not perceive the genus due to some mental lapse, would never [cognize] this [individual].
One would understand it as referring to the individual. [Objection: "But surely the word resides in the individual as qualified [by the universal].
[Page 135] [Reply:
If it resides in that which is qualified by one individual, it could not be perceived as qualified by another individual!
Therefore, the word is the cause for the cognition of the genus (*prakṛti*), and the cognition of the genus is the cause for the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*).

[Objection: "But was it not stated that [the genus] is perceived as subordinate (*guṇabhūta*)? [Reply: No; this state of being subordinate does not invalidate our position, since it is perceived in every respect. Whether it is subordinate or primary depends on the purpose: if it is uttered for its own sake, it is primary.
Now, if it is not for its own sake, but solely for the sake of another, then it is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), and there is no operation of the word with respect to it.

[Objection: "But in the case of *daṇḍī* (‘the man with a staff’), the word *daṇḍa* does not denote the staff itself, and yet the person qualified by the staff is understood; likewise here too, the generic form (*ākṛti*) would not be denoted, and yet the individual (*vyakti*) qualified by the generic form would be understood. [Reply: This is not correct.

It is said: "It is true that by the word 'staff-bearer' (*daṇḍin*), the staff itself is not directly denoted; however, it is not the case that there is no cognition of the staff-bearer when the staff has not been cognized.
For there exists the word 'staff' (*daṇḍa*) as a constituent part of the word 'staff-bearer,' by which the staff is made known. Therefore, this is correct:
that when the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) has been cognized, the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) is cognized."
"But surely, some part of the word 'go' (cow) is expressive of the form (ākṛti), while another is expressive of the individual (vyakti);
since the form is understood from it, the word 'go' does not denote the form."

Thus it is said. Nor is it the case that, just as the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍimat*) is not applied to the staff itself, so too the word "cow" (*go*) is not applied to the individual cow; for that very purpose, it was illustrated (80.12) that "the word *śyena* denotes only the universal. Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that in the absence of a connection with an individual *śyena*, the word *śyena* expresses the configuration (*ākṛti*), because it is uttered [as such];
however, no usage of the word is observed for an individual rice-grain (*vrīhi*) without a connection to the rice-configuration.
Therefore, the view that the word denotes the generic form (ākṛti) is superior—this is the siddhānta.

kha. If it is argued that there would be no ritual action, [we reply: it is an injunction regarding a different purpose; if it is argued that it is not a substance, [we reply: [it is so]. (Uddyota 1) Bhāṣya.
Now, it was stated by me: "Action would not be possible"—as in the case of the expression "he threshes the *broḍī* grains" (Bhāṣya, 1.1.25);
nor is it a word denoting a substance.

It might be argued: "Six [cows] should be given" (Pūrvapakṣa 2); and there would be no mention of seeing another, namely, "another of that same form" (Pūrvapakṣa 3). Therefore, this must be refuted. (Siddhānta 9)
Sūtra: "Because it is for that purpose, there is no division of the performance" (Uttara-pakṣa 2).
Bhāṣya: Since the word has the class (*ākṛti*) as its meaning, the performance applies to whichever individual (*vyakti*) is connected with that class.
For sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is heard in the scripture as something to be performed upon a substance; [the question is] which one? That which...

The means for performing the sacrifice is [the substance], because it is that which is employed by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), and not the generic form (*ākṛti*), since the latter is incapable [of being the direct object].

In this context, the word *vrīhi* (rice) is employed to denote the material cause (*prakṛti*) in order to specify the substratum of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*); for it will convey the generic form, and once the generic form is understood, it specifies the substratum of the sprinkling. Thus, there is no contradiction with the word denoting the generic form.

Thus, in the injunction "six cows are to be given as the sacrificial fee" (*ṣaḍ deyā gāvo dakṣiṇā*), when the number is to be applied to the chariot as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā-ratha*), the word "cows" (*gāvaḥ*) is a qualifier that expresses the generic class (*ālativacana*). Likewise, in the case of "another" (*anya*), there is a connection with "otherness" (*anyatva*) regarding a substitute for what has been lost; in that context, the word "animal" (*paśu*) expresses the generic class.

He qualifies [the meaning] by means of the form (*ākṛti*)—thus. Therefore, it is established that words such as "cow" and "horse" are denoters of the form (*ākṛti*). (Uddyota 2) (Thus ends the section on Form and Individual [Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa: A. 1, Pāda 3, Adhikaraṇa 10]).
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the venerable Śabarasvāmin’s Commentary on the Mīmāṃsā Sūtras. This concludes the Quarter on Smṛti. * * *
The Fourth Chapter.
Now begins the section concerning the fact that words such as *udbhid* and others are names of sacrifices.
(Sūtra 1: It has been stated that the Vedic corpus exists for the sake of [dharma]; therefore, everything [in it] must be for that purpose. (Pūrvapakṣa)

The texts record: "One should sacrifice with the *udbhid*, one should sacrifice with the *balabhid*, one should sacrifice with the *abhijit*, one should sacrifice with the *viśvajit*. Regarding this, there is a doubt: what...
Are terms such as *udbhid* and others injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*), or are they names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*)?

Whence does this doubt arise? Because the sentence appears to admit of both possibilities: the word *udbhidā* is connected with the verb *yajeta*. Does it enter into a relationship of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—that one should accomplish the sacrifice by means of the *udbhid* substance—or rather [does it stand in a relationship of grammatical subordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*)]? Or...
Regarding the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—in this sentence, "One should sacrifice with the *udbhid* sacrifice"—two things appear; thus, a doubt arises.
What, then, is the prima facie position? We have already stated that this is the purpose of the sacred tradition (*samāmnāya*).
A certain portion of this [Veda] is an injunction (*vidhi*), which makes known a matter not yet known, such as "One should sacrifice with Soma";

a certain portion is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), which praises an injunction by inciting one toward it, such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity"; and a certain portion is a mantra, which illuminates at the time of performance a matter already enjoined, such as "The sacrificial grass, the seat of the gods."

And so forth. Therefore, terms such as *udbhid* and others must serve one of these purposes. Among them, it cannot first be an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because that constitutes a supplementary part of a sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) for that which is to be enjoined, and there is no such thing here to be manifested of this kind. By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*): namely, that the sacrifice possesses the quality of being *udbhid*.

It is prescribed. Why? Because it favors established usage, because the injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) possesses purposefulness, and because it effects a specific course of action. Furthermore, their status as being for the sake of sacrifice is not understood from common worldly usage, nor is it defined by the Veda; therefore, they are injunctions of qualities. If it is an injunction of a quality...

In that case, the action would not be enjoined; and when an action is not enjoined, the injunction of a quality (guṇavidhāna) with respect to it would be purposeless. We say: "No"—for if it were a name, the injunction of a quality within the great Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice would be meaningful, as far as the phrase "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) extends.
In that case, [the injunction] would simply be "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," and there would be no specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣa*) regarding the performance [of the rite].

Furthermore, since they enjoin an additional matter through their connection with a quality, words such as *udbhid* will possess meaning as injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*). Therefore, they are injunctions of qualities.
Thus, this is the position reached. (Pūrvapakṣa)
This being the case, we reply:
"Or rather, it should be a name, because that which is new at its origin is not injunctive.
(Sūtra 2) [Siddhānta]. The phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) reverses the position. It should be a name.

We maintain that this [word] will enjoin an unenjoined matter, and that it will designate a sacrifice other than the Jyotiṣṭoma; for otherwise, the Vedic text (*śruti*), while expressing the instrumental case-ending and so forth, would have to indicate the possessor of the *udbhid* and other names. [The text would then mean: "One should effect [the result] by means of the sacrifice" (*yāgena kuryāt*). The meaning of the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is "one should effect by means of the sacrifice," since the sacrifice is the instrument (*karaṇa*).
And because of the mention of the instrumental case-ending, the *udbhid* and others are also instruments; and that [instrumentality] belongs to the *udbhid*.
By the word *yāgena* (by means of sacrifice), there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) due to its being the name of an action, which is consistent;

if it were denotative of a substance, there would have to be coreferentiality through the figurative indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). And between the direct statement (*śruti*) and figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the direct statement is stronger. Therefore, it is the name of an action. [Objection:
"But then the well-established status of being a term for a substance would be rejected, and the unestablished status of being a term for an action would be asserted."
It is stated: because of the mention of the instrumental case, it has the sense of an object.
Why? Because the instrumental case endings occur after nominal stems that denote an instrument, and the sacrifice is the instrument;
therefore, we shall infer that this [term] denotes the sacrifice.

"Furthermore—it might be argued that if, upon hearing the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), the cognition of a sacrifice were to arise from words such as *udbhid* and the like, then this [objection] would hold; however, our cognition does not undergo such a transformation. Therefore, [the claim] is untenable. [The opponent replies: 'The mention of the instrumental case cannot be explained otherwise.'"
If this is argued, let it be granted that it is not established; however, it is never the case when [the object] is not being apprehended—
[End of Chapter 2,
Section 8].

Furthermore, it will denote the sacrifice; therefore, they are injunctions of qualities. If it is argued that this involves *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication), it is better to assume *lakṣaṇā* than to assume the denotation of a sacrifice, for *lakṣaṇā* is well-known in common usage.

"Because it would involve the assumption of something already established. Furthermore: "If the name is being enjoined, the sacrifice is not; if the sacrifice is [enjoined], the name is not; if both were enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda).
To this it is replied: the name will not be enjoined, for it is a restatement (anuvāda).

[The names] such as *udbhid* and so forth. If it is asked, "From what [source] is their application obtained?"—to this it is replied: by virtue of the semantic power of the prefix *ut-* and the semantic power of the root *bhid-*, the word *udbhid* denotes an action;
namely, that "by means of this, the breaking open (*udbhedana*), i.e., the manifestation, of cattle is performed"—thus [it refers to] the sacrifice called *udbhit*.

Thus, because it is won by facing [the enemy], it is the *Abhijit*; because it is won by all [sides], it is the *Viśvajit*; so it is in every case. Therefore, these are names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*). As for the objection that "that which does not produce a specific activity is meaningless," even a name is meaningful through its connection with qualities and results; therefore, it is established that such items are indeed names of rituals. (Conclusion: This concludes the section [1.4.1] on the fact that terms such as *Udgitha* and others are names of sacrifices.)
Section 1: Now begins the section concerning whether words such as *citri* and others are names of sacrifices.
In which [case], there is instruction regarding qualities, primarily because of a direct connection. || 3 ||

Bhāṣya: "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā," "The Pavamāna [stotra] is fivefold," "The Ājya [stotras] are fifteenfold," "The Pṛṣṭhas are seventeenfold"—this is the illustrative example. Is the word *citrā*, the word *pavamāna*, the word *ājya*, and the word *pṛṣṭha* injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*), or are they names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*)? This is the doubt. They are injunctions of accessories because of their well-known usage, their meaningfulness, and their capacity to qualify; for these are not well-known as names of rituals, nor are they etymological (*yaugika*) terms. These are generic terms (*jātiśabda*), and *citrā* is a word denoting a quality (*guṇaśabda*).

The statement "one should sacrifice with the *citrayā*" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a sacrifice because [the sacrifice] is already known; it is not an injunction (*vidhi*) of a sacrifice. Furthermore, if one were to assume a fruit for the subordinate factor (*guṇa*), there would be no intention to express the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), as in the cases of "there are clarified butters" (*ājyāni bhavanti*) and "there are the *pṛṣṭha* chants" (*pṛṣṭhāni bhavanti*). Even when assuming these to be injunctions of subordinate factors, there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); therefore, they are indeed injunctions of subordinate factors—this is the position reached.

[Page 140] When this position has been reached, we reply: when there is doubt as to whether a term is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) or a name (*nāmadheya*), that which is taught as an accessory is connected with the primary action; the meaning is that it is the name of the action. For if it were an injunction of an accessory, the sentence would suffer from syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). In the case of the *puṃsavana*...

When [the sacrifice] has been obtained, it is not possible to enjoin by a single sentence that "the animal is the offering-material," "the animals are the fruit," and "the variegated color is the quality. For if the quality of being variegated were enjoined, it would be enjoined in the feminine gender.
That [quality] would not be prescribed for the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, nor would it be prescribed for the one performed by one desiring cattle;

likewise, the statement "the Ājya-stotras are fifteenfold" establishes the number fifteen in other cases, yet those [Ājyas] are not prescribed as being part of the Stotras, nor is there any other injunctive sentence [to that effect].
Therefore, one should enjoin these as the *ājya* [stotras], and when they have been enjoined, their number as fifteen is understood;

for both the connection of the others with the number fifteen and the connection of the *ājyas* with the stotra—which was previously unknown—are two matters that can be enjoined by a single sentence. However, if it were merely a name of the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*), this contradiction would not arise; it would simply be—

At that time, a connection with a number is being enjoined. Furthermore, by the word "ājyāni stotrāṇi" (the ājya-stotras), a quality would be enjoined only through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). Therefore, these are names of rituals (which have been enjoined in other sentences such as: "They praise with the ājyas," "They praise with the pṛṣṭhas"). As for the objection that "the name of the rituals is not well-known," [this is not a fault].

—Thus, by virtue of the well-known meaning of their constituent parts (*avayava-prasiddhi*), they are [names] other than [those derived from] the *ājigamana*. How is there an *ājigamana*? From the statement of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "Because they ran a race (*ājim īyuḥ*), that is the reason for the *ājya* nature of the *ājyas*. They are the *pṛṣṭhas* because of the mention of touch. It is the *bahiḥ-pavamāna* because it serves the purpose of the *pavamāna* chant and because of its connection with the exterior. It is the *citras* because of the variety of substances mentioned: "Curd, honey, milk, ghee, parched grain, rice, and water. Therefore, names of this kind are [names of] rituals. Now, what about...?
Are other *ānya* vessels, qualified by the number fifteen, enjoined for the acts of chanting (*stotra*)?
No, because there is no word that denotes such qualified [vessels].

But surely these two words—"fifteen" and "*ānyāni*"—will serve as the denoter; for here [it is said], "that which is touched by them is dedicated to Prajāpati. (Note: This additional phrase is found in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, and Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa manuscripts.)

[Page 141] Bhāṣya: Thus, [the author] will prescribe these for the distinguished [stotras]. These two words are not both prescriptive; one here is prescriptive and the other is a reference (*uddeśaka*). If both were prescriptive, there would be no mutual connection between them. If neither were prescriptive, the connection with the *stotra* would not be prescribed. Furthermore, it is not possible for one word here to be a reference with respect to the qualification while being prescriptive with respect to the *stotra*. Therefore, this is not a solution, because of the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*). (1.4.2 Sūtra).
Now begins the section concerning the status of terms such as *agnihotra* as names of sacrifices (*yāganāmadheya*). (The Principle of Being Named After That:
*tatprakhyanyāya*) "And that which is named after it is another scriptural injunction" (JS 1.4.4).
The Bhāṣya states: "One desiring heaven performs the Agnihotra" and "He pours the Āghāra libation"—thus they recite.

In this regard, there is a doubt: are the words *Agnihotra* and *Āghāra* injunctions of accessory materials (*guṇavidhi*), or are they names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*)? [The prima facie view is that] they are injunctions of accessory materials.

—Thus we say. Why? Because it is understood that "the oblation is for Agni" (*agnaye homaḥ asmin*), and likewise, "he pours the *āghāra* libation, which is a substance capable of flowing, such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*)"; thus, common usage (*prasiddhi*) is upheld. Furthermore, there is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the *darvihoma*, and the *āghāra* regarding the *upāṃśuyāja*; in those cases, these two possess purposefulness and produce a specific mode of activity. Moreover, in the case of the "injunction of a quality" (*guṇavidhipakṣa*), there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as in the expression "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*. In the *Agnihotra*, the injunction of a quality is understood through a compound; in the *āghāra* as well, "the *āghāra*..."
"It brings about"— thus, by the Vedic text itself, a quality (guṇa) is enjoined. Therefore, when it has been thus reached that this is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi),
[the following is said].

We reply: [The opponent] suspects that this is a case of "another name for that" (*tatpratyayānyaśabda*), on the grounds that the two qualities which are enjoined by these two [sentences] are already known from another source. For there is an injunction regarding the deity in the passage, "That which one offers in the evening to Agni and Prajāpati," and there is an injunction regarding the substance in the *āghāra* [libation] in the passage, "Having performed the *āghāra* with what has been taken four times. Furthermore, an injunction is defined as the making known of what was previously unknown; yet here, the injunction of the qualities is already known from another source. Therefore, these are not injunctions of qualities, but rather they are possible as names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*), since in that [rite] the offering (*hotra*) is made to Agni.

[Page 142] There is the act of offering (*homa*), which is the *agnihotra*; the act of pouring out in a long stream is well-known as the *āghāra*. Therefore, these are names of rituals; for the reasons such as "well-known usage" (*prasiddhi*) and so forth have already been stated [in Sūtra 1.4.10–12]. If it is argued that "this will be an injunction of fire for the purpose of what has been churned by Prajāpati," this is not so; for this [text] is capable of enjoining the fire, but not—

To prohibit Prajāpati [as the deity] would render the injunction regarding that very Prajāpati who is being prohibited meaningless; it is understood that Prajāpati is the deity, and what is so understood cannot be conceived as false. This is the resolution based on what is heard in scripture. It is said: "He pours the Āghāra libation"—this is an injunction directed toward a substance, according to the principle that "that by which a substance is intended to be prepared. By this action, the substance is processed, and once processed, it accomplishes the sacrifice.

Of which primary action is this the name? It is said: this very [action] is the unique primary action. [Objection: "But does it not lack a material substance (*dravya*) and a deity (*devatā*)? [Reply: We say that it does exist. For in the injunction, "Having poured the *āghāra*," clarified butter (*ājya*) is the material substance, and the deity is indicated by the color of the mantra. Indeed, the mantra—"O Indra, you who are the slayer of Vṛtra"—which designates the *āghāra*, either expresses the action itself or its means, and thus becomes integrated into the action. And this mantra is capable of denoting Indra; if that Indra is the means for that [action], [then the deity exists].

In this way, by means of this [mantra], the Āghāra offering can be performed; therefore, Indra is the deity, and the Āghāra is conjoined with both substance and deity; therefore, it is a sacrifice (*yajati*), and this is the name of that sacrifice—thus [it is concluded]. (9.4.3)

"And [the word] *deśam*. By that [word], such as *śyena* and so forth, which is well-known, there is a designation; and that is the name of the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*), for direct denotation (*śruti*) applies to being a name, whereas figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) applies to an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). As for the claim that "these are generic terms (*jātiśabda*) and do not denote the sacrifice," they shall denote it through the designation of similarity. For the designation occurs thus: "Just as a hawk (*śyena*) swoops down and seizes its prey, even so does this [sacrifice] swoop down and seize the hating enemy against whom they perform the *śyena* sacrifice. Through this similarity of "swooping down and seizing," the word *śyena* [denotes the sacrifice].
In a sacrifice, as in the case of "Devadatta is a lion," therefore it is a name of the ritual action.

"Just as one takes up what is difficult to grasp with a pair of tongs (*sandaṃśa*), so [it is here]; and just as cows protect [the word] 'cow' (*go*) [in the compound *gogarbhiṇī*], so [it is here]. Therefore, the word *sandaṃśa* is also a name for a ritual action, as is the word *go*. (1.4.4)
The section concerning the status of terms such as *vājapeya* as names (*nāmadheya*).

If it be argued that [the word] should be an injunction because its own name is heard as a quality—(Sūtra 6). (Purvapakṣa) Bhāṣya: It is heard in scripture, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Vājapeya. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is it an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), or is it the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*)? If such is the doubt, [the following applies].

An injunction regarding a quality is indeed seen; there is no doubt about it, for a quality is heard in the text, and when that is understood, it is impossible to say it does not exist; therefore, it is an injunction regarding a quality. (Pūrvapakṣa)
Sūtra: "Because the two actions are equal" (7).
Bhāṣya: This is not so; for these two actions would be equal—namely, the action of the Vājapeya and [the other].

And as for the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the procedural details (*vidhyanta*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* would apply to both [the Vājapeya and the Sautrāmaṇī]; and in that case, the observation of seventeen *dīkṣās* and seventeen *upasads* would not be appropriate—namely, "The Vājapeya has seventeen *dīkṣās*" and "The Vājapeya has seventeen *upasads*.
Alternatively, if it is argued that "because the two actions are equal, it is not an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*)," [then the following applies].

Therefore, this performance of the Vājapeya is for the sake of *tuṣṭi* (satisfaction) by means of the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma; in that case, the observation of the *dīkṣās* (initiations) and the *upasads* is logically consistent. Consequently, it is a name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*), as indicated by the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The attainment of this, however, is [explained] by the subsequent sūtra. (Siddhānta) Sūtra:
[If there were] a single word, [it would have to express] both its own meaning and the meaning of another. (Siddhānta Sūtra 8).

Commentary: If it were an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), the expression of the word *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice") as having both its own meaning and the meaning of another would be contradicted. If, in the phrase "one desiring sovereignty should sacrifice" (*svārājyakāmo yajeta*), it is stated for its own sake to enjoin the sacrifice for one desiring sovereignty, then it could not be restated for the sake of another to connect it with the quality of *vājapeya*. [It would have to be restated] as "by means of a sacrifice characterized by the quality of *vājapeya*."

—thus [it would follow], for in that case the sentence would be split. "But surely we perceive these as two distinct sentences directly: 'One desiring sovereignty should sacrifice' is one direct perception of two words, and 'He should sacrifice with the Vājapeya' is likewise a direct perception. This is not so; if that were the case, we would perceive four words, yet only three are perceived.

“It is said: ‘One should sacrifice’—this [injunction] will connect with both [the desire for sovereignty and the Vājapeya]. How can that which is uttered once enter into a connection with both? Because there is no difference in form; its form is exactly the same when connected with the desire for sovereignty as it is when connected with the Vājapeya; therefore, it connects with both simultaneously. This is not so. If such a form is unknown, then it is an injunction (*vidhi*); if it is already known, then it is a restatement (*anuvāda*). And it is impossible for something to be both known and unknown simultaneously. He says:

—As for what was said: "In the case of an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) that one should sacrifice (*yajeta*). If this is a restatement, by what means is the quality now enjoined? Do not say "by the word *vājapeya*," for that has not yet arrived, nor is there any derivative suffix (*kṛtya*) [to indicate an injunction].

The operation of the word-meaning is enjoined! And as for the verbal form *yajeta* (he should sacrifice), which is not a noun, it has been stated that it is a restatement (*anuvāda*). By what, then, is its operation enjoined? Therefore, the injunction "he should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is with respect to both the desire for self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) and the accessory (*guṇa*); thus, it is connected with both.

If there were an injunction for both [the sacrifice and the accessory], then the Vājapeya would not be connected with the sacrifice for one desiring self-sovereignty (svārājya). In that case, there would be two separate sentences; there would not be a single syntactical unity (ekavākyatā) between the injunction of the accessory and the sacrifice for one desiring self-sovereignty.
If [this were so], Chapter 8, Section (Pāda) 1. [Page 145]

If it is argued that "the connection [of the result] with the sacrifice belongs to one desiring sovereignty (khārājya) by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa)," we say no, because by means of the syntactical unit (vākya), the injunction applies to the sacrifice in general. If it is argued that "let there be a connection with the sacrifice in general," we say no, because of the unity of the sentence (ekavākyatā) between the sacrifice and one desiring sovereignty.
Because it is something to be understood [as such], thus the sublation of both the context and the sentence is appropriate if [the word] is a name of a ritual action;

for if it were the position that it is an injunction of an accessory (guṇavidhi), all these defects such as syntactical split (vākyabheda) and so forth would arise. Therefore, the word *vājapeya* is the name of a ritual action.
Success! (Siddha-yoga) (1.4.5 Adhikaraṇa).
The section concerning the non-naming of the *kāthāneya* and others.
But its own qualities should be enjoined, because there is no division [of the act] regarding the purpose of the injunction, provided they have not been taught by another [text]. 8.
Bhāṣya:
"That which belongs to Agni, offered on eight potsherds, is constant at the new moon and the full moon"—such passages are heard in the scripture.

In this regard, there is a doubt: are [passages] such as "that which belongs to Agni" and "that which belongs to Agni and Soma" injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*), or are they names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*)? What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? If they were injunctions of accessory qualities, many accessories would have to be enjoined.
"An oblation to Agni on eight potsherds"— since this is the case, these are not injunctions of accessory qualities (guṇavidhi). This being the position reached:

We reply: that [term] is the action (*karman*), and its qualities (*guṇa*) would be enjoined; for they are inseparable from the word ending in a *taddhita* suffix when the purpose is to enjoin the action. For in that case, the state of being dedicated to Agni (*āgneyatā*) is enjoined for the eight-pot-sherd offering (*aṣṭākapāla*). That very [offering] becomes "dedicated to Agni" (*āgneya*) if it is given having been resolved upon for Agni. Thus, by this means, the sacrifice is enjoined; that—
Such a thing being enjoined cannot be enjoined without first enjoining the cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*);

for it cannot be said that a relationship being enjoined is established without first enjoining the two related members. Therefore, these are injunctions of qualities; the cake made of rice or barley, being prepared upon the eight potsherds, is indeed the same [as the original], and thus it is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
The *Siddhānta* (conclusion) regarding the *Āṣāḍhākapāla* is stated: "He causes it to be cooked on potsherds"—
thus says the text in the tenth book of the *Mīmāṃsā*.

The Bhāṣya states: "They do not accept what has been cooked by another; therefore, in this case, there is no split in the sentence, provided that [the quality] is not enjoined by another [text]. However, where the qualities are enjoined by another statement, there it is a name, as in "He performs the Agnihotra oblation. (9.4.6)

The section concerning whether words such as *vārddhra* and others denote a genus (*jāti*). Sūtra 10: Because the word is obtained even when there is no refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the tail or the kingdom, it is not a word for that [refined object].
In the case of *barhis*, *ājya*, and *puroḍāśa*, there is a doubt:

are these words denoting a consecration (*saṃskāra*), or are they words denoting a genus (*jāti*)? We say: they are words denoting a consecration. For everywhere, the word *barhis* is applied metaphorically to grass that has been consecrated, not to unconsecrated grass; likewise, the word *ājya* is applied to clarified butter that has been consecrated, and similarly, the word *puroḍāśa* is applied to flour-cake that has been consecrated. But [an objection may be raised]:...
It is also used metaphorically for something unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), as when speakers say, "The cows have gone taking the iron," or likewise,
"Clarified butter is to be bought," or "My mother gives me a *prahlaka* with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). These [usages] occur because of similarity.

The application [of the term] is like the word "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) when applied to a mere stump. Why is this so? Because the word is used for only a part [of the whole], therefore these are words denoting a consecrated object (*saṃskāra-śabda*). Such is the position reached.
To this, we reply: since the word is found even when the *barhis* grass and other items have not been consecrated, [it is not a word denoting a consecrated object].

[They are] words denoting preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*). [Objection: But was it not said that they will apply to a single part on account of similarity? [Reply: No; for one can only say "on account of similarity" once the status of being words denoting preparatory acts is already established, and that is not yet established. How so? Because in the case of words such as *barhis* and so forth, the preparatory acts are enjoined first; therefore, when the words exist, the preparatory acts must follow, and only when the preparatory acts exist [can the status of the words be established].

The non-attainment [of the object]—thus there arises a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Furthermore, grammatical refinements (*saṃskāra*) do not occur unless they are prescribed; those which people would employ without such consideration are not [valid].

Therefore, people in the world employ *vṛddhi* and other [grammatical operations] only with respect to refined forms (*saṃskṛta*). Consequently, even in a single part, there is a genus (*jāti*); thus, that which is initially unrefined is a particularity of the pillar of the body (*yacchauyastambhaviśeṣa*), serving as a support (*upaśaya*).
[Page 147] Bhāṣya:

All observed signs ought to be signs of genus (*jāti*). Furthermore, for those things that are beyond the world (*alaukika*), it is not possible to determine their meaning from the Veda alone without depending on the connection between preceding and succeeding words. [The proponent argues: "Let the preceding and succeeding words not be meaningless"—thus he...

If it were to be postulated, that which is impossible and not perceived cannot be so postulated; yet your preceding and following words will possess meaning through worldly usage even if they are unrefined (*asaṃskṛta*). Therefore, words of this kind are indeed genus-words (*jātiśabda*). The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: regarding the rule "one covers the sacrificial pit with *barhis* grass," if the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) holds, the covering must be done with consecrated grass; in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the opposite is established. (1.4.7)
Sūtra Bhāṣya:
The section concerning the derivative (etymological) nature of terms such as *prokṣaṇī*.
The sprinkling waters [are for the purpose of the sacrifice], because of their connection with the ritual purpose. || 11 ||

It is heard in the scripture: "Place the *prokṣaṇī*s. Regarding that, there is a doubt concerning the word *prokṣaṇī*: is it based on a consecration (*saṃskāra*), or is it based on a genus (*jāti*), or is it etymological (*yaugika*)? In this regard, since the word is observed to be used when consecrations have been performed, its status as a term based on consecration is understood; however, because the word is also applied to that which has not been consecrated, it is a term based on genus.

In a certain place, people say, "We have been distressed by the *aprokṣaṇī* waters, which are unprepared. When it is argued that [the term *aprokṣaṇī*] is therefore a generic (*jāti*) word, it is replied that it is etymological (*yaugika*). Why? Because of its connection with the meaning. Regarding the term *aprokṣaṇyaḥ*, the fact that the aggregate of the prefix, root, and suffix has a generic cause is inferred from usage; however, since the root *plu* (to flow) occurs in conjunction with the prefix *pra*, the root, the instrumental suffix, and the suffix together function because of their connection with sprinkling (*secanasaṃyoga*), and thus common usage will be supported. This is so even when there is another instance of sprinkling.

If it were expressed by the word *prokṣaṇa* [as a generic term], then since that would occur in water simply through its connection with that [act of sprinkling], it would not be possible to assume a collective meaning. Therefore, it is etymological (*yaugika*). The practical application is as follows: if it is a term for a consecrated substance (*saṃskāra*), then the injunction is "Bring the *prokṣaṇī* waters"; if it is a word denoting a genus (*jāti*), then it is "Bring the clarified butter."
If it is etymological, then it is "prokṣaṇam" (sprinkling).
(1.4.8) [Page 148] Sūtra.
Bhāṣya-sarvasva: Now begins the section concerning the derivative nature of the term *nirmanthya*.
Likewise in the case of the *nirmantha*. 12.

Regarding the statement, "They bake the bricks with the *nirmanthya* [fire]," since it is observed in the context of a consecrated fire, the word *nirmanthya* refers to a consecrated fire. However, it is also seen in the sense of non-consecration, as in: "Bring the *nirmanthya* [fire]; let us eat rice. Because of its connection with the act of churning (*nirmanthana*), it is established that the term is etymological (*yaugika*) in this case, just as before. As for the purpose: when the term is based on consecration (*saṃskāra-nimitta*), the bricks must be baked with a consecrated fire;

when it is a generic term (*jāti-śabda*), they may be baked with whatever is available; but when it is etymological (*yaugika*), they must be baked with a fire recently churned, just as one says, "He ate with *nāvanīta*," meaning with butter that was recently produced by churning.
It is understood. (1.4.9 Śrauta-sūtra)
Now begins the section concerning the status of terms such as *vaiśvadeva* as names (*nāmadheya*).

If it be argued that there is an option regarding the Vaiśvadeva [sacrifice] (Pūrvapakṣa 1): In the first festival of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, concerning the Vaiśvadeva, there is a doubt: in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva," is the word *vaiśvadeva* an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*), or is it the name of the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*)?
— thus. If there is doubt [regarding this], there is no doubt: "In the Vaiśvadeva, there is an option.

The word *vaiśvadeva* is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), for the injunction of a quality is indeed understood; the Viśvedevas are enjoined in the sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya, and there is an option between them and Tvaṣṭṛ and the others.
In this way, common usage will become meaningful. (Pūrvapakṣa 1)
kha. Or rather, [the materials are not restricted] because of the context and because of direct injunction; for the context does not [restrict] the substance.
(Siddhānta) Bhāṣya: This is not so; Āgneya and the others are directly enjoined by Śruti as belonging to those sacrifices.

It is understood that the Viśvedevas [are to be invoked] by means of the direct statement, and by that alone according to the context, not by any other; nor can this be an unequal option between two equally authoritative sources, for the context is not capable of subverting what is directly stated regarding the substance. Therefore, it is a name of the ritual action. (Siddhānta)

[Sūtra 8] [Page 153] The sūtra states: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature. The commentary explains: This means that the fourfold nature of all phenomena is established based on the three natures. What are these four? First, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); second, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); third, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); and fourth, the nature of being beyond conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca-svabhāva*). Among these, the first three are explained according to their characteristics, while the fourth is explained by way of its exclusion. Regarding the first, the imagined nature, it refers to the characteristic of the grasped and the grasper as they appear within the dependent nature; because this characteristic is merely a mental fabrication and does not exist in reality, it is called the "imagined nature. Regarding the second, the dependent nature, it refers to the characteristic of the dependent origination of all phenomena; because this characteristic arises in dependence upon causes and conditions and does not exist independently, it is called the "dependent nature. Regarding the third, the perfected nature, it refers to the characteristic of the ultimate reality of all phenomena; because this characteristic is eternally free from the two kinds of grasping and is unchanging, it is called the "perfected nature. Regarding the fourth, the nature of being beyond conceptual proliferation, it refers to the characteristic of the ineffable reality of all phenomena; because this characteristic transcends all linguistic expression and mental activity, it is called the "nature of being beyond conceptual proliferation. Thus, although the fourfold nature of all phenomena is briefly explained here, it is extensively elucidated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and other treatises. Therefore, one should seek them therein. Furthermore, the meaning of the fourfold nature is also explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, and other works. One should also investigate those accordingly. The sūtra continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of emptiness. The commentary explains: This means that the fourfold emptiness of all phenomena is established based on the three natures. What are these four? First, the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*); second, the emptiness of existence (*bhāva-śūnyatā*); third, the emptiness of both existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāva-śūnyatā*); and fourth, the emptiness of neither existence nor non-existence (*naivabhāvanābhāva-śūnyatā*). Among these, the first three are explained according to their characteristics, while the fourth is explained by way of its exclusion. Regarding the first, the emptiness of non-existence, it refers to the characteristic of the imagined nature; because the characteristic of the grasped and the grasper within the dependent nature is entirely non-existent, it is called the "emptiness of non-existence. Regarding the second, the emptiness of existence, it refers to the characteristic of the dependent nature; because the characteristic of the dependent origination of all phenomena exists as a mere appearance, it is called the "emptiness of existence. Regarding the third, the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, it refers to the characteristic of the perfected nature; because the characteristic of the ultimate reality of all phenomena is neither existent—since it is free from the two kinds of grasping—nor non-existent—since it is the true nature of all phenomena—it is called the "emptiness of both existence and non-existence. Regarding the fourth, the emptiness of neither existence nor non-existence, it refers to the characteristic of the ineffable reality of all phenomena; because the characteristic of the ultimate reality of all phenomena is neither existent—since it transcends all linguistic expression and mental activity—nor non-existent—since it is the true nature of all phenomena—it is called the "emptiness of neither existence nor non-existence. Thus, although the fourfold emptiness of all phenomena is briefly explained here, it is extensively elucidated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and other treatises. Therefore, one should seek them therein. Furthermore, the meaning of the fourfold emptiness is also explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, and other works. One should also investigate those accordingly. The sūtra continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of non-self. The commentary explains: This means that the fourfold non-self of all phenomena is established based on the three natures. What are these four? First, the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*); second, the non-self of dharmas (*dharma-nairātmya*); third, the non-self of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-nairātmya*); and fourth, the non-self of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-nairātmya*). Among these, the first two are explained according to their characteristics, while the latter two are explained by way of their exclusion. Regarding the first, the non-self of persons, it refers to the characteristic of the five aggregates; because the five aggregates are devoid of a permanent, unitary, and independent self, it is called the "non-self of persons. Regarding the second, the non-self of dharmas, it refers to the characteristic of all phenomena; because all phenomena are devoid of a self-substance that is permanent and unchanging, it is called the "non-self of dharmas. Regarding the third, the non-self of the imagined nature, it refers to the characteristic of the grasped and the grasper within the dependent nature; because the characteristic of the grasped and the grasper within the dependent nature is merely a mental fabrication and does not exist in reality, it is called the "non-self of the imagined nature. Regarding the fourth, the non-self of the perfected nature, it refers to the characteristic of the ultimate reality of all phenomena; because the characteristic of the ultimate reality of all phenomena is eternally free from the two kinds of grasping, it is called the "non-self of the perfected nature. Thus, although the fourfold non-self of all phenomena is briefly explained here, it is extensively elucidated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and other treatises.

Therefore, one should seek them therein. Furthermore, the meaning of the fourfold non-self is also explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, and other works. One should also investigate those accordingly. The sūtra continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of transformation. The commentary explains: This means that the fourfold transformation of all phenomena is established based on the three natures. What are these four? First, the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); second, the transformation of the object (*ālambana-parāvṛtti*); third, the transformation of the path (*mārga-parāvṛtti*); and fourth, the transformation of the fruit (*phala-parāvṛtti*). Among these, the first three are explained according to their characteristics, while the fourth is explained by way of its exclusion. Regarding the first, the transformation of the basis, it refers to the characteristic of the revolution of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); because the storehouse consciousness, which is the basis of all deluded phenomena, is transformed into the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), it is called the "transformation of the basis. Regarding the second, the transformation of the object, it refers to the characteristic of the revolution of the objects of perception; because the objects of perception, such as forms and sounds, which are the objects of the deluded consciousnesses, are transformed into the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), it is called the "transformation of the object. Regarding the third, the transformation of the path, it refers to the characteristic of the revolution of the paths of practice; because the paths of practice, such as the stages and the perfections, which are the means of attaining enlightenment, are transformed into the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), it is called the "transformation of the path. Regarding the fourth, the transformation of the fruit, it refers to the characteristic of the revolution of the fruits of realization; because the fruits of realization, such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, which are the results of the path, are transformed into the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*), it is called the "transformation of the fruit. Thus, although the fourfold transformation of all phenomena is briefly explained here, it is extensively elucid

(Sūtra 15) (Ābhāsaniścaya). Commentary: It might be argued that by the word "Vaiśvadeva," the group of sacrifices (*yāgagaṇa*) characterized by the qualities of being directly perceived and so forth is indicated (*lakṣyate*), for therein the *āmikṣā* offering belongs to the Viśvedevas. If the group of sacrifices is indicated by the word "Vaiśvadeva," then the Viśvedevas themselves are not enjoined; how then could the word "Vaiśvadeva," which has already undergone its own [primary] application, denote the group of sacrifices?
"Who will sacrifice it, and to whom will he assign all the gods?"—thus, this mutual connection between the word *vaiśvadeva* and the *viśve devāḥ* (all-gods) is not tenable;
rather, it is merely a name (*nāmadheya*), not an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*). (Śrauta-nirṇaya).
