Therefore, because the names of the actions are for the sake of another, [the repetition applies] to the groups. (Siddhānta Sūtra 16). The auxiliary elements (*guṇa*) are for the sake of another; they are not able to cause the principal (*pradhāna*) to be repeated. Therefore, the sacrifice must be performed once; it ought not to be repeated in accordance with the auxiliaries. Furthermore, there is no contradiction because the deity is the same. In that case, within a single principal offering, there are thirty offerings.

The phrase "hayante" [are offered] does not result in the attainment of the number thirty for the oblations into the Āhavanīya fire; therefore, it is established that this is a name for the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*). (Siddhāntayukti) Bhāṣya (1.4.10).
The section concerning the status of the Vaiśvānara passage as an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) because it does not prescribe an action.
Those [mantras] which possess a prior [corresponding ritual act] are not for the purpose of injunction; their efficacy lies in the sacred tradition (samāmnāya).

17. (Pūrvapakṣa: It is heard in scripture: "Upon the birth of a son, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. In that context, various options regarding the number of potsherds are heard, such as: "When it is on eight potsherds, he purifies him with the Gāyatrī through spiritual luster," and so forth. Regarding these, there is a doubt: are the qualities such as the number eight injunctions of accessory details (*guṇavidhi*), or are they commendatory statements (*arthavāda*)? In this matter, [the opponent argues] they are injunctions of accessory details.

—this is precisely what we say. How so? For those who speak of things already known (pūrvavantaḥ)—that is, those who refer to matters already understood—are not intended for the purpose of injunction; such is the status of this sentence within the recited collection (samāmnāya).

The capacity [of the text] consists in its expressing something not previously enjoined. What is that? It is the capacity for injunction; thus it will enjoin a matter not yet determined. Otherwise, being merely explanatory praises (*arthavādas*), they would be purposeless. Furthermore, it is not possible for the twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*) to assume the status of a subordinate element (*śeṣa*). There is a direct (*pratyakṣa*) praise of the eight potsherds, whereas that of the twelve is indirect (*parokṣa*); and in the absence of a direct statement, an indirect one would be required. Therefore, these are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhis*).
(Pūrvapakṣa)

6. But if it were for the purpose of enjoining a quality, those qualities would be useless in the performance [of the rite], for there is no meaningfulness toward that [performance]. (Siddhānta) Bhāṣya:
This is not so—that these are injunctions of qualities; rather, they exist for the purpose of enjoining a quality.

They have established the number of potsherds for the *puroḍāśa* cake, yet they are unable to prescribe the performance of the sacrifice itself; for while the state of having twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapālatā*) belongs to the sacrifice by virtue of the direct statement (*vākya*), the states of having eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth belong to it only by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, those [latter] will not apply to the sacrifice. Furthermore, since the qualities such as "eightfold" form a single syntactical unit with the *puroḍāśa*, they would set aside the context and not apply to the sacrifice; and if they were unrelated to the sacrifice, they would be meaningless, while if they were related only to the *puroḍāśa*, there would be no result [for the sacrifice]. However, as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), their function as a praise of the Vaiśvānara sacrifice is appropriate.

Therefore, they are *arthavādas*—this is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). (Sūtra 19: [Objection] That [interpretation] as a supplement to it is not tenable. (This is the appearance of the prima facie view.)
The objection stated as "bhā. must be refuted—thus ends the aphorism with the introductory remark (the *uddeśa*). (Uddyota:
*ābhāsa*)
Sūtra: "Because of the lack of distinction, they would serve the purpose of praise.

(Uddyota 20) But when it is understood that [the mentions of] the eight-potsherd cake and so forth are purposeless for the sake of incitement (*prarocanā*), then, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), they constitute a praise of the twelve-potsherd cake for the purpose of inciting the Vaiśvānara sacrifice.
It will be so; for there exist specific numbers such as "not being greater than twelve" (advādaśatva) and so forth, which remain undivided within the number twelve.
Therefore, this is a praise of the parts by way of praising the whole—the cake on twelve potsherds—for the sake of its glorification.

It is applicable; for example, as in "the rim and hub of this wheel are beautiful," or "the elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry of this army are beautiful. Therefore, the praise is justified. (Uddyota)
[Objection: "Could it be the cause? (21) [Introduction]

If you view it thus—that these are merely explanatory passages (*arthavādas*)—then why would [the results] such as spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) not arise from the eight-pot-sherd offering (*aṣṭākapāla*) and the others? [The text says: "For one desiring spiritual luster, there is the eight-pot-sherd offering," and so on for the subsequent ones, according to the desire. What will happen in this way? There will be no pointlessness in the injunction of qualities regarding the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), nor will a figurative praise of the eight potsherds have to be assumed. Therefore, [these refer] to the desires.
The rules shall be as follows. (Śrāddha)

[The word] *sraḥ* [is used] because of the futility [of other motives]; it is not the cause, for the causes belong to the agent; indeed, the purpose of the qualities is what is enjoined. (Śābarabhāṣya, Adhyāya 4, Pāda 1, Sūtra 22). Commentary:
If the injunctions were for the sake of desire, there would be distinct sentences; however, this is one [sentence].

The passage begins with, "Upon the birth of a son, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara," and ends with, "In that it consists of twelve potsherds, he places cattle in this very world;

he who, upon whose birth, performs this sacrifice, becomes purified, radiant, an eater of food, possessed of sensory power, and rich in cattle"— in the midst of this [passage] are mentioned the ghee-offerings (*ājyabhāgas*) and so forth.
If these [clauses], while being heard, were not syntactically connected, they would constitute separate sentences;

for instance, regarding the scriptural statement, "When there is an eight-potherd [cake]," and so forth, by that very sentence: "By means of the eight-potherd [cake], he bestows brilliance upon him; when there is a ten-potherd [cake], by means of the Virāj, he bestows food-eating power upon him;
when there is an eleven-potherd [cake], by means of the Triṣṭubh, he bestows sensory power upon him; when there is a twelve-potherd [cake]... [and so on].

"In this very *jagatī* [meter] he places cattle; he in whom, once born, one performs this sacrifice, becomes indeed purified, endowed with splendor, wisdom, vigor, and cattle"—thus in the case of those [rites] enjoined by such passages.
In the *Mīmāṃsā-darśana-bhāṣya*:

For the causes of the agent would be such things as purity (*pūtatva*) and so forth. This very [agent] is enjoined here for the sake of a quality (*guṇārtha*) in the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, in such passages as "one who is indeed impure" (*apūta eva*). And by that [quality], these [results] such as the eightfold nature (*aṣṭatva*) are connected as direct causes—because [he possesses] the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*) through the *gāyatrī* [verse].

He purifies him, and thus he becomes purified; because the *gāyatrī* itself bestows splendor upon him, he becomes resplendent; because the *triṣṭubh* itself bestows food upon him, he becomes an eater of food; because the *jagatī* itself bestows cattle upon him, he becomes possessed of cattle—thus it is said. Thereafter...

If injunctions were possible for the sake of desire, even if they were not explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), these [passages] would indeed be purposeless. Therefore, qualities such as *brahmavarcasa* (spiritual luster) are not the cause of [the status of] ghee and so forth; consequently, ghee and so forth are merely explanatory passages (*arthavādas*). (1.4.11)
Sabhāṣya: The section concerning the purpose of the term *yajamāna* as a praise for the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) and other items.
That is the lion's roar. || 23 ||

The following is recited in the sacred tradition: "The sacrificer is the *prastara* (grass-bundle)," and "The sacrificer is the one-pot-sherd cake," and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the statement "The sacrificer is the *prastara*" an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), or is it an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*)? Likewise for "The sacrificer is the one-pot-sherd cake. What, then, is the prima facie view? It is an injunction of a subordinate quality. Why so? Because in this way it will enjoin a previously unestablished matter; otherwise, as a mere explanatory praise, it would be purposeless.
It would be so; and it is logical because it possesses meaning, therefore it is an injunction.

This is not so; for if it were an injunction, then the sacrificer would be restricted to the function of the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*), or the sacrificial grass-bundle would be restricted to the function of the sacrificer. [The text says: "He places the oblations upon the sacrificial grass-bundle."
Regarding the statement "all the *sruva*-ladles," [it might be argued that] they should be placed on the *juhū* while the sacrificer is present.

But if all the *sruva*-ladles were so placed, it would not be possible for the sacrificer to perform his duties, according to the rule: "The Brahman and the sacrificer sit to the south while the ritual action is being performed."

Furthermore, the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is not capable of performing the duties of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Likewise, if the sacrificer were to be employed for the purpose of the single-pot-sherd offering (*ekakapāla*), he would have to perform it in its entirety; in that case, there would be a total omission of all other ritual procedures (*sarvatantroparilopa*).

[Page 157] Bhāṣya: It might be so. However, a single potsherd (ekakapāla) cannot perform the duties of the sacrificer (yājamāna). Therefore, it is not an injunction. Furthermore, there is another injunction: "He places the prastara-bunch upon the upper layer of the sacrificial grass (barhis)."
"He makes the cake on one potsherd an offering of the whole"—thus, for this reason also, it is not an injunction.
What then? It is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), for the sacrificer is already known to be the *prastara* (grass-bundle), and the cake on one potsherd is likewise known.
But how is their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) understood? For the *prastara*...

Either the sacrificer is "one-cupped," yet the sacrificer is not a sacrificial cake prepared on a single potsherd; or it refers to the first handful of *kuśa* grass. How can a word for one thing be applied to another? Or for what purpose is that which is already known being mentioned? Thus [the objection stands].

It is said: that which is being known is mentioned for the sake of praise—namely, "The *prastara* (grass-bundle) is to be placed upon the *barhis* (sacrificial grass), because it is the sacrificer; likewise, the sacrificer is to be made into a single-pot-sherd offering (*ekakapāla*) entirely consumed by the fire, so that he becomes established in heaven, which is the *āhavanīya* fire."

How does the word "other" (para) function? [The answer is: It is figurative speech (guṇavāda). Why? Because this is a discourse based on qualities (guṇa). How can a word that does not denote a quality express a quality? We reply: by denoting its own primary meaning; for all these figurative words do not abandon their own primary meanings when applied to qualities.
[The words] function [in this way]; for in that case there would be the abandonment of what is well-known (*prasiddha-hāni*) and the assumption of what is not well-known (*aprasiddha-kalpanā*).

Moreover, not all [words] denote a collection of qualities (*guṇa-samudāya-vacana*), because they are seen to apply even to one devoid of those qualities; for instance, a lion cub, though unable to perform the task of enduring fatigue, is still called a "lion" when afflicted by disease. Furthermore, a word denoting a whole (*samudāya-vācin*) cannot properly apply to a single part (*avayava*), as it does with respect to all individual lions (*sarva-siṃha-vyaktiṣu*).
The established principle—that a word denotes its universal (sāmānya)—would be contradicted;

nor would it function through imagination in the absence of an actual lion, for imagination is incapable [of producing such a result]. If it is asked, "How then is the determination of cognition established by the denotation of its own object?
[the answer is: It is due to the connection with the object—once "lion" is ascertained, its habitual ferocity is generally [associated] with that.
"—is understood as 'one who acts by force,' due to the power of the cognition of the meaning;

for he who thinks, 'I shall cause the one who has committed an offense to understand [my intent],' if he utters the word 'lion,' his intended purpose is accomplished—the meaning of 'lion' is understood by force.
[Page 158]
The word "bhā" (the agent) conveys another meaning through its connection [with the action]; in this way, by denoting its own primary meaning, the connection with its qualities is understood.

But here, in the cases "the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) is the sacrificer" and "the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) is the sacrificer," what kind of connection with qualities is understood? It is the quality of "being the means for accomplishing that"—for everyone accomplishes their own purpose, and whoever accomplishes the purpose of another [also accomplishes his].
When that [word] is uttered, it comes to the heart; just as a king’s footman—
meaning a footman accomplishes the king’s business—
is recognized when the word "king" is uttered, so too here is the business of the sacrificer.

The *prastara* (grass-bundle) and the *ekakapāla* (single-pot-sherd cake) accomplish [the purpose]; they are understood when the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is understood, therefore they are indicated by the word "sacrificer. How so? They would serve as praises in the case of the increasing [of the bundle], its placement upon [the altar], and the complete offering. Therefore, such items [are to be understood in this manner].
"Explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are not injunctions (*vidhi*)"—(Sūtra 1.4.12).
This is the section concerning how words such as *āgneya* and others serve the purpose of praising the Brāhmaṇa and so forth.
Birth. || 24 ||

Bhāṣya: "The Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni; the Rājanya belongs to Indra; the Vaiśya belongs to the Viśvedevas"—such passages are heard in the scripture. In this regard, there is a doubt: are these injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*), or are they explanatory statements (*arthavāda*)? We say: they are injunctions of accessory qualities; for in this way, they will enjoin a previously unknown matter (*apūrva*). Otherwise, being merely explanatory statements, they would be purposeless. It is not an injunction [of the main act], because there is another injunction [for that].
Because of its existence, there is therefore correspondence; its mention is for the purpose of praising the injunction.

By what manner are the words "Āgneya" and so forth applied to those [offerings] which are not Āgneya? By figurative description (guṇavāda). What is this figurative description? It is the connection with fire. How so? Because they belong to the same class.

What is this state of being of the same nature? "Prajāpati desired, 'May I create offspring. He fashioned the *ṛc* from his mouth; he delighted in it with fire as its deity, the *gāyatrī* as its meter, the *rathantara* as its *sāman*, the Brāhmaṇa among men, and the goat among animals.
Therefore, these are preeminent, for they were created from the mouth. From the chest...
From his two arms he fashioned the Pañcadaśa-stoma; Indra was emitted as its deity,
the Triṣṭubh as its metre, the Bṛhat as its Sāman, the Rājanya among men, and the horse among animals.

Therefore they are full of vigor, for they were created from vigor. From his two thighs, in the middle, he fashioned the seventeen-fold [stoma]; the Viśvedevas were the presiding deities who took delight in it, the Jagatī was the metre, the Vairūpa the Sāman, the Vaiśya among men, and cattle among animals—this being said.
When one thing of a certain kind is known, another thing of that same kind also comes to mind. Therefore, these words are *arthavādas* (explanatory or commendatory statements). (1.4.13) Bhāṣya.
Bhāṣya.
Now begins the section concerning the fact that words such as *yūpa* (sacrificial post) and others serve the purpose of praising the sacrificer, on account of similarity. Sūtra 25.
It is heard in the scriptures: "The sacrificer is the sacrificial post," "The sun is the sacrificial post," and so forth.
Regarding these, there arises a doubt: are they injunctions of attributes (*guṇavidhi*) or explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)? Because they serve a purpose, they are injunctions of attributes.
[This is not the case], because it is impossible for the sacrificer to accomplish the function of the sacrificial post, or for the sacrificial post to accomplish the function of the sacrificer.
Or [it refers] to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); and because there is no other injunction, it is not an injunction itself, but rather a corroboration for the purpose of praising the injunction.

The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) arises from figurative description (*guṇavāda*). What is the quality (*guṇa*)? It is similarity (*sārūpya*). What is the similarity? It is the state of being half[-buried] and the state of being brilliant. Therefore, such [passages as these] are...
The explanatory passages (arthavādas). (1.4.94) [Sūtra]
The section concerning the fact that words such as "vyatha," "apaśu," and others have the purpose of praising cows and other animals.
Praise. || 26 ||

"It is said in the Śruti: 'Others are indeed non-animals compared to cows and horses; cows, horses, and goats are animals'; 'That which is without the Sāman is no sacrifice'; 'That which is without the Chandomas is no Sattra. In this regard, when there is a doubt as to whether these are injunctions (vidhi) or explanatory passages (arthavāda), the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that they are injunctions because they possess purposeful meaning."

It is stated: if they were injunctions (*vidhi*), then only cows and horses would be sacrificial animals (*paśu*), only the *Sāmavāya* would be a sacrifice (*yajña*), and only that which possesses the *Chandomas* would be a sacrificial session (*sattra*); [there would be no place] for other animals, other sacrifices, [Page 160]...
Otherwise, the origin of the *satra* sacrifices would be purposeless, and another injunction (*vidhi*) would not be possible.
Therefore, this dialogue is for the sake of praise: there is a censure of other animals in order to praise cows and horses;

a censure of those without *sāman*s in order to praise those with *sāman*s; and *acchandomaka* [hymns] are censured in order to praise those containing *chandomas*, just as it is said: "that which is without clarified butter is unfit for food."
That which is soiled is "without clothing"—thus [it is said]. (1.4.15 Śrauta-sūtra)
This concludes, for the most part, the section concerning the designation of creation; [it is] the section concerning abundance (*bhūmādhikaraṇa*).
The Infinite. || 27 ||

In the Bhāṣya it is heard: "He lays down the *sṛṣṭi* [bricks]. Regarding this, there arises a doubt: is this an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) or an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*)? When the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that it is an injunction because it conveys something not previously established (*apūrvatva*), it is replied: if it were an injunction, the meaning would be "he lays down bricks characterized by the *sṛṣṭi* mantra"; however, in that case, [it is not so].

A certain distinction among the bricks is resorted to—namely, that "those of such a form are for the creation, not those of such a form"; in that case, all the mantras containing the word "creation" (sṛṣṭi) would apply [to all bricks].
Consequently, other mantras not connected [to this specific purpose] would become useless. Therefore, it is a restatement (anuvāda).

—Because they are mentioned in the sequence of the *madrāḥ*, their placement is established; the mention of the *sṛṣṭis* is for the purpose of praising their creation. Moreover, if it were an injunction (*vidhi*), there would be figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); [for instance] in the passage "they praise with one," it would have to indicate those which are not *avakāśas*. But surely, "there is figurative indication even in a restatement (*anuvāda*)"? No, there is no fault in figurative indication in the case of a restatement. However, how [could it apply] to those that are not *sṛṣṭis*?

And the word "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) [is used] with respect to the acts of creation—on account of their abundance; for there, many bricks possess the characteristic marks of creation (*sṛṣṭi-liṅga*), while few possess the opposite marks. (9.4.16 Śābarabhāṣya) — those bricks which are found to be employed in the laying down (*upadhāna*) accompanied by the word "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*).
"They are called 'thrills' (hṛṣṭayaḥ)," says Mādhava.
[Page 161] Ru.
Now begins the section concerning the fact that words such as *prāvavat* and others have the sense of *sutyā*.
Because of the inherence of the indicative mark. || 28 ||

Bhāṣya: "He places the breath-like [bricks]," "He places the Śrāvyāni [bricks]"—in these injunctions, there would be meaninglessness for those mantras possessing different characteristics that are being placed as breath-like entities.

Therefore, it is a restatement (anuvāda). Because of the association with a characteristic mark (liṅgasamavāya), a word for one thing is used for another; as in "the umbrella-bearers are going," where all are indicated by a single umbrella-bearer.
And this word "living beings" (prāṇabhṛt) and the word "sixty" do not denote the group of intoxicants while abandoning their own primary meaning.

And when the words "creation" (sṛṣṭi) and "living being" (prāṇabhṛt) are used in a group, both of them are included; just as by the word "umbrella-bearer" (chatrin), used in its primary sense as a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), even one who is not carrying an umbrella is included. (9.4.17)
Bhāṣya:
Now begins the section concerning the determination of doubtful meanings based on the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa).
"In cases of doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence" (JS 1.4.29).
"One anoints the pebbles with clarified butter (*ghṛta*)," so it is heard in the scripture;
regarding this, there is a doubt: are the pebbles to be anointed with any one of the substances—clarified butter, oil, or fat—or rather with clarified butter alone? How does the doubt arise?

The doubt is as follows: In a single sentence, there is an introduction with the general term "with ghee" (*ghṛtena*) and a conclusion with the specific term "clarified butter" (*ājyena*). Since a sentence must be concluded in accordance with its beginning, the question arises: in this case, when the general term is used at the outset to indicate the specific, or when the specific term is used in the conclusion to characterize the general—which of these two, the beginning and the conclusion, is more consistent? This is the doubt.

Thus— in cases of doubt, since there is no contradiction in the initial general statement, no specific [meaning] should be assumed; however, at the conclusion, because a cognition of the general has already arisen, there is a contradiction,
and thus the mention of "clarified butter" (ghṛta) is for the purpose of indication (lakṣaṇā), as in the case of both creation and destruction.
The twenty-sixth [section]: thus, "clarified butter" (ghṛta) and "not-clarified butter" (aghṛta) are both called "clarified butter.
[Page 162] Bhāṣya:
When there is doubt, this being the case, we say: by means of a general statement that requires a specific instance...

The opening of the statement [is general], while the conclusion is by virtue of the specific. Why? Because no general rule has been enjoined, such that there would be a contradiction with the conclusion. How is it not enjoined?
Because among doubtful matters there is an absence of an injunctive word; indeed, no injunctive word exists [here].

Because of the reference to the present tense in the statement, "He places the pebbles smeared with ghee," there is no direct praise of the general class [of substances]; rather, there is an explicit praise of ghee.

The praise of ghee is by means of direct denotation (*śruti*), while the praise of the general class is by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and direct denotation is more authoritative than secondary indication.
It is superior; therefore, there is the injunction regarding clarified butter. Likewise: "He puts on a garment;

this garment, namely that which is made of linen, belongs to all the deities. And similarly: "One should sing while touching this [pillar]; for all beings subsist upon this Audumbarī pillar. (9.4.18 Śrauta Sūtra).
Sūtra:
The determination of those who are established according to their respective capacities.
Or rather, it is so because it is a part of the conceptual construction [of the object]. 30.

Bhāṣya: It is heard in the scripture, "He cuts with the spoon, he cuts with the knife, he cuts with the hand. In this regard, there is a doubt: is everything—both the liquid and the collected meat—to be cut with the spoon, as well as with the knife and the hand, or [is it otherwise]?

"Is there a fixed rule for all substances by their purpose—[namely], with a *sruva* ladle for liquids, with a *khadgī* knife for meats, and with the hand for solid masses?"—thus [it might be asked]. Since no specific distinction is stated, there is no fixed rule.

This being the position reached, we reply: "The determination is by way of purpose; the determination is by way of capability. One should take the portion with a *sruva* ladle as far as one is able; likewise, one should take that of which one is capable.
And thus: for verbal roots expressing their meaning, capacity (*śakti*) is the auxiliary factor;
it is no different from an axe.

[Page 163] Bhāṣya: If this is so, then the arrangement ought to be according to one's capacity. For instance, regarding the injunction, "He offers groats with his joined palms into the fire-vessel"—the *añjali* is the joining of both hands; that must be performed in such a way that it is not opened wide, for in that manner the oblation can be accomplished. Therefore...

Just as, for instance, from the expressions "he eats on a mat" (*kaṭe bhuṅkte*) and "he eats from a bronze vessel" (*kāṃsyapātre bhuṅkte*), it is inferred by implication that he is sitting on the mat and has placed the rice in the bronze vessel. (1.4.19)
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya composed by the venerable Śabara-svāmin. This first chapter is completed.
[Page 164] Second Chapter, Ninth Pāda:
The Section on Whether the Previous [Action] is Expressed by the Verbal Suffix (*ākhyāta-pada*).

"Words denoting actions have the sense of their own inherent nature; from them, the action should be understood, for this is the meaning that is enjoined. (Siddhānta Sūtra 1). Commentary: In the first chapter, the definition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) was established. Therein, injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and traditional texts (*smṛti*) were determined according to their true nature; the injunction of subsidiary qualities (*guṇavidhi*) and names (*nāmadheya*) were examined; and it was stated that the determination of the meaning of doubtful matters is derived from the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) or from the context (*artha*). That must not be forgotten.
Immediately thereafter, the primary and secondary [actions], as well as those that are distinct and non-distinct, will be examined;

this alone is the meaning to be described, and no other, and this indeed is the connection of the chapter. Thus, here the sixfold differentiation of action will be stated—namely, difference of word, repetition, number, quality, context, and name—and what is about to be said is first announced; for by announcing what is being demonstrated, it will be easier to comprehend.

The intellect of the listener is also concentrated; thus, this is called the "characteristic of various actions" (*nānākarmalakṣaṇa*)—this is stated as the primary subject matter of the chapter, while everything else is either introductory (*upodghāta*) or incidental (*prasaktānuprasakta*). In that regard, first this is considered: it was stated in the first chapter that "Dharma is a matter characterized by an injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*). An injunction is a sentence that expresses an action, and the meanings of words reside in the sentence. Therefore, [one must consider] whether [Dharma is expressed] by each individual word...
Is the *dharma* distinct for each word, or is it all one and the same? What, then, is the initial position? That the *dharma* belongs to each individual word.
This being the position, it is said: when the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) arises from one [word], then the other [words] are for its sake.
[Page 165]
[The opponent says: "It will be so; in this way, there will be a much less extensive assumption involving unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and the necessity of inference.
Therefore, the *apūrva* is one.

When it is one, then a doubt arises: from which [words] does it arise—from words denoting action (*bhāva*), or from words denoting substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*)? (What, then, is action? And what are those words denoting action?)

— thus [it is said]. [Examples are] *yajati* (he sacrifices), *dadāti* (he gives), *juhoti* (he offers)—and so forth. Now, one might object: "These are words for sacrifice, giving, and offering; they are not words denoting an action (*bhāva-śabda*). This is not so. These words such as *yāga* (sacrifice) and the rest are indeed words denoting an action, and from them the sense of "one should bring about" (*yaccārtha*) is understood—as in "one should effect" (*bhāvayet*), meaning "one should strive so that something comes into being. Therefore, these are words denoting an action;
whereas from words denoting substances (*dravya*) or qualities (*guṇa*), there arises the cognition of a substance or a quality, but not of an action to be brought about (*bhāvanā*).
Therefore, these are not words denoting positive entities— this is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa). What, then, is the conclusion?— that they apply without distinction.

From this it follows: the meaning is that [words] are words denoting action (*bhāvārtha*); from them, an action should be understood, such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) and so forth. Why? Precisely because they have the sense of bringing something into being (*bhāvārthatva*). Those who say "one should bring something into being" [must conclude], upon connection with the word "desiring heaven," that one should bring heaven into being.

—thus they would say; therefore, from them, an action (*kriyā*) is understood, for the action is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the production (*niṣpatti*) of the fruit. And those [actions], being connected with sacrifice, giving, and oblation, declare the arising of heaven. Why? Because this is the meaning enjoined, namely, that by means of sacrifice and so forth.

"How should one who desires heaven bring about heaven?"—[the answer is] "by means of sacrifice and so forth. And since the result is accomplished by that which is consumed [in the ritual] after having produced the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), and not otherwise, the *apūrva* is therefore understood. Consequently, from whatever word its denotation is expressed, the *apūrva* is cognized through that. Therefore, we maintain that verbal roots (*bhāva-śabda*) are the enjoiners of the *apūrva*.

However, there is no word whatsoever that directly denotes the *apūrva* (the unseen potency). Since something must be brought about by words whose meaning is an action (*bhāvārtha*), and since for one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) something must be the end to be realized—these two requirements are joined like the horse and the chariot in the "burnt-horse" fable. Expressions such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) are expectant, asking: "What? By what means? How? They become free from expectancy through the purpose expressed by the phrase "one who desires heaven. But this is not the case with words denoting substances or qualities. Therefore, [Vedic injunctions] have actions as their primary meaning.
"The words denoting action enjoin the *apūrva*—thus [it is said]. Now, why both?
[Page 166]
It has been indicated [in the Bhāṣya]: "Words denoting action have the sense of bhāva.
Some words denoting action do not have the sense of bhāva—for example, *ru*.
It is said: there exist [sacrifices] such as the Śyena, the Ekacikā, and others.

Some meanings of "being" (*bhāva*) are not words denoting action (*karmaśabda*), such as "the act of being," "existence," or "becoming. What, then, is the example here? It is: "One seeking to harm [an enemy] should sacrifice with the *śyena*," and "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrā*. Is it that one should sacrifice with the *śyena* while seeking to harm, or that one should seek to harm while sacrificing? Likewise, is it that one should [sacrifice] with the *citrā* while desiring cattle, or that one desiring cattle should sacrifice?

— this being the case, in this section there will be an inquiry as to whether [the terms] are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or names (*nāmadheya*). Likewise, regarding the statement, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," [it must be considered] whether the one desiring heaven [should sacrifice] by means of those two— the Darśa (new moon) and the Pūrṇamāsa (full moon)— which are times.

Furthermore, [in such cases as] "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," "by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices," "not by means of the Śyena," and "by means of the Citrā"—these are not words denoting an action (bhāvavacana); nor is there any connection between these and the person seeking a result, because they possess different case-endings. Therefore, words denoting substances and qualities are not enjoiners of the apūrva. (Siddhānta)

If it is argued that the meaning of all words is "being" (bhāva): (Objection) If you view it thus—that because they are words denoting non-existence (*abhāva*), words for substances (*dravya*) and qualities (*guṇa*) do not enjoin the *apūrva*—then the meaning of all [words] is "being. [For instance, in the sentence] "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices," the word "should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) establishes the connection between these two [the agent and the means].

And likewise in the cases of "one practicing sorcery with the Śyena" and "one desiring cattle [should sacrifice] with the Citrā," these too are expressions of an action because they possess expectancy. Among all expressions of an action, there is no reason for a definitive distinction that only words denoting the ritual act (*karman*) are the enjoiners of the *apūrva*, and not words denoting substances or qualities. (0)

Sva. Those [words] whose form is perceived when they arise in their own application are *nāmans*; therefore, there is no further expectation for them from anything else, because they are already established in their own application. (3)
(Ācārya-nirṇaya 1) ||
Bhāṣya:
Of those words which, upon being uttered and produced, are employed in their own respective meanings—
[Page 167]

The meaning is that it is observed [in experience] that what has once arisen persists for a period of time, rather than perishing immediately upon arising like an action (*kriyā*); such is the meaning of those words, namely, those words denoting substances and qualities. (Although it should have been stated as "those words denoting substances and qualities," it is formulated in the Sūtra as "those names"; therefore, "names" refers to these.)
It is a synonymous term. How is this known? Because nominal case-endings are pronounced for these. Which are they? *vṛkṣaḥ*, *vṛkṣau*, *vṛkṣāḥ*;
*śukaḥ*, *śukau*, *śukāḥ*—and so forth. Therefore, it has been correctly indicated. Since this...

The object is not momentary; therefore, "there is no further expectation for them"—that is, there is no primary expectation—and thus their production need not be performed, because they are "already existent," meaning they exist at the time of their own employment during their respective application. (Ābhāsa-nirṇaya 1)
Those words for which no usage is found in their own derived meaning are called *ākhyātāni* (verbs); therefore, the action should be understood from them, because usage depends upon them.

[The Bhāṣya says: "But those [words] which, when uttered, have no application to an external object—that is to say, at the time of their usage, no object is perceived—those are called *ākhyāta*s. Thus, he teaches that *bhāva*-words are synonyms (*paryāya-śabda*) for *ākhyāta*s. How is it that *bhāva*-words are synonyms? Because their case-endings (*vibhakti*) are said to be "attractive" (*āyātika*). Which are they? *pacati*, *pacataḥ*, *pacanti*.

Such are these [examples]. Therefore, the meaning of the accomplished (*bhūta*) should be understood as preceding those [words denoting what is to be accomplished]; for words denoting what is to be accomplished (*bhavya*) are uttered together with words denoting the accomplished. When that which is accomplished serves the purpose of that which is to be accomplished, its purpose is seen: the production of that which is to be accomplished—which possesses a purpose—is meaningful, and that production is brought about by the accomplished; thus, the purpose is perceived.
On the other hand, when that which is to be accomplished serves the purpose of the accomplished, nothing is seen, and an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) result must be postulated.

Therefore, sacrifice is not for the sake of the substance. Furthermore, "because the performance is dependent": the performance of these [subsidiaries] is dependent upon the person; an efficient force (*bhāvanā*) connected with the person is expressed, for it says to the person: "one should bring about [the result]."
Thus, by this [injunction], "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," the person is also understood;
[on page 168, Bhāṣya:
the sacrifice, as well as the relationship, are understood; and in the phrase "one desiring heaven [should have] wealth," the substance is understood.
And it is the person [who is denoted], not the relationship. Now, it might be argued: "This is what is meant:

the word 'one should sacrifice' (yajeta) will express the relationship between the seeker of the result and the substance—namely, that one should effect the result by means of the substance; therefore, the production of the result by means of the substance would be understood, as would the expectancy."

It is true that [the connection] is understood: by means of the sentence, "one should effect [the result] through a substance," whereas by means of direct statement (*śruti*), "one should effect [it] through sacrifice. However, when the connection with the sacrifice is enjoined—namely, "one should effect [it] through sacrifice"—then at that time there is no connection with the substance, as in "one should effect [it] through a substance. Furthermore, when the connection with the substance is being enjoined, there can be no connection with the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*); for while it is possible for one to be restated (*anūdyatām*), injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement cannot occur simultaneously.

Therefore, there is a contradiction between the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and the syntactical connection (*vākya*); and when there is a contradiction, the direct statement is more authoritative. Consequently, the substance is not connected with the person desiring the result; in that case, it would be illogical to claim that the substance—since its connection with the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) is absent—will serve the purpose of attaining heaven. This is the reason for the definitive conclusion: that verbal roots (*bhāva-śabda*) are the enjoiners of the unseen potency (*apūrva*), and not words denoting substances or qualities (*dravya-guṇa-śabda*). When [this is the case],...

If [the text] says, "one should perform by means of sacrifice," then it is a direct statement regarding the sacrifice; as for the words "by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyām*), it is through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇayā*) that the sacrifice is enjoined for both the New Moon and the Full Moon. (Ābhāsa-nirṇaya 2) (2.1.1).
[The section on] existence preceded by the absence of pain and pride.
But how is it understood that this *apūrva* exists? It is stated:
"The injunction, moreover, is the commencement [of action]. (JS 2.1.5)

The Bhāṣya says: "By the word 'codanā' (injunction), we mean the *apūrva* (the unseen potency). Furthermore, the *apūrva* exists because an undertaking is enjoined—namely, 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice. For otherwise, the injunction would be purposeless, since the sacrifice is perishable; if the sacrifice were to perish without producing something else, then both the person and the performance [would be fruitless]. (Kāśikā Saṃkara edition)
[Page 169] Bhāṣya:
If the cause were to perish, the fruit would not exist; therefore, it produces [the fruit].
"But if, on the other hand, it is postulated that the cause itself does not perish due to the force of the statement regarding the fruit..."
This is not possible; for we do not perceive any form of action other than this:

that which causes its substratum to reach another location is called "action. It does not inhere in the self, because the self is omnipresent; if it were present everywhere, its effects would be perceived everywhere.

It is the inferential mark (*liṅga*), and not that very [mark] itself, for the coming from another place; for nothing contradictory to its coming is observed when it is absent. It is understood that the substance which was inherent in it has perished, and because of that, it too has perished—even though the substratum remains unperished.

If it is argued [that the self exists], we say no, because of the perception of ashes. If it is argued that [the self] exists even when the ashes are present, we say no, because [the self] is not perceived even when [the body] is present. If it is argued that the performance of an action is the inferential mark [of the self], then, since such a thing is not observed, an alternative must be stated; if it is conjectured that it will be one of the others, such as cleanliness (*sauca*) and so forth, then it is merely a fabrication.

"When something exists, something else comes to be"—thus [it is said]. "In that case, would something unprecedented be produced? If so, there is a reason for assuming a non-specific [result], but not for assuming a specific one. If it is argued that "the action will exist without a substrate," that too is exactly the same.

It will not reach another location by means of postulating a different intrinsic nature; it remains exactly as it was. Therefore, the sacrifice is momentary (bhaṅgin), and because of its momentariness, there exists the apūrva.

What is the purpose of this inquiry? If words denoting substances and qualities also enjoin the *apūrva*, then in the event of the loss of a substance or a quality, no substitute should be taken up, as in the case of the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). However, if it is according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), then having substituted another substance or quality, [the rite should proceed].
The ritual application must be performed— thus [ends the section]. (2.1.2 Sūtra).
The section concerning the distinction between the subordinate and principal status of ritual actions.
These are twofold, being either subordinate or predominant qualities.

Commentary: This has been understood—that words denoting action (bhāvaśabda) are expressive of the act—yet words denoting action are of many kinds: such as "he sacrifices" (yajati), "he offers" (juhoti), "he gives" (dadāti); and likewise of these same kinds are "he milks" (dogdhi), "he grinds" (pinaṣṭi), "he liquefies" (vilāpayati), and so forth.

Regarding these, there is a doubt: are all of them enjoiners of primary actions (*pradhāna-karman*), or are some enjoiners of preparatory actions (*saṃskāra-karman*)? Since there is no difference in their being verbal roots (*bhāvārtha*), it follows that all are denoters of primary actions; to this we reply: they ought to be divided into two classes.

They are of two kinds: some denote principal actions (*pradhānakarman*) and some denote preparatory actions (*saṃskārakarman*); even so, they are meaningful, and since they are meaningful, it is not possible to postulate an *apūrva* from all of them. Therefore, not all [actions] are principal actions.
These are the expressive words.
Pain is the primary characteristic of the Pradhāna.
Those [actions] by which a substance is not intended to be produced are primary, because the substance is subordinate to them. || 7 ||
Bhāṣya: "This being the case, it is more reasonable to assume a subtler unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), for we perceive no decisive reason as to why [the result] should be prior rather than not.
To this it is replied: substances are not intended to be consecrated or produced by the *bhāva* (action) and the *karman* (object);
rather, those [actions] are primary (i.e., they denote the principal action), while the substance..."
Because it is subordinate; for a substance is subordinate because it is that which is most desired for the accomplishment of the action.
Distress is characterized by qualities and actions.
But where a substance is intended to be acted upon, there a quality should be understood [as subordinate], because that substance is the primary element. || 8 ||

But for those [actions] by which a substance is intended to be prepared, there a quality would be understood as the object; why? Because that [action] has the substance as its primary purpose. In direct perception, substances are not intended to be prepared by such [verbs] as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*); therefore, these are denoters of principal actions (*pradhānakarman*), since the substance is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). However, by such [verbs] as "he grinds" (*pinasti*), a substance is consecrated (*saṃskriyate*); therefore, these...
[Page 171] Bhāṣya: Words expressing qualities and actions; this alone is the reason for the definitive conclusion (*vinigamanā*). As for the purpose:

in the former view, even in a *caru* made of *preyaṅgu* grain, the grains would have to be produced for the sake of threshing; in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), they need not be produced. (2.1.3).
The section concerning the subordinate status of sweeping and other such acts.
But [the action] would be a mere ritual act (*karma*) because it does not result in completion, like the *prayāja* offerings.

(Pūrvapakṣa 1) The scripture declares: "He cleanses the *ukhā*, he cleanses the fire, he cleanses the enclosing sticks, and he carries fire around the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the carrying of fire around [the cake]...?

Is the act of sweeping a primary action (*pradhānakarma*) or a subordinate action (*guṇakarma*)? What, then, is the prima facie view? To this it is replied: An action of such a kind, which by itself is insufficient for a visible purpose, we call a mere duty (*dharmamātra*); in that case, it possesses the character of a primary action.

It may be so. Why? This is already established by the very statement of the definition itself: that which does not possess this definition is a non-Brāhmaṇa;

However, the author of the *Vṛtti*, for the benefit of his students, has elaborated upon it—[including] passages rich in the particle *iti*, those recorded as "thus he said," the nature of narratives (*ākhyāyikā*), and logical reasons (such as: "He offers with rain; therefore it is produced").

Etymological derivation (*nirvacanaṃ*): "That [curd] is the curd-nature of *dadhi*"; censure (*nindā*): "His fires are indeed suspended"; praise (*praśaṃsā*): "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity"; doubt (*saṃśayaḥ*): "Should it be offered in the *gārhapatya* fire, or should it not be offered?"; injunction (*vidhiḥ*): "The *udumbara* post is as high as the sacrificer"; the action of another (*parakṛtiḥ*): "He cooks beans for himself"; ancient history (*purākalpaḥ*): "In former times, they used to come together with firebrands."
The assumption of restriction (*vyavadhāraṇakalpanā*)—as in "as many dogs as one might receive"—[is one of the ten types of injunctions].

[As it is said: "Cause, etymological derivation, censure, praise, doubt, injunction, the action of another, ancient history, the assumption of restriction, and comparison—these ten are the injunctions belonging to the Brāhmaṇa.

—some *mantras* also abound in the particle *iti*, such as "Thus, indeed, is my mind," which is recorded as having been spoken; and there is the form of a narrative (*ākhyāyikā*), such as "Ugra was Bhujyu," where "this is your desire" serves as the reason; "therefore the waters are standing" is a definition (*nirvacana*), and "in vain... is a censure (*nindā*).

128. Now, what is the definition of *sāman*? A particular kind of chanting is called *sāman*. Now, what is the definition of the *yajus*?—it is asked. Now, what is that which is called *nigada*—is it *yajus* formulas, or is it something other than *yajus*? [The answer is: "Or rather, the *nigada* should be a fourth [category], because of its specific characteristic (*dharmaviśeṣa*).
(Pūrvapakṣa) [Bhāṣya]: The *nigadas* are not *yajus* formulas. Why? Because of their specific characteristic: "One recites the *ṛc* loudly... (*uccaiḥ ṛcā*).

"It is performed: loudly with the Sāman, in a whisper with the Yajus, and loudly with the Nigada"—this is a specific rule of dharma; therein, "loudly with the Nigada" is restated [as a known fact], provided that the nature of the Yajus as Nigada consists in its being for the purpose of addressing others.

It would remain so, and its loudness would not be perceived as a property of the *dharma*; yet it is indeed perceived. Therefore, the fourth class of sounds born from speech is called *nigada*. (Pūrvapakṣa)
Furthermore, there are designations [38] (Yukti).
Commentary: There is also a designation: "The *yajus* verses exist, but they are not *nigadas*; the *nigadas*..."
They proceed, but not the vehicles—therefore, for this reason also, there is a difference of state. (Yukti)
Sūtra: Or rather, they are *yajus* formulas, because they possess that form.
(Siddhānta) Commentary: Or indeed, *nigadas* are simply *yajus* formulas. Why? Because they possess that form; for they have that very same nature.
The form [of the Yajus] consists in its recitation as a continuous prose (praśiṣṭapāṭha) and its distinctness from the characteristics of Ṛk and Sāman.
From the statement in the Bhāṣya: "A specific dharma [arises] from speech. (Upasaṃhāra 41)

“Because of the statement,” that is, because of the capacity for communication; for indeed, some *yajus* formulas possess the capacity to communicate to other persons. (Upa. Also because of the purpose. Therefore, the specific property [of loudness] is meaningful.
And those *yajus* which are recited loudly (*udairacāryante*) are *nigadas*. Why? Because of the word "ni" (*ni-śabda*).
It is a term that expresses excellence (*prakarṣa*), just as when something is intensely red, it is said to be "completely red" (*nitarāṃ raktaṃ*).

The root *gad* signifies speaking, specifically the act of recitation. Indeed, this very excellence consists in being characterized by loudness. [Objection: But is not the quality of the *yajus* formulas, namely their being whispered (*upāṃśutva*), based on a direct scriptural injunction (*vācanika*)? [Reply: No.
We reply: A quality (*guṇa*) is that which serves as an aid to those performing their own respective functions.

Now, loudness (*uccais-tva*) does not serve as an aid to the *yajus* mantras intended for addressing others; rather, it causes an obstruction to the performance of their own specific function. Therefore, loudness is a quality for the purpose of addressing other persons. However, the statement [regarding loudness] will have another purpose, namely, for those other [mantras].
The commentary states:
Yajus formulas are not for the purpose of addressing others; therefore, it prescribes that they should be recited in a low voice (*upāṃśutva*).

Just as one might say, "From here, O Brahmin, let the [ordinary] guests be fed; from there, the wandering mendicants"—so too, by this specific quality, those very same *yajus* formulas are designated as *nigadas*. (Upasaṃhāra)

The Section on the Definition of Unity of Statement (Ekavākyatva).
Now, [the principle of] syntactic unity: a single sentence is that which, if divided, would result in a state of expectancy. 46.
Bhāṣya:

Now, among the Yajus formulas recited in succession, how is it to be understood that "this much is one Yajus"? To the extent of the collection of words by which [an action] is intended, that much collection of words is one Yajus. And by how much is it intended? By as much as the assistance to the ritual action is manifested.
Because it must be expressed as such, it is called a "sentence" (*vākya*); by that it is stated:
"Now, because of its unity, there is one sentence"—for this reason, there is the state of being a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*).

It exists; therefore, a collection of words that has a single meaning is a sentence, provided that when divided, the word remains expectant (sākāṅkṣa). What is the example? "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ... [etc.]. "But surely each word here has a single meaning. True, but not so upon its division.

[Objection: "The meaning is accompanied by a form (*sākāra*). [Reply: That unity is not tenable, because objects are manifold and because a collection of words has a distinct meaning for each. This has already been stated (Sūtras 1.1.24–25).
If it is argued that the sentence-meaning is either a distinction (*bheda*) or a relation (*saṃsarga*):"

Even so, there would not be unity of purpose, because in a multi-word [utterance] there is a multiplicity of individual words, distinctions, and relations. It is established by virtue of having a single purpose; for instance, in the case of "devasya tvā"—this entire collection of words expresses the specific act of pouring out (nirvāpa), and that is a sentence. Now, one might object: "But here [in the mantra], 'devasya tvā savituḥ prasave'..."

"Nirvapāma" is one sentence; "aśvibhyāṃ bāhubhyāṃ nirvapāmi" is another; thus there are many sentences. If "nirvapāma" were to be supplied as an *anuṣaṅga* (elliptical extension), then there would be many sentences; however, such an *anuṣaṅga* does not occur.
And if "nirvapāmi" were a subordinate element, then it would have to be repeated for each primary object (*pratipradhānam*). But that is not the case.

The recitation of the mantras beginning with "devasya tvā" is uttered for the sake of the purpose [of the act] of offering (nirvāpa); for if the means were predominant, the statement would have an invisible (adṛṣṭa) purpose. But when the offering is the primary factor, there is a visible purpose: the manifestation of the offering itself. That [offering] is then expressed as qualified by all its qualifiers; therefore—
There is no contradiction. And as to how one word is qualified by another, that has been stated [in the Sūtra] "tadbhūtānām" (1.1.25); therefore, it is a single sentence.

Now, for what purpose is both stated— namely, "because of oneness" and "because there is expectancy regarding the division"? It is said that while something may have a single meaning, it is not [the case here].
It is expectant of division, as in "May Bhaga divide for you two;

may Aryaman divide for you two"—thus, all [these words] denote a single act of division. [Objection: But surely the division qualified by Bhaga is one thing, while the division qualified by Aryaman is another. [Reply: No—this is said;
for in some recensions, the reading is "Pūṣan" instead.
Commentary:

The purpose of this [mantra] is for the general act of separation (*vibhāga*), not for a specific one; for it is observed to apply to the general case, not to the specific, and it does not explicitly refer to separation. Therefore, this sentence is optionally applied to the act of separation. Likewise: "A pleasant seat for thee... [is used].

"I prepare [the seat] with a stream of clarified butter; I fashion it so that it is easy to mount. Sit upon this nectar, O wise one, and take your stand—thou who art the essence of oblations. Thus, when there is a purposeful division, two functions are performed: the preparation of the seat and the establishment of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

Therefore, since the sentences are distinct, the former is enjoined for the preparation of the seat, and the latter for the establishment of the sacrificial cake; thus, our own position is correctly established, and there is no valid objection to the Sūtra. (2.1.14)
The Bhāṣya on the Topic of the Division of Sentences (Vākyabheda).
In the case of identical [words], there would be a split in the sentence. || 47 ||

"Īṣe tvā, jarje svā"—thus [it is said], as well as "May life be perfected through sacrifice; may breath be perfected through sacrifice. Here a doubt arises: in such cases, are there separate sentences or one single sentence? We say: it is one, because when "Īṣe tvā" has been uttered...

No visible purpose is seen [in this case], and likewise in the phrase "īṣe tvā," there is an unseen result (adṛṣṭa) due to the conventional force of the words. It is logical to postulate a single unseen result for both; thus, there will be a lesser assumption of an unseen inference. Therefore, it is a single sentence. This being the position reached, we reply: "In the case of equals, there would be a division of sentences. When they are equal—meaning when they have no mutual expectancy—the sentence is divided. By the words "īṣe tvā," one purpose is accomplished, and by "ūrje... [another].
By the word "tvā," another [meaning] is indicated. [Objection: But was it not just stated that no visible purpose is seen here?
[Response: Even if it is not perceived through means of knowledge such as direct perception, it is nevertheless understood through scripture;
for [the Vedic injunction says], "With *īṣe* thee—I cut," and "With *ūrje* thee—I cut."

Likewise, in the passage "May life be perfected by the sacrifice; may breath be perfected by the sacrifice," there is a perfection of breath distinct from the perfection of life. Now, it might be argued that only the general category is intended, and that it does not admit of distinction because of the difference in qualifiers—just as in the case of "I offer the oblation to Agni," where the act of offering is one, yet its specific instances are "at the impulse of Savitṛ" and "by the arms of the Aśvins. [Page 190] Bhāṣya.

"Just as in the case of [the mantra] 'With the hands of Pūṣan,' no division of the pouring-out (nirvāpa) is desired on account of the divisions of those [mantras], so too here, 'kḷpti' is a single meaning; it will not become divided by these specific qualifiers such as Āyu and the rest. It is replied: Here, "He causes [the sacrificer] to recite the kḷptis" refers to many [recitations].

Various *klṛptis* (preparations) are heard in the texts, and they must be explained. Among them, one *āyuḥ-klṛpti* is [expressed by] "May life be prepared by the sacrifice"—this person is able to say this; "May breath be prepared by the sacrifice"—this person [says] another *prāṇa-klṛpti*. But thus all these are expressions of specific *klṛptis*, and that is a visible purpose. Therefore, because there are multiple meanings, there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) even in that case. [Objection: "But surely there is unity due to the general expression, as in the case of the distribution (*vibhāga*). [Reply: This is not so.

In this case, the commonality [of the word *kalpate*] does not have a visible purpose in the distribution [of the mantras]. Furthermore, it is prescribed that "he causes [the sacrificer] to recite the *kṛpti*-mantras," and the phrase "May life prosper through the sacrifice" is directly perceived as a designation for the prosperity of life; likewise, there is [prosperity] for the vital breath from the phrase "May the vital breath prosper through the sacrifice."
Therefore, there is a split of the sentence. (2.1.15)
The Section on Secondary Limbs (Anumaṅgādhikaraṇa).
Sūtra 48: Or rather, there is an ellipsis (anuṣaṅga) [of the verb] to complete the sentence, because it applies equally to all.

Bhāṣya: Regarding the passage, "O Agni, that body of yours which dwells in the earth, most excellent, dwelling in the depths; that word has struck away the darkness of the waters; that word has struck away the darkness, O Agni. That body of yours which dwells in the mid-region; that body of yours which dwells in the sky"—here there is a doubt: Is the phrase "that body, most excellent" to be supplied (*anuṣaktavya*) to all [the subsequent clauses], or should a worldly (non-Vedic) syntactical supplement (*vākyaśeṣa*) be composed? What is the prima facie view? The phrase "that body, most excellent" is not a syntactical supplement to "O Agni, that body of yours which dwells in the mid-region," nor is it employed as something following after the verb *as* (to be). This being the position, we reply: there is an *anuṣaṅga* (supplying of the ellipsis).

The completion of the sentence would be "tanūrvaṣiṣṭhā," just as it follows immediately after "yā te agne 'yyāśayā," so too it follows after "yā te agne rajāśayā" and "yā te agne harāśayā. If it is argued that [the word] "irāśayā" is separated [from the preceding], that is not so;
for there is no separation of the aggregate, as the aggregate "rajāśayā" is itself uninterrupted.
[Page 191]

Since the remainder of the sentence cannot be connected with the aggregate as a whole, it must be connected with the individual members of that aggregate; and when there is a connection with each member, no distinction is perceived [between them]. Therefore, the ellipsis is to be supplied everywhere.

Moreover, a sentence-remainder (*vākyaśeṣa*) is that which is heard either after or before something expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*), provided it is capable of fulfilling that expectation. But what is the extent of "proximity" (*sannidhi*)? It is said: it is as far as both [the expectant word and the remainder] are able to take into account [one another]. And what is this [extent]? It is immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) or separation by a related word (*saṃbandhipadavyavāya*). For within that range, both are able to take each other into account; for when there is separation by a related word, the prior mental impression (*pūrvasaṃskāra*) does not disappear precisely because of that relationship. Even where there is separation by another expectant word, there too a connection exists, since both [words] are expectant.

For it must be stated that the purpose (kārya) is indeed to be expressed; the subsequent [word] requires the preceding one, and if one were not so required, it would be a careless reading. And it is possible for it to be required; therefore, just as this [word] is in proximity to one, so too is it to the other, because there is no intervention by words unrelated to both. Since both have a mutual expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), this much alone is the cause for the connection with the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa), and not mere immediate sequence (ānantarya); for even when there is an interval, a connection occurs provided there is no intervention. Therefore, there is *anuṣaṅga* (syntactic ellipsis).

Now, how should it be? Where, in the proximity of [mantras] that are already complete in themselves, another mantra capable of fulfilling them is heard—such as, "May the Lord of Thought purify you; may the Lord of Speech purify you; may the divine Savitṛ purify you with a flawless filter, with the rays of the Vasu Sūrya"—for in this case, those mantras ending in "may he purify" are already complete and do not require further supplementation.

Some say: "Will it not require the phrase 'without flaw' (*achidreṇa*)? It is true that it requires it; yet, even though it requires it, it would require only one of them. By means of one alone, this [requirement] becomes satisfied—because once it has been satisfied by one, it will not require the others. It requires them because of their lack of purpose; and being connected with one, it is not without purpose.

It exists; therefore, it does not require the other two—and likewise, because the other two are complete in themselves, they do not require it. Now, one might object: "In this supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), no distinction is perceived as to which [of the three] it requires even one, such that we could say by which it is rendered independent of further expectation (*nirākāṅkṣīkriyate*) and by which it is not. Therefore, since no distinction is understood, it must be connected with all of them. No, it is not so. It is connected only with that with which we perceive its direct sequence (*pratyakṣānantarya*).

"It is understood that 'it is combined'—this is the specific distinction; therefore, it is combined with that which immediately precedes it. Thus, there is no universal application (anuṣaṅga) everywhere. To this, he replies: "This is not so."

We perceive the immediate sequence of this [mantra] with the word *punātu* (may he purify); and we perceive the sequence of the word *punātu* itself with [the mantras] beginning with *citpatistvā*. Furthermore, this single word *punātu* is repeated again and again; from this we understand that wherever the word *punātu* is employed, the phrase *achidreṇa* (with the unbroken) must also be employed there, because they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with it. This being the case, the mantras beginning with *citpatistvā* are incomplete (*sākāṅkṣāḥ*) without the word *punātu*, and thus they require that word *punātu*, and that word *punātu* requires the phrase *achidreṇa*.

It is distinguished; therefore, by that word *punaḥ* together with its *anuṣaṅga*, all [sentences] must necessarily be rendered free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣīkartavya*). Consequently, the completion of the sentence (*vākyaparisamāpti*) is attached as follows: "In all cases, however, there are simultaneous applications. (2.1.16).

Because of the intervention [of other elements], it should not be connected [to what precedes]. || 48 ||

"May your desirable [portion] go with the wind; may your limbs be united with the sacrificial objects; may the lord of the sacrifice be united with his blessing"—thus [it is said]. Because "may your desirable [portion] go with the wind" is separated by the plural form "may your limbs be united with the sacrificial objects," the phrase "may the lord of the sacrifice be united with his blessing" does not connect [to the former]. Since the remainder, "goes," is separated by one [phrase] that has a syntactic expectancy, it [connects] from there.

The word *saṃyajatraiḥ*, being in the plural, does not connect with the preceding [word] *aṅgāni* because it is separated by [the intervening word]; therefore, it does not connect with what follows. For in that case, a distinction is understood—namely, that [the preceding word] is separated by one [intervening word].
When such a distinction is understood, the presence of a syntactical supplement (*vākyaśeṣa*) there is not appropriate.
Therefore, for the plural-ending [word] and for the subsequent [word] separated from it, there is a worldly syntactical supplement.
It must be performed—thus [it is concluded]. (2.1.17)
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya composed by the venerable Śabarasvāmin. This was the introductory quarter.

The section concerning the distinction of apūrvas based on defects:
"There is a difference of action when there is a different word, because of the connection with a specific [auxiliary] factor. (Sūtra 1)

There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, concerning which it is heard in scripture: "One should sacrifice with Soma," "He offers the sacrificial fees," and "He gives gold to the Ātreya. Do these acts—sacrificing, giving, and offering—perform their function by acting in combination, or rather by acting separately?

There is a doubt: are those who accomplish [a rite] seen to accomplish it by acting together, or even by acting separately? First, regarding acting together: three pressing-stones are seen holding a single bowl; however, pegs on a door-lintel act even separately, for in each individual one, a loop can be suspended. Therefore, a doubt arises: do the acts of sacrificing, giving, and offering oblations accomplish their purpose by acting together or by acting separately? What, then, is the prima facie view? That they act together. Why? Because it is more reasonable to assume a single auxiliary function for things whose purpose is unseen (transcendental). How so?
An object that has not been seen or heard of is understood to be non-existent;
since it does not exist, if it is seen or heard of, there is no contradiction.

If [the alternatives] were contradictory, then [a third] would have to be postulated; by that, the object would come to possess [that specific] meaning. If no distinction [between them] were perceived, then not even one [of the two] would be postulated.

And a distinction is indeed understood—that from many [actions] there arises one *apūrva*—therefore, it is the aggregate (*samudāya*) that is intended to be performed. Consequently, when a visible result is being postulated, since the individual parts possess purposefulness with respect to the aggregate, a single *apūrva* will be postulated as arising from the aggregate. Nor is the aggregate non-verbal, for the aggregate is expressed by the very words denoting its constituent parts.

Therefore, the aggregate is what is intended to be performed. Alternatively, the earlier portion of the word "yajeta" (he should sacrifice) is stated here; its recitation in sequence is as follows: "He gives gold to the Ātreya," and "He offers the Dākṣiṇā oblations."
The Bhāṣya says:

it expresses the meaning of "yajati" (he sacrifices), while the latter part [of the word *bhāvayet*] means "one should bring about"; likewise, in the case of "dadāti" (he gives), the former part expresses the meaning of "giving," while the latter part reiterates that very same [act as something to be brought about]; similarly, in the case of "juhoti" (he offers oblations), the former part expresses the meaning of "offering oblations," while the latter part reiterates that very same [act]. Thus, within a single efficient force (*bhāvanā*), the three—sacrificing and so forth—are the means.
These are prescribed by direct scriptural statement (śruti). Therefore, it is understood that the prior productive operation (bhāvanā) is qualified by these gifts and oblations;

hence it is said: "Together they accomplish a single transcendental result (apūrva). Alternatively, the act of giving enjoined by the word *yajati* is restated by the compound term *dānahoma* for the purpose of connecting it with an accessory; therefore, the conclusion reached is that there is a single *apūrva*.

This being the case, we reply: there is a distinction of the *apūrva* for each word—namely, "In the case of a different word, there is a difference of action, because of the connection with a specific [suffix]. By the word *yajeta*, the duty to perform the sacrifice alone is expressed, and not that which is denoted by the word *juhoti* or the word *dadāti*, because they are different words; for it is through their status as parts of the injunctive sentence (*prayogavākya*) that the whole [action] is understood.

The connection with existence is understood; by direct statement (*śruti*), it is understood for the constituent part [the sacrifice], as in "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*). Even though giving and offering (*dāna-homa*) are proximate, it is by direct statement that the connection with existence is understood for the sacrifice alone, not for giving and offering; moreover, direct statement is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*). Therefore, the aggregate is not directly expressed by words, for it is only conceived through syntactical unity by means of the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*).

Having extracted [the root], one should determine it; and *dadāti* is a different word from *yajati*. In this regard, although the subsequent portion, which expresses the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), is common to all [roots], nevertheless, for each [root] the preceding portion is distinct, and by that [distinction], the aggregate is a different word from another aggregate.
Thus, a different meaning is clearly established: "one should give" (i.e., one should accomplish [the result] by means of giving).

It is understood that giving alone is the instrument of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), and it does not require sacrifice (*yāga*) or oblation (*homa*) as auxiliaries. Likewise, the word "he offers" (*juhoti*) expresses a productive operation for which the oblation is the means, and it does not require giving or sacrifice. This much is understood from the verbal expression: that [the result] is accomplished by giving alone, and that it is also accomplished by the oblation alone; however, the cognition that "[it is] accomplished by giving alone" is not thereby set aside.

For the root *dadāti* (to give), being connected with its own set of causal factors (*kāraka*), does not require the sacrifice (*yāga*) or the oblation (*homa*) as its subordinate element (*anubandha*). Therefore, the sentences are distinct; there is a difference of the unseen potency (*apūrva*) for each word.

138 Bhāṣya: Thus [it is said]. Nor can the word *dāna* (giving) be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of *yajati* (sacrificing) and *juhoti* (offering), because that would entail the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) of both sacrifice and offering. Nor can giving be a restatement of the other two, because the root *dadāti* has the purpose of transferring ownership to another, whereas the other two have the purpose of relinquishment (*tyāga*). The practical application (*prayojana*) is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the transcendental result (*apūrva*) arises from the aggregate; but according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), since the sacrifice possesses the fruit, the other two are subordinate (*guṇabhāva*). Bhāṣya: Regarding the passage beginning with "He offers the *samidh* oblation" and "He offers the *tanūnapāt* oblation," and so forth—the word *yajati* ("he offers") is repeated five times. Does this enjoin a single *apūrva* (transcendental result), or is there a distinction of *apūrva*s for each repetition? Since a difference in ritual action (*karmabheda*) was stated [in the previous section] when there is a different word, whereas here the very same word is uttered again and again, therefore, there is only one *apūrva* here. [Objection: But surely, if it does not enjoin another *apūrva*, it becomes purposeless.
[Reply: It is true that it would be purposeless; however—

Furthermore, even when repeated many times, a word does not come to have a different meaning; what is understood at the first utterance is exactly what is understood at the hundredth. Therefore, the root *yajati* (to sacrifice), when repeated five times, enjoins a single apūrva (transcendental result). Nor will this repetition be purposeless.
"Tanūnapāt shall perform [the rite] with the Āghāra-offering; therefore, there is a single apūrva (unseen potency).

This being the prima facie view, we reply: "The repeated mention of the same [deity] would be for that very purpose," meaning it would effect a distinction between ritual acts. For when only that much is being enjoined, in some particular case...
Furthermore, the repetition would be purposeless. [Objection: But was it not said that [the sentence] cannot enjoin another meaning?
[Reply: It is answered: even "He offers the *samidhs*" (*samidho yajati*) is merely a restatement of what is already known;

for the sacrifice itself is already established by the injunction "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ yajeta*). In that context, [it is the deity that remains to be enjoined].

It is not possible to prescribe [this], for the deity is established there by direct Vedic statement (śruti), whereas this [other deity] is established through syntactical connection (vākya) or context (prakaraṇa); a choice between these two is not logical. This very connection of the deity with the sacrifice is the remainder [of the injunction]: "He sacrifices to Iḍā," "He sacrifices to Barhis," and "He sacrifices with the utterance of Svāhā."

[Bhāṣya: Being enjoined, it would be purposeless if the sacrifice were not performed, for it could not be carried out; however, when it is performed, it can be accomplished. Therefore, the sacrifice is to be repeated, and with each repetition, there is a distinct unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*). That which is performed in connection with the *samit* is not the same as that performed in connection with the *tanūnapāt*, because the two are different; hence, there is no modification (*vikalpa*). This is the purpose.
In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there is a single performance; in the final conclusion (siddhānta), however, there is repeated performance.
