Sūtra: But the specific procedure belongs to the Full Moon sacrifice, because its form is not mentioned [in connection with the New Moon].

(Si0) Bhāṣya: For they recite thus: "That which is the cake on eight potsherds for Agni, offered at the New Moon and the Full Moon—those two, Agni and Soma, said: 'Of the clarified butter alone... [they spoke].

"One should sacrifice in a low voice on the full moon day"—thus they offered this cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Soma at the full moon; curd for Indra at the new moon, and milk for Indra at the new moon. Likewise: "He pours the libation, he sacrifices the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), he cuts off the portion for the Viṣṭakṛt, he sacrifices the Patnīsaṃyājas, and he offers the Samiṣṭayajus. And likewise: "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the full moon day;
he who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the new moon day. In this regard, there is a doubt: do all these [constitute the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice]?

Are they all equally primary? Or rather, are the offerings such as the Āgneya and others the primary acts enjoined, while the Āghāra and other rites are auxiliary acts that provide indirect assistance (*ārādupakāraka*)? Likewise, do the two phrases "he who, knowing thus... merely refer back to the previously mentioned rites, or [is it otherwise]?

"Thus, one who knows this sacrifices on the full moon day; he who knows this sacrifices on the new moon day"—do these two [sentences] enjoin two previously unknown rites, while the others are injunctions of subordinate qualities?

This being the prima facie view—namely, that because they are different words and involve repetition, they are all equally primary—we reply: "But the context belongs to the full moon day; the two connected with the full moon and the new moon days are merely restatements of the Agneya and other rites already under discussion. Why? Because there is no mention of a [distinct] form."

"One who, knowing thus, performs the sacrifice designated as the Paurṇamāsī"— in this way, not all sacrifices are being uttered; rather, that which is designated as the Paurṇamāsī is what is enjoined, and we do not understand it in this manner.
"What is the form of the sacrifice designated as such?"—by this we may understand something; therefore we say: if they were the enjoiners of the *apūrva*, they would be purposeless;
but if, on the contrary, they are restaters of those [sacrifices] under discussion, then they refer to what is proximate.

It is understood that the sacrifices are connected with the full moon and new moon days; this is the form [of the injunction], and thus the statement possesses purpose. If it is asked, "But how will a word ending in the singular number denote many [sacrifices]?"—it is replied: it will denote them by virtue of being a term for a collective whole (*samudāya*). For previously, the sacrifices were endowed with their own forms, and there exists a collective whole (*samudāya*) established through their accumulation; the word here is used in reference to that [whole], and therefore it ends in the singular.

There is no fault here, for there are indeed words ending in the singular number that refer to a collection of many things, such as *yūtha* (herd), *vana* (forest), *kula* (family), and *pariṣat* (assembly). When these two [words, *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa*] denote the collection of the Āgneya and other sacrifices, then they alone are designated by the term *darśapūrṇamāsa*; consequently, it is these that have the connection with the fruit. However, the Āghāra and other rites [are connected to the fruit] by virtue of their proximity to what possesses the fruit.
These are the auxiliaries that provide assistance from afar.
And because of the observation of specific details, there would be an application of all [elements] equally.
(Yukti 1) Bhāṣya: Furthermore, if all [the elements] were of equal primary importance, they would not [be modified] in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
"Let the *prayāja* offerings be observed. They are indeed observed, for it is stated: "At each *prayāja*, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* [gold grain].
This would not be possible unless the *prayāja* possessed the quality of being related to the *āgneya* [offering].
Therefore, not all [the constituent parts] are equally primary.
Sūtra: But it is a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), because of its connection with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
(Pūrvapakṣa) Bhāṣya: This is not so—that [the two] are connected with the Full Moon and New Moon sacrifices.
"These are collective terms," however, "but they are the enjoiners of the two preceding rites; likewise, they are not figurative terms for those preceding ones," according to the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā.

[Page 198] Bhāṣya: It will exist. [Objection: But the form does not exist. [Reply: We shall understand the form through another sentence: "At the full moon sacrifice, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni. That which is the rite named Paurṇamāsī—of that, this is the form: Agni is the deity and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is the substance.
In the Śruti, a quality is enjoined by means of the [offerings] beginning with the Āgneya.

Or rather, it is an injunction of the accessories, because they are enjoined simultaneously; for when [the action] is enjoined by the scripture, each one of those [accessories] would be taught as being for the sake of that [action]. (Uddyota) Alternatively, the injunctions such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) and so forth would be injunctions of ritual acts (*karmacodanā*). Why? Because there is a simultaneous teaching of the accessories (*guṇānām yugapacchāsanāt*); for you intend to enjoin multiple accessories here by means of a single sentence alone.

Furthermore, when an action has been enjoined by one word, it is not possible to enjoin multiple subordinate elements (guṇas) [simultaneously], provided there is no mutual connection between them. How so? If, first of all, the intended connection were "on the full moon day, there is an eight-potherd [cake]," then the eight-potherd cake would not be connected to this purpose by way of its mere existence; what then is the eight-potherd cake?

Is it connected with the full moon (paurṇamāsī)? In that case, the verb "to be" (bhavati) occurs [in the sentence]; however, at that time, the statement "the cake on eight potsherds is dedicated to Agni" (āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ) does not even come near it, because there is an absence of connection, and thus it cannot be construed with this: "The cake on eight potsherds becomes dedicated to Agni. Alternatively, one might argue: "The offering dedicated to Agni occurs on the full moon day."

In that case, there would be no connection at all between the *paurṇamāsī* and the *āgneya-puroḍāśa*. If it is argued that "the *āgneya*-nature of the eight-potherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) is enjoined for the *paurṇamāsī*," it must be asked: by what is that eight-potherd cake enjoined for that [sacrifice]? If it is argued that "its [the cake's] being eight-potherd is for the sake of the *āgneya* [deity]," even so, this same fault remains. If it is argued that the word "*paurṇamāsī*" is connected with both [the sacrifice and the deity], then there would still be no mutual connection between the substance (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*). If, however, [it is argued that] the substance and the deity...

It might be argued that the two [offerings], being distinguished from one another, would both be connected with the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*). To this it is replied: "That which is the cake on eight potsherds for Agni occurs at the full moon"—this too is incorrect, because that [offering] is not established [elsewhere]. Or, if it were prescribed for the full moon by someone as an offering to Agni, even so, there would be an absence of the required form (*rūpa*) due to the non-prescription of a deity.
Thus, if someone were to say, "In that case, Agni shall be the deity," he should be told:

"There would be a mutual lack of connection with the purpose; for the word *āgneya* cannot be both a restatement (*anuvāda*) and an injunction (*vidhi*). [If it is argued: "We shall postulate a deity."

If [it is argued that it is] not so, because in the absence of an injunction there would be no deity—since a deity is a word denoting a relationship—that very Agni is the deity of the eight-potherd [offering], and not of anything else.

Therefore, the connection between the *āgneya* (dedicated to Agni) and the eight-potherd offering must necessarily be enjoined, such that "this is the sacrifice"; by means of that, another sacrifice becomes related to the Full Moon sacrifice.

What is enjoined is neither a substance nor a deity; nor can one sacrifice constitute the form of another sacrifice. Since there is no mention of such a form, the two [terms] connected with the *Paurṇamāsī* and *Amāvāsyā* are not enjoiners of two new (unprecedented) rites. As for what was said—that "the words *Paurṇamāsī* and *Amāvāsyā* are able to refer back to the sacrifices under discussion only through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and not directly"—this is not a fault, because when a word's meaning cannot be established directly, [indication is permissible].

In that case, even when understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it becomes grammatically correct; for example, there occurs the common usage "he stands near the fire" (*anau tiṣṭhati*) or "he stands in the pit" (*avaṭe tiṣṭhati*) [meaning "he stands near the fire" or "he stands near the pit"]. For even secondary indication is indeed worldly (*laukikī*). |||

The Upāṃśuyāja should be like the Full Moon sacrifice. (Pūrvapakṣa: Regarding the passage, "Indeed, a lack of continuity (*jāmi*) is created in this sacrifice when two cakes are offered consecutively; therefore, one performs the Upāṃśuyāja in between," and further, "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a low voice for the sake of avoiding *jāmitva*;

Prajāpati is to be sacrificed to in a low voice for the sake of avoiding *jāmitva*; Agni and Soma are to be sacrificed to in a low voice for the sake of avoiding *jāmitva*"; there arises a doubt: [Does the phrase] "one performs the Upāṃśuyāja in between" [refer to a separate act]?

—Is this [the term "upāṃśuyāja"] a designation for the collection of the sacrifices under discussion that possess Viṣṇu and the others as their deities, or rather for a distinct, unprecedented sacrifice? To this it is replied: the Upāṃśuyāja ought to be like the Paurṇamāsī [offering]. Why? Because of its connection with a name;
for a specific sacrifice is heard of in scripture as being connected with a name—the one designated by the name "Upāṃśuyāja."
Furthermore, the substance and the deity do not constitute the form [of the sacrifice], and there exist sacrifices characterized by the *upāṃśu* quality which are under discussion;
therefore, it is a term denoting a collection.

"But surely another sacrifice, possessing the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśu*), is enjoined as having form by way of that whispered nature. No, a word of such a kind cannot express a sacrifice qualified by whispering; for its expression is "the whispered sacrifice" (*upāṃśuyāgaḥ*), [according to the rule] "of *ca* and *ja*..."

According to the rule *ku-dhiṣṇyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52), the word would have to undergo the substitution of *k* for *u*; however, the term *upāṃśuyāja* is an unanalyzed (avyutpanna) word. Therefore, it is not a distinct sacrifice possessing its own specific form (*rūpavat*). Even if it were merely the general act of sacrificing (*yajati*) connected with a name, we could still not recognize it as a separate sacrifice, as its deity and substance are not prescribed. [Objection: "If that were so, then even the sacrifices under discussion would become non-expressive. [Response: Let the word *upāṃśuyāja* not be expressive; let the word *yajati* [be expressive].
It will be so; that being the case, even if the word *upāṃśuyāja* lacks naturalness due to its being a restatement (*anuvāda*), there is no fault.
