"Or rather, it is an injunction, because [the previous subject] is not under discussion.
(Siddhānta) Bhāṣya: It must be the designator of a separate ritual action, namely, "he performs the Upāṃśuyāja sacrifice.
Why? Because there is an absence of previously mentioned sacrifices; and if those previously mentioned do not exist, for what [would this be]?
Does he state a collective [view]? [Objection: But was it not just stated that there exist sacrifices under discussion which have Viṣṇu and others as their deities? [Response: They do not exist;
for those [passages] such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to with low voice" are not injunctions (*vidhi*), but rather explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

How so? Because there is no other injunction in this sentence; it is this very thing—"one performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in between"—that is enjoined in this sentence. If these two were also enjoined [as separate acts], then the sentence would be split (*vākya-bheda*). Furthermore, in this sentence, the relationship between the sacrifice and Viṣṇu and the others is understood, but there is no injunction of the sacrifice itself.

"But surely, in the case of the statement 'he performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in between,' a connection with the intermediate space is also understood. True; however, that which is enjoined there is the connection with qualities such as being performed in a low voice (*upāṃśutva*). For this is a single sentence; it cannot enjoin multiple things. How so? This sentence begins with "Indeed, a flaw (*jāmi*) is thus created in the sacrifice" and ends with "for the sake of avoiding the flaw"; the injunction regarding the *vidhi* (the *upāṃśuyāja*) is recited in the middle of it.

Being connected with that [context], it cannot constitute a separate sentence; therefore, statements such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a low voice" (*viṣṇurupāṃśu yaṣṭavyaḥ*) are not injunctions (*vidhi*), but rather explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). What, then, is an explanatory passage? The defect of "over-cooking" (*ujjīmitā*) is stated regarding the *Āgneya* and *Āgnīṣomīya* sacrifices when they are performed consecutively; to remedy this, it is enjoined: "One performs the *Upāṃśuyāja* in between. How is it remedied by that? In that [context]...

When [the sacrifice] is being performed, it is indeed known that Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, and Agni-Soma are to be sacrificed to; and thus, because of the intervention [of these deities], non-redundancy (*ajāmitā*) is understood. Therefore, thinking "I shall state the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding non-redundancy," the connection with Viṣṇu and the others is restated; for there is no other purpose for the connection with the intermediate [deities] than what is established by the direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*). How is it understood that Viṣṇu and the others are to be sacrificed to? It is understood that Viṣṇu and the others—whether they are to be sacrificed to or not—are mentioned for the sake of praising the *upāṃśuyāja* (whispered sacrifice).
[Bhāṣya on verse 202] by Rucaka.
In this regard, some [opponents] first argue: "They are indeed already established. Why? Because they are prescribed in another recensional branch (*śākhā*).
Even if they are not [already] established here, nevertheless, on account of the commonality of being performed in a low voice (*upāṃśutva*), [they apply].

"Prajāpati as the deity" and "Viṣṇu" are merely restatements (anuvāda), for Viṣṇu and Prajāpati possess the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśu*); therefore, whatever is performed for Prajāpati in the sacrifice is performed only in a whisper—such is the declaration from the traditional recitation (*samāmnāna*). Thus, even though Viṣṇu is not [explicitly] established [as a deity], one speaks of him as if he were established. However, regarding Agni and Soma, an injunctive passage is cited: "One should say these two; or rather, Agni and Soma [are the deities] of another [sacrifice], those two [should be spoken] in a whisper."
"One should sacrifice on the full moon"—therefore, this is a different sacrifice.

Because of the connection with a quality. (Ābhikaraṇa-nirṇaya) As for what was said—that it is not known which sacrifice is designated as the *upāṃśuyāja*—it is that sacrifice to which this quality is attached: "silently on the full moon day."
"Performing sacrifice"—thus [it is said]; therefore, there is no fault.
"And because of the statement occurring in the context of principal acts.

(Yukti) The statement occurs in the context of principal acts; it strengthens the status of being a principal act. Just as, upon seeing writing in a place where others are predominant, the thought arises: "This must be a foreigner"—so it is here. Therefore, it is not a term denoting a collective whole. (2.2.4)
Bhāṣya on the section concerning the non-originary nature (*apūrvatā*) of the *āghāra* and other [rites].
The Āghāra and Agnihotra [are not sacrifices] because they lack a definite form.
(Purvapakṣa) It is heard in scripture: "He pours the Āghāra," and likewise these others:
"He pours upwards, he pours continuously, he pours straight"—and so forth; and this "He offers the Agnihotra," as well as "He offers with curds."
"He offers with milk"—thus it begins. In this regard, there is a doubt:
are the pouring-out rites (*āghāra*) and the oblations (*homa*) performed by such injunctions as "he pours out upwards" and "he offers with curd"?

Regarding those [acts] that have been enjoined, there arises the question: do the two statements, "He pours the Āghāra" and "He performs the Agnihotra," merely refer back to (anuvāda) the established collections [of acts], or do these two themselves enjoin two previously unknown (apūrva) Āghāra-pourings and Agnihotra-oblations? What, then, is the prima facie view? That they are not injunctions of new acts. Why?

Because of the lack of specific form (arūpatvāt); for these two possess no distinct form different from the previously known oblations and pourings, by virtue of which they could be determined to be separate rites.
Therefore, because it concerns the subject at hand, it is a restatement of what has been previously introduced.
Sūtra:
Because of the connection with a name. (Pūrvapakṣa-yukti 1) Bhāṣya: Furthermore, there is a connection with a name, as in: "He performs the oblation named Agnihotra."

"One performs the rite called *āghāra*"; thus, two oblations (*āghāra-homa*) qualified by their names are enjoined. However, it is not understood what specific rite this one called *āghāra* is, nor what that named *agnihotra* is. [Objection: "But it is indeed understood: pouring out is *āghāra*, and offering is *homa*. [Reply: If there were only the generality of pouring out and the generality of offering...

If they were already known as the *ādhāra* and *agnihotra* offerings, then these two [terms] would be mere restatements (*anuvāda*). Alternatively, if both names were previously unestablished, even so, the general categories of *ādhāra* and *agnihotra* could not be expressed, because a name depends upon a specific instance; and since that specific instance is not perceived, the injunctions for the new *ādhāra* and *agnihotra* offerings would be untenable. Furthermore, how...?

By which word would "action" (kriyā) be denoted? For that instrument (sādhana) which is most desired (īpsitatama) is expressed by a word ending in the accusative case, while action is expressed by a verbal suffix (tiṅ). In the view of restatement (anuvāda), the collection of actions would constitute a distinct entity, and that will be the most desired instrument.
Sra.
Bhā.:
And because it is not the subject under discussion. (Pūrvapakṣa Yukti 2)
Furthermore, even in the case of the Āghāra offering, the substance and deity are not explicitly mentioned, by virtue of which it might possess a specific form.
Therefore, these two terms as well are collective designations.

[Page 204] Or rather, it is an injunction (*codanā*) because the meaning of the word is intended for performance; the repetition is for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) due to its proximity. (Siddhānta Sūtra 16) Commentary: It is not the case that this is a collective term; rather, there would be two injunctions of separate rites. Why? Because the meaning of the word is intended for performance, as in "he pours the libation" (*āghārayati*).

The meaning of the words is that "he offers" (juhoti) implies that the *homa* and the *āghāra* are to be performed; therefore, we understand that two distinct rites are being enjoined. Furthermore, the terms *āghāra* and *agnihotra* are well-known as denoting the general acts of pouring and offering; thus, their meanings are not unknown.
Therefore, they are established as being possessed of form.

As for what was said—that because they are enjoined by such [passages] as "He pours upward" (*ūrdhvam āghārayati*) and "He offers with curds" (*dadhnā juhoti*), they are merely restatements (*anuvādī*)—this is not so; for these two, the *homā* and the *āghāra*, cannot be enjoined [by those sentences]. Nor do [the sentences] "He pours upward" and "He offers with curds" [enjoin them].

This is what is meant: it is not that "the base must be made" or "the oblation must be performed"; rather, it is that "the connection with the upwardness of the base must be established" and "the connection between the curd and the oblation must be established.
Therefore, since these [connections] have not been previously established, they are not mere restatements (anuvāda). [Objection: But surely, when the connection has been enjoined...
"The oblation and the pouring would follow from the sense of the text. This is not so;

for when this [text] exists, there is a connection through direct injunction. Therefore, the oblation and the pouring do not result merely from the sense; rather, we say that they are both enjoined previously by direct audition (śruti).

[Objection: "But surely, in the injunctions 'he pours out' (āghārayati) and 'he offers' (juhoti), it is the activity pertaining to the pouring and the offering that is heard, not the connection with *dadhi* (curd), *ājya* (clarified butter), and so forth. [Response: True, it is not explicitly heard; however, the hearing of the activity is justified by its proximity (*sannidhi*) for the sake of the subordinate qualities (*guṇa*). [Objection: But surely [the activity] pertains to another word-meaning..."

The Vedic revelation is unable to express the [independent] operation. It is true that this is so; it expresses what resides within its own word-meaning, but the word denoting the quality qualifies that very word-meaning, and thus that qualified [meaning] alone will be understood.
This might be the case—that the word denoting the quality would qualify its own word-meaning.
But this operation would not be perceived as residing in the quality (*guṇa*). What would happen in that case?

Even if the quality were not being operated upon, the meaning of the word would be established. [Objection: What is the purpose of the proximity of the word expressing the quality now? [Response: It is purposeless. But how can it be purposeless? [Page 205]
[Objection: Should it not be understood as a name (*nāmadheya*)? [Response: When there is a meaning, it is not meaningless;

but when there is no meaning, what else could it be? [Objection: "In that case, it will arise from the sentence (*vākya*); for when the meaning of the direct expression (*śruti*) exists, the meaning of the sentence is not employed. [Response: This is true; however, it will be possible if [the primary meaning] is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*). How is it not intended to be expressed? Because the word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) is read without error, and because of its own word-meaning (*svapadārtha*).

And because it is distinguished by another word. Therefore, it is established that the "repeated mention" (*punaḥśruti*) in such cases as "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) is for the sake of a subordinate element (*guṇārthena*). Furthermore, the utterance of the root *juhoti* (to sacrifice) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to connect it with a subordinate element. If "if he sacrifices" (*yadi juhoti*) is a restatement, [it serves this purpose].

By what means, then, is the quality (*guṇa*) enjoined? Do not say "by the word *dadhi* (curd). But was it not just stated that the operation of the quality is understood from the sentence? True, this is so; however, if it were not being enjoined, how could it be understood? Its authority (*pramāṇa*) would not be apprehended! In the absence of authority, there would be delusion (*vyāmoha*). Thus...
In that case, the words "juhoti" (he offers) and "āghārayati" (he pours) are injunctive; of what do they express the substance? We reply: of the meaning of the verbal root.
If they are injunctive, since their own meaning has already been enjoined previously, for what purpose are they uttered again?
There is no fault, as it is for the sake of enjoining that which constitutes the meaning of the sentence; therefore, these are injunctions of distinct rites.

As it has been stated: "In the *āghāra* offering, there is no original substance or deity. What, then, is the use of a substance and a deity in this case, when its form is already known through the expression of a well-established meaning? Furthermore, since it is said, "This was indeed the fourfold-drawn [clarified butter]; having poured the *āghāra* for it," clarified butter (*ājya*) is its substance, and the injunction regarding the deity is based on the description of the mantra: "O Indra, may this sacrifice reach the heavens..."

"One pours the libation with the formula: 'A great sacrifice, O Lord of Sacrifice, accompanied by Indra, svāhā! Thus, this [sacrifice] is "accompanied by Indra" only if Indra is its deity; if this [formula] is the designation of the deity for the libation, then by it the libation is performed. Therefore, it is established that [the term refers to] a separate rite, and not a collective name for a group of acts. (2.2.5)

"Do not say so"— this should be applied according to the style of the *Vājapeyādhikaraṇa* [in the *Tantravārttika*], and the distinction is that the suffix is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*), while the meaning of the verbal root is merely a statement (*anuvāda*)— such is the *Vārttika*.
Since this mantra is recited in different forms in each manuscript and is not seen in the root text, there is no certainty that it is exactly like this.
[Page 206] The section concerning those sacrifices ending with the animal, Soma, and Pūrvanta.

The injunction regarding the animal and the Soma [is established] because of the connection with their own substances; for within the context, the connection with the substance would be purposeless, as it is not for the sake of a subordinate quality. (Siddhānta 17) — Bhāṣya.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma," and regarding this they recite: "He cuts a portion from the heart, then from the tongue, then from the chest"; likewise, [in the case of] "One should sacrifice with Soma," there too [it is said]:
"He draws the cup for Indra-Vāyu, he draws the cup for Mitra-Varuṇa, [he draws] the cup for the Aśvins."
"he cuts," and so forth. Regarding this, there is a doubt:

are the words *ālabhati* ("he seizes") and *yajati* ("he sacrifices") restatements (*anuvādau*) of the very acts enjoined by the terms *avadyati* ("he cuts off") and *gṛhṇāti* ("he takes"), or are they injunctions (*vidhātārau*) of two entirely new acts?
What has been established so far? That it belongs to the aggregate (samudāya).
Why?

It is considered whether these two actions—slaughtering (*śrālabhati*) and offering (*yajati*)—should be enjoined; however, they have already been understood through the acts of cutting out (*avadyati*) and taking up (*gṛhṇāti*), and that which has already been understood is not enjoined. Furthermore, the heart and other parts are referred to by the word "animal" (*paśu*), and by the word "Soma."

[Regarding] the juice: therefore, in the statement "one should sacrifice with Soma," the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) [of an already known act], while the phrase "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" is for the purpose of connecting it with the result; and in the statement "one should immolate the animal," the root *ā-labh* (to immolate) is for the purpose of connecting it with Agni and Soma. Furthermore, a conjunction is observed in the text: "The Adhvaryu takes these ten cups at the morning pressing. Likewise, [regarding] the Āśvina...

The sequence is: "the tenth is drawn," and "the third is offered. Furthermore, if the two preceding sacrifices were being enjoined, then the deities such as Indra-Vāyu and others would have to be enjoined therein;
and since they would serve the same purpose, they would necessarily be subject to option (*vikalpa*), just as in the case of the injunction: "He binds [the animal] to a *khadira* post..."

"He binds it to a Palāśa branch; he binds it to a Rohitaka branch"—thus [it is said]. In that case, these two would be appropriate through the observation of a combination of actions (*karmasamuccaya*). However, if this is a statement regarding a collective whole (*samudāya*), then this is properly established as being intended for the two sacrifices (*yajati*); therefore, they are both restatements (*anuvāda*) of the collective whole.
"He offers that as the third," is the reading in the Vārttika.
Bhāṣya on Saṃyutta Nikāya,
page 207.
This being the case, we reply: there is an injunction and a mandate for two previously unknown rites, namely those of the animal sacrifice and the Soma sacrifice.

Why? Because the word *soma* is well-known to denote a milky creeper, not its juice; for the word *soma* expresses the plant (*ākṛti*), not the individual substance (*vyakti*). Likewise, they apply the word *paśu* (animal) figuratively to a specific four-footed substance that has hooves, a tail, and hair, yet there are no sacrifices under discussion here whose substances possess such a form.

For whom these two [words] would be mere restatements of a composite whole? [Objection: "Is it not the case that the heart and other parts, being modifications (*vikāra*) of the animal, are restated by the word 'animal' for the purpose of establishing a connection with Agni and Soma? [Reply: This is not so; all that is said is "the animal belongs to Agni and Soma" (*paśur agnīṣomīyo bhavati*), and it is not stated that "this [composite] heart and so forth is the animal.

In that regard, if a common domestic animal (*laukika-paśu*) were taken, then the word "animal" would be used in its primary sense (*mukhya*); if, however, the heart and other parts were taken, then it would be used in a secondary sense (*jaghanya*) through its connection to the modification. Likewise, the word "Soma" is also a restatement through its connection to the modification.
It may be so. Therefore, two new (apūrva) actions would be enjoined, not mere restatements (anuvāda).

Now, [it might be argued]: "The creeper (latā) is enjoined in the sacrifices already established as being for Indra-Vāyu and others. To this it is replied: No; that [creeper] cannot be known as belonging to Indra-Vāyu by means of syntactical connection (vākya), because it is [already known] by direct statement (śruti).

For the *rasa* (juice) belongs to Indra-Vāyu; therefore, even though the original sacrifices exist, this statement regarding the connection with a substance would be purposeless if it were unable to either enjoin or refer to them.
Consequently, two new actions (*apūrvakarman*) must be enjoined, rather than being mere references (*anuvāda*) to the original ones.
"And the preparatory rites are not injunctive" (Pūrvapakṣa-siddhānta 18).

Thus far, it has been stated that even though the archetypal sacrifices exist, [the text] is not a mere restatement; now, however, it is argued that these sacrifices do not even exist as archetypes. Why?
The preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*) are not themselves injunctions, nor are sacrifices enjoined by means of the [cups] dedicated to Indra-Vāyu and others;

therefore, the taking up of the cups (*grahaṇa*) is merely a preparation for a visible purpose. However, while the cup is being prepared, there is no mention of a deity; [this reading exists as a variation in the *Kāśikā*, *Saṃkṣepasaṃhitā*, and *Pustaka* manuscripts, but it has not been cited here because, although the wording differs, the meaning is not different].

[Page 208] The mention of the name is for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*); therefore, when it is said, "He draws the *aindravāyava* cup," what is meant is that he forms a mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for Indra and Vāyu. In that case, without a sacrifice, [the action would be incomplete].

It is not tenable that [the act] "he intends" (saṅkalpayati) would constitute the sacrifice; rather, it is that very sacrifice which has been traditionally handed down (āmnāta), in the presence of which the intention can be formed. Therefore, sacrifices are not enjoined by such [passages] as "He draws the cup for Indra and Vāyu," because the sacrifices are already established through prior injunctions.
The word *yajati* is a term for a collection of names and states; likewise is the word *labhate*.

Sva. 18: Because of that distinction, there would be repetition of the action; for it would be purposeless due to the separation of the substance, since [the action] would become subordinate to the substance.
(Upasaṃhāra) Bhā.
The story of Paśu has been told in the tenth [book]. It will arise again; for now, Soma is under discussion. [Question:

"How can there be a combination of actions (karma-samuccaya)? [Answer: The deities such as Indra-Vāyu are not explicitly heard in the text—[namely,] that a sacrifice is to be performed for Indra and Vāyu, or for Mitra and Varuṇa.
"The sacrifice is to be accomplished"—if they had heard this, they would have conceived of the deity with respect to the sacrifice;

for then it would have been known that the sacrifice is accomplished by the deity alone. But rather, these deities are enjoined with regard to the consecration of the drawing (grahaṇa) for the sake of an unseen result (adṛṣṭa). In that case, the conception of Mitra and Varuṇa is distinct from the conception of Indra and Vāyu; therefore, at the time of the drawing, it produces another unseen result from the unseen result produced by that [other deity]. This is likewise for the other drawings as well. Therefore, there is a combination (samuccaya). As for the drawing...

In vessels of fixed measure, one span in height, and in water-jars of fixed measure, it is not possible to contain the entire Soma, which has been prepared in a quantity of ten handfuls; and even if it were possible, [it would still not apply] to those [rites] prescribed as obligatory (*nitya*).

First, let it not be that the injunctive statement regarding the deities is sublated by conceptual construction. Due to the hearing [of the text], because of the distinction between them—that is, because of the distinction in the connection with the deities—there is a repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the act of drawing the cup (*graha*). This is because the substances to be consecrated, which are the cups connected with the deities, are distinct. For the hearing of another connection would be purposeless; indeed, that which is performed would be purposeless. Therefore, there is a distinction of the act of drawing the cup, because it becomes subordinate (*guṇībhāva*) toward the substance to be purified (*saṃskārya*). Thus says the Vārttika.
Regarding the statement: "The animal is a single oblation."

[Page 209] Bhāṣya: It is indeed logical to take only the *yava* (barley). For if one were to take the *ṣaṣ* (six), then that very same [substance] would have been prepared for Indra and Vāyu, and that very same [substance] for Mitra and Varuṇa—thus it would not be appropriate. Therefore...

Because of the distinction in conceptualization, Soma exists separately; since it consists of various deities, it cannot be treated as a single unit. Furthermore, in the absence of an offering to the deities, it is impossible to present [the substance] to them. Therefore, the deities must necessarily be worshipped exactly as they were intended; and when these are being worshipped, the sacrifice heard in the scripture—"One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma"—is fulfilled.

Thus it is; one does not expect another deity, and the sacrifice is heard in scripture as being performed with the entire *soma* consisting of ten handfuls; that [sacrifice] is not possible without repetition—therefore, by implication, it will possess the quality [of repetition]; thus the sacrifice consists of repetitions, for it is not [performed] without repetition.

It will be endowed with all the deities and with the entire Soma. And while that [Soma] is being practiced, both sequential performance and combined performance are indeed appropriate; therefore, the observation of those two is entirely logical.
But the preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) would not be subject to option, because the substance is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) since it exists for the sake of another. (Śrauta-nirṇaya 20).

As for what was also said—that just as in the cases "he binds to a *khadira* tree" and "he binds to a *pālāśa* tree," the *khadira* and other trees are optional with respect to the preparatory rite, so too the deities will be optional—that is not correct; for in that case, [the purpose] is to bring about the preparatory rite.

The *khadira* wood and others are prescribed in the scriptures; and if Indra-Vāyu and the others were also heard in the scripture as deities for the purpose of accomplishing the sacrifice, then there would indeed be an option between them, but these [latter] are not heard in connection with the sacrifice. Therefore, they should be combined. (2.2.6)
The section concerning the schism in the formal acts of the Saṃgha:
"Because of their separate establishment, there would be a division of the Saṃgha's formal acts. (21)
Bhāṣya: There is the Vājapeya sacrifice, [enjoined by the text]: "One desiring sovereignty should sacrifice with the Vājapeya. Here, this sūtra has not been extracted from the Vārttika-latā.
In that context, there are animals dedicated to Prajāpati: "He sacrifices seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati;
for Prajāpati is seventeenfold. They are black-spotted, hornless, and uniform in appearance, for such indeed is Prajāpati. Regarding this, a doubt arises: what...
Are these seventeen acts [distinct], or is there one act characterized by seventeen animals?
What, then, is the prima facie view? That it is one act. Why? Because seventeen animals are dedicated to Prajāpati; are they intended to accomplish a single sacrifice, or...?

When there is this doubt—whether [the animals] are many or one—it is logical that there is one; for he who postulates many sacrifices must necessarily postulate only one. In that case, when only one [sacrifice] is performed, the assignment of seventeen animals becomes appropriate. And by what [means]?

We would have to assume a second and subsequent sacrifices; this being the case, there would result the assumption of an inference of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) that is most minimal. Therefore, a single sacrifice is accomplished by means of seventeen animals.
This being the position reached, we reply: there should be a distinction of acts (*karmabheda*) due to the number, because [the animals] are distinct.

If the number seventeen were to apply, that would be appropriate for many separate sacrifices involving animals, but not for a single one. Why? Because the extended injunction (*codaka*) indicates that this sacrifice must be accomplished by means of eleven portions (*avadāna*); and since those portions are obtained from only a single animal, the seizing of a second and subsequent animals would not serve to complete the required portions.
When one [animal] is being sacrificed, others may touch it for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*);
if that were so, because they would not have that [sacrifice] as their purpose, they would become *prājāpatya*s; in that case, regarding those *prājāpatya*s...

—thus it would be heard [in scripture]. Therefore, the seventeen-fold set of sacrificial portions (*avadāna*), which resides in distinctness, could not be accommodated in a single animal; rather, there is a requirement for many sets of sacrificial portions in many sacrifices.
Consequently, they would take up seventeen animals for the seventeen sacrifices, and that...
There will be consistency with the Saṅgha; therefore, there are seventeen sacrifices. [Objection:
"But surely, even in a single sacrifice, one sacrifices with seventeen sets of portions (avadāna) because of the scriptural injunction? [Reply:

This is not so—for in the case of animals, the collection of slaughter is heard of in scripture, not the collection of portions; the portions are the oblations (havīṃṣi), the means for accomplishing the sacrifice, whereas the slaughter of the animal is not [the means]. For that [slaughter]...
Distinguishing the substance which is the original material of the *avadāna*, it has assisted the primary element in its natural state;
thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter.
Even in the case of modification (*vikṛti*), the [number seventeen] will benefit the primary rite by qualifying the counter-sacrifice (*pratidrava*) of the portions (*avadāna*);
and in that context, the number seventeen modifies the animal (*paśu*), not the group of portions (*avadānagaṇa*).
Therefore, it follows that one animal should be sacrificed for each group of portions. In that regard—

The group of seventeen is not established; it must be understood in this way. If they were intended as [types of] limbs, colors, or forms—such as "a white one with seventeen parts," "a red one," and so forth—or if it meant "one of these," such as "hornless ones," "horned ones," or "single-horned ones," and so forth—since they are heard of in the scripture as being dark-colored, hornless, and uniform in appearance—it is among these that [the animal] is to be found.

It applies to many sacrifices, not to a single one; therefore, there are seventeen sacrifices. The practical purpose is that if one [animal] is lost or defective, the entire group of animals would have to be repeated; in the case of a single animal being seized, they would seize the others in succession. According to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), this is for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*); according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), only one animal is repeated, for when there is a distinction of acts, one animal does not require another animal. (2.2.3)
Sra.:
Now begins the section concerning the distinction between the *saṃjñā* and the *tarka*.
And the name [is established] because of its connection with the origin [of the word]. || 22 ||
Bhāṣya: "Now this is Jyotis, now this is Viśvajyotis, now this is Sarvajyotis.
Here a doubt arises: Is the previously mentioned Jyotiṣṭoma being referred to by these names? Or [is it something else]?

Is it that the quality of giving a thousand [cows] as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth is enjoined for the [already established] sacrifice, or rather are distinct rituals with the specific qualities about to be mentioned being taught? What is the prima facie view? That, in order to respect the context (*prakaraṇa*), this is an injunction of a quality for the ritual under discussion. But surely, by the force of the sentence (*vākya*), these qualities will be enjoined for the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other [sacrifices]. This is not a fault; for these are indeed designators of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* itself: "Jyotis" is used as a synonym (*pratīka*) for the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, and "Viśvajyotis" refers to its lights, such as the *Citra* and others.

All those [names] mentioned in the supplementary portion of the text belong to this [sacrifice]; therefore, it follows that this Jyotiṣṭoma is both the Viśvajyotis and the Sarvajyotis. Thus is the prima facie position.
[Page 212]

This being the case, we reply: indeed, names are the differentiators; for those [sacrifices], there are the names "Jyotis" and so forth, which are heard in their original injunctions (*utpattivākya*), and these [passages] are repetitions of them.
Therefore, the sentence "Now this Jyotis" is an injunction of a previous rite.
For if there were a restatement (*anuvāda*), the injunction of a specific modification of my own activity would be purposeless.

Furthermore, if a quality (*guṇa*) were enjoined with respect to what is already under discussion (*prakṛta*), there would be an option (*vikalpa*); in that case, one alternative would be sublated (*bādha*). Nor are the *Jyotirāya* and others denoters of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*; they are distinct composite wholes (*samudāyāntara*).
A different composite whole does not become identical in meaning to another merely by sharing a common component, just as [in the case of]...

The word *śālā* denotes a house; however, because of the commonality of the word *śālā*, words such as *mālā* do not thereby become denoters of a house. As for the statement, "The word *jyotis* is taken as a representative part (*pratīka*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*," this is due to the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

In that case, there would be an indirect syntactic unity with the word *jyotiṣṭoma*; that would subvert the direct syntactic unity with the word *jyotis*. And this is not to be doubted, for a sentence (*vākya*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*). Now, furthermore, [the term *jyotiṣṭoma*] is so called either because it has the sense of "shining" (*dyotana*) or because it possesses light (*jyotiṣmat*).

If it is argued that [the term] will apply to other actions, just as the word "light" (*jyotis*) refers to the *ciṭṭhat* and other luminaries, and that "all-light" (*viśvajyotiḥ*) or "universal light" (*sarvajyotiḥ*) expresses their totality—we say: no.

For the word "light" is not conventionally established in reference to the *ciṭṭhat* and so forth; to speak thus would contradict established usage. As for the claim that "on account of the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), the word 'light' denotes the *cit* (consciousness) and so on"—
Thus, it is understood through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), and not by the word itself, that "it is employed in that very sense" within that sentence;
however, where such another means of knowledge does not exist, the word cannot function there—

just as in the case of "Devadatta is a lion," the word "lion" denotes Devadatta through another means of knowledge, but this is not the case in "one should sacrifice a lion," where such another means of knowledge is absent.
It does not exist. Therefore, the two who speak of the Jyotiṣṭoma as "Viśvajyotis" and "Sarvajyotis" do not refer to the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, but rather to all other distinct rites. (2.2.8)
"In the case of prescribing what is to be prescribed after it has been praised," so says the Kātyāyana-Prāyaścitta-Purāṇa.
[Page 213] The Section on the Differentiation of Ritual Actions Based on the Differentiation of Deities.
kha. And the quality [belongs] to the prior connection, because of the equality of the two sentences. || 23 ||
In the Vaiśvadeva section of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, they recite: "He pours curds into heated milk;

that is the Āmikṣā for the Viśvedevas; the Vājina is for the Vājins. Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the Vājina an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi) within the ritual action characterized by the Āmikṣā, or is it [a separate action] from that?
Is it a separate ritual action characterized by the quality of *vājina* (curd-whey)? What is the prima facie view? That it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).

Why? Because, having referred to the Viśvedevas as "the Vājins" by means of this *vāja* (sacrificial food) which they desire, *vājina* is enjoined; therefore, both—the *āmikṣā* (coagulated milk) and the *vājina*—belong to the Viśvedevas.

And in that very same ritual action, there is an injunction regarding the quality of the *vājina* (curd-mixture). Just as when it is stated, "One performs the *agnihotra*," it is further specified, "One performs it with curds" or "One performs it with milk.
This being the case, we reply: the quality (*guṇa*), being connected with the designation of the deity which has not yet been established [by another injunction], [is a distinct act].

One should establish a separate ritual action, for in that case these two sentences become equal, as both are injunctions of two previously unknown sacrifices. But how can there be a mention of a previously unknown deity, when it was just stated that "the whey (vājina) is a restatement of the Viśvedevas"? To this it is said: here, the status of the Viśvedevas as deities is [established] in some respect.

In some cases it is by direct statement (*śruti*), and in others by syntactical connection (*vākya*); when there is a mention [of the deity] by direct statement, it is by *śruti*, and when there is a mention by the dative case, it is by *vākya*. Where the status of being a deity is established by direct statement, there it forms a single syntactical unit with the *āmikṣā*; where the dative case is used, there it is with the *vājina*. In that regard, among these, the status of being a deity is established by direct statement in one instance.

The connection with a specific substance is established by means of a sentence; in one case, both [the deity and the substance] are established by means of a sentence. Thus, here there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and sentence (*vākya*) regarding the status of being a deity; and when there is a conflict, the direct statement is more authoritative.

Therefore, it is determined that the status of being a deity belongs to the Viśvedevas in the sentence concerning the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture), but not in the sentence concerning the *vājina* (whey); by this, it is understood that this [sentence] does not [apply] through a deity-word that is not part of its own context.
[The opponent says: "There is a connection"—therefore, it is a different ritual action (karmāntara). (2.2.9 Śrauta Sūtra).
Now, as for what was described—that when it is said, "He offers the Agnihotra," statements such as "He offers with curd" are injunctions of accessories (guṇavidhi)—to that it is replied:
[Page 214] (The refutation of the doubt concerning the preceding section; or rather, the section on the unity of action based on the specific nature of the substance:
But when the word denotes the action itself and not its qualities, a quality would be understood as pertaining to that [action]. || 24 ||

[Commentary: It is appropriate that there is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*) therein; however, there is no connection with any quality not already present in the archetype (*aprakṛta*), whereas such a connection does exist with the sacrifice (*yāga*) through its archetypal nature. Therefore, this [previous] description is incorrect.
Alternatively, this is a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇāntara*): regarding such passages as "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*).
Other actions are postulated only out of a desire to avoid conceptualizing [them as distinct];

however, it is understood from the word "juhoti" that it is that very same action, not a different action; therefore, it is established that there is an injunction regarding a quality in that very context, and the option [of alternatives] arises from the specific scriptural statement. (2.2.10)
The section concerning the fruitfulness of substances such as curd and the like.
But on account of the scriptural statement of results, it must be ritual action; for the result is connected with ritual action. (Sūtra 25)
( Pūrvapakṣa ) ||
In the Bhāṣya, with reference to the Agnihotra, they recite: "One desiring sensory power should offer curds," and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the offering of curds and the like a separate sacrifice from the Agnihotra, or is the fruit [attained] through the quality of the curds and the like? What is the prima facie view?
"—it is another sacrifice. Why? "Because of the mention of a fruit"; for a fruit is heard as being desired, and that is logically appropriate to the ritual action.
[Objection: "What indeed is the observed fruit of a ritual action? It is the acquisition of grain and so forth from sowing and so forth. No..."

—Thus we say: that [result] is not established by this visible [fact]; if perception (*darśana*) were the cause, then it would be logical for that [perception] to belong to the ritual action (*karman*). When the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) has stated this, the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntavādin*), fearing the redundancy of the substance "curd" (*dadhi*), [argues that] because the principle of the section on the meaning of words (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*) is inapplicable, there is no capacity in the word.
Thinking thus, he asks: "Is it like the case where one asks, 'What indeed is the fruit of plowing and so forth?
By this [inference] based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), the *Vārttika* states: "You consider that there is a fruit from the oblation."

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī), demonstrating the defect in inference based on general observation (sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna), establishes— following the Vārttika— that the result [arising] from the oblation is understood from the word alone;
such is the appearance.
[Page 215] Chapter 2, Section 2.

Bhāṣya: [The observation of results] is seen in things such as agriculture where the result is perceptible, but not in the case of the *homa* (oblation). If it is argued that "what is observed in agriculture occurs elsewhere as well," this would lead to an over-extension (*prasajyate*). If it is replied that "it occurs because of similarity to agriculture"—that is, the *homa* is similar to agriculture because it is an action (*kriyā*), and not because it is a substance (*dravya*)—[then we respond: ... [The argument continues: ...[This is not so,] because the similarity of the *homa* to agriculture is based on its being a ritual act (*karman*), not on its being a substance. Furthermore, the similarity of the *homa* to agriculture is established by the fact that both are enjoined for the sake of a specific result, and not merely by their common nature as actions. Moreover, the similarity of the *homa* to agriculture is restricted to the specific context of the injunction; it does not extend to all actions, as the similarity is determined by the specific purpose and the particular means prescribed. Therefore, the principle of analogy (*atideśa*) from agriculture to the *homa* is limited to those aspects relevant to the attainment of the fruit, and does not apply to every detail. Thus, the inference of results in the *homa* is valid only within the scope of the scriptural injunctions governing it.

"For that [comparison] is dissimilar. Even though the *homa* (sacrificial oblation) is similar, it is dissimilar; for the *homa* has the sky (*dyau*) and the deities as its means of accomplishment, whereas the ploughing (*kṛṣi*) has the plough (*lāṅgala*) and so forth as its means. Furthermore, the *homa* consists of renunciation (*tyāga*), while the ploughing consists of cleaving (*pāṭana*). "Now, if some similarity is admitted—even in the case of a substance (*dravya*), there is some similarity such as 'existent' (*sat*) and 'non-eternal' (*anitya*) and so forth. If it is argued that because there is something more similar than a substance, one cannot say 'this is not similar,' then there is indeed something more similar to the ploughing than even the *homa*."

"Because the object is perceived—thinking thus, [one might claim] that the homologue (*homogya*) should be similar [to the subject]. But this is not established, for it is not observed anywhere that something which is similar in one respect must necessarily be so even when the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) is involved. If it is known that what is the cause of the established (*siddha*) is also the cause of the thing to be proven (*sādhya*), then that [cause] becomes its prover (*sādhaka*); but if it is not known to be a cause, then even if it is similar, it is not a prover. Therefore, whether a similar thing is a prover or not a prover must be examined. "Now, as for that action..."

That [agriculture] is seen to have a fruit, and the *homa* is also an action; therefore, it too must possess a fruit. When an action has ceased, another substance is seen as the fruit of substances and their combinations—thus, a substance would also be fruitful. Furthermore, since it is not seen in agriculture, by analogy with that, there would be no unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) from the *homa* either; or, by analogy with agriculture, there would be only rice, not the sense-organ (*indriya*). Therefore, in cases of this kind, the establishment of both the seen and the unseen does not occur. How then is the *homa* to be understood?
"What is the fruit?"—it is replied: That fruit is not understood from the word itself, because the word does not say "this is the fruit";
therefore, it is logical that the fruit comes from the oblation (*homa*), as this is understood from the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) by means of the word.

Furthermore, the fruit [comes] from the curd (*dadhi*), as understood through syntactical connection (*vākya*); and direct statement (*śruti*) is more authoritative than syntactical connection (*vākya*). Therefore, it is logical that the fruit comes from the oblation, and the curd is the fruit.
And it is also illogical;
moreover, curd is incapable of both—producing the fruit and accomplishing the oblation.
[Page 216]

[Objection: But surely this will be like the washing of a woolen blanket (*kambala-nirṇejana*); for the washing accomplishes both—the purification of the blanket and the cleanliness of the feet. [Reply: We do not say that a single thing lacks the capacity to accomplish two purposes; rather, we mean that a single sentence is incapable of expressing that curd is subordinate to both the fruit [of the sacrifice] and the oblation (*homa*).

If one were to say, "If one should produce the fruit by means of curd," it would mean that there is no oblation with curd; or if one were to say, "One should accomplish the oblation by means of curd," it would mean that there is no fruit.

If both were stated, the sentence would be split; yet this [sentence] is perceived as undivided. Therefore, the fruit does not arise from the accessory substance, and the *agnihotra* oblation is a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) from the *adhihoma*.
But because the two sentences are not equal, its quality would be understood [from the one]. (26)

But because of the word "tu" (but), the verb "pacet" (should cook) is understood as recurring [from the previous context], not as a different action; rather, the result arises from a subordinate quality (guṇa).
How so? Because those two sentences are not equivalent: "[One] should offer the Agnihotra... [and "...[one] should cook..."].

In the case of "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*), the fruit mentioned in connection with the ritual action is: "One desiring heaven should effect [it] by means of the oblation. In the case of "one desiring sense-power should offer curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya juhuyāt*), it is mentioned in connection with a subordinate factor (*guṇa*); for here it is not understood that "the oblation is to be performed for the sake of sense-power," but rather that "the oblation is to be performed with curd for one desiring sense-power"—thus, there is a connection between the oblation and the curd.

There is no origination of the oblation for the sake of the sense-faculty; rather, "he who desires the sense-faculty should perform the oblation with curd"—this is what is meant. "And which word is the expresser of human effort?
we reply: "The word 'juhuyāt' (he should sacrifice)."
"An objection: the Śruti declares this human effort as connected with the oblation (homa), while the Vākya declares its connection with curd;
and a Vākya cannot set aside a Śruti.
Nor is it possible for it to be connected to both simultaneously, for in that case the Vākya would be split."

Thus it is said. To this we reply: those who would rely upon your position would subvert the Vedic revelation (śruti) in the interim; however, in our position, only the meaning of the verbal root in "juhuyāt" (one should sacrifice) is subverted.

In your position, on the other hand, it is the word "dadhnā" (with curd) itself that is subverted; and it is understood that they recite this without negligence, for this is not the song of a careless person.
[Page 217]

The Bhāṣya states: "For it has been said that the traditional [interpretation] is indeed equal. Therefore, the fruit is not mentioned in connection with the ritual action (*karman*); however, in its connection with the quality (*guṇa*), there is no erroneous reading whatsoever, for one would certainly recite it as "one should offer" (*juhuyāt*). Thus, it must be stated for the purpose of enjoining the relationship between the restraint of the senses (*damena*) and the desire (*kāma*).

[Objection: "But even when it is being uttered, the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do) is not understood in isolation; there is no purpose in mentioning it in isolation, and furthermore, it is connected to the oblation (*homa*)."

"Therefore, this is inconsistent"—so [the opponent says]. We reply: "No. Even though this is connected with the *homa* (oblation), it is indeed the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do/make); however, there is merely a specific qualification regarding its connection with the *homa*, but this does not negate its status as the meaning of *kṛ*. [The sense is: "For one desiring sensory power (*indriya*), one should perform that which is connected with the *homa* and connected with curd (*dadhi*). [Objection: "But in this case, the fruit is mentioned in grammatical coordination (*samabhivyāhṛta*) [with the action]."

That capacity which is distinguished by the oblation— when that exists, it is precisely that which is called the "oblation"; the word "juhuyāt" (he should sacrifice) expresses the effort [of the agent], but here there is no actual oblation.

It is enjoined as a means (*sādhana*), whereas the first [element], characterized as the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is understood from the sentence as being dependent on the curd; for this very reason, it has been stated by Bhaṭṭikāra: "The accessory (*guṇa*), depending upon the oblation (*homa*), will accomplish the fruit"—just as a king's servant, depending upon the king, performs the king's work. Therefore, the fruit belongs to the curd.
"One who desires sensory power should perform [the offering] with curd, thinking, 'This is sensory power. How so? "By means of this procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the *agnihotra*. Why is this so?

Because the curd, which is the means to the result, requires a procedure; because this procedure is present in proximity; and because the meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice), which serves as the indicator of the injunction (*codanā-liṅga*), is observed.
And since this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the meaning of *juhoti*, it is therefore not injunctive. It is not.
And since there is no other injunction for the *dadhi-homa*, it is therefore not a separate ritual act;

thus, the fruit [of the sacrifice] belongs to the *dadhi*. Alternatively, because the word *dadhi* is intended to be significant, the connection between the *dadhi* and the *homa* is enjoined by the sentence; therefore, [the fruit results] from the *dadhi* by means of the *homa*.
"From that which is being connected, the result will arise"—thus [it is stated]. (2.2.11a)
[Sūtra 218] Section concerning whether the *bāravaṃtīya* and other such rites constitute separate ritual acts.
In the case of equal [sacrifices], it should be connected with the ritual action. ||27||

Bhāṣya: "One desiring the status of a Brahman should sacrifice with that very Agniṣṭoma, having made the Vāyavyā verses its twenty-one-fold Agniṣṭoma-sāman"; and, "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with this same [Agniṣṭoma], having made the Vāravantīya upon the Revatī verses its Agniṣṭoma-sāman.
Herein, this matter is subject to doubt: is it from a quality of that very Agniṣṭoma?
From the *vāravantīya* [sāman] comes the fruit of cattle; "one should sacrifice with this" is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Now, is "one should sacrifice with this" a separate ritual action? What is the prima facie view? It is not a separate ritual action; the fruit arises from the accessory (*guṇa*). Why? Because the statement "one should sacrifice with this" refers to that which is already known, not to something unknown; therefore, it is not a further injunction. One who desires cattle [should act] in this manner.

"One should sacrifice"—thus it is said, not "one should sacrifice [in this way]," for how so? "Having performed the Vāravantīya. Moreover, the phrase "of this very [sacrifice]" is a clear statement that there is no other action.
Therefore, the result arises from the accessory—this is the conclusion reached.

This being the case, we reply: in such instances where there are distinct sentences of equal status, the result must be connected with the ritual act itself—as in the statement, "Having performed the Vāravantīya on the Revatī verses for this very [sacrifice]. For this [sacrifice] does not already possess the Revatī verses upon which its Vāravantīya could be based; therefore, the Revatī verses [must be obtained through the ritual act].

The *agniṣṭoma* is a type of one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) that is a modification (*vikṛti*) [of the Jyotiṣṭoma]. It is called *trisṛt* because its *ṛkstotra* is joined with the *triṣṭubh* meter. Among the seven Soma-terminuses (*somasaṃsthā*), such as the *agniṣṭoma* and others, it is called *agniṣṭoma* because it consists of the completion of the *agniṣṭoma* terminus; it is so named due to its nature as a terminus (*saṃsthārūpatvāt*). Furthermore, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), following the *ārbhavapavamāna*, there is the *yājyā*.

The *sāman* is sung; and because the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice is completed by means of it, it is called the *agniṣṭomasāman*. That *sāman* is sung in the *ṛks* dedicated to Agni in the archetype (prakṛti), such as "yadyāyācā vā yannayaḥ.

When one desires cattle, that *sāman* should be sung over the *ṛks* dedicated to Vāyu, beginning with "revatīr naḥ sadhamādaḥ," just as it is employed in the twenty-one-fold *agniṣṭoma* in the archetype. But for one desiring cattle, [the *sāman* is sung over] the *revatīs*.
Mādhava states that one should chant the Vāravantīya Sāman upon these Revatī verses, beginning with "ityādiṣu."

[Page 219] Bhāṣya: [If it were so], they would exist, and the *vāravantīya* would be enjoined with respect to them—thus the sentence would be split! "Now, if it be argued: having taken up the preceding *revatī* verses for this [sāman], and [having enjoined] the *vāravantīya* upon them..."

Having performed [the sacrifice], one should sacrifice with this—thus it is restated. In that case, the term "agniṣṭomasāman" would not be appropriate. If it were said, "Now it occurs in the function of the agniṣṭomasāman," then the phrase "of this very [sacrifice]" would be intended [to apply]. If both were intended to be expressed, there would be a syntactical split; therefore, it is a distinct ritual act.

"Now, how is there no syntactical split (*avākyabheda*) in the case of a different ritual action? [The text says: 'Desiring cattle, one should sacrifice, having performed the *vāravantīya* chant upon the *revatī* verses. Here, a previously existing sacrifice is enjoined as qualified by all the qualifiers; thus, because there is a single purpose and a mutual expectancy when separated, syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) is established. [Objection: But surely there is a difference in meaning, for in this way a new sacrifice (*apūrva*) would have to be performed."

[The opponent says: "In the case of the *revatī* verses, the *vāravantīya* chant is something unprecedented. We say: "No. A sacrifice characterized by the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya* chant is what is enjoined; it is not the production of the *vāravantīya*. Consequently, the *vāravantīya* will be brought forth upon the *revatī* verses, and it is possible to bring it forth. It is said: "There is a relationship between the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya*..."

It would not be prescribed; and in that case, other *sāmans* might also occur in connection with the *revatī* verses, and the *vāravantīya* might occur in connection with other *ṛks*. This is not a fault, because the relationship already established by the word "with" (*latvā*) is expressed for the sake of the sacrifice; thus, the relationship is understood, and both of these meanings are conveyed.
The word *lata* is capable of expressing both the act of bringing forth (*abhinirhṛti*) and the state of being prior in time;

just as in the case of "bring the red one" (*śoṇam ānaya*), the cow already connected with the quality of redness is enjoined by the very word to be brought, and thus there is no split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), so too should it be understood here.

"But even so, there are many things: the *revatī* verses, the *vāravantīya* chant, the connection between them, the sacrifice, and the one desiring cattle. This is not a fault; for although many are heard, only one is enjoined—the sacrifice as qualified [by those elements]. "But surely the *revatī* verses are also enjoined?"
Regarding the *vāravantīya* as well: if it were not enjoined, the sacrifice qualified by it could not be understood at all;
for one cannot enjoin a qualified entity without first enjoining the qualification.

Therefore, when many things are being enjoined, there is no single purpose (*ekārthya*). To this it is replied: "purpose" (*artha*) here denotes the objective (*prayojana*); as many words as express a single objective—

[Page 220] Bhāṣya: They bring about [the result]; that many [words] do not constitute a single sentence. Nor is there the case here where there are multiple purposes; for in this instance, there is no single word that is the enjoiner of multiple intended objects.

The phrase "in the Revatīs" is not merely an enjoiner of the Revatī verses; rather, it is "the Bāravantīya [sāman] in the Revatīs. Here too, within these two words, the word "Bāravantīya" ends in the accusative case.

From this, no intended connection is understood, because there is no deviation from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Even in the case of "having performed" (*śatvā*), the verb *karoti* does not terminate in mere connection, but rather expresses a connection with a further purpose. Thus, the root *yajati* (to sacrifice), being thus qualified, is not for the sake of another; therefore, these word-meanings have a single purpose, and consequently, they constitute a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*). On the other hand, if a result were attributed to the accessory (*guṇa*), then the *vāravantīya* would be for the sake of the function of the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*, and [the injunction] "this is its *agniṣṭoma-sāman*" would follow.

There would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). If it is argued that a sacrifice qualified by all the specific details such as the *revatī* verses and so forth is enjoined for this [sacrifice] mentioned here, even so, the sentence would be split because of the connection with the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*).

"Now, suppose it is argued: 'One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Vāravantīya performed upon the Revatī verses. This cannot be so; because there would be a deficiency [of the rite] due to the absence of another verse and the lack of a specific [textual] injunction. But was it not just stated: 'Indeed, it is possible to perform the Vāravantīya upon the Revatī verses'? It is possible only when there is an explicit statement; in the absence of a statement, they are not grasped by the mention of the Vāravantīya. Well then, there will be such a statement: 'One desiring cattle should bring about the Vāravantīya upon the Revatī verses, and then he should sacrifice'—in this case, the term 'yajeta' (he should sacrifice) is a mere restatement."

If the statement [concerning] the *revatī* verses is connected with the *vāravantīya* chant, then a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) is established, and it is not an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) for the *agniṣṭut*. [Objection: "But since there is a reference to the sacrifice in the words 'one should sacrifice' (*yajeta*), there will be a relationship between this [chant] and the sacrifice as its constituent part (*aṅga*) and purpose (*prayojana*). [Reply: This cannot be so. If it were enjoined as a subordinate part (*aṅgabhāva*) with respect to the sacrifice, there would be no connection with one who desires cattle (*paśukāma*). If there were a connection to both, the sentence would suffer from syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). [Objection: "Then let the connection with the sacrifice be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), and its status as a subordinate part be established by the context (*prakaraṇa*). [Reply: This is not tenable, for direct statement (*śruti*) is indeed more powerful than context. Therefore...
Whether it be a sacrifice having the *vāravantīya* as its quality performed under the *revatī* verses, or a *revatī*-verse sacrifice having the *vāravantīya* as its quality,

we find the subsequent case-ending (*liṅga*)— the word "yajeta"— as the indicator of the injunction regarding the relationship between the sacrifice and the desire for cattle; however, it is not an indicator of the relationship between the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya*.
[Page 221] Bhāṣya:
No direct injunctive [text] is perceived. Therefore, it is established that the sacrifice, qualified by all its adjuncts, is enjoined for one who desires cattle.
"But then, when the sacrifice is being enjoined as thus qualified, that Vāravantīya [chant] upon the Revatī verses..."

"How does it become the Agniṣṭoma-sāman? It is replied: "By virtue of the scriptural statement, it will take the place of the Agniṣṭoma-sāman. For what indeed can a scriptural statement not accomplish? There is no burden too heavy for a scriptural statement. Furthermore, as for what was said regarding "of this very [sacrifice]," since that statement refers to what immediately precedes it, there is no contradiction in taking it to mean "possessing these characteristics" [of the preceding sacrifice].

The word will be used in its secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, the result does not arise from a quality; rather, it is a distinct ritual action possessing its own specific characteristics. Thus, in all such cases, the result is connected to the ritual action itself. (2.2.12)
The section concerning the identity of the *saubhara* and the *nidhana*.

[Topic 28: The connection of desires with the *nidhana* in the *saubhara* chant. In the *saubhara*, because of the mention of the person (*puruṣa-śruteḥ*), there is a connection with desires regarding the *nidhana*. (Pūrva-pakṣa) The traditional text recites: "He who desires rain, he who desires food, and he who desires heaven—let him praise with the *saubhara*; for all desires are indeed contained in the *saubhara*. Following this, it further recites: "One should employ the *hīṣ* as the *nidhana* for one desiring rain; the *ūrg* for one desiring food; and the *jagat* for one desiring heaven. In this regard, the following is considered: what...?

The *saubhara* chant has *dṛṣṭi* as its motive; *hīṣ* is another motive for *dṛṣṭi*, and then the *saubhara* itself is the motive for *dṛṣṭi*. When that [the *saubhara*] has *dṛṣṭi* as its motive, then the *nidhana* of the *saubhara* should be performed with *hīṣ*—thus [it is for one desiring vigor, with *ūrk*].

The word "ja" indicates that the deliberation is the same for one who desires heaven. How can there be a fruit other than *nidhana*? Or how can the scriptural statement be for the purpose of establishing the *nidhana*? If it is thus—[Mādhava says]: *saubhara* is a specific *sāman*; *nidhana* is the final part of a *sāman* divided into five or seven parts; and within that *nidhana*, there are specific variations such as *hoṣā* and so forth.
[Page 222] Bhāṣya:
A connection is being made—namely, "One desiring rain should perform [the rite] with 'hīṣ'";
in that case, the result would be distinct from the *nidhana*. Or, if the connection is thus: "One should make 'hīṣ' the *nidhana*."

— thus, if [the text] were heard for the purpose of establishing the *nidhana*, then the qualification "for one desiring rain" (*dṛṣṭikāmāya*) would be applied to the *saubhara*, and there would be no connection with *hīṣ*.

What, then, is the prima facie view? That another desire is enjoined regarding the *nidhana* of the *saubhara*. Why? Because of the mention of the person; here there is a hearing of human effort in the form "one should do. That must be stated when a connection is to be made between the one desiring rain and *hīṣ*.

It exists, but not in connection with the *nidhana* of the *saubhara*; for in that case, it is already established by the force of the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) itself that "one should perform the *saubhara* together with its subsidiaries. Therefore, from the expression of human effort in the phrase "one should perform," we understand that whichever alternative makes the expression of human effort meaningful, that is the preferred alternative; and in this case, it is meaningful.
"The fruit is subsequent to the *nidhana*": therefore, there is one desire in the *saubhara*, and a second desire even by means of the distinct *nidhana*.
Alternatively, "for one desiring rain"—this is a scriptural mention (*śruti*) of a person; that is, for one who desires rain.
That person is expressed by the word "one who desires to see" (*dṛṣṭikāma*). In this case, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) would enjoin [the act] with respect to the opposite alternative;

however, in the other case, the word "one who desires to see"—being a term denoting a person—would indicate the *saubhara* chant through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and thus there would be the fault of using a word in a figurative sense. And between the domain of direct statement and secondary indication, direct statement is the proper course, not secondary indication. Therefore, we perceive that [the injunction applies] to the *nidhana*.
"A second desire—thus [it is said]. And in this way, there will be an abundance of results; therefore, there is another desire at the *nidhana*."
[Sūtra 26: Since everything has already been stated as being desired, there would be a scriptural mention of desire regarding that;
however, the repetition is for the purpose of the *nidhana*. (Conclusion) [Commentary:
The word "but" (*vā*) sets aside the previous position. And that which was stated—that [the repetition] pertains to the *nidhana*—is not the case.

Regarding the phrase "another desire" (*aparaḥ kāmaḥ*): the connection is not made in this way—that one should perform [the rite] with the *hīṣ* [interjection] for the sake of one desiring rain. How then? [The connection is: "The *hīṣ* is the *nidhana* of the *saubhara*.
How so? Because when the *hīṣ* is connected with the desire for rain, it becomes the *nidhana*.
[Page 223] The connection "one should perform" would not have been established; in that case, the statement "hīṣ is the *nidhana*" would not be appropriate.

If there were a connection with both, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), and one might infer that the word "*nidhana*" was recited erroneously; however, it has been stated that such a thing is not an erroneous recitation. Therefore, there is no fault in connecting it with the desire for rain.
Therefore, there is no result other than the *nidhana*.
[Objection: "But then, how is it that there is no syntactical split (*avākyabheda*) regarding the connection with the *nidhana*?"

It is said: for one who desires sight, the Saubhara exists; the Nidhana of the Saubhara (the attainment of the Saubhara) certainly exists; in that case, one should employ "hīṣ"—this very meaning is what is enjoined. Therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); hence, this is a restrictive rule regarding the Nidhana.
It is understood. In this very way, it should be stated as "ūrk" and "ja-";
for since the entire Saubhara has "ūrj" as its *ṛṣṭi* (concluding syllable) and aims at heaven, the Saubhara can be indicated by means of words expressing desire.
Why is it indicated? The repetition of the recitation is for the purpose of the *nidhana*.
(He will establish the rule regarding the Nidhana—this is the meaning. (2.2.13 Śrauta Sūtra).

Now begins the section concerning the fact that the *cathā* belongs as an auxiliary to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.

[The opponent’s view: "But its own quality, because it is connected with a specific season, should necessitate a different ritual action, since that connection is not a subordinate element [of the original sacrifice].

(Pūrvapakṣa) There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, [enjoined] thus: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. With reference to that, it is heard in scripture: "If the Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara as its *sāman*, one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu; if it has the Bṛhat as its *sāman*, [one should draw] those beginning with the Śukra cup."
"If it has the *gajat-sāman*, [it is] for the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice"—thus it is said. In this regard, a doubt arises:
is a specific *graha*-offering enjoined for the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, or for a separate ritual characterized by the *Rathantara-sāman* and the *Bṛhat-sāman*? If, by the mention of the *Rathantara-sāman*...

By the mention of the *ṭaitsāma*, the Jyotiṣṭoma is denoted; therefore, it is a specific feature of its *bahv-āgratā* (many-pointedness). Alternatively, if it is not denoted, then it belongs to a different ritual act—this is the point.
What, then, is the prima facie view? It belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma because of the context (*prakaraṇa*). This being the position reached:

"However, it is a quality [of another sacrifice], because of its connection with a *kratu* (sacrificial rite). Here, the word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the previous position: this is not the case regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma. Why? Because of the connection with a *kratu*. How then? It refers to a different ritual action (*karmāntara*). [Objection: But surely this kind of statement—"having the *Rathantara* as its *sāman*, having the *Bṛhat* as its *sāman*"—is a description of the Jyotiṣṭoma *kratu* itself.

[Reply: No, we say; if there were no connection with a distinct *kratu*, it would be a description of the Jyotiṣṭoma. However, this is a connection with a separate *kratu*. How is there a connection with a separate *kratu*?
Is it so? Or how could there not be a connection with the Śata-sacrifice?—thus [it is asked].

"If the existence of the *rathantara* or the existence of the *bṛhat* is the cause of the specific greatness, then there would be no connection with the Śata-sacrifice—if, upon seeing the *rathantara*, the *sāman* exists..."

Then there is the sequence beginning with the *aindravāyava* cup and the sequence beginning with the *mukhya* cup; following that is the injunction of the qualities (*guṇavidhi*) for the *jyotiṣṭoma*. Now, does it possess the *rathantara-sāman* or the *bṛhat-sāman*, or neither?
[Page 225] Chapter 2, Section 3.
168. Bhāṣya:

The indicative mark (*nimitta*); from that follows the connection with the hundred sacrifices. What is the meaning of the phrase "if it has the *Rathantara* as its *Sāman*"? This is the meaning: if the *Rathantara-Sāman* is the qualification of this sacrifice (*kratu*).

—Thus [it is said]. Why is this so? Because of the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the compound word; for a compound occurs only between words that possess semantic capacity, and such capacity exists only when there is a relationship of qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*).
Furthermore, a qualifier must be something unique (*asādhāraṇa*); in this case, the meaning is as follows: if it were *rathantara* alone...

"Sāman" means only the *ṛk* itself and nothing else; furthermore, there are many *sāmans* belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma, such as the Gāyatra and others. Therefore, these two words are not denotative of the Jyotiṣṭoma. Consequently, even if it were an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) for the Jyotiṣṭoma on account of the context (*prakaraṇa*), [it would still not be so].
—thus it is understood; nevertheless, setting that aside, by virtue of the direct statement (*vākya*), it must belong to both the *rathantara-sāman* and the *bṛhat-sāman*.
[Objection: "But just as the Jyotiṣṭoma is not characterized by the *rathantara-sāman*, so too it is not for the other two."

Is there some [sacrifice] characterized by the Rathantara-sāman? It is replied: this sentence—"If the Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara-sāman"—will establish a distinct ritual action (karmāntara) characterized by the Rathantara-sāman. [Objection: But there is no injunctive word here. [Reply: It is said:

there is this word "should be" (syāt). [Objection: He says, "This cannot enjoin, because due to its connection with the word 'if' (yadi), such a word serves only to indicate a condition for something already existing."

"It exists, but not for the purpose of an injunction. To this we reply: regarding this sentence beginning with "if," namely, "If the Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara-sāman," there exists an intermediate sentence: "The Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara-sāman. The meaning of that intermediate sentence is one thing, and the meaning of the sentence beginning with "if" is another. The sentence beginning with "if" cannot itself enjoin; rather, it is the intermediate sentence that will enjoin it. Furthermore, the existence of either the Rathantara-sāman or the Bṛhat-sāman, being heard as a condition (*nimitta*), is not purposeless.

It occurs [in this way]. Therefore, if the connection with "yadi" (if) were not intended to be expressed, and that [connection] being unintended, this sentence—"the Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara-sāman"—would be for the purpose of enjoining the Rathantara-sāman as a permanent rule; in that case, "yadi" would be meaningless.

Alternatively, one may supply the word "roceta" (should so desire), such that it means "if he should so desire. Or else, it is just as in these cases: "One should eat ṣāṣṭika rice with milk; if one should eat śāli rice, one should sprinkle it with curd."
[Page 226] Bhāṣya: By a sentence of this kind, the eating of *śāli* rice is enjoined;
in the same way, it should be understood that here too [the following] is enjoined: "If the Soma sacrifice should have the *Rathantara-sāman*..."

"One should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu"—thus it is said. But how, then, is the eating of *śāli* rice enjoined by that sentence? It is replied: the connection should be understood through transposition—namely, "if one should desire the addition of curd, one should eat *śāli* rice.

[Objection: "But surely we do not find the optative suffix following the root *iṣ* (to desire); rather, they record that suffix as following the root *sic* (to sprinkle). [Reply: That suffix indeed follows the root *sic*.

When uttered, it conveys the sense of desire; for we consider it to be used in the expression of a wish—thus, here too, if the meaning were "one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu" in the sense that one *wishes* to draw them, then it would mean "one should perform [the sacrifice] so as to have the Rathantara-sāman. But if this were the case, it would be a mere matter of wish, not an injunction regarding a specific order of the cups. It is replied: just as in this worldly sentence, if...

Just as one understands from the mention of "curd as a condiment" (*dadhyupasecana*) that one should eat rice with curd as a condiment—because it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the statement "one should eat rice"—so too here, because of the mention of the specific priority (*agrātā*) and because it forms a single syntactical unit with that, it is understood that the *Rathantara-sāman* is qualified by that priority. Alternatively, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) here expresses the relation of cause and effect:

"The Soma sacrifice characterized by the *Rathantara-sāman* must be made the cause for the cups (*graha*) having the *Aindravāyava* first. Therefore, because of its connection with the entire sacrifice (*kratu*), this accessory (*guṇa*) should give rise to a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).
In this way, the conjunction of the entire sacrifice will become meaningful.
Furthermore, there must be a preceding cause (nimitta) and a subsequent effect (naimittika). How so? For it is only when a cause exists that the effect can come to be, not when it does not exist.

And that which is yet to come is not existent; furthermore, the *Rathantara* Sāman is something yet to come—how then can it be the cause for a specific excellence of the vessel (*graha*) belonging to a prior time?
Moreover, it is beyond doubt that the [sacrifice] in the *Jagatī* meter is a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*), and by analogy with that, the others are as well.
It is understood that this refers to a different ritual action; therefore, it is not an injunction for a group of Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices.
