But because of the difference in gender for a single [entity], it might be stated for the sake of a specific purpose; [nevertheless,] oneness [is established] because it is a statement of a subordinate quality (guṇavākya).
(Siddhānta) Bhāṣya: By the word "but" (tu), the previous position is set aside. It is not as was said—that [the mantra] expresses the performer of the sacrifice.

—Thus [it is asked]. How then? [The answer is: It is a specific feature regarding the precedence of the cups (*grahāgratā*) belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma itself. Why? Because of the power of the context (*prakaraṇa*). [Objection: But was it not said that, by the force of the sentence (*vākya*), it belongs to another sacrifice—one characterized by the *Rathantara* sāman or the *Bṛhat* sāman? This has been refuted: even within the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, there are those characterized by the *Rathantara* sāman and those by the *Bṛhat* sāman. [Objection continued: Again, this is criticized because since the Jyotiṣṭoma possesses many sāmans, the qualification by either the *Rathantara* or the *Bṛhat* cannot be established. To this it is replied: the qualification is indeed established.

Because the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are optional, there exists that performance in which the Rathantara is absent; and there also exists that performance characterized by the presence of the Rathantara Sāman. Thus, this Rathantara, by its very existence, serves as a differentiator because of its uniqueness. Therefore, [it applies to] the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Thus, there are those for whom the *rathantara* is the *sāman* and those for whom the *bṛhat* is the *sāman*.

Now, as for what was said—that there must be a prior cause and not a subsequent one—this is not so; for a cause can certainly exist even if it is yet to come, just as the performance of agricultural and domestic tasks occurs because of the thought "it will rain. Moreover, that is observed in experience.

And this is a scriptural sign (*nimitta*); it must be according to the literal statement. Furthermore, this optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the word "syāt" occurs with reference to all three times. Therefore, even a future event may serve as a sign. As for the claim that "the *jagatsāman*" is a different ritual action—that is because of its similarity [to the other].

[Objection: "The Rathantarasāman [rite] is also a different ritual action. [Reply: Because a Jagatsāman is impossible, it would follow that it is a different ritual action; however, since the names 'Rathantarasāman' and 'Bṛhatsāman' refer to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice itself, it is not a different ritual action. (2.3.1) [Topic 1: The Rathantarasāman and Bṛhatsāman Rites are Not Different from the Jyotiṣṭoma] The doubt arises whether the Rathantarasāman and the Bṛhatsāman rites are different from the Jyotiṣṭoma or not. The opponent maintains: "The Rathantarasāman is a different ritual action. Why? Because the name 'Jyotiṣṭoma' is applied to a sacrifice that possesses both the Rathantarasāman and the Bṛhatsāman. However, when the Rathantarasāman alone is mentioned, the name 'Jyotiṣṭoma' does not apply, because the Jyotiṣṭoma cannot exist with only one of these two sāmans. Therefore, since the name 'Jyotiṣṭoma' is absent, the Rathantarasāman must be a different ritual action. The established conclusion (siddhānta) is: It is not a different ritual action. Why? Because the name 'Jyotiṣṭoma' is applied to the sacrifice characterized by the Rathantarasāman. Just as the name 'Devadatta' applies to a person even when he is seen only with one eye, so too the name 'Jyotiṣṭoma' applies to the sacrifice even when it is characterized by only one of the two sāmans. Furthermore, the Rathantarasāman is prescribed as an alternative to the Bṛhatsāman; therefore, the Rathantarasāman is not a different ritual action. As for the argument regarding the impossibility of the Jagatsāman, that is irrelevant, because the Rathantarasāman is indeed possible within the Jyotiṣṭoma. Thus, it is established that the Rathantarasāman and the Bṛhatsāman rites are not different from the Jyotiṣṭoma. (2.3.1) [Topic 2: The Abhyuditeṣṭi is a Modification of the Darśapūrṇamāsa] In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa), there is a passage: "If one should perform the full moon sacrifice when the moon has already risen, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. Because the name 'Vaiśvānara' is not found in the original Darśapūrṇamāsa context. Since the name 'Vaiśvānara' is not mentioned there, and since the deity is different, this must be a different ritual action. The established conclusion is: It is a modification of the Darśapūrṇamāsa. Why? Because the Vaiśvānara offering is connected to the same procedure (tantra) as the Darśapūrṇamāsa. The Vaiśvānara offering is not an independent ritual action; rather, it is a modification of the Darśapūrṇamāsa. How so? Because the Vaiśvānara offering is connected to the same procedure as the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and because the Vaiśvānara offering is mentioned in proximity to the Darśapūrṇamāsa. Now, the section concerning the qualification for other sacrificial rites (*kratvantara*).
In the Aveṣṭi sacrifice, because of its connection with the term "yajña," it is said that the ritual (kratu) is the primary element. || 3 ||

There is a triad of kings: "A king desiring sovereignty (*khārā*) should sacrifice with the Rājasūya. With reference to that [sacrifice], they prescribe an offering named the Śunāsīrīya-iṣṭi: "An oblation of rice-cake on eight potsherds for Agni; gold is the sacrificial fee," and so forth. With reference to that [iṣṭi], it is enjoined: "If he should sacrifice as a Brāhmaṇa, having placed the oblation for Bṛhaspati in the middle, he should offer the oblation."

"Having offered, one should sprinkle [the oblation] with clarified butter: if he is a Kṣatriya, [he offers] to Indra; if he is a Vaiśya, [he offers] to the Viśvedevas. Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the mention of the Brāhmaṇas and others for the purpose of indicating a condition (*nimitta*), or is this sacrifice enjoined for the Brāhmaṇas and others?
"In what way would it be for the purpose of a condition? Or in what way would it be an injunction of a sacrifice?"

—Thus [it is said]. If the term *rājanya* applies to Brāhmaṇas and others as well in some manner, then it has the sense of a cause (*nimitta*); but if it applies only to the Kṣatriya, then such scriptural mentions are merely restrictive (*prāpaka*).

What, then, is the prima facie conclusion? That the word has a causal sense (*nimittārthatā*). Therefore, it is described in this way: the word "king" (*rājan*) is etymological (*yaugika*); he whose function is kingship (*rājya*) is a king. What, then, is the function of a king? The inhabitants of Āryāvarta employ the term "kingship" for the protection of the countryside and cities, as well as for the extraction [of taxes] from them; and the learned teach that "the function of a king is kingship. By this, we consider—

"He who possesses this action is the king"— just as, for example, those who did not know a certain man named Udamegha, but knew his son as Mededhi, would be able to infer that "he who is his father is Udamegha," because such a designation applies specifically to the son of Udamegha; in the same way, the word "king" [is applied] due to the connection with kingship.
—Thus it is understood.

—“But surely, even when a Kṣatriya does not subsist by the duty of protecting the country and the city, speakers in the Andhra region still apply the word ‘rājan’ to him. We do not say that they do not apply it;
rather, because the word ‘rājan’ has its basis in a specific function, [the term applies] also through connection with that [function].

[Page 229] We shall now demonstrate that the word "king" (rājan) applies here; for people indeed employ the word "king" even for a Kṣatriya who possesses those [qualities]. Since this is established, and by virtue of the context as well as the co-occurrence with the word "if" (yadi), there will be an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi) pertaining specifically to the Rājasūya, and not [to other sacrifices].
It will prescribe a different ritual for the Brāhmaṇa and the Vaiśya.

Alternatively, the universal practice that contradicts the universal practice would lack authority; for those local people indeed accept the universal practice. Moreover, worldly matters are not subject to dispute.
They are more reliable than those who sing [the Vedas] incorrectly; likewise, the conduct of those inhabitants of Āryāvarta—
who are devoted to the means of acquiring words and their meanings, who speak correctly, and who perform their duties—
is more excellent than that of the Mlecchas dwelling in border regions.

Therefore, the word "rājan" (king) is used in its etymological sense; the scriptural mentions [of the classes] are for the purpose of indicating the causal conditions, and the injunction regarding the qualities of the Rājasūya is not a separate ritual action.

This being the position, we reply: In the case of the Aveṣṭi, however, the mention of the Brāhmaṇas and others is primarily for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratu*), intended to enjoin the Aveṣṭi sacrifice for the Brāhmaṇas and so forth, and not for the purpose of indicating a causal condition. Why?

Because [the right] has not been attained by Brāhmaṇas and Vaiśyas. How is there non-attainment? Because the Rājasūya is prescribed for the Kṣatriya—[in the injunction]: "A king should sacrifice with the Rājasūya. [Objection: But was it not said that the word "king" (rājan) is etymological? [Reply: This too is incorrect, because it denotes a caste (jāti). [Objection: It was said that since both meanings are denoted, due to the connection with the word "if" (yadi) and the context, it is not logical to enjoin a different ritual action. To this, we reply: the denotation of both is not tenable. Why? If, first of all, it were a word denoting caste...
The King said: "In this way, because it is his duty, his sovereignty (*rājya*) will consist in the protection of the realm;
therefore, the usage of those residing in Āryāvarta will not be contradicted.
Now, if the word 'sovereignty' (*rājya*) were eternally connected with the act of protecting..."

The word "rājan" (king) will be based on that [act of ruling] as the cause for its application to the Kṣatriya caste; thus, its usage among the Āndhras will not be contradictory. Therefore, one must not accept—on the basis of observing such usage—that both the words "rājan" and "rājya" (kingdom) are eternally connected to the caste and the act of protection respectively. What, then, is the final determination? It is the action of one belonging to the royal caste.
[Page 230]

Therefore, protection is expressed by the word "rājya" (sovereignty); for thus the learned, remembering this, apply the suffix *ṣyañ* to denote its action (*karma*), and they do not record the elision of the suffix to denote its agent (*kartṛ*), nor the restoration of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
Consequently, sovereignty is the king's action; the king is not the agent of sovereignty.

[Objection: "But surely, whoever performs the protection of the country and the city, the world addresses that person with the word 'king' (rājan). [Reply: It is said in response: The world employs [the term] through connection (*yoga*); the word *rājya* is well-known in the sense of "protection. However, we have stated that this word *rājya* in the sense of protection exists because of its connection to a king (*rājayogāt*). Therefore, the word *rājan* is not established by popular usage alone; rather, the word *rājya* arises from its connection to that [king], while the word *rājan* is applied even to a Brāhmaṇa or a Vaiśya when they possess that [quality of protecting].
It is so employed; however, they do not remember it thus—that one is a "king" simply by virtue of connection with kingship.

As for what was said—"That which is inferred from the inference [of the act] to be the agent of kingship is the king, just as Udamegha is the father of Śrādamegha"—it is replied: the application [of the term] is based on inference.
We infer that "the king is the performer of the kingdom," and we observe people employing this [expression] directly with respect to a Kṣatriya. Likewise, we also infer the connection:
"the king is the performer of the kingdom"; however, [the expression] "the kingdom is the action of the king" [is used].

They remember; and while inferring, they have inferred memory, whereas while remembering, they perceive [the object] directly through perception. Therefore, in that case, memory is stronger—so it is said. "Whosoever exercises sovereignty, there people employ the word 'king'; it is not that the king's action is sovereignty. Therefore, we consider that the connection with sovereignty is the basis for the application of the word 'king'."
The cause [of the application of the word "kingdom"] is the connection with a king (*rājayoga*), and not the connection with a kingdom (*rājya*)—this is what we do not say;
that we understand the connection with a king to be the cause for the application of the word "kingdom" based on usage (*prayoga*).
How then? Based on traditional authority (*smṛti*). For traditional authority is more powerful than usage.
From the application [of the rule], memory may be inferred.

However, according to the *Siddhāntakaumudī*, following the *vārttika* "rājā'se" on the basis of the sūtra "patyantapurohitādibhyo yak" (Pāṇini 5.1.128), it prescribes the suffix *yak* in the case of "rājakarma rājyam" (the king’s duty is sovereignty). In both instances, the meaning is the same; thus, there is consistency with the present context.
[Page 231] Chapter 2, Section 3.
175 bhā.

Furthermore, it has been stated that the status of being the cause for the application of the term "kingdom" (rājya) is inconsistent; for even when one does not perform the protection of the realm, people of Andhra still call him a "king. [Objection: But is it not the case that the application of the term "kingdom" follows from the connection with a king? [Response: This too is inconsistent, for it is not necessarily so for a king...

"Everything, including the blinking and the movement of the eyes, is called 'sovereignty' (rājya). If we were to say that [the soul] is the instrumental cause (nimittabhāva) of this activity, then we would be subject to such a reproach;
however, we maintain that it is the *muktyā* (liberation/cessation) that constitutes the instrumental cause. Therefore, whatever action belongs to one of royal lineage—"

We accept that the word "king" is qualified by birth (*jāti*). As for what was said—that even the Śūdras accept someone as a king because of his connection with sovereignty—that has been refuted: the application [of the term] is weaker than the traditional law (*smṛti*). As for what was said—that the inhabitants of Āryāvarta are authoritative compared to other customs—it has been stated that the usage of the word is equal in both cases. Therefore, the word "king" is based on birth; likewise, because of the connection with the sacrifice (the *Rājasūya*), the injunction for the sacrifice is the *Aveṣṭi*. (2.3.2)
Sūtra:
"The section concerning the injunction of the *pradhāna* (the principal rite).
[It applies] to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), because it is subsidiary to everything. (4)

The Bhāṣya states: They recite this—"A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring, a Rājanya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn. In this regard, a doubt arises: Is the mention of the Brāhmaṇa and others for the purpose of an occasion—that is, that Brāhmaṇas and others, when establishing the fires, should do so in spring and the other seasons—or is the establishment of the fires (ādhāna) itself enjoined for the Brāhmaṇas and others? How would there be the status of an occasion, and how would there be the injunction of the establishment?
This depends on whether the two words "Brāhmaṇa" and "in spring" are connected with one another.
Therefore, hearing [the Veda] is for the sake of the sign. Now, "a Brāhmaṇa should have faith"—this is the injunction of faith for the Brāhmaṇa. It is the same for the Rājanya and others as well.
Why?

What, then, is the conclusion reached?—that the mention [of these words] is for the sake of an occasion (*nimitta*). These words are devoid of form; what is the similarity of the occasion? [It is] the Brāhmaṇas—

[Page 232] There is a co-utterance (*samuccāraṇa*) of the Brāhmaṇas and others with the spring season and so forth; thus, that which was previously unknown is now made known. [Objection: "But there is indeed a co-utterance of the Brāhmaṇas and others even with the act of establishing the sacred fires (*ādhāna*). [Reply: Certainly there is such co-utterance, yet it is not the case that their connection with the *ādhāna* is unknown.

By what is it obtained and known?—it is by the scriptural injunctions regarding desires (*kāma-śruti*). What are these scriptural injunctions regarding desires? "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice," "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *darśa-pūrṇamāsa* [new and full moon sacrifices]," and so forth. How is the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires) [established] by these scriptural injunctions?
Is it obtained? It is said: by implication. One should act in such a way that the *agnihotra* is accomplished; one should act in such a way that the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are accomplished.
And these rites are not accomplished without the *gārhapatya*, *āhavanīya*, *anvāhāryapacana*, and so forth; for they prescribe that [the oblation] is offered in the *āhavanīya*.
"He offers; thereby Soma becomes sacrificed for and pleased by him"—thus it is stated, and so forth. By implication, this means that the Āhavanīya fire and other such fires must be established;

since that cannot be accomplished without the *ādhāna* (the rite of laying the sacred fires), it is understood that the *ādhāna* itself must also be performed. By whom should it be performed? By those for whom there are scriptural injunctions regarding specific desires (*kāmaśrutayaḥ*). And these apply without distinction to Brāhmaṇas and the other classes. Therefore, the connection to the *ādhāna* belongs to these [classes].

[The word] "viditaḥ" [is used]. Moreover, if the connection with the Brāhmaṇas and others were enjoined by both [the words], there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). For in that case, a single meaning would not be enjoined!
Therefore, the scriptural texts have the sense of indicating a condition (*nimitta*)—this is the position reached.

This being the case, we reply: "In the case of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*), because it is subsidiary to everything. These scriptural statements are the means for establishing the fire-installation. Why? Because the fire-installation is not stated by any one of the means of proof—such as direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth—to be subsidiary to all ritual acts; rather, it is because the fires are subsidiary to everything, and the principal act is subsidiary to them. What follows from this? If that is so, [then the following applies].

"The fires are obtained through the scriptural injunctions regarding desire (*kāmaśruti*), not through the act of laying them (*ādhāna*). [Objection: "But surely the laying of the fires is the means for obtaining the fires. [Reply: It is said in response: "The laying of the fires is not the sole means for these fires; rather, it is like the production of other substances."
"He becomes recognized"—thus [it is stated] in the Kāśmīra-Kṛṣṇa manuscript.

[Page 233] And since means such as purchase (*krayaṇa*) and so forth exist for the fires, the same applies to the sacrificial fires (*agni*); thus, production is not mandatory. Therefore, in one case the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) would apply, while in another it would not—whichever [case it may be].

In this view, there is no [inherent] attainment; rather, it is that very injunction which will necessitate the production [of the fires] for Brāhmaṇas and others, as in the statement: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires for his own sake. When this [injunction] exists, then the Āhavanīya and other fires become established solely for one's own sake, and not otherwise. And this being the case, it is understood that the Agnihotra and other rites are not to be performed with artificial or borrowed fires; therefore, only those fires produced by oneself (ātrima) are [valid] for them.
The practitioner (sādhaka) is thus determined. And how is it understood that the installation (ādhāna) has the self as its purpose?

For the middle voice ending (ātmanepada) in the word "bādadhīta" is possible only when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent; in the absence of this statement, if one were to resort solely to the scriptural injunctions regarding desire (kāma-śruti), the installation would not have the self as its purpose.
Moreover, while these direct scriptural injunctions for the installation exist, the injunctions regarding desire cannot override them.

It would be necessary to postulate another scriptural injunction for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), such that these [other] scriptural passages would be mere restatements of the already established *ādhāna*.

If these [passages] did not exist, those who do not accept a separate scriptural injunction for the *ādhāna* would have to accept such an injunction, because the scriptural passages concerning specific desires (*kāmaśruti*) speak of the *agnihotra* and other rites which are impossible to perform without it.

However, since these [passages] do exist, for those for whom the *ādhāna* has been explicitly stated, [the *kāmaśruti* passages] refer to the *agnihotra* and so forth as being dependent upon that very *ādhāna*.

It is understood that the subsequent scriptural injunctions regarding desire (*kāma-śruti*) refer to those [who have already established the fires]. Here it is said: there exists a scriptural injunction for the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) as an independent act, namely, "He who, knowing thus, establishes the fire, overcomes his rival who seeks to prevail. Accordingly, the scriptural mentions of Brāhmaṇas and others are intended to specify the occasions (*nimitta*) for that which has already been established.
[The opponent says: "They will exist; this repetition is for the purpose of prescribing the collection [of materials].
[We reply: No, we say this, because this sentence is distinct from the sentence prescribing the collection of materials.
For one thing conveys a different meaning—namely, "he places the fire-pan on the altar"—and another conveys "he pours water [into it]."
"For when there is the prescription of a single meaning, there is a single sentence; however, these two meanings are distinct, therefore there is a split of the sentence here.
To this it is replied: since the scriptural injunction "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring" exists...
The repeated mention (*punar-śruti*) does not enjoin the act of kindling (*ādhāna*) alone; rather, it enjoins water as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*).
When that [water] is enjoined for a single purpose, it does not result in multiple purposes. [Objection: "But..."
"This rule is for one who possesses faith; that repetition of the text is for the sake of a specific quality. We say: "No.
That first text is connected with the Brāhmaṇas and others, while this is a mere repetition (punar-śruti) standing alone.
Why?

For she (the Vedic text) enjoins by means of a word; we observe a sign occurring therein: "This is the praiseworthy establishment [of the fires]"—thus he says. From that, we understand the praiseworthiness of the establishment. And thus, we maintain that the scriptural statement "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires" is the injunctive text (*vidhāyikā śruti*), and not some other statement of praise contradicts our position; for it is possible that what is enjoined by one [text] may be praised by another.

It is for the purpose of saying "it is praised. However, if it were said that this [passage] is injunctive (*vidhāyaka*), then the established position (*mata-pakṣa*) would be contradicted. How so? An injunction (*vidhāna*) is the making known of what was previously unknown. If a new thing (*apūrva*) were made known by a statement of praise, then the *piṇḍa* would not have been made known as something new;
in that case, the word whose function is to make known the new would be obstructed! But it is not so.

When the injunction is expressed by the optative suffix (liṅ), the statement of praise is subordinated; for even when the injunction is known through another sentence, the statement of praise is still logically possible. Furthermore, that which is the injunction is conveyed by direct audition (śruti), whereas praise is understood through syntactical connection (vākya); and direct audition is more authoritative than syntactical connection.
"But is this not also a sentence: 'A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires'? It is replied:

In this case, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) prescribes the act of establishing the fires (*ādhāna*), which is its own primary meaning; however, by means of the connection with the Brāhmaṇa and other [classes], it praises the meaning of another word—that one who thus acts against his rival or enemy.
"It endures"—thus [it is said]. [Objection: "But surely, you have concluded that the injunction of multiple attributes occurs through a single sentence.

[Response: This is not a fault; for it has been stated that when a sentence is intent upon enjoining an attribute, there is indeed an injunction of multiple attributes—according to the rule: "But those attributes should be enjoined because they are not divided [from the action], provided they are not established by another [means] regarding the object of the injunction" (Jaimini Sūtra 2.2.6). Therefore, while the scriptural text connected with the Brāhmaṇas and others is injunctive, this [present text] is a restatement of the fire-laying (*ādhāna*) alone.
It is established that the procedure for the collection of materials has been commenced.

As for what was stated [at 176.17], that "if multiple qualities were enjoined, there would be a syntactical split" (*vākyabheda*), this would indeed be a syntactical split if two things qualified by those quality-injunctions were to be enjoined; however, a single installation (*ādhāna*) qualified by both qualifiers will be enjoined.

[Page 235] Bhāṣya: Therefore, there will be no split in the sentence. Consequently, it is established that the scriptural injunctions are the means for enjoining the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) for Brāhmaṇas and the other classes. (2.3.3) [Adhikaraṇa].
Now begins the section concerning the subordinate status of the Dātrāyana and other [subsidiaries].
[The view that] there is another injunction regarding the *ayanāni* because of the attachment of a specific name.

(Pūrvapakṣa 1) The *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are prescribed as the archetype (*prakṛti*), and it is stated: "One desiring offspring should sacrifice with the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*; one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *Sākaṃprasthāpya*; one desiring food should sacrifice with the *Saṃkramayajña*. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the fruit [resulting] from these merely due to a quality (*guṇa*) of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices themselves, or are they distinct rituals (*karmāntara*) of this kind? What is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)?
— "It is another ritual act. Why? Because of the attachment of a specific name (*saṃjñopabandhāt*).

Although, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the word *yajati*, it is understood that this is indeed the same sacrifice previously mentioned, nevertheless, because it does not bear that name, it is understood that a different sacrifice is to be enjoined.
Sūtra Bhāṣya Sūtra.
And because [the agent] is devoid of qualities, there is an injunction for action. (Pūrvapakṣa 2)
Furthermore, no quality (*guṇa*) is perceived here that the injunction (*codanā*) might intend to enjoin;

and if it were not a different sacrifice, [the injunction] would be utterly meaningless. Moreover, if a quality were being enjoined, then a connection between the sacrifice and that quality would be understood—and thus its performance [would follow].
If it were prescribed—meaning, if it were not being restated as something already known—then only the sacrifice would be understood; thus, its performance would be understood as what is enjoined.

And the sentence is completed with respect to the fruit. (Pūrvapakṣa 3. For this reason also, it is a different rite. How so? Because the sentence is completed with respect to the fruit: "One desiring offspring should sacrifice. Thus, for one desiring offspring, the sacrifice is enjoined as the means; it is indeed enjoined.
If so, it is a different action.
[Page 236] Sūtra: "Or rather, it is a modification, because of the context. (Siddhānta) *The reading in the Kātyāyana-Śrautasūtra is "sākaṃ prasthāyīyena" (with the Sākaṃprasthāyīya).*

The Bhāṣya states: "In this manner, the qualification for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices itself would apply to rites of this kind, such as the Dākṣāyaṇayajña and others; thus, the context (prakaraṇa) is maintained."
Sūtra:
And because of the observation of an indicative mark [the rule is established].

(Siddhānta and Hetu) Bhāṣya: An indicative mark also demonstrates this point: "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa for thirty years, if one is a performer of the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice; [otherwise], for three [years]."

"One should sacrifice for exactly fifteen years; for it is here that that perfection is attained. One should sacrifice at two full-moon festivals and two new-moon festivals; for it is indeed here that that perfection comes to be. If the Dākṣāyaṇayajña is merely the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices themselves, then [it is as follows].

In that case, the purpose would be the possession of thirty [qualities], and consequently, it would be logical for him to receive the favor of those thirty qualities; therefore, this too is not a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*).
Sūtra: "The attachment of a name [is] due to its quality" (10).
(Ābhāsa-nirṇaya. Bhāṣya: As for what was stated—that it is a different rite because of the attachment of a name—if the word *dākṣāyaṇa*...

In no way whatsoever can it be construed as a term for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; therefore, it must be a distinct ritual (*karmāntara*). However, it is possible to understand it through its connection with the quality of repetition (*āvṛtti-guṇa-sambandha*)—namely, "the *ayana*" (course). Here, "repetition" is what is meant by *ayana*; "these belong to Dakṣa" are the *Dākṣas*, and their *ayana* is the *Dākṣāyaṇa*. But who is Dakṣa? One who is energetic (*utsāhī*). Thus...
Even if [the opponent] maintains that there is a simultaneous departure (*sahaprasthāna*), meaning a connection of qualities (*guṇasambandha*), this applies everywhere.

If it is possible to state a connection of qualities between the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, why is it said that the sacrifice being perceived is something else? Or rather, why should the context (*prakaraṇa*) be set aside?
Sūtra Bhāṣya:
The conclusion is not distinct [from the preceding]. (Śrauta-nirṇaya 2)

As for what was said—that the sentence is complete with respect to the fruit, meaning that the performance of the sacrifice is enjoined for one desiring offspring and so forth—it is not so; for the completion [of the sentence] with respect to the fruit is indistinguishable from those [other cases].
[Page 237]
Chapter 2, Section 3.

Other sentences that are free from doubt regarding the result of a quality— those sentences which enjoin a result for a quality— are concluded as being statements of the result of a quality (such as, "for one desiring sensory power, [he should offer] with curd").

"One should offer oblations"—such [statements] as these are not distinct from that [case], for here too a result is declared to arise from a subordinate factor (guṇa). [Objection: "How is it that this is not connected thus: 'One desiring offspring should perform the sacrifice'? [Response: How then [is it connected]? It is: "One desiring offspring should perform the *aṣṭakā-yajña*. Here, by the term "*aṣṭakā-yajña*," the connection of the sacrifice with its specific time and the performer is indicated, but not a different sacrifice. Therefore, the result is declared to arise from a subordinate factor within the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices under discussion; no other sacrifice is enjoined. Thus...
This is to be understood from the *Sākaṃprasthāpya* and the *Saṃkrama-yajña*—thus [ends the section].
(2.3.40) Bhāṣya.
Now begins the section concerning whether those [rites] associated with specific materials and deities constitute distinct sacrifices.

[Topic: The Consecration of the Animal. Sūtra 12: "And the consecration [is subsidiary] because it is not mentioned in the context and because it does not have the word 'action' [as its primary referent]. (Purvapaksha) Something is taught independently of any specific context: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal dedicated to Vayu; one desiring Brahmanic glory should offer a pap (caru) dedicated to Surya. Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices as well, they recite: "He should touch the pole-axle (īṣā); he offers four handfuls. In this regard, there is a point of doubt: Is the touching [of the animal] in the Darśapūrṇamāsa the same as the touching [prescribed] here? Or is it different? [The Purvapaksha continues: It is the same. Why? Because the action is identical. Just as the action of touching the pole-axle is performed in the Darśapūrṇamāsa, so too is the action of touching the animal performed here. Furthermore, the agent is the same. Therefore, the action is the same. Moreover, the purpose is the same. Since the purpose is the same, the action must be the same. Consequently, the consecration of the animal is merely a preparatory act (saṃskāra) for that same action. Why? Because it is not mentioned in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and because it lacks the word denoting the primary action itself. Thus, the consecration is a preparatory rite. This is the prima facie view. [The Siddhanta follows: But it is a distinct action. Why? Because of the difference in words. The word used here is "one should sacrifice" (*ālabheta*), whereas in the Darśapūrṇamāsa it is "he touches" (*ālabheta*). A difference in words implies a difference in actions. Furthermore, the context is different. The context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa is distinct from the independent injunction. Also, the purpose is different. The purpose of the Darśapūrṇamāsa is the attainment of heaven, while the purpose here is prosperity or Brahmanic glory. Since the purpose is different, the action must be different. Therefore, the consecration of the animal is a separate action. This is the established conclusion. [The Purvapaksha rejoins: But the purpose is the same. How so? By means of the animal. Just as the Darśapūrṇamāsa is accomplished by means of the cake (puroḍāśa), so too is the prosperity accomplished here by means of the animal. Therefore, the purpose is the same. [The Siddhantin replies: No, because the means are different. The means of accomplishing the Darśapūrṇamāsa is the cake, whereas the means of accomplishing prosperity here is the animal. Since the means are different, the actions are different. Therefore, the consecration of the animal is a separate action. This is the final position. [The Purvapaksha further argues: But the purpose is the same. How so? Because of the connection with the result. Just as the Darśapūrṇamāsa is connected with the result of heaven, so too is this connected with the result of prosperity. Therefore, the purpose is the same. [The Siddhantin replies: No, because the connection is with a different result. The connection with the result of heaven belongs to the Darśapūrṇamāsa, while the connection with the result of prosperity belongs to this independent injunction. Since the results are different, the actions are different. Therefore, the consecration of the animal is a separate action. This is the established conclusion. [The Purvapaksha concludes: But the purpose is the same. How so? Because of the commonality of the name. Both are called "animal-sacrifice" (*paśuyāga*). Therefore, the purpose is the same. [The Siddhantin replies: No, because the application of the name is based on similarity. The name "animal-sacrifice" is applied here due to the similarity of the procedure, not because the action is identical. Therefore, the consecration of the animal is a separate action. This is the final position. [The Purvapaksha finally argues: But the purpose is the same. How so? Because of the mention of the same deity. Just as Agni is the deity of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, so too is Agni the deity here. Therefore, the purpose is the same. [The Siddhantin replies: No, because the deity is different. The deity of the Darśapūrṇamāsa is Agni-Soma, whereas here the deity is Agni alone. Since the deities are different, the actions are different. Therefore, the consecration of the animal is a separate action. This is the established conclusion. [The Purvapaksha concludes: But the purpose is the same. How so? Because of the commonality of the substance. Just as the Darśapūrṇamāsa uses the cake as its substance, so too does this use the animal as its substance. Therefore, the purpose is the same. [The Siddhantin replies: No, because the substance is different. The substance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa is the cake, whereas the substance here is the animal. Since the substances are different, the actions are different. Therefore, the consecration of the animal is a separate action. This is the final position. In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice, is the offering (*nirvāpa*) a prescription of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), and does that which is performed as a subordinate quality not depend upon the archetype (*prakṛti*)—as in the case of "the white horse" and so on? When it does not depend upon the archetype, then what: is it merely as stated [in the text], or are these two acts accompanied by a sacrifice (*yajimatī*)?

What, then, is the prima facie view? That these are injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*) for the two previously mentioned acts of seizing (*ālambha*) and offering (*nirvāpa*). Why? In this context as well, there is another reading: *guṇāt phalam* (the fruit [arises] from the quality), found in the Kāśīmudrita and Kīramudrita manuscripts.

The word exists [in the text]: "But surely [one] should sacrifice" and "[one] should offer"—these two are not injunctions.

To enjoin whiteness in the touching and the rice-pap (caru) in the offering. Therefore, there is no separate touching nor a separate offering; rather, these are injunctions of qualities (guṇavidhi) regarding the two acts already under discussion.

Though specified by many words, only one [entity] is expressed; thus, having analyzed their identity of meaning, these words here possess expectancy, and therefore their status as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) is established.

"One places the *caru* (gruel)"—this is indeed a direct (pratyakṣa) statement. "One places the *vāīspatya* (belonging to Vāiśvapati)"—this is inferential (ānumānika). What, then, is the conclusion? That it is a different sacrifice. Why? Because the previous [animal] dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ and Pāvīman is qualified by both attributes; how could it be referred to by the word "pātnīvata" alone?

Moreover, if the release of the one dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ were being enjoined, the qualification "having been consecrated with the paryagni rite" would not be appropriate. Therefore, we say: [it refers to] that which has been consecrated with the paryagni rite.

"It is prescribed that the *pānīvata* [cup] is offered; this is indeed the same sacrifice"—this being the position reached, we reply: it is not a different ritual action (*karmāntara*), but rather the same previous one, by means of the word "re-offering" (*utsarga*).

An exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is being enjoined. What will result from this? First, the character of being a sacrifice (*yajimat-tā*) will not be obscured; second, the word *utsṛjati*, enjoining the *utsarga* (relinquishment) by direct statement (*śruti*), will not be sublated by the syntactical connection (*vākya*);

When the state of being dedicated to Pātnīvata is being enjoined, the act of relinquishment (utsarga), which is already established by implication, would be restated by means of the verbal root. Furthermore, since the state of being dedicated to Pātnīvata for the preceding [offering] is already known, it cannot be the object of an injunction; therefore, there is a restriction of the previous ritual action. As for what was said:

Let there be no [question of] substance and deity; the verbal root *yajati* (to sacrifice) is directly present. Therefore, the conclusion reached is that one performs a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*) designated as *śrābhyas* and designated as *atyugras*.

We reply: this being the case, we say that when a name alone is heard that lacks a specific substance or deity, it is a prescription for a particular repetition of the cup-drawings within the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice itself. Why? Because:

First of all, this [name] belongs to the *graha* (the vessel for drawing the soma), not to the sacrifice, because it is directly connected with the act of drawing (*grahaṇa*), whereas the sacrifice is mediated by it. In order to enjoin another ritual act— for that [term] denotes a sacrifice already enjoined, as there is no distinction [otherwise]— it is established that by the word *yajati* (he sacrifices), the Jyotiṣṭoma itself is expressed, and by the words *aśva-dābhya*, two other cup-offerings (*graha-abhyāsa*) are enjoined. [Objection: But surely, since the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa are directly perceived [in their respective contexts], those [words] do not denote substances; thus there is no fault. (Kātyāyana Saṃhitā, Commentary on Pāda 1, Adhikaraṇa 2).

[Page 247] And regarding the two months, it is not a prescription of a subordinate element (guṇavidhi). Why? Because this is stated after the phrase "having performed the Upasads," and there are no Upasads belonging to the Agnihotra or the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Therefore, a prescription of the month is impossible in that context.

"Now, it might be argued: 'The *upasad* offerings are also enjoined here. However, in this case, since multiple qualities would be enjoined within this single sentence for the purpose of enjoining those qualities, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

On the other hand, in this [other] view, the word *agnihotra* does not qualify the action; therefore, there will be no syntactical split. Consequently, it is established that this is a distinct ritual act."
(2.3.11a) Section on Optional Sacrifices such as the Vyābhreya.
And the fruit [arises] even in the absence of action. || 25 ||
Bhāṣya: Without reference to any specific context, it is heard: "One desiring to be free from disease should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni;

one desiring rain should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Soma; one desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra-Agni. Here a doubt arises: is the fruit enjoined for the archetypal (prakṛta) offerings to Agni and the others, or are these distinct rituals separate from the archetypal ones?

What is established? That there is an injunction of results regarding the archetypal rites (*prākṛta*). Why? Because the *Āgneya* and other rites, being already known, are recognized here; therefore, they are restated (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of connecting them with the results.
This being the position reached, we reply: And a result, when heard in proximity to a ritual action, is a differentiator [of that action].

How so? If it were a restatement (*anuvāda*), it would not be possible to enjoin a result, because there would be no injunctive force; for it is understood that what is not being enjoined cannot be intended as a means. Furthermore, if "one desiring radiance" (*rukkāma*) were enjoined here, then according to Mādhava, "one desiring radiance" and "one desiring splendor" (*tejaskāma*) [would be the injunctions].
In the Mīmāṃsā system (Bhāṣya): Because the Āgneya and other sacrifices are non-eternal, while [the Veda] is eternal, their connection cannot be established!
Thus it is in all cases. Therefore, these are distinct ritual acts. (2.3.120)
The section concerning the fact that the *aveṣṭi* does not have food as its result.
But because there is no separation while one is present, the repetition is for the sake of the fruit. (26)

There is the Aveṣṭi sacrifice, beginning with the injunction, "There is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni," and so forth. With reference to that, it is stated: "One should cause one who desires sovereignty to sacrifice with this. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is this a separate rite from the Aveṣṭi, or is it the Aveṣṭi itself? What is the prima facie view? It is a separate rite, according to the previously stated reasoning. This being the position, we reply: In the context of the established ritual, the re-statement for the sake of a specific result pertains to the Aveṣṭi itself; it is not a separate rite.
Why? Because of non-distinction; this word "etayā" (by this) is not able to denote a separate sacrifice distinct from what is heard, for this word is a reference back to that which is proximate.
Therefore, this Aveṣṭi is enjoined for one desiring food. What is the purpose?

If it is the Aveṣṭi sacrifice, then the oblations are those dedicated to Agni and the others; if, however, it is a different ritual, then it is a sacrifice characterized by the Śraviṣṭha [deities]. (2.3.13) This is the section concerning the fact that the mention of Agni and the others serves the purpose of praise.
Sva. [The Agneya sacrifice] should be understood as being repeated because of the reason already stated. (Purvapaksha) || 27 ||

In the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, having prescribed—“The cake for Agni on eight potsherds is constant on both the new-moon day and the full-moon day”—it is stated again: “The cake for Agni on eight potsherds is on the new-moon day. Regarding this, there is a doubt:
should one sacrifice with the offering to Agni twice on the new-moon day, or only once? Which [is it]?

Is it obtained? — Because it is the cause for the [shape] of the Āgneyī brick, it is recognized through repetition; for if there were a repetition of the same thing without distinction, it would indeed be purposeless. Thus [it is concluded].
[Page 253] But because there is no distinction from the action, it is not enjoined by the repetition. || 28 ||
(Sūtra 1) Bhāṣya:

This is not the case—that the Āgneya [offering] should be performed again. Why? Because there is no word expressive of repetition. [Objection: "But surely the Āgneya, being uttered again, will enjoin a further action. [Reply: We say, "No. A word, when uttered again, cannot express that "the same purpose must be performed again," for that which belongs to it...

The meaning of that which is uttered for the first time shall be the same even if it is uttered a hundred times; it cannot be anything else. [Objection: But surely, enjoining again what has already been enjoined without distinction is purposeless.
[Response: Let it be purposeless as you wish, but it is not capable of [establishing] anything else.
To say that it would be appropriate for [the repetition] to be meaningless, but not for it to express a different meaning;
therefore, it should not be repeated twice.
Śrībhāṣya.
Or rather, the repetition is for another purpose. (Sūtra 2)

Alternatively, it is argued that the repetition is not purposeless; it will serve as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). To this it is replied: "What is the purpose of the explanatory praise? Since the *Āgneya* has already been enjoined by the preceding sentence which includes the explanatory praise, for what other purpose would the scripture (*śruti*) enjoin it again?"
How could it be applied? It has been stated that whatever is a mere scriptural statement (*śrutimātra*) which does not serve as an injunction for anything is purposeless:
"Because the Veda (*āmnāya*) has action as its purpose, those [passages] whose meaning is not [action] are purposeless" (Sūtra 1.2.1; p.
38). And whether heard or unheard, the meaning is exactly that much, just as it is heard.
"And even a deity not previously mentioned establishes its status as a constituent part; thus it is so.
To this it is replied: "Or rather, the repetition serves another purpose; it is not for the sake of enjoining the *āgneya* [offering], but for the sake of enjoining the *aindrāgna*.
The *āgneya* cake on eight potsherds indeed occurs at the new moon sacrifice."
"He does not become successful by means of Agni alone; rather, Agni accompanied by Indra is more effective. Therefore, the offering to Indra and Agni (Aindrāgna) must be performed. (2.3.14).
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya of the teacher Śabarasvāmin. *** ===
The fourth quarter of the second chapter.
This concludes the section concerning the lifelong performance of the *agnihotra* sacrifice.
No; lifelong practice is a property of the ritual act, because of the context. (Sūtra 1)
(Purvapaksha)

In the *Bahvṛcabrāhmaṇa* it is heard: "One performs the *agnihotra* as long as one lives," and "One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives. Here there is a doubt: is lifelong performance a repetition of the ritual action (*karmadharma*), or is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the agent (*kartṛdharma*) being enjoined?

Regarding the question "Is it lifelong?"—how is there repetition as a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*), or how is there a restriction as a property of the agent (*kartṛdharma*)? If the act of offering (*juhoti*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) and "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*) is the injunction (*vidhi*), then there is repetition as a property of the ritual action; if the opposite is the case, then...
There is a restriction regarding the duty of the agent—what, then, is the prima facie view? It is repetition [of the act], based on both the nature of the action and the context.

Why? Because of the context; for if this is the interpretation of the statement—that *juhoti* and *yajati* are restatements (anuvāda) and "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*) is the injunction—then the context is upheld, and therefore there is repetition. By doing so, the praise of the sacrifice will be consistent: "This Agnihotra is a sacrificial session (*satra*) that lasts until old age, as are the New and Full Moon sacrifices."
And [the word] "ca" is used because of the commonality of long duration; therefore, there must be repeated practice.
Or rather, it belongs to the agent, because of its connection with the scriptural statement. (Siddhānta)

Bhāṣya: Here we say—there would be no lifelong practice, for a restriction is enjoined upon the agent. Why? Because of the connection with the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). In this way, the meaning will be determined by the direct statement; otherwise, there would be an implied figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*). How so? [The phrase] "as long as life lasts" (means...)

"One should perform it for that much time"—this Agnihotra, completed at evening, cannot be performed throughout the entire duration of one's life. Nor can the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices be completed within the full span of a lifetime, as they conclude on the full moon and new moon days. If it is argued that "even if performed during only a portion of the time of one's life, it becomes a hundredfold by virtue of that time," this is not so.
(Chapter 2, Section 2) [Page 255]

Commentary: For that which is already established by implication need not be enjoined by the word. Since the time is limited by the duration of life, it must be completed within that period; thus, repetition follows from the sense, and that—

For this [obligation] is heard as something to be performed, and it is not expressed directly by the roots *juhoti* (he offers) or *yajati* (he sacrifices); rather, it is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as "one should offer for as long as one lives" or "one should practice for as long as one lives. And direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful than context (*prakaraṇa*). If this is the syntactical analysis of this sentence, then "for as long as one lives" is a restatement (*anuvāda*), and "he offers" and "he sacrifices" are the injunctions.

[The opponent argues: "In this way, the words *yajati* and *juhoti* will retain their own primary meanings; likewise, the word *yāvajjīvam* (as long as one lives) will denote living itself and will not be characterized by repetition. Thus, the rite is enjoined with living as the occasion: 'If one is alive, one must offer. Here, living is the occasion (*nimitta*), not time; because the occasion is fixed, [the rite] is fixed."
By that [word], action is expressed; a restriction regarding the agent's property is enjoined—thus it is said.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*); for how could it be restricted by the introductory statement?
Otherwise, that [introductory statement] would be purposeless. (Sūtra 3; Commentary 1)

There is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*): "Indeed, even he who is a performer of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is cut off from the heavenly world if he should let the full moon or the new moon day pass by.

How is this an indicative mark? For if the sacrificial session (*sattra*) were a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*), it would have to be completed within the duration of one's life; in that case, there could be no passing over of the [specific] time. And in that case, the other [text] would be purposeless.
There may be the prescription of expiatory rites and so forth.
And [the scripture] shows its own completion; if it were time, there would be a division of the ritual acts. 4.

There is seen an indication of completion (*vyapavarga*) [of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*], namely: "Having sacrificed with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, one should sacrifice with the *soma*. If, after sacrificing with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, there is a time for the *soma*, it is clear that those two [the *darśapūrṇamāsa*] are not performed throughout one's entire lifetime.

These two [rites] are completed. Now, if living (jīvana) is the occasion (nimitta), a distinction between the rites (karmabheda) is established: having completed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one should perform the Soma sacrifice as a different rite.

Furthermore: "He who offers the Agnihotra but does not sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa is indeed one who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni); he makes those deities who are entitled to the offerings become merely contemplative."
—Thus there is the statement of one who is anxious; when that portion of the oblation which is fixed is not being given, there is the statement of one who is anxious.
But as for that portion of the oblation which is unfixed, they are anxious about it, thinking, "This will be ours"—thus [it is said].
Fixed...

And that portion belongs to the obligatory (niyama) alternative, not to the optional (kāmya) alternative; for the optional Agnihotra and the Full and New Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa) are rites performed for specific desires. Therefore, it is the obligatory alternative. Moreover, it is heard in scripture: "This sacrificial session (sattra), namely the Agnihotra and the Full and New Moon sacrifices, lasts until old age and death; by these two, one is released from both old age and death. This statement, which determines release from old age and death, is consistent with the obligatory alternative. For in the case of the optional alternative, one would be released even through non-performance!
But because of impermanence, it could not be so. (He0 3)

The word "but" (*tu*) in the commentary indicates a further point of view; from this as well, we see that the duty and the rule belong to the agent. If the preceding *homa* were merely an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*), then that single Agnihotra *homa* mentioned in connection with a specific desire would be the only obligatory (*nitya*) rite, and no other would be obligatory.
In that case, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) would be contradicted: "The Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are indeed lifelong; by these two, one is released from old age and death."

—Messenger! How is it contradictory? The statement that definitively establishes liberation from old age and death is appropriate according to the view of necessity (*niyamapakṣe*), whereas according to the view of desire (*kāmyapakṣe*), one would be liberated even without practice.
And likewise for contradiction, as before. (Sūtra 6; Commentary 4)
Bhāṣya: Furthermore, we see that prior practice is not enjoined as a subordinate element (guṇa). Why? Because of contradiction;

a contradiction would arise, for the modifications (vikāra) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, such as the Saurya and others, would also have to be practiced throughout one's life. Thus, the meaning of the independent injunction (anārabhyādhikaraṇa) would be rendered nullified. Moreover, we see that there is a restrictive rule (niyama), and this will be consistent with the praise and the state of continuity.
[Page 257] On the other hand, because the rule of duty pertains to the agent, the scriptural injunction regarding time would be the occasioning condition. || 7 ||
Bhāṣya:

If a restriction were enjoined as a property of the agent, then living would be the occasion; when living is the occasion, the rite is prescribed. In that case, the rite is completed upon its performance, and likewise...
The observation of liberation would otherwise be unaccounted for; therefore, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) concerning the agent is enjoined.
Now begins the section [dealing with] the unity of ritual action based on the recognition [of identical rites] across all recensional branches (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-eka-karma-tā-adhikaraṇa*).

kha. Because of the mention of specific names, forms, and dharmas, of repetition, of censure, of incapacity, of words indicating completion, and of penance, as well as because of the observation of other purposes, there would be a difference of ritual acts in the various Vedic branches. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 8 ||

Bhāṣya 1: Here, other recensions (śākhās) are cited as examples, such as the Kāṭhaka, the Kālāpaka, the Paippalādaka, and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt: regarding a ritual action that exists in one particular recension...

The Agnihotra and other rites are heard [prescribed] in one place; when they are heard again in another recension (*śākhā*), do they differ from it or not? We see that they differ. Why? Because of the difference in name:
one is named *Kāṭhaka*, while the other is named *Kālāpaka*; thus, there is a difference due to the difference in name.

"Is this not merely the name of a book? True; we say it is also [the name] of rituals—for there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and identity of case-ending (*ekavibhaktitva*) between the rituals and such [names].
Furthermore, because of the difference in form: in one recensional branch (*śākhā*), [there is] an *agnīṣomīya* [offering] on eleven potsherds (*ekādaśakapāla*).

They recite: "In one [instance], a cake on twelve potsherds"—thus, since the form is different, how could it not be a separate ritual action? Furthermore, because of a difference in the properties (*dharma*), the Taittirīyas, while studying the *Kārīrī* passages, [recite] on the ground...

Some perform the practice of providing food, while others who study the Śākhins do not; likewise, some who study the Agnihotra bring water-jars for their teacher, while others do not; some who study the Aśvamedha bring fodder for the horse, while others do not; and others [perform] another [practice].

They practice the Dharma; for instance, the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and other rites are desired by some as a means of assistance, yet they are not so desired by others. How could that very same [rite] not be desired by one person, or how could it be fit to be desired by another? From this it is understood that there is something else. Furthermore, because of the consequence of tautology: if the ritual action (*karman*) were one and the same based on all recensions (*śākhā*), then in a single [recension]...

The mention in another *śākhā* of a rite already prescribed in one *śākhā* would be a mere repetition and thus purposeless; however, this fault does not exist in the case of [the rites being] distinct. Therefore, for this reason also, there is a difference between the rites. Furthermore, because of the statement of censure: "In the morning, they speak untruths; before sunrise, they offer oblations."

"Some followers of certain Vedic branches censure the *agnihotra* performed before sunrise, saying: "Those who recite the *divākīrtya* [hymn] at a time other than day—when the sun is not yet their light—that is not their light. Others, however, censure the *agnihotra* performed after sunrise, saying: "If they offer when the sun has risen, it would be like serving food to a guest who has already eaten his fill. Since this contradiction exists within the recognition of all Vedic branches (*sarvaśākhāpratyaya*), it does not pertain to a difference in the ritual action itself; therefore, even on this basis, there is no difference [between the rites]."
Furthermore, due to incapacity, they would indeed be unable to bring about the conviction that [the sacrifice] is for all deities;

in that case, it would have to be admitted that a rite is being enjoined for a purpose not previously commenced. However, this is possible when there is a difference in the ritual acts; therefore, there is a difference in the ritual acts.

And because of the statement regarding completion: even when not completed, there is a statement of completion; some say, "Our fire-sacrifice is completed here," while others designate it as incomplete. This would not be possible if it were a single ritual action, for it would not then be completed in one place.
It is not so in other cases; rather, it is logical that there is a difference, therefore there is a distinction.

Furthermore, because of the prescription of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*): some authorities prescribe an expiation for the transgression of performing the *agnihotra* before sunrise, while others prescribe an expiation for the transgression of performing it after sunrise, as well as for its omission.

If the ritual action were one and the same, such a twofold increase [in the occasion for expiation] would not be possible; however, if the actions are distinct, then that which applies when it is not yet risen...
The *homakarma* (fire-oblation rite) is performed when [the moon] has risen; the other [rite] is also performed when it has risen; therefore, there is a distinction.

Furthermore, because of the observation of another purpose, this is heard in scripture: "If they have previously intended to consecrate themselves, whether the householder [is consecrated] first, or the followers of the householder..."—thus, they [consecrate] him alone.

[Page 259] Bhāṣya: They should undertake the *ṛtu* sacrifice that has the *ṛk-sāman*; for the *rathantara* belongs to them. Now, if they desire [to perform it]—thus, the observation of the twelve-day (*dvādaśāha*) sacrifice is appropriate both for those who have already performed sacrifices and for those who have not performed sacrifices before, provided there is a difference of ritual acts; it is not possible if there were a single ritual act. How so? It is heard in the *Tāṇḍaka*: "This indeed is the first of sacrifices, namely the *Jyotiṣṭoma*."... [text continues] ...ya [the *agniṣṭoma*].

"By performing this [sacrifice] without having first performed that [other], one would produce a miscarriage; it perishes"—this [statement] would apply everywhere; in that case, the observation of the initiations for the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) would not be possible; therefore, there is also a difference of ritual acts (*karmabheda*).
Now,
there is another indicative mark: "If one were to pile [the fire-altar] with five layers,
he would enter upon a smaller sacrificial rite, a smaller progeny, fewer cattle, and a smaller reputation."

If it were the case that [the sacrificer] would become worse, then, since the measuring of the five [posts] is prohibited by the statement "if he measures according to the altar," there is the observation of the measuring of the altar;

however, that is appropriate only if there is a difference in the ritual acts (karmabheda), for the observation of the measuring of the altar by one who performs the cooking is not appropriate if there is a single ritual act (ekakarmatva). How so? For some authorities record:
"The intervals between the sacrificial posts (yūpa) are the measure of a chariot-yoke"; that would apply everywhere, and in that case, for us...

If there were identity [of the rite], the honor of the altar would be the honor for us, and the observation of the honor of the altar would not be possible; therefore, there is also a difference of action (*karmabheda*).

Furthermore, there is the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*): in some [recensions] regarding the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is heard, "Two *virāj*s of the recited verses remain over," while for others, "Three *virāj*s of the recited verses remain over. There is a contradiction if there is a single action, but not if there are multiple actions.
In one *jyotiṣṭoma* there are two [offerings], and in another there are three; therefore, there is a difference in the ritual acts (*karmabheda*).
Furthermore, it is heard in the *Sārasvata*: "Those who offer the *puror̤āśa* sit down;
those who offer the *sānnāyya* keep the calves away. Those who offer the *sānnāyya* are those who have already performed their first sacrifice.
The Puror̤āśins are the opposite; the observation of both [groups] at the Sārasvata [sacrifice] is consistent only if there is a difference in ritual acts.
If it were a single ritual act, all would have the Jyotiṣṭoma as their archetype, and in that case, such an observation would not be possible.
