And the fruit [is for the person], because it has the person as its purpose. (Sūtra 5)

The fruit is also taught with reference to the person who desires, "May heaven be mine"—for him there is the sacrifice; not that heaven itself should obtain its own self. Why? Because of the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*); this [usage] occurs when the result is intended for the agent. The sacrifice is employed with the thought: "How might the person experience the fruit of the action? Therefore, the fruit [belongs to the person].
The human purpose is heard [in the scripture] as resulting from the sacrifice, not for the sake of the self's accomplishment; therefore, it is a subordinate element (śeṣa).
[Page 271] Sūtra. Chapter 1, Section 1.
And the person [is subordinate] because he exists for the sake of the ritual action. || 6 ||

Commentary: A person (*puruṣa*) is also heard of as being subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) in such cases as the measuring of the *audumbarī* post. Therefore, this [assertion] is not definitive: namely, that Bādari considered subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) to apply only to substances, qualities, and preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*).
Now, the venerable commentator (Vṛttikāra), having reached a firm conclusion, states:

"The status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣabhāva*) is restricted solely to substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*) in relation to the sacrifice; it is relative."

In the case of the others: the sacrifice has primacy with respect to the substance, but is subordinate with respect to the fruit; the fruit has primacy with respect to the sacrifice, but is subordinate with respect to the person; the person has primacy with respect to the fruit, but is subordinate with respect to such acts as the measuring of the *audumbarī* post. Therefore, the restriction is accepted: substances, qualities, and purificatory rites are necessarily subordinate to the sacrifice.
"They are indeed subordinate factors"—thus [ends the section].
(Sūtra 3.1.3) This is the section concerning the fixed scope of the *nirvapa* and other rites according to their respective purposes.
The connection [of the word] is for the sake of those [meanings]. (Nirukta 1.7)

There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, [enjoined by the injunction]: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa. In that context, certain duties (dharma) are heard: the pouring out [of the grain], the sprinkling, the husking—such are the duties pertaining to the vegetable offering (auṣadha); likewise, the purifying, the melting, the taking up, the placing down—such are the duties pertaining to the clarified butter (ājya); and likewise, the fetching of the branch, the driving forth of the cows, the leading forward of the cows—such are the duties pertaining to the Sānnāyya. Regarding these...

There is a doubt: should all [the rites] be performed in relation to the medicinal herbs, the clarified butter, and the Sānnāyya offering, or should only those which, when performed in a particular context, serve a purpose, be performed there?
[Objection: But they are indeed heard as being connected [to specific acts], such as "He threshes the rice-grains" and "He pounds the rice-grains."

"He grinds"—thus it is said. Certainly, [the acts of] threshing and so forth are enjoined as constituent elements (padārtha) by direct Vedic statement (śruti), whereas their connection with rice and other materials is established by syntactical connection (vākya); therefore, there is a doubt.
[Page 272]
[Commentary: What, then, is the prima facie position? They are connected with a purpose—that is, with a practical objective.

Those [acts] which, when performed in a particular context, serve a purpose, should be performed there. Since acts such as spreading [the grass] up to the pouring out [of the butter] do not provide assistance to both the *āgneya* and the *saumya* offerings, they should not be performed in that [combined] context.

Thus, acts such as winnowing and so forth pertain to both the medicinal herbs (auṣadha) and the cooked oblation (sānnāyya); acts such as fetching the branch and so forth pertain to both the forest herbs (āraṇya-auṣadha) and the cooked oblation. [Objection: But surely all [acts] are heard of in connection with all [substances]. [Reply: We do not know this very thing—whether they are heard of or not—and thus it must be investigated. Even if they were heard of, nevertheless, because they would be of no assistance, they would simply not be performed.

But all the ritual acts prescribed [in the context] should belong to the sacrificer himself, because there is no distinction based on connection and no distinction based on the context. (Pūrvapakṣa 8)
The Bhāṣya states:
That which is obtained from the *bhr̥t* (the sacrificial fee) would be performed only where it serves a purpose;
however, all these ritual elements (*padārtha*) are enjoined by the *jagatī* [meter], and therefore, not only where...

The purpose is seen to be directly perceptible; therefore, they should be performed only there. Where, then? They are understood to be prescribed everywhere, wherever they have been enjoined. Why? Because, due to the lack of distinction in connection and the lack of distinction in context, it is understood that for all the *ānya*, *auṣadha*, and *sānnāyya* offerings, the relationship between the end to be accomplished (*apūrva*) and the means is equally specific—that when performed in one place, they become performed for the sake of the *apūrva*. Likewise, the context is undifferentiated, such that wherever they are enjoined, they are considered enjoined for all.

It is understood; therefore, all [auxiliaries] must be employed everywhere. As for the objection that these do not assist in every case—it is understood from the force of the injunction that they do indeed assist in every case—and this assistance will be of an unseen (adṛṣṭa) nature.
The action would be non-existent because its purpose has been lost. (Siddhānta) || 9 ||

Bhāṣya: This is not so—that all [auxiliaries] must be employed everywhere. It has already been stated that those which do not provide assistance in a particular place do not deserve to be performed there. [Objection: "But surely, by the force of the injunction, all will provide assistance everywhere. [Response: We say, "No."
Sūtra:
But the fruit.
Because of the absence of the object when there is a dissociation [of the word] from its activity, the meaning of the word would not exist.

There is no rule by which all [words] would assist in every instance; nor do we perceive such assistance through perception or other means of knowledge. Even presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) would necessarily apply only where there is an injunction by means of a word, and not otherwise. And if...

If spreading [the grass] and other such acts were not helpful to the two *sānnāyya* offerings, their recitation within that context would be inexplicable; therefore, an invisible benefit (*adṛṣṭa upakāra*) would have to be assumed.

However, these acts are themselves recited for the sake of the vegetable substance (*auṣadha*), for the result—such as the removal of husks—is understood to arise from the activity of threshing and so forth performed along with it, and there is a visible purpose served by that. It is not [an invisible one].

Therefore, the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is accomplished even without that [mantra]; and since this [cake] exists, the recitation within the context is purposeful. And when that is purposeful, there is no grounds for assuming an unseen result (adṛṣṭa). For this reason, it is not possible to assume such a result. Moreover, if that were the case...

If the production of rice and other grains were not observed [to result from the action], then, because rice and the like would not exist in the absence of that [action], the benefit [of the action] would have to be regarded as consisting merely of the word-meaning, independent of any observed benefit; consequently, even for the *ājya* (clarified butter) and *sānnāyya* (curd-mixture), an unobserved (*adṛṣṭa*) benefit would have to be assumed whenever they are being prepared. Therefore, actions such as spreading [the flour] are not to be performed everywhere. The same applies to actions such as purifying (*utpavana*) and fetching the branch (*śākhāharaṇa*). Thus, not all actions are to be performed everywhere;
actions such as spreading are not for the *ājya* and *sānnāyya*, but only for the vegetable-based oblation (*auṣadha*).

It is established that the acts of purifying and so forth apply to the other [milk], not to the medicinal herbs or the curdled milk; and the acts of fetching the branches and so forth apply to the curdled milk, not to the other medicinal herbs. (1.1.4)
Sūtra Bhāṣya:
The section concerning the fixed application of the *sphya* and other implements according to their respective associations.
And the substance, because of its connection with the origination [of the rite], should be enjoined for that very purpose. || 11 ||

There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices; regarding them, they recite: "The sacrificial post and the potsherds, the Agnihotra-ladle and the sacrificial stake, the black antelope skin and the wooden mace, the mortar and the pestle. [Page 274] Bhāṣya.
"The pestle and the millstone—these indeed are the ten sacrificial implements.
In this regard, a doubt arises: are these [implements] enjoined for whatever purpose can be accomplished by them here, or only for that which is specifically connected with each?

To whom, then, [should they belong]?—this is the question. What, first, is the prima facie view? That they belong to whoever is capable [of using them]. Why? Because in this way the injunctions will be meaningful; otherwise, they would be mere restatements (anuvādas) and thus purposeless. Furthermore, there is no distinction regarding the context with respect to all ritual items, and the connection with the sacrifice expressed by the term "sacrificial implements" (yajñāyudhāni) is equally applicable to all. Therefore—
"All [the substances] everywhere"—this is what follows from the prima facie view.
This being the case, we reply: "And the substance, because of its connection with the originative injunction, should be enjoined for that purpose alone."
Whatever substance is connected by a scriptural statement with a specific action must be performed by that very substance;

for example, by the statement "he digs with the *sphya*," the *sphya* serves the purpose of digging, and that digging is not to be performed by anything other than the *sphya*. And when this is the case, [the following] is established:

Thus, this must be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that very *sphya*: "These indeed are the sacrificial implements of the sacrifice. In this way, there is a restatement for each individual item, as it has been obtained by its respective scriptural injunction. For example: "He cooks on the potsherds," and "He [cooks] the oblations with the *agnihotra-havanī*."

"He pours out [the grain], he winnows it with a winnowing basket, he spreads the black antelope skin beneath the mortar, he places the wedge upon the grinding stone, he pounds with the mortar and pestle, and he grinds with the grinding stone and muller"—thus [it is said]. Due to the context (*prakaraṇa*), all [implements] would apply everywhere; however, by virtue of the specific statement (*vacana*), they apply according to that statement. Furthermore, the term "sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudha*) also establishes a general purpose, and thus it must indeed be understood as such;
for a general statement serves to enjoin a particular, whereas a direct statement enjoins a particular through its own specific wording.
Therefore, it is established that whatever is connected with something by way of its origin is to be employed in that very same thing. (3.1.5)
"He places the lower grinding stone upon the yoke-pin," according to the Kātyāyana-Śrautasūtra (Kātyāyana-Prayoga-paddhati),
Chapter 3, Section 1. [Page 275]
Section on the Non-Confusion of the Qualities of the Bāhyakhyā and Others. (The Cāraṇi Principle)
[Sūtra 12: When there is a single purpose, there should be a restriction on the substance and the quality due to their performing a single function.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, with reference to the purchase [of Soma], it is heard in scripture: "One purchases Soma with a reddish-brown, tawny-eyed, one-year-old cow. Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the quality of redness (aruṇimā) belong to the general context of the sacrifice, or does it belong specifically to the one-year-old cow in the act of purchase itself? But how can there be such a doubt when the connection with the purchase is so clear from the statement, "one purchases with a reddish-brown [cow]"?

Is there doubt regarding that which is being traversed? It is replied: Here, indeed, the word teaches that the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*), though formless, is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the action, by connecting it with the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-vibhakti*) which denotes an instrument, as in the expression "with the ear. And a formless object cannot be the means of accomplishing an action. Therefore, we understand the connection of the quality of redness with the act of buying; for an authoritative word will not express a meaning that is impossible to accomplish—thus [it is concluded].

A conceptual construction might perhaps be possible; that is, when seeking a mode of authority for the statement, the intellect turns toward the thought that there is some kind of relationship— and if, upon further investigation, we were to perceive the capacity for a connection with an action through syntactic unity (ekavākyatā), [then it would be so].

We shall assign the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) to the act of purchase itself; however, if it were not perceived by those who are attentive to their own [textual] authority, no connection whatsoever would be established. Therefore, having accepted a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), we shall determine this to be a property of the entire context (*prakaraṇadharma*). Thus, "this must necessarily be deliberated upon. What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It is that it should be assigned to the entire context. Why? Because there is no distinction in its connection and because there is no distinction in the context. [Objection: But surely the sentence is more powerful than the context; therefore, due to syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), the quality of redness will be connected with the purchase.

—Thus it is said. This is not understood in that way; for even by a hundred statements, it is not possible to enjoin a meaning that is not [already] established. Indeed, one might say: "One should burn with water. [Page 276] Bhāṣya. Even so, it is elsewhere read as *ekahāyinyā*. One cannot enjoin a matter through words that lack a basis in reality. For if someone were to say, "One should burn with water," [it would be impossible].
"One must protect oneself from fire"—does this statement possess consistency in its purpose? Nor is it logical for that which has no visible purpose to be a means for an action.
Therefore, because there is no connection [between the two], there is no syntactic unity in the case of "He buys with a red [cow]."
Why?
Because this word is certainly not expressive of a quality (guṇavacana); rather, it is expressive of a substance (dravyavacana).

Because of the connection with gender; those specific substances are female, male, or neuter—and thus, when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) occurs in the feminine, the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is applied.
And we perceive the feminine suffix in the word "aruṇayā" (with the red one). Therefore...

"The word *aruṇa* denotes a substance"—this [view] is untenable. For it is that very substance, when delimited by its redness (*aruṇimā*), that acquires the status of being denotable by the word *aruṇa*; that same substance, when possessing other qualities, cannot be expressed by the word *aruṇa*. This [word] refers only to the quality of redness.
The word *jagat* does not deviate [from its primary meaning], whereas a substance (*dravya*) does deviate;
and for those who possess causes, a non-deviating cause is desired. Therefore, it is understood that its own meaning is a quality (*guṇa*).
Thus, its status as a word denoting a quality is understood from direct perception, because the feminine suffix (*śrī-pratyaya*) is observed.

But surely, the inference that *aruṇā* is a nominal stem denoting a substance is set aside by perception, for perception is stronger than inference; therefore, it is a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*). How then is its connection with the feminine suffix [-tī] established? For even a word denoting a quality can possess a feminine gender, just as one says "the cognition is red" (*aruṇā buddhiḥ*), so too "the [cow] is red" (*aruṇā*). If it is a word denoting a quality, then [it must be connected] with the verb "to buy" (*krīṇāti*).
It is not connected [to that]. Therefore, by effecting a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), there is an insertion into the entire context—thus [it is concluded].
"Now, if it is not connected with the word *krīṇāti* (he buys), then in that very sentence..."
"It will be connected with the word *ekahāyanī*, and there will be no split in the sentence"—this is not so;

for the word *śravaṇa* denotes the quality alone, not both the substance and the quality, while the word *ekahāyanī* denotes the substance alone, not accompanied by a quality. Thus, between these two—

Without the genitive case-ending which expresses the relation, how can the related entity be understood? [Objection: "Indeed, even without the genitive, there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) because of the mention in the same case-ending.
[Page 277]
"1 pādaḥ | 217 lā. We shall understand it as 'a blue lotus'"; that is untenable, because of the form [of the cognition].

The word *aruṇa* denotes a quality (*guṇavacana*). However, its syntactic unity with the word *ekahāyanī* must be assumed on the basis of their connection through a single case-ending and their proximity;

having thus accepted this syntactic unity, one must establish coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *ekahāyanī*. Furthermore, syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than gender (*liṅga*). Therefore, that [objection] is unfounded.

In this regard, it is said: when a word functioning as a mere expression of a quality does not obtain a connection with anything else, then—in order that it not be purposeless due to its lack of instructional value—it attains the status of referring to a substance (*dravya*). In that state, becoming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the proximate term *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) which is joined by the same case-ending, it becomes a term in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). And having done so, the expression "a blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*) is established.
And this word *aruṇā* (red) functions in that particular state; for it has no purposeful application within the context if it were severed from its own primary meaning. Why?
Because by the very same reason that it is not connected with the act of buying (*krīṇāti*), the meaning of the word is not a non-material factor of the action.

It becomes a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*); yet it is not by means of substances that are the instruments of action (*kriyāsādhana-dravya*), for a word denoting a quality alone is not capable of denoting a substance— this is the very reason why,
even in the absence of a connection with the context, when that [quality] is connected there as well, it denotes the action.

It would have to be connected either with [the sacrifice] or with the substances that accomplish it; however, both of these are untenable. Therefore, in order to avoid meaninglessness, the word *aruṇā* (red) is connected with the proximate word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow), and thus there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
This is not so; this word *aruṇā* cannot function as a qualifier of the *ekahāyanī*.

What is the reason? Because it is uttered with the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), which denotes an instrument; therefore, by the force of this heard instrumental case, it must be an adverbial adjunct (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) of the action.

For grammatical factors (*kāraka*s) are connected with an action, not with a substance. Thus, by the force of the direct statement (*śruti*), it is an adverbial adjunct of the action; yet, because it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), it is also an adjectival adjunct of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*).
Moreover, direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*); therefore, this [word] has no connection with the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*).
[Objection: But surely, since a quality (*guṇa*) cannot be connected with an action, its status as a grammatical factor (*kāraka*) would be unintended (*avivakṣita*).

[Page 278] Bhāṣya: "The capacity (*śakti*)—thus the connection with the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) has been determined. Even so, this is not tenable if the expression of the case-factor (*kāraka*) is unintended. If, by this word denoting a quality (*guṇa-śabda*), a substance (*dravya*) is intended to be expressed, then there is no distinction from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*); thus, the nominative case (*prathamā-vibhakti*) would result. For the third case (*tṛtīyā*) cannot express a connection with that which is most proximate, nor can another meaning be postulated on the grounds of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*) when it is not possible, as in the case of the expression "he stands in the fire" (*agnau tiṣṭhati*).

The young student: When [the word] has been spoken, since it is not applicable to a horse or a cow, it is determined to refer exclusively to something in proximity to fire; likewise, this word ending in the nominative case cannot in any way apply to a meaning that is non-distinct from the base meaning (*prātipadikārtha*). Therefore, let it be understood that [the word] is perhaps purposeless; its connection with a one-year-old heifer (*ekahāyanī*) must not be determined.

He said: "We do not say that the agent is not denoted by the word *aruṇā* (red); rather, it is clearly the agent qualified by the quality of redness that is denoted by this [word]. However, sometimes something is intended to be enjoined (*vidhitsita*), while at other times that which is subordinate is what is intended to be enjoined, and that which is primary is merely restated (*anuvāda*). For example, in the case of the word *daṇḍī* ('staff-bearer'), it is understood as a term in which the person is primary and the staff is subordinate; sometimes..."

However, when a person has already been established, a statement is uttered for the purpose of prescribing a quality of the staff, such as: "The one with the staff recites the directions"; likewise: "The priests wearing red turbans perform the ritual.

Similarly here also, even if the quality is not subordinate but the factor (kāraka) is primary, nevertheless, once the factor has been restated, it is appropriate for the statement to serve the purpose of prescribing a quality.

"Therefore, the connection with the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) is logical, and there is no split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). This is not sound. For here, this word *ekahāyanī* is uttered in order to make known the previously unapprehended relationship between the *ekahāyanī* and the act of purchasing (*krīṇāti*). How then can it be connected with the word *aruṇā* (red)? This very point, though already stated, is being questioned again and again.
*kārakavibhaktiḥ* according to the Prācīna-puṣpa;
*uparatiḥ* according to the Cit-pāṭha.
[Page 279]

Bhāṣya: "But how is it that, when the word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) has an equal syntactic connection (*samabhivyāhāra*) with both the act of buying (*krīṇāti*) and the quality of redness (*aruṇaguṇa*), one must accept its connection with the act of buying and not with the quality of redness? [Answer: Because of the authority of the word (*śabdaprāmāṇyāt*). For indeed, the case-ending expressing the connection with the action is attached immediately after the word *ekahāyanī*, but not [after the word *aruṇayā*]."

It expresses a connection with a quality (*guṇa*). [Question: "Which [case-ending] expresses a connection with an action (*kriyā*), and which expresses a connection with a quality? [Answer: When the characteristic of a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is intended in relation to an action, the second case (*dvitīyā*) and so forth are employed; however, when the *kāraka* status is not intended, but rather a mere relationship (*sambandha*) is intended, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used. We do not see the sixth case here, yet we do see—
Indeed, [the word *ekahāyanī*] is connected with the third [word, *krīṇāti*]; therefore, we accept a relationship between the word *ekahāyanī* and the verb *krīṇāti*, not with the word *aruṇā*.

"How then does the relationship 'a blue lotus' (*nīlam utpalam*) arise here? It is replied: it does arise, but it is not characterized by direct syntactical connection (*śruti*), rather it is characterized by sentential connection (*vākya*).

In the proximity of the word *utpala* (lotus), the term *nīla* (blue), which depends upon it, does not enter into a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) without abandoning its own primary meaning; rather, being uttered for the purpose of denoting a specific lotus, it enters into a relationship [with it]. [Objection: "In this case as well, a relationship with the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) through redness (*aruṇimā*) is joined by means of the sentence-characteristic (*vākyalakṣaṇa*), just like that [previous case]. [Reply: We say—no. For direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful than syntactical connection (*vākya*), and direct statement, being superior, expresses a connection with the action (*kriyā*), not a connection with a quality (*guṇa*). "If..."

Furthermore, by the force of the scriptural repetition (*śruti*), a connection with the ritual action might be accepted; yet, because it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), there is also a connection with the accessory (*guṇa*). This is not possible: that which is uttered as being connected with one thing cannot, while remaining in proximity to it, be connected with another, just as [a wife] cannot [be connected to two husbands simultaneously].

Just as the word "king" in the expression "the king's man, [belonging] to Devadatta," being uttered for the purpose of qualifying the wife, is not connected with the man; so too here, the word *ekahāyanī*, being uttered for the purpose of qualifying the purchase, does not deserve to be connected with the word *aruṇā*.
‘Āc—True, this is so; in the absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) is not a cause [of syntactic connection].

However, in every case, the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is established only when the word-meaning is sublated, and not otherwise. For it is a general rule that there is a sublation of the specific application by means of the general; thus, those things accepted through the general [rule]...
[Page 280]

Mīmāṃsā—In the tenth [book], it is stated that the specific arrangement of word-meanings is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). This has been declared [in Sūtra 1.1.25]: “The collection of those [word-meanings] which have attained their state [of being related] with an action is for the sake of the meaning, because the [sentence] meaning is caused by that. In this regard, while word-meanings are apprehended through perception and other means, the sentence-meaning, however, is inferential (*ānumānika*). Let this be understood: a word functioning solely in its own isolated sense is not an instruction; it enters into syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with another proximate word, and not otherwise.

Thus, although here the word *ekahāyanī*, being connected with the verb *krīṇāti* (to buy), has fulfilled its purpose and does not require a connection with another word, the word *aruṇā* (red), failing to obtain a connection with another word, would be meaningless; therefore, it enters into syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the word *ekahāyanī*. But was it not said that [the word *aruṇā*] is for the sake of connecting with the action, not for the sake of connecting with [the word] *aruṇā*?

We say that the word *aruṇā* (red) is for the purpose of connecting [the quality] with both [the cow and the purchase], in order to avoid its being meaningless. Even that which is performed for one purpose is capable of serving another purpose as well;
for example, bricks are brought forth for the sake of the sacrificial altar, yet water is also drunk from them.
"And it is touched [by the other]. Likewise here as well, the word *ekahāyanī*, being uttered for the purpose of connecting with the body, will coalesce with the word *aruṇā*; nothing is corrupted.
Therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). This is not so, even though this word *aruṇā*...

"Lest it be purposeless," [one might argue] that it should be connected with the *ekahāyanī* (the one-year-old cow); even so, it ought to apply to everything within the context, for the expression "he does not buy this Soma" is not capable of restricting it; indeed, this is not uttered as a qualifier—what then?
It is enjoined as something not previously established (*apūrva*).

[Objection: "But even when enjoined as something new, it will be connected with the other [element], just like the word *ekahāyanī*. How so? For a word being uttered for a specific purpose conveys its meaning only through that which serves that purpose."

It is for that purpose alone that it is postulated; it exists as something present in the intellect. Therefore, by means of that which is present in the intellect, the word can be connected with its desired meaning. This is not so; for only that which, when not being connected, would be meaningless, is connected, and nothing else. Why is this? Because when [the general property] is being connected, the universal...
If it were restricted to a specific instance, then the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) would be sublated by the syntactical connection (*vākya*). Furthermore, this [word],
not being connected with the act of buying (*krīṇāti*), does not become meaningless, because it is connected with those [actions] contained within the context (*prakaraṇa*).
"He will be connected with one-year-old cows.
Now, it was argued that "even in this context, his connection is untenable.

It is not untenable; for when a single meaning is being enjoined within a single sentence, it cannot be connected with another, because of the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*). Indeed, the mode of expression for that which is being enjoined is different.

[This applies] to one who is connected with a quality. That which is being enjoined is made known as if it were already known; that which is being restated is [made known] as if it were already known for the sake of connecting it with a quality. And a word being uttered once cannot be both "as if known" and "not as if known. The word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow), when being enjoined in connection with the purchase (*kraya*), would be "as if known"; and when being connected with the word *aruṇā* (red), it would likewise be "as if known. However, there is no fault in a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) [if this occurs]; but in the context (*prakaraṇa*), by means of other sentences...
And these other substances and actions, having been obtained, are connected with this [injunction] prescribed by another sentence;

thus it becomes logical that while one thing is enjoined there, another is restated in a different sentence. Therefore, due to the distinction of connection and the lack of distinction in the context, the application is to all substances within the entire context.
This being the case, we reply: "When there is a unity of purpose, there should be a rule of single performance for the substance and the quality.

Where the unity of purpose of a substance and a quality is heard in scripture, there the substance and the quality should be restricted to a single ritual act. Why? Because of their single performance—that is, because they have a single function.

For a single function of substance and quality is heard in scripture: their connection with the act of purchase. How is this understood? From the fact that they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*). How is there a single syntactical unit? Because the meaning of "with a red, tawny-eyed, one-year-old [cow]" is not yet complete due to its expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) for both the speaker and the listener; however, it reaches completion with "he buys Soma," because of the unity of these two. If they have a single function, why does no option (*vikalpa*) arise? This is not so; for according to the rule "those having a single purpose may be optional" (*ekārthāstu vikalperan*), they would possess the character of being optional.
— Thus, this objection is improper. How so? An objection is indeed that which establishes one's own position and acts against the opposing position; but this is not so.
*The reading "ekahāyanībhiḥ" does not appear in the Pāṇinian school manuscript (pā0 so0 pustake). [Page 282] Mīmāṃsā Darśana.*

The alternative (vikalpa) acts against our position; our position is that there is no connection with the fire-drill (araṇi) by means of purchase. Nor is it an alternative, because their effects are different. [Objection:
But was it not just stated—"the effect is one"—and even there...

This is contradictory—for previously it was stated that "because it is formless, a quality is not connected with action," whereas now the opposite is being asserted, namely, that "both the substance and the quality accomplish the single purpose of the purchase. It is replied: this is not a case of option (*vikalpa*), nor is it a contradiction; rather, there is a single effect, but there is a difference in capacity, for the substance [accomplishes it] directly.

Action returns the favor; however, quality is the means for accomplishing excellence. If this is so, then quality does not bring about the action itself, but rather it is the qualifier of the means. This is not so; for the very capacity of a quality to bring about an action consists in its making the means more effective. Furthermore, an action requires a qualification of its means.

For a quality (*guṇa*), acting as a sign (*cihnabhūta*), indicates the means (*sādhana*); if the sign were absent, it would not be indicated—namely, "which is the means of the action?"—and consequently, we would be unable to determine the action to be performed. Thus, the quality becomes the means of the action. And this being so, there is no option (*vikalpa*).

It is as follows: just as in the case of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and [instruments] such as a sword, for the locus indeed supports the agent (*kartṛ*) and the others; for if they were not supported, they would be unable to bring about the action. Likewise, the agent provides support for the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the others; if they were not supported, they would be unable to bring about their respective purposes.
However, when another means (*sādhana*) is prescribed for that very assistance toward the effect which is the object of the primary means' assistance, [that other means is subordinate].

In that regard, there is an option (*vikalpa*), as in: "One should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*) and "One should sacrifice with barley" (*yavair yajeta*); both serve the purpose of producing rice-grains.
If this is so, then it follows that this very thing [the one-year-old cow] becomes an injunction (*vidhāna*).
And that qualifying factor is the quality of redness; in that case, the same fault would follow—namely, the split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
We do not say that the word "red" (*aruṇā*) is connected with the word "one-year-old cow" (*ekahāyanī*);

rather, it is connected only with the verb "to buy" (*krīṇāti*), for thus it is heard in the scripture: "One should effect the purchase by means of the quality of redness. And as to how it is effected by that [quality],...

Thus, one must strive accordingly; and since a quality (*guṇa*) does not bring about an accomplishment (*sādhana*) without a substrate, it follows by implication that it functions as a qualifier of the accomplishment, just as in the case of: "the action brings about the result. [Page 283] Bhāṣya.

"One should cook in a pot"—in this case, since the pot is designated as the instrument for accomplishing the action, one employs the pot for both containing and supporting [the food]; the same should be understood here as well. Therefore, there is no contingency of a split in the sentence.
"But even so, would there not be a split in the sentence? How?
Because completion is observed—each [word] constitutes a separate sentence, just as in the case of Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra."
In the expression "bhojyantām" (let them be fed), the verb "to eat" (bhuji) is completed with each individual;
and as in the case of "he whose father and grandfather do not drink Soma. So too here: "he buys with a red one," "he buys with a one-year-old cow. This is not our position.
[Objection: Even so, the quality of redness (aruṇimā) will apply only to the purchase, not to the entire context. [Reply:
True, this fault does not occur;
however, it follows that the purchase could be made with a one-year-old cow that is not red, and with a red cow that is not one-year-old. In that case—

As for what was stated—that there is a restriction regarding substance and quality—that proposition is abandoned. We do not, therefore, say that there is a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). How so? For it is the purchase (*kraya*) to which both the substance and the redness (*aruṇimā*) are taught, and not the purchase to them. Furthermore, the subordinate element (*guṇa*) does not differ with respect to each principal element (*pradhāna*);
rather, the subordinate element differs with respect to each principal element. And this [rule] exists.

The illustration is: "the completion of the sentence occurs with the aggregate"—as in, for example, "Let the Gargas be fined one hundred," or likewise, "Having pressed [the Soma] and having struck [it], they consume it.
Therefore, the purchase is enjoined as qualified by both qualifiers.

"But how, given both these examples, can it be determined with certainty that the completion of the sentence occurs only in the aggregate and not in each individual part? To this we reply: here, both the substance and the quality of redness are connected to the action.
The two [substances] are perceived as mutually unconnected; likewise, the purchase is perceived as qualified by both the substance and the quality of redness, not by either one alone.
In that case, if this statement refers to both the substance and the quality of redness, then there is undoubtedly a connection with the purchase for each individual component.

Now, if it is stated with the desire to prescribe the purchase (*kraya*), then just as this [cow] is qualified by the state of being one-year-old (*ekahāyanī*), so too is it qualified by the state of being white (*avaṇi*); thus, a necessary connection between both must be accepted. Furthermore, in this case, neither the substance nor the color is what is primarily desired; rather, what is desired is—

[The word] *krayaḥ* [is the subject], for by means of it the substance *soma*, which belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma, is obtained. The substance and the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) must both be employed for the purpose of purchase; otherwise, they would not be connected. Therefore, the purchase is enjoined, and it is understood that it is not qualified by either one [of the two factors] alone—thus it is determined here that the completion of the sentence occurs with the aggregate. And when this is so, there is no other substance apart from the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) that serves as the means of purchase, nor is there anything other than the redness (*aruṇa*).
Another quality is a qualifier of the means of accomplishment—thus, the restrictive rule (niyama) is established.

To this we reply: if the quality enters into a relationship with the means of accomplishing the purchase, then, even though the sentence is distinct, because it serves as the means for the purchase, the redness (āruṇimā) [belongs] to this substance.

It does not enter [into the syntactical unity]; for what purpose is syntactical unity established as the primary goal? To this it is replied: For if the sentences were separate, the purchase would be understood as having the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) as its means, and the redness (*aruṇa*) would be another purchase having redness as its means; the quality of redness would not be known as belonging to that very same purchase which has the one-year-old cow as its means. In that case, whatever...

The act of purchase is qualified by the quality of redness; therein, another means of accomplishment also becomes applicable by implication, and the quality of redness, qualifying that as well, would be connected with it. However, this difficulty is avoided when there is syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*). Therefore, it is rightly stated: "When there is oneness of purpose between the substance and the quality, there should be a restrictive rule because of their serving a single function" (3.1.6).
The performance of all [the rites] beginning with the planetary offerings (*graha*) is based on the context of the *samsthā* and so forth. (And there is the principle of singularity.
Kha. Sūtra 13: That which is joined with singularity belongs to one [offering], because of its connection with the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). (Pūrvapakṣa)
There exists the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, [stated as]: "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with Soma. (Bhāṣya).
*The reading "niyogataḥ" is found in the Prācīna manuscript.
"It is concluded," so it says in the Prāyaścitta-puṭa [Page 285].
And this is heard in the Bhāṣya: "He cleanses the cup with the fringe of the *daśāpavitra*," and likewise...

In the Agnihotra it is heard: "He sweeps away the grass from the fire"; likewise, in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices it is heard: "He carries fire around the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). In this regard, there is a doubt: should the sweeping and other rites be performed for one cup, one fire, and one sacrificial cake, or for all the cups, all the fires, and all the cakes?

[Is it] of all the *puroḍāśas*? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? One cup (*graha*), one fire (*agni*), and one *puroḍāśa* are to be taken here. Why? Because of the connection with the scriptural statement (*śruti*). These items are connected with the scriptural mention of singularity; for among these, a single substance is heard in the scripture, and in a ritual characterized by eating, that which is [prescribed] by the word is what [is to be used].

Our authority is as follows: when it is said, "One should sacrifice a man," only a single man is sacrificed; likewise, here too, only one cup is to be wiped, only one fire-altar is to be moved, and only one sacrificial cake is to be carried around with the fire.
Or rather, it applies to all [the organs], because the defining characteristic is common to them all; for a defining characteristic is indeed non-distinctive. || 14 ||

Bhāṣya: This is not so; it is not the case that these ritual acts, such as cleansing and the rest, are to be performed upon substances qualified by singularity, such that "all the cups are to be cleansed," "the pits are to be dug for all the oblations," and "only the sacrificial cake is to be carried around with fire. Why? Because the cleansing and other acts are enjoined after the substance has been indicated by the singular number, and that indication is non-distinctive (applicable to all).

Regarding all substances, no distinction is perceived therein as to which vessel is to be wiped and which is not; because of the comprehension of the general term and the non-comprehension of any particularity, there is the cognition of all. The same applies to the fire and the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*). [Objection: But surely the singular number is heard in the text; that [number] specifies [the object].

This is not so; for the singularity that is heard [in the text] would express singularity in the case of the *paca* and other vessels, but it would not exclude the second and subsequent ones, since singularity is its denotation, not the second and so forth.
Mādhava says: "The *daśāpavitra* is a cloth."

[Page 286] Bhāṣya: Since there is no prohibition by that [text], why should acts such as sweeping— which are obtained through the general statement regarding the second [vessel] and so forth— not be performed?

In this regard, it might be argued: since the singular number heard here applies only when there is a single substance, what else could it do regarding a second or subsequent substances other than excluding them? For if the singular number were not to exclude the second and subsequent substances, [the rule would be meaningless].
It would indeed be purposeless, yet it is capable of excluding the second and subsequent [offerings],
just as in the case of "He takes up the horse's bridle"— which excludes the donkey's bridle— so too should it be understood here.

This is not so; the statement— "With this [verse] 'imāmagṛbhṇan,' [one takes] the horse's halter"— is intended to express the relationship between the *mava* and the halter that exists therein, and not [to enjoin the application of the verse].

By this reasoning, since taking is already established by the very indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the word "takes" (*ādatte*), a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṅkhyā*) of the *bhava* is appropriate. However, in this case, as for the singular number heard in reference to the substance (*dravya*), even though it is heard, it ought not to be an eliminator (*nivarttaka*) because it is not being enjoined (*avidhīyamānatvena*), just as, for example:

Suppose someone, pointing to an injunction, were to say: "If anyone should eat this, whether it be a dog or a cat, he must be warded off. In that case, if the act of eating were enjoined as the occasioning condition (*nimitta*)—and not the connection with the dog or the cat—then even a crow arriving there would have to be warded off; for although the dog or the cat is mentioned, their connection [to the eating] is not enjoined as the occasioning condition. Likewise here, since the connection with oneness is not being enjoined, even though oneness is heard, in the ultimate sense...

"It should be wiped"—this is what [the opponent suggests]. However, there is no word here that prescribes a connection between the substance and the number one. "But surely [the word] 'he wipes' (saṃmārṣṭi) [prescribes it]. No, this is not a prescription for the connection between the substance and the number one.

To what, then, does it apply? It is precisely the injunction regarding the connection between the substance and the cleansing that is established by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) within its own word-meaning; otherwise, the meaning of another word would have to be enjoined by syntactical connection (*vākya*). And syntactical connection prevails only when direct statement is impossible, not when direct statement is possible.
Therefore, since unity is being enjoined as a qualifier, it cannot exclude the second and subsequent [cups]. This being the case, the cleansing and other rites are not performed for a second [cup].
[Page 287] Chapter 3, Section 9.
227 bhā.
It is either unexpressed or prohibited; for just as that which is heard with respect to one [element] is understood, so too it is with respect to the second and the rest.

Moreover, this is a fault: that unity would not be restricted to the substance with respect to objects such as the act of wiping (*saṃmārga*). For the act of wiping and so forth does not function as a qualifier for that substance in which unity might be restricted; rather, it is the act of wiping and so forth that is enjoined here.

It is not prescribed as a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the substance, for it cannot be enjoined simultaneously [with the substance] and yet uttered as a characteristic; indeed, only that which has a well-known relationship (*prasiddhasambandha*) is able to function as a characteristic, and a word-comprehended object of this kind does not have a well-known relationship unless it has been enjoined. Furthermore, the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) and so forth are enjoined; therefore—
It is not a qualifier; and if it is not a qualifier, one cannot maintain that unity is restricted to the substance.
"Now, suppose unity is mentioned in connection with the sweeping (*sammārjana*). Even in that case, there would be two possible courses:

The primary object is either the oneness (*ekatva*) or the cleansing (*sammārjana*); yet both of these are untenable. First of all, it is not possible to perform the cleansing of oneness. Nor does the cleansing, when performed upon the substance, benefit the oneness in any way.
Furthermore, there is no purpose served by benefiting the oneness, for it is not heard in the scripture as being a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*). Now, if...
"Unity is subordinate with respect to the cleansing"—this too is not correct. Why?
Because it is incorporeal; for that [unity] does not effect the cleansing. Even though another incorporeal thing, by qualifying the means, effects the action, nevertheless this [unity] does not.
It must be so; for here the word *saṃmārja* does not have the sense of purification (*saṃmārga*), and purification is enjoined for the sake of the cup (*graha*).
For that [cup] possesses a purpose, whereas purification would have its purpose merely inferred.
If the cup were to assist the purification, then one would be assisting that which assists it—thus [the relationship is established].
Oneness would be an auxiliary to the cleansing (*sammārga*), but it is not so; therefore, there is no connection between oneness and cleansing. [Objection:
"But even though it is the primary element, the *mahā-āhuti* and so forth certainly accomplish the cleansing; therefore..."

That means of accomplishment, being thus distinguished, will assist that [result], just as the ritual properties (dharma) applied to the curd and milk for the purpose of oblation assist in the cooking; and likewise those applied for the purpose of wrapping.
[Page 288]

[The opponent says: "The enclosing-sticks (paridhis) possess the characteristics of the sacrificial post (yūpa) because they serve as a means of binding; therefore, this is not a valid solution. To this, it is replied: We do not say that those things which do not serve that purpose are incapable of providing assistance.
What then? [We mean that] when the principal element, such as the horse and so forth, is used as a defining characteristic...

It is said: at that time, there is no connection between oneness and the large number (mahat) and so forth, nor with the cleansing (saṃmārga) and so forth. How so? Because whenever something is mentioned here as a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇatvena), there is a correspondence (saṃvāda) in that regard, but it is not enjoined for the sake of cognition. "For what purpose, then, is it mentioned? [The answer is: "Something else will be enjoined for it"—this is that very point.

Having perceived the cup (*graha*) and so forth, its cleansing (*saṃmārga*) and other such acts are enjoined. If, therefore, a further connection with oneness were enjoined either with respect to the substance "cup" or with respect to the ritual act such as cleansing, the sentence would be split due to the enjoining of two distinct relationships. Now, it might be argued: "The cup..."

If it were the case that after having caused [the cup] to be offered, its connection with oneness is enjoined—and not its connection with the cleansing and so forth—then it would have to be admitted that the study of the cleansing and other rites is a mistake; but this is not so. Therefore, the singular number is not connected with either [of the two]. Thus, this oneness renders no assistance to the cup, nor to the cleansing; it is merely restated as it already exists. Therefore, this is not [the case].

"It is intended to perform even a small portion"—thus, the *sammārjana* (sweeping) and other rites must be performed for all the great fires. Why? Because of the connection and because there is no distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*).

[Objection: "If singularity is not intended to be expressed, why is the singular number uttered there? Surely, when plurality is intended, the plural number ought to be used. [Reply: We do not deliberate on this point—namely, whether the singular number ought to be uttered or ought not to be uttered.
— When this is being recited, what is to be understood? Is it only in one [instance], such as the *sammārgī*, or in all? In this regard, it has been established that it applies to all.
Furthermore, the purpose of the case-ending is not merely to express [the number]; what then?

Even in the case of the relationship between the *kāraka* and its connection, when unity is not intended to be expressed, this [number] will be uttered for the sake of the *kāraka*-connection; therefore, it is not meaningless.
Moreover, the base (*prātipadika*) signifies the cup (*graha*), while unity is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*). What follows from this?
[Page 289] Bhāṣya:

If this is so, then this is heard: the case-ending expresses the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by direct denotation (*śruti*) itself. Now, if this is the case, what is the harm? [Is it not possible that] the sweeping (*saṃmārga*) [is connected to the cup]?

"How will it be connected?"—for it would be connected with the sentence by that [word], and not by direct statement (*śruti*); for that which is being connected with one sentence cannot be severed from it to be connected with another. But if it were not being connected with the single act of cleansing (*sammārjana*), then...

It is not the case that [the action] is performed as qualified by oneness, nor does anything go wrong; nor is the cleansing (saṃmārga) and so forth qualified by oneness, but rather it is enjoined for the cup (graha) and so forth alone—so why should it not be performed for the second and the third?
But when there is an injunction, because it is for the sake of another, it should be understood according to the scriptural statement. 15.
(Śrauta-nirṇaya)
HT.

Now, as for what was stated [at 225.10, Pañjikā]: "Just as in the case of 'one should sacrifice a beast' (*paśum ālabheta*), where only a single beast, male or female, is sacrificed, so too is this [the case here]"—there is indeed a scriptural authority (*śruti*) on this point.

And the meaning of the word *paddārtha* (the purpose of the substance) is purification (*sammārga*). In that case, the animal is for the purpose of the sacrifice. What follows from this? That which one sets aside for the sake of the sacrifice benefits the sacrifice; for a sacrifice cannot be performed with what has not been set aside. However, purification is not to be performed upon a vessel by means of anything whatsoever that is intended for it—such that by setting aside the vessel, one would benefit the purification—and rather, this singleness of the animal is enjoined with respect to the sacrifice. [Objection: But surely...

(225 | 7 pa0) — "The case-ending directly expresses the capacity residing in the meaning of the nominal stem by its very power (*śruti*"; this [number] will enjoin it in the sacrifice through syntactical connection (*vākya*), and it has been stated that *śruti* is stronger than *vākya*. True; where a direct relationship is intended to be expressed, and where it is not so intended, that which is understood through *vākya* remains unprecluded.

Therefore, one male animal is sacrificed. However, the singularity of the cup (*graha*) does not assist the act of cleansing (*sammārga*), and thus it cannot qualify the cup. Consequently, it is not intended to be expressed."
— thus. (3 | 1 | 7 a0) | The reading is ‘paricchitti’ in the Bāla-vyākhyāna and Soma-siddhānta manuscripts; likewise in the Kāśī-kāśīmudrita manuscript.
[Page 290]
The section concerning the non-application of cleansing and other rites to the *camasa* cups and similar vessels.
No; for on account of the [mere] performance of the ritual, there would be an absence of fixed order among the qualities. (Pūrvapakṣa 16)

Bhāṣya: There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, and in that context it is heard: "He cleanses the cup with a fringed filter. Regarding this, the following has been understood: all cups are to be cleansed. This meaning has been understood. Now, this is being deliberated: should the *camasa* vessels also be cleansed?
Or not?
What, then, is the prima facie view? That everything, including the *camasa* cups and so forth, is to be cleansed.
Why? Because there is no distinction in their connection [to the ritual] and because there is no distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*). Just as...
For there is a connection with the *apūrva* (transcendental result) in the case of the cups (*graha*), and likewise for the bowls (*camasa*).
Just as the cups are mentioned in this context, so too are the bowls. Therefore, the cleansing (*sammārjana*) applies to all of them.
[Objection: "But the cups are explicitly heard in the text; they will therefore exclude the bowls."
[The opponent says: "It is recited [in the text]. The mention of 'cup' (*graha*) will be for the purpose of illustration;

that is, the *soma*-vessel beginning with the *graha*, in which the *soma* being poured might spill—when this has been stated, all of that must be wiped clean; just as when mealtime has arrived, the cooking-pots [must be cleaned]."

When it is said, "Let them be wiped," all those things that are fit for use in eating are wiped; it is understood that the mention of the "pot" (sthālī) is for the purpose of illustration. It should be seen that the same applies here as well. [Objection: In the world, practical usage is characterized by its purpose; whatever object is wiped for a specific purpose, [that alone is wiped].
Whether it has been stated or not, that [act] must indeed be performed. But here in the Veda, [the connection] is defined by the word;

and since the word "cup" (graha) indicates the cleansing (sammārga), why should the word "cup," which is directly heard in the text, be assumed through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā)? It is said: [it is so] because of the act of cleansing—namely, in the cleansing.
This word is capable of enjoining human effort by the mere act of hearing; however, in relation to the connection with the cup (*graha*), it would require a syntactical sentence (*vākya*).

Since direct audition (*śruti*) is more authoritative than a syntactical sentence, the word *graha* must therefore be explained through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) rather than according to its literal sense. Consequently, whatever among you is fit for the refinement of cleansing (*sammārjana*) must be cleansed; such a quality does not remain restricted solely to the cups.

[Page 291] Or rather, there is a fixed determination of the meaning because of its connection with the Vedic text, since that [text] possesses the status of a means of valid knowledge (*śabda-pramāṇa*). (Siddhānta)

Or rather, the wiping (*saṃmārjana*) would apply only to the cups (*graha*), and not, by extension, to the bowls (*camasa*). Why? Because the purpose is connected with the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*);
for the cup (*graha*) that is being heard [in the text] must not be abandoned. If it were abandoned, the very scriptural statement "the cup" would be contradicted;
thus it is understood that what those venerable ones say is merely the song of the careless, and this is not proper. Therefore...
Since the word "ten" indicates the cup by implication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is the connection of that cup with the act of cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) that is enjoined.
And one cannot enjoin a connection without enjoining the act itself; therefore, this very word enjoins the cleansing. Nor will the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) be contradicted. Why? Because...

"One cleanses"—this [injunction] can enjoin the act of cleansing as something already existing through human effort, as established by direct Vedic audition (śruti), and there is no distinction here whether the cleansing is being produced for the first time or is being connected with something else. Therefore, even when there is a connection with the cups (graha), the direct audition is not sublated;
thus, it is proper that the cleansing be restricted to the cups themselves based on direct audition.

"Now, it has been argued that because there is no distinction regarding the prior conjunction and because there is no distinction regarding the context, this injunction would apply to the *camasa* cups as well, and not be restricted to the *graha* vessels alone. To this, it is replied: It is able to enjoin [the action] there only by forming a single syntactical unit with those elements that possess the context; it cannot do so otherwise.

Having set aside the unity of expression; and that [unity] is inferred from the context (*prakaraṇa*), whereas this [connection] is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) along with the word "one" (*eka*). Therefore, there is no injunction within the context; for having abandoned its own purpose in connection with the oneness of the cup (*graha*), it is not able to enjoin it. In the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "The sacrificial post (yūpa) of the Vājapeya has seventeen spokes. therefore, it must apply to that part of the Vājapeya which is similar to a sacrificial post.
And there is the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice; because of its being made of *khadira* wood and its having the dimensions of half [the standard], it resembles a sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

When it is placed therein, the term "Vājapeya" applies directly (*āñjasena*); otherwise, the word "Vājapeya" would have to be applied to the animal sacrifice which is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the Vājapeya by means of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus it is said.

It should be understood thus: "But surely, even in our own view, the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) refers to the half-vessel by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). To this we reply: in every respect we accept the use of secondary indication; however, in our position, the context of the *vājapeya* sacrifice is upheld. Therefore, it finds its place in the half-vessel. This being the prima facie view, we say: "Because it would otherwise be purposeless, [it applies] to its subsidiaries"; for the word *vājapeya*—first of all—[is not applicable there].

It is a term denoting a specific *somayāga*; it has no direct requirement for a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), yet it has as its subsidiary (*aṅga*) the *paśuyāga*, and the purpose of that [subsidiary] is to connect the animal with the post. If seventeen-foldness were prescribed directly for the *vājapeya* post, then because such a post does not exist [in that context], the statement would result in being meaningless. In the animal sacrifice there is a sacrificial post (*yūpa*); it is that [post] which ought to receive the application of the term. And whatever assists that which is its benefactor becomes connected to it.
It is through a direct relationship alone, and not one that is separated by one [intermediary]—thinking thus, it becomes connected;

just as in the case of "Devadatta’s grandson," he is separated from Devadatta by his son, yet he is connected to Devadatta by a direct relationship. Therefore, this very [relationship] is [the one intended].

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "He clenches his fists, restrains his speech, and announces the initiated one"—and likewise, "He washes both hands and wipes them on the grass. In this regard, there is a doubt: are the clenching of the fists and the restraint of speech for the purpose of the announcement, or do they find their place within that specific context? Likewise, what about the washing of the hands?
Is it for the purpose of spreading a mat of grass (*ulaparāji*), or rather for performing all the ritual acts within the context?

What, then, is the prima facie view? Washing the hands is for the purpose of purifying the hands, and the restraint of speech (*vāgyama*) is for the purpose of purifying the person; by restraining his speech, one becomes single-minded and performs the ritual acts. Thus, there arises an expectancy as to which specific acts these two purifications serve. When this expectancy exists, it is satisfied by immediate proximity (*ānantarya*).

Therefore, because of the immediate sequence, [one might think] that the vow of silence, the clenching of the fists, the washing of the hands, and the spreading of the *ulaparāja* grass are for the purpose of the *Avadāna*.
This being the prima facie view, we reply: there is a connection with all those things studied within the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Mādhava says: "A bed of *ulapa* grass has been prepared there to serve as a mattress."

"—thus, and not for the purpose of spreading [the grass]—in this sense he spreads [it].

In the section on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is recited: "One makes the cake for Agni four-fold. Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the making four-fold apply to the offering to Agni, the offering to Agni-Soma, and the offering to Indra-Agni everywhere; or does it apply to the offering to Agni alone? What is the prima facie view?
The making four-fold applies to all the remaining offerings, because the term "for Agni" (*āgneyam*) is common to all, being connected with the quality of having Agni as its deity.
It is understood that this [quality] would apply to the Agniṣomīya offering as well, and even to the Aindrāgna offering. Why? Because both of those are "belonging to Agni" (āgneya);
for that which has Agni as its deity, even if another deity is also present, it is still "belonging to Agni.
It is just as, for example, the mother of both Ḍittha and Uvittha is [still] the mother of Uvittha.

It occurs; so it is here as well. If there were no mutual relationship between the cake for Agni and the cake for Agni-Soma, then the fourfold cutting would be restricted to the cake for Agni alone. But such a relationship does exist; therefore, there is no restriction, just as one cuts off the *prāśitra* portion from all [the cakes] after dividing the head of the cake for Agni.
The cutting off of the *prāśitra* portion; likewise also the making into four parts.

Or rather, there is a fixed determination [of the meaning] because of the connection with the object; since the indicative mark (liṅga) is connected with the object, the mention of the quality is for the purpose of definition. (Siddhānta 27)

The *vājagdaḥ* (the portion of the omentum) turns away one side, or rather, it should remain fixed; the making of four portions belongs to the *āgneya* (offering to Agni) alone, and it cannot be common to both. Why? Because of its connection with the specific purpose.

By means of the deity Agni, there is a connection with that which has a single deity, but not with that which has two deities—namely, the Agnīṣomīya and the Aindrāgna. Why? Because for that which has Agni-Soma as its deity, the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) is made characterized by both qualifiers; in that case, Agni is a deity only in dependence upon Soma, not independently. And for that which has Agni as a deity in dependence upon Soma, the secondary derivative suffix (taddhita) is not produced from it, for that suffix is said to be applied only to those [words] that are semantically independent (samartha).

And that which is dependent is incapable [of syntactic connection]. Therefore, there can be no designation of a dual-deity offering by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) ending in *agni*, which refers to a single deity independently. Consequently, the fourfold division (*caturdhīkaraṇa*) occurs only where Agni is the independent deity; for the connection of the meaning of the secondary derivative with the indicative mark of the deity occurs through semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), and not when such capacity is absent.

Now, as for what was said—that just as the cutting of the *prāśitra* portion is performed from all [the cakes], so too is the making of four parts—it is correct that the connection there is made with the *prāśitra* cutting, namely: "He cuts the *prāśitra* of the cake dedicated to Agni (*āgneya*). [Objection: "How then is it that 'having divided the head of the cake dedicated to Agni'? [Response: In that context, one part is "he cuts the *prāśitra* of the cake dedicated to Agni," while the second part is "having divided the head of the cake dedicated to Agni. Thus, in that case, it refers to the cake dedicated to Agni.

It is understood that [the portion] is cut from the head; there is no fixed rule as to whether it is from the head of one [animal] or from another. For if that [portion] were not dedicated solely to Agni, then, in order to avoid its being purposeless, it would have been accepted as being dedicated to two deities.

Something is required [as a correlate]. And since such a relationship exists there—as in the expression "the mother of Ḍittha"—the statement is logical. (3.1.15 a0)

[Page 303] The section concerning the primary application of mantras whose meaning is not manifest. (Vahnyadhikaraṇa).

Sūtra: "The status of being subsidiary to the ritual act should belong to mantras because of their capacity to express meaning; therefore, there is an inherent connection with the purpose, due to the eternal association. (1)

Bhāṣya: Here, the mantras are the examples, such as "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods," and so forth. Is the application of these mantras restricted to their primary meaning alone, or also to their secondary meaning?
What, then, is the primary meaning, and what is the secondary? It is said:
that which is understood from the word itself is the first cognition, the primary; it is like a face (the foremost).

— Thus, that which is understood from a well-known meaning through some connection is called "primary" (*mukhya*). However, that which is understood later, like the hindquarters (*jaghana*), is "secondary" (*jaghanya*); and because of its connection with a quality (*guṇa*), it is "figurative" (*gauṇa*).

"If this is so, then all of this is primary; for everything is understood from the word itself. Just as when it is said, 'The fire burns,' there is a cognition of the burning, even so, when the word 'the boy is fire' is uttered, there is a cognition of the boy. Now, if it should be argued:

"That [meaning] which is understood from a word without an accompanying term (*nirupapada*) is primary (*mukhya*); that which is understood from a word with an accompanying term (*sopapada*) is secondary (*gauṇa*)"—this is not tenable; for whatever the form of a word may be the cause for a certain meaning, that very same form remains even when it is accompanied by an accompanying term.

Even in the case of the word without an *upapada*; nor is it possible that when the cause (*nimitta*) exists, the effect (*naimittika*) should not exist. "What follows from this? If this is so, then one cannot say: "Without an *upapada*, its meaning does not arise; but once the *upapada* has appeared, its meaning will arise. Furthermore, the meaning of the whole (*samudāyārtha*) cannot be understood [in that way].

For the distinction [between word-meaning and sentence-meaning] is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Now, if it is argued that "the sentence-meaning arises from the word-meanings," this is not possible; for a sentence-meaning does not arise from word-meanings that have not been connected. Therefore, let it be stated thus: this very word *agni* denotes burning.

"The word *agni* itself is the designator of the *bhāṇavaka*"; therefore, there is no distinction such that the primary sense is superior to the secondary sense. If it is argued, "That which is well-established is primary, while that which is only slightly so is secondary"—this too is not tenable.

Familiarity is indeed cognition, and there is no distinction within cognition itself. If it is argued that "that which is employed frequently is primary (*mukhya*), while that which is employed rarely is secondary (*gauṇa*)," this is not so; for even when employed rarely, a word cannot convey its meaning if it lacks the capacity [to do so]. Therefore, since it is understood from the word itself, it is primary.
[Objection: An objection is raised: "There is a distinction here; the *māṇavaka* (the young student) is not understood from the word 'fire' (*agni*).

How is this known? It has been stated [at 1.3.36]: 'It is improper for a single word to have multiple meanings. Why is it not the other way around? [Reply: It is said: we observe that people, disregarding the cognition of the *māṇavaka*, understand the flaming [fire] from the word 'fire'.
But they do not understand the young boy from the word "fire" while disregarding its similarity [to fire]. Why is this so?
Because the word "fire" is restricted to whatever object is intended to be expressed that resembles fire;
for it is precisely for this reason that it is observed to cease when the similarity has departed. Therefore...

Similarity is not the cause for the application [of the word] to this [boy], nor is that similarity perceived when the burning [of fire] is absent. Therefore, the word "fire" has burning as its cause with respect to fire, but not with respect to the boy; therefore, it is used in its primary sense (*mukhya*) with respect to fire, not with respect to the boy. It is exactly the same regarding the cognition of grass.

In that case, sound is not the cause for a cognition similar to [the cognition of] grass. Thus, since this condition exists, there arises the inquiry: "Does the word have a primary sense, or does it also have a secondary sense? What, then, is the prima facie position? That there is application both to the primary and the secondary sense. Why?

Since both are possible, both—the grass itself and that which resembles grass—can be conveyed by the word "barhis" (sacrificial grass). Grass is conveyed directly, while that which resembles grass is conveyed through the cognition of grass. And whatever can indeed be conveyed by the word "barhis," which serves as a means for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, all of that must be conveyed, because there is no reason for making a restrictive selection.

Furthermore, if this is accepted, the eating of the *pūṣan*-portion and other such acts are not displaced from the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*); rather, they will denote the deity under discussion by means of a figurative expression (*gauṇa-abhidhāna*).

This being the case, we reply: the *mantra* must be employed in its primary sense (*mukhya*), not in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*). Why? Because both [uses] are impossible. For, due to its recitation within the context (*prakaraṇa*), it enters into a single syntactical unity with the principal act; thus it follows that one should accomplish with this *mantra* whatever can be accomplished by it. And since it is capable of assisting through its connection with the expression of the primary meaning, it does not intend to denote a secondary meaning.
Therefore, there is no application [of the word] in a secondary sense. [Objection:
"But surely, from the cognition of the primary sense, the secondary sense can be conveyed. [Response: This is true;
however, its purposeful utility is already fulfilled by the cognition of the primary sense alone—thus, it does not apply to the secondary sense.

There is no evidence for its application in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*). However, by its application in the primary sense (*mukhya*), its lack of purpose (*ānarthakya*) is avoided; once the lack of purpose has been avoided, a secondary denotation does not follow, for a word does not denote a secondary meaning without first denoting the primary one. Therefore, due to the absence of evidence, it should not be applied in a secondary sense.

Furthermore, because the secondary sense (*gauṇa*) possesses the capacity for communication, many means of approach are obtained; and it has been stated [in *Śābarabhāṣya* 9.4.30] that this capacity consists in being a part of the word—namely, "because it is a part of the conceptualization arising from the meaning. In that context, with respect to the secondary sense, there is necessarily...

If [the mantra] were applied [to the mouth], it would be sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the absence of another means. If it is argued that "the recitation of the mantra is the means of valid cognition," we say no; for that [recitation] lacks the capacity to exclude other means. [Objection: But surely this same fault applies even to its application to the mouth.
[Reply: No, it is said; for if it were not applied even to the mouth, it would not [be a mantra at all].

It would benefit the primary [meaning], and in that case, its arising [in the secondary sense] would be entirely purposeless. Therefore, there is a distinction between the secondary and the primary. Furthermore, one who applies a mantra to the secondary meaning should be asked: "Why do you not cause it to convey the primary meaning? (Note: some manuscripts read "notlakṣyante" instead of "na lakṣyante").

306]: If he should say, "There is no figurative cognition otherwise," one should reply to him, "There are other means for figurative cognition as well.
Then, if he, being thus challenged, should reply, "The primary cognition is also occasional..."

If one were to say this, he should be told: "In that case, it is not necessarily to be applied in a secondary sense; for when one employs the primary meaning in order to produce the secondary cognition, it follows that the application is actually to the primary meaning itself. Furthermore, the purpose is served by the meaning as it is understood, not by the mantra as the means of expression;
therefore, the secondary sense may be conveyed by other means as well."

It is that which is to be made understood; it is not that very [secondary] thing itself which must be employed by me. Even if there were a need for a means of communication (*pratyāyaka*), even then the purpose would be accomplished by the primary means of communication alone—thus, it would certainly not be employed in a secondary sense. Therefore, it is established that the comprehension of the task occurs through the primary and the secondary [meanings] directly.

Therefore, it shall be carried out wherever it is purposeful, and not otherwise.
