In the *Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*, it is heard in the *Anvākhyāna*: "With the mantra, 'The dweller, the gatherer of riches,' one worships the Gārhapatya fire with the verse addressed to Indra. Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the worship be performed for Indra, or for the Gārhapatya fire? But why is there a doubt when the statement "one worships the Gārhapatya" is so explicit? It is said in reply:
"But for some, it is recited as 'rasī' at certain times," so says the Vārttika.
[Page 307] Bhāṣya:

Since the attendance is performed by means of the sentence, that is a consecration (*saṃskaraṇa*) through words of praise, not merely standing nearby; nor is it possible to effect the naming of Agni by means of the Indra-invoking verse.

Therefore, regarding the statement "he worships the Gārhapatya fire," the doubt might arise that this worship is for the sake of the Gārhapatya—that it should be intended as worship directed toward the Gārhapatya. However, there is no such word [expressing that], whether ending in the instrumental case or the locative.
Consequently, an inquiry arises: how is this to be understood? This is the point.
What, then, is the prima facie view? It is that, by virtue of the inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*) and because [worship directed at the Gārhapatya] would be impossible, it is worship of Indra.

Regarding the worship of the Gārhapatya fire: if it is asked, "Why is the accusative case used?"—the answer is that it is either used when the desired object is not intended to be primary, or it emphasizes the mere relationship. Alternatively, the word *gārhapatya* functions as a qualifier of the act of worship due to its connection [with it]. Therefore, the worship qualified by the Gārhapatya fire must be performed for the sake of Indra.
For a qualification serves to specify the primary action itself.

Since it is thus established that [the *aindrī* verse] pertains to the *gārhapatya* by virtue of its location, we reply: on account of the direct statement (*vacana*), the *aindrī* verse should be used for a purpose other than its literal meaning; it is not the case that this worship (*upasthāna*) is for the sake of Indra—the *aindrī* verse should be used for a purpose other than its literal meaning. Why?
By virtue of the force of the statement—since there is this statement, "He worships the Gārhapatya with 'O Mother'"—the accusative case-ending on *gārhapatya* indicates its predominance.
What indeed could a statement not accomplish? There is no burden too great for a scriptural injunction. Therefore, the worship is for the sake of the Gārhapatya fire.
The designation [of the sacrificer] as one from whom [the fee] is to be taken would be based on his own quality, because the relationship is not caused by the scripture. (Sūtra 4, Purvapakṣa-Nirṇaya)
[The Bhāṣya says:

"Now, it might be argued here: 'In this case, the worship of the Gārhapatya fire will not be performed with the verse addressed to Indra. To this we reply: It will be so because of a direct scriptural injunction. And he says:

Even with a hundred utterances, one who says, "One might cause fire to be understood by the word 'Indra'," would be contradicted; just as [one might say], "One should sprinkle with fire," or "One should illuminate with water. For the relationship between a word and its meaning is not caused by human convention;
rather, it is eternal and is understood from worldly usage—thus it was stated [in Sūtra 1.1.5]: "The [relationship] is innate..."
[Page 308] Bhartṛhari says:

"The relationship of a word with its meaning is eternal. [Objection: "But is there not also an artificial relationship between a word and its meaning characterized by convention, such as 'Devadatta' or 'Yajñadatta'? [Reply:
There is indeed such a case, where there exists a sentence that establishes that relationship.

However, this sentence does not establish a relationship between the word and its meaning; rather, it means that one worships the Gārhapatya fire with the word "Indra" by virtue of a well-known relationship. For it is not possible for one thing to be designated by a word belonging to another.

To say this, what purpose would speech serve here? Bhāṣya: To this it is replied—“Or rather, there may be denotation through a quality, because a relationship is the cause of cognition”—even though this sentence does not prescribe the relationship between word and meaning.

Although it is the cause [of the name], nevertheless, by this word "Indra," it is possible to effect the designation of the Gārhapatya fire. Why? Because of the connection with a quality, this designation will be figurative;

for there are indeed designations based on a quality, such as "Devadatta is a lion" or "The young Brahmin is fire. In the same way, here too, the word "Indra" is applied to the Gārhapatya, which is not actually Indra.

It will come to pass; and he possesses a resemblance to Indra: just as Indra is the means for accomplishing the sacrifice, so too is the Gārhapatya fire. Alternatively, Indra is so called from the root *ind*, which signifies sovereignty (*aiśvarya*); and the Gārhapatya fire also possesses sovereignty over its own function.

Therefore, the meaning which is conveyed by the word "Indra," once it has been understood, will convey the sense of the Gārhapatya fire either through similarity or through the quality of sovereignty; thus, there is no fault. (3.2.2)

How would it be enjoined with reference to the act of killing? Or how would it indicate the time?

If the connection were made thus—"O preparer of the oblation, come! while striking—then it would be taught as being subordinate to the act of striking; but if it were "while striking, he cooks," then it would indicate its time. And this being the case, [the statement] "he understands thus" is a restatement; he performs the summoning (*śrāhāna*).

For he who says "come" (*ehi*) is one who summons (*āhvayati*); in that context, he will cause the intoxication to be understood through some quality. Therefore, it should not be employed in the *nākāna*.

Bhāṣya: This is not so—it is taught as a definition. What then? It would be a definition of time. Why? Because in the expression "he makes it long" (*ciram karoti*), the state of being long (*cirtvam*) is enjoined; for if this were enjoined within this very same sentence, there would be the fault of enjoining multiple subordinate qualities (*anekaguṇavidhāna*).

The sentence would be split! Therefore, the connection is not thus—"while threshing"—but rather, "he causes [the wife] to thresh. [Objection: But even in this view, both the mantra and the time are being enjoined; therefore, that same fault would occur. [Reply: No.

We reply: At the very time of the announcement (*āvahana*), the offering (*havis*) is to be understood as clarified butter (*ājya*); in that context, this very connection is restated (*anūdyate*), while the mere tripling (*trir-āghāraṇa*) is what is enjoined (*vidhīyate*). As for the claim that the word is for the purpose of indicating the time (*kāla-lakṣaṇārtha*), this is not a fault; for indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is indeed common in worldly usage, and here too, since the action is already established by its very form (*rūpa*), it is merely restated, and having been so enjoined, it is performed.
By means of another sentence, the threshing is able to indicate the time; therefore, it should be employed for the purpose of summoning.
In the Mīmāṃsā system:

the meaning of a sentence can be established only in conjunction with what has been immediately cognized; and when unrelated words are uttered, there is no immediate cognition, and thus no syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) occurs.
Therefore, [the opponent suggests]:

"Alternatively, by means of another method such as meditation (dhyāna) and so forth, one may first comprehend the meaning of the preceding word and then produce the meaning of the sentence. That [sentence-meaning] would be non-Vedic, being preceded by human intellect.

It would be as follows: just as when one takes a verbal root from one section (anuvāka) and a noun from another, a sentence-meaning is produced, so too would it be in a case where one produces a sentence-meaning after having understood the meaning of the preceding word through some other means such as meditation (dhyāna). Therefore...
It is determined that syntactic unity does not exist when there is an intervention by unrelated matters;
therefore, there is no syntactic unity between the *sāmidhenī* verses and the *upavīta*. [Objection:
"But the *upavīta* is prescribed in proximity to the various ritual variations (*kalpa*) of the *sāmidhenīs*, which are present in the immediate consciousness."

"Therefore, it will be connected with the *sāmidhenī* verses"—to this we say: "No. For the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *sāmidhenīs* has indeed ceased, due to the intervention of the *nivid* formulas.

By means of syntactical connection (*vākya*), the optional forms of the *sāmidhenīs* enter into a relationship [with those *nivid* formulas], and the context does not persist; furthermore, by the statement of these optional forms, the *sāmidhenīs* are no longer the subject under discussion.

O venerable ones! For in that case, their statement does not mean "they are to be performed," but rather, "they are to be connected with the numbers. And even that is established by syntactical connection (*vākya*), not by context (*prakaraṇa*). In that regard, for a quality whose single-sentence unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the *sāmidhenī* verses is not established when those *sāmidhenīs* are not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*), there is no connection with them. Therefore...
It is established that whatever is to be performed in a ritual context must be done while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī).

[Page 318] Bhāṣya: There should be an application (viniyoga) of those [verses]. "Now, for what reason are the indicative power (liṅga) and the ritual action (karman) specified? All [the verses] would be applied only to the function of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*;
there would be no application among the *sāmidhenī* verses. But then, on account of the name (*samākhyāna*)...

And because the function of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses has already been fulfilled by the sequence of the *liṅga* (indicative power), their application to the *sāmidhenī* verses becomes established; just as when the sequence of the *agnivāruṇī* sacrifice has passed and the *saumāraudrī* sacrifices have not yet arrived, it is stated that "those [verses] are to be placed among the *sāmidhenī*s as *dhāyyā*s," so too are the two *dhāyyā*s: "pṛthuyājāstaṃ sambādhe."
Both [terms] are thus explained. Therefore, both should be designated.
(3.2.7 Śrauta-sūtra; Śabarabhāṣya).
The section concerning the application of the vital breaths in the act of propping up the sacrificial post.
And the rule regarding mantras applies to those who do not possess that [qualification], because they are disciplined in their respective offices. (Pūrvapakṣa 20)

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "One worships the Āgnīdhra with an Āgneyī [verse], the Sadas with an Aindrī, and the Havirdhāna with a Vaiṣṇavī. Regarding this, there is a doubt: should one worship using only those [verses] from the present context that possess such indicative marks (liṅga), or should verses with such marks be brought in from the Daśatayas?

What, then, is the prima facie position? Since a mantra is enjoined by its indicative power (*liṅga*) within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), it must be brought from among the *Daśatayas* (the ten maṇḍalas of the Ṛgveda). For the mantras beginning with "āgneya" are capable of denoting those [verses] belonging to the *Daśatayas*. Furthermore, this particular mantra under discussion has already been employed for another purpose.

Even here, it does not deserve to be taught; for the teaching of what has already been taught is indeed not logical in such a case. Of what kind [of thing]? That which has been taught with respect to a particular distinction does not deserve to be taught elsewhere by means of a general mark. How so?
If that mark were its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), then that [object] would be distinguished by it.
"One should touch" (upaspṛśet) — thus [it is stated in] Vyāsa’s Soma-puṣpa.
[Page 319] Bhāṣya:
Since one performs this by means of this very indicative mark (liṅga), it is therefore not [merely] taught.

It exists; now it is taught that "one performs [the rite] with such a mark"—if this were so, then it would not be perceived [as something new], and therefore a further teaching of such a kind for that which has already been taught in such a manner is not logical. Consequently, those [verses] from the *Daśataya* which possess the marks [are what are intended].
[They] have been grasped. [Objection:
"But surely, by the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is proper to grasp those that are under discussion.
[Reply: It is said in response: for an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger than context. [Objection: "If there is a contradiction..."

The context would be sublated by the indicative mark (*liṅga*), yet there is no contradiction between these two; for we do not, out of a desire to favor the context, sublate the indicative mark while adopting the subject matter (*prakṛta*) that possesses that mark. However, if we were to adopt the subject matter as being devoid of that mark, then we would indeed sublate the indicative mark.
We shall, therefore, accomplish both—the context and the indicative mark. This is not so, because [it is sublated] by the indicative mark.

There arises the conviction that "it must be performed even with the *dāśataya* [verses]," for even the *dāśataya* verses can indeed be designated by the term *āgneyī*. That conviction, which is produced by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and conceived as being "because it is suitable" (*miṣṭayā*), exists in accordance with the context (*prakaraṇa*); and if that context...

If it is followed, it is treated as false; if, however, it is not followed, it is correct. Therefore, there is a contradiction; and when there is a contradiction, the weakness of the context [prevails]. It is said:
"That [mantra] must be favored by this act of worship because it possesses the indicative mark (liṅga). No.

The *madvya* (soma-pressing) is ten-fold; and when that is undertaken at the Mahāvrata, it is undertaken in its entirety. However, when the ten-fold *madvya* is undertaken, whatever *madvya* would otherwise apply by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside, provided there is no contradiction.
But here, there is no contradiction between the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the context; rather, the specific form [is determined] by the context.

It is understood that from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) the universal (*sāmānya*) is inferred, and the individual (*vyakti*) is one thing while the universal is another. Therefore, the individual possessing the indicative mark should be adopted as the subject at hand. To this it is replied: This is true; when the subject at hand is adopted, the context (*prakaraṇa*) is not sublated, and the indicative mark is also favored. However, the cognition produced by the indicative mark is rendered somewhat false. [Objection: "But the individual is not the primary meaning of the word; how can the cognition be sublated when the individual is not being adopted? [Reply: It is said: This very point is not [the case].
[Page 320] We understand that here the possession of gender is not a factor; rather, the mention of the nominal suffix (taddhita) is the other [factor].
In that case, the mantra is indicated by the deity, for it is the specific manifestation of the mantra that is the means of accomplishment, not the general category.

There is no other [basis] whatsoever; rather, it is the deity itself that is the commonality by which the means of accomplishment (sādhana) is to be characterized. And no distinction is perceived, such as "this is that one" or "this is not that one.

Since no distinction is apprehended, all its indicative marks (liṅga) must be accepted; thus, even when there are many individual instances, the cognition arises, and it conforms to the context (prakaraṇa).

"Bābhravya says: This is improper. If this were the case, one would not have to adopt only those [mantras] belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*); one might also adopt those from the modified form (*vikṛti*). But has it not been said: 'The instruction regarding a mantra used for another purpose does not constitute an instruction for it when used for a different purpose'? It is replied: Not necessarily; that very same [mantra] may occur in another context, as may others, in a general sense.

By means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is not the case that anything is thereby corrupted. [Objection: "But this is indeed corrupted; neither the indicative mark nor the context (*prakaraṇa*) is upheld. [Response: True, they are not both upheld;
however, the context is not even worth considering, because it is obstructed by the cognition arising from the indicative mark.

Moreover, neither the indicative mark (*liṅga*) nor the context (*prakaraṇa*) is to be favored; rather, there occurs a determination of that [mark], and when it is understood that "this is fruitful," one proceeds accordingly. [Question: "What follows if this is so? [Answer: This follows: the indicative mark is not favored anywhere. Thus, when another [mark] has been determined, activity cannot occur [based on the first]. Therefore, it is understood that the verses from the *Daśataya* [collection] are to be taken.
Or rather, it is designated by its own name, because of both the context and logical consistency. (Siddhānta) || 21 ||

Commentary: That which is denoted by the name [Jyotiṣṭoma] alone must be understood [as the referent]. Why? Because of both the context and logical consistency; for that [sacrifice] is the subject under discussion, and it is proper to have a cognition of what is already under discussion.
How so? It is not possible to enjoin an operation of the *bhava* (the act of being) with respect to the Jyotiṣṭoma.

Precisely because [the act] has already been obtained, the injunction of a specific operation is appropriate, since that specific operation was not previously established; furthermore, if it were enjoined for the sake of giving without regard for the context, there would be a syntactical split (vākya-bheda)— [namely, that one should both] perform the attendance and [do so] by means of this particular mark.
[Page 321] Furthermore, the instruction would be purposeless because of its lack of connection with anything that possesses a result, and the *upasthāna* does not possess a result. (Yukti 1)

Bhāṣya: "But surely, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it would be an auxiliary to the Jyotiṣṭoma. If the connection between the *upasthāna* and the Jyotiṣṭoma were intended to be expressed, then the *upasthāna* would be enjoined in relation to the Jyotiṣṭoma, and through the context, it would form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with it. However, when indeed the connection of the *upasthāna* with the sacrifice (*mava*) is intended to be expressed, then [it applies] to all *upasthānas*."

The *maya* (the mantra) attains [application] by overriding the context (*prakaraṇa*); the context cannot serve as a specifier. Or, if there were a connection with both, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). In our view, however, this fault does not arise;

for when an action is performed in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* by means of either the *Āgneya* or the *Aindra* [mantra], it is then another specific act of worship (*upasthāna*) belonging to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* that is enjoined.

Everything is restated—thus there is no fault. Alternatively, only the mere connection with the *agnīdh* (the priest), the *haviḥ* (the oblation), and the *sadas* (the sacrificial hall) is enjoined; "he approaches" (*upatiṣṭhate*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), meaning that by means of this mantra he approaches the *agnīdh*, i.e., he sits down near him. Therefore, mantras of this kind occurring in the archetype (*prakṛti*) are to be adopted.
And because [the rule] has been taught for all. (Sūtra 23; Yuktis 2)
As for what was said—that "the [verses] under discussion have indeed been taught for another purpose"—that is answered as follows:

this has already been replied to. Furthermore, it is not the case that none of them have been taught; for in the *Bācastoma*, when the *Āśvina* recitation is being performed, one urges on the sun. Therefore, there is no distinction regarding the subject matter at hand. Consequently, only those [verses] under discussion are to be taken. (3.2.8)
*Jyautiṣṭomika* (pertaining to the Jyotiṣṭoma), according to the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā Pūrvabhāga.
[Page 322] The section concerning the application [of mantras] according to their indicative marks (*liṅga*), such as the *bhakṣa-mantra* and others.
By means of both the indicative mark (liṅga) and the name (samākhyā), the section (anuvāka) has the purpose of [reciting] the portions for consumption (bhakṣa).
Bhāṣya (Pūrvapakṣa).

Regarding the consumption [of the Soma], it is heard [in the scripture]: "Enter me for long life, for health, for the increase of wealth, for splendor, and for offspring. Come, O Vasu, before the dawn;
as one dear to me, I shall hold you with my arms, O Soma, who are rich in men. May the men look upon you, O divine Soma, with auspicious eyes. O Lord of bay horses, touch my limbs gently."

Do not be thirsty; O auspicious one, attend upon the seven seers for me; do not go beyond my navel or my head. May Vāc, the delightful, the overcoming, the banner of sacrifices, be satisfied with the pressed Soma—she who belongs to the troop of the six seasons, the troop of the seven seasons, and the troop of the Ādityas, O goddesses of the boundary, you who find the thought.

"Of the morning pressing, of the midday pressing, of the third pressing; of that which has the *gāyatrī* metre, of that which has the *triṣṭubh* metre, of that which has the *jagatī* metre; of that drunk by Indra, drunk by Narāśaṃsa, drunk by the Pitṛs; of the honeyed [Soma] offered, I, being offered, partake"—such is the beginning [of the passage]. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is this entire section (*anuvāka*) to be employed for the act of partaking (*bhakṣaṇa*), or is some portion of it to be used elsewhere as well? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That the entire section serves the purpose of partaking, on account of both indicative mark (*liṅga*) and syntactical connection (*samākhyā*).

The entire *bhakṣānuvāka* (the section on eating) should be employed for the act of eating. Why? Because this word "I eat" (*bhakṣayāmi*) is clearly to be employed for the act of eating; it is capable of expressing eating and nothing else. Furthermore, its other words are indeed expressions that qualify the act of eating; wherever there is the phrase "I eat," there [these qualifiers apply].
They are employed as follows:

"Nanu ehi vaso"—beginning with these words and ending with "sadhyāsam"—is for the purpose of purifying (pavana), forming a single unified meaning through its own collection of words that are mutually expectant, and is distinct from the sentence regarding consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*). "Nṛcakṣasam"—beginning with these words and ending with "avasyeṣam"—is the statement regarding inspection (*avekṣaṇa*). And "hindame gātrā harivaḥ"—beginning with these words [is likewise].
[Page 323] Bhāṣya:
"Do not speak falsely; do not go beyond what is intended"—this concludes the section for the sake of correct digestion.
Since the subjects are numerous, how can it be possible to state so many sentences?

"All this constitutes a single sentence, which is employed for the act of eating"—this is the objection. It is replied: "It has already been stated that all these are qualifiers of the eating. [End of section] "In this regard..."

"Even so, the sentence would be split, because it is impossible to express the qualifiers and the qualified simultaneously. It is replied: "We do not intend to express the qualifiers; rather, a single substance is enjoined as qualified by the qualifiers, such as the taking up (*grahaṇa*) and the looking at (*avekṣaṇa*). [The opponent objects: "This is not correct, because the words denoting the qualifiers would then have their own meanings unexpressed and would instead be subordinate to the qualification of the act of eating (*bhakṣaṇa*); this is understood only through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And between the primary sense (*śruti*) and indirect indication, the primary sense is the proper course, not indirect indication. Therefore, there is not a single sentence."

To this it is replied: although these acts such as seizing (*grahaṇa*) and so forth are understood from the great Vedic texts, they are not all intended; rather, only one act—eating (*bhakṣaṇa*)—is to be conveyed, for that is what is explicitly heard (*śruta*), whereas the qualifiers are not heard. There is no purpose in conveying them, and there is indeed a purpose [for conveying the eating].

As many word-groups as constitute a single unit, so many are one sentence. Therefore, this is a single sentence for the purpose of a specific consumption; thus, it must be applied to the act of consumption. Furthermore, there is the designation "the *bhakṣānuvāka*," and the entire *anuvāka* is not merely a part.
"But surely, how can a worldly word belonging to common usage (*laukika*) restrict a Vedic auxiliary (*aṅga*)?"—
even though it is worldly, it is nonetheless beginningless (*anādi*) by virtue of its recitation (*anuṣākana*).

[The relationship. What follows from this being so? This follows: it mentions an *anuvāka* (section) as being co-uttered (*samabhivyāhṛta*) with the act of eating; and such co-utterance occurs only when a relationship exists, just as in the case of "the cook" or "the reaper"—from such co-utterance we shall infer the relationship. Now, in matters of this kind, the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is not to be understood through inference alone;
it is understood only from an injunction (*vidhāna*), and not otherwise. Furthermore, a name (*samākhyā*) is not injunctive.

To this it is replied: the name (samākhyā) will bring about proximity in the mind regarding the relationship, and the injunction of performance (prayogavacana) will enjoin it; therefore, the Śalalūnuvāka is to be employed for the act of eating.

In the *Mīmāṃsā-darśana*, Bhāṣya: The meaning of a sentence can be established only together with that which has been immediately cognized; and when unrelated words are uttered, there is no such immediate cognition.
There is no syntactic unity [between them].
Therefore, together with that which is separated [by the intervening text], one should first understand the preceding matter by means of another method, such as meditation (dhyāna), and so forth.
It would produce a sentence-meaning that is non-Vedic and preceded by human intellect;
it would be like the sentence-meaning produced by taking a verb from one section and a noun from another, where [the meaning] is constructed by someone else.

Having understood the preceding matter through meditation and so forth, one should generate the meaning of the sentence. Therefore, it is determined that syntactic unity does not exist when there is an intervention by unrelated matters;
consequently, the upavīta does not have syntactic unity with the *sāmidhenī* verses. [Objection: "But..."
The *upavīta* is prescribed in proximity to the various forms of the *sāmidhenī* verses that follow immediately after;
therefore, it will be connected with those *sāmidhenīs*. We say: "No. For the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *sāmidhenīs* has indeed been interrupted by the *nivit* formulas.
By means of syntactical connection (*vākya*), the various forms of the *sāmidhenīs* enter into a relationship with the optional (*kāmya*) rites, but not [with the *upavīta*].
The context continues, yet the *sāmidhenī* verses do not become part of the primary subject matter (*prakṛta*) by virtue of the word "option" (*kalpa*).

For there is no statement regarding them therein that they "should be performed"; rather, [the statement] is that they "are to be connected with numbers. Furthermore, even that is established by syntactical connection (*vākya*), not by context (*prakaraṇa*). In that case, since the *sāmidhenīs* are not part of the primary subject matter, for which accessory would there be syntactic unity?

It does not exist with the *sāmidhenī* verses; there is no connection between it and them. Therefore, it is established that whatever is to be performed within the context [of the sacrifice] must be done while wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*).
(3 | 9 | The section concerning the non-existence of *laṭ* [the present tense] in the case of drinking one hundred vessels and so forth; [The Maxim of Mutual Non-Connection])
kha. And because qualities are for the sake of another, there would be no connection [between them] due to their equality. || 22 ||

In the *bhāṣya* on the establishment of the fire (*agnyādheya*), it is stated that the *vāraṇa*, *vaikaṅkata*, and *pālāśa* vessels are for the purpose of the *śrauta* oblations, intended for the *homa*.

[Page 325] In the *bhāṣya*: "May the six [cups] of Soma satisfy; I partake of the portion of the *vastumadgaṇa*, O divine Soma, which is pressed by the mind, belonging to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), having the *gāyatrī* meter, drunk by Indra, full of sweetness, and offered—offered, I partake. In this regard, there is a doubt: does the formula begin with "mandra" and so forth?

Is there one mantra ending with "tṛpyatu," another beginning with "vasumadgaṇa," and yet another beginning with "uta mandrā" and ending with "bhakṣayāmi"? What, then, is the prima facie view? There are two mantras; for if these two exist, satisfaction is one thing and eating is another, and thus, due to the difference in purpose, there is a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). As it has been said: "By virtue of its form and the instruction [of the ritual], there is a displacement of the purpose."

"Because it is enjoined"—this being the position reached, we reply: because of the mention of qualities, the single [verse] beginning with "mandra" should be used; for satisfaction is mentioned as a qualification of the act of eating, as in the words, "I eat; may my speech be satisfied."

"Now, [one might object]: 'The word "tṛpyatu" is one thing, and "tṛpti" is another; this [latter] occurs as a future passive participle (bhaviṣyantī) when there is a subordinate word (upapada) denoting an action.'"
In that case, there is a connection between two actions, as in "I eat" and "he satisfies"; but here, in "I eat, may he be satisfied," there is no such connection.
It is replied: this [desire], "may he be satisfied," is not understood as part of the injunction. Where, then, is it understood?

Whether it be in the sense of a prayer (*prārthanā*) or in the sense of the time having arrived (*prāptakāla*), the connection is made either as "if I speak" (*yadi bhakṣayāmi vāk*) or "the time has arrived for me to speak" (*yadi vā bhakṣayāmi vācaḥ taptaḥ prāptaḥ kālaḥ*). Thus, because of the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), when there is a single meaning and a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*), it is appropriate [to treat them as one]. But [it may be argued that] these two sentences are independent (*nirākāṅkṣe*).

"Having broken the form, they are made without expectancy. To this it is replied: even if these two sentences were to express two distinct meanings that are independent of one another, nevertheless, since the visible purpose is the manifestation of the breaking (*bhañjana*) and not the satiation (*tarpaṇa*), there is indeed a single purpose (*aikārthya*).

How much more so, then, when it is understood that the quality itself is being expressed? Therefore, because of the designation of the quality, there should be a single mantra beginning with "mandra" and so forth—thus [it is concluded]. (3.2.10a)
[Page 326] The section concerning the application, through modification (*ūha*), of the mantras beginning with "indrapītasya" in all instances of consumption.
kha. Because of the specification of gender, there is no absence of [offerings] to Indra among those of equal injunctions.
cha.
Bhāṣya.
The state of being a mantra. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 27 ||
This very case is my illustration: here there exist both offerings to Indra and those not to Indra, and there are also the ritual consumptions (*bhakṣaṇa*) for them. In this regard, there is a doubt:

is there a consumption of the intoxicating portion (*mada*) in both the offerings to Indra and those not to Indra, or is the consumption of the intoxicating portion only in the offerings to Indra, while for those not to Indra there is only the consumption of the *śramavaka*? What, then, is the prima facie view? [That it applies] to those not to Indra.
"The eating [of the *śramavaka*] is [the rule]. Why? Because these offerings are governed by the same injunction;

among them, the mantra "of that drunk by Indra" (*indrapītasya*) is unable to denote what has not been drunk by Indra, and in a single context (*samānaprakaraṇa*), there can be no abandonment [of the primary meaning] in the absence of an explicit statement.
Because it does not express any other meaning, therefore, in such cases, the eating is merely for the sake of removing fatigue. Thus [it is concluded].
Or rather, it is according to the deity; for that indeed shows its being the archetype. || 28 ||
Alternatively, it should be characterized by the *ahargaṇa* according to the respective deity.

Why? Because the *dhruvacamasas* constitute the archetype (*prakṛti*). What, then, are the *dhruvacamasas*? They are those belonging to the opening of the pressing (*savanamukhīya*) at the *śukra* and *manthin* rites; they are dedicated to Indra, and their offering constitutes the archetype, while the others are the modified forms (*vikṛti*). How is this understood? From that archetypal nature.

For it shows this. How? "Of the *anuṣṭubh* metre"—thus, in the *ṣoḍaśin* [rite] at the *atirātra*, the formula for the consumption [of the soma] is modified. What is the indication here? By saying "it is modified," it shows a transformation.

"Now, this might be an objection: [one might say] 'No,' for it is heard that 'it does not bend. How then does it bend? It bends by means of the *anuṣṭubh* metre; thus it bends the formula for consuming. This very point is applicable in the case of modifications."

[Page 327] Bhāṣya: Therefore, these are modifications; consequently, even in the case of those offerings dedicated to Indra, the *maya* (the "meat" portion) obtained through the extended application (*codaka*) need not be abandoned. It is said: "It has been stated that these are modifications—this is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) presented;
now let the logical principle (*nyāya*) be stated. It is replied: Soma dedicated to Indra is drawn.
And it is measured; therefore, while Soma exists in those [cups] dedicated to Indra, there is no Soma at all in those not dedicated to Indra.

Thus, all the properties of Soma apply only to the cups dedicated to Indra, while the others are without such properties and remain expectant [of them]. But how is it known that "Soma dedicated to Indra is both taken and measured"? It is known from the wording of the mantra:
"For Indra thee, the possessor of cattle"—such mantras serve to designate Soma as dedicated to Indra.

It is capable—thus it does not refer to anything else. Therefore, the Soma belongs to Indra; consequently, the ritual properties (dharma) of Soma apply to those [vessels] dedicated to Indra. However, other great vessels, being expectant (sākāṅkṣāṇi), will take up the ritual properties from what is heard in scripture—this is the logical principle (nyāya). Therefore, the mantra should be recited according to the respective deity.
—Thus it stands; for now, this matter remains unresolved, and since this is the case, another point of inquiry will follow. (3.2.11) [Adhikaraṇa]
In the case of the Soma-consumption at the *vyabhyunīta* [offering], Indra also has the status of being indicated;
however, in the case of those [offerings] that are *abhyunīta*, there is an indication of all [deities], because of their specific nature. (28)
(Pūrvapakṣa 1)

Furthermore, there are Soma-libations that have been drawn again (abhyunīta). At the very movement for the *yukta-anvārambha*, these are the libations at the beginning of the pressings (*savanamukhīya*). Having offered them with the four cups of the central priests (*madhyataḥkārin*) upon the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls of the Hotṛ, and having offered once each with the cups of the *hotraka*s upon their *vaṣaṭ* calls alone, Soma is then drawn again into those very vessels while they still contain remnants. For in that case, the Adhvaryu gives the direction: "O cup-bearers of the central priests, offer upon the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls; O cup-bearers of the *hotraka*s, having offered once..."
"Having drawn up the *śukra*, turn back!"—therein the Hotṛs sacrifice to various deities;
the Maitrāvaruṇa sacrifices to Mitra and Varuṇa with the verse, "We invoke Mitra... [Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.13.24 states: "Once, once."]

[Page 328] Bhāṣya: Here, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin recites "O Indra, we [choose] you, the bull... (RV 8.96.1); the Potṛ recites "The Maruts, by whose victory... (RV 1.165.1); and here [the Neṣṭṛ recites for] Tvaṣṭṛ and the wives [of the gods].
"O Agni, bring the wives here"—with these words, the Āgnīdhra [invokes] the fire with "Like a bull, like a barren cow. And there, at the previous *vaṣaṭ*-call, Indra was worshipped with those cups;
having been poured out again, Mitra, Varuṇa, and the other deities were worshipped, while the remnant therein belongs to Indra.

And [the case] of Mitra, Varuṇa, and the others. In this regard, there is a doubt: is there an indirect reference (upalakṣaṇa) to both Indra—the deity for whom the offering has already set out—and to Mitra, Varuṇa, and the rest; or rather, should Indra not be indirectly referred to? What, then, is the prima facie position? There should be an indirect reference to all of them when they are again invoked.

Why? Because of its specific nature; for in each cup (camasa), there is the remnant of those two, and in the archetype (prakṛti), it was stated that "the remnant belongs to her to whom it was offered, and he has drunk from it"—that same thing must be said here as well. Therefore, in each cup, there is the mention of both.

What is meant by "because of the observation of the majority"? These words are heard being concluded within a passage that belongs to the majority of the Vedas and begins with the Veda: "Prajāpati alone was this universe in the beginning; he performed austerity. Having begun with the statement, "The Ṛgveda from Agni, the Yajurveda from Vāyu, and the Sāmaveda from Āditya," this is heard at the conclusion: "The Ṛc is performed loudly, the Sāman loudly, and the Yajus in a low voice. Bhāṣya: "Loudly"—this is what is obtained. Why? Because this is performed by means of the Sāmaveda through the Vāravantīya and other chants; therefore, these Sāmans should be sung loudly.

Sūtra: This being the case, we reply: one should either set aside the primary for the sake of the subordinate, or set aside the subordinate for the sake of the primary; it is logical that the subordinate should be set aside so that the primary may be upheld. Why? Because the subordinate exists for the sake of the primary. One engages in the subordinate with the thought, "How may the primary become endowed with its quality through the performance of the subordinate? If, by disregarding the subordinate, the primary suffers a loss of its quality, then the very purpose of engaging in the subordinate is defeated.

It is not attained. Now, thinking "I shall make the principal act possessed of its quality," one who is occupied with the quality causes the quality of the quality to fall away; his own purpose is not lost, nor does he set out to make the principal act possessed of a quality. For the chanting of the Sāman is the quality and the laying of the fire (ādhāna) is the principal act; since the principal act belongs to the Yajurveda, it has the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutā*). That [quality] sublates the loudness (*uccaistva*), which is the property of the quality belonging to the Sāmaveda.
Therefore, the Sāmans should be chanted in a low voice. (3.3.2)

The scriptural statement regarding both [is established] by the preponderance [of evidence]. 10.
In the Yajurveda, they recite the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. Likewise, there is an identical recitation in the Sāmaveda.

When the cognition has already been formed [by one Veda], the hearing of the second [recitation] is for the purpose of [indicating] a subordinate element (guṇa). In this regard, there is a doubt: what...?

Is the Yajurvedic tradition for the purpose of ritual action (*kriyārtha*), while the Sāmavedic is for the purpose of qualities (*guṇārtha*), or is it the reverse? Whichever tradition is for the purpose of ritual action, those [mantras] will be *vamā*. What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Since no specific distinction is perceived, there is no certainty as to whether the Sāmavedic is for the purpose of ritual action or the Yajurvedic.
"He employs [it]," according to the Kāśmīra manuscript (Kā0 krī0 pa0).

This being the case, we reply: it should be determined by the preponderance of qualities; for it is understood that where more qualities are enumerated, there the injunction has ritual action as its purpose. Indeed, wherever there is an injunction regarding what ought to be done, there a requirement for the performance of that act is expected. Where...
And since the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is required, it is logical that there be an injunction regarding that procedure.

Furthermore, those numerous qualities constitute the procedure; by means of this mark of the procedure, we infer the injunction for the performance of the action. Just as when many who resemble kings are seated, he who has a white umbrella and a fly-whisk is recognized as the king.

Even though it is not explicitly stated, [it is known] by the mark of royal insignia. Likewise, by the mark of what ought to be performed and by the abundance of qualities, the injunction for the Jyotiṣṭoma belonging to the Yajurveda is inferred.
Therefore, the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma is [governed] by the Upāṃśu [chanting], for the Jyotiṣṭoma is indeed [prescribed] by the Yajurveda.
That which is impelled by it is performed; that which is not impelled cannot be performed—thus it is said.

Sūtra: [A rite] not connected by direct statement [is connected] by context, because it requires a procedure. 11.

The causes for application have been stated: *śruti*, *liṅga*, and *vākya*. *Śruti* is the accusative case-ending, as in "the *gārhapatya* [fire] with the *aindra* [verse]. *Liṅga* is the inherent capacity of the words, as in "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods. *Vākya* is the syntactical connection.
"He buys"—thus [it is said]. Now, are these the only grounds for application (viniyoga)? No, it is replied. What other ground is there? With this very question the discussion begins;
and indeed, a discussion often begins with a question, as in: "What is the name of this river? or "What is the name of this mountain?"
What is this "result"?

It is explained as follows: that which is not connected by direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), or syntactical connection (*vākya*) is [connected] by context (*prakaraṇa*), because of the requirement for a procedure (*itikartavyatā*). A statement that falls within the vicinity of something requiring a procedure and is capable of fulfilling that requirement enters into a single syntactical unity with that primary subject matter.

When things that possess a sequence are taught in their successive order, an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) toward a particular property is inferred at the turn of each subsequent item; when such expectancy exists, there is the state of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*). Therefore...

When the sacrifices (*yāga*) possessing a fixed sequence are mentioned in the supplementary texts (*anumantraṇas*), the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice is mentioned in its proper order with the mantra "Thou art the burner. And likewise, in the case of the *aindrāgna* ritual, there is a mantra of similar origin belonging to one who has an enemy.

Mādhava [states that] when there arises an expectancy—such as "What is the fruit of the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) and so forth? or "What is the result of not performing the New and Full Moon sacrifices?"—the context (*prakaraṇa*) is established in the form of syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*).

"Succession" (*krama*) is the state of occupying the same location; this is the essential nature of succession. It is of two kinds: that produced by recitation (*pāṭhakṛta*) and that produced by meaning (*arthakṛta*). Regarding these, Mādhava states that even that produced by recitation is of two kinds: "as it occurs" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) and "in proximity" (*sannidhi*). Now, are these alone the causes for application (*viniyoga*)? No, it is said. Furthermore, designation (*samākhyā*) would also be such a cause. How is designation a cause for application?
Designation occurs when a relationship exists, just as in the case of "cook" or "reaper";
there, upon perceiving the word "cook," one understands that his relationship is with the act of cooking (*pacati*).

It is understood in this way even in the case of the Veda. Having perceived a word whose connection with its meaning is uncreated and conventional, there arises a comprehension of that connection. What is the example and the purpose here? The example is: the rites designated by the name *adhvaryava* are to be performed by the *adhvaryu*, and those designated as *hautra* by the *hotṛ*. Sūtra 14: In the case of a conflict between direct statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), syntactical connection (vākya), context (prakaraṇa), position (sthāna), and name (samākhyā), each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding because of its remoteness from the purpose.
