[The text says:
"He worships the Gārhapatya fire"—thus it is stated. Then one reflects: what?

Is the worship to be performed for Indra or for the Gārhapatya fire? There is no fixed rule [on this point], or is it for the Gārhapatya alone? If these two reasons possess equal force, then there is an option (*vikalpa*).

Now, if direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful, then the Gārhapatya fire alone is to be worshipped. But what here is the direct statement? And what is the indicative mark (*liṅga*)? The direct statement is the hearing of the word "Gārhapatya"; the indicative mark, however, is the capacity of the word "Indra" to denote a specific deity, as in: "When, O Indra, dost thou not fail us, nor desert the donor? Now, what [is the conclusion]?

What is called a sentence (*vākya*)? A collection of words that together express a single meaning is a sentence. If this is so, then the following is also a sentence: "He worships the Gārhapatya fire with [the verse] addressed to Indra," and this too: "Never indeed art thou a deceiver. In both cases, the words together express a meaning; therefore, this deliberation regarding one sentence versus another does not apply here.

Regarding *śruti* and *liṅga*, or rather, if *śruti*, *liṅga*, and *vākya* are to be distinguished— such that "this is the difference between *śruti* and *vākya*, and this is the difference between *liṅga* and *vākya*"—
that is now explained: first, that which is the capacity of a word to denote its own meaning...
That sign (*liṅga*) by which the meaning of a word is understood from the mere hearing of the word is understood through *śruti*;

for *śruti* is "hearing. It has already been stated that a sentence consists of one or more words having a single meaning. All this is present in every sentence, yet it is distinct [from other means of proof].

It is observed here that, by the mantra "Never indeed art thou neglectful," Indra is to be worshipped; this is not understood merely from hearing this particular word, nor does any other word uttered in its proximity possess the capacity by which this could be understood.
Indeed, in this [mantra], the word "Indra" [is present].

There exists [a person] who is capable of understanding a specific deity, and there is a purpose served by that deity being so understood; therefore, the word "Indra" is employed in the invocation to Indra, and the remaining words are subordinate to it because they form a single syntactical unit with it, and not [because of the thought]:
"O Indra, you are never a killer, but rather you give breath to those who offer oblations."
Mādhava says the meaning is that "you take pleasure in the sacrificer."
In the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra-bhāṣya:

Thus, in this verse, the worship of the Gārhapatya fire occurs by virtue of the power of a certain word; however, it is from the direct hearing of the word "Gārhapatya" itself that we understand the fire.
Not from the indicative mark (*liṅga*). If, however, the indicative mark is stronger, then Indra is to be worshipped;
if there is the mention of the Gārhapatya fire, then the Gārhapatya [is to be worshipped].

In that case, it is the conflict between the indicative mark and the syntactical connection (*vākya*) that must be deliberated here, not the conflict between the direct statement (*śruti*) and the indicative mark. If the indicative mark is stronger, then because of the capacity of the word *indrāgnī* to denote a specific deity, there is the worship of Indra; but if the syntactical connection is stronger, then the Gārhapatya.

"It should be approached; for this sentence [states]: 'He approaches the Gārhapatya fire with a verse addressed to Indra. This is not so. Although this is a sentence, there is also a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) here;

and that which is the direct scriptural statement contradicts the indicative mark (*liṅga*), not the sentence. How so? For even though the sentence is more powerful... [the direct statement is stronger].

Regarding the phrase "He worships with the Aindrī [verse] at the *liṅga*": this must enter into syntactic unity with the word *gārhapatya*; for if it did not, it would contradict the *liṅga*. That meaning which is understood from the direct hearing (*śravaṇa*) of the word *gārhapatya* becomes set aside when the *liṅga* is more powerful; that [meaning] is not connected with the worship. For in that case, the word *gārhapatya* would have to denote either Indra or proximity to Agni. But rather, direct audition (*śruti*) is the authoritative means of knowledge.

Consequently, by this indicative mark (*liṅga*), the worship of Indra would be set aside. Therefore, this conflict is strictly between *śruti* (direct statement) and *liṅga* (indicative mark), not between *liṅga* and *vākya* (syntactical connection). Alternatively, there is no predominance of either Indra or Gārhapatya regarding the act of worship due to their forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*). Why, then [is there predominance]? Because of the presence of the word "Indra," Indra has predominance; because of the hearing of the accusative case-ending, Gārhapatya has predominance.
Thus, there is a conflict between *śruti* and *liṅga*.
How so?
What, then, is the prima facie position? That these two reasons possess equal force.

This is also a reason, this as well—(both scripture and indicative mark). For no distinction whatsoever is perceived regarding the form of one cognition as compared to another cognition, such that "the form of this one is as fragile" or "the form of this one is as firm. [Objection: "But surely..."

For the cognition arising from an inferential mark (liṅga) is indeed accompanied by doubt, as if it were the form of something fragile, whereas the cognition arising from sacred scripture (śruti) is free from doubt. This is not tenable, because [the cognition] arises from an inferential mark [Page 347].
The cognition arising from indicative mark (*liṅga*) is accompanied by doubt, whereas there is no comparison at all between that and the sacred text (*śruti*).

However, since the cognition arising from indicative mark is indeed free from doubt, it can be set aside by the sacred text. [Objection: But surely there is never a cognition free from doubt arising from indicative mark.
[Reply: This is not so; for if that were the case, there would be no such thing as an "indicative mark" at all.
[The cognition] would not be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). [Objection: "Let it not be a means of valid knowledge;

rather, there is a connection (*saṃprayoga*) with objects whose nature has been fully ascertained through a logical mark (*liṅga*). Or else, its lack of validity is quite clear and beyond doubt. How so? Because one knows: 'This [cognition] is capable of bringing about this object.'"

"From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) alone, it is understood that whatever is capable of accomplishing something cannot be expected to accomplish it in the absence of an explicit statement; therefore, the indicative mark is not the means of application (*viniyojaka*).
To this, it is replied: when a certain matter is recited in proximity to another matter that possesses a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), [the former is understood as belonging to the latter].

It is understood that this [word] serves as its means of accomplishment; yet, when there is doubt as to how exactly it will provide assistance, a definitive conclusion arises through the force of implication (*sāmarthya*): "In whatever matter this is capable, therein it can be employed. Therefore, it constitutes an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

[The opponent says: "It is the *pramāṇa* [the means of knowledge]. And there is no reason for a decisive determination (*vinigamanā*) regarding the relative strength of the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Therefore, these two causes possess equal force: by the indicative mark "kadā cana starīrasi," Indra is to be worshipped; by the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), the Gārhapatya fire is to be worshipped. Because there is no contradiction, we understand this very same meaning: even though one cause is stronger, it is capable of subverting that which is weaker only when they are in conflict, not when there is no conflict. And here there is no contradiction whatsoever, such that one might worship Indra with this mantra and the Gārhapatya fire as well.
This very thing is the contradiction: that which is enjoined as a single presentation is [here] performed repeatedly.

"It is repeated"—this is merely the established principle that "accessory elements (guṇas) are repeated for each principal element (pradhāna) according to their distinction," and there is no contradiction here. However, this indeed is the contradiction: when the Gārhapatya fire is being worshipped, the word *indra*, which denotes the name, must depend upon either an accessory quality or a connection with an action;

whereas if Indra himself were the one to be worshipped, the word *indra* would be independent [of such factors]. And in this matter, there is no authority [for the latter view]—this is a certain reading.
[Page 348] Bhāṣya:

"In the case of both the primary and the secondary, the understanding applies to the primary. We say: this is not so. The secondary would be sublated by the primary only in the event of a contradiction, but there is no contradiction here;
for they would conflict if they were denoted simultaneously, but in this case, it is something else.
In the case of ritual application (*prayoga*), one [word] denotes Agni and the other denotes Indra; therefore, these two grounds are of equal strength.
This being the position reached, we reply: between direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), the direct statement is stronger. Why?

"Because of the remoteness of the meaning. What does this "because of the remoteness of the meaning" mean? It means the remoteness from the purpose. But what is the meaning here? The meaning of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is: "He worships the Gārhapatya fire"—this is proximate. "Indra is to be worshipped"—this is remote. How so? Because it is not heard in the text that "Indra is to be worshipped by means of the mantra beginning with *kadā ca nastarīrasi*. Even though there is the capacity for the mantra to denote Indra...
"Because of the absence of a *bacca* [substitution], Indra is not to be invoked"—thus they sing.
Now, it was indeed said: "It is understood that [the mantra] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) because it is recited in the context (*prakaraṇa*);

its application (*viniyoga*) is by virtue of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*). This is not so; for it has already been stated (at 1.2.50): "Since Dharma has the Word as its sole source, that which is not based on the Word should be disregarded."

—Thus, both this context (*prakaraṇa*) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) are themselves wordless (*aśabda*). Furthermore, regarding a matter of such a nature that transcends the domain of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), comprehension is not possible without a word. Therefore, we consider that the indicative mark is subordinate to the meaning of the direct statement (*śruti*). "Even if this is so, provided there is no contradicting direct statement..."

There is no determination of meaning from an indicative mark (*liṅga*), for that very indicative mark as a means of valid cognition does not exist at all. Why, then, should the *śruti* (direct statement) be distinguished by this? We say that, in that case, even the deliberation regarding the relative strength of *śruti* and *liṅga* is not tenable. To this, it is replied: For one who seeks the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) and possesses the context (*prakaraṇa*), the mantra falls upon the *samits* (kindling sticks) by virtue of its own power of being recited; and since [the sacrifice] has a requirement for procedure, it is accepted as a supplementary part of the sentence, such that "one should sacrifice with this mantra. What has been said?
Does it occur? When the sacrifice is being performed as something desired to be accomplished, it might assist me; however, without the mention of Indra, this [mantra] is not capable of assisting me.
(Chapter 3, Pāda 1).

Bhāṣya: By this, the following is stated: "Indra is to be denoted by this [word]. Therefore, this meaning is rooted in direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) itself. If it is rooted in direct statement, it cannot be sublated by another direct statement. Thus, as for this indicative mark (*liṅga*), either it is not an authority at all, or it ought to be treated as an option alongside direct statement. We reply: it shall neither be non-authoritative, nor shall it be treated as an option. How so? It has been established that the meaning is one that is characterized by both direct statement and indicative mark.

Therefore, it is not invalid. However, since another meaning is understood from the direct Vedic text (*śruti*) by depending upon the syntactic unity inferred through reasoning (*ānumānikī*) and the capacity of the indicative mark (*liṅga-sāmarthya*)—namely, that "the worship of Indra is performed with this mantra"—while the direct Vedic text itself says "one worships the Gārhapatya fire," there is this discrepancy (*viprakarṣa*). First, there is the cognition of the indicative mark; then, by virtue of its capacity, the word is requested for this meaning. This is as follows:

In the event of a conflict with direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), [the indicative power] is not possible; for this is clearly heard: "By this mantra, the Gārhapatya fire is to be worshipped. Since this is firmly established, and since the sentence (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) have already fulfilled their function once this has been determined, it cannot be assumed that "this person performs worship of Indra" by means of the word. Therefore, due to the remoteness of the meaning, the indicative power (*liṅga*) is sublated by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
And because an option is improper; for an option is improper,

since in that case non-existence would be like a permanent rule on one side— as when it is heard in scripture, "With the Aindrī verse he worships the Gārhapatya fire," if non-existence were postulated as an alternative, then that which is not heard [in the text] would become the [prescribed] act, whereas that which is heard...

Furthermore, there is a loss [of consistency], and as great as the fault is in abandoning the meaning of what has been heard (śruta), so great is it in the postulation of what has not been heard; for in both cases, established tradition (prasiddhi) is obstructed. Therefore, because an option (vikalpa) is improper, we understand that between direct statement (śruti) and indicative mark (liṅga), the direct statement is stronger. Now, as for what was said—that sublation (bādha) is proper when there is a contradiction, and that no such [contradiction] exists here—

Regarding the contradiction: there is indeed this contradiction, in that the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) expressing the worship of Indra exists while the sentence (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) have not yet had their capacity established; however, once their capacity has been established, such a statement is no longer applicable. Nor can it be that both the sentence and the context simultaneously have their capacity established.
[Page 354]
Since it is possible for [the meaning] to exist through both direct statement and the capacity [of the words], there is a contradiction; and when there is a contradiction,
direct statement (śruti) is more authoritative than indicative power (liṅga).

What is the example of a conflict between an indicative mark (*liṅga*) and a sentence (*vākya*)? "I prepare a pleasant seat for you; with a stream of clarified butter I fashion it well. Sit upon it, O immortal one, be established there, O essence of grain, being well-disposed"—thus [the mantra says]. Herein lies the doubt.

—Should the mantra beginning with *kiṃ kṛtvo* be employed both at the spreading [of the grass] and at the placing of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), or should the portion ending with *kalpayāmi* be used for the spreading, while the portion beginning with *tasmin sīda* is used for the placing of the cake? If the syntactical unity (*vākya*) is more authoritative, then the entire mantra is to be used in both cases.
How so? Because the phrase *tasmin sīda*, etc., enters into a single syntactical unit with the preceding phrase *suṣevaṃ kalpayāmi* by depending upon it: "That which I prepare, in that [seat]..."

"Sit"—thus [the word]. Now, if the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is more powerful, then it applies to the making of the seat within the *kaṣpaya* vessel. How so? Because the phrase "I make a pleasant seat for you" is capable of denoting the making of a seat; and the phrase "sit upon that" is likewise capable of denoting the placing of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Thus, it is employed in the act of placing.

—What, then, is the prima facie position? These two means of proof possess equal strength; for while it has been stated that *śruti* is stronger than *liṅga*, it is not said that *liṅga* is stronger than *vākya*.

Alternatively, the sentence itself is stronger than the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Why? Because that [sentence] is even sublated by direct statement (*śruti*), yet a stronger cause cannot be sublated. Therefore, we determine its fragility; for that which is sublated by one thing can also be sublated by another.
"To set aside"—this being the position reached, we reply: between *liṅga* (indicative power) and *vākya* (syntactical connection), *liṅga* is stronger.

Why? Because of the remoteness of the purpose (*arthaviprakarṣāt*). What is this remoteness of the purpose? It is understood that "this mantra is a subsidiary of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices" because it is recited in proximity to that which possesses the *prakaraṇa* (context). In that case—

Because of the capacity of the term "sīda" (sit down) to denote the act of placing the *puroḍāśa* cakes, this mantra is employed for that specific placement; there is no authority by which it could also be employed for the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*). Likewise, the mantra "I prepare a pleasant seat for you" (*syonaṃ te sadanaṃ kṛṇomi*) also attains the status of being an auxiliary to the New and Full Moon sacrifices solely through the power of its recitation within that context (*prakaraṇa*).
[Page 355] Bhāṣya:
Precisely because it has its application in the *upastaraṇa* (spreading of the base) by virtue of its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), the cake (*puroḍāśa*) has already fulfilled its purpose;
it does not deserve application in the act of placing (*sādana*). For there is no [functional capacity] of that which is being separated from this [act].

There is some purpose [to this]. Thus, the mantra "sit upon this" lacks the capacity for the act of spreading [the base], and the mantra "pleasant" lacks the capacity for the act of placing the sacrificial cake. The capacity for spreading arises by attaining syntactic unity with the preceding [mantra], and the capacity for placing arises because the preceding [mantra] attains syntactic unity with the subsequent one; however, neither has such capacity in its own form. Therefore, there is this remoteness of purpose (*arthaviprakarṣa*).

As for the direct capacity of the phrase "syonante" (O pleasant one) to denote the act of preparing a seat, that is primary. However, the capacity of the phrase "tasmin sīda" (sit upon that), which attains syntactic unity with the preceding part, is secondary. Thus, because of the expressive power of the former part, its application to the act of spreading [the grass] is stated; this is the proximate sense of the indicative power (*liṅga*) relative to the *śruti* (direct Vedic statement). But as for the latter part, once its expressive power has been produced, from that...

The meaning of the direct statement (*śruti*) is thus separated by the indicative mark (*liṅga*), and therefore becomes remote. Likewise, for the subsequent [verse], it is proximate in relation to the act of placing the cake (*sādana*), while for the preceding one, it is separated by the indicative mark. Therefore, due to this remoteness of meaning, the indicative mark is stronger than the syntactical connection (*vākya*). Consequently, although the word "pleasant" (*syonam*) is required by the subsequent [verse] and thus could be employed in the act of placing the cake, nevertheless, having set aside the syntactical connection, it must be applied specifically to the act of spreading the base (*upastaraṇa*).
And regarding the [mantra] "sit upon this" used for the act of seating:
it is argued that just as the word "syonante" has the capacity to denote the act of spreading [the seat], so too does it have the capacity to enter into syntactic unity with what follows;
and such capacity is an indicative mark (liṅga). Therefore, when the sentence is split...
"The indicative mark (liṅga) itself becomes sublated"—this is true;
yet even this is an indicative mark, and indeed an indicative mark characterized in this way refers only to a remote object.
From the indicative mark comes syntactic unity (ekavākyatā), from that comes the capacity for expression (abhidhānasāmarthya), and from that comes the meaning of the direct statement (śruti).

Remoteness of meaning (*viprakṛṣṭārthatā*), and remoteness of meaning is the cause for sublation (*bādhana*). Therefore, [the claim] that "it is not sublated" is inferior. The reading *etadapi* is found in the Kāśmīra manuscript.
The commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: "It will form a single syntactical unit with what follows. Thus, in the case of "sit upon that," it does not form a single unit with what precedes either.

Moreover, for that which has attained syntactical unity with what follows, no visible purpose is observed; however, the spreading [of the grass] and the placing [of the vessel] are indeed visible purposes. Why? Because the spreading and the placing are directly enjoined by scripture (*śruti*). Thus, there is the placing and the placing for the subsequent [act], but not within a single syntactical unit with the preceding one. Furthermore, these two do not fail to perform their respective functions individually without a syntactical unity with the preceding and subsequent [parts]. Therefore...
The former is to be applied to the former [context], and the latter to the latter— thus,
even by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*), that which was stated [previously] is sublated by direct statement (*śruti*).
That [the latter] should be set aside—this is not so. For it is not logical that even by another means that which has already been set aside should be further set aside;

rather, that which has been set aside should be favored for the sake of its meaningfulness. With respect to the *śruti*, its meaning is remote; with respect to the *vākya*, its meaning is more proximate. Therefore, the *liṅga*...
"It is more powerful."

Now, how is it when there is a conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*)? What, then, is called "context"? Context is the statement of that which is to be performed, which stands in need of a procedure (*itikartavyatā*). For it is the commencement of the act of stating that [procedure]; it depends upon the beginning of the injunction and its conclusion. Syntactical connection has already been explained. What is an example of a conflict between these two? It is the *sūktavāka* recitation. For therein, the deities of the full moon sacrifice and the deities of the new moon sacrifice are mentioned; they do not admit of being unified into a single syntactical whole with one another.

In that case, by the force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), the word "Indra-Agni" should be employed in the full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*); however, the word "Agnīṣomau" should be employed in the new-moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*). Now, a doubt arises regarding the appropriate remainder: "They two, being great, have grown more powerful"—should this be employed as many times as it is recited in the *sūktavāka*, for both the full-moon and new-moon sacrifices, since the context (*prakaraṇa*) is more authoritative? Or rather, where...

That which has been extracted and brought forth by Indra and Agni must be employed in that very context; for the sentence is more powerful—thus there is doubt regarding all such cases. What, then, is the prima facie view? That these two grounds are of equal strength. Why?
[Page 357]
Chapter 3, Section 1.

Commentary: Furthermore, there is expectancy for the one [word] and also for the other; when the expectancy is equally satisfied, there is no reason for a deciding factor. Therefore, they possess equal force. Now...
Or rather, the sentence is weak, for it is sublated by the indicative mark (liṅga).

This being the position reached, we reply: the sentence is stronger than the context (prakaraṇa). Why? Because of the remoteness of the meaning (arthaviprakarṣa). What is this remoteness of meaning? In a sentence, when each individual word is analyzed...

It becomes expectant; it becomes entirely complete. In that case, there is the state of being a single sentence (*ekavākyabhāva*) through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), whereas in the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is not directly perceived. How so? When something complete falls near that which is expectant of the "how-to" (*itikartavyatā*), the expectant nature of that subject matter (*prakṛta*) is understood; it is inferred that they do not yet constitute a single sentence. And by assuming the capacity for expression through the state of being a single sentence, the formulation occurs: "This is what is expressed"—such is the conceptual construction. This is the remoteness of meaning: namely, that the direct audition (*śruti*) of the sentence is more proximate [than the context].

The context is remote. Therefore, regarding the injunction "He offers the prastara with the sūktavāka," when there is a separation of those words denoting the deities of the full moon sacrifice and those denoting the deities [of other sacrifices], there must also be a separation and application of their respective remnants; thus, even if...

By the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is inferred that the supplementary portions concerning the deities of the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with those expressing the deities of the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*). However, there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) [of connection] with the words for the deities of the new moon sacrifice; and where there is contradiction with what is directly perceived, inference is not possible. Furthermore, once the context has become meaningful, there can be no further requirement for those [words] that have already attained their purpose.
The expectation can be established as possible.
Now, as for what was said— that it is indicated by the indicative mark (liṅga), and therefore also by the context (prakaraṇa)—

"It must be sublated"—no; for that which is sublated by something else should be understood as fragile even in other instances. Now, if it were fragile, it would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) at all. However, the power of a sentence to sublate is with respect to a context (*prakaraṇa*), not with respect to an indicative mark (*liṅga*); for this context is remote from the meaning relative to the indicative mark.
[The word "prati"] refers to a proximate object; by that sentence, the context (prakaraṇa) is set aside—thus [it is said].
[Page 358] * "paripūrṇam adhīti" as found in the Yā0, So0, and Pu0 manuscripts; likewise in the Kā0 and Kau0 manuscripts.

Bhāṣya: Now, what is the example when there is a conflict between context (*prakaraṇa*) and sequence (*krama*)? In the context of the *Rājasūya*, the narrative of Śunaḥśepa and other elements are prescribed in the sequence of the *Abhiṣecanīya* [rite]. If context is stronger, they are subsidiaries (*aṅga*) to all [the rites of the Rājasūya]; if sequence is stronger, they belong to the *Abhiṣecanīya* alone.

What, then, is the prima facie position? These two causes are of equal strength. Why? Because we do not perceive any distinction by which we might understand that "this one is stronger. Therefore, these two causes are of equal strength. Moreover, the context [is set aside] by the syntactical connection.
[The opponent argues: "It is sublated; therefore, it would be sublated even by sequence.

To this, we reply: Context is stronger than sequence. Why? Because of the remoteness of the purpose (*arthaviprakarṣāt*). What is this remoteness of the purpose? It is because that which possesses context has a requirement (*sākāṅkṣatvāt*).

There is syntactic unity with that which is recited in proximity, even if it is complete, and not with that which is recited in sequence; for sequence is merely the recitation of many items being recited in a specific order of proximity. In that case, it must be understood that although the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) of what is recited in proximity to that which possesses sequence is not actually perceived due to the force of the specific proximity of the recitation, it nonetheless exists. In the case of context (*prakaraṇa*), however, [the expectancy] of that which possesses the context is directly perceived.

Furthermore, there can be no simultaneous syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between that which possesses a context (*prakaraṇavat*) and that which possesses a sequence (*kramavat*), because such a unity is not established by the Vedic text itself; thus, there is a contradiction. In that case, the direct (*pratyakṣa*) expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) within the context is capable of subverting the inferred (*ānumānika*) sequence, because syntactic unity arises from expectancy, the capacity for expression (*abhidhāna-sāmarthya*) arises from syntactic unity, and the literal meaning (*śruty-artha*) arises from that capacity. Thus it stands.

The *śaṭa* (direct statement) prevails over the *prakaraṇa* (context), while the *vimalaṭa* (syntactical connection) prevails over the *krama* (order). Therefore, between *krama* and *prakaraṇa*, the *prakaraṇa* is more powerful.

Now, as for what was said—that since it is set aside even by a *vākya* (sentence), it must also be set aside by something else—that is not so; for it is right to favor that which has already been set aside, and not...
"That which is sublated must be sublated"—thus [it is said].
Now, what is the example for a conflict between order (krama) and name (samākhyā)? Which is stronger? [The example is:
in the section named *Pauror̤āśika*, there is [an injunction] in the sequence of the *Sānnāyya* [offering].
Regarding the mantra "śundhadhvam devāya karmaṇe," the word *mayaḥ* is recited for the purpose of purification (*śundhana*).
In that context, since there is a combination [of mantras], does the power of the combined [text] prevail over the *puroḍāśa*?
[Page 359]
In the Mīmāṃsā system,
the meaning of a sentence can be established only with that which has been immediately cognized; however, when unrelated words are uttered, there is no immediate cognition,
and thus no syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) occurs.
Therefore, [the opponent might suggest]:

"Alternatively, by means of another method such as meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth, one may first comprehend the meaning of the individual words and thereby produce the meaning of the sentence. But that [sentence-meaning] would be non-Vedic, being preceded by human intellect.

It would be like that sentence-meaning which is produced by taking a verb from one section (anuvāka) and a noun from another; it would be such a case where one produces the sentence-meaning after having understood the meaning of the prior word through some other means, such as meditation. Therefore...
It is determined that syntactic unity does not exist when there is an intervention by unrelated matters;

therefore, the upavīta does not form a single sentence with the *sāmidhenī* verses. [Objection: "But surely the upavīta is enjoined in proximity to the various recensions (*kalpa*) of the *sāmidhenīs*, which are present in the immediate consciousness."
"Therefore, it shall be connected with the *sāmidhenī* verses"—this we deny. For the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *sāmidhenīs* has indeed been interrupted by the intervention of the *nivid* formulas.
By means of syntactical connection (*vākya*), the optional forms of the *sāmidhenīs* enter into a relationship [with the result], and the context does not persist;
nor are the *sāmidhenīs* brought back into the context by the statement of these optional forms.

O venerable ones! For in that context, their words do not mean "they are to be performed," but rather, "they are to be connected with numbers. And even that is established by syntactical connection (*vākya*), not by context (*prakaraṇa*). In that case, regarding the non-contextual *sāmidhenī* verses, there is no syntactical unity for a quality that has no connection with the *sāmidhenīs*; therefore, it has no connection with them. Consequently...
It is established that whatever is to be performed in a ritual context must be done while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī).
(3 | 9 | The section concerning the absence of connection in the drinking of one hundred vessels and so forth; [The Principle of Mutual Non-Connection]) ||
kha. And because qualities exist for the sake of another, there would be no connection [between them] due to their equality. || 22 ||

In the Bhāṣya on the Mīmāṃsā-darśana, regarding the establishment of the sacred fire (agnyādheya), it is stated that the *vāraṇa*, *vaikaṅkata*, and *pālāśa* vessels are intended for the *āghāra* libations and for the purpose of *homa* offerings. [Page 360]

Bhāṣya: A sentence-meaning can be established only with that which is immediately perceived; and when unrelated words are uttered, there is no immediate perception [of a connection], nor does there arise a single syntactical unity (ekavākyatā).
Therefore, it must be with the separated [word]...

"Alternatively, having understood the meaning of the constituent parts (*pūrvapadārtha*) through another means such as meditation (*dhyāna*), one might produce the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*). That [sentence-meaning] would be non-Vedic and preceded by human intellect,
just as, for example, taking a verb from one section (*anuvāka*) and [a noun] from another...

That which is produced as the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) by means of a word-meaning (*nāmapada*) would be of such a nature that, having understood the preceding word-meaning through another means such as meditation (*dhyāna*), one produces the sentence-meaning. Therefore,
it is determined that syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) does not exist when there is an intervention by a disconnected meaning.

Therefore, there is no syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the *sāmidhenī* verses and the *upavīta*. [Objection: "But since the *upavīta* is recited in proximity to the various arrangements of the *sāmidhenī* verses which have been recently perceived in the mind, it must therefore be connected with the *sāmidhenīs*. [Reply: We say, "No," for the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *sāmidhenīs* has indeed ceased, due to the intervention of the *nivit* words.

For it is by means of the direct statement that the optional variations of the *sāmidhenī* verses enter into a relationship [with the ritual], and the context does not persist; nor, moreover, do the *sāmidhenīs* become established as part of the archetype (*prakṛta*) by virtue of the statement regarding the variations. For there is no statement regarding them there that says, "They are to be performed"; what then?

They are to be connected with numbers—this too is established by syntactical connection (*vākya*), not by context (*prakaraṇa*). In that regard, for a quality that does not have a single-sentence relationship with the *sāmidhenī* verses when those *sāmidhenīs* are not the subject under discussion, there is no connection with them. Therefore, it is established that whatever is to be performed within the context must be done while wearing the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītin*).

kha. And because qualities exist for the sake of another, there would be no connection [between them] due to their equality. || 22 ||

Bhāṣya: Regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the vessels made of *vāraṇa* wood and the *vaikaṅkata* wood are for the purpose of the *śrauta* oblations, intended for the act of offering (*homārtha*).

But because the primary [element] is not connected [with the others], it should therefore be extracted from that [context]. (Siddhānta) || 16 ||

The twelve-fold *upasada* would be displaced. Why? Because of its lack of connection with the *jyotiṣṭoma*. How is there no connection? Because the syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the *ahīna* sacrifice is directly perceived.
[Objection: "But surely the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself is figuratively called an *ahīna*. [Reply: No, it is said—no.
When the primary meaning is possible, it is not appropriate to adopt a secondary sense. [Objection: "But surely there will be a negative compound (nañ-samāsa).

[Reply: We say no; for if that were the case, the word *ahīna* would have an acute accent on its first syllable (*ādyudātta*), yet this word has an acute accent on its middle syllable (*madhyodātta*). Therefore, setting aside the context, this is a characteristic of the *ahīna*.
Moreover, there is a designation:

"The *sāha* itself has twelve *upasads*, as does the *ahīna*. If the *sāha* were one thing and the *ahīna* another, then such a designation would be appropriate; and since the statement of this designation exists, [it follows that it belongs] to the *ahīna*.
— thus [ends the section] (3.3.80).
This concludes the section concerning the excellence of the *pratipad* [verses] such as the *kula*.
Or rather, it is connected with the singular, dual, or plural [number], because of the injunction regarding that [sacrifice]. (Siddhānta 17)

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard [in the scripture]: "Since you two are indeed the lords of heaven"—with these words, one should perform the *pratipad* for two sacrificers; "these are the flowing drops"—with these words [for one sacrificer].

"For many sacrificers"—thus [it is stated]. In this regard, there is a doubt: do these two *pratipad* verses belong to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* itself, or should they be displaced to the *Dvirātra* and other sacrifices that involve many sacrificers, such as the *Kulāya* and the *Ahiṃsaka*? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? [They belong] to that which is connected with a plurality of performers.

Because of the lack of connection with the Jyotiṣṭoma, the two *pratipads* should be displaced; for the word *pratipad* does not denote a verse to be recited at the commencement of a *stotra*, according to Mādhava.
The reading "gvamindaraḥ" is found in the Cā0 So0 Pu0 and likewise in the Kā0 Kī0 Pu0.
The same applies to what follows as well.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, two sacrificers are heard of, just as in the case of the Kulāya sacrifice: "By this [sacrifice], a king and a domestic priest, desiring union, should sacrifice."

If it is argued that [the rule] applies to what is performed for a purpose within a fortnight, (Pūrvapakṣa) || 18 ||

If you think that the two steps should be increased, this is not so, for the context would be contradicted. If it is argued, "Let it be contradicted, because there is no connection [of the Jyotiṣṭoma] with two sacrificers or with many sacrificers," [we reply:

In the Bhāṣya, it is stated regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices: "They perform the joint offerings with the tail of the animal (*jāghanī*).

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is this injunction part of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, or is it for the animal sacrifice (*paśu*)? How would it apply to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, and how would it apply to the animal sacrifice?

If the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are enjoined with reference to the tail (*jāghanī*), then there is a displacement [of the offering from its original context]; but if the tail is enjoined with reference to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, then it remains within the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices themselves. What is the prima facie view? Displacement. Why is it displaced? Because the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are enjoined with reference to the tail—how so? From the word [indicating] the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
—the injunction [is established] by means of the sentence regarding the tail (*jāghanī*); moreover, the word (*śabda*) is stronger than the sentence (*vākya*).

"The Patnīsaṃyājas have already been prescribed. True, they have been prescribed; however, they are now prescribed again in connection with the *jāghanī* (the tail), meaning that they must be performed in connection with it.

This being the case, the Patnīsaṃyājas at the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are not defective even without the *jāghanī*; rather, the *jāghanī* is merely disposed of there. Therefore, wherever the *jāghanī* [is present]...

In that context, her performance is purposeful, and it applies to the animal sacrifice; however, the word "patnī" (wife) does not apply here to the tail (*jāghanī*) of the animal, which consists of the four portions of the *vyāghāraṇa* offering.
Mādhava maintains that this is merely a partial name [of the sacrifice].
In the two months, a partial contradiction being set forth is not expressed as a separate word;
therefore, there is an elevation (*utkarṣa*) of this injunction. Thus it is said.
Or rather, it is an injunction, because it conveys something not previously known. (Siddhānta) || 21 ||
Why?
Because the tail (jāghanī) is enjoined as a subordinate element (guṇa) of the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings.
Since it is not previously established (apūrvatvāt), the tail has not been previously obtained as a subordinate element of the Patnīsaṃyājas; therefore, [it is enjoined].

By the word *khāja*, the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are enjoined; their connection with the tail (*jāghanī*) is not previously enjoined. And where a connection is enjoined, there the injunction pertains to one of the two [relata], while the connection itself is necessarily implied. Alternatively, where the injunction pertains to the connection, the two relata are necessarily implied; and where both are intended as the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there they are expressed by the word *kha*.

A relationship is enjoined; however, where one of the two is by way of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), there, having defined one, the other is enjoined. And here, the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings function as the defining characteristic. How is this understood? Because of the connection with the *patnīs*, not all sacrifices are intended, but rather only a specific one is defined, for which the *patnīs* serve as the means of accomplishment.

Sūtra: "Now, why is it that the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are not prescribed by indicating the tail (*jāghanī*)? By syntactical connection (*vākya*), there is the injunction of the tail (*jāghanī*), while by direct statement (*śruti*), there is [the injunction] of the sacrifice; thus, it has been stated that an injunction of the sacrifice here is not possible because it would entail a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, there is the injunction of the tail. If this were so, the *patnīsaṃyāja* sacrifice at the New and Full Moon sacrifices would be defective in the absence of the tail; therefore, there is no displacement (*anutkarṣa*).
If it is argued that it is a partial [application], [we reply: No. (Ābhāṣya) 22.
Now, as for what was said— that because a single part, the tail (jāghanī), does not serve the purpose of the animal, it must therefore be transferred (utkarṣa)— that must be refuted.

307. Commentary: [Objection: But surely there is a contradiction regarding the meaning of *cara*. [The Bhāṣya] says here: "It is true that the word *caru* is used for rice that has been clearly cooked, as in 'rice (*caru*) is being clearly cooked'; however, its clear cooking is not the cause [of the application of the term].
If clear cooking were the cause, it would not be used for rice that is merely kneaded! Even there..."

For it is employed [in common speech] thus: "A flour-cake (*piṣṭakacarū*) is being prepared. Therefore, whatever is the commonality between these two is the cause [of the application of the term]; this is what is being stated. It is not because of being a name for cooking (*pakti-nāmatvāt*), nor is there a contradiction regarding the *caru*. How so? Because it is a name for cooking; this word *caru* is a name for cooking. The word *caru* is a designator of that which is produced by internal heating through non-exposure to fire (*anavalāvitāntaruṣmapāka*). Therefore, speakers apply it to both ground rice (*piṣṭa-odana*) and plain boiled rice (*viśada-odana*).

[They] say: "It is the *caru*. The purpose has already been stated: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the pouring out (*pevaṇa*) applies to both [the *puroḍāśa* and the *caru*], whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it applies to the *caru* alone. Because there is a single conjunction with one [of the two]. (Siddhānta) 38.
The *Bhāṣya* states: "The grinding of the offering for Pūṣan is known to occur only in the case of the *caru*. Now, a doubt arises:

does this apply only to an offering for Pūṣan dedicated to a single deity, or also to one dedicated to two deities? What is the example of an offering for two deities? In the *Rājasūya*, there are the latter two offerings connected with three [deities]:
the cake on eleven potsherds for Soma-Pūṣan, and the *caru* for Indra-Pūṣan, which is dark-colored.

Regarding the term "sacrificial fee" (dakṣiṇā), the example there is the offering to Indra and Pūṣan. What is the prima facie view?—that grinding applies only to that which has a single deity. Why? Because of the connection with the singular [deity].
And as in the case of the fourfold making [of a decision].
The *cara* is accomplished; "the *ca* is added" is the reading according to the Pāṭhayā and Sārasvata schools.

In the case of an offering to two deities (*dvidevatya*), the ritual rule would be contradicted: [the rule] regarding the grinding of the portion for Pūṣan would not apply to the other.

In that situation, if the portion of Pūṣan were ground, the other would remain unground; consequently, there would be an uneven cooking, and since the term *caru* (rice-pot offering) is based on the act of cooking, that term would be contradicted. Now, if...
Thinking it would not be contradictory, they might grind a portion for another deity as well; thus there would be confusion regarding the portions.

What is the fault in that? That the portion of one deity might be offered to another! Therefore, the grinding should be performed exactly as prescribed in the scriptural text, even when the offering is intended for a single deity.

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is recorded: "The *nivīta* is for humans, the *prācīnāvīta* is for the ancestors, and the *upavīta* is for the gods; he wears it as the *upavīta*, for that indeed constitutes the mark of the gods. Regarding the statement "the *nivīta* is for humans," there is a doubt: is this an injunction (*vidhi*) or an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)?

—Thus [it is asked]: when there is an injunction, is this a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*) or a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*)? Or, since the injunction occurs within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), does it pertain to human beings therein, or does it find its place in a ritual action where humans are the primary factor?—thus [it is asked].

What is established? That it is an injunction (*vidhi*) and a duty of humans (*manuṣyadharma*). If it is an injunction, then by enjoining this unprecedented matter (*apūrva-artha*), it becomes purposeful; otherwise, it would be a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) and thus useless. If it is an injunction, then "the *nivīta* for humans" is a designation where the human is the primary factor (*puruṣapradhāna*). How is this understood? Here, humans are not being enjoined; rather, the *nivīta* is enjoined for humans, and what is not enjoined [is not purposeful].
It becomes an auxiliary; for if humans were also enjoined [as the beneficiaries], there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, the *nivīta* is an aid to humans.
[Objection: But surely, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is an aid to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). [Response: No, because of the context.

For this reason also, it is not an injunction. Why? Because it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with an injunction. If the other [passage] were also an injunction, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), for there is no syntactical unity between one injunction and another injunction due to the difference in their modes of expression. What is the purpose of the repetition? It is for the sake of praising the *upavīta* (wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder). How is there praise of the *upavīta*? [It is shown by] the fact that the *nivīta* (wearing it around the neck) is unsuitable for the divine rites known as the Darśapūrṇamāsa, for that belongs to humans;

"Just as among actors there is such a style as that of Devadatta, so too among Brahmins there is such a style"—this mention of other styles is for the purpose of praising the dress of Devadatta; likewise, here too, the mention of the *nivīta* is for the purpose of praising the *upavīta*. This is an injunction (*vidhi*), namely "One should not speak untruth at the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," and not a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Why? Because of a different connection (*saṃyogāntara*): in the case of the performance of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), the person is connected with the observance;
here, however, the connection of the person is with the prohibition of a specific thing. How could it be otherwise?

What is being heard will be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of something else; therefore, there is a triple injunction for the prohibition. [The opponent] says: "We accept this—that it is an injunction—but we maintain that it is a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*), because human effort is what is directly stated in the scripture. To this we reply: when all [the elements] have arrived, what is heard is the performance of the action (*kriyānuṣṭhāna*), not any particular factor of action (*kāraka*).
How is this understood? From the suffix (*pratyaya*), since we perceive the action as that which is to be performed.
"But do they not also perceive the agent? True, they perceive him, but not from the word.
From what, then? From the sense; for when an action is enjoined as something to be performed,"
[Page 384] Bhāṣya:

In that case, the operation of the causal factors (*kāraka-vyāpāra*) is understood by implication; that which is understood by implication is not directly expressed by the word (*śrauta*). And that which is not directly expressed by the word is not understood from the sentence (*vākya*). How, then, could it be understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*)?
It will be contradicted.

He says: "From the teacher's instruction that 'the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together,' it is understood that the agent is the meaning of the verbal root and the object is [also] its meaning; for the teachers prescribe the suffix *śap* in the sense of the agent and the suffix *yak* in the sense of the object, thus teaching both the agent and the object as the meanings of the suffix."
Therefore, it is said that the meaning of a word is both the agent and the action.

It is replied: the meaning of a word does not arise merely from the statement of a teacher or from the statement of the author of the Sūtras; rather, it is understood through the suffix. And the action, being perceived as something to be performed, [is understood].

It is understood that [the suffix] causes the factors of action (kārakas) to be conveyed. Furthermore, the Teachers maintain that neither the agent nor the object is the meaning of the suffix. [Objection: "But surely the *lakāra* is heard in the sense of both the agent and the object. [Response: It is not heard in the sense of either the agent or the object; rather—

“In one [object], the singular number; in two, the dual number; in many, the plural number”—this is another statement therein, and there the connection is made thus: “when there is one agent, when there are two agents, or when there are many agents. In this same way, the connection with oneness and so forth applies to the object (*karman*). In that case, it is not expressed as “it occurs when the agent is one and...,” [but rather the grammatical number is determined by the state of the object].

How, then, is it?—the singular number is used when there is a single agent; that is to say, when the agent is one. Likewise in the case of duality and plurality, and likewise with respect to the object (*karman*). When explained in this manner, the intended meaning of the word becomes consistent with worldly logic, the words of the Sūtra become consistent with reason, and this very [interpretation] is also the traditional teaching (*āgama*). That is to say: when oneness and so forth are the meanings of the case-endings (*vibhakti*), then the object and so forth function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*).

"Now, it might be argued that this too is the case: when *karman* and so forth are the meanings of the case-endings (*vibhakti*), then *ekatva* (singularity) and so forth function as qualifiers. To this we reply: indeed, *karman* and the rest are obtained through the force of the meaning (*arthaprāpta*); they do not constitute the direct denotations (*abhidheya*) of the word. However, *ekatva* and the rest are not obtained from the meaning; therefore, they are the actual denotations of the word. Consequently, although *ekatva* and so forth are qualifiers, nevertheless, it is the qualifier itself that is expressed [by the suffix]. This is just as in the statement, "The priests wearing golden garlands perform the ritual," where the state of wearing a golden garland is a qualifier.
[Page 385] Bhāṣya: Even so, that very thing is what is enjoined; therefore, the oneness of the agent is not the meaning of the word.

[Objection: "But surely, because the agent is one, there is the singular number; because the agents are two, there is the dual number; and because the agents are many, there is the plural number. Therefore, it is understood that the agent is certainly the meaning of the word. [Reply: This is not so, for this is not known through inference. Rather, the agent is understood precisely from the comprehension of the action to be performed.
"It is understood"—this is perception (*pratyakṣa*); that [perception] is not sublated by anything whatsoever.
When there is an indication in the singular number, the oneness of the agent is understood; when there is an indication in the dual number, duality of the agent;
when there is an indication in the plural number, plurality of the agents—that too is perception. Which, then, could be inference (*anumāna*)?

"It ought to be set aside"—just as when a word expressing a genus (*prakṛti*) is in the dual number, a plurality of substances is understood, whereas in the singular number, the oneness of the substance is understood; so it should be seen here as well.
Therefore, it is not based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*); and if it is not based on direct scriptural statement, the context (*prakaraṇa*) will not be sublated.

As for the argument that "the human effort [of performance] would be purposeless in the view that the action is a property of the sacrifice (*karmadharma*), because of the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*),"...
"Because of the statement regarding what is to be performed"—to this it is replied: if it were an auxiliary (*aṅga*), it would be grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*);

however, that which is not enjoined does not become an auxiliary. Therefore, for the sake of being an auxiliary, it must be enjoined even under this view. Hence, we consider this [to apply] to that which belongs to the context.

The prohibition is as follows: "Therefore, that which is false is not a part of speech"—meaning that whatever has been resolved upon is the constituent part, and that alone must be performed; having resolved upon an offering of rice, one must not present an offering of barley.
He asks: "Since falsehood must be avoided by both parties as well, what is the purpose of deliberation? It is replied: In the former position, it is a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*).

In that case, according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the expiation (prāyaścitta) is that prescribed by Smṛti; according to the final conclusion (siddhānta), it is the ritual duty (dharma) pertaining to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice;
and in that specific instance, the expiation is that belonging to the Yajurveda. (3.4.1)

The person [is] like a snake, because it has that as its purpose. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 14 ||
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "The Aṅgirasas were our ancestors, the highest...

In the Mīmāṃsā-darśana [Bhāṣya]:

"The meaning of a sentence can be established only with that which is immediately perceived; however, when unrelated words are uttered, there is no immediate perception, and thus there is no syntactic unity."
Therefore, [the opponent suggests:

"Alternatively, by means of another method such as meditation (*dhyāna*), one may first comprehend the meaning of the prior word and then generate the meaning of the sentence. That [sentence-meaning] would be non-Vedic, being preceded by human intellect.

It would be like this: just as when one takes a verb from one section (anuvāka) and a noun from another, a sentence-meaning is produced; such would that [sentence] be, wherein one might produce a sentence-meaning after having understood the meaning of the preceding word through some other means, such as meditation. Therefore...
It is determined that syntactic unity does not exist when there is an intervention by unrelated matters;
therefore, there is no syntactic unity between the *sāmidhenī* verses and the *upavīta*. [Objection:
"But the *upavīta* is recited in proximity to the various forms of the *sāmidhenī* verses, which are present in the immediate consciousness."
"Therefore, it shall be connected with the *sāmidhenī* verses"—this we deny. For the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *sāmidhenīs* has indeed been interrupted by the intervention of the *nivid* formulas.
By means of syntactical connection (*vākya*), the optional variants of the *sāmidhenīs* enter into a relationship [with those formulas], and the context does not persist;
nor are the *sāmidhenīs* brought back into relevance by the statement of the variants.

O venerable ones! For in that case, their statement does not mean "they are to be performed," but rather, "they are to be connected with the numbers. And even that is established by syntactical connection (*vākya*), not by context (*prakaraṇa*). In that regard, for a quality whose single syntactical unity with the *sāmidhenī* verses is not established, there can be no connection with those verses. Therefore...
It is established that whatever is to be performed in a ritual context must be done with the sacred thread worn over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī).

kha. And because qualities are for the sake of another, there would be no connection [between them] due to their equality. || 22 ||

Bhāṣya: In the establishment of the sacred fire (agnyādheya), the vessels made of *vāraṇa* wood and the *vaikaṅkata* wood are for the purpose of the *śrauta* oblations; they are intended for the act of offering (*homārtha*).
Chapter 8, Section 4. [Page 387]

[Objection: "But surely the context (*prakaraṇa*) cannot restrict the word *jañjabhyamāna* to a single part [of the ritual], for syntactical connection (*vākya*) is indeed stronger than context. [Reply: We do not say that the word *jañjabhyamāna* is excluded from the person outside the context by means of the context. Rather, we say that it is excluded from the person who is not part of the context.

"It is turned back"—this is what is said; however, a result must be postulated there. [Objection: "But surely a result is heard directly in the scripture: 'He indeed places the prāṇa and apāna within himself. [Reply: We say, "No.
For we do not perceive here an injunctive word such as, "He should place the prāṇa and apāna within himself"; this is a statement in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*), not an injunction.

However, it serves as a praise for the mantra; therefore, this [mantra] is not fruit-bearing when used apart from the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Consequently, it is understood to be a purificatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*) for the person performing the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

If it is argued that this is understood as "the act of human consecration" (puruṣasaṃskārakarma) performed only by one who is performing the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa)—this is not so. Why? Because even one who yawns elsewhere than at the New and Full Moon sacrifices is indeed denoted by the word "yawning" (añjabhyamāna). It is not [restricted].

And this has been stated: "It is excluded by the context; therefore, it is displaced. To this, it is replied: It is not at all excluded, but rather there is no purpose for it being refined [by the context].
[Objection: "But surely, even with regard to the refinement of the person (*puruṣa-saṃskāra*), there is no purpose within the context. [Reply: It is replied:

The consecrated person shall perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices. [Objection: Even if there is a displacement [of the sacrifice], the consecrated person will perform another [rite]. [Reply: It is said—consecration does not become a subordinate element (guṇa) for another, because that other is not the subject under discussion (aprakṛtatvāt). [Objection: Even for the subject under discussion, it is not a subordinate element, because of the syntactical statement (vākya).

Because it is understood as a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*). It is replied: due to its lack of purpose (*ānarthakya*), it is not understood as a property of the person. Therefore, this [injunction] forms a single syntactical unit with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices under discussion, and not with any other fruit-bearing rite, because there is no context (*prakaraṇa*) for that;
therefore, there is no displacement (*utkarṣa*).

As for the argument that the prohibition within the context—namely, the statement "In this case, one should say"—is an injunction of performance whose own literal meaning is not intended to be significant; if that were so, it would be a mere restatement of what is already established by scripture, and there would be no purpose in enjoining its connection with the person.
Bhāṣya-sūtra [Page 388]
In the Mīmāṃsā system, it should be extracted on account of the designation. (Sūtra 16: Concluding Siddhānta)

Now, as for what was described—that just as the twelve-fold *upasads* are extended, so too should this [the *sāhna*] be extended—it is replied: that [extension] is designated by the scriptural statement (*vākya*) for the *ahīnas*, and the *ahīnas* possess results; however, the word "deficient" (*hīna*) does not apply to the *jyotiṣṭoma* there, because it would be used figuratively (*gauṇatva*) and because of the specific designation: "The *upasads* of the *sāhna* are indeed three."

"Dependent"—thus it is said. Therefore, it is appropriate that the state of having twelve *upasads* is extracted from the context (*prakaraṇa*), because its connection to the person is purposeless, whereas another element possessing a purpose exists within the context. (3.4.5)

And [the gift] to Śaṃyu is [established] because of the surrender of everything. || 17 ||
In the *Bhāṣya* on the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard: "The gods said to Yama Bārhaspatya, 'Bring this [offering] to us.
To this great statement, there follows this declaration: "'What shall I gain from my offspring? they asked. [He replied: 'Whoever should threaten a Brāhmaṇa, him you shall strike with your staff.'"

"Let him who reviles another be punished with a thousand [pieces of gold]; let him who sheds blood be punished for as many years as he might collect grains of dust by wading through it—he shall not recognize the world of the ancestors for that many years. Therefore, one should not threaten a Brahmin, nor strike him, nor cause him to shed blood.

In this regard, there is a doubt: is the prohibition of threatening (*avagoraṇa*) enjoined for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, or is it taught for the person? What is the prima facie view? On account of the context, the prohibition of threatening and so forth applies to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; that is to say, during the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, one must not threaten anyone by the neck, nor should one inflict violence, nor shed blood.
Another means must be resorted to for the sake of providing sustenance; therefore, they invite him to the meal (*āmbāhāryeṇa*).
Regarding this, the Vārttika states: "The word 'saṃghā' is an elliptical expression indicating the prohibitory statements concerning the killing of Brahmins, cows, and so forth."
[Page 389] Chapter 3, Section 8.

325. [The opponent says: "It follows from the context (*prakaraṇa*). This being the position reached, we reply: "And in both cases, there is an extraction (*utkarṣa*) from the context. Why? Because of the total surrender (*sarva-paridāna*); this [gift] pertains to the Brāhmaṇa in all his states."

A prohibition has been stated, namely that acts such as threatening (*avagoraṇa*) and so forth should not be performed even in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. [Objection: "But surely, by virtue of the *prakaraṇa* (context), these are duties belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa. [Reply: True, they belong to the *prakaraṇa*; however, in this case, it is a duty for one who threatens, established by means of a *vākya* (direct syntactical connection), and a *vākya* is more powerful than a *prakaraṇa*. [Objection: "But could it not be that the act belongs to the *prakaraṇa* because it is being enjoined? [Reply: No, it is said; in that case, a result would have to be assumed, whereas here [the result] is already established, for it exists here.

The injunctive case-ending—as in "one should punish with a hundred," "one should punish with a thousand," or "one should know the world of the birds"—therefore, there is a displacement (*utkarṣa*) of such [passages]. (3.4.6 Śrauta Sūtra).
This is the section concerning the prohibition of conversation with a woman in her menses as being for the benefit of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
[Siddhānta: It is [not] so, because there is no prior prohibition, as in the case of a servant’s stained garment. (Sūtra 18) (Siddhānta)

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "One should not converse with a woman in her courses; one should not eat her food. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the prohibition of conversing with a menstruating woman a restriction on the conversation that is an auxiliary part of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, or is it a prohibition for the person in all circumstances?
Is it a prohibition? What is the prima facie view? That, by virtue of the context, it is a rule of prohibition regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

This being the position, we reply: the conversation with one wearing soiled clothes (*malavadāsas*) should be displaced from the context. Why? Because of the prior exclusion; for it is heard in scripture: "If on the day of the vow the wife should be in her courses, one should sacrifice after having excluded her."

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is a dialogue between the Adhvaryu and his wife: "This is your world, O lady. This [practice], being liable to occur, would be prohibited; for it is said in some readings that "it is not established because of the absence of restriction," and this is likewise found in the Bhāṣya.
[Page 390] Bhāṣya:

Since there is no prior exclusion for those performing the sacrifice, how could a contradiction arise such that it would necessitate a prohibition? Therefore, the rule regarding "one with soiled clothes" should be displaced.
The dialogue together.
Sūtra 18: And because of the prohibition of food.
And there is a prohibition regarding food: "One should not eat the food of a woman who has not bathed after her menses, nor indeed [should one eat] the food of a woman.

This is a prohibition against sexual intercourse that is enjoined; however, since it is not applicable within the context [of the ritual], it is determined that this is a duty of the person (puruṣadharma) extracted from the context.
The section concerning the fact that [qualities] such as possessing a golden stream are attributes of a person.
a. But when it is not in the context [of a specific rite], that property [belongs to all] because of its distinction from that [context]. (Siddhānta) || 20 ||
In the Bhāṣyasūtra, it is heard without reference to a specific context: "Therefore, gold of beautiful color should be worn; he [who wears otherwise] would be of ugly color."

"He becomes an enemy"—thus it is said. "One should be well-dressed; one indeed maintains one's form"—thus it is stated. In this regard, there arises a doubt: is this a ritual duty (prakaraṇadharma) or a personal duty (puruṣadharma)?
To this, it is replied: "But that duty belongs to one outside the context, because of its specific nature; therefore, it is a personal duty."
It would be of such a nature. Why?
Because there is a distinction for this [element] from that which is studied within the context (*prakaraṇa*); this is not studied within the context, provided it is recited outside of the context.
It would be a dharma pertaining to all contexts; its recitation outside of a specific context would not produce any particular distinction. Therefore, such a thing is a dharma of the person.
But because it is not a substance, the remainder should belong to you. (Pūrvapakṣa 21)

But the word "tu" (but/however) [indicates] a fivefold modification. It would not be a property of the person; rather, it would be a subsidiary element of the Agnihotra and other rites. Why? Because of the absence of a material substance (*adravyatvāt*). Here, no material substance or deity is heard mentioned, by the hearing of which one might assume that "one should sacrifice with a wife."
But in the absence of a connection between a substance and a deity, this root *bhṛ* (in *vibhakti*) expresses "bearing" and denotes a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*).
[Page 391]
The residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of ritual actions manifests as the form of the *śrāva* for that which remains, and not otherwise;
therefore, the *agnihotra* and other rites are its residue. Thus, one must be well-clad.
kha.
Because of the connection with the Veda. (Pūrvapakṣa-yukti 1)

Bhāṣya: The connection with the Veda expressed as "the office of the Adhvaryu" (ādhvaryavam) is appropriate for that which is subordinate; for it is by the Adhvaryu that the subordinate element is performed, and it is not a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*). For the Adhvaryu is the performer of the rites such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa, together with their subsidiaries and the subsidiaries of those subsidiaries. Therefore, this too is a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*).
Such are the types [of arguments].
And because of the connection with substances, [the word "sacrifice" is used]. (Pūrvapakṣa-yukti 2)

Furthermore, the instruction here refers to a substance, because of its connection with the accusative case— as in "gold is to be worn. And the consecration of a substance is purposeful under the view that it is a subsidiary to the ritual act,
whereas it would be useless if it were a duty pertaining to the person.
Śāṇḍilya [maintains] that there would be a connection with the fruit for one's own [self], like a conjunction; therefore, it is an action (karman). (Pūrvapakṣa-siddhānta 24)
[The Bhāṣya says: "Or rather, the connection of such things with the fruit would be a property of the person; for if they were the properties of gold or cloth, they would be purposeless. [Objection:
But surely the ritual act will be accomplished by means of the consecrated gold or cloth. [Reply:
This is not so, because gold cannot assist the ritual act as its constituent part (aṅga), since there is an absence of direct scriptural statement (śruti) and the other criteria."

It is a constituent part of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*). Therefore, there is a connection with the result for those [statements] of this kind, such as "therefore his rival becomes ill-favored" (*durvarṇo 'sya bhrātṛvyo bhavati*).

[Objection: "But surely this is a statement of present fact (*vartamānāpadeśa*). [Reply: True, this is so; however, in order to avoid meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*), a connection must be sought through an injunction of result (*phalacodanā*). And from another...
It is simpler to modify that which belongs to a single sentence than to seek [an external element].
"Puruṣapradhāna" is the reading in the Kāśikā-saṃgraha-pustaka.
Why?

The Bhāṣya says: Direct [connection] exists with one [text], while indirect [connection] exists with another; there is a modification of the present tense and an ascertainment of the intended meaning regarding the relationship.

Therefore, such an instruction concerning a primary act would be like the connection of the Prajāpati-vows with their fruit—namely, "By this much he becomes freed from sin. It should be viewed in the same way here as well. Consequently, such a thing is a duty of the person (puruṣadharma). (3.4.8)

The remainder belongs to all rites within the context, because there is no distinction. (Pūrvapakṣa) 25.

Bhāṣya: Here, the examples are the *jayas* and others which are connected with ritual actions, such as: "One should offer the *jayas* in whatever rite one desires success," "He offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*," and "He offers the *abhyātānas*. Regarding these, are they subsidiary (*śeṣa*) to all actions, such as agriculture and the like, or only to Vedic rites such as the *agnihotra*? Their status as subsidiaries follows from their connection with specific determined rituals and from the fact that no separate fruit is heard [for them]. Which...?
Is this then established?— that they are the remnants of all ritual acts, because no specific distinction has been stated.
Bhāṣya:
Sūtra 26: "The oblations, however, should be restricted [to the Āhavanīya fire], because of their connection with the Āhavanīya.
This is not the case—that [the oblations] are auxiliary members even of all rites, such as plowing and so forth.

These are oblations; therefore, they should be restricted [to those who possess the Āhavanīya fire], for there is a connection with the Āhavanīya fire in the case of oblations, as it is said: "When one offers in the Āhavanīya, by that the Soma-drinker becomes worshipped and gratified.
Consequently, these [oblations] are auxiliary to him who possesses the Āhavanīya fire. Not [to others].
One who desires should seek success; *cittacca svāhā* and so forth are the *jamā*s.
*Ṛtāvādityādamo rāṭraśvataḥ*; *babhirśvatānām* and so forth are the *abhvatānā*s—so says Mādhava.

Furthermore, the *bhāṣya* states: "The ladles (*sruc*) and other implements are used in the *āhavanīya* fire, and there is no *gārhapatya* fire for them, from which the *āhavanīya* would have been carried forward (*praṇīta*). Therefore, [the rites] such as plowing (*karṣaṇa*) do not [apply]."
Jayā and the others.
And the remainder [is established] from the traditional designation. (Sūtra 27) (Hetu)
Bhāṣya: From this as well, we see that [the *jaya* offerings and so forth] are subsidiary to the sacrificial altars (*vedikā*). Why?

Because of the name (*samākhyāna*). For since the *jaya* offerings and others are recited in the Veda named "Ādhvaryava," they will be performed by the *adhvaryu* priest. [This applies even] to the plowing and other such acts [performed] by the *adhvaryu*.

Because they would exist even when performed by one who is not an Adhvaryu priest, they would subvert the [specific] designation; therefore, they are subsidiary to the Vedic rites—thus [it is concluded]. (3.4.9)
The section concerning the necessity of performing a sacrifice upon receiving a Vedic horse.

8. [Objection: In the case of a worldly sacrifice, there would be a fault due to the *iṣṭi* offerings; however, in the case of a Vedic sacrifice, there should be no fault on account of the sacred scripture.
(Pūrvapakṣa) || 28 ||

There is the *Aśvapratigraheṣṭi* sacrifice, concerning which it is said: "Varuṇa indeed seizes him who accepts a horse; as many horses as he may accept, so many four-potherd offerings to Varuṇa should he present. In this regard, there is a doubt: does the sacrifice apply to the acceptance of a horse in a worldly context, or in a Vedic context? What, then, is the worldly acceptance of a horse, and what is the Vedic? [The worldly] is when one is begging for it in the world...
Or, when one obtains a horse without asking for it, there is worldly acceptance (*śvapratigraha*) of it;
so too in the Vedic context, as in "In the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, a thousand horses are the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)," and "In the Agniṣṭoma, a cow or a horse.
Regarding this, it is said: since there is a commonality of being Vedic, [the rule] applies to the Vedic case—this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Mādhava maintains that the word *pratigraha* (receiving) in this context refers to giving (*dāna*). Bhartṛmitra objects: "In common worldly usage, it would be a fault (*doṣa*), for a fault is indeed heard in scripture: 'Varuṇa seizes him who accepts a horse as a gift'—and this is that very case."
"Where there is a fault, there [is a penance]—and that [fault] occurs when acceptance is made in the worldly sense from a Śūdra or from another person of sinful deeds;

thus it is established that because of the connection with a fault, it pertains to the worldly. [Objection: "The mention of the fault is not for the purpose of qualifying the scope of the penance, but rather for the purpose of praising the penance."

It is said: this would be so for the purpose of destroying a fault (*doṣanirghātārtha*). This ritual is the "Release from Varuṇa" (*varuṇapramocana*); it ought to apply to the worldly (*laukika*) case, because the seizing by Varuṇa exists in the world, whereas in the Vedic case of receiving a horse (*aśvapratigraha*), that [seizing] would not exist. However, its performance is understood through the Śālāki [textual] statement. And if there were sin (*pāpa*) resulting from that, it would not [be the case].
Its status as something to be performed would be understood [only if it were beneficial], for the fruit of sin is certainly not something to be performed.

[Objection: "But even in the case of Vedic acceptance (*pratigraha*), there is sin for one who accepts from an improper person. [Reply: It might indeed be so, if the acceptance itself were intended as the goal;
