It has been established in this section that there is no sacrifice prescribed by the Veda for the acceptance of a dog's marrow.
Or rather, it is an explanatory supplement (arthavāda), because there is no possibility of falling [into sin]; therefore, it should be understood as applying to the journey.

Bhāṣya: And that which was stated is not the case—namely, "He who receives a horse from a Śūdra or from any other evildoer in this world should offer this *iṣṭi*; for he is said to be seized by Varuṇa"—where "seized by Varuṇa" refers to one afflicted with *jalodara*, whose abdomen swells with fluid; *jalodara* is precisely what is well-known in the world by that name.

"And for him, the worldly acceptance of horses is not the cause"—thus is the reading "prati anupaghātāt" found in the Kāśīmudrita-saṃskaraṇa-pustaka; likewise it is in the Bhāṣya as well, on the next page.

It is known, and it is not enjoined by this [passage]; therefore, the onset of dropsy does not result from the acceptance of a horse.

Now, if sin is expressed by the word *varuṇa*, then the intention is that he "binds" [the sin]—this is the meaning. In that case, when the well-known [meaning] is abandoned, the word *varuṇa* would merely denote hair, as it binds [it].

It is said: in that case, even regarding the acceptance [of a gift], one might be seized by Varuṇa; due to the affliction of guarding, nourishing, and being anxious about it, this sacrifice would not be established. [This refers to] "the worldly acceptance of a dog"—thus, the well-known [proverbial] usage would be contradicted. Therefore, this is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

By means of the comparison—"as much as there is benefit for one seized by Varuṇa in being released from Varuṇa, so much [is the benefit] by this"—this is a glorification: the acceptance of a suitable [gift] is like being seized by Varuṇa, and the sacrifice which is performed is like the release from that [seizure], just as by one seized by Varuṇa.

The release must necessarily be performed; this case is exactly like that—therefore, whatever might be understood [as the result] should be accepted. For in the case of worldly acts, a result must be postulated, whereas in the Vedic act where there is the taking of the *ajavata* cup, [the release] will become a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that very act, in conjunction with the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*).

Since syntactic unity is to be understood through a connection, it is more parsimonious for that syntactic unity with a remote statement of the result to be established; thus, it is logical that the *iṣṭi* applies to Vedic giving. (3.4.10)
The predominance of the *dātu*, *vāta*, and *vīrya* [is established].

Bhāṣya: "As many horses as one might accept, so many four-potherd offerings to Varuṇa (vāruṇa-catuṣkapāla) should one perform. What is the prima facie view?—"And because the action is not enjoined, there is a difference of agency"; the sacrifice is not enjoined for the agent of giving, but we understand it to belong to the one who is bound by the acceptance—namely, as many horses as...

In the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya it is stated: "He should accept [the gift]; he should offer as many cakes on four potsherds to Varuṇa.
Therefore, this rite is to be performed by the officiating priest who accepts the gift.
Sūtra: That [gift] should belong to the officiating priest because of the indicative mark. (Conclusion)

This [fault] does not belong to the recipient, but rather to the causal agent (the giver). Why? Because of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). What is the indicative mark? It is the connection of the preceding words with the subsequent words according to their respective meanings; for this is heard: "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa. Here, Prajāpati is celebrated as the giver of the horse, and Varuṇa as the recipient.
And [the word] "he" (*saḥ*) reaches toward the deity [of the syllable *khāṃ*]. Thus, the word "he," being dependent, requires the previously mentioned remainder of the sentence;

it attains syntactic unity with that [remainder] by referring back to Prajāpati. Furthermore, due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it is appropriate for this to be a reference to Prajāpati alone, and not to the object [of the verb], because of their lack of coreferentiality. "He..."

The word "paryadīryata" (he was rent asunder) refers back to Prajāpati mentioned previously; thus, it attains syntactic unity with that [preceding passage]. "He saw this four-potherd oblation"—this is Prajāpati himself—"he offered it"—this is Prajāpati himself—"thereupon he was released from the grasp of Varuṇa"—this is Prajāpati. And... [the rest of the sentence follows].

"He takes this"— this reason is to be refuted, because it is said that since Prajāpati, having given a horse to Varuṇa, fell away, therefore whoever accepts (or gives) a horse, him Varuṇa seizes, and he falls away. But since he was released by means of the offering to Varuṇa, therefore even another who gives a horse [is released] by means of the *vāruṇī* [offering].

"It is to be offered"—thus the Varuṇī sacrifice is praised as a means for the giver of a horse; it must be performed by one who has given such a horse. Therefore, having given a horse, one should offer the Varuṇī sacrifice.
"O friend, surely it is said: 'He who receives a horse should perform the offering.

This being so, if the statement begins in one way and concludes in another, both the beginning and the conclusion would be meaningless. Therefore, the meaning of the word must be determined by the beginning."
It should be interpreted according to the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), or, in the case of a conclusion being absent, according to the introduction (*upakrama*).
In this regard, [on page 397] in the Bhāṣya:

"Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa"—this should be interpreted in accordance with the conclusion, namely, "He recovered the horse from Varuṇa," when [the conclusion is present]; but when [it is not], it must follow the introduction.

[The doubt is: Does the concluding statement mean "he receives the horse for yoga" or "he causes the horse to receive [the reward] for yoga"? In this regard, the first option must be accepted—"the primary sense prevails because of the injunction, as in common worldly usage"—since there is no contradiction; the latter, however, is contradicted.
It must be understood through secondary figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
Furthermore: "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa"—from Varuṇa... [TT]

"One should accept the horse"—this would have to be construed as highly improper. The word "pratigṛhṇāti" (he accepts) can, by some capacity or other, express the meaning "pratigrāhayati" (he causes to be accepted); for he who performs that action, and by whom the action is accomplished even through a secondary means, is the agent of that action.

It can be said that just as one who arranges for six horses to pull [a cart] is called "one who ploughs," even though he does not himself perform the ploughing, because he practices that which is conducive to it; so too here, he who gives is "one who practices that which is capable of receiving. Therefore...
It can be said that "he who gives receives"— therefore, having determined this, it is understood that when it is stated "he who gives receives," the Varuṇī sacrifice is prescribed for him. (3.4.11)

They recite this: "One who has vomited Soma should offer a caru-oblation of Śyāmāka grain to Soma-Indra. In this regard, there is a doubt: does the Soma-Indra oblation apply to the vomiting of worldly Soma-drinking, or to that of Vedic Soma-drinking? What is worldly Soma-drinking, and what is Vedic? It is replied: it is Vedic Soma-drinking.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma and in those sacrifices lasting seven nights or ten nights, there is the drinking of Soma that is worldly (laukika)— that is, when Soma is consumed for the purpose of nourishing the bodily constituents (dhātu-sāmya). What, then, is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)?
—"In the same way as that [case of] 'intoxication from drinking' (pānavyāpaca), the sacrifice should apply to worldly vomiting, not to Vedic [vomiting];
thus is the prima facie view refuted. Just as it was stated there that [the rite applies] to worldly vomiting because of the mention of a connection with a fault, so too here.

In this case as well, hearing occurs through a connection with a defect, as in the worldly saying: "He who drinks Soma is carried away by his sense organ (indriya) or by his vigor (vīrya). This is intelligible because, when one has consumed [Soma] for the sake of balancing the bodily constituents (dhātu-sāmya) and it is subsequently destroyed by vomiting, the state of imbalance of the constituents results in being carried away by the sense organ.

If it is argued that there would be no fault in the Vedic rite [if one vomits], [we reply]: in that case, the remainder must be drunk; since the act enjoined by the word has been accomplished, there is no fault. Even if one vomits, the act of drinking has nevertheless been performed therein; therefore, the purpose of the injunction has been fulfilled, and thus there is no fault.
It may be so. Therefore, in the event of an accident involving the drinking of Soma in the worldly sense, there should be an offering to Saumendra.
But in the case of the Vedic, there would be a fault; however, in the case of the worldly, there would be no fault because of the purpose. (Siddhānta) || 33 ||
[The view is that] this [prohibition] should apply to the Vedic drink in the event of its mishap, but not to the worldly one.

Why? Because of "defect" (*doṣāt*); for a connection with defect is heard in the scripture: "He is indeed deprived of his sense-organ and vigor. In the case of the worldly [drink], however, there is [only] the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātusāmya*).

When it is being performed, nothing is faulty; for in the world, people drink that very thing for the purpose of vomiting. Even if this were merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), nevertheless, in order to avoid the assumption of a separate result, it is logical to assume that it applies specifically to the Vedic rite—thus [is the conclusion]. (3.4.12)
The *saumendra-caru* is fit for the officiant’s authority in the event of the sacrificer’s incapacity.
That [is so] because there is no distinction in all cases. (Pūrvapakṣa 34)

Why? Because there is no distinction; no specific qualification is mentioned [Page 399].

the Sūtra and Bhāṣya.

Or rather, it should belong to the master. Why? Because it is for his sake; the ritual act is for his sake, since the Soma is vomited by him.
As for the rite dedicated to Soma and Indra performed here, that too is for his sake alone; for this is heard in the scripture as being for the benefit of the one who has vomited Soma. Thus...

Regarding those who vomit Soma: that which can assist the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) but not the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), for that is not a rite intended for the priest when Soma is vomited. and what is done for that purpose would not serve the benefit of the sacrificer. Therefore, the [rite for] vomiting should not be performed by the priests.

[This applies to] the sacrificer, because when the consecration of the Soma is ruined, his ritual act becomes defective;

"Whatever was to be done has all been done; at that time, there is no other substance remaining."

—Thus, the re-application (*punaryoga*) should not be repeated. Why? Because that substance is for the purpose of accomplishing the sacrifice; it is not the case that the substance must be connected with the sacrifice. For if the oblation (*havis*) were to be connected with the sacrifice, then, by means of the sacrifice, there would be two portions to be offered.

If it were connected [to the sacrifice], there would still be another thing to be connected; thus, for the sake of connecting that, the injunction (*niyoga*) would have to be repeated. But the sacrifice is not for the purpose of connecting with the substance;

rather, the substance is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the sacrifice. [The substance] is employed so that the sacrifice may reach its completion—how else could it be accomplished? Therefore, once the sacrifice is completed and the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is achieved, there is no further role for the injunction.
"It is logical that the primary [act] should proceed according to the subordinate [factors].

"How is it that substance is not the primary [factor], such that there would be no proceeding from it? Because [the result arises] from the sacrifice.

Regarding the fruit [of the action], it is said: "When there is the mention of both the accomplished and the to-be-accomplished, the accomplished is taught for the sake of the to-be-accomplished. Furthermore, no visible benefit to the substance is produced by the sacrifice;
therefore, having offered the oblation, a remnant must be left over.

There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices; therein are the subsidiary rites, such as the eating of the *iḍā* portion, the *āśis*, the *sauviṣṭakṛta* offering, and so forth. Regarding this, there is a doubt: should these be performed from each individual oblation (*havis*), or from only one oblation? What is the prima facie view? They should be performed from one, because they do not serve as the motive for the oblations; the subsidiary rites are not the motivating factors for the oblations.

If they were impelled by all the remaining rites, then all would be impelled and thus performed for all; however, these are for other purposes and need not necessarily be employed in the remaining rites. Nevertheless, due to proximity, they must be performed from some [of those rites] or another.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "This is for the Brahman; this is for the Hotṛ; this is for the Adhvaryu; this is for the Agnīdh. Is the division among the officiating priests for the purpose of hiring (*parikraya*), or for the purpose of consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*)? What is the prima facie view? The division is for the purpose of hiring. Why? Because there is no mention of consumption.

It is heard [in scripture]: "It is to be eaten. Whatever fault there is in the abandonment of what is explicitly stated (śruta), that same fault exists in the postulation of what is not explicitly stated (aśruta). This division has the sense of "becoming" (bhava) as its purpose. Why? Because of the absence of giving. How is there an absence? For one who possesses power (*prabhavatā*) is able to give, not one who lacks power. Why is there no power? Because it has been resolved by the sacrificer: "This is for the deity."
Thus, the learned do not themselves transact with what has been dedicated to a deity;
therefore, one who follows the practice of the learned cannot prevail [against it], and consequently,
there is no purchase.

Now, as for what was said—"It is not heard [in scripture] that one must consume [the portion]; and as great as the fault is in abandoning what is heard, so great is the fault in postulating what is not heard"—to this we reply: there is a connection with the portions of Brahmā and the others, expressed by such phrases as "This is for Brahmā. In that case, either the portions would benefit Brahmā and the others, or Brahmā and the others would benefit the portions. However, no visible purpose is served by the portions benefiting Brahmā and the others.

However, by means of portions that serve as offerings for Brahmā and the others, a visible benefit can be produced in some manner through their being consumed. Therefore, the distribution is for the purpose of consumption. If it is asked, "What then is the benefit? [the answer is: those who are satiated possess the capacity to complete the remainder of the ritual action.

The word *udgātṛ* has a connection with the cup (*camasa*) through direct syntactical statement (*vākya`); however, the plural suffix (*bahuvacana*) has a connection with the word *udgātṛ* by way of direct denotation (*śruti*), whereas there is no connection whatsoever for the plural suffix with any other officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). Therefore, the claim that "the cup belongs to many" is untenable. To this, it is replied: this word *udgātṛ* is capable [of expressing the group].

To express plurality, they "sing out" (*udgāyanti*) through connection with the action; thus they are called *udgātṛ*s. Who are they? [They are] the *prastotṛ*, the *udgātṛ*, and the *pratihartr̥*. From this indication in the plural number, we shall understand that the word *udgātṛ* is derived based on its connection with the inferred action. For in this way, both the plural number and the word *udgātṛ* will be appropriately applied. Therefore, the cup belongs to those who perform the *stotra*.

[The opponent argues that] all the Chāndogas should consume [the Soma] after performing a thousand Brahma-rites. Why? Because of the connection with singing (*gāna*). This position is not tenable. How so? Because there is only one [singer] in that case.

The connection is with *udgāna* (chanting), while the other [term] is connected with *gāna* (singing). For singing is one thing and chanting is another; *gāna* consists merely of the act of singing and is both worldly and Vedic. The second [term] is the well-known designation for the second section (*parvan*) of the Sāman, derived from the root *gai* preceded by the prefix *ut*. In that context, it is said "one alone performs the *udgītha*," meaning there is only one *udgātṛ*, not many. Therefore, because of the connection with *udgāna*, [the term refers to the office].
That "there will be many" is also untenable. Why?

Because of the connection with the Veda: there is a specific recensional tradition called *Audgātra*, as well as the ritual acts of the *Udgātṛ*; one who performs or studies the *Audgātra* is called an *Udgātṛ*.

How so? It is well known that "the work of the Udgātṛ" is *audgātra*; thus, if it is clear that the agent of *audgātra* is the Udgātṛ, it is understood that the term refers to the Udgātṛ. Even when the specific action is not explicitly named, one says "*audgātra*" to refer to the action characterized by that person for whom the Udgātṛ is well known. This is because of the word itself.
He for whom the *audgātra* is well-known says, "He is the performer of that," even though it is not explicitly stated;

just as he for whom *Audamegha* is well-known says, "His offspring, even though not explicitly stated, is *Audameghi*"; and he for whom *Audameghi* [is well-known, he likewise speaks of his progenitor].

In this way, both the plural number and the word *udgātṛ* will be appropriate, and there will be no other defect whatsoever.

Having restated, "They consume the cup," the text speaks specifically of the *camasins* (the cup-bearers), and then says, "Now, all indeed desire a share of this *hāriyojana* [cup]. For this is a single sentence, as indicated by the use of the word "now" (*atha*) in the phrase "now, of this"; that word requires something immediately preceding it.

The word "all" (*sarva*)—that is, the particle *eva*—by its inherent force, refers back to all those previously mentioned; therefore, we consider that this [sentence], "Now, of this *hāriyojana* cup," forms a single syntactical unit with the preceding [sentence], "Just as the *camasins* consume the other cups according to their respective cups. Consequently, for the *camasins* who are present...
This is the distinction: as in the case of the other cups, [the offering] is divided; but in the case of the Hāriyojana cup, everyone partakes of it entirely.
But [the opponent argues]: "Since it is a rule for all, the scriptural injunction regarding the *camasa* cups refers only to half of that. (30)
Bhāṣya (Āhnika 3).

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position. It is not the case that "only the cup-bearers (camasins) desire [the soma] at the Hāriyojana [offering]. Rather, all are enjoined in relation to the Hāriyojana; the connection to be enjoined is "all drink," and it is not possible to enjoin the connection "only the cup-bearers.
For two distinct connections cannot be enjoined as something unprecedented (*apūrva*) within this single sentence.
To establish this, there is therefore a different mode of expression:
according to Mādhava, by the words "Thou art the steed for the yoking of Hari," the horse being seized at the *mava* [libation] is designated as "the steed for the yoking of Hari" (*hāriyojana*).
[Bhāṣya] Chapter 3, Pāda 5. [Page 419]

What, then, is this? It is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*): "Just as the *camasins* consume the other cups (*camasa*s)," meaning that the *camasins* consume the cups, and while they are consuming them, each consumes according to his own cup; however, in the case of this *hāriyojana* [cup], it is not only the *camasins* who consume it.

"All indeed"—thus [it is said]. What will happen in this way? The word "all," denoting all things, will not be restricted to a single part. Furthermore, two related entities will not exist within a single unprecedented sentence. Therefore, this position is superior.

For this scriptural mention of the *camasa* (cup) is for that purpose; it is the *camasin*s (those who drink from the cups) who are mentioned for the sake of praising the *hāriyojana* cup. How so? Because the *hāriyojana* is of great value, since everyone desires to partake of it, whereas each individual [desires] the other cups; those [other cups] are not of great value, as they are inferior to the *hāriyojana*. (3.5.9)
The section concerning the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance as the cause for consuming [the sacrificial portion].
And one should consume [the portion] after the utterance of "vaṣaṭ. || 31 ||
[Question:

Is the name (*samākhyā*) alone the sole cause for consuming [the sacrificial portion]? [Answer: We say: no. For the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance (*vaṣaṭkāra*) is also a cause for consumption; the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is a ground for consuming. How so? Because of a scriptural statement (*vacana*). For it is heard in scripture thus: "The first consumption belongs to the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ*."

Since eating is not already established [as a duty], this word is not for the purpose of enjoining primacy; rather, it enjoins the very act of eating as qualified by primacy—thus [it is concluded]. (3.5.10)
Mu.
Bhā.
Section on the fact that both the *homa* (oblation) and the *abhivayana* (pouring over) are also causes for the consumption [of the remnant].
And because of the oblation and the extraction [of the Soma]. || 32 ||
There is another reason for the *homābhiṣava* (the offering and the pressing). How so? Mādhava says that in the injunction regarding the *havir-dhāna*, the *hotṛ* is the performer (*vighaṭaka*).
[Page 420] Bhāṣya:
"Having pressed with the stones, having offered in the *āhavanīya*, and having gone back to the *sadas*, one eats the portions."

"—they eat"—this sequence is not prescribed [by that statement] at this point, because the eating has not yet been established once the oblation (*homa*) has been performed. Since both the action and the sequence would have to be prescribed, the sentence "having offered" (*abhihutya*) would suffer from syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Furthermore, this sequence is already established by the purpose (*artha*). Therefore, [the eating occurs] immediately after the offering.

No one moves from their purpose; rather, someone is entitled to the performance [of the act]. Furthermore, the acts of offering (homa) and pressing (abhiṣava) are not enjoined as being subordinate parts of the eating (bhakṣaṇa), because the pressing is for the sake of the offering, and the offering is for the sake of the fruit [of the sacrifice]. Therefore, the eating is prescribed for those who perform the offering and the pressing; that is, "those who press and those who offer, they eat. (3.5.11)
The section concerning the drinking of Soma by the *baghaṭkāra* and others from the *camasa*.
Sūtra 33:
Because of the direct instruction regarding the cups for oneself, the procedure for the remaining [cups] is unmanifest. (Pūrvapakṣa)

Bhāṣya: This is heard [in the scripture]: "Let the Hotṛ’s cup go forward; let that of the Brahman go forward; let that of the Udgātṛs go forward. In this regard, there is a doubt: should those who perform the offerings and the pressings in the cups, as well as those who utter the *vaṣaṭ* call, consume [the soma], or not? What is the prima facie view?
They should not consume it, because the cups have been specifically assigned to the respective cup-holders (*camasin*) by direct instruction: "Let the Hotṛ’s... and so forth.

By specific statements such as "the cup of the Hotṛ," and by the general statement regarding those who perform the oblation and the pressing— that the Soma which is to be consecrated by consumption should be [consumed] from the cups by the priests— what other occasion for action could there possibly be now?
"What is that which is unmanifest and has a general cause? It will apply to the remainder—that which does not belong to the cup-bearers."

Or rather, [the word "svaḥ"] would refer to the sacrificer himself because of his being the cause; and there is no designation of the cups [as belonging to others], because that word refers to the maker. (Siddhānta 34)

[The Bhāṣya says: Or rather, there may be a consumption of the *vaṣaṭ*-offerings and so forth in the cups (*camasa*s), for the reason for them is obtained there, and it is not prohibited. [Objection: But is it not directly perceived [that the cups belong] to the cup-holders (*camasin*s)?
[Page 421]

[Objection: They should be excluded because of the specific instruction. [Reply: It is said: "The cups are not designated for others, because the agent is the one who consumes them. Expressions such as "Let the Hotṛ’s cup go forth" and so on are unable to exclude the Vaṣaṭ-maker and the others; for these are prescriptive instructions, not prohibitions.
Therefore, the Vaṣaṭ-makers and the rest should also partake in the cups.
Sūtra:
And because another [substance] is seen in the cup. (Yuktidhikaraṇa) 35.
Furthermore, in the *camasa* cup, [the text] indicates other *camasin* priests: "He hands over the cups to the *camasādhvaryu*s;
he carries them away at the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ*. There is only one...

The cup belonging to the Khaś is kept for the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* call; therefore, the observation of the distribution of many portions would not be consistent if those who utter the *vaṣaṭ* call and others did not consume [the Soma] from the cups. Therefore, they do consume it.
"Now, where many persons consume [the offering] from a single vessel, what is the order there? It is replied:
"The section concerning the Hotṛ’s priority in consumption."
In a single vessel, the Adhvaryu should consume first, one after the other. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 36 ||
For the sequence belongs to him in whose hand the Soma is.
Bhāṣya-sūtra:
Or rather, the Hotṛ [should perform it], because of the wording of the mantra. (Siddhānta) || 37 ||
The Bhāṣya states: "Or rather, the Hotṛ should eat first; for it is said, 'O you of beautiful color, O you of beautiful color, for thus [it is]';
and likewise, 'Even before the Hotṛ, they have eaten the sacrificial food,' and similarly, 'Like a Hotṛ, drink first for us.'"
And because of the scriptural statement. (Sūtra 38; Hetu 1)
This statement occurs: "The first portion belongs to the *baṣaṭ*-utterer.
This statement is this very sūtra, which was recorded in the *Sūtrasaṃgraha*.
[Page 422]

In the Mīmāṃsā system, one should not think: "Because multiple qualities are being enjoined, the priority [of the first] is not intended to be significant"—for since the priority is not otherwise established, this is not a restatement (anuvāda) but rather an injunction (vidhi); and for one who enjoins by means of a compound, it is not difficult to enjoin multiple qualities.
Sūtra:
And because of the sequence of the causes. (He0 2)

Commentary: For the utterance of "vaṣaṭ" is first the occasion for the Hotṛ priest, and thereafter the oblation is the occasion for the Adhvaryu; and according to the sequence of the occasions, there is a conformity to the order in the sequence of the things occasioned. (3.5.13)
Sūtra Bhāṣya: The Section Concerning the Requirement of Prior Permission for Consuming [the Remnants].
The consumption [of food] is permitted by verbal authorization. || 40 ||

Now, regarding the case where the Soma in a single vessel is not consumed by many: should it be consumed there after having asked for permission, or even without asking for permission, or only after having asked for permission?

When the conclusion that there is no fixed rule follows from the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is stated: "It must be consumed after having asked for permission. Why? Because of a scriptural statement (*vacana*); this scriptural statement occurs: "Therefore..."
"Soma is not to be drunk by one who has not performed the preparatory rites"—this is the statement regarding the permission for the preparatory rites.
(This is a *prāptisūtra*. [3.5.14])
The section concerning the request for permission by means of Vedic speech.

Now, since it is established that one must eat only after being permitted, the question arises: should permission be sought by means of common (laukika) speech, or by means of Vedic (vaidika) speech? Since there is no restrictive rule, the prima facie view is that it may be done with common speech; to this, we reply:
Sva. One should request permission with the words "Having taken it up, invite [the gods]," because of the indicative mark [of the mantra]. || 41 ||
Bhāṣya:
It is weak because of the two indicative marks of requesting permission; it is handed down in the tradition as being for the purpose of requesting permission on account of those indicative marks.
[Page 423]
By virtue of its capacity, it is applied; therein, regarding the purpose already accomplished, the worldly [means] is set aside. (3.5.15, Section 15)
Bhāṣya: The section concerning the response in Vedic discourse.
And that [objection] is, in fact, a rejoinder. || 42 ||

This has been understood: by the statement "one should not cause it to be uttered with means impaired by that," [it is meant that] one should not utter it. Now, there is a doubt regarding the response: is the response worldly, or is it this very [Vedic] one? What is the prima facie view? This [Vedic response] is employed in the context of the *praśna* (question); therefore, another, worldly response ought to be used. To this we reply: "And that" response is this very same one.
"But surely this is a powerful indicative mark (*liṅga*): 'Upayasva' (Come hither). It is said in reply:

"That which precedes it—the word 'Upayasva'—will serve as the response, since it is capable of being a response. [Objection: "This traditional recitation (*samāmnāya*) is reversed; for first there ought to be the question, and after that the response. [Reply: "By implication (*arthāt*), it is first..."
It will serve as a response; for the seeker is indeed weaker by virtue of the sequence.
The section concerning the request for permission regarding a single vessel from the *Śrīmad-Bhāṣya*.
Because there is a commonality of the single vessel for those [who drink together]. || 43 ||

This is what is being deliberated: should anyone at all be asked for permission, or only one who shares the same vessel? Since the statement is made without qualification, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that "anyone at all. To this, it is replied: that request for permission should be made by those who share the same vessel. Why? Because...

Soliciting permission (*anujñāpana*) is a subsidiary factor (*aṅga*), and its form is as follows: when one intends to do something that ought to be done by another, one says, "Please permit me," as in the case of eating together.
[Page 424]

Or, one whose mind desires to practice [virtuous conduct] makes the mind of another conformable to it. This is not possible at all in the case of various vessels, for there it is not the case that one person must act while another desires to do so; nor does one show honor in such matters as eating together and the like.
But when the Soma is in a single vessel and is to be consecrated, a division into equal portions follows by rule;

in that case, if it were drunk without being divided, it might happen that one person would drink what was intended for another to drink, and in such a situation, a formal request for permission is possible— [namely,] "You should drink with faith."

"May I drink; perhaps I might drink more or less than you, so please permit me"—thus there is a possibility of requesting permission. Or, "If I were to drink from the same vessel as you, I might disturb the serenity of your mind"—thus there is a possibility of requesting permission. Therefore, this [practice] should apply only to those who drink from the same vessel. (3.5.17)
The section concerning the existence of the eating of the *yaṣṭu* by oneself.
The consumption [of the offering] is removed by the removal of the *yājyā*, just like the *pravara*. 44. (0)

Bhāṣya: There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; therein, regarding the seasonal offerings (ṛtuyāga), it is heard: "He gives the direction to the Hotṛ, 'O Hotṛ, sacrifice this,' or he himself, having sat down, sacrifices. When he sacrifices himself, then there arises a doubt: does he have a share [in the fruit] or not?
Is it not so?—to this it is replied: if the *yājyā* were removed, the eating would not be removed; rather, the eating would belong to the *hotṛ* alone, and not to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
Why? Because the *yājyā* is one thing and the eating is another, and furthermore...
When one thing is being removed, another is also removed; just as when that very *yājyā* verse is being removed,
the *pravara* is not removed, so it is with this case as well.
"Now, [it is argued]: 'He utters the *vaṣaṭ* over the *ājya*';
wherever there is the *yājyā*, there is the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, and wherever there is the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, there is also the consumption [of the offering].
[This is not so,] because [the rule does not apply] to the *sambhojana* and so forth—so reads the Kāṇva-saṃhitā manuscript. The same applies elsewhere.
[Page 425] Chapter 3, Section 5. ||
It is said: first of all, the *vaṣaṭ*-call is not a constituent part of the *yājyā*, by which [it would be so].

This [offering] is not included by the mention of the *yājyā*. As for the statement, "He utters the *vaṣaṭ* over it," the Hotṛ will utter the *vaṣaṭ* even over that which is being employed by another; for, by virtue of the scriptural injunction, there is the removal of the *yājyā*, but not the removal of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance. For as far as the scriptural word extends, that which is based on the word must indeed occur, since the scriptural statement refers specifically to that.
Or rather, it belongs to the sacrificer, because of the arrival of the cause; [sūtra 45] (the established view).
The one who has sacrificed should be the one to consume [the portion]. Why? Because of the arrival of the cause;
the cause of the consumption is the *vaṣaṭ*-call, and that arrives along with the *yājyā* verse.
For it is heard in scripture: "He utters the *vaṣaṭ*-call over the *yājyā*."
It has not been stated that "the Hotṛ utters the *vaṣaṭ* while the sacrifice is being performed by the sacrificer. This is not a valid solution: one must sacrifice without pausing;

the sacrifice is accomplished by the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, not by the *yājyā* alone. Therefore, the sacrificer must not pause until the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, even if another person were to utter the *vaṣaṭ*.

The sacrificer [is distinct] from the officiating priests; moreover, he should not act as a priest for another. For he is enjoined as one who is to sacrifice (*yaṣṭavya*), not merely as one who recites the *yājyā* verses. This is because of the injunction that "having sat down himself, he sacrifices," which prescribes sitting down for the sacrifice along with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*).
Because it has already commenced, there is no loss of its status as the *pravara*. 46. (0 Ni.)
Now, as for what was said: "Just as the *pravara* is not removed, so too is the *bhakṣa*."

It is said: because it is impossible, the *pravara* (the ancestral invocation) is not removed; for how could that which has already passed be removed by the *hotṛ*? Moreover, if performed at a lost opportunity, it would be defective for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). And a defective rite cannot accomplish its purpose in any way. Nor is this [removal] obtained here through the *codaka* (the general rule of transfer). If it were argued that whatever is possible is what is obtained through the *codaka*—
"That which has been brought about but cannot be maintained is not truly brought about"— this is the nature of things.
The reading in the Kāśīmudrita-puṣpaka manuscript is: "sāne yāge vidhānāt."
[Please provide the text to be translated.]
In the *Mīmāṃsā-darśana-bhāṣya*,
it is stated that there is here an injunction regarding the *apūrva*; if it is possible [to establish] it in the manner described, then so be it.
It must be performed; if it cannot be done [in its entirety], then it should be performed wherever it is possible.
Therefore, it is logical that there should be no removal of the *pravara* (ancestral lineage), rather than performing it where it would be defective.
"Of the food"—thus [it is stated]. (3.5.18)
The section concerning the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) not being a modification of the sacrificial oblation (*haviṣ*).
The fruit-cup (phalacamasa) is a modification of the consumption [of Soma] occasioned by a specific cause, because of its connection with the Vedic text.
47 || (Pūrvapakṣa) ||
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard [in scripture]: "If he should officiate for a Rājanya or a Vaiśya,
and if he should desire to distribute the Soma, having fetched branches of the Nyagrodha tree..."
"Having ground [the fruit] and rubbed it in curds, one should offer that as the portion for him to consume, not Soma"—thus it is stated.

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the *phalacamas* a modification of the act of consuming (*bhakṣa*), or is it a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyā*)? (Does it mean "one should consume the *phalacamas*," or rather, "with the *phalacamas*...")

[Should one] sacrifice?—What is the prima facie view?—"The fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) is a contingent modification of the act of eating (*bhakṣa*). For it forms a single syntactical unit with the explicitly stated act of eating—as in "He should give that to him as food"—but there is no word "he should sacrifice with it" (*tena yajeta*). Therefore, it is a modification of eating.
Or rather, it is a modification of the sacrifice, because the consecration is for the sake of that [sacrifice]. 48.
The modification of the soma-drink is the fruit-cup (the meaning being that one should sacrifice with the fruit-cup).
How so? Because this act of consuming is for the purpose of consecrating the soma, and it applies to the fruit-cup as well.

If the eating is for the purpose of consecrating the *phalacamas* (fruit-cup), it would be purposeless because the *phalacamas* has no other use. "Now, if the eating is the primary act," then [the prohibition] "not Soma"—[in the Mādhavīya, the reading is *stibhinī*; there, the meaning is that *stibhinī* refers to a bud].
Fifth Chapter, Fifth Section.

The restatement "262 bhā. is not tenable. However, if it were a modification of the sacrifice (ijyāvikāra), then the preparation of the fruit-cup (phalacamasa) would be appropriate. Therefore, it is a modification of the sacrifice.
The Commentary on the Sūtra says:
"He asks: How can there be a modification of the sacrifice when there is a connection with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice)?"
—Thus it is said. It is replied: there is a connection with the sacrifice (*yajati*). How so?

It is understood that "if one should cause a *rājanya* or a *vaiśya* to sacrifice, having ground shoots of the *nyagrodha* tree... he should offer that to them as food," for the purpose of causing the sacrifice. For if there were a connection with eating (*bhakṣa*), the preceding [clause] would not be connected with the subsequent one, [as in] "if [one should eat] the *soma* by means of eating..."

"One should desire to consecrate it; one should consecrate it with Nyagrodha-sticks"—thus [it is said]. Therefore, there is no connection with eating; for the sacrifice is the subject under discussion, and it will be connected with that, so there will be no fault.

[Objection: "But surely, from the statement 'one should give that portion to him,' it is understood that [the substance] is a means for consumption (*bhakṣa*), not a means for sacrifice (*yāga*), because of its immediate proximity to the word *bhakṣa*. [Reply: It is said in response:
Since the connection [of the substance] with what is being heard would otherwise be purposeless, it is connected to the subject under discussion [sacrifice].

—so it is said; but how is there a connection with eating? It is because that substance of the sacrifice which is to be eaten becomes [available] through the *codaka* (extended injunction); therefore, it acquires a connection with eating, and by means of this connection with eating, the very connection with the sacrifice is indicated (*lakṣyate*), provided that it is intended by that. Thus...

He becomes that which is to be consumed; therefore, from this statement regarding consumption, it is understood that he is worshipped by means of it all the more. This is the construction involving a restrictive interpretation: "One should offer that as a portion to him," meaning "one should make that his portion"—that is, one should act in such a way that he becomes that portion.
And if he is worshipped by means of it, then he indeed becomes that portion.
Therefore, he must perform the sacrifice—thus [it is said].
From the oblation. (He0 1)
There is a statement regarding a specific modification of the sacrificial substance: "When they offer other cups, he approaches that [particular cup] with a young blade of Darbha grass and offers it.

Since there is a modification of the substance, the mention of the "young blade of Darbha grass" as a quality in relation to the act of offering becomes appropriate. Therefore, for this reason as well, there is a modification of the substance.
[Page 428] Ratnabhāṣya Sūtra.
Bhāṣya-sūtra:
And because of the simultaneity with the cups. (Sūtra 50; Second Hetu)

"When they draw out the other cups, then they draw out this cup"—this observation of the drawing out (*unnayana*) is appropriate when there is a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyā*), not when there is a modification of the consumption (*bhakṣa*). Therefore, it is indeed a modification of the sacrifice.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (51) (0 3)

From this as well we see that it is a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyāvikāra*). Why? Because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). What is the indicative mark? It is the restatement of the prohibition of Soma:

"One should give him that portion to consume, but not the Soma. When there is a modification of the sacrifice, the Soma is not consumed. Therefore we see that it is a modification of the sacrifice. (3.5.1)
The section concerning the fact that only those who are Brāhmaṇas are to be made to approach the cups belonging to the Rājanya.
[The rule applies] because of the commonality among those who have entered [the sacrifice] subsequently. (Pūrvapakṣa 52)

In the Rājasūya sacrifice there is the Daśapeya; regarding it, it is heard in the scripture: "A hundred Brāhmaṇas consume the Soma; ten by ten they approach each individual cup. Here, a doubt arises concerning the cup of the Kṣatriya: should the Kṣatriyas approach that cup, or [should others do so]?
"Are they Brāhmaṇas?"—this is the question. What is the prima facie view? They are Kṣatriyas (Rājanyas). Why?

Because it is prescribed that "ten by ten should follow each cup"; thus, for those following, a number is enjoined. In the case of the single class of Kṣatriyas, the number ten is enjoined; that very class of Kṣatriyas is meant, and therefore ten Kṣatriyas should follow. In this way, there would be one hundred Brāhmaṇas.

And among those [participants], the word "hundred" is a restatement (anuvāda). And that which has the form of a restatement indicates what is already established—as in the expression, "He eats the portion. Therefore, the Rājanyas should follow along with the Rājanya's cup.
Some say: "The Brahmins and Rājanyas [should eat] from a single cup."
Chapter 3, Section 5. [Page 429]
"It contradicts [the rule]"— this is not a fault, for one does not become impure by means of Soma (sū.).
Thus it is heard in the Bhāṣya.
Or rather, it refers to Brāhmaṇas, because the word is used in the same sense. (Siddhānta) || 53 ||

Or, Brāhmaṇas should approach the Rājanya-cup. How so? Because of the scriptural injunction, "A hundred Brāhmaṇas consume the Soma"—this rule regarding the number applies specifically to the Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, there are a hundred Brāhmaṇas; for the purpose of their consumption, ten each are prescribed for every single cup as they approach. Consequently, ten Brāhmaṇas from among the hundred Brāhmaṇas should approach the Rājanya-cup. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the fifth quarter of the third chapter in the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya composed by Śabarasvāmin.
In the Mīmāṃsā system, the sixth quarter of the third chapter.
Śrī Bhāṣya Śrī.
Bhāṣya-sūtra:
The section concerning how the injunction regarding *khadira* wood and so forth applies to the archetype (*prakṛti*) in cases such as the *svāhākāra*.
The entire purpose [is established] because it is not a separate topic. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 1 ||

Something is stated without reference to a specific context: "He whose *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira* wood cuts [the portion] with the very essence of the meters; his oblations become full of essence. And:

"He whose *darvī* spoon is made of *parṇa* wood does not go to a miserable world," and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the quality of being made of *khadira* [an injunction] regarding the *sruva*, and the quality of being made of *parṇa* regarding the *darvī*?
Does [the rule] apply only to the primary sacrifice (*prakṛti*), or does it apply to both the primary and the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)? What is the prima facie view?

"It applies to all purposes because there is no specific context; such a rule pertains to both the primary and the modified sacrifices. Why? Because of the absence of a specific context; they are not heard within the context of any particular rite, and therefore, by virtue of the direct statement (*vākya*), they should apply everywhere."
Or rather, it belongs to the archetype, because of the principle of non-repetition. (Siddhānta) || 2 ||

Or rather, the vessels mentioned as not being taught in connection with any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*) should find their place in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*). Why? Because of the avoidance of redundancy; thus, there will be no redundancy. What is the fault in redundancy? We say it is impossibility—if they were present both in the archetype and in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).

It exists; if it exists in the archetype (prakṛti), then by the force of the extended application (codaka) alone, it is obtained as a modification (vikṛti). Therefore, it does not require the non-contextual injunction (anārabhyavidhi). Consequently, because there is no need for it, the non-contextual injunction does not enjoin it therein. For this reason we say:
it is for the sake of the archetype alone.

The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the previous position. We say that this is not an *anārabhyavidhi* (unattached injunction) for all purposes; rather, its purpose is for the *maṇḍapa* (the sacrificial shed). Why? Because of the completeness of the injunctive meaning: the general rule (*codaka*) brings forward the entire [archetypal] procedure. The *anārabhyavidhi* does not establish a new, independent *apūrva* (transcendental result) that is devoid of expectancy. For that [result] belongs to the vessels by virtue of the sentence, not to the sacrifices; the sacrifices, due to their connection with the indicative marks of the injunctions, require the archetype, and thus they attain syntactic unity with it. And the archetypal elements are capable of satisfying their expectancy, whereas the *anārabhyavidhi* is not.

[Page 433] These are injunctions (*vidhi*). Therefore, the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) must necessarily be produced; and if it is produced, there is no need for the *anārabhya-vidhi* (injunction not dependent on a specific context). Furthermore, even if that [injunction] were to operate because of the absence of [other] purposes such as the *prakaraṇa* (context), it would not be connected with the modified sacrifice (*vaikṛta-yāga*). Therefore, [it does not apply] to the modified sacrifice.

The general rule (*anārabhyavidhi*) is not connected with the modified (*vaikṛta*) primary rite; rather, the general rule is a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) either for that modified primary or for the archetypal (*prakṛti*) rite—such being the case when there is a prohibition due to the force of the extended application (*codaka*). Since the archetypal supplementary statement is already established, the general rule will not apply. Therefore, the general rule serves a significant purpose.

But the occasional (*naimittika*) [element] belongs to the archetype, because it is a modification of that, due to a specific connection. (10)

"It should be performed by one desiring the word of Brahman"—in such cases as these, there arises a doubt: does it find its place in the archetype (*prakṛti*) or in the ectype (*vikṛti*)? Because of the specific injunction: although the *khadira*, *pālāśa*, and *rauhitaka* woods are mentioned without distinction, as is the *camasa* cup, the *godohana* vessel and the *bilva* wood are specifically enjoined; and by a specific injunction, a general injunction is sublated. that which is obtained through the general rule is indirect and based on indication (*lakṣaṇā*), whereas that which is [obtained] through the particular rule is direct.

That [word] is directly perceived by the Vedic text (*śruti*), and direct textual statement (*śruti*) is stronger than indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*); moreover, what is directly perceived is stronger than what is remote. Therefore, it must apply only to the archetype (*prakṛti*). (3.6.3)

Even though they are to be brought into being, the visible rites would be performed for the sake of the fires that already exist. It is not heard as being dependent upon the archetypes; it is not [dependent on them].

Furthermore, there exist in this case direct scriptural statements (*śruti*) and other means of proof which establish its status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*). Therefore, such an inquiry is appropriate in those instances;
however, in the present case, there is no basis for establishing its status as a subsidiary. Consequently, the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is not connected with Agni.
It is employed for ritual action; since the fires are for the purpose of all rituals, they are said to be "for all purposes.

There are the Pavamāna sacrifices, beginning with "To Agni Pavamāna" and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the Pavamāna sacrifices be performed using a fire consecrated by the Pavamāna sacrifices, or not? What is the prima facie view? Regarding those very Pavamāna sacrifices...

The fire consecrated by the Pavamāneṣṭi should be the archetype (prakṛti). Why? Because of the principle of the extended application (codaka), just like the Prayājas; for just as the Prayājas occur in these [sacrifices] by virtue of the codaka, so too should the fires consecrated by the Pavamāneṣṭi be present.
Or rather, not so; because they have that as their purpose. (Siddhānta) || 17 ||

Or rather, there should be no consecration by means of the *iṣṭi* sacrifices for the fires during the *pavamāna-iṣṭis*. Why? Because there is no basis for the claim that it "might occur in some cases."
[Page 437] Bhāṣya: Because they are for that purpose; it has been stated that those Pavamāna-iṣṭis are for the purpose of consecration (saṃskāra).

And whatever is indeed a subsidiary (aṅga) is grasped by the extended application (codaka); however, the consecration of the Pavamāna-iṣṭis is prompted by the fire-altar (agni), not prompted by the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa); therefore, it is not drawn forth by the codaka.

Moreover, the Pavamāna-iṣṭis depend upon a primary archetype (prakṛti) that is devoid of the preparatory rites of an iṣṭi, because at that stage the Pavamāna-iṣṭis themselves have not yet been prescribed. (Sūtra Bhāṣya 3.6.6).
The section concerning the fact that the *upākaraṇa* and other rites belong to the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice.
The ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice is common to all, because there is no distinction in the context.
18 || (First Pūrvapakṣa) ||

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, as stated: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma"; likewise, there are the Savanīya and Anubandhya animals.

Furthermore, there are the duties pertaining to the animal—such as the bringing near (*upākaraṇa*), leading forward (*upānayana*), tying with a cord (*akṣayā-bandha*), binding to the sacrificial post (*yūpa-niyojana*), immolation (*saṃjñapana*), and dismemberment (*viśasana*)—do these apply to all [the animals]?

[The question is: Do these [ritual] properties belong to the Agniṣomīya, the Savanīya, and the Anubandhya animals; or to the Agniṣomīya and the Savanīya; or to the Agniṣomīya alone? What is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)? Because there is no distinction, they belong to all the animals. How is there no distinction? All the animals are mentioned in the context (prakaraṇa) of the Jyotiṣṭoma; since they have entered that context, the properties of the animal sacrifice (paśudharma) are connected to all of them, and there is no specific distinction made among them therein. This being the prima facie view, we reply: these properties should belong to the Savanīya, as they are common to all.

The ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice would apply [to all] if there were no distinction within the context; however, there is indeed a distinction within the context, as the properties of the animal sacrifice are recited specifically within the context of the Savanīya offerings.
"In the Agniṣṭoma, an animal dedicated to Agni (āgneya) is to be sacrificed, for the Agniṣṭoma belongs to Agni.
In the Ukthya, an animal dedicated to Indra and Agni (aindrāgna) is to be sacrificed, for the Ukthya-stotras belong to Indra and Agni.
In the Ṣoḍaśin, a he-goat (dṛṣṇi) dedicated to Indra is to be sacrificed, for the he-goat belongs to Indra."

The Ṣoḍaśī sacrifice: A ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī is to be offered at the Atirātra; for it is stated in the Bhāṣya, "Sarasvatī is indeed speech" (page 438). Having introduced this subject, the ritual details of the animal sacrifice are prescribed. Therefore, these should belong to the Ṣoḍaśī itself, because of the context.
Sūtra: And because of the position, [the rule] applies to the preceding one. (Second Pūrvapakṣa)

As for what was stated— that by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), these [rites] are for the sake of the *savanīya*— we accept this; and by virtue of the sequence (*krama*), they belong to the *agnīṣomīya*, for it is in the sequence of that [latter] on the day of the *apavarga*.
It has been traditionally handed down; therefore, it applies to both as well.
According to some, [the rite] is to be performed on the next day; in that case, the prior mention of the [first] day is for the purpose of indicating a subordinate quality. (Siddhānta 20)

According to some reciters of the Vedic branches (*śākhins*), there is a scriptural injunction for the *savanīya* animals to be performed on the following day; with reference to that, this repeated mention of them is for the purpose of a specific quality (*guṇa*). "But what is the quality for the sake of which this scriptural statement exists? It is said: the grouping of the animals, [as expressed by] "Just as a fish, once caught, shakes off the person..."

"Thus, these [details], being unknown, cause people to stumble"—having thus stated the fault in not knowing them, the text prescribes the quality of the *vapā* (omentum) offering by means of a *pravara* (introductory formula), asking: "How, by means of these, are the *savana*s provided with animals? This scriptural statement (*śruti*) is for that purpose, because it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the *vapā*-offering. What follows from this? If this is so, then the animal-ritual details (*paśudharma*) do not belong to the *savanīya* offerings by virtue of context (*prakaraṇa*), but rather belong specifically to the *āgnīṣomīya* sacrifice by virtue of position (*krama*). Why?

Furthermore, what is that scriptural injunction? "Having drawn the Āśvina cup and having encircled the sacrificial post with the Trivṛt [cord], he dedicates the Savanīya animal to Agni. Thus it is said.
[Objection: "If it is argued that by means of that [substitution], there is a prescription of time for the superior [rite]. (21) (Ābhāsya)

Bhāṣya: This is not so—that [the offering] is for the sake of the Agniṣomīya alone by virtue of sequence; rather, it is for the sake of the Savanīya due to the context (*prakaraṇa*). The recitation on the previous day is for the purpose of injunction, while the statement regarding the Aśvin cup is for the purpose of enjoining a temporal qualification. How so? By means of that performance of the omentum-offering (*vapāpracāra*), this time is enjoined for what has been postponed. When the performance of the omentum-offering at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) has been prescribed, the immolation of the animal (*paśvālambha*) also follows there. Since there would otherwise be no fixed time for it, the Aśvin cup [is prescribed].

"Having taken hold of the vessel"—this merely prescribes the time. "Having encircled the sacrificial post with the rope, he performs the dedication"—this is a restatement (anuvāda). For otherwise, there would be [the fault of] the encircling... [Page 439] Bhāṣya.

The time would have to be prescribed, as well as the *upākaraṇa* (the ritual dedication); in that case, because multiple qualities would be enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, the characteristics of the animal sacrifice pertain to the *savanīya*.

Not so, because it is only a part. (22) (Ābhāsasiddhānta)

For the omentum is but one part of the substance; therefore, because the preparatory rites (*upākaraṇa*) are subsidiary acts (*sannipātī*) intended for the consecration of the omentum, they do not undergo displacement.

From this also we see that the rites pertaining to the animal sacrifice belong to the Agniṣomīya [animal]. Why? Because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
