They would belong to the Agniṣomīya and not to the Savanīya, because of the absence of those two deities in the latter; and the scripture also indicates this. Therefore, they are for the sake of the Agniṣomīya.
There is no injunction for the sake of a subordinate quality. 27.

(This is the sūtra following the preceding word: "But surely, the animal cake-offering (paśupuroḍāśa) is for the purpose of covering the gaps. We say: no; "there is no injunction for the sake of a subordinate element," meaning there is no injunction for the purpose of covering the gaps; that is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda), as has been stated. Therefore—

The purpose is for the consecration of the deity; therefore, if they are for the sake of the Agniṣomīya, the observation of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) at the *savanīya* stage is logically consistent, but not if they were common to all. Therefore, the animal-ritual characteristics (*paśudharma*) are for the sake of the Agniṣomīya—thus [the conclusion]. (3.6.7) [Page 441] 3.
As in the case of the *yathāyatha*.
The section concerning the fact that the bringing of branches and other such acts possess the character of being *dohada* (ritual inducements) for both [the sacrificer and the deity].
3.77 Sūtra: Because of the difference in time between the two milkings, the boiled [mixture] would be unconnected [to the rite]. (Pūrvapakṣa)

There is the evening milking, and likewise there is the morning milking. There are certain duties pertaining to the milking, such as the fetching of branches, driving out the cows, the recitation of the *prastāva*, the milking of the cows, and so forth. Do these pertain only to the evening milking, or to both?

Thus it is said. What, then, is the prima facie position?—The two milkings are not connected with the ritual duties; they are cooked [prepared]. Why? Because in the sequence of the evening milking, they prescribe the fetching of the branches and so forth on the day of the Upavasatha, and the evening milking takes place on that very same day.
Therefore, in due order, those [acts] intended for the evening milking possess the characteristics of the milking.
Sūtra Bhāṣya:
Because there is no distinction of context, the scriptural injunction regarding time applies to that which is connected with it.
28 || (Siddhānta) ||

For the context (*prakaraṇa*) is common to both; just as it applies to the curds, so too does it apply to the milk. And since order (*krama*) is stronger than context, therefore the properties of the *doha* (milking) pertain to the purpose of both. Furthermore, the preparation of the evening milking does not take place on the previous day; when then? On the following day. How so?

Thus they prescribe: "The curds for Indra on the new moon day; the milk for Indra on the new moon day. For on the new moon day, both [substances] along with their auxiliary parts are enjoined. This evening milking is performed on the previous day; this is the very nature of curds—that what is commenced on the previous day is completed on the following day. Therefore, [this applies] to the evening milking.
"They are prescribed in the sequential order"—this very point does not even exist. Therefore, the *dohada* rites pertain to both purposes. (3.6.8a)
The section concerning the fact that the *sādana* (seating) and other rites belong to the nature of the three pressings (*savanatraya*).
In the same way, there is the mention of the cups (grahas) within another Soma-pressing.
In the Śabarabhāṣya:
There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, [as stated in the injunction]: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma."
[Page 442] Bhā. Thus: In that context, ten cups (grahas), beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu, are prescribed for the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana);
regarding them, certain ritual duties (dharmas) are heard: "The other cups are set down on a leveled spot; the *dhruva* cup is set down on an unlevelled spot."

"One wipes the cup with the *daśāpavitra*. There are other cups at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) and others at the third pressing (*tṛtīya-savana*). Regarding these cups belonging to the midday and third pressings, there is a doubt: should the rules for the cups be performed for all of them, or only for those cups that belong to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*)? What is the prima facie view? [That they apply] to the cups belonging to the morning pressing.
[If it were argued that] they [the mantras] would [apply], because they are recited in sequence for those [specific rites] and not for others—
this being the position reached, we reply: "In another pressing," that is, from the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) [into] the midday pressing (*mādhyandina*).
And at the third pressing, the drawing of the cups ought to be exactly like that;
for the context is the same for all of them, wherein these ritual details are recited.
By direct statement (*vākya*), they are enjoined for the cups in general, and since both sequence (*krama*) and direct statement are stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*), therefore—
"The properties of the planets"—thus [it is stated] in Śrautasūtra 3.6.8.
Sūtra Bhāṣya:
The section concerning the application of the threefold nature of the girdle and other attributes to all sacrificial animals.
And the girdle [is part of the sacrifice], because of the observation of an indicative mark. || 31 ||

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, as it is stated: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. In that context, a rope is mentioned, along with its specific characteristics: "It is made of three strands, it is made of Darbha grass, and it must be braided from fibers that have been pounded. Regarding this, there arises a doubt: do these characteristics apply to the rope of the Agni-Soma animal?
Are the ropes common to both the *savanīya* animal sacrifice and the *agnīṣomīya*, or are they for the *agnīṣomīya* alone?
What is the prima facie view? That, on account of the context (*prakaraṇa*), they belong to the *agnīṣomīya* rope alone.
This being the position, we reply: they are common to both. Why? 1.

"From the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga)," a mark exists; for it says thus: "Having drawn the Āśvina cup and having encircled the sacrificial post with the triple cord, he dedicates the animal to Agni.
[Page 443]

The *bhāṣya* shows the girdle (*raśanā*) in the context of the Savanīya animal sacrifice. If that [girdle] is common [to both], then this scriptural indication is consistent. If it were for the Agnīṣomīya sacrifice alone, then it would exclude the original girdling of the Savanīya; and in the case of the Savanīya, there is another, non-original girdling where the state of being a *triṣṭubh* is observed. How so? "That indeed [is] the Aśvina..."

"Having taken the house and having gone out, he encircles the sacrificial post with the cord"—thus it is stated. And if that cord were not common [to all], then the encircling would have to be performed with a cloth, yet the text shows the use of a cord.
Therefore, the cord is common; and because of its commonality, that [encircling] is also common.
Are they common? From this indicative mark (*liṅga*), there is the commonality of the rope.

What indeed is the principle here? It is replied: by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it belongs to the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice]; by virtue of the syntactical connection (*vākya*), it belongs to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) in general. (3.6.10)
The section concerning the fact that even for the *śyena* and *dābhya* vessels, the act of placing [them] and so forth is identical: Sūtra 32.
That which is distant and not connected with others [is included] because of proximity.
HTT.
sra.
(pūrvapakṣa) ||

Regarding that which remains distant from the Jyotiṣṭoma, such as the Aśva and the Ādabhya cups mentioned in the section on the *anuvākyās* for the *upasad* rites: there arises a doubt—should the ritual properties (*dharmas*) of the cups prescribed in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma be performed here, or not? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? They should not be performed, because they are not in proximity (*asannidhāna*). Just as, according to the statement "he mixes the cup for Mitra-Varuṇa with milk," the mixing applies only to that specific cup and not to all, so it is here as well.
The category of phenomena belongs only to those [treatises] situated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*, not to all of them.
Or rather, it is connected [to the primary act], because the subsidiary is for its sake and is dependent upon it.
33 || (Siddhānta) ||
[The Bhāṣya says: Or it may be connected with the dharma; such a thing would be so even if it were not situated within the context.
Why? Because the sentence (vākya) is stronger than the context (prakaraṇa). [Objection: But surely [it applies] elsewhere to the action... [Page 444]

In the Mīmāṃsā system, [it is argued that] the *āgrayaṇa* and other vessels would not benefit the Jyotiṣṭoma. It is replied: they will indeed benefit it, because the *aṃśu* and *ādabhya* vessels are for that purpose—that is, for the sake of the Jyotiṣṭoma—as subsidiary elements.
The properties of a *graha* (cup) are auxiliary to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice on account of being a *graha*;

whatever *graha* assists the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it must possess all those properties. Therefore, the properties of a *graha* must also be performed for the *Śukra* and *Ādābhya* cups. Thus [it is concluded].
It should be established according to the instruction and so forth in the Bhāṣya. (Ā0 Ni0) || 34 ||

As for what was said—that "one mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk"—that is appropriate because of the explicit scriptural statement regarding the mixing (*śrayaṇa*), which establishes the rule by overriding the general context (*prakaraṇa*). But here it is the opposite:
in that case, the context applies to all cups, while the sentence applies to specific ones; here, however, [the rule applies] to all these cups.

The sentence [is the authority] for specific cases; the context [is the authority] for those within a specific section. Therefore, the ritual properties (dharmas) apply even to that which is not situated within a specific context. (3.6.11)
Sūtra Bhāṣya:
The section concerning whether the *citriṇī* and other bricks are subordinate parts (*aṅga*) of the fire-altar (*agni*).
In the section concerning the subsidiary parts of the fire-ritual, it is the same as that [case]. 35.

The *citriṇī* bricks are mentioned without reference to a specific fire-altar: "He lays down the *citriṇī* bricks," "He places them," "He lays down the *bhūteṣṭakā* bricks. However, within the context (*prakaraṇa*), there are properties of the bricks: "One should make the brick unbroken and not black."

Likewise, there is the injunction: "One should join the bricks with ashes. In this regard, a doubt arises: should these ritual requirements (dharmas) be performed for those [bricks] mentioned outside of the specific context (aprakaraṇa), or not? What is the prima facie view? They should not be performed. Why? Because they are not in proximity (asannidhāna). This being the position, it is replied: a subsidiary act of this kind should be treated exactly like that [case previously discussed]. Just as...

The *grahas* (libations); in this context, the sentence is more powerful than the subject matter (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, because these bricks have no other purpose. (3.6.12) [Page 445], in the chapter.
Sixth quarter.
The section concerning whether the removal of pride and so forth constitute the specific characteristics of Soma alone.
Sūtra: Because the purpose is different, there should be no common rule of application. || 36 ||
In the *Bhāṣya* on the *Bhāṣya*, it is heard in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice: "If he should officiate for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya..."

"If he should desire to consume the Soma, one should fetch Nyagrodha-sticks, crush them, mix them with curd, strain them, and offer that as his consumption, not the Soma"—thus [it is said]. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there are Soma-rites, such as measuring, bringing down, purchasing, pressing, and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt: are these rites prescribed equally for both the Soma and the fruit-cup (phalacamasa), or are they Soma-rites [only], while the fruit-cup [receives them] because it is a modification of that?
— thus [ends the discussion]. (The purpose of the deliberation in this section is whether those who desire specific qualities should engage in the ritual or not.

What is the prima facie view? — "They are subject to the same injunction, because there is no division within the context. This being the position, it is replied: "That which is contingent (*naimittika*) of such a kind is not subject to the same injunction."

It may be so. Why? Because of their inequality. The fruit-cup (*phalacamas*) is not equal to the *soma*; the *soma* is prescribed as a constant (*nitya*), whereas the fruit-cup is contingent (*naimittika*). What follows from this? If that is the case, then the ritual properties (*dharma*) also, being prescribed as constant, cannot be performed as if they were contingent. If they were common [to both], then they would be enjoined there without reference to a specific context (*anārabhyavidhi*).

Moreover, the *phalacamas* is an occasional rite (*naimittika*); it adopts the properties of the *soma*. In that case, those properties, being common [to both], would be stated twice—so they argue! Therefore, the injunctions are not identical. (3.6.13)
The section concerning the performance of the primary ritual duty even in the case of substitutes.
And the substitute is like that [original]. (Pūrvapakṣa) 37.
There is a substitute for a substance prescribed in the sacred text, just as when the *barhis* grass is being carried away, *nīvāra* grains are used.

In this regard, there is a doubt: are the *nīvāra* grains subject to the same injunctions, or not? What is the prima facie view?—"The substitute is like that [original], just as in the case of the *naimittika*..."

The *bhāṣika* [accentuation] is not subject to the same rule as the permanent [Vedic accentuation]; likewise, a substitute is not equal to the original because it lacks that status. This is the point.
What is the inequality? [The inequality is that] the [rites] are prescribed for *vrīhi* rice, not for *nīvāra* wild rice;
thus there is a lack of parity. The [rites] are prescribed for *vrīhi*, while for *nīvāra* they are [permitted] only by way of necessity (*arthāpatti*).
They come into being.
Likewise, because the purpose is one. (Siddhānta) || 38 ||

Bhāṣya: This is not so—that the substitute is not of the same rule (asamānavidhāna). For that which exists [in the substitute] is exactly as it is heard [in the scripture]; there is no relationship of original and modification (prakṛti-vikārabhāva). Why? Because the nature of rice (vrīhitva) is the cause for the properties of rice to apply to individual grains of rice, and it does not exist in the place of [the original].
Sūtra of the Hevajra Tantra,
Chapter on the Emanation.
It is heard in scripture: "it becomes wild rice (nīvāra)"; therefore, there is no relationship of original material and its transformation.
"How then do the properties (dharma) exist in *nīvāra* grains? It is replied: those individual instances (*vyakti*) which are delimited as being *vrīhi* rice exist in the *nīvāra* grains;
it is for the sake of those [instances] that those properties are produced, both of those instances and of others.

This same rule applies to those [grains] contained within the rice. What is the similarity? Both are characterized by the nature of being rice (*vrīhitva*). Therefore, they are subject to the same injunction (*samānavidhāna*).
And because it does not possess the characteristics of the Śāstra. (Yukti 38)
Furthermore, there is no relationship of original and modification (*prakṛti-vikārabhāva*) between a substitute and that which is prescribed by scripture. Why?

Because the substitute is characterized by its purpose; for a substitute is employed on account of the purpose, and it cannot be understood from the purpose itself that "the state of being *nīvāra* takes the place of the state of being *vrīhi*.
Therefore, there is no relationship of original and modification between a substitute and that which is prescribed by scripture. (3.6.14)
The section concerning the performance of the primary ritual duty even when substitutes have been prescribed.
The mention of the accessory is for the purpose of restriction. 40.
Now,
regarding that substitute which is prescribed by scripture, does it share the same ritual details (*sāmānavidhya*) as the original, or not?
[Page 447]

[The opponent] says: "As in the case of the text, 'If one should not find Soma, one should press Pūtīka plants. We say that this is not a case of equal injunction (*asāmānavidhya*), for it is the opposite of what was heard [in the primary rule].

This being the position reached, it is replied: 'The mention of the accessory (*guṇa-śruti*) is for the purpose of restriction. Here too, the substitute (*pratinidhi*) is indeed characterized by its functional purpose (*artha-lakṣaṇa*); when Soma is unavailable, a substance similar to Soma is obtained."

In that case, when a substance very similar [to the original] is available, one that is slightly similar is restricted [as the substitute]. When another [substance] is to be substituted, it is substituted for another in the place of what was heard [in the scripture]; not, however, by virtue of being a sacrificial substance. (3.6.15)
The section concerning the mutual subsidiarity of the rites beginning with the *dīkṣaṇīyā*.
Sūtra: But the concluding rites have the same application, because there is no distinction in the context. 41.
(Purvapaksha) ||

—Bhāṣya: There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; therein, the terminuses (saṃsthās) are recited: Agniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, and Atirātra. In that context, there are ritual duties such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā and others. Regarding these, a doubt arises: are they intended for the Jyotiṣṭoma in its entirety, including all its terminuses?
The *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites have been mentioned; are they intended for the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice alone, or for all sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthās*)?
What is the prima facie view? The injunction applies equally to all terminuses.

Why? Because there is no distinction in the context; there is no specific indication in the context by which it could be known that these are prescribed with reference to the *agniṣṭoma* terminus alone. Therefore, the terminuses are subject to the same injunction.
Sūtra-bhāṣya: And there is a designation as if they were equal. 42 || 60 ||
The designation occurs as if it were identical across the various contexts: "If it is an Agniṣṭoma, he offers the oblation;

if it is an Ukthya, he anoints the enclosing sticks; if it is an Atirātra, he should proceed toward the Havirdhāna shed while muttering this very Yajus. From this specific statement regarding every state, it is understood that even that which is general applies only to one who is in every state.
For if the injunction were not common, it would belong only to that which has the Agniṣṭoma as its concluding form; [in that case],
one would not mention the Agniṣṭoma here, even though it is not being mentioned.
There is a connection with the *dharma*—thus we understand that because every state is mentioned, this is a section concerning all states.

Moreover, it is heard in scripture: "One should sacrifice a goat dedicated to Agni at the *agniṣṭoma*, a second one dedicated to Indra-Agni at the *ukthya*, and a third, a spotted bull dedicated to Indra, at the *ṣoḍaśin*. The mention of a second and a third is consistent only if there is a common injunction (*samānavidhi*). For indeed, two [goats] are [required] at the *ukthya*.
The two [stotras] exist as conditions: the Agniṣṭoma-stotra and the Ukthya-stotra;

and there, the two occasional animal sacrifices are the one for Agni and the one for Indra-Agni. Therefore, the observation of a second [animal sacrifice] is appropriate there. The same applies to the Ṣoḍaśin and the Atirātra, insofar as there is a relationship between the archetype (prakṛti) and its modification (vikāra).

But because of the direct Vedic statement (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), the *Āgneya* [offering], which is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) by means of the *Aindrāgna* and others, would sublate it;

in that case, the observation of the second [offering] and so forth would not be possible, yet it does occur. Therefore, the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are the properties (*dharma*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma in its entirety.
The modifications [of the mantra] apply when there is a connection with desire, because of the equality of the obligatory [mantra]. 43.
(Sūtra) ||

Bhāṣya: This is not so—that they are of equal injunction (*samānavidhāna*). What then? The *ukthya* and other forms are modifications (*vikāra*). Having accepted the *agniṣṭoma* as the standard form (*saṃsthā*), the ritual duties (*dharma*) such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others are prescribed. Why? Because the *ukthya* and others are heard in connection with specific desires (*kāmasaṃyoga*): "One desiring cattle should take up the *ukthya*; one desiring vigor should [take up] the *ṣoḍaśin*."

"One should praise; one should cause one desiring offspring to sacrifice with the Atirātra"—thus it is heard. A desired quality (guṇa) being heard does not enter into the permanent rite. How so? Because in such a case of a desired [quality], the production of the fruit results from that very quality: "One desiring cattle should take the Ukthya cup," not "one desiring the Jyotiṣṭoma" or "one desiring the taking of the Ukthya"; rather, it is so that cattle may come to be.

The meaning is that one should grasp [the rule]. How so? In this regard, a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) must necessarily be expected; because of proximity, it is understood that it is the procedure of the obligatory (*nitya*) rite.
But how is it determined that this very procedure belongs to the obligatory rite?
[Page 453] Chapter 3, Section 3.
Now, is this [meditation] intended for those seeking specific desires (kāmya), or is it common to all? It is replied:
Wherever there is a desire for a quality, it occurs only when that action is being accomplished,

and not otherwise. Regarding the question— "Is that procedure (*itikartavyatā*) which presents itself in close proximity [to the action] a property of the means (*sādhana*) or of the end (*sādhya*)?"— it is determined to belong to the end (*sādhya*).

It must be that this [means], not being present when the goal is unaccomplished, is connected with the means; for in this way that specific procedure is enjoined: "by this one should assist the achiever in the means. And there is no such manner by which, while the action is not being accomplished, the achiever could be made effective by it.
Therefore, for the achiever as well...

By one who accepts a specific *itikartavyatā* (procedure), this must also be accepted regarding the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*): namely, that the *jyotiṣṭoma* is the object to be accomplished and the *saṃsthās* (termini) are its means of accomplishment; therefore, it is established that this *itikartavyatā* belongs to the *jyotiṣṭoma*. Now, why is it not common [to all]? Because it is prescribed as if it were permanent (*nityavat*), precisely when...
The Jyotiṣṭoma [is performed] at that very time for initiation; however, when one desires cattle in the Jyotiṣṭoma, then it has the Ukthya as its concluding form.
The ritual duties (dharmas) of the Jyotiṣṭoma must always be performed, even once the Ukthya form is reached; therein, the duties of the Jyotiṣṭoma must always be performed—those [duties].

And [the statement] "for the sake of the *ukthya* and other forms" contradicts what precedes it by what follows, if it were not always for the sake of the *ukthya* and others; yet if it were for the sake of the *ukthya* and others but not always, both [positions] would be mutually contradictory. Therefore, it is not common to all. Furthermore, if that which is recorded as if it were permanent (*nityavat*) were actually non-permanent (*anitya*), then that recording as if permanent would be [inconsistent].

If it were made non-permanent, then its traditional injunction as if it were permanent would be contradicted; therefore, this applies to the Jyotiṣṭoma which has the permanent *saṃsthās*, and not to the optional [Jyotiṣṭoma] with *saṃsthās* such as the *ukthya*.
Or rather, because it has already been stated, they will belong to the *prakṛti*. || 44 ||
For it is said there:
"Is not the *agniṣṭoma* termination also heard of as being for the sake of a desired result?"

Regarding what has been handed down in tradition, one [rite] is obligatory (*nitya*) and one is optional (*kāmya*); there, by the force of the two sentences, the obligatory rite itself will become endowed with desire, and there is no violation of its obligatoriness.
[The Bhāṣya says: "There is not"—meaning that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites will be the *dharmas* (procedural details) of the *jyotiṣṭoma* when it is in the form of the *agniṣṭoma*.
Sūtra Bhāṣya Sūtra (Sūtra Commentary on the Aphorisms)
But because of the scriptural statement, there is a combination. (Sūtra 45) (Ābhāsara-Nirṇaya)

Now, as for what was said— that the observation of the second and third [offerings] is possible only if there is a common injunction (samānavidhi) and not otherwise— that statement will hold true; it is not an actual observation, for in the Ukthya sacrifice, the offering to Indra-Agni is enjoined as the second, and likewise, in the Ṣoḍaśin, the offering to Indra is enjoined as the third.
And because of the prohibition of the previous marks. (Yukti 46)

Furthermore, we see from this that there is a relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*). Why? Because of the prohibition of the previous indicative marks (*liṅga*): "If it is an *agniṣṭoma*, he offers an oblation;

if it is an *ukthya*, he anoints the enclosing-stick and does not offer an oblation. This observation of the absence of the oblation would not occur if there were uniformity of rule (*sāmānavidhya*) based on the authority of the statement when the occasion has arisen.
Sūtra: Because of a specific quality, there is a designation for the one [entity]. (Ābhāsara-Nirṇaya)

[Commentary: Now, as for what was stated—namely, "the designation"—this is a designation of the single person authorized by means of a quality not [himself] authorized, according to the reasoning already set forth; and the mention of the Agniṣṭoma is a restatement. (3.6.16)
Thus ends the sixth quarter of the third chapter in the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya composed by Śrī Śabarasvāmin.
Sūtra-bhāṣya [Page 455]
The section concerning whether the *bārhaspatya* and other offerings are subsidiary to both the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) or subsidiary to one of them.
On account of the distinction of the context, that which is not connected belongs to the principal [action]. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 1 ||
The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are well-known; therein there are the *barhis* (sacrificial grass) and its properties, as well as the altar (*vedī*) and its properties.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: do the *barhis* and so forth, along with the properties of the *barhis* and so forth, belong to the primary sacrifice alone, or to both the subsidiaries and the primary? What, then, is the prima facie view?

"—because of the specific context, that which is unconnected belongs to the primary [rite]; such qualities belong to the primary. Why? Because of the specific context; for the context belongs to the primary rites."
And their connection is through the context; therefore, it belongs to the principal.
[The rule applies] neither to the subsidiaries nor to all [the principal acts], because their status as subsidiary is not prompted by that [specific purpose].

[Commentary: These ritual properties (dharmas) belong to all [elements], both the subsidiaries (aṅga) and the primary acts (pradhāna). Here, subsidiarity (śeṣatva) does not arise from the context (prakaraṇa), for that is characterized by utility: whatever benefits something is subsidiary to it. And these properties benefit all the subsidiaries and primary acts. How is this understood? From the syntactical connection (vākya). In the statement, "He places the sacrificial offerings (havīṃṣi) on the altar (vedi)," only the altar is understood from the sentence; the primary offerings would [otherwise] be understood from the context. But the sentence is stronger than the context; therefore, [the offerings are placed] on the sacrificial grass (barhis).
"He establishes [the point]—thus:

[The opponent] says, 'If the context is set aside by the syntactical connection (*vākya*), then even in common worldly usage these properties (*dharma*) are stated for the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). What is the fault in that? [The reply is: In all cases, the properties must be performed."

[They] attain [them]. It is said: from the context, it is understood that they are indeed auxiliaries of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Therefore, they should not be performed in worldly (secular) rites.
"If this is so, then the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) themselves are also not denoted by the word 'Darśapūrṇamāsa'; therefore..."
Even in those cases, they do not apply. It is said: although the subsidiaries are not part of the Darśapūrṇamāsa—[in the Mīmāṃsā-darśana on page 456]—the same principle holds.
The [rites] denoted by the word [bhāvanā] are auxiliaries to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices;
the ritual duties (dharmas) performed in these will assist the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Therefore, they must be performed for both the subsidiaries and the primary sacrifice.
If it is argued that [the rule applies] even from afar. (Ābhāsya) || 3 ||

For that [statement] is not [authoritative], because its purpose is that [very thing]. (0 Ni.)

Therefore, the properties which assist the Darśapūrṇamāsa apply only where they serve the purpose of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and not elsewhere. But because of the connection with the fruit, the principal [act] is connected with its owner.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, shaving the hair and beard, the drinking of milk, and various austerities are prescribed;
regarding these, there is a doubt: do they serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the primary rite, or do they serve the purpose of the primary rite alone?
What, then, is the prima facie view? They serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the primary rite—according to the principle established previously.
It has been attained.

This being the case, we reply: this [ownership] belongs to the master; therefore, it pertains to the principal [the person]. Why? Because of the connection with the fruit. This relationship of the person is with the sacrifice: the sacrifice is the giver of the unseen result (*apūrva*), and the person is the recipient. "But is there not also another relationship—namely, that the sacrifice is the object to be accomplished (*nirvartya*) and the person is the accomplisher (*abhinirvartaka*)? [We answer: No, because of the fruit.

The person is mentioned for the purpose that "there will be a connection"—for he does not accomplish the sacrifice; rather, it is the sacrifice that will come into being through its own existence. Why, then, [is the person mentioned]?

Does the fruit arise for one who brings [the sacrifice] to completion? It is said that the *saṃskāras* (purificatory acts) perform a refinement (*saṃskurvantīti*). They produce a capacity in that which is to be refined toward its specific purpose. And the purpose of the person is to obtain the fruit, not to bring the sacrifice to completion. Therefore, those *saṃskāras* belonging to the person render the person capable of receiving the fruit, not capable of accomplishing the sacrifice. [The opponent] says: "If they do not produce a capacity for the accomplishment of the sacrifice, then how are they properties of the sacrifice?"
[They] exist. It is said: they serve as assistance for the sacrifice while it accomplishes its own purpose.
And what is its own purpose? That which connects its performer with the fruit [of the action]. Therefore, the purificatory rites of the master are for the sake of the primary [act]. (3.7.2)
The section concerning whether the sacrificial altar and other such elements belong to both the subsidiary and the principal rites of the Soma sacrifice.
And because of the connection with the desire to act. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 7 ||
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard in the scripture: "Thirty-six steps toward the east, twenty-four on the rear side, and thirty on the back; as much as we are able. Regarding this, there is a doubt:
is this altar for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the primary rite, or is it for the sake of the primary rite alone? What [is the conclusion]?

Is it already established? — Because of the connection with the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), [the agent] is one who seeks the primary object. What is this "desire to act"? It is the thought, "We shall be able. This [scriptural injunction] is heard for the sake of that which is desired to be done: "We shall be able to perform this."
And what he intends to perform is the primary rite (pradhāna), not the subsidiaries (aṅga); for the primary rite possesses the fruit, whereas the subsidiaries do not.

"Now, if the ancillary parts (aṅgas) are not intended to be performed, for what purpose are they performed? It is said in reply: the ancillary parts are performed even though they are not intended [as ends in themselves]. Although...
Those [subsidiaries] are not themselves desired to be performed; nevertheless, while they are not desired to be performed, something else is desired to be performed by means of them.
Therefore, those [subsidiaries] are performed—[namely], that which is desired to be performed, for which the altar (*vedi*) exists.
Therefore, it serves the purpose of the primary rite. (Thus much has been established as a conclusion. (3.7)

Because it is designated as such. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 8 ||

There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices; regarding them, it is heard in scripture: "One should touch the Pūrṇamāsī with the Caturhotṛ formula, and the Amāvāsyā with the Pañcahotṛ formula. —“The full moon day and the new moon day”—thus it is said. Therefore, the touching belongs to the principal rite.
Kha. But since the fruit is heard in connection with that [rite], therefore there should be a desire to perform the whole. 8.

The fruit is heard as resulting from the rite together with its subsidiaries; therefore, it is the rite together with its subsidiaries that is intended to be performed. Even if the subsidiaries themselves are not the object of the intention, this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) following the presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the preceding section. This is the present Sūtra.
It has been shown.
