By the naming of the qualities, there is the naming of all the purposes. (Siddhānta) || 10 ||

Bhāṣya: As for what was said—that because the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* denote the primary [sacrifices], the touching (*abhimarśana*) belongs to the primary oblations—it is not so; there should be touching of the subsidiary oblations as well. Why? Because of the mention of a quality; there is a mention of "touching as a quality. What is that mention? That which says "touching as a quality" regarding the *paurṇamāsī* and the *amāvāsyā*.
And thus, the touching (abhimarśana) with the accusative ending must be performed for the sake of the Full Moon sacrifice, and the touching must be performed for the sake of the New Moon sacrifice.
Therefore, wherever it is performed—whether at the Full Moon or the New Moon—it should be done in every instance where it is beneficial;
whatever is connected to the Full Moon or the New Moon, whether directly or through a sequence (praṇāḍyā), [must be performed].
Or rather, whatever is performed here and there benefits those two; therefore, the offering of the principal oblations as well as the subsidiary oblations must be performed. (3.7.4)
Section Kha: The Topic Concerning the Subordinate Purpose of Initiation and the Sacrificial Fee.
But the initiation fee for the principal [rite] is [determined] by the scriptural statement. || 11 ||

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, initiations (dīkṣās) are prescribed: "There are three initiations. Likewise, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) are prescribed: "Its sacrificial fee consists of one hundred and twelve [cows]. Regarding this, there is a doubt: are the initiation and the sacrificial fee for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the principal rites, or only for the principal rites? What is the prima facie view? Since persons are for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the principal rites, [the initiation and fee must be for both].

"The initiation and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) are for the sake of both the subsidiary and the principal rites"—this being the prima facie view, we reply: the initiation and the sacrificial fee belong to the principal rite. Why? Because of a scriptural statement; for there is indeed a scriptural statement:
"The initiations are for the Soma sacrifice; the sacrificial fees are for the Soma sacrifice. For there is no [contradiction] to the scriptural statement.
Bhā.: There is indeed such a thing as an excessive burden. Therefore, the initiation fee (*dīkṣā-dakṣiṇā*) [is determined] by the scriptural statement (vacana).
Kha.
Bhā.
"Of Soma"—thus [it is said].
And because cessation is observed. (12) (Yukti)

It demonstrates the cessation of the initiations (*dīkṣā*). How so? "When you have performed the sacrifice with the animal, what then is its initiation?"—"In that he offers the *ṣaḍvīta* oblation, that is its initiation"—thus there is a statement even in the absence of an initiation.
It occurs; therefore, the initiation and the sacrificial fee pertain to the auxiliary parts—thus [it is concluded]. (3.7.5) [Sūtra]
Sūtra Bhāṣya:
The Section on the Non-subordinacy of the Sacrificial Post to the Inner Altar.
Likewise, the altar belongs to the sacrificial post. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 13 ||

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, as it is said: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. In that context, with reference to the sacrificial post (yūpa), it is heard: "The sacrificial post is indeed speech; if one were to fix it within the altar (antarvedi), it would burn [the sacrificer]; if [he fixes it] outside the altar (bahirvedi), it would not be secured. Therefore, he fixes half within the altar and half outside the altar so that it is secured."
"It exists; it does not depart"—thus it is said.

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the altar (*vedi*) taught as being a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) by the phrase "within the altar" (*antarvedi*), or is it stated for the purpose of defining a location by the phrase "half within the altar, half outside the altar" (*ardham antarvedi bahirvedi*)? How [is it] as a constituent part of the sacrificial post, or how [is it] otherwise?

Is it characterized by location?—thus [the question]. If the intended meaning is a connection between the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the interior of the altar (*vedi*), then the post must be made connected to the altar by way of being an accessory (*aṅga*) to it;
but if [it means] that place where the post, while being measured, has its upper part both inside and outside the altar, that...

Since the location is being taught, it is therefore characterized by its location. What is established? "Just as the altar belongs to the consecration and the sacrificial fee of the primary rite, so does the altar belong to the sacrificial post; likewise, the sacrificial post is to be measured; likewise, it is to be measured [as it is being erected].
[Page 461]

The altar exists within the sacrificial ground (*vedi*). Thus, the scriptural mention of the *vedi* will also be upheld; otherwise, the word *vedi* would have to indicate a location through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). When there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and secondary indication, direct statement is preferable, not secondary indication. Therefore, the altar is indicated as being a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Or rather, it refers only to one's own country, because it forms a single syntactical unit with the word "non-pupil" (aśiṣya). (Siddhānta) || 14 ||
The Bhāṣya states: Or rather, by the word "vedi" (altar), only a location is indicated, not that the altar is an accessory (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Why?

Because there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with what is not to be enjoined (*aśiṣyeṇa*); namely, the syntactic unity of the passage, "He fixes half within the altar and half outside the altar," exists with that which is not to be enjoined, if [the word] indicates a location. Now, if...

The altar (vedi) is mentioned as being a constituent part of the sacrificial post (yūpa); therefore, the mention of "outside the altar" (bahirvedi) would not be intended as an injunction. When the altar is taught as a subordinate element of the post, the utterance of the words "outside the altar" serves no useful purpose whatsoever.
Sūtra-bhāṣya:

"Now, if it were to enjoin even the space outside the altar as a subordinate part of the *yūpa*, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, when the altar is indicated as a subordinate part of the *yūpa*, the word 'outside the altar' [is used]."

In every respect, it should not be enjoined. However, if it is characterized by location (*deśalakṣaṇa*), then, since it is being characterized by a specific location, the word "outside the altar" (*bahirvedi*) would be stated as a qualification; otherwise, it would be understood that the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) may be placed in any place whatsoever within the interior of the altar (*vedyabhyantara*). Now, if...

Furthermore, when the word "bahirvedi" (outside the altar) is heard, whichever location is intended for the measuring of the altar— whether it be *antarvedi* (inside the altar) or *bahirvedi* (outside the altar)— that location is what is sought to be indicated;
and that cannot be indicated without the word "bahirvedi"— thus [the word] must necessarily [be used].
He is to be instructed; therefore, it is the characteristic of place—thus [ends the section]. (3|7|6 Śrauta-sūtra)
The section concerning the fact that the *sāmidhenī* verses are not subsidiary to the *havirdhāna* cart.
"Regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses, they say 'they recite them after that' because of the statement concerning the two *havirdhāna* carts. (15) (50)

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "And when they press [the Soma], they recite the Sāmidhenīs" (Bhāṣya, p. 462). The meaning is that one should connect the Sāmidhenīs with whichever Havirdhāna shed they are pressing in. In this regard, there is a doubt: is the Havirdhāna enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the Sāmidhenīs, or are the Sāmidhenīs qualified by the Havirdhāna?

Should the *sāmidhenī* verses be recited, or is the location for those reciting them indicated by the *havirdhāna* cart? What, then, is the prima facie view? The *havirdhāna* is enjoined as an accessory (*aṅga*) to the *sāmidhenīs*; that shed in which they press the Soma is [the locus].

"One should connect [the act] with the *sāmidhenī* verses"—from this statement, "the *sāmidhenīs* connected with the *havirdhāna* are to be recited," it follows that since they constitute an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *sāmidhenīs*, the scriptural mention of the *havirdhāna* will be upheld; otherwise, one would have to imply a specific location.
Therefore, the *havirdhāna* is an auxiliary of the *sāmidhenīs*.
Or rather, it is only the region that is directly perceived as the object of the Soma sacrifice. (Siddhānta) || 16 ||

This is stated for the purpose of indicating the location— that the *sāmidhenī* verses are to be recited in that place where they press the Soma— because the pressing of the Soma is a perceptible primary ritual act performed by him,
as it is said: "He places the Soma in the southern *havirdhāna* shed."

First, these [logs] are to be taken up for the purpose of placing the Soma; likewise, the *sāmidhenī* verses are also to be taken up for the purpose of kindling the fire. However, in this case, only this much is heard: "They press the Soma near the *havirdhāna* (Soma-cart); those [verses] connected with it are also to be taken up for the purpose of kindling the fire for the *sāmidhenīs*. In that regard, it is not known: do the *sāmidhenīs*, being connected, assist the *havirdhāna*, or does the *havirdhāna* assist the *sāmidhenīs*?
To this it is said: the *sāmidhenīs* certainly do not [assist] the *havirdhāna*.

They assist [the sacrifice], for they are not yet enjoined as such—namely, that "the *sāmidhenī* verses are to be recited. What then? The connection of those verses with a specific part of the *havirdhāna* is what is enjoined; specifically, between the two carts named *havirdhāna* situated in the southern and northern sections within the *havirdhāna* pavilion, it is the southern cart that is denoted here by the words "that" (*tat*) and "which" (*yat*). The pressing of the *soma* takes place in its vicinity. Mādhava maintains that the word *uta* here functions in the sense of the word *atha* (meaning "then" or "thereupon").
[Page 463] Bhāṣya:
Furthermore, that which is not enjoined cannot be a subsidiary (*aṅga*), nor is it enjoined in this manner: "The *havirdhāna* cart should be taken up and connected while they are following.

How then? A specific connection with the *havirdhāna* is heard in relation to the *sāmidhenī* verses; what is enjoined is the connection with the *havirdhāna*, and there is no connection of the *havirdhāna* with the *sāmidhenīs*.
[The place] has already been obtained, which would otherwise be merely restated for the sake of a specific detail. With what, then, is the injunction connected?
For the function regarding the *soma* is directly perceived, whereas the function regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses is not directly perceived by the injunction.
However, there is a connection between the location and the *sāmidhenī* verses, [as seen in the text]: "behind..."

The word "vedim" is understood as indicating a location; it refers to that which is adjacent to either the northern or the southern [shed] when no specific rule is prescribed. In that context, the statement "where they press [the Soma], that is the Ambāṣṭha" becomes appropriate. Therefore, the mention of the *havirdhāna* (Soma-cart shed) is for the purpose of indicating a location.
Sūtra-bhāṣya:
"Now, why does this connection not occur— namely, that in which [the injunction]..."

"They offer oblations; this [act] is connected with the *sāmidhenī* verses"—this cannot be so. For if it were thus, two distinct matters would have to be enjoined: the connection with the injunction of the oblation and the connection with the specific injunction of the *sāmidhenī* verses; in that case, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, it is not so.
The connection is as follows: [the word] "messenger" (dūtī).
And the designation is likewise [indicative of that]. (Yukti 17)
And the designation is likewise the same, as we have taught: "The *havirdhāna* [shed] is for the sake of Soma. (3.7.3 Āhnika)
The section concerning the performance of other limbs by another wife.
The fruit of the ritual act belongs to the performer, because that is its characteristic; therefore, it should be performed by oneself. (Pūrvapakṣa 18)
Bhāṣya II:

Ritual actions are the examples— namely, "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," and "One desiring heaven [should sacrifice] with the Jyotiṣṭoma."

"One should sacrifice"— regarding this, there is a doubt: are these rites to be performed by oneself entirely, or should one perform only the pouring of the oblation (utsarga) oneself, while another performs the remainder?
Or rather, is it that another person performs the remainder? What is the prima facie view? It should be performed by oneself. Why? Because the fruit belongs to one who performs it oneself.
How is this understood? "Because that is its defining characteristic"; the word is the defining characteristic of this meaning—that [the act] is performed by oneself.
The fruit accrues to one who performs [the rite]. What is that word? It is "one desiring heaven should sacrifice.

This refers to whoever desires heaven; it is said that, becoming the agent in the sacrifice, he shall accomplish the fruit. And by becoming the agent in the sacrifice along with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), he obtains the fruit.
Therefore, it should occur through one's own application.
But in the case of the disposal, because it is subordinate, the performer of the subsidiary acts is the same as that of the principal;
therefore, it may be performed by another or by oneself. (Pūrvapakṣa 18)

In the act of relinquishment (*utsarga*), there is primacy. How so? He who performs the relinquishment has thereby accomplished everything. How so? Relinquishment is equivalent to hiring (*parikraya*); through it, those hired perform everything.
Therefore, he who performs the hiring has himself accomplished everything.
It occurs thus: therefore, one should perform the act of discarding alone by oneself; the remainder may be done by another or by oneself.
Whether it be oneself or another [should perform the purchase], because of the scriptural injunction for purchase and because of the prohibition regarding one's own self. (Siddhānta) 20.

The remaining [acts] must have a different agent. Why? Because hiring (parikraya) is not prescribed; for although many modes of securing the services of persons are available, hiring is specifically restricted. Therefore, all ritual items (padārtha) must be performed by those secured through hiring. Furthermore, hiring oneself is contradictory; if one were to perform them oneself, it would be as if performed by one who has not been hired.
In that case, the scriptural injunction regarding the hiring [of assistants] would be rendered meaningless, or it would have to be assumed to serve an invisible (transcendental) purpose.
Therefore, the remaining ritual acts should be performed by others who have been hired.
However, for one who performs the *utsarga* (the act of relinquishment) himself, everything becomes performed by himself. (3.7.8)
[Page 465] The section concerning the specific rules for the officiating priests who have been hired.
In that case, there would be no restriction on the number of agents for the purpose, because there is no specific distinction.
Bhāṣya 21 || (Pūrvapakṣa) ||
In that case, since they have been hired for those ritual procedures (*itikartavyatā*), there would necessarily be a restriction on the number of performers.
Why? Because of the absence of specification; no specific rule regarding the number of performers is recorded in the scripture.
Their number is determined by the purpose: as many as are required to accomplish the ritual procedure belonging to the Aṅgirasas.
Choose!
Or rather, because of the difference in scriptural injunctions, there should be separate [deities] for each name. || 22 ||
Bhāṣya-sūtra-bhāṣya (The Commentary on the Aphorisms of the Bhāṣya)
As many as are the names of performers heard in connection with the ritual acts—so many [priests] are to be chosen;
and these names are distinct, as they are heard [in the texts]: "The Adhvaryu distributes those [cups] in front;
the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the Manthin; the Neṣṭṛ leads the wife forward; the Unnetṛ..."
"He draws up the cups"— likewise, "the Prastotṛ chants the Prastāva, the Udgātṛ sings the Udgītha, the Pratihartṛ chants the Pratihāra, the Subrahmaṇya recites the Subrahmaṇyā,
the Hotṛ recites the morning litany (Prātaranuvāka), the Maitrāvaruṇa gives the directions (Preṣyati) and recites the responses (Anuśaṃsati)."

The Acchāvāka performs the sacrifice; the Grāvastut recites the Grāvastotrīyā hymn—this much is the purpose in the ritual action. Therefore, these must necessarily be performed exactly as they are heard in the scripture; there exists no other element apart from this that is not taught by the direct statement (*vākya*), for that is understood through the name (*samākhyā*). Consequently, one should select only this many.
If it is argued that [the distinction] arises from a difference in the parts of a single [entity], [we reply: no. (23) (0)

If it is thus proposed—that one should choose from among these many—it is not so; rather, whoever intends to perform a particular action is designated by the specific word corresponding to that very action.
[Page 466]
In the Bhāṣya on the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra, it is stated: "Even though there is only one [agent], he may perform many ritual acts by means of many names;
therefore, there is no fixed rule."
Sūtra: "For [the names apply] at the time of origination" (24).

Bhāṣya: This is not so; for at the time of the origination of persons—that is, when persons are being produced—their designations differ: "He chooses a Brāhmaṇa," "He chooses a Hotṛ," "He chooses an Udgātṛ," "He chooses an Adhvaryu," and so forth. Therefore, there is a need for those with such names in the ritual action; they must necessarily be chosen. Consequently, these...

The mention [of the number] in the act of choosing (*varaṇa*) is not an injunction, because there is no purpose for it; nor is it a restatement (*anuvāda*), for the Veda would not say "so many are to be chosen"—that would be entirely meaningless. Furthermore, this [mention] is capable of conveying a specific number; therefore, this statement is for the sake of that specific number which is understood from them. Consequently, [the number is] sixteen.
The [rites] must be performed; thus, Soma would have the sacrificer as its agent, and the same applies to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Sūtra Bhāṣya:
A separate section concerning the Camasādhvaryus.
And the Camasādhvaryus [are distinct], because they are designated by means of them. || 25 ||

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there are the Camasādhvaryus, as it is said: "One should choose the Camasādhvaryus. Regarding them, a doubt arises: are they some among these [already mentioned], or are they others distinct from them? What is the initial position? Since they are enumerated among those [already mentioned], they must be some among these very ones. To this we reply: the Camasādhvaryus should be others, distinct from them. Why? Because of their designation by means of them; for there is a designation of these [Camasādhvaryus] by means of those [previously enumerated] who have been specifically counted.

[The text] says: "There are cup-attendants (camasādhvaryu) for those who act in the middle; there are cup-attendants for the Hotraka priests. [Objection: "But surely those very individuals who are mentioned in the archetype (prakṛta) should be the cup-attendants. [Reply: We say, "No. Why? "Because they are designated separately," as in: "the cup-attendants for those who act in the middle..."
[Page 467] Bhāṣya:
Regarding the statement "the Camasādhvaryus of the Hotrakas," this genitive case occurs because of a relationship of dependence;

they are designated by means of the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and the priests are their masters, not the sacrificer (yajamāna). Furthermore, it has been asserted by us that these [Camasādhvaryus] are distinct from the attendants of the sacrificer. This is not [the case].

The Camasādhvaryus are to be chosen by the sacrificer to perform their duties, yet they are to be chosen by the officiating priests (ṛtvij). Furthermore, there is a distinction even in their very originative injunction: "One should choose the Camasādhvaryus. (3.7.10)
No.
Bhā. Ma.
(Noble Commentary on the Mahāyāna)
Bhāṣya:
This section concerns the plurality of the Camasādhvaryus.
But [their number] is determined by the mention of "many" in the original injunction. (Sūtra 26)

Regarding these very persons, there is a doubt: is there no restriction—as to whether it be one, two, or many—or must they be many? When the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that there is no restriction, it is replied: they must be many. Why? Because in the original injunction, the plural number is heard: "the Camasādhvaryus."
One becomes widely learned at the time of birth; therefore, there are many.
The section concerning the rule regarding the number ten for the *camasādhvaryu* priests.
The number ten [of the cups] is established because of the observation of an indicative mark.

(3 | 7) Regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it has been stated that there are *camasādhvaryu* priests and they are many. When the doubt arises as to how many "many" there are, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there are three, on the strength of the plural number.

We reply: "The number ten [is established] because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga); they should be ten, for it is heard in the *Daśapeya*, which is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*: 'There are ten *camasādhvaryu* priests; ten by ten they follow each cup (*camasa*). For this reason, it is the *Daśapeya*."

By stating "there are," he indicates that there are ten *camasādhvaryu* priests; if there were only three, this indication would not be possible. Therefore, this number exceeds three, and if there were not ten, this indication would likewise be untenable. Consequently, [there must be ten].
In the Mīmāṃsā system (Bhāṣya):
there are ten [cups], and there are ten owners of them. Therefore, because of the existence of a purpose [for each].
Ten members are required; and when those ten are admitted, other groups are also included, and by that means there would likewise be ten. (3.7.12) [Adhikaraṇa]
Śrī Bhagavadgītāsūtraṃ (The Sacred Verses of the Lord)
Bhāṣya:
The section concerning the distinctness of the *śamitṛ* (the slaughterer).
And the Śamitṛ priest [is distinct] because of the difference in name. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 28 ||

There is the *śamitṛ* (the immolator), with the injunction: "Bring forward the *śamitṛ*. Is he one among those who have been mentioned by name, or is he someone other than them? What is the prima facie view? Since there is a mention [of names] in the act of choosing him, it follows that he is one among those [already mentioned]. To this, it is replied:

"And the *śamitṛ* [is distinct] because of the difference in terminology—the terminology differs, such that it is said, 'This rite is to be performed by one who has this designation'; therefore, one who bears this designation must be produced. Because of the mention of this [term], a distinction from the *saṃstaritṛ* is understood; therefore, the *śamitṛ* should be someone else."
Furthermore, there is the scriptural injunction: "If one should offer the *komā* and *vaikartana* portions to a non-Brāhmaṇa,

he should give them to a Brāhmaṇa"— thus there arises a suspicion regarding the non-Brāhmaṇa status [of the recipient], and that suspicion is not applicable in the case of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).
[The rule applies] because of the context and because of the lack of connection with the origination [of the action]. (Siddhānta 28)

It is true that [the term] is understood as referring to those who have already entered the Saṅgha, but it is not understood as referring to those who are currently being born; in that case, because of the distinction in the action of a single individual, it is thus also logically consistent. As for what was said—"he becomes one born from a non-Brāhmaṇa"—that refers to the sacrificer:
"if the sacrificer should be a non-Brāhmaṇa. Now, if...

"One should not be a non-Brahmin"—thus, from the perspective of impurity (*mala*), the *śamitṛ* (the slaughterer) is connected [to that prohibition]. It is replied: he is called a *śamitṛ* because he "pacifies" (*śamayati*); this word is etymological (*yaugika*) and applies even to those engaged in the primary rites. Furthermore, since the *śāmitra* (the function of the slaughterer) is recorded in the section on the duties of the *adhvaryu*, it must be performed by the *adhvaryu*.
[The variant reading in the Kātyāyana Saṃhitā-pustaka is: "Because there is no purpose [for it], it is not added to the tenth chapter."]

[Page 469] Bhāṣya: Therefore, because of the act of pacifying (*śamana*), the *adhvaryu* is the *śamitṛ*. This being the case, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), who is not part of the original context (*aprakṛta*), becomes connected [with the role]. (3.7.13) [Adhikaraṇa].
The section on the eight separate legal cases concluded. *Sra.* (End of chapter).
Upagamyāṣṭapṛthakkādhikaraṇam. (The section on the eight distinct matters following the approach).
And the Upagās [are to be sung] because of the observation of indicative marks. || 30 ||

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there are those called the *santapanīya* chanters; because of the difference in their names, they are understood to bring about a mixture [of functions]. This being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), we reply: some of them alone should be [the chanters]. Why? Because they are enumerated at the time of origin and because the word is etymological. This is an indicative mark (*liṅga*): "The Adhvaryu should not chant as an assistant. If there were others besides these, he would not have prohibited the Adhvaryu, since [the prohibition] would not apply [to him].

Since, however, he prohibits [the purchase from anyone else], we understand from this that it must be one of those specifically mentioned in connection with the originative injunction. (3.7.14 Śrauta-sūtra).
Section Kha: The Topic on the Distinctness of the Soma-Seller.
But the seller is different, because his action is not enjoined.

HIT. There is a doubt regarding the seller of Soma: is he one of those [classes] such as the *adhvaryu* and others, or is he someone other than them? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Since they are enumerated, it follows that he is one of them. To this we reply: "The seller, however, must be another. For the act of selling is not enjoined; rather, the act of buying is enjoined, and therein lies the purposeful action.

Furthermore, the Adhvaryu and other priests are produced for the purpose of performing the constituent parts of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; however, no sale of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself is heard of in the scripture. Therefore, none of them [the priests] is [to be purchased]. (3.7.15)
[Page 470] The section concerning the non-universality of the rule regarding the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Sūtra: Because the performance of the ritual action belongs to all [the priests] without distinction, they are all officiating priests (ṛtvij). || 32 ||
Bhāṣya-sra-bhāṣya (The Commentary on the Bhāṣya on the Sūtras)
( Pūrvapakṣa ) ||

Regarding these persons who are mentioned in connection with the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice: are they all officiating priests (ṛtvij), or only some among them? What is the prima facie view? All of them. Why?
"Because of the performance of the ritual action, all perform the means of sacrifice; therefore, all who sacrifice during the season are priests (*ṛtvij*), and no distinction is relied upon— namely,
that 'only these sacrifice during the season' are priests, while these are not."
— thus [it is said]. Therefore, [the rule applies] to all officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). [Objection:

But surely a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṅkhyā*) is heard in the text: "There are seventeen priests for the Soma sacrifice, the sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*). [Response: It is replied that in a restrictive enumeration, many [implications would follow].
The statement "defects exist" will result in both literal exclusion and figurative denial.
Or rather, it is not so, because of the enumeration. (Siddhānta) || 33 ||

Nor indeed all [the priests]. Why? Because of the enumeration; for it is heard thus: "There are seventeen priests for the Soma sacrifice, the Adhvara ritual. This is not an injunction (*vidhi*), because a greater number [of priests] is already established by other means. It is not a restatement (*anuvāda*), because there would be no purpose for it. And if it were not even an enumeration, it would be utterly meaningless.

"Is it not the case that in the restrictive enumeration (parisaṅkhyā), there is the abandonment of one's own meaning, the assumption of another's meaning, and the sublation of what has been obtained? It is replied: the abandonment of one's own meaning is not a fault, because it has already been established. And the assumption of another's meaning follows from the cognition [of the text]. How so? When the office of the priests (ṛtvij) is already known, the statement "there are seventeen priests" is made; thus, the word "priest" is again connected with the number seventeen.

It is manifested [by seventeen], and not manifested by more than that. In this regard, it is understood that when the word "officiant" (*ṛtvij*) is connected with persons and manifested again, it is understood that those in excess of seventeen are excluded. Here, is the connection with the seventeen intended, or is the exclusion of the additional ones intended? Since the connection with the seventeen is not the purposeful factor, it is understood that the exclusion of the additional ones is what is intended.

He says: "But surely, even when the additional [priests] are being excluded, the exclusion does not apply; for they do not fail to sacrifice during the season, nor would those sacrificing during the season cease to be *ṛtvij*s. It is replied: "True, but not because of the exclusion by the word *ṛtvij*."

It is not connected [to the prohibition], but rather, by the force of the negation itself, they do not perform the duties of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). What, then, are the duties of the officiating priests? They are: "The officiating priests fast," "He shaves the officiating priests," and "He gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests."

He asks: "How could that which is the duty of the *ṛtvij*s not belong to some who possess the word *ṛtvij*? It is replied: In that case, the word *ṛtvij* is of two kinds—based on the performance of seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtuyajana*) and based on selection and maintenance (*varaṇabharaṇa*). Of these, the acceptance of the [word] based on sacrifice would be purposeless; therefore, it is understood as being based on selection and maintenance. He says: "But in this way, there is indeed mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): those who are *ṛtvij*s are to be selected, and those who are selected are *ṛtvij*s"—this is mutual dependence. It is replied:

The meaning of "one does not choose the priests" is not that those who are already priests are to be chosen; how then? It is that they become priests through the act of choosing. In this way, the use of the accusative case will be appropriate, as in the expression "he chooses the Adhvaryu priest. Furthermore, the act of choosing will thus serve a visible purpose.
If someone were to ask, "How does it come about through one's own desire that there is an Adhvaryu?", I would say, "It comes about. How?
[One might think: "This ritual act must be performed with the word 'evam' (thus)," yet there is no such word; and as for that which does not exist, if it can be brought into being, [then it exists].

He becomes the performer; just as in the case of the scriptural injunction "one offers with the *juhū*," where a *juhū* is made even though it was not previously existing, so too should this be understood. In that regard, when the connection with the term "officiant" (*ṛtvij*) is to be established without restriction, it must be established by means of a specific selection (*varaṇa*). Thus is the rule.

It is excluded. Therefore, there is no mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya). Consequently, the restriction (parisaṅkhyā) is that only seventeen priests (ṛtvij) are to be appointed by means of the purificatory rites (saṃskāra)—thus the seventeen priests are established as the performers.
Thus [ends] the commentary on the Sūtra.
If it is argued that [the result follows] after half a month, (Ābhāsya) || 34 ||

If you think thus—that this is stated according to the aforementioned position, whereas according to the position of the *apoddhāra* (separate mention) there are seventeen priests—then that must be refuted.
"It is not the case that all [persons] lack qualification. (0 Ni0) Bhāṣya:

This is not so; for here there is no mention of all persons, such that there would be a partial statement (*avayutya-vāda*) with respect to them; rather, it is where a higher number is mentioned that [the rule applies].

There is a partial statement (*avayutyavāda*), as for example: "When there is a cake on twelve potsherds, that which is on eight potsherds..."—but here no higher number is mentioned. Therefore, it is not a partial statement. (3.7.16)
Sūtra Bhāṣya:
The section concerning whether Brahmā and the others mentioned in the passages regarding initiation and sacrificial fees are indeed the seventeen officiating priests.
But there is a restrictive rule regarding the sacrificial fees, because of their connection with the Vedic revelation.

It has been established that there are seventeen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Which are those seventeen? This is the point of inquiry. What is the prima facie view? There is uncertainty. To this, we reply: there is a restriction by means of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), because of their connection with the Vedic text; they should be restricted through their association with the fees, for it is thus recorded in scripture: "He gives the sacrificial fee to the officiating priests."

—Thus, having spoken thus, in the subsequent sentences concerning the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), Brahmā and others are heard: "He gives to the *agnīdh* priests," "then to the *brahman* priest," and "then to such-and-such and such-and-such"—only certain specific individuals are thus heard mentioned. Such are those who are so heard.
They are indeed the officiating priests (ṛtvij); therefore, no others can possibly be more qualified than them, for such is the restriction established by those [scriptural] authorities.
Chapter 3, Section 7.
And their status as sacrificers has been stated, because of the injunction for their initiation (dīkṣā). || 37 ||
bhā.
(yu0) || [Commentary: (the second half)] ||

Having stated, "Those who are the officiating priests (ṛtvij) are the sacrificers (yajamāna)," the text demonstrates the initiation (dīkṣā) in a subsequent passage concerning the sequence of initiation for the Brahman and others. How so? "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati, initiates the Brahman; then the Udgātṛ, then the Hotṛ. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having initiated him, initiates the Ardhins."

The Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin from the Brahman, the Prastotṛ from the Udgātṛ, and the Maitrāvaruṇa from the Hotṛ. Then, having initiated him, the Neṣṭṛ initiates the third group: the Āgnīdhra from the Brahman, the Pratihartṛ from the Udgātṛ, and the Acchāvāka from the Hotṛ. Then, having initiated him, the Unnetṛ initiates the fourth group: the Potṛ from the Brahman and the Subrahmaṇya from the Udgātṛ.

The Grāvastut priest is initiated by the Hotṛ; thereafter, another Brāhmaṇa initiates him, or a religious student (brahmacārī) sent by his teacher—so it is said. And initiation (dīkṣā) is a refinement (saṃskāra) of the sacrificer.
Therefore, the seventeen priests, beginning with the Brahman, [are the ones to be initiated]. (3.7.17)
The section concerning the fact that the officiating priests (ṛtvij) are seventeen, including the master of the sacrifice (khāmin).
The seventeen priests, including the master, [are entitled to the sacrificial fee] because of their commonality of function.

Bhāṣya: This has been stated—that there are seventeen priests—and these are the Brahman and the others. In this regard, a doubt arises: is the Sadasya the seventeenth among them, or is it the Gṛhapati? What, then, is the prima facie view? That the Sadasya is [the seventeenth], for he is a performer of the ritual action, whereas the other is the master.
Furthermore, whoever is a laborer must be hired, and the officiating priests (ṛtvij) are hired;
therefore, the Sadasya is the seventeenth priest. Moreover, they prescribe for him a cup and his formal selection (varaṇa);
a priest is to be selected, not the master [of the sacrifice]; therefore, the Sadasya is the seventeenth.
This being the position reached, it is said in reply: "The master is the seventeenth, because of the commonality of the ritual action.

The master should be the seventeenth among them. Why? Because of the commonality of the ritual action; in the sacrifice, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are the performers, and in the sacrifice, the householder (*gṛhapati*) is also a performer; therefore, he is an officiating priest.

[Page 474] Bhāṣya: Because of the commonality of sacrificial ritual. As it has been stated—"They prescribe him; they prescribe his cup and his selection; therefore the Sadasya is the seventeenth"—it is replied: They prescribe only the Brahman priest; both the selection and the cup belong to the Brahman alone, for he is the one who exists in the *sadas* (the sacrificial hall); therefore, the master is the seventeenth. (3.7.18 Śrauta Sūtra).
The section concerning the restriction of the agency of the Adhvaryu and others among those who speak the Yajus formulas.
And because of the context, the root *bhū* possesses the sense of both the original material and its modification for all purposes.
All their purposes are accomplished because they have been employed, and the fires [are established] because of their own specific time. || 38 ||
(Pūrvapakṣa) ||

The seventeen priests of the Jyotiṣṭoma have been established. Now, in this regard, there arises this doubt: should all the duties pertaining to the person be performed by them, as well as those pertaining to the fires?

Is the fire-ritual (agnikārya) performed with the Gārhapatya and other fires, or is it some particular state? What, then, is the prima facie position? "They [the fires] are for all purposes because they are employed; and the fires are for their own time. Thus, those fires would be for every human purpose, and the fires for the fire-ritual. Why? Because they are required by those rituals, there is a specific appropriation of them for each respective purpose.
The restatement is justified because of their own specific time; and the fires are accompanied by all the paths—this has been established. (3.7.19) [Sūtra]

"Furthermore, as for those [fires] such as the Āhavanīya and others, their being for all purposes is entirely irrelevant and is not mentioned even by way of incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*), because the reason—that they are for a specific time—is also ineffective. Moreover, in the rejoinder (*uttarapakṣa*), there is no reference whatsoever to the subject (*pakṣa*) or the reason (*hetu*) of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Starting from this point, [the text continues]: "This is indeed a statement of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), because there is no expression of a refutation. Therefore, it is described in this way: it is not the case that the universal purposefulness (*sarvārthatva*) of these fires was made the subject of the prima facie position; rather, according to the logic stated in another sutra concerning a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*), the prima facie and final positions are like those regarding the installation (*ādhāna*)."

They must be established: are the Āhavanīya and other fires for the sake of the archetype (*prakṛti*) alone, or rather with respect to both the archetype and the ectype (*vikṛti*)? In that regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they are for the sake of the archetype, just like other *anārabhyavāda* (unattached) injunctions; as it has been stated, "Or rather, [they belong] to the archetype, because of the specification of direction.
This being the position reached, it is replied: the fire-altars (*agni*) should serve all purposes. Why? Because of their having their own time;
the meaning is that they possess independent origination. Thus, this has been described: the establishment of the fire-altars serves all purposes due to its own specific time.
In this context, the Vārttika beginning with "tvādityatra" should be recalled.
[Page 475] The established conclusion (siddhānta) of the section concerning the restriction of agency for the Adhvaryu and others specifically to the duties of the Adhvaryu and so forth.
Sūtra: There would be a restriction [of the application] of the ritual act due to its connection with that [specific person], because the connection has a purpose. (Conclusion) || 40 ||
Commentary:

"From that connection" means from the connection with a specific person; [the ritual] is restricted such that those [acts] which are designated by a particular person must be performed by him. In this way, the connection of these [acts] with the persons will be meaningful: the *adhvaryava* by the *adhvaryu*, the *hautra* by the *hotṛ*, and the *audgātra* by the *udgātṛ*.
"By the Udgātṛ"— thus [ends the section].
(3.7.20a) This is the section concerning the occasional sublation of the agency established by the name of the ritual manual (*samākhyā*).
Its exposition is by means of the explanation of its instruction. || 41 ||
Bhāṣya: Is this the universal rule—that everything designated by names must be performed by the persons whose names they bear?

We say: no; for there is a specific assignment based on direct instruction (*upadeśa*) and specific designation (*samākhyā*). As for direct instruction: "Therefore, the Maitrāvaruṇa gives the directions and recites the responses. As for designation: "The *potrīyā* [verse], the *neṣṭrīyā* [verse]. This is an exception to the general rule of designation.
And there is also the observation of an indicative mark to that effect. || 42 ||

Bhāṣya: Where it says, "One should listen to the Hotṛ reciting the Prātaranuvāka," this indicates that the Hotṛ is obtained for the Prātaranuvāka by virtue of its designation (*samākhyā*). Likewise, there is this further indicative mark (*liṅga*): "The *udgītha* belongs to the Udgātṛs; the *praṇava* of the Ṛks belongs to the Uktha-reciters."

"This very sūtra, which serves as a supplement by preventing over-extension (atiprasaṅga) regarding application through name (*samākhyā-viniyoga*), constitutes a separate section (*adhikaraṇāntara*," so says the *Śāstradīpikā*.
[Page 476] Bhāṣya: "The *pratihāra* belongs to the *adhvaryu*s"—thus it shows a distinction established by convention;
likewise, this also serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*): "He who knows his own [portion], O *adhvaryu*, becomes possessed of his own."
"This belongs to the Adhvaryu himself when he causes [the Hotṛ] to announce"—

this shows the restrictive rule established by the name [of the office]. (3.7.21) [This concludes the section concerning] the Maitrāvaruṇa as the performer of both the recitation and the command when they are combined.
The recitation of the *praisha* belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa, because of the direct scriptural instruction. (Pūrvapakṣa) 43.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, as it is stated: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. Regarding this, they recite: "Therefore, the Maitrāvaruṇa priest gives the directions and also recites the responses. In this regard, there arises a doubt.

—Should the Maitrāvaruṇa priest function at all recitations (anuvacana) and all commands (praiṣa), or only where there is a command within a recitation? What, then, is the prima facie view? He should function at all recitations, because there is no distinction; for no specific distinction is adopted, such as "in this particular recitation..."
"The Maitrāvaruṇa is here"—thus [it is said]. Therefore, in all recitations (anuvacana) and in all directions (praiṣa), there should be a Maitrāvaruṇa.
Or rather, it is the section concerning the *puro'nuvākyā*, because of the proximity of the *praiṣa* (direction). 44.
(Sūtra 10)
The Bhāṣya says: Or rather, the Maitrāvaruṇa should recite the *puronuvākyā*. Why?

Because the Maitrāvaruṇa is present where both the *praiṣa* (direction) and the *anuvākyā* (invitatory verse) are mentioned together; he is not present where there is only the *anuvākyā*, nor where there is only the *praiṣa*; [but he is present] where both are found.
They are combined; in that case, he would be [the one performing both], for they prescribe him as such when the two are combined— namely,
"therefore the Maitrāvaruṇa gives the directions and also recites"— and from the word "and" (ca), it is understood that the two are combined.
Sūtrabhāṣya [Page 477]
And because the Hotṛ is seen [performing it] during the Prātaranuvāka. (Yukti) || 45 ||

From this also we see that the Maitrāvaruṇa does not participate in all recitations. Why? Because [the text] indicates the Hotṛ specifically in connection with the morning recitation (prātaranuvāka). How so? [It says]: "When he should overhear the Hotṛ as he is reciting the morning recitation, then the Adhvaryu should take [the cup]. Therefore, the Maitrāvaruṇa does not participate in all recitations. (3)
7 | 22 (Śrauta-sūtra) ||
In the cup-offering, the duties are to be performed by the *camasādhvaryu*s; because of their designation, the *camasādhvaryu*s [are the performers] of the cups. (Sūtra 46, Pūrvapakṣa)

HIT. There are the *camasādhvaryus*; regarding them, a doubt arises: should the *camasādhvaryus* offer the cups, or should the *adhvaryu* do so? We say: the *camasādhvaryus*. Why? Because they perform the duties of the *adhvaryu* with respect to the cups; thus they are called *camasādhvaryus*.
Therefore, they should offer oblations—thus it is said.
Sūtra: Or rather, the Adhvaryu [should perform it], because of his being the one who extends the ritual. (Siddhānta) || 47 ||

The Bhāṣya states: Either the Adhvaryu should offer the oblation; for this is the logical rule—that whatever constitutes an Adhvaryu-function, the Adhvaryu should perform it, and since the offering (*homa*) is an Adhvaryu-function, therefore the Adhvaryu should offer it.

[Objection]: "But surely the Camasādhvaryus [should offer], because of the specific designation (*samākhyāna*); the Camasādhvaryus shall offer. [Reply]: No, it is said in response. They are called *camasādhvaryus* because they are engaged in the service of the cups (*camasa*). If the Adhvaryu offers by means of them, then the offering must also be performed by those Camasādhvaryus. If the Camasādhvaryus offer and not the Adhvaryu, then [the Adhvaryu's role would be lost].
Therefore, the Camasādhvaryus would not be like that; hence, they should not offer the oblation.
And there is another *camasa* cup, because it is seen [in the texts]. (Yukti 48)

The Bhāṣya also shows another Camasādhvaryu in connection with the *camasa*. How so? "He hands over the *camasa*s to the Camasādhvaryus; he carries them away at the *vaṣaṭ*-call; another, having carried them away... [Page 478] Bhāṣya.

It is understood that he hands it over to the *camasādhvaryu*. How so? It is understood that "he moves toward the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer" means for the purpose of consuming [the soma]. Therefore, the handing over is to the *camasādhvaryu*; he who offers the oblation is the one who hands it over.
Consequently, [the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer] is someone other [than the *camasādhvaryu*].

"He offers"—thus it is said. Furthermore: "He who knows what belongs to the Adhvaryu becomes possessed of property; the ladle is the Adhvaryu's property, the Vāyavya cup is his property, the Camasa is his property.
Now, this Camasa is not his [the Adhvaryu's] own property, for it belongs to the sacrificer (yajamāna). It is the Camasa of this [sacrificer].
By saying "kham," he indicates the offering with the Adhvaryu's cup.

In the Bhāṣya:
There is the Śyena sacrifice prescribed for the Udgātṛ, and the Vājapeya for the Adhvaryu. In that regard—

There is a doubt: should the ritual acts in the Śyena sacrifice be performed by the Udgātṛ priests alone, and in the Vājapeya by the Adhvaryu priests, or in both cases by various priests? What is the prima facie view?—“On account of the instruction of the Veda (that is, on account of the designation), as in the previous case. Just as, for example:

On account of the designation "Adhvaryava," the Adhvaryu performs the constituent acts; likewise, "when there is a difference of Veda, they should be according to the instruction"—that is, whatever act is taught in a Veda designated by a particular name, its constituent acts must be performed by that very person; for it is taught there as being complete with its auxiliary parts.
Therefore, in the *Śunaḥśepa* sacrifice, the acts are to be performed by the Udgātṛs, and in the *Vājapeya*, by the Adhvaryus.
[Page 479] Or rather, it would be his own duty because of the force of the qualification; for that which is unmanifested is to be performed together with the remainder. (Siddhānta) || 51 ||

Bhāṣya: Either it would be its own duty (because of the inclusion of that [Prākṛta dharma]), or, being connected [to the archetype] through the force of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), it should perform it along with the subsidiaries—so it is heard.

And those subsidiaries exist in the Jyotiṣṭoma; they are not seen there [in the archetype], so in that Jyotiṣṭoma, there are no priests other than those [already present], and with them it forms a single syntactical unit.
[Objection: "But the name is perceptible, whereas the extended application (codaka) is inferential. [Reply:
It is true that the name is perceptible, but it is merely worldly; in that context, it must be inferred.

The Vedic word would have syntactic unity with that [direct injunction], whereas the *codaka* (extended application) has syntactic unity with a directly perceived procedure (*itikartavyatā*) studied in a remote context. Therefore, the *codaka* is more powerful. As for what was said—"on account of the name"—to that it is replied: "In the case of the remainder, it is indistinct."

It will be determined by name—that which is not obtained through the general rule (*codaka*) shall be restricted by the name. For example, in the *Śyena* sacrifice, it is said, "they pierce with thorns"—thus the *udgātṛ*s will perform the piercing; and in the *Vājapeya*, it is said, "they offer with leaf-cups"—thus the *adhvaryu*s will perform the offering. (3.7.24)
Thus ends the seventh quarter of the third chapter in the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya composed by the venerable Śabarasvāmin.

The hiring of the master [is an act] for the sake of the ritual action, because the action has that as its purpose. || 1 ||

Regarding this, there is a doubt: are the priests to be purchased by the Adhvaryu, or by the master [the sacrificer]? What is the prima facie view? [It is] on account of the designation (*samākhyāna*).
When it is argued that [the ritual] should be performed by one who has studied the Veda (*adhyāyī*), we reply: "The act of hiring (*pariśraya*) is the duty of the master (*svāmikarma*). Why?

Because the action is for his sake; for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is one who desires the fruit, and he who desires the fruit must perform it himself. If he hires [assistants], then he performs everything himself."
— thus it is understood; if, however, he does not purchase [the services], he would not perform all [the rites]. Therefore, the owner must purchase [the services].
For the others, it would be by means of speech. || * 2 ||

But the preparatory rites (saṃskāras), depending on the capacity of the person, should remain fixed according to the Veda, just like the ritual acts themselves. (Pūrvapakṣa)
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "He shaves his hair and beard, cleanses his teeth, pares his nails, and bathes. Regarding this, there is a doubt:

are such acts to be performed by the Adhvaryu priest, or by the sacrificer? What is the prima facie view? They are to be performed by the Adhvaryu; for purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are restricted according to the Veda, based on the designation (samākhyāna).
By the person, like a ritual act—just as other matters taught in a particular Veda are performed by the person designated by that same name, so too are these [rites]. Thus [it is said].
[Objection: But [the acts] belong to the sacrificer, because they have him as their primary purpose, like the ritual act itself.

(Siddhānta) [Commentary: Or rather, they should be performed by the sacrificer. Why? Because the person is the primary element. How is the person the primary element? The fruit of the action is understood to be intended for the agent; therefore, these acts produce in the person the capacity to perform the ritual work. And there is no one [else] by whom...

By means of performing the action, capacity is produced; for that purpose, one purchases men. One purchases them from those things desired, so that by whatever means a person's capacity arises, it must be performed by that very means, like the primary action. Just as the primary actions serve the purposes of the sacrificer, so too does this.
And because of the designation. (Sūtra 5) (Haituka).

For the connection of the persons with the acts of shaving and so forth must be inferred, because it would serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*); whereas [the connection] with the directly contributing subsidiaries (*ārādupakāraka*) is already established. And when a [connection] is already established, one should not infer another.
It is possible to conceive [it thus]; therefore, the convention would not be the regulator when the person is primary.

And because [the result] exists in relation to the injunction. (Hetuvāda)

for since they are impossible [directly] with respect to substances, they are postulated in relation to them. And in the absence of proximate substances, they would apply to remote ones; but when they are possible with respect to a proximate substance, then they do not apply to remote ones.
They should be performed by the sacrificer, because their purpose has been fulfilled; therefore, they belong to the sacrificer.
Because they are unequal, they would have different rules of application. (Sūtra 8) [0 Nigamana]

(This is a sūtra following the preceding word: "Now, why are they not of equal injunction? Because the injunctions are made without distinction, they would apply to all persons. To this it is said:

— This injunction does not apply equally to all persons. Why? Because of inequality; for these [persons] are unequal with respect to this injunction. What is the inequality? That which is prescribed for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is not prescribed for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). How is it prescribed for the sacrificer?
—how is this understood? [It is understood] that "the one who desires [the result] should perform [the acts] himself. [Objection:

But since there is no distinction, they are prescribed for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) as well. [Reply: We see that they are not prescribed for them because of the absence of purpose. How is there an absence of purpose?

Acts performed by the officiating priests are neither performed nor caused to be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), because the purchase (*parikraya*) is for the sake of what is heard [in the scripture]; and acts performed by oneself do not benefit the one who desires [the result]. They are purposeless; therefore, they are not prescribed for the officiating priests—this is their commonality. Consequently, they do not share the same injunctions. (3.8.2)

The section concerning the sacrificer's status in relation to austerity.
And austerity [is effective] because it results in the attainment of its fruit, as is seen in the world. || 8 ||

Regarding austerity (tapas), it is heard: "I do not eat," "I do not drink," "I do not consume food. In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the austerity that of the officiating priest (ārtvija) or that of the sacrificer (yājamāna)?
What is the prima facie view? On account of the designation (samākhyāna), it follows that the austerity is that of the officiating priest. Thus...
To this we reply: the austerity belongs to the sacrificer. Why? Because it is for the sake of accomplishing the fruit;

austerity is for the purpose of achieving the fruit, and the fruit of the sacrifice is accomplished by one who has perfected his austerity. How is this understood? For austerity is suffering, and suffering is the fruit of demerit (*adharma*); demerit acts as an obstacle to the fruit of the sacrifice, for it is detrimental. As long as that [demerit] exists, [the fruit does not arise].

Therefore, it ought to lead to what is beneficial; thus, dharma and adharma are counteracted by the experience of their fruits. Consequently, dharma is heard of as resulting in the experience of the fruit of suffering.
That which is to be produced as suffering by that [adharma] is this very thing—thus it becomes something with a perceptible purpose.

One should not assume an unseen principle (*adṛṣṭa*); rather, the sacrifice, being connected with that exhausted merit through the enjoyment of its fruit, will bestow the result. Furthermore, the accomplishment of the fruit belongs to the sacrificer, not to the officiating priests. Therefore, austerity is a duty of the sacrificer.
And the remainder of the sentence is like that. (Yukti)
The *Vākyaśeṣa* also illuminates this very meaning: "When indeed nothing remains within a person, when the black of his eye vanishes, then he is most fit for sacrifice (*medhyatama*)";
thus, when there is fasting, then there is *medhā*, and *medha* is sacrifice.
Sacrifice is renunciation; "it is accomplished through austerity" is the completion of the sentence, and the sacrificer is the one who renounces. Therefore, austerity belongs to the sacrificer.
For the others, it should be by means of speech; this is the distinction. (11)
Is this the general rule—that all austerity belongs to the sacrificer?
No.
[Page 484]
Bhāṣya: "Because of the statement regarding others"; and where there is a statement, it concerns the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), as for example: "All the officiating priests fast. (3.8.3).
The commentary [states]:
"The removal of expectancy; [this concerns] the red turban and so forth, in relation to the section on the universal dharma."
And because it is a quality, there would be no restriction by means of the Veda. || 12 ||

Now, as for what was stated— that "the austerity belongs to the officiating priest because of its designation"— it is not designated by that name because it is a subordinate factor; for where the person is subordinate, there the designation serves as a regulator.

Or likewise, in the Śyena sacrifice it is heard: "The priests proceed wearing red turbans and red garments"; similarly, in the Vājapeya it is heard: "The priests proceed wearing golden garlands. In this regard, there is a doubt: should the wearing of red turbans be performed by the Udgātṛs in the Śyena, and the wearing of golden garlands by the Adhvaryus in the Vājapeya; or rather, should both be performed by all the priests? What [is the conclusion]?
Is it thus established?—that by virtue of the designation (*samākhyāna*), the [rite] in the Śyena sacrifice is performed by the Udgātṛs, and in the Vājapeya by the Adhvaryus.
This being the position reached, we reply: "And because it is a subordinate factor (*guṇatva*), there would be no restriction by means of the Veda";
for the red turban and the golden necklace are subordinate qualities (*guṇa*), while the person is the primary factor (*pradhāna*).

Therefore, the red turban and the golden garland are heard in scripture as qualifications of the person, not as something to be performed; hence, the person is the primary factor. What follows from this? If this is so, then when the persons are the primary factors, the name (*samākhyā*) is not restrictive—this has been stated.

Moreover, because it is heard as a subordinate element (*guṇatva*), this injunction is understood to apply to all priests; for a subordinate element being taught in proximity to a principal element (*pradhāna*) is prescribed with respect to each principal element.

How, then, could that which is obtained by direct statement (*vacana*) be restricted by a name (*samākhyā*), even though such a name exists? Therefore, in both cases, [the rite is to be performed] by all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
“A ritual act of this kind should be performed”—thus [it is stated]. (3.8.4 Śrauta Sūtra)

Likewise, desire [is established] through its connection with purpose. (13)
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, they recite: "If he should desire, 'May Parjanya rain,' he should erect the Sadas shed low. Regarding this, there is a doubt:
Is the desire that of the officiating priests (ṛtvij), or is it that of the sacrificer (yajamāna)? Why so? If...

Should the desire belong to the Adhvaryu priest, or to the sacrificer?—thus arises the doubt. What is the prima facie view? The desire belongs to the officiating priest, because of the designation; for the Adhvaryu is the one who performs the ritual action, and he is connected by the sentence with the act of "measuring," therefore the desire belongs to the officiating priest. This being the position, we reply: "The desire should be such as austerity [is]; that is to say, the desire belongs to the sacrificer. Why? Because of the connection with the purpose; the sacrificer is connected with the fruit of the sacrifice along with its constituent parts.

—thus it is understood. Because of the specific verbal suffix (*upagraha*), as in "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma"—due to this specific suffix, and because of [the rule] "he should measure," it is understood that the Adhvaryu acts for the sake of another. Now, as for what was said—that [the mantra] forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the person who has a need—it is replied: even so, there is a single syntactical unit with the original statement regarding the sacrificer.
"One should measure [the altar] while desiring [a specific result]."
There would be [a distinction] for the others because of their designation; this is the specific point. || 14 || (The Distinction) ||

Where there is a specific designation, there the desire belongs to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), as in: "Whatever desire the *udgātṛ* desires for himself or for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), that he brings about by singing. If [the phrase] "for himself" were to be restricted to mean "for the sacrificer," then both the mention of the "sacrificer" and the word "or" (*vā*) would be rendered purposeless. Therefore...
It is understood that by designating the sacrificer, the Udgātṛ refers to himself—thus [it is concluded]. (Sūtra 3.8.5)

In this context, such examples as "O Āyu, give me life" and "O Agni, you are speech; give me speech" have been cited by me. Regarding these, there is a doubt: are they to be performed by the officiating priests (ṛtvij) or by the sacrificer (yajamāna)?
Based on the name [of the section], it is initially concluded that they are to be performed by the officiating priests.

This being the case, we reply: these [words] should be like that; just as there is a desire, so too a word denoting the self is appropriate. In the phrases "May there be life for me," "May there be vigor for me," and so forth, the fruit of action is denoted by such expressions as "life" and "vigor," [meaning] "O Agni, accomplish the fruit of my action for me. Thus, here the fruit of action is proclaimed for the sake of generating enthusiasm.

And it is the sacrificer who exerts himself through that [fire], not anyone else; for the fruit of the action belongs to the officiating priests, and the fire is not for their sake, since that [fruit] is already established.
That which belongs to the sacrificer is for the sake of the fire, and being unestablished, it must be brought about; thus, it generates exertion so that there may be no deficiency.
Even when the officiating priest exerts himself for what has been accomplished, he exerts himself solely for the sake of the fruit of the ritual act belonging to the sacrificer;
in that case, a word denoting the self [of the priest] would not be appropriate, whereas a word denoting the self [of the sacrificer], when applied to the sacrificer, is non-figurative. Therefore...
The duties of the sacrificer.
And because it is seen [to occur] even in separation. (Yukti 16)

And in the case of separation from the fires, there is a ritual attendance during travel [expressed by the mantra]: "O Agni, being thus, [attend] you who are there. Furthermore, one who is away on a journey does not become a priest (*ṛtvij*) for the fires;
this word denotes one who performs the ritual action. However, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) indeed remains [connected] to the fires.
Even when away from home, the sacrificer, having made arrangements for the *agnihotra*, departs;
and it is possible for the renunciation [of the offering] to be performed even by one staying in a foreign land.
By specifying that very particular form of attendance (*upasthāna*) for one who is away, [the text] demonstrates the attendance of the sacrificer himself. For that very reason...
And there should be such persons as these for the sacrificer—thus [it is said]. (3.8.6 Śrauta Sūtra).

"—Because of the designation, they belong to the Adhvaryu. This being the prima facie view, it is replied: "Both should employ them. Why?

should both the learned and the unlearned be made to recite, or only the learned? What is the prima facie view? Since there is no distinction specified, both the learned and the unlearned.

This being the position reached, we reply: it is indeed the knower (*jña*) [who is entitled]. Why? [The opponent argues: "In the Mīmāṃsā system, one would be entitled [to perform rituals] immediately. We say: "No. The performance [of rituals] is heard to occur after the study of the Veda; the study of the Veda is not itself grasped by the injunction for performance. Why?
Because it is heard in the Veda as an independent injunction regarding action: "Therefore, you must study your own portion of the Veda (svādhyāya)."
Thus, while this statement exists, it cannot be postulated that by such injunctions as "one should offer the Agnihotra," it is meant that "the Veda is to be studied.
In that case, when only the oblation is enjoined, one who is capable of studying the Veda is qualified [to perform it], but not otherwise.
[The opponent asks: "By knowing how much, however, does one become a learned person (vidvān) entitled [to perform a sacrifice]?"—[the answer is:
by that much which, once known, enables one to accomplish the sacrifice as it has been described.
Therefore, he who knows that much is entitled to that sacrifice.

"Now, it might be argued: 'From the injunction "one should study the Veda," it follows that the entire Veda must be studied; one is not entitled [to perform rites] by means of a mere portion of the Veda. To this we reply: The study of the Veda is to be performed for the sake of knowing the sacrificial rites (*kratu*). In that regard, when one particular rite is to be performed, knowledge of another rite does not serve a visible purpose. Therefore, knowledge of other rites need not be taken into account for the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform a specific rite. For the sake of knowing one rite, there is the textual portion (*grantha*) of that specific rite; yet all rites [are contained within the Veda].

How are they to be known?—it is heard that the study of the entire Veda is to be performed separately and separately; therefore, one who knows the meaning of his own words (the portion he has studied) would be entitled [to perform the rites]. Consequently, for one who does not know the meaning of his own words, there is no ritual action at all; how could such a person be permitted to recite? Therefore, it is stated [that knowledge is] a means to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
—this alone should be recited—thus [it is said]. (3.8.8a)

On account of the designation, they should belong to the sacrificer in the ritual action; it is understood that they belong to the sacrificer because of their specific designation, just as [the mantras] are designated as "pertaining to the Potṛ" (potrīya) or "pertaining to the Neṣṭṛ" (neṣṭrīya).
Or rather, it is the Adhvaryu [who performs it], for the designation is based on reasoning directed toward that purpose. || 20 ||

The Adhvaryu should perform these [acts], for it is understood from the designation (*samākhyāna*) that the Adhvaryu was hired for that purpose: "All these constituent elements (*padārtha*) are recited in the *Adhvaryava* section; their mention in the *Yājamāna* section is merely a reference (*indatā*), and a reference is an act performed in proximity. In that case, the Adhvaryu will perform the constituent elements, and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) as well...

"Making [the two] proximate"—this is impossible. In that case, regarding the conflict between the subsidiary (aṅga) and its quality (guṇa), because the purpose is for that [subordinate], the quality of being a pair (dvandvatā) must be set aside. Therefore, these ritual items belong to the Adhvaryu.
As for what was stated— that it is "because of the designation"— that must be refuted; it is now said in reply:
"An explanation preceded by logic": on account of this explanation, the sacrificer must accomplish the staff-bearing; the sacrificer should say, "Accomplish this and that.
Furthermore, regarding certain ritual items, there is an authorization (anumantraṇa) for the sacrificer, and the designation [of the office] will be based on that;
however, the unprecedented [element] would be displaced. As it was said: "Just as in the case of the *potrīya* and the *neṣṭrīya* [offices]."

— thus, it is the same here as well; to this it is replied: it is logical that there, the removal of the calves by means of a *palāśa* branch is one action, while the placing of the pot to hold the milk produced by milking is another action; Mādhava maintains that these two together constitute a single *indram*.

[Page 490] Bhāṣya: Because of the designation (*samākhyāna*), here the staff (*daṇḍatā*) belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamānīyā*), whereas the ritual acts (*padārtha*) belong exclusively to the Adhvaryu priest. Therefore, there is no fault. (3.8.9) [Adhikaraṇa].
