Sūtra: In case of conflict, the instrument [is decisive], because of a specific relation; the other is different from them, since it is from that [instrument] that their distinction arises. // 21 //

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma; for its sacrificial post (*yūpa*), there are two formulas for encircling it: one is the instrument [formula], "Thou art the enclosure of the Adhvaryu," and the other...

The mantra "hotā yuvā suvāsāḥ" is a *kriyamāṇānuvādī* (an after-recitation). Since both of these mantras are obtained in the *Kuṇḍapāyināmayana* sacrifice through a series of extended injunctions (*codaka*), a doubt arises: what is it? In that context, the appointment of priests is prescribed as: "He who is the *hotṛ* is also the *adhvaryu*. Should the *hotṛ* perform the duties of the *adhvaryu*, or should he perform the *hotṛ*-duties consisting of the *kriyamāṇānuvādī*? What is the prima facie view? There is no fixed rule.

This being the prima facie position, it is replied: in case of conflict, the instrument [the mantra] should be used—namely, "O Adhvaryu, thou art the encircler"—and not the Hotṛ's descriptive recitation of the action in progress, "Thou, young and well-clothed.
Why? Because of the distinction in their application; for there are two distinct applications in that context.

In the case of the *hautra* functions, it is by means of the *codaka* (extended application); in the case of the *ādhvaryava* functions, it is by direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śravaṇa*), as in: "He who is the *hotṛ* is the *adhvaryu*. Thus, the duty of the *adhvaryu* is enjoined directly;
and direct statement is stronger than inference. Therefore, the performance of the *ādhvaryava* function is [enjoined] with the mantra: "Thou art the encircler."

The Hotṛ should perform it. [Objection: "But who would perform the Hotṛ’s duties if they are obstructed? [Response: Another person would do so—whichever among them has a specific qualification; that is, another person from among the Hotṛ's attendants, whoever possesses the required expertise or a specific distinction of preeminence. (3.8.10)
Bhāṣya 3,
Chapter 8, Section 8.
The section concerning the distinct agency in the acts of commanding and executing the command.
And because, in the case of the *praiṣas*, there is the authority of another. || 22 ||

Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, an injunction (praiṣa) is recorded there: "Place the sprinkling waters; set down the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the ladles; prepare the strainer; bring the clarified butter. In this regard, there is a doubt: is the one who utters the injunction the same as the one who performs the action enjoined?

Furthermore, is it that one person is for the command (*praiṣa*) and another is for the object of the command (*praiṣārtha*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That there is only one person for both the command and the object of the command. Why? Because of the designation (*samākhyāna*), and because [the distinction] that "another" exists is not heard in the text.

[Objection: "But surely a command to oneself is contradictory. [Reply: It is said in response: it will not be a command; we shall explain the *loṭ* suffix as expressing the time for action (*prāptakāla*). [Objection: Even when it expresses the time for action...
"The second person and so forth are established only when *yuṣmad* and the others are the *upapada*; there is no confusion of persons.
It is replied: "The second person and so forth occur when there is the intention (*vivakṣā*) to speak of *yuṣmad* and the others;
when it is intended to say 'the time has come for you,' then the second person occurs only with *yuṣmad*."

Nor [is there a conflict] between "us" and "the rest. Indeed, when only this much is intended—that the time for the action has arrived—it is not specified whether it is "for you" or "for me"; therefore, the second person and so forth need not occur in accordance with "you" and the others. Furthermore, it is impossible to intend both simultaneously, as in: "The time for the matter has arrived, and [it is] for you."

For in that case, the sentence would be split. Therefore, one might say either "the time for you" at the time when the word-meanings are already known, or "the time of the word-meaning for you" once "you" has been ascertained. In that situation, the time of the word-meaning must be stated, not [the time of the person].

For there is a purpose served by that [second person] being remembered when it refers to you (the *yuṣmad-artha*), since it is understood that "it must be performed by you"; however, the referent of "you" (*yuṣmad-artha*) is not [the primary object] in that way. Therefore, based on the designation (*samākhyāna*), the direction (*preṣa*) and the matter directed toward (*praipārtha*) belong to the Adhvaryu alone.

This being the position, we reply: "The *pra* [prefix] is used for mutual [direction] when those meanings are intended. Why? Because of the "governing of another" (*parādhikārāt*); for the *pra* is appropriate in the case of directing toward another, not toward oneself. [Objection: But was it not said that it will apply to the sense of "time having arrived"? [Reply: It is said in response: [Page 492] "It is not so; because of the connection with the root *i* (to go) and because of the presence of the prefix *pra*, it is understood as expressing direction toward another. Furthermore, since the *pra* is taught in the governing rule of others, it is understood as expressing direction toward another, not toward oneself. As for the statement that it will apply to the sense of 'time having arrived,' that is not correct; for in that case, the *pra* would be meaningless, since the sense of time having arrived is already expressed by the suffix alone. Moreover, if it were merely the sense of time having arrived, one would expect the form *prāptaḥ kālaḥ* rather than *prāptakālaḥ*. Therefore, it must be understood as expressing direction toward another. Thus, it is established that the *pra* is used for mutual direction when those meanings are intended. This is the conclusion.

Bhāṣya: No; when a *praiṣa* (an injunction to another) is possible, it is logical that it denotes "the arrival of the proper time" (*prāptakālatā*). For in that case, the sense of the second person (*yuṣmad-artha*) which is understood is not intended to be expressed—so it is said—and in this instance, the meaning of a *praiṣa* is indeed possible. Therefore, it is an injunction (*praiṣa*); and if it is an injunction, it is established that the meaning of an injunction must be distinct [from the mere arrival of time]. (3.1.26)
Mahābhārata,
Śāntiparvan.
The section concerning the respective roles of the Adhvaryu and the Āgnīdhra in the matters of the *preṣa* (command) and the *praiṣa* (authorization).
But the Adhvaryu [is the performer], because of the scriptural observation. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 23 ||

Now, this being the case, a doubt arises: should the Adhvaryu direct the Agnīdhra, or should the Agnīdhra direct the Adhvaryu? Since there is no specific rule, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that there is no fixed restriction. To this we reply: the Adhvaryu should be the one who carries out the purpose of the direction mentioned. Why? Because it is so observed (darśanāt).

The following is seen [in the scripture]: "One should hold the *sphya* crosswise; if one were to hold it lengthwise, the *sphya* is indeed speech, and speech would overwhelm the *adhvaryu*. Thus, the *sphya* is in the hand of him who gives the command;
"one should overwhelm the *adhvaryu* with the *sphya*" refers to another *adhvaryu*, distinct from the one who gives the command.
It indicates this; therefore, one should direct the Āgnīdhra priest with the call.
Or rather, it is figurative, because of the commonality of the action. (Siddhānta) || 24 ||
Indeed,

Venerable Sir, it is not the case that "the *preṣa* (command) belongs to the *āgnīdhra* and the purpose of the *preṣa* belongs to the *adhvaryu*"; rather, would the *adhvaryu* himself command the *āgnīdhra*, such that both the command and the purpose of the command belong to the *adhvaryu*?
Since both [actions] will take place there, the designation "Adhvaryava" (pertaining to the Adhvaryu) will be upheld.

Therefore, the Adhvaryu alone should be the primary [agent]. What is his primacy? It is that he must perform the entire sacrifice according to the designation. Now, as for what was said—that the Adhvaryu is seen to be the performer—this is replied: it is true that he is seen [to perform it].

But there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for one who is merely reflecting upon the performance of the purpose of the *praisha* command. Therefore, this is a false view; for that view which lacks a means of valid cognition is a delusion, such as the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. However, there is indeed a means of valid cognition for the Agnīdhra priest in the performance of the purpose of the *praisha*. Therefore, the Agnīdhra is the performer of the action, not the one who causes it to be performed.
[Page 493] Chapter 3, Section 8, Part 1.

Furthermore, the word *adhvaryu* is observed [in this context]. Therefore, it is used figuratively; because he performs the ritual acts prescribed for the *adhvaryu*, he is called "the *adhvaryu*," and likewise "the *āgnīdhra*. Consequently, the *praiṣa* (direction) belongs to the *adhvaryu*, while the object of the direction belongs to the *āgnīdhra*.
Thus [ends the section]. (3.8.12a)
The section concerning the desirability of the fruit for the master [of the sacrifice] in the case of mere instruments. (This is the principle of the year. Sūtra:
The fruit belongs to the officiating priest in the case of instruments, because it is purposeful. (Pūrva-pakṣa) 25.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is prescribed: "With the words, 'O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations,' he places the fire first. Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the fruit be invoked for the priest—namely, "O Agni, may splendor be [mine] in the invocations"—or for the sacrificer? What is the prima facie view? That it is for the Adhvaryu priest alone. Why?

In this way, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) will be preserved; otherwise, there would be an implied indication (*lakṣaṇā*), whereby [the word] would indicate the sacrificer by means of the self. Therefore, the fruit must be desired for the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).
What is the meaning? By means of this fuel-stick being held, the sacrifice will be accomplished.

In that regard, regarding the points of competition among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the statement of the *adhvaryu* is: "I shall be the most eloquent," and likewise, "I shall be the most energetic."
Or rather, [the fruit belongs] to the master, because that [sacrifice] is for his sake. (Siddhānta) || 26 ||

The statement belongs to the sacrificer, because the ritual action is for his sake; for this ritual action, together with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), is performed for the benefit of the sacrificer, as indicated by the specific verbal suffix (*upagraha-viśeṣa*); such is the purpose of this [action] along with its parts.

The accomplishment of the fruit belongs to the sacrificer, while the glory belongs to the Adhvaryu priest who has well-recited the *pravara*. Why is this so? If it is thus, then from the mention of the fruit, the necessity of performing the act for the sake of that fruit is understood. Regarding this, Mādhava says: "The meaning is: 'May that fruit characterized by splendor (*varṇa* = *tejas*) belong to me—that fruit which belongs to those mantras whose oblation (*havana*) is distinguished.'"* *viśvā* refers to those mantras; *varṇa* therein signifies splendor. The sense is: "May that fruit [characterized by] splendor belong to me. Thus says Mādhava.
In the Mīmāṃsā-darśana-bhāṣya,
regarding the *agny-anvādhāna* performed for the sacrificer while the declaration of the fruit is being made, by means of this mantra:
Because of the connection with the fruit, it becomes manifested as something performed; it is not [manifested] by the recitation of the Adhvaryu’s glory.

Therefore, the fruit must be attributed to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Now, why is this mantra not one belonging to the sacrificer? It is replied: because the *agny-anvādhāna* (the adding of fuel to the fire) [is performed by the Adhvaryu].

By designation, it is the *ādhvaryava* (the office of the Adhvaryu); and thus, in the performance of the subsidiary acts, the mantra makes the Adhvaryu its agent, as expressed by the words, "He [the Adhvaryu] performs with this mantra. Therefore, the mantras belong to the Adhvaryu.
Furthermore, even in the phrase "O R̥tvij," the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) designates himself [as the R̥tvij] through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇayā*).
Just as soldiers, when victory resides in the king, designate it as "ours," so too [is this case].
Sūtra: And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (He0) || 27 ||
The indicative mark (*liṅga*) also demonstrates this meaning, for it declares thus:
"Whatever blessing (*āśis*) the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) invoke, that belongs to the sacrificer alone"— thus [it speaks of] blessings.
Therefore, we say this as well: [the text] shows that the sacrificer is for the sake of the sacrificer;
the fruit is to be desired—this is the very purpose stated for the position.
(3 | 8 | 13 Śrauta Sūtra) | The section concerning the status of the fruit of the ritual action as a duty of the officiating priests within the context of the instruments of action.
But their own ritual acts bear fruit for them, because they possess an object in relation to their master. || 28 ||

Commentary: This has been established—that among the various instruments [of action], the fruit is to be wished for for the master (the patron). Is this the universal rule? No; so he says, that in some cases the fruit is also to be wished for for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), where the fruit pertains to the ritual act itself, as in the case of the mention of the fruit [in the Kāṭhaka-Saṃhitā].

Regarding this, the Adhvaryus say that the quality [of the Soma] is "that which makes one intoxicated" (*mayaḥ karoti*); it is explained as such because of the passage: *sa uccarate nena madeaiti* (Kauśika Sūtra 20.50).
Chapter 3, Section 8.
"O Agni and Viṣṇu, I am about to step forward; move apart so that you do not burn me.
This refers to one who, being scorched at the end, is able to perform the ritual action; it is the power of the ritual action belonging to the sacrificer.
The assistant, the messenger, and the officiating priest—the fruit [of their service] is to be wished for here. Thus [it is said].
Sūtra: Also because of designation. (28)

And where there is a designation (*vyapadeśa*), there the office of the officiating priest (*ārvtijam*) applies: beneath the southern *havirdhāna* cart, there are four *uparava* holes with openings facing inward and a span (*prādeśa*) between them;
having inserted his hands there, the *adhvaryu* asks the sacrificer, "What is here?
He replies, "Auspiciousness. The *adhvaryu* responds, "May that be ours together"—this is the designation.

There is [a result] for both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer (yajamāna). The statement "May that be ours together" (*tannau saha*) expresses the claim of both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer. Therefore, in this case, the fruit of the Adhvaryu must be invoked [as a separate result].
The section concerning whether the preparation of a substance serves the purpose of both the subsidiary and the principal acts.
There is no preparation of the substance [for all rites], because there is no distinction in the context for all actions. || 30 ||
In the *Bhāṣya*, regarding the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, there arises a doubt concerning the rules for the sacrificial ground (*vedi*) and the rules for the sacrificial vessels (*vedidharma*):

are they for the sake of both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary rites (*pradhāna*), or are they for the sake of the primary rites alone? Since the context (*prakaraṇa*) suggests they are for the sake of the primary rites—this being the prima facie view—it is replied: it is not so; the preparation of the substance (*dravyasaṃskāra*) is for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the primary rites. This [prima facie] position is merely set forth for the purpose of the subsequent discussion, as has already been explained. (3.8.15)
O Agni and Viṣṇu, you two who possess the forms of *khukhu*—I, the Adhvaryu, have not transgressed against you; I have not overstepped your presence. May you two become like lightning flashes to me.
Therefore, do not cause me, who am embodied, to suffer; do not inflict upon me the divine affliction in the form of fever and other ailments.
"Do not do so," said Mādhava.

The section concerning the non-connection of unprecedented and original dharmas with the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
But because of the specific instruction, there is no eligibility for one who has previously undergone a modification. || 31 ||

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, as it is stated: "The initiated one who sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. Regarding this, it is heard in the scripture: "He covers the pit for the sacrificial post with sacrificial grass (barhis), and he anoints the sacrificial post with clarified butter (ājya). In this regard, a doubt arises: should the ritual properties (dharma) pertaining to clarified butter and sacrificial grass be applied to those two, or not? What is the prima facie view? They should be applied. Why? Because of the scriptural statement.

Since it is the prescriber of the ritual properties for both the *barhis* grass and the clarified butter (*ājya*), that same scriptural injunction is obtained here as well through the force of the extended application (*codaka*); nor is this *barhis* and *ājya* devoid of purpose.
Therefore, the ritual properties should be performed here.

This being the case, we reply: "On account of the specific instruction, there is no application of what is new in the modified sacrifice. These ritual duties have been specifically instructed as those which assist the primary act by means of the ghee and the sacrificial grass (barhis) used for the original purpose; and those which are beneficial to the primary act [are thus limited].

The *dharmas* (ritual details) are extended here by analogy; for it is the principal act (*pradhāna*) that is considered the object of the injunction (*codaka*), not the *dharmas*, since the similarity with the injunction pertains to the principal act and not to the *dharmas*.

Furthermore, when another connection is possible, there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between a known element and a proximate one that serves a different purpose, as in the case of "the king's wife."

[The example] "the man of Devadatta"—how much more so, then, in the case of something remote? For it is indeed well-known that subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) arises only in dependence upon a principal (*pradhāna*); here, however, only an extension (*atideśa*) is being made. If subsidiarity were to be established in dependence upon the ritual items (*padārtha*), then even the subsidiaries would have to be proven [as such]. Furthermore, the ritual properties (*dharma*) being depended upon would become common to all; thus, alas, it would not be appropriate. Moreover, because of the observation of specific indicative marks (*liṅga*), the ritual properties would be restricted; in that case, the following observation would not be possible:
"They proceed with the omentum at the morning pressing, and with the sacrificial cake at the midday pressing. Likewise...

"The father does not increase, nor the mother, nor the navel; for he is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Therefore, by whatever means they are performed in the archetype (*prakṛti*), they must be performed by those same means in the modification (*vikṛti*), and not by other means. Furthermore, the spreading [of grass] over the sacrificial post-hole (*yūpāvaṭastaraṇa*) does not exist in the archetype, nor does the anointing of the sacrificial post (*yūpāñjana*).

42.8 Bhāṣya: Therefore, the archetypal (*prākṛta*) properties would not apply there, because it is something unprecedented (*apūrva*). (3 | Ma.)
8 | 16 (Śrauta Sūtra)
The section concerning the requirement that the *vidhṛti* and *pavitra* be made from the *paribhojanīya* sacrificial grass.
And in case of conflict, because of the specific scriptural statement, the unmanifest [is used] in the remainder.

In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the texts prescribe: "He makes two strainers (*pavitre*) out of two blades of *darbha* grass, equal in length and cut at both ends, measuring a span (*prādeśa*)," and likewise, "He makes two separators (*vidhṛtī*) of the measure of an *ara*. Regarding this, there is a doubt: are the two separators and the two strainers to be made from the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) intended for strewing the altar, or from something else? What, then, is the prima facie view? They are to be made from the sacrificial grass intended for strewing the altar. Why? Because that [grass] is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), and because the properties (*dharma*) apply without distinction.

"For the sake of all the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), therefore [it should come] from that. This being the position reached, we reply: it should be made from something else. Why? Because of contradiction. How is there a contradiction? It is heard in the scripture: "He strews the altars in three or five layers. How then could that which is used for strewing be made into the *vidhṛti* and *pavitra*? For it is not possible for one thing to serve both for strewing and for those other purposes.

And [this applies] to the *vidhṛti* and the *pavitra*. Thus, both the stated injunction and the possession of multiple qualities would be impossible; therefore, it should not be made from that [grass]. [Objection: "If it is not to be made from that, then from what? [Response: Such an unmanifested remnant exists;
there is indeed a sacrificial grass called *paribhojanīya*, and from that it should be made."
(3 | 8 | 17 śra0) | Section on the Deposition of the Ordinary Puroḍāśa and Other Offerings.
Ba. But there is the removal of one part because of its connection with something existing. || 33 ||
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard [in the scripture]: "He places a fragment of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) in the vessel for Indra and Vāyu;
parched grains (dhānā) in the vessel for the Aśvins; and curd-mixture (payasyā) in the vessel for Mitra and Varuṇa."

Thus [it is said]. In this regard, there is a doubt: should it be performed from something else, or from those belonging to the archetype (*prakṛta*)? [Page 498] Bhāṣya: What is the prima facie view?—that it should be from something else, according to the previous reasoning. To that, it is replied:
—Therefore, there is the removal of one part. Why? Because of the connection with what is present;

for the *puroḍāśa*, the *dhānās*, and the *payasyā* are present there, and it is logical that the connection be with them alone, not with anything else—thus, the consecration belongs only to the *puroḍāśa* and the others, not to the *aindravāyava* and the rest. Why? Because the accusative case is observed in relation to the *puroḍāśa* and the others.
Furthermore, the benefit is directly perceived through the removal of a single part, not through a connection with Indra, Vāyu, and others;
in this way, there will be an assistance to the archetype (*prakṛti*). Therefore, that [benefit] should be performed for the archetype by means of direct instruction (*upadeśa*);
nor is there here an intention regarding a specific portion being taught, nor is there a state of having multiple subordinate qualities (*guṇabhāva*) by another.
And the other [oblation] is established as being offered with a chip—thus [ends the section]. (3.8.18)
The section concerning whether the *upayaj* ritual rule in optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) serves the purpose of the primary rite.
In its own modification, the subsidiary serves all purposes, just as in the archetype. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 34 ||
The Bhāṣya states:

They prescribe this—"The optional sacrifices (iṣṭis) belonging to the Yajñātharvaṇa should indeed be performed in a low voice (upāṃśu). Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the low-voiced nature for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the primary, or for the sake of the primary alone? What is the prima facie view? "In the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), it is for its own sake."
The remainder would apply, because there is no distinction between the subsidiaries (aṅga) and the primary rites (pradhāna), just as in the archetype (prakṛti);

for just as in the archetype the characteristics of the altar (vedi-dharma) and the characteristics of the fire-altar (āhavanīya-dharma) are for the sake of both the subsidiary and the primary, so it is here as well.
Or rather, its own primary meaning [is intended], because the subsidiary part is not enjoined. (Siddhānta) || 35 ||

Or rather, this [rule] would apply to the modifications (vikṛtis) for the sake of the principal [rite]. In this way, it was stated that this [rule] serves all purposes, setting aside the context (prakaraṇa) by means of syntactical connection (vākya) so as to serve both the subsidiaries and the principal. Now, that very same syntactical connection is specified as "the optional (kāmyā) iṣṭis," and the optional ones...

There are principal sacrifices and subsidiary sacrifices; the subsidiary sacrifices are for the sake of the principal sacrifice. Therefore, the subsidiary is not independently enjoined. That which is enjoined as possessing a fruit through a specific desire is precisely that which is connected with this procedure of low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*).
[Page 499]
Chapter 3, Section 8.
Commentary: It is connected [to the principal act]. Therefore, the low-voiced recitation (upāṃśutva) is for the sake of the principal act.
Bhāṣya-sūtra-bhāṣya (The Commentary on the Aphorisms of the Bhāṣya)
Śrīmad Bhagavadgītā, Chapter 19.
The section concerning the application of ghee to the limbs of the hawk-shaped sacrificial cake.
In the absence [of the primary], there is no [application] of its subsidiaries due to the distinction of proximity. || 36 ||

In the Śyena sacrifice it is heard: "Clarified butter prepared with fresh butter (navanīta) is the oblation. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the fresh butter for the principal rite, or for the subsidiary rites? What is the prima facie view? It is for the principal rite, because that is the context; thus, by the authority of the scriptural statement, the principal rite is to be accomplished with fresh butter.

This being the case, we reply: "In the event of impossibility, it should apply to its subsidiaries" (i.e., the subsidiaries of the Śyena sacrifice). How is there impossibility? Because the primary sacrifice has Soma as its substance. [Objection: But surely, on account of the scriptural injunction, fresh butter (navanīta)...
It will be so. "Clarified butter is not used in the Śyena sacrifice"—this is the meaning of the sentence. What [is meant]?

Clarified butter is the ghee in the Śyena—thus, the connection with clarified butter is enjoined, while the connection with the Śyena is restated. And [there is] no direct [connection] of the Śyena [with the clarified butter].

There is a connection with clarified butter (ājya) [in general], but it exists specifically for the components of the Śyena sacrifice. For that which possesses [this connection], non-congealed butter (anavanīta) is prescribed, "because of the specific proximity."
If it is argued that the same applies even in the case of the fire-installation (ādhāna), [we reply: No. (Ābhāsasūtra 37)

If it is seen thus— that "clarified butter is a constituent part of the Śyena sacrifice"— then it would also apply to the Pavamāna offerings at the fire-consecration (ādhāna), for those offerings also assist the Śyena,
since the Śyena is accomplished in a fire consecrated by them.
It is not so, because the subsidiary (aṅga) is not the subject under discussion, since that [the primary] is the cause of it. || 38 ||

No; for in the context of the Śyena sacrifice, neither the Pavamāna offerings nor the fire-installation (ādhāna) are heard as being primary. What follows from this? If that is so, there is no connection whatsoever between the fire-installation and the Śyena.

[Commentary: There is a connection; the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) belongs to the fires, and the fires belong to the Śyena sacrifice. Therefore, there is no fresh butter (*navanīta*) in the Pavamāna offerings. This—that the establishment of the fires benefits the fires—is not the reason for [the butter] being a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the Śyena. If any one of the [criteria such as] context (*prakaraṇa*) were present, that would be the reason. Therefore, there is no [connection] between the Śyena and the establishment of the fires.
There is a relationship—thus [it is said].
The section concerning the fact that the butter for all the limbs of the Śyena sacrifice is distinct.
Or rather, [the connection is established] at that time because of the observation of the indicative mark (liṅga). (Pūrvapakṣa 38)

Commentary: Now this is doubted: is clarified butter (navanīta) for the subsidiaries performed at the time of the Soma-pressing (sutyā), or for all [subsidiaries]? It should be for those at the time of the pressing, because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga); for this is heard in scripture: "He immolates the animals together. In that regard—
The reiteration: "In the place of the Agniṣomīya [animal], there is the Agniṣomīya cake," Śrautasūtra Bhāṣya.

"In place of the Anubandhyā, there is that belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa"—thus he shows two other positions; by this it is understood that the statement regarding the Śyena prescribes a specific rule for the subsidiaries performed at the time of the Soma-pressing.
Or rather, it belongs to all, because there is no distinction.
(Sūtra) ||
And the butter should belong to all the subsidiaries. Why? Because there is no distinction; since there is no specific qualification, it belongs to all the subsidiaries.
Sūtra: The observation of an indicative mark is as stated by logic. (Śrāddhaniyama)

Commentary: As for what was stated regarding the *liṅga* (indicative mark), that must be refuted. First of all, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that the statement concerning the Śyena sacrifice applies to the subsidiaries whose time is identical [to the primary]. However, as for the observation (*darśana*), because it lacks a foundation in a valid means of knowledge, it is a false observation, like a mirage. How so?
"But why is there a grasping of the wind in the middle?"—because of logical necessity (*nyāya*). What is the logical necessity?
It is the favoring of the sequence. In this way, even though it is not explicitly stated in the text, the sequence is favored.
[Page 501]
Therefore, clarified butter is [the essence] of all the limbs. — Thus [says Bhāskara].

bhā.
The section concerning the fact that one's own [relatives] consist of flesh.
But the meat belongs to the Savanīya offerings, because of the specific injunction.
The Śākya sacrifice lasts thirty-six years. Regarding this, they recite:
"On each day that has concluded, the householder goes out hunting; the sacrificial cakes for the *savanīya* offerings are made from the meat of whatever wild animals he kills there. In that regard—

There is a doubt: whether the *tarasa* (flesh) takes the place of all possible *puroḍāśa* cakes, both those belonging to the *savanīya* offerings and others, or only those belonging to the *savanīya* offerings? What is the prima facie view?
That all *puroḍāśa* cakes should consist of flesh; for it is not possible [to substitute flesh] for the *puroḍāśa* cakes...

In order to prescribe that [the sacrificial cakes] consist of flesh and to qualify the *puroḍāśas* by means of the word "savaniya," the sentence would indeed be split. Therefore, all *puroḍāśas* consist of flesh.

This being the position, it is said in reply: "But the meat should belong to the *savanīya* offerings. Since it is stated, "The *tarasa* [flour-cakes] are the *savanīya*s," a connection between the *tarasa* and the *savanīya* is enjoined; however, the statement "the *puroḍāśa*s are the *tarasa*s" is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). Why is this so? Because the word *savanīya* cannot be a restatement with respect to all *puroḍāśa*s, whereas the word *puroḍāśa* is applicable to the *savanīya*s. Therefore, the word *puroḍāśa* is the restatement. Thus, [it follows that...].
"In place of the *savanīya* grains and other offerings, meat [should be substituted], because there is no distinction in the act of cutting."
If it is argued that [the application of the rule] is improper in the absence of the rasa of devotion, [we reply: no. (Ābhāsya)
If you think, "In the case of the *savanīya* offerings, the word 'puroḍāśa' will be a restatement (*anuvāda*)," [we reply:
the word 'puroḍāśa' does not apply to parched grains (*dhānā*) and the like, and it is improper to resort to figurative usage (*bhakti*) when a primary sense is possible.
[Page 502] Or it may be so, because it is a characteristic mark of the archetype, as in the case of the Vairāja.
(Ābhāsa-nirṇaya) Bhāṣya: In the archetype, the Jyotiṣṭoma, this word "puroḍāśa" applied to the *dhānās* and other offerings is figurative.

It is employed in its primary sense when [the referent] is proximate; here too, it is used only in a figurative sense, for they are indeed proximate by virtue of the term *savanīya*. Just as the application of a word occurs in the archetype (*prakṛti*) due to the presence of its characteristic mark (*liṅga*), so it is in the modification (*vikṛti*); for example: "those with umbrellas are going," or "those with banners are going. As in the case of: "The *ukthya* sacrifice has the *vairūpa* chant, the twenty-one-fold [stoma], and the *ṣoḍaśī*."

By the word *sāman*, which possesses the natural characteristic (*prakṛtiliṅga*) of being a *vairāja-sāman*, it is understood that [the sacrifice] has the *vairūpa* as its *pṛṣṭha-stotra* and the *vairāja* as its *pṛṣṭha-stotra*; likewise here too, the Savanīya offerings consist of meat.
Thus ends the eighth pāda of the third adhyāya in the Mīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śabarasvāmin. And the third adhyāya is completed.
[Page 503] Sūtra 4, Fourth Chapter, Ninth Section.
Now begins the section on the thesis (pratijñā).
Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into that which serves the purpose of the sacrifice and that which serves the purpose of the person. 1.

In the third chapter (*adhyāya*), the definition of the application of subsidiary elements (*śeṣa-viniyoga*) was stated through direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyāna*). Now, here, the nature of that which is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and that which is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) are investigated: what is for the sake of the sacrifice? What is for the sake of the person? Furthermore, the inquiry into what is instigating (*prayojaka*) or non-instigating, into fruit-injunctions (*phala-vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), subsidiaries (*aṅga*), and primary acts (*pradhāna*)—that too is simply the investigation into what is for the sake of the sacrifice and what is for the sake of the person. How so? A subsidiary is for the sake of the sacrifice; a primary act is for the sake of the person; and a fruit-injunction is for the sake of the person.

An explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) may serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*); likewise, a certain motivating factor may serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) while being motivated by the purpose of the sacrifice. Therefore, it was stated in the aphorism: "The desire to know [the distinction] between that which serves the purpose of the sacrifice and that which serves the purpose of the person.
In this regard, the words *atha* and *ataḥ* have already been explained in the first aphorism of the very first chapter. Now, regarding the word *atha*:

The subject at hand requires a definition for the application of the remaining [elements]. Therefore, the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) introduces a specific inquiry into what serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). That which is for the sake of the sacrifice is *kratvartha*; that which is for the sake of the person is *puruṣārtha*. The term "inquiry" (*jijñāsā*) is also understood in this very context as "the desire to know" (*jñātum icchā*). Thus, this is the formal proposition (*pratijñā-sūtra*): "An inquiry into what serves the purpose of the sacrifice and what serves the purpose of the person. (4.1.1) — Now begins the section concerning the definitions of *kratvartha* and *puruṣārtha*, accompanied by two alternative expositions (*varṇaka*).
In the case of one's own [body], there is a desire for that in which a person finds pleasure; this desire is characterized by the object [itself] because it is not distinct from it. (JS 4.1.2)
Bhāṣya:

Now, what is the definition of that which is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), and what is the definition of that which is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)?—thus the definition should not be forgotten here; this is an additional reading found in the Kaṃ0 Saṃ0 manuscript.
Bhāṣya:

O Vācaṃya, for indeed comprehension is easier when the instruction is given by means of a question-and-answer method rather than through a prolix exposition. Therefore it is said: "In that which a person finds pleasure," (and in that which, when destroyed...)
That object in which a person finds pleasure is an object that serves the purpose of man (*puruṣārtha*). Why?

Because "the desire for it" arises through the [attainment of] the object itself, not through the scripture; for the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) is understood from the scripture, and not otherwise. Indeed, the purpose of man is inseparable from pleasure.
Whatever is a means for accomplishing pleasure is a human end (*puruṣārtha*). Once the human end has been defined, that which is its opposite is the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*);
thus, the definition of the purpose of the ritual is established. (First Section)

Or rather, the Sūtra is explained as follows: In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is prescribed: "He strews [the grass] so that it is not seen through; he thus makes him possessed of offspring and cattle so that they are not seen through. Likewise, there are such injunctions as: "For one desiring cattle, he should make the altar (vedi) filled with the dust of the teacher's feet; for one desiring cattle, he should make the sacrificial ladle (veda) knee-high; for one desiring cattle, he should bring water in a milking vessel," and so forth. In this regard, a doubt arises: Are such items as these for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*)?

Or is it for the sake of the human agent? What is the prima facie view? It is for the sake of the sacrifice. Why? Because a direct benefit to the sacrifice is seen from them: the spreading of the earth and the strewing of the altar are mentioned [in the scripture]—as stated in (3.1.30): "In the case of substances, qualities, and purificatory acts..."
Bādari says: "Therefore, they are for the sake of the sacrifice"—this is the position reached.
This being the case, we reply: that in which there is pleasure for a person is indeed for the sake of the person; since pleasure is produced from them, therefore these are for the sake of the person.

[Objection: But was it not said that a visible benefit to the sacrifice is observed? [Reply: It is true that it is observed, but not for the benefit of the sacrifice from these aforementioned results.

These [subsidiaries] are heard in the texts, yet it is not the case that whatever assists something is its subsidiary; rather, as has been stated (Sūtra 3.1.2), "That which is heard as being for the sake of another is its subsidiary"—because "the subsidiary exists because it is for the sake of another. (Second Exposition)
Or rather, the acquisition of wealth is the illustration; here, the acquisition of wealth [is governed] by various restrictive rules.
The reading "puṣyākoṭena" is found in the Kaśmīr manuscript (ka0), the Saṃkṛta manuscript (saṃ0), and the Pūrvapakṣa manuscript (pu0).

This is what is meant: that which is performed depending on a goal sought by oneself is for the sake of human purpose (puruṣārtha), while that which is for the sake of assisting it is for the sake of the ritual (kratvartha); this must be remembered according to the Tattvaratnamañjūṣā.
Chapter 4, Section 1.

It is heard in the Brāhmaṇa that the acquisition of wealth occurs for a Brāhmaṇa through receiving gifts and the like, for a Kṣatriya through victory and the like, and for a Vaiśya through agriculture and the like. In this regard, there is a doubt: is the acquisition of property for the sake of the sacrifice [performed] by these means?
Or is it for the sake of the person? What is the prima facie view? It is for the sake of the sacrifice. Because of the restrictive rule (*niyama*);

if this were for the sake of the person, the restrictive rule would be purposeless. This is understood through direct perception: that wealth acquired both through restrictive rules and without restrictive rules gratifies the person. Therefore, it is for the sake of the sacrifice; moreover, its syntactic unity with the scriptural injunctions regarding desires (*kāmaśruti*) is observed.

Otherwise, it would form a single syntactical unit with the fruit-statement (*phalavākya*) concerning the object of inference. There is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*), such as: "One whose consecrated fire should burn his house while he is an *āhitāgni* should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat; one whose gold should be lost should offer the *Āgneya* and other oblations"—and so forth; this is enjoined in the event of the destruction of the substance.
If the acquisition of property has the purpose of ritual action (*karman*), then this [acquisition] also has the purpose of ritual action when a connection exists;

otherwise, it is inferred that it has the purpose of ritual action even when no connection exists, and its fruit would have to be postulated. Therefore, the acquisition of property is encompassed by the direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*) of the root *yajati* (to sacrifice).

It is understood that whatever, without which the sacrifice cannot be accomplished, is embraced by the Vedic text (śruti) as belonging to the sacrifice; therefore, it is for the sake of the ritual (kratvartha).

This being the position reached, we reply: it is for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha). When this object is performed, pleasure arises for the person; therefore, his desire for it is characterized by the purpose of maintaining the body. For one whose body is maintained, there is clearly wealth, and for the embodied being—
A sacrifice is prescribed; therefore, the application of existing property is declared.

For even without the word explicitly expressing the acquisition of property, the sacrifice is indeed accomplished when the acquisition of property is understood from the scriptural injunction; thus, the appropriation of property serves the purpose of the person.

Furthermore, if the acquisition of wealth for the sake of ritual action were based solely on the scripture, then that which was acquired in such a manner could not be employed elsewhere; in that case, there would be a total abandonment of all established principles. Moreover,
All ritual acts would become dependent upon the acquisition of wealth; in that case, this [scriptural statement] would not be tenable:
"Indeed, he who performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices is cut off from the world of heaven."
The reading in the Kāśīmudra edition of the Purāṇa is "khargāt."
[Page 506] Bhāṣya:
"One would cause the new moon day or the full moon day to pass by"—and this being the case, this auxiliary, occurring outside the time of performance, would be of no benefit. Nor is it...
It ought to be understood as being accompanied by faith, for there is a scriptural statement regarding it: "One should take up the sacred fires in the spring";
yet this [taking up] is not an auxiliary (aṅga) [to the sacrifice].
Now, as for what was said—that the injunction of restriction is purposeless with respect to the acquisition of property for the sake of human ends—[that is not so].

Regarding the statement "it exists": it is replied that the status of being for the sake of man (*puruṣārthatā*) is not thereby excluded, for that [status] is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), whereas you designate it as imperceptible (*parokṣa*) through logical reasoning. And the imperceptible cannot be a sublater of the perceptible; therefore, although another unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) might be postulated on account of the restrictive injunction, the visible gift (*dāna*) is not negated. Consequently, that which is the purpose of man—

Since there is pleasure, and for its sake the acquisition of wealth—in this case, the sacrifice must be performed with rice, whether that rice was acquired for the sake of pleasure or acquired for the sake of the ritual; there is no distinction here. Even rice acquired for the sake of pleasure is simply rice.
Even rice acquired for the sake of ritual action remains simply rice; therefore, the acquisition of a substance is not included within the injunction of performance (*prayoga-codanā*).

Now, as for what was said—that in your view the syntactic unity of the restriction is with an inferred or non-manifest verbal expression, whereas in our view it is with a perceptible injunction of performance—this is not a fault. For even in the case of eating, [the unity is] with the perceptible act of eating, not with the statement of the result. How so?

[Question: Then what? [Answer: It is understood that "the unseen (adṛṣṭa) arises from the restrictive rule (niyama)," just as in your own position. [The opponent] says: "In our position, it is understood that because of the state of being a single sentence with that which possesses a fruit, it assists that which possesses a fruit. [The author] replies: In our position as well, there is that which possesses a fruit...
Thus, there is the state of being a single syntactical unit; however, this much is the distinction: for you, the result is scriptural (śruta), but for me, it is perceptible (dṛṣṭa).
Now, as for the indicative mark (liṅga) that was mentioned—that ritual action is heard [to be prescribed] in cases such as the burning of a house—[it is as follows].

To this it is replied: even though the acquisition of property is not for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), nevertheless, when burning [of the house] occurs as the occasion (*nimitta*), the injunction of the *Jāmadagnyā* and other rites for the sake of a result or for the status of being an auxiliary to the ritual action (*karmāṅgabhāva*) is indeed logical. Therefore, the acquisition of property is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), for it is inseparable from pleasure (*prīti*). — (Third Section) (4.1.2).
[Page 507] The Section Concerning the Human Purpose of the Vows of Prajāpati.

438kha. When that [substance] is relinquished for the sake of the ritual act which serves the purpose of the person, there is no room for doubt regarding the authority of the scripture; nor is the substance intended to be modified, because it is connected with that specific purpose. Therefore, the mention of the person in relation to the action [is for the sake of the person]. || 3 ||
Bhāṣya:

Here, the vows of Prajāpati serve as an example: "One should not look at the rising sun, nor the setting sun," and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt: are these for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*)?
Are the *prajāpati-vratas* for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) or for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*)? What is the prima facie view?
That they are for the sake of the sacrifice. Why? Because in this way, it will not be necessary to assume a separate fruit. But is it not the case that their fruit is indeed heard in scripture?
"By this much, one becomes beset by sin"—thus it is said. It is replied: this statement is not intended to express a result;
rather, this word is merely a description of a present state. Therefore, wherever the sun is to be looked upon...
This being the prima facie view, we reply: even when that [pleasure] is relinquished, the ritual acts serve the purpose of the person. In this regard, there is a prohibition;
for one who is exerting effort or resting, there might be some restriction that constitutes an auxiliary part of the ritual action.
This being the prima facie view, we say: even upon the relinquishing of that [pleasure], the ritual acts are for the sake of the person.
They would be of such a nature; these are taught as belonging to the agent, not to the action.

That connection which is established by the force of the meaning is what is intended to be enjoined, whereas the connection with the action already exists. Furthermore, the *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) is more authoritative than even the words of one's father or mother when it is unsurpassed; for one personally realizes [the truth] through it, as it stands in the place of the sense organs. It is not...
And by such means as these, some visible benefit for the substance is accomplished. Therefore,
because of its connection with that human purpose, a person is enjoined to an action of this kind.
Moreover, the human effort [of the speaker] would be employed merely to indicate the injunction regarding the object, while the effort itself would not be intended to be expressed.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that where the gaze upon the sun is reached, there is a prohibition against looking at it when it is rising or setting—it is true that the prohibition is logical; however, the scriptural text should be followed accordingly.

[Page 508] Bhāṣya: Otherwise, a restriction (niyama) would be implied; however, here a restriction is heard directly from the word: "his vow"—therefore, this is a restriction: that while the sun is rising...

"Regarding the term *īkṣitayaḥ*: moreover, [in the passage] 'By this much he becomes unjoined with sin,' a fault connected to the person (*puruṣa*) is mentioned, not one connected to the ritual act (*karman*).
Therefore, the Prajāpati-vows have the person as their purpose. The characteristics of the cows are likewise."
"Letters other than *ṛ* should be substituted for the agent (*kartṛ*)"—such rules as these [are intended].
But because the scripture makes no distinction, the results should be according to what is heard in the Vedic texts. || 4 ||
(Śrauta Sūtra)

The Bhāṣya says: If this is so, then these [acts] as well would be for the sake of the person—such as "he offers the *samidh* oblation," "he offers the *tanūnapāt* oblation," "one should not speak untruth," and so forth.
For here too there is a mention of human effort, and here too no substance is intended to be prepared (*cikīrṣyate*).
Sūtra:
Or rather, when the cause is not perceived, there is no connection of the meaning with that purpose. (5) [Niyama]

Or rather, this is not the case—that even the *samidh* and other such offerings would result in human goals (*puruṣārtha*). For if no specific cause were perceived, the Prajāpati-vows would indeed be for the sake of the person; however, in that context, no cause such as direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) or the like is perceived by which it could be understood that they are subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the ritual acts. Therefore, they are for the sake of the person. This is because of the purpose.

There is no connection [of the *prajāpati-vrata*] with the ritual action (*karman*); however, in this case, the means known as "context" (*prakaraṇa*)—namely, the *samidh* and so forth—is taken as the basis by which they are understood to be for the sake of the ritual action.
Therefore, the comparison is unequal; and such being the case, the human effort is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
And likewise among those who have become like the world. (Yukti) || 6 ||

In common worldly practice as well, when something connected with a result is heard in relation to things that have already achieved their purpose and are thus useful, it is understood to be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that; thinking thus, they [perform] either fasting or recitation.
Chapter 4, Section 9.

Having taught [the rites], they consider themselves successful; they do not say, "This is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of that which possesses a purpose," nor do others, thinking thus, consider them ill-spoken. Therefore, the *samidh* and other such acts are subsidiaries of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*), not the vows of Prajāpati (*prajāpativrata*).
—Thus it is established. (4.1.3 Śrauta-sūtra)
The section concerning the restatement of the sacrificial implements (yajñāyudha).
Sūtra: But substances, being without distinction, should be offered, lest they be rendered purposeless.
Bhāṣya (Pūrvapakṣa):
There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices; therein it is recited: "The potsherds and the sacrificial cakes."

"The *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), the *śamyā* pin, the mortar, the pestle, the lower grinding stone, and the upper grinding stone—these indeed are the ten sacrificial implements.
Regarding this, there arises a doubt: are these substances to be given away, or [used] by one's own [self]?

Are they to be connected with their own respective meanings? To establish this, the following must be considered: Is this an injunction (*vidhi*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*)? If it is an injunction, there is an offering; if it is a restatement, the connection is according to the literal sense. What is the prima facie position? It is an injunction, because in that case there is a specific motivation for action, whereas otherwise it would be a mere statement.

It would be purposeless. Furthermore, upon their being given away, the term "sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudha*) remains applicable—meaning they are the weapons of the sacrifice, that is, the means for accomplishing the sacrifice. Otherwise, by the literal hearing of the text, they would be the implements of digging and so forth; only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) could they belong to the sacrifice. Moreover, the number [ten] is thus made consistent, because of the connection with a single sacrifice; otherwise, due to the connection with multiple purposes, the number ten would not be consistent. Therefore, they should be given away.
That which is prescribed without distinction must pertain to the primary rite by virtue of the context.
But the connection of substances is with their own respective purposes, because they serve distinct purposes; therefore, they should be used according to the scriptural text. (Siddhānta) || 8 ||
This is not the case; it is not an injunction stating "they are to be given," but rather a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already established.
[Page 510]

Because of its nature as [an injunction]—as in: "They heat [the grains] on the potsherds; he cooks them in the *agnihotra-havani* vessel; he pours out [the grain] with the winnowing basket; he separates [the chaff]; he spreads the black antelope skin beneath the mortar; he places the grinding stone upon the wedge; he threshes with the mortar and pestle that have been sprinkled; he grinds with the grinding stone and millstone that have been sprinkled"—thus, by its own [nature].

By their own statements, [the materials] are obtained for the acts of digging and so forth; thus, the statement regarding those already obtained is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Context (*prakaraṇa*) is also set aside by the direct statement (*vākya*); furthermore, the word "sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudha*) is appropriate on the side of being a restatement, not on the side of an injunction (*vidhi*), for that word "implement" would be figurative (*gauṇa*) when applied to the *syena*-shaped pieces and the like.

The number [mentioned] will also be intended as referring to the recitation [of the text]. And it is quite clear that the *syena*-shaped pieces and the like are employed by means of digging and so forth—for there is indeed an injunction there, such as "they dig with the *sphya*," and so on; but there is no injunction that "the sacrificial implements must be made."
Therefore, in the case of the *udghāta* and so forth, there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already established by the sentence.
Sūtra.
Tsaṃyukta-āgama.
And they are enjoined in matters of purposeful action. (Yuktidīpikā 1)
The purposeful acts (*arthakarma*), such as the *puroḍāśa* cake and others, are enjoined; these too would undergo modification.

In that case, there is sublation (*bādha*), not combination (*samuccaya*). This is because the *puroḍāśa* and other offerings are connected with the sacrifice independently, as are the *syena* and other rites. Or rather: "And the purposeful acts are enjoined."

They are enjoined in the ritual of the Paridhānīyā [funeral hymns]: "They burn the one who has maintained the sacred fires with the fires and with the sacrificial vessels. If they were to be given away, they would not be present there; therefore, they also must not be given away.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (Sūtra 10) (Yukti 2)
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga), namely: "Fourteen oblations are offered on the full moon day; thirteen on the new moon day.
Therefore, for this reason as well, it is a restatement (anuvāda).

The section concerning the desire for expression regarding the oneness of the animal (*paśvekatvādivivakṣādhikaraṇa*), also known as the *paśvekatvanyāya*.
443. Sūtra:
"In that case, there is oneness [of the mantra], as it is not a constituent part of the sacrifice, because the purpose is subordinate. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 11 ||
Bhāṣya-sūtra-bhāṣya (The Commentary on the Aphorisms of the Bhāṣya)

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, as it is said: "The initiated one who sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma"; likewise, "He yokes two oxen"; and similarly, in the Aśvamedha, "He sacrifices kapiñjala birds to the spring."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is the singularity, duality, and plurality intended to be expressed (*vivakṣita*), or are they not intended? In that context, the meaning is that singularity, not being a constituent part of the sacrifice (*ayajñāṅgabhūta*), is not intended to be expressed; for [in the case of the singular], the purpose (*artha*) is subordinate, and the substance (*ālambha*) is not subordinate.

Or rather, the number belongs to the act of joining. To what, then? To the animal, the two oxen, and the *kapiñjala* birds; for the case-ending, by virtue of direct audition (*śruti*), expresses the meaning of number as residing in the meaning of the nominal stem.
It could express it as a subsidiary element of the sacrifice only through syntactical connection (*vākya*), and direct audition is more authoritative than syntactical connection.
Therefore, it is not intended as a constituent part of the sacrifice—[one might object]:
"Let it not be a constituent part of the sacrifice; nevertheless, it is intended as a constituent part of the animal victim and so forth."

It is possible. There is no purpose whatsoever served by whether the limb of the animal and so forth is mentioned or not mentioned; for the purpose is served by the sacrifice's own constituent part being unimpaired.
Indeed, even if a limb of the animal or the like is impaired, the sacrifice remains deficient, and sacrifices [yield] their fruit.
Not so for the animal and the like. Therefore, whether the quality of the animal and so forth is unknown or known, there is no purpose served; thus, that is not intended to be expressed.
For it is said that only that which possesses a purpose is intended to be expressed.
And because there is a single accentuation. (Yukti 12)

Furthermore, there exists certain speech by which it is understood that something was not intended to be expressed—for instance, "If they should steal the Soma, one cow should be given as the sacrificial fee.

For if this were intended to be expressed, he would not have said "one" (ekām), because the singular number in the word "cow" (gām) is itself intended to be significant; likewise, this applies to the case of "two ewes, two milch-cows," and so forth.
The word "de" (that) is an indicator; in the Mīmāṃsā system, the doubling of the syllable "avo" is not intended to be expressed. [Page 512]
Bhāṣya: Thus. In the verse "three lalāmas," the mention of the word *śroṇi* (hip) is also a [supporting] mark;
Sūtra Bhāṣya.
The plural number in the word *lalāmāni* is not intended to be significant.
If it is argued that [the meaning] is understood—(Ābhāsya 13).

If you view it thus—that the number is not intended to be expressed—then that is not correct;

for the number is understood as being an integral part of the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-vacana*), just as when it is said, "Bring the animal" (*paśum ānaya*), only one is brought; or when "animals" (*paśū*) is said, two are brought; or when "animals" (*paśūn*) is said, many are brought.
And that which is so understood is the word-meaning (*śabdārtha*); therefore, [the number is indeed intended].

That number is a constituent part of the sacrifice is understood from the word; and that which is understood from a word does not fail to be intended unless there is a specific reason [to the contrary].
The word "own" [refers to the sacrificer] because it is a means of valid cognition, as in the previous case. (0 Ni0) || 14 ||

Bhāṣya: This is not so; what is perceived is true, and this is not a non-verbal meaning arising from delusion or the like. Why is this? Because it is understood from the syntactical connection (*vākya*) that [the number] is an auxiliary of the sacrifice, yet the syntactical connection is sublated by the direct statement (*śruti*). Therefore, in the sacrifice, unity and so forth are not non-verbal meanings. For even a verbal meaning is perceived, as in the case of "He runs ahead. He is called "ahead" (*pūrva*) because there is another behind him; thus, when "ahead" is said, [it refers to one who has another behind him].
Another [meaning] is understood, but it is not understood that "another runs," because of the hearing [of the word];
likewise here too, from the word "animal" (paśum), singularity is understood, but not [its application] to the sacrifice. Just as...

For when it is said "previously," the other [element] is merely understood, but it is not enjoined for any purpose; likewise here too, the number is merely perceived, but it is not enjoined as something to be performed in the sacrifice, nor in the animal victim.

But if it is asked, "Why is it not prescribed in the case of the animal sacrifice?"—the answer is: because of the absence of an injunctive [word]. Even the claim that "the verbal form will be the injunctive" is not tenable.

—Since that [sentence] "He should sacrifice" (śrālabhate) is an injunction of the relationship between the substance and the deity, it cannot also enjoin the relationship between the number and the numbered; for in that case, the sentence would be split. Therefore, the number is not intended to be significant.
Chapter 4, Section 1.
[Objection: It is perceived like its own word; for when that [word] occurs, it is seen. [Response: Its cognition is [inferred from] the manifestation (bhā).
Sūtra: It is as in the case of others. (Siddhānta) || 15 ||

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position: it is not the case that number is not heard by means of a word in the sacrifice; for the meaning is perceived as expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).
In common worldly usage, when one says "bring a cow" (*paśum ānaya*) with the singular ending, the act of bringing is qualified by the oneness of the cow.

It is understood that in the command "Bring two animals," what is cognized is that which is qualified by duality; for in that case, singularity departs and duality arises. And it is understood that when something arises upon the addition of another element, that [new element] is its meaning—just as with other words. For example, when "Bring the horse" is said, the bringing of a horse is understood; and when "Bring the cow" is said, the bringing of a cow is understood.
In the case of bringing a cow, where a horse departs and a cow appears, it is thereby known that the word "horse" has the horse as its meaning and the word "cow" has the cow as its meaning.

As for what was said—that "by the *śruti* (direct Vedic statement), the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) is sublated"—it is replied: it is not that the *śruti* is set aside, nor is there no meaning of the sentence; rather, the *śruti* merely expresses the number inherent in the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Such a number is enjoined in the sacrifice by the sentence. For the meaning of the nominal stem is connected both with the verbal expression and with the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*); thus, the act of offering (*ālambha*) is understood as qualified by that [number]. In that case, because they share a single purpose, they constitute a single sentence (*ekavākya*).

It is logical [that the number is intended]. For if the number were prescribed with respect to the animal, a single verbal form would not be able both to enjoin the meaning of the verb and to establish the relationship between the number and the thing numbered.
Therefore, the number is intended to be significant in the sacrifice.
And there is an indicative mark (liṅga) to that effect. (Sūtra 16; Yuktisthāna 1)
What [is it]?—thus [it is asked]. "The two ears are dedicated to Yama, the ointments are dedicated to Rudra, those of the form of the sky are dedicated to Pajanya;

of these, the one dedicated to Indra and Agni is the tenth"—if multiplicity (*citvam*) is intended, then the one dedicated to Indra and Agni becomes the tenth. Likewise, "the black ones are dedicated to the Earth, the smoky..."

Having introduced them with the words, "The atmospheric ones, the firm divine ones, the variegated lightning ones, and the perfected star-ones," he says: "This which consists of the five [days] is indeed the form of the half-months.

Bhāṣya: "Of those possessing ten. Therefore, we also see that the number is intended to be expressed.

— thus [it is said]. As for what was stated—that the phrase "one cow" shows that the singular number is not intended to be significant—it is replied here: this is stated in order to enjoin the connection with the number of cows; for otherwise, the connection with the cow as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) would be understood as being enjoined.

Therefore, this applies even when gender is intended to be significant; for instance, the statements "two cows" (*dhenū*) and "three khalas" (*khalān*) are restatements (*anuvāda*). This concludes the portion of the preceding section concerning the significance of gender. (4.2.5) [Adhikaraṇa]. This also follows from the section on the significance of gender.
And likewise, there is an indicative mark [to this effect]. (Sūtra 17) (Yukti 2)
And by doing so, the gender (liṅga) which shares the same phonetic form will also be intended;

in that case, this following observation becomes applicable: "In spring, at dawn, one sacrifices a black-necked animal to Agni; in summer, at midday, a lioness to Indra; in autumn, in the afternoon, a white cow to Bṛhaspati. There it is heard: "They are pregnant. Since pregnancy is a quality of females, this will indicate that [the animals] are female.
Likewise, it is stated: "The horse, the bull, the he-goat, the ram, and the man—these belong to Prajāpati.
In that context, it is heard: "They are possessed of testicles for the sake of possessing virility"; since being possessed of testicles is a quality of males, this indicates the inclusion of males.

Or it is another topic (*adhikaraṇāntara*); for there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) to that effect—namely, the topic concerning number (*saṃkhyādhikaraṇa*) is seen within the topic concerning gender (*liṅgādhikaraṇa*). [The objection is: "Gender is not intended to be expressed, because it is sublated by the syntactical connection (*vākya*) rather than by direct statement (*śruti*); nor is it heard as if it were intended to be expressed"—thus, there is an indicative mark.

In the statement, "The auspicious cow is the *somakrayaṇī* (the cow for purchasing Soma)," because of the feminine gender (*strīvacana*), it is understood that the gender is indeed not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). [Objection: "But why is a male deer not brought when one says, 'Bring a doe'? [Response: It is not so; that is merely a non-verbal [indication], just as in the case of the phrase, "It runs ahead. Or rather, the gender is intended to be significant, because the meaning of the sentence is established by the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). Likewise...
And there is the indicative mark (liṅga): "They become pregnant," and likewise, "They become eunuchs" (muṣkarāḥ) [Page 515],

Bhāṣya: As for what was stated—namely, "The cow is for the purchase of Soma"—therein the feminine gender (*strī*) is not intended to be significant; likewise, in the statement, "He sacrifices men and elephants to Prajāpati," the mention of "men" (*puruṣa*) is not intended to be significant. The section concerning the invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*) of those things that depend on a substratum.
The meaning would be understood as existing without distinction among all substrata. || 18 ||

In this context, the examples of the dependent (*āśrayin*) categories are [the following sacrifices]: the final fore-offering (*uttama-prayāja*), the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*), and the *sviṣṭakṛt*—these sacrifices serve as the examples. Regarding these, there is a doubt: is the sacrifice merely a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the deity, or is an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*) produced in the deity by means of the sacrifice? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)?—[It is that] in the case of the dependent sacrifices...

"In the absence of any distinction, the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is understood"—this being the case for such types of bases, the meaning of the verbal root as *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is to be understood specifically in other verbal forms, namely *yajati*, *dadāti*, and *juhoti*. This has been stated [in the Bhāṣya]: "That which has come into being (*bhūta*) is taught for the sake of that which is to be brought into being (*bhavya*)" (Mīmāṃsāsūtra 2.1.4).
But in the case of its own injunction, there is no commencement [of a separate rite], because it is already differentiated; for it is not enjoined by another. (Sūtra 19) (Śrauta)

In this injunction, however, there is no commencement of a new [apūrva] for the former [act], because the verbal form is designated as having a different case-role (*vibhakti*)—that which has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) does not produce an *apūrva*, whereas that which indeed has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) produces an *apūrva*.
And this [act] has a visible purpose; for when this sacrifice is performed, the deity...
Those ritual items which, by means of a single part, depend upon another's substance, a deity, or both, and thereby consecrate them, are called "dependent" (āśrayin); this is your view.
[Page 516] It is recorded in the Bhāṣya that even in the case of the sviṣṭakṛt offering,
the substance is disposed of, and it is not by any other word.
In this case, something previously unknown is being enjoined; therefore, the sacrifice itself is the purificatory rite.

[The word] *sra* [denotes the substance] when there is a desire to act upon a substance; and in the case of a verbal root meaning an action (*bhāva-artha*), there is a state of being subordinate (*guṇabhūtatā*) based on its dependence [on another], which constitutes subordination (*guṇībhāva*). (Siddhānta 20)

Or rather, there may be an unseen result (*apūrva*) from this; for even when there is a desire to honor the deity, the sacrifice is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to that purpose of purifying the deity and to the presentation of the substance. In that context, the deity is remembered by means of the mantra; while that mantra is being employed for a visible purpose, the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) is heard as having a transcendent (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose. For that [act of relinquishment], there is no visible effect whatsoever, other than its being based upon the deity.
It is understood that this [offering] is dedicated to the deity and is unprecedented (apūrva). (4.2.7 Śrauta Sūtra)

[This occurs] due to the equality or inequality of the purpose and the substances and actions. || 21 ||

The third subject has been concluded; from this point forward, the equality and inequality regarding the purpose (*artha*) of substances and ritual actions will be discussed—namely, in some cases there is equality, and in others there is inequality: the inequality between *āmikṣā* and *vājina*, the inequality among the means of purchase (*krayaṇa*), and the equality of the staff (*daṇḍa*) in being held by both the Maitrāvaruṇa priest and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Thus it shall be treated in various instances.
The equality and inequality [of the results] must be observed—thus [ends the discussion]. (4.1.8 Śra.)
The reading in the Kaśmīra and Sāradā manuscripts is *akhiladarpi*; the reading in the Kāśmīra and Kīra manuscripts is *viṣṭakṛtyāpi*.

Regarding substances and actions such as the staff, the fetching [of water], and so forth, "equality" means they are employed for the same purpose; "inequality" means they are employed by one [factor] but not by the other. The meaning is that what follows this will be explained;
thus ends the section.
