(The Vājinanyāya:
Since they are produced from a single source, everything should be equal. (Pūrvapakṣa 22)

In the Vaiśvadeva section of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "One pours curd into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas, and the whey (*vājina*) for the Vājavantyas. Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the pouring of curd into heated milk serve as the motive for the *āmikṣā*, but not for the *vājina*?

Or rather, both? What is the prima facie view? Both. Why? Because it is understood that when something is performed and another thing is produced as a useful result, the former is the motivator (prayojaka) of the latter; and when the curd-mixture (dadhi) is brought in, both are produced from it—the *āmikṣā* as well as the whey (*vājina*). Therefore, [the bringing of the curd] would be performed for the sake of one or the other, if—
If there were a reason for determining [one over the other], it would be so; however, since no distinction is perceived, it is understood that both purposes are served by bringing [the substance].
Therefore, this single accomplishment is instigated by both.
Or rather, because the production of the flavor of the mixture [results] from the contact of the curds with the milk, the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) should be the primary element. 23.

Bhāṣya: This is not the case—that both [the curd and the milk] are the motivators; rather, the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) is the motivator. Why? Because that which is produced from the curd and the milk is not the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). If that were the oblation, then it would be understood as a specific distinction that both [substances] are produced from those two [alone]. What...?
What is the sacrificial oblation (*havis*)? It is milk mixed with curds. Why is this so?
Because it is called "belonging to the Viśvedevas" (*vaiśvadevī*), not that which is produced from it.
[Objection: But surely, because of the feminine gender designation, the *āmikṣā* (curdled milk) is the oblation, and that is produced from it.

"It is produced, and the whey-offering (*vājina*) is also produced"—this is not so, it is said; for that very milk, when heated and mixed with curds, becomes *āmikṣā*. Therefore, the mark of the three [milkings] is without fault. He asks: "If the offering (*havis*) is milk mixed with curds, then why is it said that *āmikṣā* is the motivator? It is replied:
In the Mīmāṃsā system, Bhāṣya:
"It will be combined. We say: "No."

By the specific sentence, "He purchases [the Soma] with a one-year-old cow," the one-year-old cow taught for the purpose of purchase is connected to the sentence concerning the foot-dust because it is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*); and a sentence is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*). Now, having been mentioned for the purpose of purchase as a one-year-old cow, she—being proximate—would be connected to the sentence concerning the foot-dust by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*). That which...
"O Parārthin, this step of hers is to be grasped. Therefore, the leading [of the cow] is connected with the purchase;
the step is not the motive.

What, then, is the purpose of this inquiry? If both [the purchase and the step] were motives for the leading of the one-year-old cow, then when the seventh step of the one-year-old cow [is taken] upon the pressing-stones...
When it is deposited, then the one-year-old cow should be led again for the seventh step;
when the step is not the motive factor, then the one-year-old cow need not again be made to follow six steps—thus [is the conclusion]. (4.1.9)
The section concerning the non-application of the scattering of husks and ashes upon the potsherds: Sūtra 26.
And the act of naming the purpose [of the potsherds] is for the sake of that which is yet to come, because the connection is caused by that; for it is for that purpose that the injunction is made.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "He bakes the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) on the potsherds," and likewise, "He scatters the husks with the cake-potsherd. Regarding this, there is a doubt: do both—the baking of the cake and the scattering of the husks—motivate the use of the potsherds, or is only the baking the motivator, and not the scattering of the husks?
What is established? Since there is no reason for a definitive conclusion [favoring one over the other], both [alternatives] are possible.

This being the position, it is said: that which has an expression connected to a purpose—that is, an expression whose purpose is the accomplishment of a specific aim—is like "the cake-pan" (*puroḍāśakapālam*); [here] the pan is for the sake of the cake.
The cake-offering potsherd. How is this understood? First of all, at that time the cake does not exist, such that there could be a present relationship with the potsherd;
for that very reason, it is not past either. Thus, this [relationship] of the potsherd is with the cake that is yet to come.
Chapter 4, Section 1.
There is a connection [between the potsherds and the cake], and there is also a connection with that which is to come about; it arises from that cause.
Therefore, whatever potsherd is employed for the sake of the *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake), by means of that, the husks are to be scattered. Thus it is said.

And this being the case, when a pan is taken up for the purpose of pouring out the husks in the absence of a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) during the cooked rice (caru) offering, that [pan] would not be a "cake-pan" (puroḍāśakapāla); and if it is not so, the husks cannot be poured out by means of it. Therefore, there is no pouring out of husks upon the pans.
The instigator; for cooking is the instigating act. (4.1.10)
The section concerning the non-employment of excrement and blood in the animal sacrifice.
Sūtra 27: Because of the non-sacrificing of the animal, there is no ritual action regarding its blood and dung.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma; regarding it, it is heard in the scripture: "He cuts a portion from the heart, then from the tongue," and so forth; likewise, "He discards the blood, he throws away the dung, and having removed the outer skin of the thick parts, he discards it. In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the sacrifice of the animal performed by means of the portions such as the heart and the rest?

Is it the one who performs the act, or is both the single piercing and the removal of blood also the instigator? What is the prima facie view? "Because they result from a single action, everything should be equal" (4.1.22 Sūtra);
thus, both are instigators.
This being the position, we reply: in the case of the animal sacrifice, the piercing and the blood are not instigating factors.

Indeed, the purpose of the animal sacrifice is for that [blood], as it is said: "From it he pierces and pours out the blood"; this refers neither to the animal nor to anything else. The animal belongs to Agni and Soma by virtue of the direct statement (vākya): "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma.
The blood and the fat would belong to the animal by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa), but context is overridden by the direct statement.

"But surely, these two—the bristles and the blood—are prescribed; therefore, the certainty is that it is the animal intended for sacrifice, and not any other. If this is so, then the bristles and the blood are non-contributory (*aprayojaka*). What is the purpose [of this discussion]? When they are equal [in status], in the absence of bristles and blood, another animal should be seized; however, if the bristles and blood are non-contributory, there is an omission [of them].

Sūtra 28: [The production of a whole] from its parts occurs because of the conjunction of existing substances with one another.

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "He cuts off [the portion] for the Sviṣṭakṛt from the northern half. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the Āgneya sacrifice the motivator (prayojaka) of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), while the Sviṣṭakṛt is not a motivator, or are both motivators? What is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)?

"Because they are produced as one, everything would be equal"—this being the position reached, we reply: a substance consisting of a single part (*ekadeśadravya*) of this kind would be the motivator (*prayojaka*). Why? Because of the connection with what is already present; it does not motivate the whole (*avayavin*) through the action upon a single part. Rather, a single part of the already existing whole is to be taken up; in that case, the scriptural authority (*śruti*) prevails, and not [the requirement of the whole].

"One should take the possessor of the part"— as when one says, "Give a piece of sugarcane to this person," or "Give a fragment of a sweetmeat to him," it is understood that one should not take the sugarcane itself,
but rather take a piece from the existing sugarcane, or a fragment from the existing sweetmeat.

"One should take [a portion]"—thus it is said. Therefore, the substance is for another purpose; from its upper half, one should offer [the portion], and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) exists for the sake of Agni. Consequently, the sviṣṭakṛt offering is not the motive [for the preparation of the cake]. Thus it is concluded.
[Objection: "Because of the specific designation, it is for the sake of something else. (Sūtra 28).

[Page 522] "Let there be a share for me," he said. "Then choose," they replied. He said, "The *uttarā* alone shall yield for me, yielding again and again. The Bhāṣya states: There is the Vājapeya sacrifice, [enjoined by the text] "One desiring sovereign rule should sacrifice with the Vājapeya.

There is a doubt: should another vessel be produced for the purpose of holding the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings in order to sprinkle the omenta (*vapā*) of the *prājāpatya* animals with it, and then the omenta of the *prājāpatya* animals should be sprinkled with that [remnant]; or rather, should the remnant not be held, and thus the omenta of the *prājāpatya* animals should not be sprinkled with it at all? Furthermore, at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), there is the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings; at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*), when the time for the *vipralaṣṭa* has passed, the immolation of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati is heard [in scripture]: "They release those that have been carried around the fire (*paryagnikṛtān*); he immolates the one belonging to Brahma at the time of the *brahmasāman*. And thus the *juhū* ladle becomes occupied. Therefore, another vessel must be produced, just as in the case of the *anuyāja* offerings.
A vessel is produced for the purpose of holding the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya), because of the scriptural statement, "He sacrifices the after-offerings with speckled butter"; so it is here as well.

Or rather, it is not [the case], because of unworthiness; but unworthiness arises from being only a part.

Nor should the omenta of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati be sprinkled with clarified butter. Why? Because there is no remnant (*śeṣa*). Because it is a single portion; for that which is a portion of another thing taken for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings is the remnant. What follows from this? If this is so, a single portion being enjoined as an operation does not enjoin the whole (*avayavin*) as something to be taken up.

He says: "One should not cause the production [of the substance]; the maintenance of what has been produced will follow as a matter of course. It is replied: Because it is a single part, the sprinkling does not necessitate the substance itself; for this is merely a single part of a substance whose purpose has already been fulfilled.

It is established that [the act] is for the purpose of pouring out, not for the purpose of sprinkling. [Objection: "But surely, because of the use of the accusative case, the oblations (*haviṣ*) would be the primary object. There is a need for the empty vessel, not for the clarified butter as an oblation. Therefore, there is no purpose at all for the omenta of the Prājāpatya offerings being besmeared with clarified butter; for what reason, then, should the remnant be retained? Thus it is asked.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "Having passed over the iḍā, he pours together [the butter] toward the barhis. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the pouring together (samānayana) of the clarified butter (ājya) and its ritual requirements (dharmas) a motivator (prayojaka), or is it not a motivator? What is the prima facie view? It is not a motivator. Why? Because this portion of the clarified butter intended for the prayāja and anuyāja offerings is being poured together; thus, according to the previous principle, it is not a motivator.
It has been established; therefore, this is stated: "The drawing together [of the butter] is the mouth, because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).

What is the indicative mark? It is heard in the Śruti: 'There are other [portions] taken four times each; for he is not one who is about to perform the after-offerings (anuyāja)'—if it were for the sake of the fore-offerings (prayāja)."

Regarding the *samānayana*: then, one *caturgṛhīta* portion is brought together there; even one [portion] belongs to the *anuyāja*s. And thus, the *iḍā* of the *ātithya* rite is concluded—meaning that in the absence of the *anuyāja*s, one *caturgṛhīta* portion is to be taken for the purpose of the *samānayana*, but not for the purpose of the *anuyāja*s. In that case, the observation of many *caturgṛhīta* portions is logically consistent.
For otherwise, in the absence of the after-offerings (anuyāja), one would not indeed take four portions in the upabhṛt;
thus, the plural number in "those four portions" (tāni catugṛhītāni) would be untenable. Therefore, the bringing together [of the butter] is the motive.

"But surely a mark (liṅga) is taught; what is the attainment [of the purpose]? It is said: A visible purpose is seen there, namely that the *prayāja* offerings are to be made. It is for a visible purpose; therefore, for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings, the clarified butter from the *aupabhṛta* vessel is brought over.

Among the five *prayājas*, the third *prayāja* is designated by the word "iṣṭ" with a plural ending. Sūtra: In the case of an occasional rite, because it is a modification, something else should be the primary element of the sacrifice.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is an occasional (naimittika) injunction: "One should perform the Bārhadratha-sāman for a Brāhmaṇa, the Pārthuraśma for a Rājanya, and the Rāyovājīya for a Vaiśya.
Likewise, in the case of the fire-altar (agni), there is an occasional injunction: "One who is building the first [fire-altar] should build it with a thousand [bricks]."

"One should collect [wood] in two thousand pieces for the second [fire], and in three thousand pieces for the third"—thus it is heard in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices: "One desiring cattle should fetch water with a milking vessel;

one desiring spiritual luster, with a bronze vessel; one desiring stability, with an earthen vessel. These are occasional (naimittika) injunctions. Regarding them, there is a doubt: are these very occasional acts intended for the permanent (nitya) purpose, or is there something else for the permanent purpose in each respective case?

What is established here? Are these [elements] themselves [to be used]? Why? Because in this case, the *brahmasāman* and so forth must necessarily exist; for they have been enjoined and require proximate means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

Yet, they do not possess their own prescribed means of accomplishment, and contingent elements (*naimittika*) present themselves nearby; therefore, by means of those [elements] belonging to the archetype (*prakṛta*) which are proximate, these [elements] [are supplied].

They are rendered free from expectancy—this is logical. How so? For that which is contingent (*naimittika*) is understood from the proximate sentence; nothing else is heard. And whatever fault there is in abandoning what is heard, exactly the same fault exists in the postulation of what is not heard.
He says: "But surely those [rites] were introduced for the purpose of the *nimitta* (contingent occasion). It is replied:

This is not a fault; even that which is introduced for one purpose may be connected with another, just as irrigation channels are constructed for the sake of rice, yet water is drunk from them and used for ritual sipping (*upaspṛśyate*).

And so it should be understood here as well. Alternatively, there is indeed an intermediate sentence here, such as "one should lead [the water] with a *godohana* vessel"; that, being connected to a specific desire (*kāma*), establishes the leading of water by means of the *godohana*. And it is not possible to discard what has been directly stated (*śruta*). As for this reading "pāthurasyam," it is the reading found in the Kāśīmudrita (Kāśī printed) edition.

The word "of one desiring cattle" (paśukāmasya) is capable of expressing its connection with the desire for cattle; it cannot, however, set aside the meaning of the intermediate sentence, nor can it negate what is already understood.

It cannot be said that [these texts] are without cause or are unintended; for there are indeed sentences that possess a double meaning, such as "The white one runs" or "He who goes among the Alambusas.
Therefore, these occasional (naimittika) injunctions must indeed serve the purpose of the obligatory (nitya).
Thus the prima facie view having been stated, we reply: when a contingent rite (*naimittika*) is heard in the scripture, there should be "another" [action] for the sake of the sacrifice.

Why? Because it is a modification (*vikāra*)—that is to say, because it is prescribed in reference to a specific condition (*viśeṣa*); for that contingent rite is heard in connection with a specific circumstance, and in the absence of that [circumstance], [the original rule applies].

It cannot be so in the case of a specific [rule]. Therefore, in each case, something else [applies] apart from the occasional [application].

"Of such a kind"—thus he said:

It is possible to supply an ellipsis in a sentence, for this sentence is indeed complete: "The Viśvajit sacrifice is to be performed. There is no word here that is expectant (sākāṅkṣa), by means of which one might supply something and connect it with a result, as in the case of a deceptive instruction on an unsafe path, such as "Go by this way," where the road is safe; this sentence is complete and does not require an ellipsis made by a deceiver. In the same way, this sentence too is complete and does not require an ellipsis.

Moreover, this sentence would be connected only with that which is being enjoined: "The Viśvajit sacrifice is to be performed" and "this is the fruit"—these are two distinct matters, whereas it has been established that a single sentence conveys a single meaning. Therefore, a sentence of this kind is indeed purposeless.
Karma is the messenger.

for words are recognized as meaningful through the meaningfulness of their referents. For those things which are incapable in terms of their meaning, there is no connection even when they are in immediate proximity; therefore, that is merely a fragment of the Vedic revelation (śruti).

Bhāṣya:
"Or rather"—this is the rejection of the previous position. Nor is it the case that this [injunction] is without fruit;
for the injunction is understood through its purpose. Through what purpose?

[The opponent replies] by means of the expression "that which ought to be done" (*kartavyatā*). [The proponent asks: "But surely the 'ought-to-be-done-ness' of an activity (*vyāpāra*) is contradicted by perception. [The opponent replies: "It is not said of the activity itself. Of what, then? Of something else by means of the activity. Thus, the sentence now remains expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*).
In that case, an ellipsis (adhyāhāra) is appropriate, for a construction can indeed be made even by means of ellipsis;
as when "the door, the door" is said, it is understood: "Let it be closed," or "Let it be opened. But how is it known that an ellipsis must be supplied here?
By the force of the scriptural tradition (āmnāna); thus this tradition will become meaningful, and it is capable of making the meaning understood. Therefore, [it is not the case that...].
It is meaningless.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that whatever word is supplied is of human origin, and therefore what is understood through it is not authoritative? [Reply: We shall not supply anything new; rather, [we will supply] by means of the Vedic [text].

Thus, we determine that this [word] forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with another word recited elsewhere. [Objection: "This is not possible; for a word that occurs in close proximity is capable of contributing to the meaning of a sentence, whereas one that stands at a distance is not. To this it is replied: even a word that is separated [from its partner] sets aside the intervening factor and, by virtue of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), [attains its connection].
When something revolves in the mind, it is quite sufficient to produce a specific [cognition];
for example:
"O messenger, do you see that tree growing far away as it runs?"
I tell you, O large-eyed one! You who cook an old ox!

Bhāṣya: Thus you see from here—the word "śabda" becomes "buddha"; that [word], by means of these intervening words, [is connected] with the word "jaradgavam," which has arisen at a distance, like a tree.
Sūtra Bhāṣya Sūtra.

The commentary [states]: being connected by setting aside the intervening factors, it is connected; for, by the reason that "the meanings of these [words] are purposeful," even those "statements" which are separated are connected—those which...

Furthermore, [the phrase] "therefore, indeed" (*athato hi*)—being incapable even when there is immediate sequence (*ānantarya*)—does not deserve a mutual connection with [the preceding], just like [sentences] such as "she who milks the old bull" (*yā pinaci jaradgavam*). Therefore, there will be no human authorship (*pauruṣeyatā*). [Objection:
But surely, even here, the dependence is human. [Reply: It is said: No, it is not dependent.

It is known that this [word expressing the desire for a fruit] serves as a means for the comprehension of the meaning of the Veda; since there can be no dependence on anything else in the immediate proximity, another kind of dependence is resorted to by virtue of the power of the sacred tradition (*āmnāna*). Therefore, it is "a part of that scriptural statement" (the meaning is: although the word expressing the desire for a fruit is situated at a distance, it constitutes a part of that sentence).
And the meaning of the sentence is like the meaning of the subordinate element. (Yukti)

"Just as in the case of the statement, 'The boar for King Indra,' where a prescription of a subordinate quality occurs through an injunctive word situated in another sentence, so too may there be a prescription of a result; just as in the case of the restriction [implied by] the statement, 'Varuṇa indeed seized him at the outset,' so too should this [present case] be understood. (4.3.5)
The section concerning the single fruit of the Viśvajit and other sacrifices.
All that [is performed] for every purpose, because there is no specific instruction. (13) (50)

"Therefore, one performs [the rite] for the ancestors on the previous day"—thus it is established that such an action is indeed fruitful, as in the case of "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit. However, this is doubted: is this action productive of all fruits, or of a single fruit?
What is established?—"That is for all purposes. Why? "Because there is no specific instruction," according to the Mīmāṃsā system. [Page 570]

Bhāṣya: Nothing specific is indicated here as to what particular fruit results from this. If there were such a thing, it would be known. Therefore, it is for all purposes, because there is no distinction.
Sūtra:
Or rather, it is one, because the injunction is one. (Conclusion) 14.

[The Bhāṣya says: "There would be a single result, or [the injunction] would not be for all purposes. Why? Because of the unity of the injunction (*codanaikatvāt*), and because of its expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatvāt*), this is connected with the word denoting the person seeking [the result]—as has been stated. And that which is capable of being connected even with many is connected with one; having been connected with one..."

It becomes free from expectancy; it does not deserve to be connected with anything else. Therefore, it is logical that there is only one injunction of what is to be done (*kartavyatā-codanā*); consequently, there is a single result (*ekaphalatā*).
Sūtra-samuccaya-bhāṣya (The Commentary on the Compendium of Sūtras)

That [result] would be heaven, because it is common to all. || 15 ||
(Sūtra 10)

In regard to examples of this kind, it has been established that there is a single result. Now, however, a doubt arises: is it any [result whatsoever], or is it heaven? The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is any [result], because no specific distinction is stated. To this, it is replied: "That [result] would be heaven, because it is common to all."

"For all men indeed desire heaven. Why is this so? Because heaven is pleasure, and everyone seeks pleasure. What follows from this? If it is so, then the word, which expresses without distinction, will not be restricted to a specific [class of persons] when it says, 'one should sacrifice' or 'one should act. Therefore, such [acts as these] have heaven as their fruit."
"And because of the conviction [regarding it].

(Yuktidīpikā 16) Furthermore, in the world there exists the conviction that heaven is the fruit of an action whose fruit has not been explicitly enjoined; thus it is said: "Devadatta has made a grove; heaven is certain for him."
[Page 571] Bhāṣya:
"Devadatta has come from the pond; his attainment of heaven is certain"—if this is so, how is it known? It is through this reasoning that there arises a conviction regarding heaven.

When actions that have heaven as their fruit are to be performed, they do not explicitly utter the word for the fruit; it is simply understood. Therefore, from this also, we understand that in such cases, heaven is the result. (4.3.7)
The section concerning the fact that the *rātrisatra* has its fruit stated in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
(The Principle of the Night-Sacrifice Session).
Sūtra 17: Kārṣṇājini maintains that in a sacrifice, the explanatory passage concerning the fruit is like a subsidiary element. (Pūrvapakṣa)

In the *Bhāṣya*, regarding the nights (*rātrīs*), it is heard: "Those who perform these [rites] indeed become firmly established; those who perform these become endowed with Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasvin*). In this regard, there is a doubt: are these explanatory passages concerning results (*phalārthavāda*), or are they injunctions of results (*phalavidhi*)? What is the prima facie view? They are explanatory passages concerning results—so says *Kāṇījini*.

[The opponent] thought: "Why? Because these words have the form of explanatory passages (arthavāda) concerning results. What is this similarity? It is the absence of the injunctive suffix (vidhi-vibhakti), just as in the case of "subsidiary elements" (aṅga); for example, in such passages as, "He whose sacrificial ladle (sruva) is made of khadira wood cuts [the portion] with the very essence of the meters."
Sva. (Sūtra 18): Ātreya [holds that] the fruit [belongs to the sacrificer], because of the specific instruction; for where it is not heard, there must be inference.
Bhāṣya (Siddhānta).

The teacher Ātreya, however, maintained that for such [passages] there is indeed a "fruit," and not that they are merely explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) regarding a fruit. Why? Because even though no fruit is explicitly heard in these cases, there must be a scriptural injunction for a fruit (*phala-codanā*) existing as a supplement to the sentence. Therefore, while another [injunction] might be assumed to exist indirectly and thus separated, this one is already established as being immediate;
for the direct connection of these [passages] with "firm standing" (*pratiṣṭhā*) and the "possession of Brahman-splendor" (*brahmavarcasa*) is perceptible.
Only the case-ending of the injunction is to be expected from another source.
[Page 572] Bhāṣya.

[Objection: "But how can the mere injunctive suffix alone come from elsewhere [as a separate entity], such that it will be connected with this verbal root-meaning, such as *pratiṣṭhā* (establishment) and so forth? [Reply: It is said: It will exist together with the verbal root-meaning, not alone; therefore, there is no fault. Now...

Or rather, that same injunctive suffix which enjoins the nights will also enjoin this specific result, such as "firm foundation," through the performance-injunction (prayogavacana); or else, together with the praises, it will be the enjoiner of the firm foundation and so forth. Thus [it is argued].
kha. The praise [of the limbs] is for the sake of another, because it serves a different purpose. (0 ni0) ||

Now, as for what was said—that just as in such passages as "He whose *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira* wood," the mention of a fruit (*phalaśruti*) is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), so it might be here as well—it is appropriate that there the mention of a fruit is an explanatory praise, because a direct injunction of a fruit is impossible there and because an explanatory praise of a fruit is possible. As it has been stated: "In the case of substances, purificatory acts, and rituals, the mention of a fruit must be an explanatory praise, because they exist for the sake of another" (Sūtra 4.3.1). (Section 4.3.8)
The section concerning the fact that optional rites yield the specific results as stated.

In the case of an optional rite, [the agent] is constant [in his purpose], just as in the case of a sacrifice, [the performer] is constant in his purpose regarding the sacrificial limb for the sake of the ritual.
20 || (Pūrvapakṣa) ||
The optional rites (*kāmyāni karmāṇi*) are the examples—such as, "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer the *saurya* oblation," and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt:

is heaven both the fruit and the desired object (*kāma*) of these rites, or is it only the desired object? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Heaven should be a constant factor in an optional rite. Why? Because a general term denoting the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*) is not restricted to a specific [object].
For it is possible for this [term] to be connected even with the word "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), though situated at a distance.
An objection is raised: "But surely a qualifying term is heard—namely, 'desiring Vedic splendor' (*brahmavarcasakāma*)? This is not a qualifier;
it is merely an incidental attribute (*upādhi*), just as when one has set out to fetch firewood.
He says: "You must also fetch vegetables"—thus, while fetching wood, the fetching of vegetables is made a condition (*upādhi*). What is this "condition"?

Why is it performed?—Because it is taught as a secondary injunction in proximity to the authority for fetching wood: "When there is the fetching of wood, this other thing must also be done. Similarly, here too, when heaven is the fruit, another fruit is taught: "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should bring about heaven by means of sacrifice. For the statement regarding the fruit of spiritual luster in that case does not preclude the fruit of heaven; just as in the case of a subsidiary of the sacrifice which serves the purpose of the rite, [it is said]: "One desiring cattle should fetch water with a milking vessel"—one who desires cattle [uses] the milking vessel.
One should bring it forth—thus.
Sūtra: And when the cause has ceased, [the effect follows] by necessity. (Yuktidīpikā 21)
Bhāṣya-sūtra-bhāṣya (The Commentary on the Sūtras of the Bhāṣya)

Furthermore, when the cause has ceased, or when the desire for the fruit has vanished, or when the fruit has been obtained, a rule of completion is observed; as seen in the *Dṛṣṭikāmedhyā* rite: "If it rains, [the rite] ends right then."

"One should offer the oblation; if it does not rain, one should offer it on the following day"—if heaven were not [the result], for what purpose would there be this rule regarding completion? Therefore, heaven is permanent.
Or rather, desire is enjoined through its connection with that. (Siddhānta) || 22 ||

Either desire (*kāma*) would be the fruit, not heaven; for its injunction (*codanā*) occurs through connection with that [desire], not through connection with the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*). Its syntactic unity (*ekavākyabhāva*) with the one desiring heaven is inferential, whereas [its connection] with the word expressing desire is perceptual; and the perceptual is stronger than the inferential. Therefore, desire alone is the fruit—so it is concluded.
Because it is a subordinate quality in the subsidiary part. (Śrāddhaniyama 1) || 23 ||

Bhāṣya: Now, as for what was said—"just as in the case of a subsidiary of the sacrifice"—that is appropriate, because "in the case of a subsidiary, [the connection] is due to its being a subordinate factor. In that case, the connection with the ritual (*kratu*) and with the desire is directly perceived—as in: "He who may be desirous of cattle..."

"He should accomplish the carrying forward [of the water] by means of the milking vessel"— thus [it is said]; however, there is no direct scriptural statement here that one who desires the power of Brahman should perform the sacrifice.

In the *Bhāṣya* on the *Mīmāṃsā-darśana*, it is stated: "[The sacrifice] would bring about heaven. How, then, [is it to be understood]? "He who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should bring that about by means of that sacrifice. Therefore, it is not like a subsidiary (*aṅga*).
It ought to be so. Thus.
And when [the fire] has been extinguished, there is a restrictive rule for that purpose. (Sūtra 24) (Commentary 2)

Bhāṣya: Now, as for what was said—that when the desire for the fruit has ceased, or when the fruit has been obtained, the rule of completion is observed—to that we reply: "The rule applies when [the desire] has ceased; it is for that purpose. That is, the rule applies when [the desire] has ceased. For what purpose? To avoid the reproach of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). For one who, having commenced [a rite], does not complete it, the learned would immediately reproach him.
—saying, "He is a base man who has already begun [the sacrifice]"; for the learned (śiṣṭas) censure those who, having intended the oblation for the gods, do not bring the sacrifice to completion.

Therefore, it must necessarily be completed; in that case, this scriptural observation will be appropriate: "If it rains, one should offer only as much as has been prepared. Therefore, regarding optional (kāmya) sacrifices...
"Desire alone is the fruit"—thus [it is stated] in the sūtra (4.3.9).
This is the section concerning the fact that the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices are for the purpose of all desires.
(From here onwards, two sections [will be discussed]: the Darśapūrṇamāsa principle).
And [the desire for all objects] is [fulfilled] by the desires for the subsidiaries, because of the context. (Pūrvapakṣa 25)

Bhāṣya: This is recorded in the sacred tradition: "For one specific desire other sacrifices are performed; for all desires, the Darśapūrṇamāsa [are performed]. For one specific desire other rituals (kratavaḥ) are performed;
for all desires, the Jyotiṣṭoma [is performed]. In this regard, there is a doubt: what...?

Is this, together with the desires for the subsidiaries (*aṅgakāma*) and the desires for the subsidiaries of the subsidiaries (*aṅgāṅgakāma*), a restatement (*anuvāda*) or an injunction (*vidhi*)? What is the prima facie view? It is a restatement; that which is "the attainment of all desires" (*sārvakāmya*) is being restated, along with the desires for the subsidiaries and the desires for the subsidiaries of the subsidiaries. For there indeed exist desires for the subsidiaries and desires for the subsidiaries of the subsidiaries, such as: "For one desiring cattle, [the altar] should be made of loose soil."
Chapter 4, Section 3.
"One should construct the altar with a dug-out pit and filled with earth for one desiring a firm foundation"— such [injunctions] as these;
likewise, "If he should desire, 'May Parjanya rain,' [he should place] the *sadas* low."
Regarding the phrase "minuyāt," we consider it proper to regard this as a restatement (anuvāda), since what is being expressed here is precisely that which has already been enjoined.
Sūtra:
"Or rather, it is the instruction regarding the fruit, because of its association with the word denoting the primary [act]. (26)
(Sūtra) ||

The Bhāṣya says: Or rather, it is an injunction of results. Why? Because there is a connection with results through the word denoting the principal [sacrifice], as in "the Darśapūrṇamāsa for all [desires]" and "the Jyotiṣṭoma for all [desires]";
and by the mention of the principal, the possession of all results is enjoined for that principal. Therefore—

It is not a restatement (*anuvāda*). If it were to depend upon the desires for the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the desires for the subsidiaries of the subsidiaries (*aṅgāṅga*), then the word would have to be taken in its secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*); however, direct denotation (*śruti*) is more authoritative than secondary indication. Therefore, the injunction is established by the statement of performance (*prayogavacana*). (4.3.10)
The section concerning the separate performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites for each respective fruit.
(The Principle of the Accomplishment of Yoga)
And that [application] belongs to all [the fires], because there is no distinction. (Pūrvapakṣa 27)

Bhāṣya: It has been stated regarding examples of this kind that there is an injunction for all desires in the primary rite. Now, the following is doubted: do all desires [fulfill themselves] in a single performance of the great rite, or successively? That is to say, are "all" desires fulfilled in one performance? How so?
What is established?
That the Darśapūrṇamāsa and the Jyotiṣṭoma are the cause for all desires; and if they are the cause—
"Will there not indeed be a limit to all desires?"—
therefore, all desires [are to be fulfilled] simultaneously.
3 m [Page 576] sva. The accomplishment of yoga is not possible, because the object is not connected with its production. || 28 || (Siddhānta) ||

And this is not the case—that all desires [should be fulfilled] simultaneously; rather, "succession is the logical conclusion," meaning that desires would occur in succession. Why? "Because the object is not connected with simultaneous production. These objects called desires do not all arise at once;
simultaneous production of all things is impossible due to contradiction. Or alternatively:
It is not [the case] because of the statement "due to being connected with origination," for this is a statement regarding the origination of desires;

it is a statement characterizing those [desires] that have already arisen, namely, "from all those desires, the Darśapūrṇamāsa and the Jyotiṣṭoma [are to be performed]. It is not that all desires are heard of as being [inherently] part of the ritual action, such that "all" [desires] would apply.
"For it is from those [desires] that action is prescribed. Therefore, the concomitance of desires is not understood. (4.3.11).
Or rather:
The section concerning the fact that optional rites possess fruits pertaining to both this world and the next.
(Another interpretation: And that [is] for all, because there is no distinction. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 27 ||

Desire-driven rituals (*kāmyāni karmāṇi*) serve as the illustration: "One desiring Brahmanic luster should offer the *saumya caru*; one desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni; one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrayā* [offering]; one desiring a village should offer the *vaiśvadevī sāgrahāyaṇī*.
Regarding these, there is a doubt: do the desires [fulfilled] belong to this world, or to the next?

"In this world?"—what is the prima facie view? "In that [world], there are desires, because there is no distinction; just as there is heaven, so too are these [desires] there. For cattle and the like are not perceived in a place where [existence] is eternal, and whatever is perceived immediately [after death],"...

That is understood from the word "tataḥ": just as at whatever time the rubbing occurs, at that same time the fruit [arises] in the act of rubbing; [the reading in the Śrauta-sūtra and Soḍhala-puṣpa is "sāgrahīṇīm"].
Chapter 3, Section 3.

[It is] pleasure; and that which is perceived at a later time, its cause is likewise something else entirely, namely perception.

However, there is no cause for the assumption of a body other than the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Therefore, it should be understood that the fruit consisting of specific sense organs, a body, and so forth—which is capable of connecting with a person—arises from a ritual action whose fruit is [normally] animal-based. For that very point is shown by the following: "Kaikaya..."

Desiring to know, he said to Dālbhya, "Sacrifice for me with this *iṣṭi* that secures a kingdom. He replied, "O gentle one, you do not indeed understand that which secures a kingdom; sacrifices are performed for the sake of that specific desire [which bears fruit] in another birth"—thus [he spoke of] the fruitfulness of future lives.
He shows this; therefore, the optional rites have their fruits in another birth.
[The opponent says: "No, because the accomplishment of yoga is connected with the production of the object. (28)

Here indeed is the accomplishment of their yoga; yoga does not arise through mere origination.
He who desires [results] from the sacrificial animals should perform it by means of this sacrifice—thus [it is said], but not [otherwise].

In this regard, it is understood that [the effect] is not possible in this life; and as for the claim that "it is not perceived immediately thereafter," that is not so, for it is not apprehended through perception or inference, but its existence is established by means of scripture (*śabda*). As for the argument that there must be another cause at a later time—

—Thus [it may be argued], but this is not a fault; there will be another [reason], and this too. For example, as in the statement, "For such-and-such a desire these sacrifices are offered"—to this it is replied:
such is the thought of this seer—"In this case, because his reward is [already] attained, I do not cause you to sacrifice for that."
"Whose fruit it is in the next world, by him I shall cause [the sacrifice] to be performed"—thus it is; therefore, this objection is refuted. (4.3.12a)
The section concerning the status of the Sautrāmaṇī and other rites as subsidiaries to the Cayanā (piling of the altar) and other rituals.
Sūtra 28: [The injunction applies] to the inherent relation, because the connection [of the word] is purposeful. (Conclusion)

Bhāṣya: "Having performed the *Niścita*, one should sacrifice with the *Sautrāmaṇī*; having sacrificed with the *Vājapeya*, one should sacrifice with the *Bṛhaspatisava*. In this regard, there is a doubt: is there a relationship between the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the purpose (*prayojana*)?

Is this, moreover, a connection for the purpose of time? We reply: it is a connection between a subsidiary element and its purpose. For in this way the matter is applied by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*); otherwise, time would have to be indicated (*lakṣyeta*) through secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*). And when there is a conflict between direct statement and secondary implication, direct statement is the proper course, not secondary implication. Therefore, the Sautrāmaṇī is a subsidiary of the Agni, and the Bṛhaspatisava is a subsidiary of the Vājapeya.
Sūtra:
If it is argued that "time" [is meant] when there is a mention of time. 30.

Bhāṣya: If you view it thus—that there is a relationship between the subsidiary action and its purpose—then why does this not become an injunction of time? For the word "having piled" (*citvā*) is indeed of the nature of an injunction of time [referring to the time after the piling has been completed].
Sūtra: It cannot be so, because there is no inherence with the purpose. (31) (Ābhāsaniyoga)
Bhāṣya:

This is not so, because of the lack of inherence (*asamavāya*). [There is] no inherence of the word with its purpose—that is, with the meaning of the word—and the meaning of the word is the act of piling (*cayana*); therefore, there would be a lack of inherence with the *Sautrāmaṇī*.

And [the time for] the Vṛhaspatisava is [determined] by means of the Vājapeya; otherwise, one would subvert the context (*prakaraṇa*). For when heard in the context of the Agni[-cayana], the sacrifice is understood as occurring at the half-month, and in the context of the Vājapeya, it is understood as occurring at the Vājapeya. Otherwise, its characteristic and time would have to be understood as belonging to both contexts. Therefore...
The relationship between the constituent parts and the purpose—thus [ends the section]. (4.3.13a)

If it is argued that it serves both purposes, (Pūrvapakṣa) || 32 ||

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the scripture declares: "Having completed the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice, one subsequently offers the Vaimṛdha. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the Vaimṛdha an auxiliary (aṅga) to both sacrifices, and is its connection with the Paurṇamāsī merely for the sake of timing; or is it a relationship between an auxiliary and its specific purpose? What is the prima facie view? If this is the case, then the Vaimṛdha serves the purpose of both. Why? Because of the context (prakaraṇa).

Because of the force of the scriptural mention of both [the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa], and because of the similarity in form with an injunction regarding time, [the word] "having completed" (saṃsthāpya) [is used].
Sūtra.

Thus [ends] the Sūtra.
Not so, because of the unity of the word. (Siddhānta 33)

There is a single word—*anunirvapati*—and within a single sentence, it cannot enjoin two distinct relationships: namely, that between the Vaimṛdha sacrifice and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, and [the relationship] with the time of the Full Moon. For a sentence is understood to have only a single purpose.

As for what was stated—"on account of the context"—that must be refuted.
Because of the connection with non-origination. (Siddhānta) || 35 ||

Bhāṣya: This is not so; this very [text] is the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) for the *vaiśvānara* sacrifice. That [injunction] would either form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyabhāva*) with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices due to context (*prakaraṇa*), or it would belong directly to the *paurṇamāsī*. In that case, direct connection (*pratyakṣasaṃyoga*) is stronger than context;
and there is a direct connection with the *paurṇamāsī*, whereas [connection] by way of time (*kālena*) is indirect (*parokṣa*). Therefore, it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *paurṇamāsī*.
"Vaimṛdha"—thus [ends the section].
(4.3.94a) This is the section concerning the time for the Anuyāja offerings and others, which is between the Āgnimāruta and the Vaimṛdha.
But [if it is argued that] time would exist in its own non-arising, [we reply: no, because [time] is connected with a purposeful action.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "They proceed with the after-offerings (anuyājas) after the Āgnimāruta [offering]," and "Having cast away the enclosing-sticks (paridhis), he offers the Hāriyojana [oblation]. Regarding this, there is a doubt.

—Is it an injunction of an auxiliary (aṅga), or rather an injunction of time?—If it were an injunction of an auxiliary, there would be direct scriptural statement (śruti); if it were an injunction of time, there would be figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). Therefore, it is an injunction of an auxiliary—thus [the prima facie view].
[Page 580]

We reply: In the statement regarding non-origination, there would be a lack of temporal sequence; the *agnimāruta* is a subsidiary of the *soma*, while the *anuyājas* are subsidiaries of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*). In that case, there is no mutual connection between those two. Likewise, the *paridhis* are subsidiaries of the animal sacrifice, whereas the *hāriyojana* is a distinct primary rite. [And so is] the *anuyāja*.
The Agnimāruta [offering] has already been reached, and the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) between those two has not yet been reached; that is what is being prescribed.

Likewise, this applies to the Hāriyojana [offering] and the throwing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi-praharaṇa*). This being the case, no benefit whatsoever is conferred upon the Hāriyojana by the throwing of the enclosing sticks.
Or rather, [the *hāriyojana* cup] serves the purpose of the throwing of the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*). [Objection:

"But surely the throwing of the enclosing-sticks would be assisted by its being placed on top? [Reply: It is said in response: No, for the throwing of the enclosing-sticks is not to be performed for the sake of being on top; indeed, that [purpose] already exists.
Furthermore, since that [animal] exists, its state of being "above" it certainly exists;
therefore, the relationship is one of time. (4.3.15)
The section concerning the fact that the *soma* sacrifice and others follow the time subsequent to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
Sūtra: In a matter concerning the time of origin, the time [of the rite] should be [the determining factor], because the sentence has that as its primary purpose. (37)

Regarding this, it is heard: "Having performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma. In this regard, there is a doubt: is this an injunction for an accessory (aṅga), or for a time (kāla)? What is the prima facie view? On account of the direct Vedic statement (śruti), it is an injunction for an accessory. This being the position, the reply is given: in this doubt concerning whether it is an injunction for a time or an accessory, it must be a time, because of the syntactical connection (vākya).

Because that is the primary subject; for this sentence has time as its primary subject and is not intended to enjoin a sacrifice. Its lack of intent toward that [sacrifice] is due to the fact that it does not state the form [of the rite]. How is there no statement of the form? Because of the absence of a deity. How is there an absence? Because it is not heard in scripture. For whatever is heard [mentioned] for someone becomes that person's deity; indeed, a deity is understood through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), and not otherwise.

By means of perception and the other [pramāṇas]. Therefore, there is no injunction of a previously unestablished sacrifice; since this is a restatement for the purpose of specifying time, this fault does not apply—for that which has its deity already enjoined is what is being restated. Thus, [Page 581]...

In this context, the relationship is one of time (*kālārtha*). He demonstrates this: "The New and Full Moon sacrifices are indeed the chariot of the gods; when one who has performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices sacrifices with Soma, he alights at the end of his journey upon the choice portion of the gods"—thus, on the path already shown.

Just as it is comfortable to travel by chariot, so too is it comfortable to sacrifice with Soma for one who knows the New and Full Moon sacrifices; for him, the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites which have the Darśapūrṇamāsa as their archetype become well-practiced. In this way, the explanatory passage (arthavāda) becomes meaningful. (4.3.14)
The section concerning the fact that the fruit of the Vaiśvānareṣṭi accrues to the son.
In this regard (from here onwards, there are two sections concerning the principle of the Jāteṣṭi).
But the connection with the fruit would not apply to that which is not enjoined, because it does not constitute the entirety [of the action]. (38)

Bhāṣya: "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born. There is a doubt: is this for one's own supreme welfare (*ātmaniḥśreyasa*), or for the supreme welfare of the son? We say it is for one's own supreme welfare; these ritual acts that bestow results do not pertain to another. Why? Because of the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the context of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*); as in: "If one potsherd should be lost, [one should offer] one month of the year... [and so forth].

"If [the sacrifice] should be abandoned, or if the sacrificer should die, he should offer a cake on one potsherd to Heaven and Earth. If two [cakes] should be lost, two months of the year would have been abandoned;
if the sacrificer should then die, he should offer a cake on two potsherds to the Aśvins.
He sets it out with a shaking motion for the protection of the sacrificer. Thus it is said.
It shows that when the skull is destroyed, there is a rite whose fruit is the supreme good for the self;

it should be understood in the same way here as well, therefore [it leads to] the supreme good of the self—this is the reading in Mādhava’s Nyāyamālā: "The Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices," at the conclusion.
"In the case of the determined, bare path," so says Mādhava.
(Bhāṣya on Sūtra, Page 582).

Bhāṣya: This being the position, we reply: there would be no connection with the fruit for the father; the statement regarding the fruit pertains to the son as a subordinate element, not to the father. How so? It is heard thus: "Vaiśvānaram..."

One should offer an oblation on twelve potsherds when a son is born. In that there is an offering on eight potsherds, he purifies him with the *gāyatrī* through spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). In that there is an offering on nine potsherds, he bestows brilliance upon him by means of the *triṣṭubh*. In that there is an offering on ten potsherds, he bestows the enjoyment of food upon him by means of the *virāj*. In that there is an offering on eleven potsherds, he bestows sensory power (*indriya*) upon him by means of the *triṣṭubh*.

"In that there is an offering on twelve potsherds, he bestows cattle upon this very person in the Jagatī meter; he for whom, when born, one performs this sacrifice, becomes purified, radiant, an eater of food,
possessed of sensory power, and rich in cattle"— thus, the fruit belongs to him who is born.
It is heard in scripture that there is no such thing as an excessive burden for a word; therefore, the fruit belongs to the son.
As for what was said—that these ritual acts do not bestow results upon another—that is now addressed.

Since the fruit belongs to the son, that pleasure is one's own; therefore, the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is not contradictory. It is with reference to this very pleasure of one's own self that the statement occurs:
"The son is indeed one's own self."
"Truly, you are born from limb after limb; you are produced from the heart.
You are indeed the self named 'son'; live for a hundred autumns! Thus [he says].
But the connection with the impairment of the limbs is for the purpose of indicating the cause [of the penance]. 38.
(Ācārya-nirṇaya) ||

Now, as for what was said—"if one potsherd should be lost," and so forth—it is replied: the connection of the destruction of the auxiliary parts (aṅga) is appropriate as a causal condition (nimitta), and not otherwise; for when a potsherd is lost, looking for it is not prescribed for the purpose of searching for that [lost sherd], nor indeed...
When a *kākīnī* has been lost, its search is conducted by means of a *kārṣāpaṇa*. (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.17)
Sūtra-bhāṣya [Page 583]
Or thus: the section concerning the sequence of the Jātaka rites following the Vaiśvānara sacrifice.
But the connection with the impairment of the limbs is for the purpose of indicating the cause. || 38 ||
In this regard, there is the injunction: "Upon the birth of a son, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.

A doubt arises: is this to be done immediately upon birth, or after the birth-rite (jātakarman) has been performed? We say: it is to be done immediately upon birth; for when the occasion (nimitta) has arrived, the rite contingent upon that occasion (naimittika) must be performed.
This being the case, we reply: [the rite is performed] "after the birth-rite (jātakarman) has been performed. Why? Because of the capacity [of the child].

For it is only when the birth-rite has been performed that the consumption [of the sacrificial food] is prescribed for him. If the sacrifice were performed before the birth-rite, the time for the consumption would be postponed;
in that case, he would not be able to sustain his body. Now, as for what was said—"for when the occasion has arrived..."—[that refers to the occasion of the birth-rite].

"It must be understood as being occasional (naimittika). It is said: "The connection with the impairment of the limbs is for the purpose of an occasion (nimitta). "Impairment" refers to the birth of a son; that is the past occasion, not something belonging to the time [of the rite] itself. And that occasion does not cease even when the *jātakarman* has been performed.
In the other alternative, time would be lost, and there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in this case.
Therefore, [the rule applies] "when the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) has been performed.
Now, is this on any day within the ten-day period, or rather at its own specific time? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That it may be on any day whatsoever.

Thus, an absence of restriction would result. To this it is replied: [The sacrifice should be performed] on either the full moon day (paurṇamāsī) or the new moon day (amāvāsyā). Why? Because of the scriptural statement (śruti); for it is heard thus: "He who, having sacrificed with an animal or with Soma, should sacrifice, he should sacrifice on either the full moon day or the new moon day.
For the forest (the Vedic tradition) is not overburdened; otherwise, in the other case, the [proper] time would be lost.

In this view, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). On the other hand, if one were to perform the *antaḥśrāddha* on another lunar day or at another time, one would not be able to bring together all the constituent parts (*aṅga*s). This refers to both time (*kāla*) and purity (*śauca*); such is Mādhava’s intention, as this constitutes a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).

[Page 584] Bhāṣya: One should not undertake it [immediately]. Therefore, one should perform it after the ten-day period has passed, either on the full moon day or the new moon day. Sūtra Bhāṣya:
The section concerning the necessity of performing the auxiliary rites of the Sautrāmaṇī and others at their own specific times.
The primary time for the subsidiaries is determined by their connection with the principal rite.
40 || (Pūrvapakṣa) ||

It has been stated that there is a relationship between the subsidiary and the purpose in such injunctions as, "Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī," and "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava.
This is now being deliberated: should it be performed immediately upon the mere piling [of the altar], or in the midst of that very rite?

Or should it be performed at its own time? Likewise, in the Vājapeya, should the Bṛhaspatisava be performed [at the time of the main sacrifice], or at its own time? The "time of the principal" should apply to these two. Why?
Because the subsidiaries have the time of the principal; for there is indeed one time for the principals.

And regarding the "limbs" (subsidiary rites), it will be stated: "But the limbs, because they are prescribed [as part of a whole], should be taught along with the principal rite. Having performed the *agnicayana* (fire-piling), one must not stop at that alone;
another sacrifice known as the *sautrāmaṇī* must be performed. Likewise, the *vājapeya*.
Having brought that about, one would not be finished by that much alone; one should further perform the sacrifice known as the Vṛhaspatisava. Thus it is said.
But when [the rite] has not been commenced, there should be an injunction [for it] at its own proper time, because of its similarity to that [commenced rite].
41 || (Siddhānta) ||
Bhāṣya:
This is enjoined as another sacrifice in the context of the "cessation" (*apavarga*) of the sacrifice, and this cessation applies to all [the constituent acts].
It does not occur when the auxiliary parts of the sacrifice are omitted; nor is it as you think—this topic has not been recorded here in the Vārttika, the Tattvaratna, or the Śāstradīpikā.
"it occurs when [the rites] have been performed"—this is the reading in the Kāśikā, the Kriyākalpataru, and the Purāṇa.
Chapter 4, Section 3.

"Once the sacrifice itself is completed"—why? Because of its connection with the instrumental case-ending (*karaṇavibhakti*), as in "by means of the Vājapeya sacrifice" (*vājapeyena iṣṭyā*). The performance is understood to include the subsidiaries (*sāṅga*), not the rite alone without its parts; otherwise, there would be a performance in the middle of that [ritual]. If...
Having observed the Vājapeya—[if it were] intended as a mere state [of the sacrifice], then one would understand that the primary element alone is to be accomplished under the name "Vājapeya";
but this is not the case. Therefore, the meaning is: "having performed all the constituent parts (aṅga) as they have been described."
If this is so, then when the preparatory rite has been completed and the time for the *vājapeya* has passed,
the sacrifice is performed; because of the commonality of its injunction (*codanāsāmānya*), the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) belonging to the *jyotiṣṭoma* applies,

and it must therefore take place at the time obtained through its own archetypal injunction (*codaka*), namely, the time of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, due to the commonality of the injunction of the *sautrāmaṇī*.

He says: "In the case of the Vājapeya, because of the expression 'having sacrificed' (*iṣṭvā*), it is understood that one must first complete the sacrifice; however, this does not apply to the fire-altar (*agni*). In that case, because of the expression 'having piled' (*citvā*), the meaning would be 'having completed the piling' (*cayana*). It is replied: "This is not so; for it is heard in the scripture as 'having piled the fire' (*agniṃ citvā*), [meaning] by means of the piling of the fire."
The meaning is "having consecrated" (*saṃskṛtya*). By the term "fire" (*agni*), the piled altar (*cayana*) is designated; its benefit is not merely its placement on the ground.

If the sacrifice takes place upon the ground, then there is a benefit to the fire through the piling. The phrase "having brought that about" (*tam abhinirvartya*) is understood to mean "having brought the sacrifice about in the fire situated on the ground," as long as the fire remains on the ground.

There is no sacrifice; for as long as the fire is not assisted by the piling (*cayana*), the fire cannot assist the sacrificer. The assistance rendered by Soma is not merely the act of establishing it on the ground.
Therefore, it is understood that even in that case, one must first bring the sacrifice to completion. (4.3.19)
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya composed by the venerable Śabara-svāmin.
[Page 586] The section concerning the fact that gambling and other such acts are constituent parts of the sacrifices performed in the Rājasūya.
And because of the commonality of the word "context" (prakaraṇa), there is no status as a subsidiary part for the injunctions. || 1 ||
( Pūrvapakṣa ) ||

There are Vedic rituals such as the *anumati* and others; sacrificial animals such as the *malha* and others; Soma offerings such as the *pavitra* and others; and acts such as the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) of an anthill—these and similar rites are those involving wooden implements. Likewise, there are these: "He plays with dice," "He defeats a Kṣatriya," "The earth causes him to suffer from hemorrhoids," and "He is consecrated. Of these...
In proximity [to the specific sacrifices], it is heard: "One desiring sovereignty over the earth should sacrifice with the Rājasūya.

This word "Rājasūya," being heard as formless in the proximity of sacrifices that possess specific forms, is understood to be a designation for the entire collection [of those sacrifices]. In this regard, there is a doubt: does the word "Rājasūya" denote the entire collection consisting of the Anumati and the other [sacrifices], or does it denote some of them and not others? What is the prima facie view? That it denotes all of them.
Why? Because of the commonality of the word "context" (*prakaraṇa*). The word "context" is common to all.

Regarding the term *rājasūya*: a king (*rājan*) dies (*sūyate*) therein; therefore it is called *rājasūya*. Alternatively, it is the sacrifice (*yajña*) of a king, thus *rājasūya*. Since this [term] occurs in proximity to that specific context and there is no distinguishing factor [to the contrary], it ought to be expressive of all [the constituent rites]; and that which is denoted by the word *rājasūya* follows from that.
The fruit arises. Therefore, all [these] are primary—thus [it is said].

She is old and possesses breasts adorned with jewels. Mādhava states that she is one who possesses the strength to carry a load on her back at whatever age she may be; thus she is called *yaṣṭīhī*. Regarding the term *yaṣṭohī*, the reading in the Śrauta-sūtra (ŚrSū) and the Padapāṭha is *praṣṭhauhī*. The same applies to the subsequent [verse].
Chapter 4, Section 4.
Or rather, they would be subsidiary acts, because they are distinguished [from the primary sacrifice]. || 2 ||
Bhāṣya-saṃgraha-bhāṣya (Commentary on the Compendium of Explanations)
(Sūtra) ||

"Or rather"—this marks the rejection of the previous position. Those which are "non-sacrifices" (*ayajñiyāḥ*) are "subsidiaries" (*aṅga*), such as gambling (*videvana*) and so forth. When it is stated, "One should achieve sovereign power (*khārājya*) by means of the sacrifice known as *rājanaya*," sovereign power is accomplished by the sacrifice itself, not by what is not a sacrifice; and gambling and the like are not sacrifices. Therefore, they would be subsidiaries of the fruitful sacrifices.
"Being heard"—thus [it is stated] in (4.4.9).
The section concerning the fact that the *videvana* is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the entire royal consecration (*rājasūya*).
That which is situated in the middle belongs to him who is in the middle. (Pūrva-pakṣa)

In the midst of the *abhiṣecanīya* [sacrifice] within the *rājasūya*, the gambling with an eight-year-old cow and so forth are prescribed. Regarding these, there arises the doubt: are they an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *abhiṣecanīya* alone, or of the entire *rājasūya*? It is replied: because they are prescribed in the middle, they belong to the *abhiṣecanīya*; thus, the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) will be maintained.

Or rather, it should apply to all [the fires] because of their equality and because of the injunction; for its context is not stated for the purpose of indicating a specific location in the middle. (Siddhānta) || 4 ||
Commentary: The acts such as gambling (videvana) would be an auxiliary (anga) to all the injunctions (codanā), beginning with the Anumati sacrifice.

Why? Because of the "injunction" (codanātaḥ) and because of their "equality" (samatvāt). These injunctions, beginning with the Anumati, are equal; they are all fruitful and are primary (pradhāna) rites. For all of these...

"Context (*prakaraṇa*)," [it is argued], does not apply to the *abhiṣecanīya* alone. By sequence (*krama*), they would pertain to the *abhiṣecanīya*, but by context, they pertain to all [the rites]; and context is stronger than sequence. Therefore, they do not belong to the *abhiṣecanīya* alone. Rather, since the *videvana* and other rites have their place in the middle of the *abhiṣecanīya*, those performed therein benefit all [the constituent parts]. (4.4.2)
