"Or it is a limb of the animal," for its purpose is for the anointing of that [animal], since it is heard in scripture: "He anoints the animal with the *kharu*"; thus, that anointing necessitates the production of the *kharu*. If this *kharu* is for that purpose, then it serves a visible [purpose].
If its purpose is for the sacrificial post, then since the purpose is transcendental (adṛṣṭa), it must be performed; therefore, it is an auxiliary to the animal sacrifice.
The statement regarding the price [paid for the cow] would be due to devotion. (Ābhāsa-nigamana) 28.
With what devotion? He spoke thus:
"The sacrificial post (yūpa) is indeed to be cast into the fire."
"The donkey is thrown [into the pit], and by that means the sacrificial post (yūpa) is cast down"—this is like a ransom; it is a praise expressed through this figurative usage.
What is the purpose? It is when eleven animals are tied to a single sacrificial post.

When they are being yoked, then, according to the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), there is the anointing (*samañjana*) of only one animal; whereas, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is for all of them. And it is said: "If the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the rite, then the anointing is for only one; but when there are many animals at a single post, the anointing is for all. (4.4.10).
"But in the case of all [the others], it is the reverse"— this is the reading in the Kāśī-kṛṣṇa-puṣpa manuscript.
[Page 600] Furthermore,
there is the section concerning the manifoldness of the bases and so forth.
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the offerings are the primary elements, because there is no distinction [to the contrary].
28 || (Pūrvapakṣa) ||

The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are well-known; regarding them, the following are heard in scripture: the Āgneya, Agnīṣomīya, Upāṃśuyāja, Aindrāgna, and Sāṃnāyya sacrifices, as well as the two Āghāras, the two Ājyabhāgas, the Prayājas, Anuyājas, Patnīsaṃyājas, the Samiṣṭayajus, and the Sviṣṭakṛt.

In this regard, there is a doubt: are all these sacrifices principal (pradhāna), or are some of them subordinate (guṇabhūta)? What is the prima facie view? All the offerings (ijyā) contained within the Darśapūrṇamāsa are principal, because of the general injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," which applies without distinction to all the sacrifices.
The fruit is heard [in the scripture], and that which possesses a fruit is the primary act; and all these are sacrifices. Therefore, all of them are primary.

Or rather, there are some [verses] which are indeed subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) themselves, in which there is praise as being a subsidiary; for praise is generally [intended] as such. (Siddhānta) — Bhāṣya.
"Or rather, there might be certain subsidiary parts (*aṅga*).

Which, then, are they? Those in which there is praise by way of being a subsidiary part, such as: 'These two *āghāra* offerings are indeed the two reins of the sacrifice; these two *ājyabhāga* offerings are indeed the two eyes of the sacrifice; and when the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s are performed, that is indeed the armor of the sacrifice.'"
"It is performed, or the armor [is provided] for the sacrificer's victory over his rival"—thus it is said.

The reins are a part of the chariot, the eyes of the one who possesses eyes, and the armor of the one who possesses armor; for a praise based on commonality is appropriate, provided that those parts are indeed praised as such.
Consequently, the praise becomes meaningful; therefore, the limbs are praised as limbs.
"Among others, he is praised with conciliation"—this is the reading in the Kāṇva-Kṛṣṇa-Puṣpasūtra.
Sragdharābhāṣya, page 601.
Chapter 4, Section 4.
And likewise, there is the observation of another indicative mark. (31) (Yukti)

And by doing so, the observation of another purpose becomes logical: "At each *prayāja* offering, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* grain. And it is not the case that he performs the *prayāja* offerings [as a primary act].
And he does not offer the after-offerings—thus it is said.
But the cause is not distinct [in the case of the Pradhāna], because the quality exists within the primary causes.

Commentary: This reason, namely "praise," is not distinct [in its application]. For even the Āgneya and other offerings are praised as being constituent parts (*aṅga*), as in: "The Āgneya is indeed the head of the sacrifice;
the Upāṃśuyāja is the heart; the Agniṣomīya is the two feet. And the head is a limb of that which possesses a head.

"The heart [belongs] to that which has a heart; the feet [belong] to that which has feet"—this is a praise of everything as being a limb. Consequently, everything would become a limb, and thus there would be no principal element (*pradhāna*);
and if there is no principal element, of what would anything be a limb? Therefore, this is not a limb.
Sūtra 33: [The statement] "the observation of another purpose when it is not stated for its own sake" is [a reason] because it is for the sake of another. (Yukti)

Bhāṣya: Now, as for what was stated—“The observation of something else [serves] another purpose; therefore it is not a means of proof, for that sentence is intended for another purpose and is not for the sake of enjoining the *prayāja* and other such rites that are already observed; therefore, another authority must be sought for this, namely another scriptural statement (*śruti*) or logical reasoning (*nyāya*)”—[this is addressed].
Or, in its absence, it becomes like the sight of a mirage; when the reasoning is not properly established, it is indeed non-probative.
The reading in the Kāśmīra manuscript is "tatra."
[Page 602] However, there is a distinct application of the two designations, both on account of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and on account of specific designation (*vyapadeśa*).
Furthermore, that which constitutes the primary characteristic is the possession of a fruit; in proximity to that, [there are those things] not connected [to it].
That [act] would be a constituent part [of the sacrifice], because it shares in the causal factor, and no connection with anything else is heard. (Sūtra 34; Purvapakṣa-Nigamana)

But the word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position. As for what was said—that all [the constituent parts] are equally primary—it is not so; the actions denoted by the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* are the primary rites.
Why? Because of the connection with the fruit: the fruit is heard [in scripture] as being connected to those things denoted by the term *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—thus [it is said]. But which are those denoted by the term *darśapūrṇamāsa*? They are those in whose injunctions there occurs the word *paurṇamāsī* or the word *amāvāsyā*; these are the Āgneya and the others. [Objection: "But for those denoted by the word *amāvāsyā*, no fruit is indeed heard [in the text]. [Reply: It is said in response: "The application of these two designations—namely, *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā*—is to the two groups taken separately."
And thus, regarding the collection consisting of the three [rites] beginning with the Āgneya, the word *paurṇamāsī* applies to that [collection], while the word *amāvāsyā* applies to the others.
[Objection: "How is it that the dual form *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* is heard [in the text]?"
[The sacrifice has] two purposes, "also because of the designation. How is there that designation?

By the use of the dual number—namely, "by means of the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa"—for the words *darśa* and *māvāsyā* have a single meaning. How so? [It says]: "Of these two, the Darśa is the first and the Pūrṇamāsa is the latter;
now, if one begins with the Pūrṇamāsa first, it is performed out of its proper order. One beginning the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa should offer a pap to Sarasvatī, and a cake on twelve potsherds to Sarasvant."

"Sarakhati is indeed the new moon (amāvāsyā), and Sarakhan is the full moon (pūrṇamāsa). Having prepared both of these in their proper order, he begins for the sake of prosperity; he indeed prospers, and furthermore, it is for the sake of forming a couple. In this passage, by using the word *darśa* as a base form and stating it is synonymous with the word *amāvāsyā*, [the author] demonstrates that they have the same meaning.
And it is possible to characterize the new moon day as "darśa" by means of the non-perception of the moon,
just as one is characterized as "sight-endowed" (cakṣuṣmat) by means of the eyes when the eyes are absent.
[Page 603]
Chapter 4, Section 4.

From this designation and from scripture (i.e., from what is heard in the world), we conclude that they have indeed the same meaning. Furthermore, that which possesses fruit is the primary characteristic, whereas the other is secondary.
That which is heard in proximity to something is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that. How so?

That which is heard in proximity to a requirement for procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*), being capable of fulfilling it by way of specifying the procedure, ought to be its auxiliary; otherwise, if the syntactical supplement (*vākyaśeṣa*) were not supplied, one would have to postulate a separate result (*phala*).

[The opponent] says: "But surely, it is only the fruit of the Darśapūrṇamāsa that is here attached [to the other rites]. It is replied:—It is possible for it to be attached; however, the sentence concerning the Darśapūrṇamāsa would remain expectant (sākāṅkṣa).

Another procedure for this [main sacrifice] would have to be postulated, though it is not heard in scripture; likewise, another [procedure] would have to be postulated for these [subsidiaries] such as the *prayāja*s. If this [independent] procedure were understood, the [subsidiary] procedure [of the main sacrifice] would be abandoned; therefore, subsidiariness is established because of the principle of "having a share. Furthermore, no connection with a separate fruit is heard for these [subsidiaries]. Therefore, not all [acts], such as the *āghāra* and others, are equally primary; rather, they are subordinate acts (*guṇakarman*).
Furthermore, qualities conjoined with names are prescribed, and they are not applicable to the subsidiaries.
I [shall explain] how specific qualities associated with specific names are prescribed, such as:
"One should touch the Pūrṇamāsī with the Caturhotṛ-mantra, and the Amāvāsyā with the Pañcahotṛ-mantra"— thus in all cases.

If there were no knowledge of the distinction that "in this collection there are four *hautra* priests" and "in this [other] there are five *hautra* priests," then this would not be possible. Furthermore, such an injunction of subordinate qualities (*guṇavidhāna*) exists; therefore, our position alone is correct. Moreover, the praise of the *āghāra* offerings and so forth will be logically consistent as being subordinate elements.
The reading in the Kāśī edition is "canyamānam".
And the scriptural mention of the cause is equal for others; thus, there is a relationship of subordinate and principal between the members.
36 || (Āraṇyaka) ||
Commentary: Now, as for what was stated—that the praise of the Āgneya and other offerings as being limbs would indicate their status as limbs—that must be refuted.
Sūtra.
Since there is a connection at the time of origination, there should therefore be an instruction regarding the subsidiary parts.
37 || (Śrāddha-nirṇaya) ||

Bhāṣya: This is not a fault; even though these [sacrifices] are principal, there will be praise based on their sequence of arising—namely, that for a person being born, the head is born first, the middle part in the middle, and the feet last; and likewise, by analogy, the Āgneya sacrifice is first, the Upāṃśuyāja in the middle, and the Agnīṣomīya last—it is from this similarity that this praise arises.
— thus.
Sūtra: And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose. (Yukti 38)

The Bhāṣya states: "Fourteen oblations are offered on the full moon day, and thirteen on the new moon day. Otherwise, there would not be fourteen oblations on the full moon day, nor thirteen on the new moon day. Therefore, it is established that the Āgneya and other rites are the primary acts (*pradhāna*), while the Āghāra and other rites are the auxiliary acts (*aṅga*). (4.4.4)
Chapter 11, Section 11.
Sūtra:
[This is] the section concerning the subsidiary status of the consecration (dīkṣā) and other rites within the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, they are equal, for the cause is indeed undifferentiated.
38 || (Pūrvapakṣa) ||
There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, [enjoined] by the text: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. And the reading in the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya-puṣpa is "abhisambandhaḥ."
Chapter 4, Section 4. [Page 605]
Commentary: In that context, there exist sacrifices such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others, and on the day of the Soma-pressing (*sautya*), there is the Soma sacrifice.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the sacrifice in general the primary element here, or is it specifically the Soma sacrifice?

—Thus [it is asked]. What is the prima facie view? All [the sacrifices] in the Jyotiṣṭoma should be equal. Why? Because the reason is undistinguished: it is heard in scripture that the fruit results from the sacrifice, and all these are sacrifices;
and that which possesses a fruit is primary. Therefore, in the Jyotiṣṭoma, all sacrifices [are equal].
The primary cause—thus [it is said].
But because the connection of the qualities with the originative injunction exists, there is a scriptural statement of the cause; therefore, Soma should be the primary element. (Siddhānta 40)
Bhāṣya: "But the connection of the *guṇas* occurs through the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*). Of which *guṇas*? Of the *jyotis-stomas*. By which originative injunction?"

What is the connection? [It is stated: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. From this, it is heard that heaven results from the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, not from sacrifice in general; and where there are *jyotis* (lights) as *stomas*, that is the Jyotiṣṭoma. Of what are the *jyotis* the *stomas*?

We say it belongs to the Soma sacrifice; for thus it is recorded in scripture: "What indeed are these lights? They are the *stomas* of that [sacrifice]—the ninefold, fifteenfold, seventeenfold, and twenty-onefold; these indeed are the lights, and they are its *stomas*. Because of their co-occurrence, the *stomas* are an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Soma sacrifice—as in: "Having either taken up a cup (*graha*) or having lifted a bowl (*camasa*), he introduces the hymn (*stotra*)."
And those *stomas*, such as the *trivṛt* and others, [are established] by scriptural declarations such as: "The *bahiṣpavamāna* is *trivṛt*;
the *ājya* [stotras] are *pañcadaśa*," and so forth.

Therefore, the Soma sacrifice characterized by the *trivṛt* and other *stomas* is the *jyotiṣṭoma*. And that which is the *jyotiṣṭoma* yields the fruit; and that from which the fruit arises is indeed the primary [element].

— thus [it is asked]. "But how are the Viṣṭads and others *lights* (*jyotīṃṣi*)? It is said: whether they be lights or not, they are at least designated by the word "light. [Question: "Why are they called lights? This is the reading in the Kāśikā commentary.

[Page 606] A word exists even by its mere utterance, especially in the case of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, things receive the designation "light" (*jyotis*) because they shine, as in the verbal root *dyut* (to shine) or *dyot* (to illuminate); that is, they are illuminated.

Or rather, in the context of praise, they "illuminate" by means of those words. Therefore, the Soma sacrifice is the Jyotiṣṭoma, and it is the primary rite, while the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites are subordinate.
Sabhāṣya: And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose [in the scripture]. (41)

Furthermore, an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is observed, such as: "The *dīkṣaṇīyā* is indeed the head of the sacrifice," and likewise, the subsidiaries (*guṇa*) such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* are seen in the modification (*vikāra*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, for example:
"One should give gold weighing twenty-four *mānas* at the *dīkṣaṇīyā*."

"In the Prāyaṇīyā [offering], there are twenty-four measures"—thus, because of this equality, the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites would not proceed [as subordinate]. Therefore, the Soma sacrifice itself is the primary act. (4.4.12)
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter in the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya composed by the venerable Śabarasvāmin. And this chapter is completed.
[Sūtra 1] Now begins the section concerning the fixed order of sequence. (The year, the month, and the day.)
(The Principle of the Greater Authority of Direct Assertion)
The sequence [of the Vedic texts] is characterized by direct revelation (śruti), because that is its authority. || 1 ||
In the fourth chapter, the definition of the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the non-instigator (*aprayojaka*) was treated; that must be kept in mind.

Here, now, the definition of the rule of order (*kramaniyama*) is stated, which is explained by means of direct statement (*śruti*), meaning (*artha*), textual sequence (*pāṭha*), performance (*pravṛtti*), and context (*kāṇḍa*), as well as the relative strength and weakness of these [criteria] beginning with *śruti*. First, however, the order of *śruti* is considered: should the order of ritual items (*padārtha*) be adopted according to the direct statement?

Or is there no fixed order? What is the prima facie view? Since the agent is one and the ritual items are many, and since a sequence is inevitable, there is no fixed order because of parsimony and for the sake of expeditious performance. This being the position, we reply:
"The sequence is characterized by direct Vedic statement (śruti), because that is its authority. Here, "direct statement" means explicit mention.

Regarding the syllables, that sequence which has them as its cause is the correct sequence; for the meaning of Vedic texts is based on the authority of the revealed scripture (*śruti*), and there is no other authority for these [meanings]—so it has been stated in Sūtra 1.1.2. "What is the example here? If it refers to the sequence of initiation (*dīkṣā-krama*), after stating, "Those who are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*)," it prescribes their order of initiation: "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the Householder (*gṛhapati*), initiates the Brahman priest, then the Udgātṛ, then the Hotṛ; then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having initiated him..."

He consecrates the third group: the Brāhmaṇacchaṃsin from the Brahman, the Prastotṛ from the Udgātṛ, and the Maitrāvaruṇa from the Hotṛ. Then, after the Neṣṭṛ has consecrated him, he consecrates the third group:
the Āgnīdhra from the Brahman, the Pratihartṛ from the Udgātṛ, and the Acchāvāka.
[The Hotṛ]; then, having initiated him, he initiates the Neṣṭṛ, the Potṛ—thus is the reading [in the manuscript].
*iti* is the reading in the Mo0 Pu0.
[Page 608] The *momamā-damana* belongs to the Brahman priest; the *subrahmaṇya* belongs to the Udgātṛ priest; the *grāvastut* belongs to the Hotṛ priest; thereafter, another [priest] [performs it].
"He initiates a Brāhmaṇa, or a religious student sent by his teacher"—thus it is said.
The sequence should be performed without a fixed rule, as in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa); however, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), this very sequence must be followed.

Regarding this, it is said: "The scriptural statement is improper. To this we reply: Is this not correct? No; we say it is not correct. Then is it logical? We do not say that the sequence is incorrect; rather, we say that the restatement of what has already been stated is improper. It is replied: The utterance of what is correct remains logical even if repeated many times, whereas the utterance of what is incorrect is improper even once. He says:
It is not said that there is no repetition when something already known is stated again by means of a salutation;
for even the non-forgetting [of it] occurs, as in the thought: "That task must be performed by Kṛttikā."
By Kṛttikāra. The ninth color-section.
"There is a purpose"— thus it was said: "There is a purpose."

There is no difference for the author of the Sūtra, or rather, this is indeed a different matter; for in that context, the doubt, inquiry, and conclusion are entirely different—namely, the doubt: "Is Dharma based solely on the authority of Śruti, or is it based on other means of knowledge? [The answer is: No, because perception and the other means of knowledge serve as instrumental causes for apprehension.
"It has that [Veda] as its authority, and because it transcends the senses, it is characterized by *codanā* (injunction)"—this is the inquiry.

"It is indeed characterized by *codanā* alone"—this is the conclusion. Here, however, once its authority is established, there follows the determination of the correctness of the sequence of linguistic usage. This is the second section (*varṇaka*).

Alternatively, the investigation of the Vedic text concerns this: is it an injunction that the constituent elements (*padārtha*) are to be performed, or is it the sequence (*krama*) that is enjoined? Since it is impossible to enjoin multiple things simultaneously, there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the sequence, while the injunction pertains to the constituent elements; for, as in the case of the sentences concerning the portions of the offering (*avadāna*), the injunction of the constituent elements is by direct statement (*śruti*), whereas the injunction of the sequence would have to be by syntactical connection (*vākya*). Therefore, the sequence is not [the object of the injunction].

"It is enjoined"—this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). "But surely, in the sentences concerning the portions to be cut off (*avadāna*), the sequence is enjoined. True, it is enjoined, but by means of the textual order (*pāṭha*), not by direct statement (*śruti*); for the sequence [is determined] by those who are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), according to Pāṇini-Sūtra 5.1.16.
Puṇya-pāṭhaḥ.

[Page 609] Bhāṣya: As for the statement "the sacrificers," since initiation (*dīkṣā*) is already established, the scriptural text is intended to prescribe the sequence; this is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Therefore, there is no tautology. || 3 ||
The description of colors. (5.1.1 Śrauta Sūtra).
Sūtra Bhāṣya.
The section concerning the fact that sequence is in some cases based on the nature of the objects themselves.
And because of the meaning. || 2 ||

Is this the universal rule—that in all cases [the order] must depend solely on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*)? For it has been stated: "Dharma is characterized by injunction" (Sūtra 1.1.2). This being the position, we reply: "And from the purpose (*artha*), that is, from the capacity (*sāmarthya*), the order is enjoined. For the order of ritual items (*padārtha*) is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). That which assists something while it is being accomplished is subordinate to it; and when [a certain order] is adopted, the ritual item [is properly performed].

Thus, it does not become [an essential part]; it is not a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*), for even without it, there is no deficiency. In this way, wherever the subordinate status of the sequence is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), in those cases one must follow that very [sequence] according to the purpose (*artha*), as in:

"He gives a gift upon birth; he takes [the child] with joined palms upon birth; he breathes over the newborn. By implication (*arthāt*), one should first breathe over [the child], and then take him with joined palms.

"It should be grasped, and then the boon should be given"—thus, since the release (vimoka) was prescribed first and its connection [with the boon] later, it must be performed in the reverse order according to the sense. However, as for the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*, though they are recited in reverse order, they should be performed in that same reverse order; here, the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*) does not apply.
It is measured [by its purpose], since the *anuvākyā* is for the purpose of indicating the deity, while the *yājyā* is for the purpose of the actual offering.

The injunction "He offers the *agnihotra*" is recorded first, and "He cooks the rice" is recorded later; yet, because it is impossible [otherwise], the rice must be cooked first. However, the *preṣa* (direction) and the *praiṣārtha* (the act directed) are recorded in reverse order, and they must be performed in that reverse order. (5.1.1)
(2nd Adhyāya)
The reading "anumīyate" is found in the Kāśī and Krīta editions.
[kha] • [Page 610] The section on the non-existence of a self.
The section concerning the non-restriction of sequence in certain cases.
Elsewhere, there is no fixed rule.

Commentary: In another case, there is no fixed rule regarding the order [of performance], as in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, where the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings recited in various different Śākhās—such as "I gratify the spring among the seasons" and so forth, and "One for me" and so forth—are not restricted to a specific sequence. (5.1.3)
Sūtra Bhāṣya:
The section concerning the fact that in some cases the sequence [of meditations] follows the order of the textual recitation (the principle of the order of recitation).
Or rather, it should be restricted by sequence, because plurality and singularity are subordinate qualities thereof.
(Sūtra 10)

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is prescribed: "He offers to the Samidhs, he offers to Tanūnapāt, he offers to Iḍ, he offers to Barhis, he offers with the utterance of Svāhā. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is their performance to be carried out in an unrestricted order, or [is there a fixed sequence]?

Should the very order of the recitation be restricted? What is the prima facie view? Since there is no scriptural injunction that establishes a restriction, there is no fixed order. This being the position, we reply: it should indeed be restricted by the order [of recitation] within a single sacrifice. Why? Because they possess that quality; for it is understood that ritual items possess the quality of following that [recited] order, just as one performs the actions in sequence: "one should bathe," "one should anoint," and "one should eat."

The meaning of words is understood from the sentence; for example, when instructions regarding unseen purposes are being given, someone might say: "Incense should be offered to the deity, flowers should be scattered, he should be anointed with sandalwood, and an oblation should be presented to him; when this is done, the deity is pleased. To him, another replies: "It is not so; incense should not be offered first; flowers should be scattered first. Thus he thinks.
—By this, the priority of the offering of incense is stated. Therefore, this sequence of these [offerings] is based on explicit scriptural injunction (vācanika). |||
[Page 611] If it is argued that this is not based on verbal testimony (*aśābda*), [we reply]: it would indeed be so, because it is a statement consisting of words (*vākyaśabda*). (Sūtra 5) (0)
If you say, "I see it thus," then, this being the case, the sequence is indeed non-verbal (*aśābda*).
How so? The meaning of a sentence is preceded by the meanings of the words, and from the words, only the word-meanings are understood.
This would be so if the hearing of a collection of word-meanings were the conveyor of the meaning; however, the aggregate is not the conveyor—thus it was said:
"The recitation of those [words] which have become part of that [sentence] is for the sake of the action."
In this regard [at Sūtra 1.1.25], since there is no expressive word for sequence, this perceived sequence is merely an illusion.
In this way, the existence of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) will be supported; otherwise, even that would be set far apart!

It is like the case of the water-pot. And it will be shown: "He cuts from the heart first, then from the tongue, then from the chest"—if the order of recitation were restrictive, then this [sequence] would not need to be enjoined; for if the order of recitation were restrictive, [the sequence] would follow from that very order of recitation.
One would obtain.

There would be a prohibition for the sake of one's own purpose; since [the number] two or one is for the sake of another, there is a connection with its own meaning; therefore, the word "one's own" (sva) should be used. || 6 ||
(Śrauta Sūtra, Adhyāya 12, Khaṇḍa 6)

Bhāṣya: Since there is a single agent in a single sacrifice, and since the sequence exists because it pertains to multiple constituent elements (padārtha), in that case, this very sequence would be determined by inference. Why?
Because the Veda is "for the sake of another" (parārtha); for the Veda is indeed for the sake of another, whatever is [taught] by it.

It is possible to perform it; for each respective purpose, this is traditionally handed down (samāmnāyate), and by means of it, the ritual element (padārtha) can be enjoined, and it can also be understood at the time of performance.
Therefore, the Veda and the ritual element are to be adopted for the sake of enjoining [them], and also at the time of performance.

It is not possible to distinguish [the purpose] as "this is enjoined for performance" versus "this is for the sake of understanding"; since no distinction is perceived, it is employed for both purposes.
The reading "padāmāmiti" is found in the Āsoḍhapurāṇa (A0 So0 Pu0).

[Page 612] It is understood thus: and it can be practiced by this sequence and not by another; for this very reason, when there is a deviation from the order of recitation, it is said that "it is ruined," otherwise [it would not be so].

For indeed, when that which is the purpose of something is being accomplished, what could possibly be lost? An unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) might be postulated, but that is improper when a visible result (*dṛṣṭa*) exists. Therefore, the word itself is the sequence—that very word which denotes the ritual items is also the denoter of the sequence.
Sūtra Bhāṣya:
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose [in the scripture]. (Yukti) || 7 ||
And thus it shows another purpose: "He lays down the bricks in an inverted order;

he recites the Ṣoḍaśin in an inverted order; the Aśvin is called the tenth [verse], yet he offers it as the third"—if the laying down and the reciting were without a fixed rule, this statement regarding the inversion would be meaningless. For there is no way in which the non-inversion could occur.

Likewise, the restatement of the oblation for the third day of Āśvina would not be appropriate if the rule were determined by the order of recitation. Similarly, it is stated in some places: "One practicing malevolent magic should offer in reverse order; thus he drives back his very vital breaths."
While performing [the ritual] in reverse order, he demonstrates the direct order; this is logical if the performance follows the sequence of the recitation.

Otherwise, everything would be in direct order, and the demonstration of the reverse order would not be possible! Likewise, when it is stated, "He brings together the fourth and the last," it is said, "He brings together the *iḍā* and the *barhis*"; by that...
It shows that the *barhis* is fourth; this [position] is established by the order of the recited text (*pāṭhakrama*) as the regulating factor.
The section concerning the fact that sequence in some cases follows the order of initial application. (The Principle of the Order of Initial Application.)
Because of its own activity, it initiates those qualities that are simultaneous with it. || 8 ||
(Sūtra 10)

In the Bājasaneyaka, it is heard: "At the Vājapeya, one immolates seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati. Regarding those animals, the ritual duties such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and so forth, which are obtained through the rule of extension (codaka), apply therein.
[Bhāṣya, p. 613:

The first object must be commenced from some point or other; however, regarding the second and subsequent objects, a doubt arises: should the second object also be commenced from that very same point, or...

Is there no fixed rule regarding the second [repetition] and those that follow? What, then, is the prima facie position? Since there is no scriptural injunction that establishes a restrictive rule, there is no fixed rule.
(Bhāṣya-sūtra)

This being the case, we reply: since the first [item] has been commenced, the second and subsequent items must likewise be commenced from that very point. Why is this so? "Because of the commencement of that," for all constituent parts (padārtha) must not be separated from the time of the principal rite; for the principal...
The intended or performed [action] is for their sake; for there is a statement of concomitance, namely:

"the primary act must be performed together with the constituent elements. However, because many constituent elements are enumerated, a separation is inevitable; nevertheless, it is possible [to perform it] as long as it is not separated by more than one [element].

The ritual act must be performed; therefore, an interruption by exactly that many [steps] must necessarily be made, and one must not be interrupted by more than that. If one were to begin the second ritual act from elsewhere, then one would be interrupted by even more [steps], and thus one would subvert the injunction regarding the performance (*prayoga-vacana*).
[Objection: "But if that were the case, there would be some excessive interval. [Reply: It is said: By abandoning those intervening factors that are permitted, there is some additional merit.
It is so; therefore, from whatever point the preceding section has begun, from that very point the subsequent one must begin.
If it is argued that "all [the mantras] apply" (sūtra 8, Purvapakṣa).

If you think thus— that because it is not remote from the primary, the injunction of performance (prayogavacana) applies— then that section on the subsidiary elements (guṇakāṇḍa) must be completed within a single [performance], as in the case of the Saurya and other such rites.
Not so, because it has not been performed. (Sūtra 10) [Ācārya’s Siddhānta]
Bhāṣya: This is not so; for indeed, they would not be performed together in their simultaneous application.
The reading in the Kāśīmudrita-pustaka (Kāśī edition) is: "The second category of objects (*padārtha*) also should not be commenced."

If it is argued that it is like the case of different categories [of words], [we reply: no. (Ā) || 11 ||
Now, as for what was stated— namely, "just as in other sacrifices such as the Saurya and others"—
that must be refuted.

Not so, because of the lack of inherence. (0 Ni.)

Bhāṣya: For them, an order does not follow from the sense [of the text] such that it could be regulated; for a regulation must pertain to subsidiaries (*aṅga*), otherwise the status of being a subsidiary would have to be created for that which is not already based on a subsidiary. (5.1.5)
Now begins the section concerning whether sequence follows the order of position.
And because of the connection with the place of origin. || 13 ||
The Bhāṣya states: "One should cause one who desires offspring to sacrifice with the twenty-one-fold Atirātra; one who desires vigor with the twenty-seven-fold;
one who desires stability with the thirty-three-fold"—thus it is heard in scripture. In that regard, by means of scriptural tradition (āgama)—

This is called "filling the gaps. In that regard, when the *āgama* (supplementation) is being performed, should all the *ṛc*s be brought in according to an unrestricted order, or rather according to the sequence of the *kāṇḍas*? What is the prima facie view? That it is without restriction. Why? Because in the *atirātra* sacrifice, these [verses] come to be required by the meaning of words such as "thirteen" and so on; and for those that thus become required, there is no sequential order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). This being the case, it is said in reply: when these...

Position is established in the traditional recitation (samāmnāya); by that, these [mantras] are restricted. Those which were recited first must be employed first, for this is the observed purpose of sequential order:
namely, the manifestation of what follows, which is indeed intended to be performed. Thus it is with words such as "nine" and so forth.

Since these [rites] are obtained simultaneously in the Atirātra, the order of recitation is not their domain; thus they are of indefinite order—this is the reading in the Kāśikā and Kiraṇāvalī manuscripts.
↑ Regarding the statement "the recollection of what has been said," this is the reading found in the Kāśmīra-Kṛṣṇa manuscript.

Thus, there arises the thought that this is a separate section (*adhikaraṇāntara*). However, since the restriction here is established by the very order of the recitation of the traditional texts (*samāmnāya-pāṭha-krama*), it is understood as a mere repetition; thus, the Sūtra is interpreted otherwise.
It is described [as such] because of its place and its connection with the origin. 13.

In the Sādyaska sacrifice, it is heard: "One sacrifices the animals together. Regarding this, the following meaning has been established: the three animals are to be sacrificed at the time of the *savanīya*.

Now, in this case, based on the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*), should the *agniṣomīya* be sacrificed first, or, based on the order of position (*sthānakrama*), should the *savanīya* be sacrificed first? What is the prima facie view? That the *agniṣomīya* comes first. Why? Because of the order of the text. This being the case, we reply:

The *savanīya* [offering] comes first because of its position; for if the *āgnīṣomīya* were to come first, the position of the *savanīya* would be obstructed by the injunction: "Having taken the *āśvina* cup and having thrice encircled the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)... [Objection: "But even so, the order of the recited text (*pāṭhakrama*) would be sublated. [Reply: Let it be sublated.
For the word "saha" (together) is recorded there for the purpose of prohibition; and since the position of the Āśvina cup is not prohibited, it must not be set aside. (5.1.6)
Bhāṣya: The section concerning the fact that the sequence of the wheel follows the sequence of the thief.
Or rather, the sequence of the subsidiaries follows the sequence of the principal [actions], because they exist for the sake of that. || 14 ||

"The two Sārasvatas [cups] exist; for it is heard in scripture: 'This indeed is the divine pair'—regarding this there is a doubt: do the ritual properties of the one dedicated to the three deities come first, or those of the one dedicated to the two deities?"

—Thus [it might be argued]. Since there is no scriptural injunction (śāstra) that establishes a restrictive rule, there would be no fixed order; this being the position reached, we reply: "Or rather, the restriction should be according to the primary sequence.

For indeed, the recitation of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the deity Viśvedevas comes first: "The divine Sarasvatī is breath" (*prāṇo devī sarasvatī*). Therefore, because the offering to the deity Viśvedevas occurs first, [the order is determined by that].
The Sādyaskra is a specific variety of Soma sacrifice.
Sarasvatī and Sarasvan; those two deities are the meaning of the word *sārasvata*.
[Page 616] It must be so; therefore, the rites pertaining to Śrī should be performed first.
For in this way, the principle that the subsidiaries (aṅga) share the same time as the principal (pradhāna) is maintained; otherwise, there would be an interruption by those ritual elements.
By implication, it is permitted that there may be an intervention even by more than those [specified].
(5.1.7) This is the section concerning the superiority of the order of recitation over the order of principal items in the case of the *catra* sacrifices.
But in the case of the archetype, because it is expressed by its own word, it should be understood according to the sequence. || 15 ||

In the *Bhāṣya* [it is stated]: Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), first the properties of the vegetable offerings (*auṣadha*) are prescribed, and after that, those of the clarified butter (*ājya*).

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the properties of the clarified butter be performed first according to the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*), or according to the order of the textual recitation (*yathāpāṭha*)? When it is argued that the properties of the clarified butter should come first by following the order of the principal acts, we reply: No. It is *malatī*.

It should be understood according to the order of recitation; for the word "kha" (in the sense of "as") refers to their order of recitation, and that would be subverted if it were performed otherwise. Furthermore, the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavacana*) is a restatement of the simultaneity [of the rites]; if the constituent parts (*padārtha*) are brought into proximity according to their own order, that injunction will not be subverted. Moreover, the word "kha" occurs in the order of recitation—as in "The Veda is to be studied"—whereas the syntactic unity with the injunction of performance is more clearly established through the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*). (5.1.8)
The section concerning the superior strength of the recitation of mantras over the recitation of the Brāhmaṇa.
But in case of a conflict, it should be according to the mantra, because of the capacity of its form in usage; therefore, that is the place of origin.
In the Bhāṣya on the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the mantra-text for the Āgneya offering comes first, while the Brāhmaṇa-text follows later.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: which [order] is more authoritative? It is said: there is no fixed rule, because there is an absence of a scriptural injunction that would establish such a rule. The Vārttika states:
"The meaning is that an unexpressed order is merely a mental construction (kalpa)."

Bhāṣya, Chapter 5, Pāda 1.

This being the case, we reply: the recitation of the mantra is more powerful. Why? Because of the capacity of its form for application; that is, the mantra possesses the capacity of its form for application. That by which the mind is applied to its intended purpose, and for that which is being so applied, the sequence is observed for the sake of a visible result.
"But surely the recitation by the Brāhmaṇas has that same purpose. It is replied:
"That is the place of origin; furthermore, its purpose will be for the sake of the production of the ritual action" (5.1.9).
The section concerning the greater strength of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) over the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance).
Sūtra: On account of that statement, in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), it should be according to the principal [deity]. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 17 ||

Commentary: There is a sacrifice named Adhvarakalpā, [prescribed as follows]: "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu; Sarasvatī should have a portion of clarified butter; there should be an oblation of cooked rice (caru) for Bṛhaspati.
In this regard, there is a doubt: should the ritual procedure of the offering to Bṛhaspati—which is a modification of the offering to Agni—be performed first?

Regarding the bodily acts (*kāya*), is the injunctive statement (*codaka*) stronger because of its application-statement (*prayoga-vacana*), or is the application-statement of the modification (*vikāra*) of the *upāṃśuyāja* stronger than the injunctive statement? What is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? "In this modification, it should be according to the primary [acts], because of that statement.

For in the modification, the sequence of their direct statements exists; therefore, the application-statement which brings together those [acts] present is indeed perceptible (*pratyakṣa*), whereas the [application] of their properties is inferential (*ānumānika*).
For that [extension] was obtained by means of the *codaka* (the general rule of transfer). Therefore, the direct statement of the application (*prayogavacana*) is more powerful;
by it, the inferential *codaka* is sublated.
Or, in the case of a misconception, [one should act] according to one's own nature, following the sequence of one's natural disposition.
18 || (Siddhānta) ||

The primary rule regarding the constituent parts is: "In the case of a modification (*vikṛti*), it ought to be exactly as it was in the archetype (*prakṛti*) when there is a conflict. Why? Because of the connection with the archetype; for whatever [is prescribed] in the archetype...

The *dharmas* ought to be exactly the same in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)—thus, if they were performed according to the order of the primary sacrifice (*mukhyakrama*), they would not be performed as they are in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*). For the injunction (*codaka*) [governs] the performance...
[Page 618]

Because of the statement [of the *bhāṣya*], it is more powerful, for it both produces and brings about [the application]. Having observed those things brought about, the statement of the performance (*prayoga-vacana*) summarizes them; having arisen with respect to those things already brought about, being caused by that bringing about, it cannot sublate the *codaka* (the general injunction) which was previously brought about at a later time.
Even though it is directly perceived, because it is extrinsic, it will be applied only according to what has been established.
Therefore, first are the characteristics of the Vārhaspatya [offering], and then those of the Āgneya—thus [it is concluded].
The section concerning the location of the natural property of something known [to exist] somewhere; (the Sākamedhīya-nyāya).
kha. The modification (vikṛti) should take place at that same time as the archetype (prakṛti), because it possesses the nature of the archetype, just as prescribed by the learned.

In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the Sākamedha is the third section; its constituent parts are: "An eight-potherd cake for Agni Anīkavant in the morning, a pap for the Maruts Sāntapanas at midday, and boiled rice in the milk of all [the cows] for the Maruts Gṛhamedhins in the evening.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: are these offerings to be performed over ten days, or are they to be completed on the same day (sadyaskālā)?

—Thus [it is asked]. What is the prima facie view? The modification (*vikṛti*) ought to have the same time as that [of the archetype], because "as it is taught"—that is, as the archetype has been stated, so should the modification be; for it possesses the characteristics of the archetype. Therefore, whatever is a modification, it [should take place] at the time of burning.
It ought to be so.

Or rather, even if it were performed immediately when connected with a specific order and time, there would be a loss of the characteristics of the archetype (prakṛti) because of the inference of the rule [from the modified sacrifice]. (Siddhānta 20)

Bhāṣya: Those objects which are mentioned at different times—namely morning, midday, and evening—are understood to occur sequentially on a single day, just as it is said: "Devadatta eats cake in the morning, eats various kinds of food at midday, and whatever exertion he performs in the afternoon, all that belongs to the same time. (Pātañjala-yoga-sūtra-bhāṣya).
The reading.
[Page 619] Bhāṣya:
"He eats sweetmeats"—this is understood to mean on a single day.
Therefore, modifications (vikṛtis) of this kind have an immediate time (sadyaskālā), for they are to be performed at the same time [as the primary sacrifice].
That which is obtained through an injunction and is inferential would be sublated by the *sadyaskālā* sacrifice, which takes the form of direct perception.
Sūtra Bhāṣya Sūtra (Sūtra Commentary)
If it is argued that there is an extension of time. (Ā) || 21 ||

If you think: "It is heard that [the sacrifice] is to be performed with its constituent parts (sāṅga) in the morning, and likewise at midday and in the evening"—then there will be a displacement (utkarṣa); thus it will be performed with its parts at these times, and there will be no sublation of the time for the *agrahāra* (the taking of the portions), as one will commence with the *anīkavant* cup in the morning.

The second [offering] is sacrificed in the morning. Thus, the Sāntapanīyā will begin on the previous day at midday and be sacrificed on the following day at midday; likewise, for the Gṛhamedhīya, there is the commencement on the previous day in the evening and the sacrifice on the following day in the evening—this is so because of the direct statement (*vākya*).

It has been stated that "one day is traversed. To this it is replied: for the meaning of a sentence arises from the capacity of the word-meanings; however, in this case, there is no such capacity of the word-meanings by which one day could be traversed.
Not so, because of the connection with that. (Ābhāsa-nirṇaya 22)

Bhāṣya: This is not so. Why? Because of their connection with that—namely, the principal acts are heard in scripture as being connected with the subsidiaries at a single time. How so? For the principal act together with its subsidiaries is heard [to be performed] at the morning time, and likewise at midday and in the evening; the subsidiaries are not [heard] separately for the morning time and so on. In that case, if the subsidiaries were at different times and the principals at different times, the sacrifice would not have been performed with its subsidiaries at those [intended] times. Therefore, these [sacrifices] are indeed of the same-day performance (*sadyaskāla*).

Regarding the cognitions—furthermore, it is heard in scripture: "One should perform the burning [of the sins] with the Sākamedha sacrifices"; this is appropriate for those rites performed on the same day (*sadyaskālā*). (5.1.11)
The reading is "sāntapanīyāḥ" according to the Cāndra and Somaśambhu recensions; in those cases, the ritual action everywhere conforms accordingly.
The reading in the Kāśikā (Kā'kī0 pu0) is "tatsambhavāt" (because of its possibility).
In the Mīmāṃsā system.

The section concerning the postponement of the *anuyāja* offerings and so forth, and the anticipation of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth; [this is] the principle of "that which begins with X ends with Y" (*tadādita-dantanyāya*).
Because the limbs have their primary time [of performance], there would be a displacement [of the main rite] as previously stated.
23 || (Pūrvapakṣa) ||

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "They perform the after-offerings (anuyājas) after the Agnimāruta [saṃsthā]"; this is an upward displacement (utkarṣa). Likewise, in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, it is said: "They offer the fore-offerings (prayājas) while the animal is standing"; this is a downward displacement (apakarṣa). In this regard, there is a doubt: in the case of the upward displacement, is only the after-offering displaced, and in the case of the downward displacement, is only the fore-offering displaced; or rather, in the upward displacement, is everything from the after-offering onwards displaced, and in the downward displacement, is everything up to the fore-offering displaced?
And [is it] up to the end of the *prayāja*s?—so [it is asked]. What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It should be as much as has been stated;

there would be an extension (*utkarṣa*) or a contraction (*apakarṣa*). Why? Because "the subsidiaries have the time of the principal," and thus the other [subsidiaries] will have the same time as the principal. In that case, the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), which establishes their simultaneity, will be upheld.
Or rather, because of the connection starting from that [point], there would be an extraction [of the rule] ending with that.
24 || (Siddhānta) ||

In that case, it should be understood that in the case of an increase (*utkarṣa*), [the sequence] begins with that, and in the case of a decrease (*apakarṣa*), it ends with that. Why? Because of the connection: that which is recited after the *anuyāja* offerings sets aside what would have been obtained by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) as being intermediate to the principal act;
rather, by the force of the textual order (*pāṭha*), it is performed after the *anuyājas*. Likewise, whatever follows that is [placed] after that.
"Beyond this: in this way, when one [element] is elevated, it elevates the entire section of qualities;
likewise, when it is depressed, it depresses it"—thus [ends the discussion]. (5.1.12)

The section concerning the precedence of the preparatory acts over the principal acts, established through the sequence of their performance.
For those whose time has been fixed by their engagement [in a specific rite]. || 25 ||
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard at the time of the Prātaranuvāka: "O Pratiprasthātṛ, [prepare] the Savanīya [oblations]... (Note:

Having offered the *savanīya* oblations, are the subsequent ritual items—beginning with the *pracaraṇī-homa*—belonging to the Soma sacrifice (*saumika*), or do they belong to the cake-offering (*puroḍāśa*) prior to the *alaṅkaraṇa* (decoration)? What is the prima facie view? There is no fixed rule, because there is an absence of a scriptural injunction (*śāstra*) that would establish such a restriction.

— This being the case, we reply: "By means of the sequence of performance, there shall be a restriction for those items whose time [of performance] is determined; for it is while one item is being performed that it restricts the preceding item, and that [subsequent item] is recited after it."

It should be performed later; however, because of the scriptural injunction regarding the performance of the Soma-related ritual act, namely the *pracaraṇī* oblation, the sequence is set aside. Furthermore, the decoration of the *bahiṣpavamāna* is prescribed after [the oblation];
therefore, that [decoration] precedes the ritual acts such as the pouring out [of the grain].
Thereafter, the Soma-related ritual acts are to be performed.
And because of the contradiction with the scriptural statement. || 26 ||
Furthermore, the verbal expression would be contradicted: one addressed with "Adorn yourself" might instead undertake acts such as sprinkling water [for purification].
In our position, however, when told "Adorn yourself," one will understand only the act of adorning;
in that case, regarding the act of adorning, the *loṭ* suffix denoting the proper time will be favored. Therefore, in this instance, the sequence follows the order of the original injunctions. (5)
[The discussion] concerning the extraction [of the *dhūpa* offering] when the preparation of the broth has been performed: (The Principle of the *Dhūpa* Offering).
But because of the lack of connection, that modified [offering] alone should be extracted. 27.

In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, which has the Darśapūrṇamāsa as its archetype, there is a modified (vaikṛta) act concerning the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), namely: "During the initiations (*dīkṣā*), he cuts the sacrificial post. When that act is brought forward, it also brings forward the subsequent acts, such as the carrying forward of the fires (*agnīṣomīya-praṇayana*) and so forth.
In the Mīmāṃsādarśana-bhāṣya,
regarding the doubt as to whether [the action] draws [the result] near or not— the Bhāṣya states: "It draws it near, because of the connection."
It is understood.

This being the case, we reply: that which is additional in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), when it is being deferred, cannot cause even those elements mentioned in the scriptural injunctions—such as the carrying forward of the fire for the Agnīṣomīya animal—to be deferred. Why? Because of the lack of connection; the ritual action regarding the sacrificial post (yūpa) belongs to the animal sacrifice, and [the elements in question] precede it.

It belongs to the Soma sacrifice; there is no mutual connection between those two. The ritual element belonging to the Soma sacrifice does not assist the animal sacrifice, nor does it assist the animal itself. For if it were to assist them, then its sequence, while providing assistance to that which assists, would become a subordinate factor.

It might be so, but this is not the case; therefore, there is no restriction regarding their mutual order. Consequently, only the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is drawn forward. Moreover, by drawing forward only the sacrificial post, once the word has fulfilled its purpose, there will be no subversion of the own-order (*svakrama*) of the Soma-related rites—so it is said. (5)
The section concerning the displacement of the offerings made in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.
And one should not exalt what is incidental, because of its lack of connection. || 28 ||

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard [in the scripture]: "They perform the after-sacrifices (anuyājas) after the Āgnimāruta [offering]. There arises a doubt: when the after-sacrifices are displaced [to a later time], do they displace the two oblations belonging to the Dakṣiṇāgni fire or not? The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that they do displace them because of their connection.

To this, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is stated: these two [oblations] do not deserve to be displaced. Those after-sacrifices which belong to those two [fires] are connected to them; they are not employed by others [belonging to different fires]. Therefore, the purpose of those [after-sacrifices] has already been accomplished.
— Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, there is a sequence of constituent elements (*padārtha*), but not of the purposes of those constituent elements;
for we shall explain that the constituent elements assist simultaneously.

Moreover, the production (*utpatti*) of constituent elements possesses a sequence because their production is expressed by distinct words, whereas the purpose of the constituent elements does not, since it is declared by a single injunction of simultaneous performance. Therefore, because there is no displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the production of the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), the oblation pertaining to the southern fire (*dākṣiṇāgnika-homa*) [is not displaced].
"They would be displaced"— thus [it is argued]. Furthermore, by displacing merely the *anuyāja*s,
once the word has fulfilled its purpose, there will be no subversion of the own-order (*svakrama*) for the two oblations belonging to the *dakṣiṇāgni*.

Thus. (5.1.15 Section)

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the altar (vedi) is prescribed for the time following the covering of the sacrificial oblation (haviḥ-abhivāsana). This [altar] is drawn forward to the new moon day (amāvāsyā), according to the injunction: "On the day before the new moon, one prepares the altar.
When it is thus drawn forward, it draws along with it those ritual items (padārtha) that follow it.
Is this not so?—this is the doubt. It is replied: "Because of the connection, it is drawn back.

This being the position reached, we say: "As before"; on the new moon day preceded by the preparation of the altar, the construction of the altar is prescribed on the preceding day, while for both [the new and full moon sacrifices], the covering of the oblation occurs on the following day.

Regarding the statement, "Having performed the *abhivāsana* (covering with grass), the altar (*vedi*) should be prepared on the new moon day"—there is no basis for this in any of the means of knowledge such as direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*), and so forth; therefore, the rites ending with the *abhivāsana* should not be postponed.
Furthermore, if the *abhivāsana* were postponed, the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) would be reduced to ashes. (5.1.16)

In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, there is an offering called the Sāntapanīyā, which is a constituent part of the Sākamedha; it is prescribed that "one offers a caru-oblation to the Sāntapana Maruts at midday. Regarding the doubt as to whether this [offering], when postponed due to some divine or human obstacle, would cause the Agnihotra to be postponed or not—it is said in reply: "The Sāntapanīyā, however, would cause [the Agnihotra] to be postponed, because of the force of the fire," so reads the text in the Pā0 Ma0 Pu0.

The Agnihotra is like the Soma-sacrifice because of its deficiency; for if it were not postponed, the Agnihotra would become defective when the fire has been drawn out at the time of the morning pressing (Prātaḥsavana). Therefore...
It should be postponed, just like a *savana*; for example, just as the morning *savana*, when postponed due to an obstacle from either a divine or human source, postpones the midday *savana*—
so too should it be understood in this case.

And because there is no intervention. (Yukti 31)

In this way, the Sāntapanīya will not be separated from the Agnihotra; thus, the sequence will be maintained. Moreover, a fault is heard regarding a disruption of the sequence: "Verily, that [sacrifice] is cut off from the sacrifice, when the ritual of one [deity] is performed while another's is being extended."
But because there is no connection, one should not transpose [the element]. (Siddhānta) || 32 ||
The Sāntapanīya is not a subsidiary part of the Agnihotra, nor is the Agnihotra a subsidiary part of the Sāntapanīya;
therefore, that [Sāntapanīya] is not to be performed after the Agnihotra, and consequently, the Agnihotra is not to be postponed.
And because the occasion [for the rite] has been reached. (Yukti 33)
Furthermore, the specific occasions for the Agnihotra have been established: "He offers in the evening, he offers in the morning;
he offers when the sun has risen, he offers when it has not yet risen; he offers when it has just set, he offers at the twilight;
he offers after seeing the stars. These must not be transgressed; therefore, there can be no postponement. As for what was said regarding "deficiency" (vaiguṇya), [that objection is refuted].

Even by means of the *utkarṣas* (transpositions), there is a deficiency because of the difference in time. If it is argued that "the injunction regarding the secondary time should be set aside due to the attainment of the primary limbs," we say no; for time is merely a causal condition (*nimitta*), as in the case of [the rule regarding] the *pratibala* and so forth.

Commentary (bhā.): Upon the disappearance of that [impurity], the entire rite should be performed immediately; for the occasion (*nimitta*) is heard as something not to be taken up (*anupādeyatvena*). It should be observed. Now, as for what was stated— that that which possesses the *savana* [cup] must be postponed— that is addressed in the Sūtra-bhāṣya (Sūtra 6.5.1).

And the Ṣoḍaśī [cup] [is connected with the Ukthya], because of its conjunction with the Ukthya. || 35 ||
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, with reference to the Ṣoḍaśin, it is heard in scripture:
"He draws it apart from the Ukthas," provided that by chance there is no obstacle, whether divine or human.

The *urathyā* verses are displaced; does it then follow that the *ṣoḍaśin* [stotra] should also be displaced, or not?—thus there arises a doubt. What is the prima facie view? It should not be displaced. Why?
Because in this way, the *stotra* of the *ṣoḍaśin* will be performed at its own proper time.
"When the sun has reached the zenith at the time of twilight, one begins the Ṣoḍaśin-stotra"—thus it is said. Therefore, there is no displacement [of the ritual].
This being the position reached, we reply: "And the Ṣoḍaśin must be displaced. Why?
"Because of its connection with the Ukthya": for there is indeed a displacement of the Ṣoḍaśin, as it is said, "He draws it out after the Ukthyas. Therefore, the Ṣoḍaśin must be displaced.
As for what was said—that the exclusion of the Ṣoḍaśin will occur by means of the time of the Ṣoḍaśin-stotra—[that is not so].
To this it is replied: for one who conforms to the order of the stotra, the order of the principal acts would be contradicted.
Therefore, the order of the stotra should not be followed; it is impossible to conform to both [simultaneously].
For one either performs the stotra after drawing the cup (graha), or after ladling out the soma into the chalice (camasa). Thus it is said.

kha. In a combination [of substances], each of the principal qualities should possess all the functions. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 1 ||

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "One immolates seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati. And in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, the ritual duties for the animal are prescribed and extended [to this sacrifice] by the general rule (codaka). Regarding these, there is a doubt: should one begin the ritual duties from the first animal?

Having performed [the first], one should then begin the second from the beginning; however, should the first be performed for all [the items] first, and then the second? What is the prima facie view? All [the rites] should be completed for each individual [item]. Why? To favor the proximity of the primary acts; otherwise, the proximity of the primary acts would be disrupted! Just as in the case of many [items]...
Just as in the case of the sacrificial cakes offered when horses are being accepted, there is no sequential performance of those belonging to the same class,
so it is here as well.
kha. [The response] for all [the priests] is of a single kind, because the sequence has been established. (Siddhānta) || 2 ||
Commentary: A simultaneous performance (*anusamaya*) of those of the same class must be carried out. What will happen by doing so?

The totality (*sahatva*) will be favored; that totality is heard [in scripture] in the statement: "Having performed the *vaiśvadevī* sacrifice, they proceed with the animal sacrifices" (*paśubhiś caranti*), which indicates the simultaneous performance of the animals at one time.

[Objection: "But if this is so, then the subsequent ritual act would be separated from the preceding ritual act by the operation of another animal. [Response: This is not a fault; even in this case, the required sequence is indeed maintained—for that very operation which occurs in relation to the other animal is itself [part of the same process], and it is not a separate ritual act.
There is an intervention by another entity.

Bhāṣya: Now, as for what was said—that when there are many sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), there can be no sequential performance (*anusamaya*) of those of the same kind—that must be refuted. To this it is replied: It is appropriate in that case that "there is repetition because of a specific cause"; for if a sequential performance of the same kind were carried out, once the placing on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) of a thousand [cakes] had been performed, the first one would burn, and its churning (*mathana*) could not be accomplished.

"The performance [of the ritual] follows the acceptance of many thousands of horses—this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). The sequential performance according to the sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) must be accepted—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). (5.2.2).
This is the section concerning the sequential performance of the collection of items such as the handfuls and the potsherds.
And in the cases of the Muṣṭika-pālāvadāna, añjana, abhyañjana, vapana, and pāvana, [the action is performed] with one [mantra]. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 4 ||

In the case of the *muṣṭi* (handful) and other such items, there is a doubt: is the performance to be done with one handful, or with four handfuls? What is the prima facie view? It is with one handful. Why?
Because the pouring out of one handful is a single ritual act (*padārtha*), not the pouring out of four handfuls.

How so? When one handful has been poured out, the state of "having performed the pouring" (niruptatva) is established; it cannot be said that "nothing at all has been poured out," nor does the act of pouring fail to occur once it has been performed. Furthermore, there is no purpose served by pouring out merely a single handful, for [the rite requires more].
In one [case], there is a sequential attainment of all dharmas in their entirety; this is called "attainment in succession."
"In the case of a mere handful [of grain], it is restricted," so reads the Kāśikā and Kiraṇāvalī manuscripts.

[Page 629] Bhāṣya: In a single [act], four [handfuls] are possible when not yet poured out; for the word "four" has coreferentiality with the "handful. Therefore, the performance should be carried out by means of the handful. Thus—
"one piles the kapālas," likewise, "he cuts from the middle, he cuts from the front," and likewise, "he anoints, he anoints, he shaves, he purifies."
But all [the auxiliary acts] have a single purpose because they possess that quality. (Sūtra 5)
(Sūtra 10)

Having completed one's own [offerings], however, one should perform the *anusamaya* (concluding rite); for the substance to be poured out is not to be done in a single handful, because the pouring out consists of four [handfuls]. How is there a count of four? [It is so] by virtue of the word "four."
Because of its connection with the act of offering (*nirvapati*). Thus, it is logical that multiple qualities are enjoined along with the action;

otherwise, if there were a connection with the handfuls (*muṣṭi*), a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result, and it would become a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the offering itself. The same applies to the placing [of the potsherds] (*upadhāna*) and so forth, as in the case of "the cake on eight potsherds" (*aṣṭākapālam*).

Because of the injunction, "He offers on eleven potsherds," and because of the statements, "He cuts off twice, he anoints thrice, he purifies with twenty-one [stalks]," the actions and qualities belong to the *saṅgava* and the other [pressing times]. Therefore, there is simultaneous performance (*anusamaya*) by means of the entire collection. (5.2.3)
The section on the occasion for the rule regarding the offering of the Avadāna.
But when [the word] *sra* is joined [with another], it follows from the context that it must be a limb of that [other], because the other exists for its sake.
Bhāṣya: In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "He cuts off two portions of the sacrificial cake. Regarding that—

There is a doubt: is there a sequential performance (*anusamaya*) with each portioning (*avadāna*), or with each portioning followed by the final offering (*pradānānta*)? What is the prima facie view? We say: it is with each portioning. Why?
Because they are distinct ritual acts (*pṛthak-padārtha*); for the act of portioning is indeed a distinct ritual act from the act of sacrifice (*yajati*).
Because of the finality [of the act] and because of the verbal root *ava-dā* (to cut off). This being the position reached, we reply:

"But when connected, on account of the commencement, it must be a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that; for the other is for the sake of that. The cutting off (*avadāna*) is not a separate ritual act (*pṛthak padārtha*), as it is the commencement of the offering (*pradāna*); otherwise, the verbal root *ava-dā* would have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*)."
[Page 630] There would be an investigation regarding the *darbha* grass for me! Furthermore, the repetition is for the purpose of prescribing a specific number. Therefore...

The offering (*vadāna*) is a constituent part of the sacrificial substance (*padārtha*), and the simultaneous performance of these parts is not enjoined by the injunction of the ritual procedure (*prayoga-vacana*);
therefore, there is a sequential performance (*anusamaya*) up to the end of each individual offering—thus [it is concluded].
(5.2.4a) Sūtra.
The section concerning the sequence of the detailed exposition of speech and so forth.
But because of the scriptural statement, the application of collyrium and other rites should extend up to the end of the winding of the cord.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma (agnīṣomīya-paśu), the ritual acts such as the anointing of the sacrificial post (yūpa) are prescribed.

When these acts are extended to the set of eleven posts (yūpaikādaśinī), a doubt arises: should there be a sequential performance (anusamaya) of each individual act, such as the anointing and so forth, for each post, or should it be performed from the anointing up to the final encircling (parivyāṇa) for each post?
What is established?—The acts beginning with anointing (*añjana*) should extend up to the encircling (*pariyāṇa*).
Why?

Because of the scriptural statement (*vacana*); for there is this statement: "The sacrificer should not release the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) from the anointing until the encircling. And it is not possible [to perform] many [acts] by means of the anointing and so forth [alone].
The performance should be carried out consecutively, and not with intervals; therefore, the sequence ends with the encircling.
The creation of the Dānavas would arise from a cause, just like the growth of a tree.

The injunction regarding the performance (*prayogavacana*), which brings about simultaneity (*sahatva*), will be followed; thus, there is *anusamaya* (sequential performance) according to the individual items (*padārtha*). Furthermore, "non-abandonment" (*anavasarga*) was performed by implication in the archetype (*prakṛti*), as it constitutes assistance.

By the sacrificer [commanding] the Adhvaryu, the purpose of the new production is thus seen; otherwise, it would be for an unseen purpose. Furthermore, the general rule (codaka) does not bring about what is already accomplished by the purpose itself.
Therefore, one should release [the animal] because of the reason that it is to be raised up with another sacrificial post (yūpa), as follows:

Nor is there a sequential performance (anusamaya) by way of individual ritual items (padārtha); rather, there should be a sequential performance by way of the entire group of items ending with the encircling (parivyāṇa). For the non-abandonment of the large [sacrificial post] is effected by the verbal injunction;
indeed, even without the sacrificer, the Adhvaryu is able to erect the sacrificial post.
If it is argued that this is for the sake of "facility," then the injunctive word would be contradicted! In this way, it would merely serve a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārthatā).

Indeed, it must be restricted! Just as facing east is prescribed for eating, [the order] cannot be established through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). Therefore, there is *anusamaya* (consecutive performance) according to the section on the constituent parts (*padārtha-kāṇḍa*), and the injunctive statement of performance (*prayoga-vacana*) is merely a logical principle; the general rule (*codaka*) is stronger than that. Furthermore, the increase in the number of priests (*pātravṛddhi*) should be performed according to the purpose (*artha*). (5.2.5)

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, there are animals dedicated to Prajāpati. Regarding them, a doubt arises: should one take the portions for the deities from each individual animal, and then the portions for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, and then the portions for the Iḍā; or should there be a sequential performance (anusamaya) by means of the portions for the deities with those for the deities, the portions for Sviṣṭakṛt with those for Sviṣṭakṛt, and the portions for the Iḍā with those for the Iḍā? What, then, is the prima facie view? That the rites should be performed for each individual animal.

Having cut off [the portion], it must then be offered; because this is stated in the archetype (prakṛti), it follows by extension (codaka) that this same act is required even for the Prājāpatya offerings.
[The deities are distinct] because of their separate functions. (Siddhānta) || 11 ||

This is not so; [the phrase] "by the deities" (*daivataiḥ*) refers to those belonging to the deities (*daivatānām*), "to the Sviṣṭakṛt" (*sauviṣṭakṛteḥ*) refers to those belonging to the Sviṣṭakṛt (*sauviṣṭakṛtānām*), and "by the Airas" (*airaiḥ*) refers to those belonging to the Airas (*air̤ānām*). Why? Because of "the unity of the ritual action" (*aikakarmyāt*); thus it becomes performed together. And as for the cutting of the portions (*avadāna*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*) by virtue of the scriptural statement—"the portions for the deities"—[it applies here as well]. "The deities... [and so forth].

[Page 632] Bhāṣya: "Having cut off [the portion], one should not offer only that much; the portions for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt (sauviṣṭakṛta) should be cut off. Having cut off the portions for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, one should not offer only that much; the portions for Iḍā (air̤a) should be cut off"—thus it is heard in the archetype (prakṛti). That [rule] applies here to the deities by means of the divine [portions].

While performing the *anusamaya* (concluding) offerings, one would not subvert this natural order of ritual procedure: having first cut portions for the deities (*devatāni*), one does not yet offer them, but rather cuts the portions for *Sviṣṭakṛt* (*sauviṣṭakṛtāni*).
Then, having cut the portions for *Sviṣṭakṛt*, one does not yet offer them, but rather cuts the portions for *Iḍā* (*air̤āni*).
The sequence is according to each individual object—thus it is said.

Therefore, in this way, the *manotā* will not be omitted; otherwise, it would occur only by turns.

— thus [ends the section]. (5.2.6a)

In the Rājasūya sacrifice, there is the Nānā-vāja-iṣṭi, beginning with: "One should offer an eight-potherd cake to Agni Gṛhapati; a porridge of Śyāmāka grain to Soma Vanaspati," and so forth. However, in that context, there is the archetypal *vahanti* (carrying) mantra. Regarding this, there is a doubt: [Should the archetypal mantra be used, or should a new one be composed?]
In that case, is there a single mortar used in succession, or are there many used simultaneously?

Why is there this doubt? If the spreading of the black antelope skin and so forth are distinct ritual acts (*padārtha*), then there is a difference [between them]; but if the spreading of the black antelope skin and so forth, up to the production of the rice grains, constitute a single act, then [there is no difference].

The meaning of the term is "that which is common" (*tatra*). What, then, is the prima facie position? It is that there is "one" [common element]. Why? Because of its "pervasion" (*vibhava*) through alternation;
since the purpose is accomplished by the employment of one, the employment of a second would be useless. Therefore, it is "common."
