There would be an increase in the number of mortars, for a fixed sequence established by the textual recitation is only possible when there is simultaneity; furthermore, there is a sequential performance (anusamaya) of the constituent acts,

and the acts of spreading [the grass] underneath and so forth are distinct acts because they conclude with the state of being a *yati* (a pause or interval), as is evident from the spreading underneath and other such actions.
Because it is expressed by the words; therefore, there is increase. Thus [it is said].
Sūtra 15: "Or rather, there is one [mortar], because of the state of being rice-grains, since the purpose is that.

(Uttara-pakṣa) Bhāṣya: "Or rather, there is one" mortar to be used in succession; for there is indeed a single ritual act beginning with the spreading [of the grass] and ending with the rice-grains, starting from the spreading and concluding with the husking.

This is the remainder of that very [argument]: since the act of threshing (*hanti*) is for the purpose of producing rice, in this way, the acts of spreading [the grass] and so forth, as well as the threshing, will not have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*). Therefore, it is a common ritual procedure (*tantra*). Thus [it is concluded].

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal offering to Agni and Soma; regarding that, it is heard in the scripture: "He performs the after-offerings (anuyājas) with speckled butter. In this regard, there is a doubt:

is there one vessel for the holding of both the fore-offerings (prayāja) and the after-offerings, as well as for the speckled butter, or are they distinct? What is the prima facie view? That there is one. Why?
In the archetype there is one [vessel]; likewise here too, it should be by means of one.

There would be a deficiency in the *prayāja* offerings, and a deficiency in the *anuyāja* offerings. Furthermore, it is not possible to perform distinct actions within a single vessel. Even if a boundary were established, that which is being offered...

for it has the bowl of a mere living being, and it is single-bowed.

"Regarding the objection that this leads to a fault: it is not so. And it is not possible to take [the substance] for the purpose of the after-offerings (anuyāja) by means of the breaths that effect the departure; for in the case of the *pralati*, the taking occurs at one time, and here too it must be performed at one and the same time. Regarding the doubt as to whether the *upahomas* (subsidiary offerings) should be performed first or last, it is replied: the archetypal (*prākṛta*) should come first, and the modified (*vaikṛta*) at the end.
Why? Because the supplement (*śeṣa*) is prescribed for that which has been enjoined and completed, just as a toy is provided for a child who has already been born.
"Through self-restraint, the bodies [are purified] by means of the journey," and so forth; these are the *maurācyātayaḥ*, which are the *māriekomāḥ*—thus says the practitioner (*sādhaka*).
Ātreya holds that the immediate sequence (*anantarya*) is primary, because it is expressed by a word of equal status and because there is no scriptural statement [to the contrary].

There would be a separation, because they are not heard [in that context].

There is no fixed order; or rather, just as the preparation of the fire-pan (*ukhā-sambharaṇa*) and other rites precede the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice according to the sequence of the direct textual recitation (*pratyakṣa-pāṭha-krama*), so too should the fastening of the golden ornament and the rest [precede].

This being the case, we reply: the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of the consecrated person (*dīkṣita*) must be performed first. Why? Because both the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) with respect to the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* offering and the extended injunction (*codaka*) indicate that they are to be performed after the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*. As for their mutual internal order, there is no direct order of recitation—such as that which establishes the priority of the *Ukhā-sambharaṇa*—that establishes their precedence. However, there is indeed a prior recitation of these purificatory rites in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

The latter [text] pertains to the modification (*vikṛti*) regarding the fastening of the gold plate (*rukmapratimocana*); therefore, the sequence should be exactly as stated, with the modified element at the end. [Objection: "But for what purpose is this conjunction (*sannipāta*) suspected?

In the *bhāṣya* it is stated: regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) dedicated to Agni and Soma, it is heard in scripture, "He performs eleven *prayāja* offerings; he performs eleven *anuyāja* offerings. Regarding the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, it is heard, "He performs nine *prayāja* offerings; he performs nine *anuyāja* offerings. Regarding the *Agni* sacrifice, it is heard, "There are six *upasad*s. In this regard, there is a doubt: does the number eleven apply to each individual *prayāja* and each individual *anuyāja*, and likewise, does the number nine apply to each [individual *prayāja* and *anuyāja*] in the *Cāturmāsya*s, and likewise in the *Agni* sacrifice?

Regarding the *copasads*, is there a separate set of six for each, or is it a single group (*saṅgha*) to be accomplished by all together? What is the prima facie view? That the number is distinct for each principal act (*pradhāna*). Why? Because the acts are distinct, and with respect to those principal acts, the group is heard [in the scripture].

And when a subordinate element is enjoined in proximity to a principal element, it is repeated for each principal element; just as in the injunction "he sacrifices the after-sacrifices with speckled butter," the quality of being speckled is repeated for each after-sacrifice, so too is desire.
Or rather, because of the complete destruction [of the original], a modification should be understood. (Siddhānta) || 2 ||
[Commentary: It might be assumed that the collection (*saṅgha*) is to be accomplished by all [the constituent parts]. Why? Because a collection resides in distinctness;

in the absence of distinctness, it would have to be assumed through repetition. One would repeat it only as long as there is no possibility of distinction; whereas as long as it is possible, there is indeed a residence in distinctness.

It is logical; therefore, the *saṅgha* (the assembly) must indeed be accomplished by all. As for the argument that "it is like the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*)," it is not so; for the state of being speckled (*pṛṣattā*) is not possible for a single [animal], nor does it reside in individuality, nor does its performance upon a single [animal] benefit all of them through that means.

[Page 639] Bhāṣya: Therefore, it must necessarily be divided; however, it assists by means of a single performance (*tatreṇa*), for that [performance] is dependent upon the other. This being the case, the injunctive statement of performance (*prayogavacana*) which brings about the greatness [of the sacrifice] will be upheld. (5.3.1) [Adhikaraṇa].

Regarding the *upasads*, there is a doubt: does the repetition follow the manner of a "beaten stick" (*daṇḍakalitavat*), or do they expand from their own respective positions? What, then, is the prima facie view? This is the rule for things that are to be repeated: namely, like a "beaten stick. For when it is said, "Let the section (*anuvāka*) be recited three times," one begins from the beginning, completes it, and then begins again from the beginning; therefore, the repetition is like a beaten stick.
This being the case, we reply: it ought to increase from its own place. Why?

Because the sequence has been established; the sequence established for the *upasads* is that "having performed the first, the middle one should be performed, and after that the last. In that context, if there were a repetition like a "beaten-stick" (*daṇḍakalita*), then having performed the last [again], when the first is repeated, that increase is made in its proper place. This is not the case when there is an increase from its own place.
This is a fault. Therefore, there is an increase in its own place—thus [it is concluded]. (5.3.2 Śrauta Sūtra)

In the Bhāṣya on the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses, it says: "He recites the *sāmidhenīs*.

There is a doubt: should they be placed at the end, or should they be placed between the *samidhyamānavatī* and the *samiddhavatī* verses? What, then, is the prima facie view? But what indeed are these things called *dhāyyās*? We do not find any established usage (*prasiddhi*) for this word. It is said in reply: * **The Definition of Dhāyyā:** A verse that is recited in the middle of a *sūkta* (hymn) is called a *dhāyyā*. Why? Because it is placed within the hymn. The *dhāyyās* are the *sāmidhenīs*. Why? Because there is this statement of the venerable Pāṇini:

“In the words *pāyya*, *sānnāyya*, *nikāyya*, *dhāyyā*, *māna*, *chavi*, *nivāsa*, and *sāmidhenī*, [the suffix *ṇya* is applied]” (Pāṇini 3.1.129). — Thus [it is asked]. It is replied: He says that this [verse] consists of the *triṣṭubh* itself, namely the *uṣṇih* and the *kakubh*. How so? Because at the end of the praise, it says, "The vigor is that of the *triṣṭubh*"; thus, the statement "the *uṣṇih* and the *kakubh* belong to this *triṣṭubh*" is a metaphorical attribution of the cause to the effect.

In the *Sva-stoma-viṣṭi* [sacrifice], at the *vahiṣpavamāna* [laud], the additional verses (*āgantavaḥ*) should be placed before the *paryāsa*;

for it is so observed in the *dvādaśāha*. (Pūrvapakṣa) There are sacrifices characterized by increased *stomas*: "One should cause one desiring progeny to sacrifice with a twenty-one-fold *atirātra*; one desiring vigor with a twenty-seven-fold; one desiring stability with a thirty-three-fold."

Thus, in that regard, the completion by means of the King (the *rājāpūraṇa*) will be stated. Now, when the modified (*vaikṛta*) *bahiṣpavamāna* chants are being performed, a doubt arises: "Is the insertion of the modified elements at the end, or before the *paryāsa*? What is the prima facie position? "The adventitious elements (*āgantavaḥ*) should be placed before the *paryāsa*, for it is so seen in the *dvādaśāha*: 'There are two triplets, the *stotriya* and the *anurūpa*; there are triplets containing the word *vṛṣan*; the last is a triplet.'"
Regarding "paryāsa" (inversion): here too, due to the prior inversion, there must be adventitious [defilements].

The meaning is as follows: Mādhava holds that among the three *ṛks* belonging to the *anurūpa* and *pratyāsas* of the ordinary [stotras], one should perform the insertion (*dṛṣaṇa*) with an *ṛk* whose word-potency (*śabda-śakti*) is appropriate for the middle of the two *ṛks*—the *anurūpa* and the *pratyāsa*—which have arrived through the rule of extension (*codaka*).

And the term "perversion" is a designation for the limit. (Yukti)

In common usage, the word *paryāsa* is seen to mean "end," as in the expressions *kṣetraparyāsa* (the end of a field) and *nadīparyāsa* (the end of a river). Thus, the *paryāsa* will be placed at the end.

For a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is not set aside by a syntactical connection (*vākya*). If, on the other hand, it is connected with "other than the Jyotiṣṭoma," then the claim regarding the *saṃsthās* (termini) is even less tenable. Verily, he who resorts to another sacrificial rite than the threefold one sets that [other] ablaze; he who resorts to the fifteen-fold one sets that ablaze; he who resorts to the seventeen-fold one sets that ablaze.

The section concerning the relative strength of direct statement (śruti) and meaning (artha) over the order of recitation (pāṭhakrama).

That which follows the sequence [of the text] is established by both the meaning and the words, because of the specific nature of the revelation and because of its orientation toward the meaning. || 1 ||

Bhāṣya: Here, an investigation is conducted regarding the sublation of the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) by the order of direct statement (*śrutikrama*) and the order of meaning (*arthakrama*). Is the order of recitation equal in strength to those two, or is it sublated by them? What is the prima facie view? They are of equal strength; for the order of recitation is indeed a cause, as are the order of direct statement and the order of meaning.

And there is no distinction regarding authority; therefore, there is no fixed rule—this being the position reached, we reply: the order of the text is indeed set aside by direct statement (*śruti*) and by the sense (*artha*). Why? Because of a specific direct statement and because of the predominance of the sense. What is the specific direct statement? Where...

In that case, direct audition (*śravaṇa*) is the cause [of knowledge], whereas the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is inferential; through the order of recitation, one understands the sequence of memory, namely, "It is to be performed in this manner. Because that [order of recitation] possesses a purposeful meaning, its performance is established by that single justification. However, by direct audition, the performance itself is understood through direct perception as being thus. It is the same with the *arthavāda*. Why? Because it is intent upon the meaning; for it exists for the sake of the meaning.
"For the sake of the principal," it brings about the principal—thus everything is performed.
Therefore, the textual recitation (*pāṭha*) is set aside by those two.
What is the example and what is the purpose? In the Śruti: "The Āśvina [cup] is the tenth..."

It is said: "They offer that third [oblation]. For instance, the *agnihotra* oblation is prescribed first and the cooking (*śrapaṇa*) afterwards; such is how it should be performed if the order of recitation is stronger.
In the Siddhānta, the cooking comes first, and after that the oblation. (5.4.1)

In the acts of cutting off, sprinkling, and placing, there should be an immediate sequence because of their magnitude. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 2 ||

There are the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; therein, the ritual details for the curd (dadhi) are prescribed first, and those for the āgneya [cake] afterwards, yet the offering of the āgneya occurs first. In this regard, there is a doubt:
should the cutting, the sprinkling with clarified butter, and the placing of the curd be performed first, according to the order of the sequence of performance?

Or rather, should it be according to the order of the principal [offerings], so that the offering of the Āgneya comes first? What is the prima facie view? That there is no fixed rule. This being the position, we reply: in the case of the portions to be cut off (*avadāna*) and so forth, the offering of the curd (*dadhi*) comes first according to the order of procedure (*prāvṛttika*). Why? Because if this were permitted, no other intervening factor would be postulated as more significant than these intervening factors; moreover, the scripture shows that the curd must indeed be offered first.
Or rather, it is according to the manner of the gift, because that is its purpose. (Siddhānta) || 3 ||

Or rather, they should be performed according to the order of offering (*yathāpradānam*). For that which has its offering first, its portions (*avadāna*) must come first; therefore, [the portions] belong to the Āgneya [offering]. Why? Because the acts beginning with the portions are governed by the injunction for the offering;

these acts begin with the offering and do not constitute separate ritual purposes—this has already been stated. Thus, both the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) and the portioning (*avadāna*) belong to that [offering].
It is performed solely with the intention of offering (*pradāna*). The placing (*āsādana*) as well is for the purpose of offering (i.e., the act of setting down is for the sake of the offering);
thus, there is a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*). Therefore, the performance of the subsidiaries follows the order of the primary [rite]. Thus it is concluded.

As for the claim that the performance of the *dāna* (giving) comes first—this is due to the sense of the matter, not because of the textual order. And between the order of performance (*prāṣṭattika*) and the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*), the order of the principal acts is stronger. For if the order of the principal acts were adopted, one single item would be separated by a long interval of time; whereas if the order of performance were adopted, there would be a separation of equal duration for all items. Therefore, the order of the principal acts is stronger.
— thus it is said. Now, as for the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that was stated—"one should first take a portion of the curd"—[as found in the Bhāṣya on page 662], it is replied:
this will be intended in that sense. Therefore...

The section concerning the rule regarding the sequence of the Darśa and Soma sacrifices.
In the case of speech and so forth, there is priority of the injunction. (80) || 5 ||

In the Bhāṣya, it is recorded that the state of being preceded by an *iṣṭi* sacrifice is traditionally taught. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the state of being preceded by an *iṣṭi* or the state of being preceded by the *soma* sacrifice an option, or rather, is it only the state of being preceded by an *iṣṭi*? What is the prima facie view? It should be only the state of being preceded by an *iṣṭi*. Why? Because of the scriptural statement.
There is this statement: "The New and Full Moon sacrifices are indeed the chariot of the gods;

he who, having performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices, performs the Soma sacrifice, comes to rest in the choice abode of the gods upon a chariot that is clearly visible. There is no excessive burden on the authority of such a statement. Therefore...
It is precisely because it is preceded by an *iṣṭi*.

[The time for the Soma sacrifice] belongs to oneself; for some [authorities], because of the statement regarding the lapse of the season and the lunar mansion for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), it would otherwise be meaningless at the end of that [period]. (Siddhānta 6)

Bhāṣya: We accept that the *iṣṭi* comes first; however, "for some, the *Soma* sacrifice should occur before the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*s. Why? Because of the statement regarding the non-establishment [of the fires] involving the passing over of seasons and lunar mansions: "He who, intending to sacrifice with *Soma*, establishes the fires, need not wait for a season nor a lunar mansion"—meaning that he who establishes the seasonal rite (*kratu*) of the *Soma* sacrifice need not wait.
"One should not wait for a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) nor for a season (ṛtu); one should install the fires immediately"—this expresses immediate succession;
otherwise, the statement regarding the bypassing of seasons and lunar mansions would be meaningless.

If immediate succession (*ānantarya*) were not intended, then disregard for those very two—the season and the lunar mansion—would have been stated for whichever one was mentioned; therefore, there is immediate succession between the Soma sacrifice and the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*).
Furthermore, the suffix of the present tense is clearly expressed in the phrase "one who is about to sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yakṣyamāṇaḥ*);
and that [suffix] does not denote the state of being preceded by an *iṣṭi* (sacrifice) unless it is so intended. At that time...
If it were intended to refer to the present time, the word "there" (tatra) would be contradicted; therefore, it is understood that the intention is to express immediate succession.

In the *Bhāṣya*, regarding the *Ādhāna* (the fire-consecration), this point has been established: namely, that it may be preceded by an *Iṣṭi* sacrifice or preceded by a *Soma* sacrifice. Now, there arises a doubt: does it apply to all three social classes (*varṇas*)?

Is there the state of being preceded by the *iṣṭi* sacrifice or the state of being preceded by the *soma* sacrifice? Or is it that for a Brāhmaṇa there must be the state of being preceded by the *soma* sacrifice alone? Or is it that only the *Paurṇamāsī* (Full Moon) sacrifice is postponed, while for a Brāhmaṇa both forms [of the sacrifice] are [postponed]?
Alternatively, is this a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*) which occurs after the *soma* sacrifice? Or rather, is it a single performance?
Is there an option for the Brāhmaṇa between both alternatives?
What is the prima facie view? That for the three castes, there is either the precedence of the *iṣṭi* or the precedence of the *soma*.
Why? Because there is no distinction; we perceive no specific difference. This being the position, we reply:
The Brāhmaṇa’s [sacrificial sequence] should have the Soma sacrifice as its predecessor. Why? Because of "exaltation" (utkarṣa).

For exaltation is heard in scripture: "The Brāhmaṇa indeed belongs to Agni by deity; having sacrificed with the Soma, he becomes one belonging to Agni-Soma. That which is the Paurṇamāsa oblation—therein indeed..."

"One should offer it as a secondary oblation; thus it becomes dedicated to both deities"—for what indeed could a scriptural statement not accomplish? Therefore, for a Brāhmaṇa, the Soma sacrifice must necessarily come first.
Or rather, it is the full moon day, because of its connection with the Vedic text. (Siddhānta) || 11 ||
As for what was stated—that for a Brāhmaṇa there is only the sequence beginning with Soma—that is not so;

As far as the statement 'chaviḥ' goes, it is based solely on the explicit word of the text (*vācanika*); in such a case, logical reasoning (*nyāya*) has no application.

Because it would be a mere partial element and because it would be fruitless, even if it were stated, it would not be performed; whereas when the whole is transferred, the result occurs. Therefore, by implication, there is a transfer of the whole, so that the instruction regarding the entirety will be meaningful. Or rather, another distinct rite characterized by the full-moon sacrifice is enjoined—this is the injunction of a separate action; this arises from the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), and thus it sublates the syntactical connection (*vākya*). Therefore, it is a distinct rite.
But time [is determined] from the absence of a specific rule; this would be the case. (Siddhānta 2)
There is no authoritative evidence that this [word] denotes a different ritual action.
There is direct perception that it denotes the ritual action under discussion; and that which is supported by authoritative evidence is what should be accepted.
Furthermore, it is improper for a single word to have multiple meanings. When the primary sense is possible, the word "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is used in the sense of "dharma."
It would have to be assumed [as a separate rite]. Furthermore, its form is not perceived, because no description of its form is given;

thus, it is not a different ritual action. Therefore, by means of a well-known name, there should be a reference to the ritual action under discussion for the purpose of prescribing a time. And because it possesses a result, there is a displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the entire [action], specifically for the Brāhmaṇa.
And the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is likewise. As for the claim that direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*), it is said in response to this:

"His deity is this"—thus there is for the sacrificer, who is a person, a connection with the deity.

He will indeed prepare the oblation for Prajāpati, or for Viṣṇu. Therefore, its being "dedicated to Agni-Soma" (agnīṣomīyatva) is not the reason for its status as such in its later state. It cannot be said that [the term] *aindrāgna* [is used here]; for a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) does not arise from a word that is expectant of further syntactic connection. Or rather, there should be simultaneity because of the scriptural statement. (Uttara-pakṣa)
Bhāṣya: This is not so; the modifications (*vikṛti*) would not have the time of burning as their time; rather, they would have the immediate time (*sadyaskāla*).

Why? Because there is this scriptural statement: "He who is about to sacrifice with the *iṣṭi*, the animal sacrifice, the *soma* sacrifice, or the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, he [should do so] on the full moon day or the new moon day."
"Or one should sacrifice"—this statement refers to the sacrifice together with its constituent parts (sāṅga). Therefore, the full-moon sacrifice [is to be performed] with its constituent parts.

(5.4.3) This is the section concerning the postponement of the modifications of the *sānnāyya* and other offerings after the *Soma* sacrifice.
The modifications of the *sānnāyya* and the *āgniṣomīya* [animal sacrifice] after the *soma* sacrifice follow the model of the archetype (*prakṛti*). 25.
Commentary: Here, the modifications (*vikāra*) of the *sānnāyya* and the modifications of the *agnīṣomīya* are the examples.

First, regarding the modifications of the *sānnāyya*, such as "the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) is the animal-sacrifice," and "a Brāhmaṇa desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarccasa*) should offer a cake on eleven potsherds made of *śyāmāka* grain to Agni and Soma in the spring"—these and others are the cases. In this regard, there is a doubt: are these...?

[Should they be] before or after the Soma? Or rather, after? What is the prima facie view? That they should be both before and after, because no specific distinction is perceived. This being the position, we reply: "They should be after the Soma," for their archetype (*prakṛti*) is after the Soma, and by the rule of extension (*codaka*), these [rites] must also follow it.

The *jaṅgha* should be from the Soma [sacrifice]. From what part of the Soma sacrifice is it for the *sānnāyya*? From the statement: "One who has not sacrificed with Soma should perform the *sānnāyya*. Regarding the *agnīṣomīya* [offering] as well, there is the statement: "A Brāhmaṇa is connected to Agni by deity; having sacrificed with Soma, he becomes so.
Therefore, at that time, he should subsequently offer that very *paurṇamāsa* oblation"; thus, then, it belongs to both deities.
Since this is so, its modification also ought to occur after the Soma sacrifice.

Bhāṣya: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma"—thus and so forth is the traditional scripture (samāmnāya). In this regard, there is a doubt: is heaven subordinate and the ritual act primary, or is the ritual act subordinate and heaven primary? Why is there this doubt? Because here both "one desiring heaven" and "should sacrifice" are specified.
— thus it is also stated. Here, a relationship between the sacrifice and the desire for heaven is understood;
and regarding that relationship, an inquiry arises as to whether the sacrifice is connected as the means (*sādhana*) or as the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
In this regard, if a sacrifice is enjoined as something to be performed for a person desiring heaven—

namely, "A sacrifice is to be performed by one who desires heaven"— it is understood that it is accomplished for one characterized by the desire for heaven; thus, the desire for heaven is taught there as being directed toward the sacrifice by the person.
Therefore, that [result] is accomplished for him and not for anyone else— namely, "he who desires heaven, that person is able to accomplish the sacrifice. Now,
if the desire of one who desires heaven is enjoined as something to be performed, then [the sacrifice is] qualified by that [desire].

The sense of "that which is to be done" (kartavyatā) is accepted as the sacrifice being the means for the agent. And this [sacrifice] is understood from this uttered sentence to serve the purpose of both—namely, that "either the sacrifice is to be performed, or the desire is to be attained. Yet this cannot occur simultaneously; for when there is the desire, there is not yet the sacrifice, and when there is the sacrifice, there is not yet the desire, due to the difference in the modes of verbal expression (vacanavyakti).
Saṃjaya has been reborn;
for him who desires heaven, there is [the attainment of] the sixfold [perfections]. (Note: *seksaprati* is an additional reading found in the Pā0 So0 Pu0.)
The statement is due to a difference in devotion; therefore, "tasmāt" (therefore) is the reading in the Kāśmīra and Kṛṣṇa manuscripts.

Likewise, there is this other doubt: is heaven (*svarga*) pleasure (*prīti*), or is it a substance (*dravya*)? If heaven is a substance, then the ritual action (*karman*) is primary and the substance is subordinate. But if heaven is pleasure, then the sacrifice (*yāga*) is subordinate and heaven is primary. Why is there this doubt? Because here, desire (*kāma*) is neither subordinate nor primary.
Or rather, there is no such scriptural statement; rather, only a general relationship with the sacrifice is understood from this [text],
whereas the fact that the substance serves the purpose of the ritual action follows from its inherent nature, and the fact that human effort serves the purpose of the fruit [follows] likewise.
What, then, is the established position?—that heaven (*svarga*) is subordinate (*guṇataḥ*) and the ritual action (*karman*) is primary (*pradhānataḥ*).
Regarding this, they explain as follows: "Heaven is a substance (*dravya*). How is this understood?
For all words, common worldly usage (*laukika-prayoga*) is the means for knowing their meaning.

And in that worldly usage, the word *svarga* is observed to denote a substance: "Fine silken garments are *svarga*; sandalwood is *svarga*; women of eight years are *svarga*. Whatever substance is pleasurable is expressed by the word *svarga*. Therefore, because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), we conclude that "pleasurable substance is *svarga*. If it is argued that "the application of the word [to these things] is based on analogy," we say no.
Because there is nothing in the world comparable to it by which this might be illustrated, therefore it is not an illustration. [The opponent says: "Heaven is a substance.
[The author] says: "No; pleasure is heaven, not a substance, because of the deviation [of the former from that definition]."

For that very same substance, at a certain stage, the word "heaven" (svarga) does not denote it; yet, at no stage does it fail to denote pleasure (prīti). Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), it is understood that the word "heaven" applies to pleasure.
—Thus [it is asked]. Why?
Because it is not the case that the word "heaven" (svarga) is a denoter of pleasure.
Because it is a qualifier; that which is a qualifier is not denoted by the word itself.

For example, in the expression "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*), the word for the person is occasioned by the staff; the fact that the staff serves as an instrument for the action of that substance is understood from its own nature, as is the fact that the effort of the person is for the sake of pleasure (Kātyāyana-vārttika).
Puṇya-pāṭhaḥ (The Recitation of Merit)
Having reflected thus, he said: "Indeed, no one at all reads this *Kāśikāvṛtti*."
[Page 674] Bhāṣya: It is the sign, not the denoted object.
Thus, this word "svarga" (heaven) does not denote joy itself, but rather denotes the means for attaining joy.

"Now, it is well known in the world that the word 'heaven' (svarga) refers to a specific region—a place where there is neither heat nor cold, neither hunger nor thirst, neither discontent nor fatigue;
only those who have performed meritorious deeds go there after death, and no others. To this, it is replied: if...

In that regard, some go there after exerting themselves and return from there without having produced [the result]; therefore, that place is of such a nature that it is perceived directly (*pratyakṣa*), and not known through inference (*anumāna*).
[Objection: But surely other perfected beings (*siddha*) have seen it, and they have come here.

If this is argued, we reply: there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that, namely, that "there exist such established things, and having seen them, they would have spoken. Therefore, a place of such a kind simply does not exist.

"But surely, it is understood from common worldly experience, from narratives, and from the Veda that heaven is a place of such a kind. That is not so; because humans have no connection with such a place, their word is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*). Narratives, too, are composed by humans.
It is not to be disregarded. Even the Vedic [passage] concerning those in heaven does not indeed have an injunction as its primary purport;

rather, it forms a single syntactical unit with another injunction and has praise as its purport. Although such a place might exist by implication from the mention of exclusive happiness, nevertheless, for our position...

There is no contradiction; the word "heaven" (svarga) is a means for producing pleasure. Since there is no worldly usage [of the word] for that particular place, how could the word "heaven" be its designator?

When heaven is a substance characterized by pleasure, then we say: "In the connection of substances with an action, there is a relationship as a subordinate factor (guṇa)"—for it is heard [in scripture] that "the sacrifice is to be performed here."

For one who desires heaven, there must necessarily be a relationship between heaven and the sacrifice; therein, the substance is the "existent" (bhūta) and the action is the "to-be-accomplished" (bhavya). It is logical that the existent serves the purpose of the to-be-accomplished, because its utility is perceptible;
however, it is not the case that the to-be-accomplished serves the purpose of the existent, for in that case, the perceptible benefit would be abandoned.

"But how, again, is it understood that the sacrifice is enjoined as something to be performed? If no one goes there having remembered it, nor returns from there having performed it, then that place is not directly perceived as being thus enjoined; therefore, it is not apprehended through inference. (This is the reading in the Kāśikā-kārikā-puṭa.)

Bhāṣya: If it is argued that from this sentence the necessity of performing even the desire (*kāma*) is understood, we reply:
the necessity of the desire is known from the sentence, whereas the necessity of the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is known from direct audition (*śruti*).

Moreover, direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is more authoritative than syntactical connection (*vākya*). Therefore, this is the meaning: "One desiring heaven should perform the sacrifice"—that is, the sacrifice must be performed by one who desires heaven.
Furthermore, that which brings happiness is to be performed, while that which brings suffering is not to be performed; and the Veda declares this [sacrifice] to be "to be performed."

Therefore, it is understood that sacrifice will have happiness as its fruit; however, it is accomplished for one who has the desire, and not for anyone else. Thus, the desire for heaven is subordinate to the sacrifice, just as the desire for wealth is subordinate to every ritual action; by that [desire], [the sacrifice is performed].
In the case of [the injunction] "one strives to bring the sacrificial substance," this is restricted by a visible means; however, here, one is restricted solely by the desire for heaven.

Just as that [desire], having been obtained, is subordinate, so too, being thus, it is restricted by a visible means alone, not by an unseen benefit (*adṛṣṭa*). Therefore, by means of the subordinate desire for heaven, one will strive toward the substance of heaven in order to accomplish the sacrifice. Even if it were by an unseen means, there would still be no fault.
Sūtra:
But it is not effective, because it is for that purpose. (Siddhānta)
But by the word "tu" (but/however), the [opponent's] position is set aside. Therefore, they describe it thus for now:

"Heaven is pleasure. Why? Because you have stated: "The word 'heaven' applies to a substance qualified by pleasure. If this is so, then it ought to apply first to pleasure itself; for the word does not deviate from that, whereas it does deviate from [the substance].

Regarding the substance: that very substance which is the means of pleasure and for which the word "heaven" (svarga) stands as a designation, when it no longer serves as a means of pleasure, it is no longer denoted by the word "heaven.
Therefore, [the word] expresses pleasure. As for what was said—that it is like the word "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin)—[that is not the case].

Just as that [word "staff"] also, once the staff has been perceived through the word, produces a cognition of the person possessing the staff (daṇḍin)— since the word "staff" is internally present therein and is the designator of the staff— here, however,
the word "heaven" (svarga) alone is the designator of the pleasure.
If it is argued that the word [denotes] pleasure, then the sacrifice would be subordinate and pleasure the primary object. Why?
Because human effort is for that purpose; for a person exerts effort for the sake of pleasure, and therefore [the sacrifice is not the end].

In the Mīmāṃsā system, it is understood that pleasure (*prīti*) is the means of accomplishing the sacrifice (*yāga*). For it is substance (*dravya*) that is the means of accomplishing the sacrifice, not [pleasure].

Since sacrifice occurs without [inhering in] a substance—because the word *yajati* (he sacrifices) applies to the action involving a substance and a deity—the sacrifice takes place even in the absence of pleasure (*prīti*). Furthermore, if the sacrifice were not for the sake of pleasure, it would be an ineffective action and would not reach one who accomplishes it; for that which has pleasure as its purpose is what is accomplished, and nothing else.

[Objection: "But surely the sacrifice is heard [in scripture] as something to be performed. [Reply: It is said: True, it is heard as something to be performed; however, the desire (kāma) is also understood as something to be performed. For, by direct statement (śruti), the sacrifice [is enjoined].
[The injunction] pertains to desire by virtue of the sentence; nor does it apply to both [desire and heaven], because that would entail a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). It is replied:

although the sacrifice is heard as something to be performed, nevertheless it is not to be performed [as an end in itself]. That which bestows pleasure is to be performed, but the sacrifice bestows pain; therefore, it is not to be performed according to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), [since it is directly perceived as painful].
And it is a giver of suffering. [The opponent argues: "Because of the statement that it ought to be performed, it becomes a giver of happiness through inference.
It is replied: And inference is not a valid means of knowledge because it contradicts perception.
Therefore, the sacrifice is not to be performed if it does not have pleasure as its purpose.
"Now, it will be connected with another statement of the result"—this is said [by the opponent]. We reply:

even when being connected, that which is not itself enjoined as a duty is not understood to possess a result merely by virtue of its proximity. Therefore, so that it may not be purposeless, the attainment of heaven must be the thing to be performed (*kartavyatā*).

It is understood that human effort is qualified by the sacrifice; thus, the sacrifice would be its instrument (*karaṇa*). Therefore, it has been correctly stated—that the sacrifice is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) and heaven is the primary object (*pradhānabhūta*).
— Sūtra: And because of the connection with each respective object, for there is indeed a relation through action; therefore, it should be an instruction regarding the action. (Yukti) || 3 ||
Bhāṣya:

We do not assert that the sacrifice is subordinate merely out of fear of its being purposeless; rather, the sacrifice is enjoined as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the purpose known as heaven. [Objection: "But surely the sacrifice is enjoined by the Vedic text as something to be performed (*kartavya*). [Reply: True, it is so; however, [otherwise] there would be purposelessness (*ānarthakya*).

But it is not so; for if the sacrifice were not enjoined as leading to heaven, then a person desiring heaven, even though enjoined to perform that [sacrifice], would be rendered purposeless since it would be fruitless. In that case, [regarding] this...
[Page 677]

[Commentary: [If it were so,] there would be the futility of the instruction; furthermore, since the two things being enjoined would be mutually unrelated, there would be the contingency of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) does not enjoin its own meaning; rather, it is merely referred to (*uddiśyate*). In that case, the duty to perform [the action] belongs to the desire understood from the sentence.

It is understood that the sacrifice possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇatā*). And thus, there will be no contradiction with direct perception regarding the necessity of performing the sacrifice. Therefore, "there must be an instruction regarding the action; the action is enjoined with respect to heaven, not heaven with respect to the action. [Objection: "What follows if heaven is not enjoined? [Response: This follows from it: for a subordinate element (*guṇa*) cannot be either unenjoined or obtained through implication. Therefore, heaven [is the object].
"Primarily [the result], and the action [is the means] by way of its quality"—thus it is said.
Furthermore, "He for whom heaven is desired should perform the sacrifice"—this seems incoherent, as one desires one thing while performing another. Now, if...
"It is held that from this [connection], 'therefore one comes to be in heaven,' it is understood"—
no,
for those for whom the word is the means of valid knowledge, comprehension without the word is not logical.
We understand this relationship from the sentence itself; for example, if one were to say, "One who desires to fetch wood should go to the forest," one would say this:
"The capacity of going to the forest for the purpose of fetching wood is perceived there by another means of knowledge."
— thus [it is argued].

"Now, if it is thought: 'Let there not be the futility of the instruction; therefore, presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) will arise'—" we reply: this capacity does not belong to the futility of the instruction, namely, that the pleasure resulting from sacrifice would be understood as its fruit without a statement of the fruit. Granted...
Let its lack of purpose be granted; it never acquires efficacy.

For indeed, the taking up of water by one desiring to burn does not—merely because it is useless for burning—produce a power of burning in it. Or rather, a sacrifice is enjoined for one who desires heaven.
—Thus, by resorting to an alternative interpretation, this [word] will possess meaningfulness.

[Objection: "But even in the other view, the sacrifice is enjoined for one who desires heaven; heaven does not arise from the sacrifice. [Reply: This is not so; for in that view, indeed, for one who is seeking heaven...

The performance (anuṣṭhāna) follows the sacrifice; it is prescribed as the means to that [sacrifice]—thus there is no fault in the Bhāṣya. If it is argued that there is no statement that "that performance is for the sake of heaven," [we reply: performance occurs for the sake of a desired object, and for one who desires heaven, heaven [is that desired object].

It is desired that the inclusion of the qualification "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) is precisely for the purpose of specifying a particular performance of that [sacrifice]; thus, it is faultless. Therefore, there is an instruction regarding the act of sacrifice for one who desires heaven;

hence, heaven is primary and the ritual action is secondary—this is the statement "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) with reference to one who desires heaven. Thus, this definition of eligibility (*adhikāra-lakṣaṇa*) is established.
It occurs. (Sūtra 1.1.1)
The section concerning the eligibility of humans alone for sacrifices and other rites.
Since action is for the sake of its fruit, the scripture must apply to all who are qualified. (Pūrvapakṣa)
The Bhāṣya states this: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa; one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma"—and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt:
is this stated with reference to every being whatsoever, or with reference only to one who is capable? What is the prima facie view? That it applies to all.
Because there is no distinction. [Objection: "But trees and the like do not desire anything;

how could they have the qualification [for ritual action]? [Reply: We say: let it be that insentient things lack it, but one might indeed say "one should sacrifice" with reference to animals. [Objection: "But even animals..."
They do not desire anything at all; so we say. Yet they do desire happiness, for it is observed thus: those tormented by heat approach the shade, and those afflicted by cold approach the sunlight.

[Objection: "But surely animals perceive immediate results; they do not seek results that occur at a later time, yet Vedic rituals have results that occur at a later time. [Reply: It is said in response—

Even at other times, people are seen desiring results— for instance, we observe those who fast on the fourteenth day and those who [fast] on the eighth day for the sake of [attaining] the power of a hawk. Nor can there be a suspicion of disease in these cases,
because they occur with fixed causes and because even those who have not abstained from food are seen at that time.
[Page 679] Bhāṣya:

Because they are observed at other times even though they have the same food; and there are indicative marks (*liṅga*) in the Veda—such as "The gods indeed performed a sacrificial session" (*devā vai satram āsata*)—which demonstrate the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of deities, sages, and trees.

"An objection is raised: surely they are not entitled [to perform the rite] because they are unable to carry out the injunction in its entirety. The reply is: some are indeed able to perform the sacrifice;

therefore, injunctions such as 'one should sacrifice' (*yajeta*) will apply to those who are capable. However, the statements regarding the *viṣṇukrama* steps and so forth will not apply to those who are incapable. In that case, one for whom the *viṣṇukrama* steps and the like have not been prescribed will perform only the sacrifice. Who is he?"

What is the fault? Even the "possession of property" exists for them through metaphorical usage, as in "the village of the gods," "the village of elephants," or "the village of the bull"—it certainly exists. Therefore, even non-humans who are capable have the right [to perform sacrifices].
Or rather, because of the connection with the Vedic text, the injunction is understood as pertaining to the agent himself. (Sūtra 5)

The word "but" (vā) excludes the alternative view. It is not the case that animals and the like also possess the qualification [for ritual action]. Then for whom does it apply? For one who is capable of performing the entire rite in its completeness. And these, such as animals and so forth, are not able to perform it in its entirety.
In order to bring about [the result] through action, therefore, action is not the means for their happiness; for how could that which cannot be performed be a means?

It is not [the case] for the gods, because there is no other deity [to whom they could offer], for it is impossible to perform a renunciation directed toward oneself—indeed, that would not even be a renunciation—and it is not [the case] for the seers.
Due to the absence of a common lineage (*śrārṣeya*), those such as Bhṛgu and others do not share the same *gotra* with [other] Bhṛgus and others;
nor is their capacity perceived through direct observation.
Furthermore, the commentary stating that "Bhṛgu and others are of the same *gotra* as Bhṛgu and others" is incorrect, for our [scriptural] tradition is based on the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
For the Mīmāṃsakas, because even for Bhṛgu there was the possibility of a prior birth from another [source], it is possible that before that he was likewise [born] in this very manner;
thus, the status of being a descendant of a Ṛṣi (ṛṣibhārgavatva) indeed exists, and therefore the objection regarding the lack of qualification for the Ṛṣis is not tenable.

As for the claim that "the gods have no qualification because they lack a physical form," this argument is also improper for those who maintain that the deity is intended to be the word itself. This other [objection] can be refuted.
Moreover, animals do not seek results that bear fruit at a later time, for they desire what is immediate.
[They] desire [the results]. But has it not been said: "We observe animals who seek results at a later time; dogs and hawks fast on the fourteenth and eighth days"? It is replied:
they do not fast seeking results in another birth. "How is this known?"

Because they lack the study of the Vedas—those who study the Veda know this: "Having performed this action, one obtains this fruit in the hereafter"—but these people do not study the Veda, nor the Smṛti scriptures, nor do they learn it from others; therefore, [it is] not [so].
They know the Dharma. How could those who are ignorant perform it? Therefore, they do not fast for the sake of Dharma.

[Objection: "For what purpose, then, is their fasting? [Reply: It is said: because of illness, they have no appetite. [Objection: "But how can there be illness at a fixed time? [Reply: It is said: *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "ucyate," indicating the response continues beyond the supplied excerpt.*
Furthermore, there are diseases that occur at fixed times, such as those recurring every third or fourth day;
therefore, human beings possess the qualification [for Vedic rites]. Moreover, animals do not possess ownership of property, for they are never seen to utilize property according to their own will;

thus, they lack mastery over wealth. As for the expressions "the procession of the gods" or "the procession of elephants," that is merely figurative. Therefore, animals also do not possess the qualification [for Vedic rites].
Furthermore, those indicative marks—such as "The gods indeed performed a sacrificial session" (*devā vai satram āsata*) and so forth—are explanatory passages (*arthavādas*);

they serve the purpose of praising the injunction (*vidhi*). For in all of them, there exists another injunction, and an injunction does not form a single syntactical unit with another injunction, because their modes of expression differ.

This is indeed praise: namely, that the sacred texts (*śruti*) are so powerful that even the gods remain satisfied with their duties, even animals possess proximate consciousness, and even insentient trees [attain results]; how much more so, then, learned human beings?
"But surely those who are not qualified for the Viṣṇukrama and other rites will simply perform the sacrifice;

for even Indra cannot abandon the sacrifice merely by uttering the word 'Indra. Therefore, this commentary intends that the deity is indeed for the sake of the rite (*cartha*)," so says the *Mantraratna*.
Nor do they understand it from their teachers; thus [it is stated] in the Kāśmīra and Krīta manuscripts.

[Page 681] Bhāṣya: It is not so; the qualities (guṇas) are taught in relation to the sacrifice, not in relation to the agent. Therefore, if the sacrifice were performed merely as such, there would be a deficiency (vaiguṇya), and thus there would be no connection with the fruit. "But how [is it that they are taught] in relation to the sacrifice?"

[If it is asked: "How are they taught?"—[the answer is: falling from the proximity of the word for sacrifice (*yāga*), which has a requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā-ākāṅkṣā*), they are able to satisfy that requirement.

Otherwise, if the words expressing qualities were merely enjoining the agents, the statement of the fruit—which would have its requirement unsatisfied—would be entirely purposeless. Furthermore, there would have been a syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*) with the statement of the fruit; in that case, because of the mutual requirement, the sentence would have been interrupted. Now, this very [statement]...

"The sentence will prescribe the qualified action for those who are capable, and the unqualified [action] for those who are incapable. This is not so; because there would be a conflict between the two capacities in the utterance of the *sallat* [the specific injunction], the sentence would be split, for it is indeed expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) with respect to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Therefore, there is an instruction for the sacrifice with its constituent parts (*sāṅga-yāga*), and no instruction for a sacrifice devoid of its constituent parts (*niraṅga-yāga*). Consequently, [the entitlement belongs] only to human beings.
Regarding the heading "adhikāraḥ":

Commentary:
"In the case of an unborn embryo (*garbha*), there is the designation of 'feticide' (*bhrūṇahatyā*); therefore, by killing an unborn embryo, one becomes a feticide.
A feticide is the worst of evildoers; he is the slayer of one who benefits both worlds.

A *bhrūṇahan* is a destroyer of sacrifice; he is one who commits the killing of the means of sacrifice. Therefore, they designate the sacrifice by the word *bhrūṇa*, for it either sustains (*bibharti*) everything or brings about prosperity (*bhūti*).
Thus, a *bhrūṇahan* is one who destroys the sacrifice, because [the sacrifice] is connected with merit (*puṇya*).
The restatement is as follows: if an embryo that has not yet been discerned is killed, it is possible that a male might be killed;
since the one authorized for the sacrifice would then be killed, the killing of the sacrifice would constitute the sin of *bhrūṇahatyā* (the killing of an embryo).
Otherwise, if there were authorization for both [male and female], then [it would apply] even when [the sex] is discerned.

Furthermore, if it were not understood [as a specific gender], there would be a "sacrificial slaughter" (yajñavadha); in that case, the mention of the ununderstood would be considered meaningless. Therefore, the case-ending expressing the masculine gender is intended to be significant.

Similarly, having killed an Ātreyī, one becomes a bhrūṇahan (a killer of an embryo). They say that an Ātreyī is one who has a fetus; she is called "Ātreyī" because "atra" (in the womb) exists in her. Therefore, it is understood that there is qualification for men as well; just as in the case of "one should sacrifice an animal," only a male animal is sacrificed because of the specification of gender, so it should be seen here as well. This being the position reached, we reply: "But Bādarāyaṇa [holds] it is the class (jāti), because there is no distinction; therefore, it should apply to women too, since the meaning of the class is not different. The word "but" (tu) in the Bhāṣya sets aside the previous position. It is not the case that only the male has the qualification; rather, Bādarāyaṇa considered the female (jāti) to be qualified as well. And he says: "But what about this [word] 'tu'? (Cā0 Mo0).

"Is it understood that the genus (*jāti*) is expressed by the word, such that it is the one under discussion? We certainly do not say that the word here is governing (*adhikāraka*) because it denotes a genus;

The word [is the authority]; by that characteristic, the one entitled [to perform the sacrifice] is expressed by the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*).

In this regard, the characteristic is common to both woman and man. Therefore, it is understood from the word that both women and men are entitled. In that case, by what [means] is the entitlement determined?

If it is argued that even if [the word] were meaningless, there would still be no absence of the cessation of the individual (khīniṣṭatti), [we reply: in the case of a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṅkhyā*), there is the abandonment of one's own primary meaning (*svārthahāni*), the assumption of another meaning (*parārthakalpanā*), and the sublation of what was already established (*prāptabādha*). Yet, there is no meaninglessness here, because it serves the purpose of specification (*nirdeśārthatvāt*). Therefore, the individual (*vyakti*) should also be understood, because the meaning of the genus (*jāti*) is qualified [by the individual].
Because it is enjoined, it is according to the scriptural statement.

In this case, this secondary derivative (taddhita) suffix has arisen from the word *atra*; for a secondary derivative arises only from words that possess semantic capacity (*samartha*), and the word *atra* lacks such capacity.

And since it says, "it remains," it is understood all the more clearly that the word *akṣa* denotes a man. Therefore, the entitlement belongs to two men.
