Otherwise, an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) would have to be postulated. Therefore, for the sake of the incidental fruit, another person desiring heaven should perform the sacrifice for another.
Not so, because of its eternity. (Ābhāsa-nirṇaya) || 10 ||

Bhāṣya: This is not so; for that very person who obtains the fruit of the primary action, it is also fitting that he should obtain the incidental fruit as well. In this way, the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is performed for one's own purpose; indeed, there is no distinction in the self-interest of the *ādhāna* whether it pertains to the primary fruit or the incidental fruit.
Everything indeed ought to be applicable to one who possesses faith, and [the status of] being obligatory (*nitya*) would be contradicted;

for if one should sacrifice desiring long life and so forth, then it is not obligatory, and if it is obligatory, then one does not desire long life and so forth. Therefore, the established principle should not be set aside, nor...
And the person is enjoined as the primary agent, whereas his singularity is intended [only] because it is subordinate;
therefore, one alone should sacrifice.
Sūtrabhāṣya [Page 714]
If it is argued that the action is likewise [momentary], (Ābhāsvara) || 11 ||

Now, as for what was stated—that it shows the sacrifice for two or many [sacrificers]: "Since you two are the lords of heaven," one should employ this as the *pratipad* for two sacrificers; "These drops of ours, O Indra," one should employ this as the *pratipad* for many sacrificers—this injunction regarding the *pratipad* in a ritual involving two sacrificers or many sacrificers is [an instance of] *karman*.
If it should be argued that "it would be so," that must be refuted.
Not so, because of inherence. (Ābhāsa-nirṇaya) || 12 ||

Bhāṣya: This is not so; for a combined rite is indeed found to exist with two sacrificers and with many sacrificers by virtue of a scriptural injunction, just as in the case of the Ahīna sacrifices. In those cases, the prescription of the Pratipad will be meaningful. Therefore, "one should sacrifice"—so it is said. (6.2.2)
The section concerning the rule of completion even for one who has begun a rite performed out of desire.
But it should be restricted by one's own inclination, because the commencement [of an action] is caused by the performance [of that inclination].
13 || (Siddhānta) ||

In the Bhāṣya: "One desiring offspring should sacrifice," "One desiring a village should sacrifice"—thus ritual acts are traditionally handed down. In this regard, there is a doubt: must that which has been commenced be completed as a matter of obligation (*niyogataḥ*), or may it be abandoned or left unfinished according to one's own will? What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? It should be completed as a matter of obligation. Why? Because it is heard [in scripture] in this way:
"—let Kāma sacrifice this"—thus they teach the meaning of that verb: "it expresses [the action] from its commencement until its completion.
From the beginning up to the final conclusion—this much is the specific operation that constitutes its meaning, and not [meanings] such as "cooking" or "giving," for in those cases...
"Only the mere existence of the action is indicated; it is not something that must be commenced and brought to completion"—thus says the Bhāṣya.
And thus even worldly people understand the meaning of the verb; in that regard, there is no... [Page 715]... [text fragment].
It is understood that at the outset, human effort is enjoined;
for since they do not necessarily begin what is enjoined, but rather necessarily complete it, therefore neither beginning nor completion is the meaning of the word. What then? Completion.

The meaning of the word is the completion [of the action], because the commencement has already reached its purpose. Therefore, it is understood that completion is the meaning of the word. If that [completion] is the meaning of the word, it is enjoined as something to be performed; however, there is no statement of what is to be performed regarding the commencement. Therefore, it is not [the meaning].

The undertaking is mandatory, but the completion is not necessarily so. Therefore, even if the desire for the fruit ceases once the rite has been commenced, or if one obtains the fruit, in that state as well, the completion of what has been commenced must certainly be performed.
(Bhāṣya)
"But surely the object of desire is the purpose, and that is expressed as something to be performed. This is not so;
for while that [purpose] constitutes the meaning of the sentence, the fact that the sacrifice itself must be performed is understood through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).

Therefore, a sacrifice commenced by one desiring a village must be brought to completion; the mention of the desire for a village and so forth serves as the *nimitta* (the occasioning cause). When an occasioning cause has arisen, that which is to be performed is prescribed; even when that occasioning cause has ceased, it must still be performed. It is enjoined that the commencement must be completed; thus, even when the occasioning cause has ceased, it remains to be done, for what has ceased does not become non-arisen, and its arising is the occasioning cause itself.

It is not a mere entity. Therefore, even when the desire for the fruit has ceased, what has been commenced must be brought to completion; for the motive for an action is its commencement, and that [motive] persists until completion.
Sūtra: Or rather, there is no fixed rule because of the desire for results, as in the case of that which has not been commenced. (Pūrvapakṣa)
The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position. [The answer is: "There is no fixed rule," or rather, "there is. Why?

Because of the desire for a result (*phalārthitvāt*). For one who desires a result—that is, one who wishes to bring about a result—an alternative means is prescribed, not a mandatory duty (*kartavyatā*); for if that were being prescribed, it would belong either to the result or to the sacrifice.

Or it might be so; however, the result need not be stated at all, for one need not be instructed that "that which someone desires must be performed by him," as in the case of the Veda: "This must be done by me.
[Page 716]

[The opponent says: "Thus [the agent knows the end], but he does not know the means; he desires that [means], and this is taught: 'Sacrifice is the means'—it is accomplished by means of sacrifice. But there is no obligation to perform the sacrifice itself, because that would contradict perception; for the sacrifice is visibly painful. If, however, it is another thing that is to be accomplished by means of the sacrifice, then there is no contradiction; [but] regarding the obligation to perform the sacrifice...

The fruit is desirable, yet there is no authoritative basis for its being something that must be performed. Furthermore, instruction regarding what is to be done pertains to matters that are possible and so forth; therefore, the sacrifice is not something that must necessarily be performed.

Rather, having referred to that which is desired by one who seeks the fruit, the injunction prescribes the sacrifice as the means to achieve it according to how it is established; consequently, it does not necessarily have to be completed, just as—

That which has not been commenced need not necessarily be commenced; likewise, that which has been commenced need not necessarily be brought to completion. As for the claim that "the meaning of a sentence is sublated by direct statement," it has already been stated that where the meaning of the direct statement is impossible, there the meaning of the sentence is accepted.
Therefore, there is no fixed rule.
Or rather, it is a restriction [of the agent], because the agent is caused by that; therefore, it must be the cause of that [action].
15 || (Uddyota) ||
The Bhāṣya says:

For the commencement is indeed the cause of the completion. How so? "That" would be the reason for the agent. What is the reason? It is the possession of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatā*). For the learned do not censure one who completes a task of this kind once it has been commenced; they do not reproach him as being a person who merely begins but does not finish.

"He is not to be associated with"—thus there is the fault of being censured by the learned. Therefore, having begun [the rite], one must complete it. [The opponent] asks: "But for what reason do the learned censure him? It is replied: "Why should we concern ourselves with the reason for their censure? (6.2.3).
And those who are opposed to the root [scripture] without independence are not learned; they are indeed unlearned.

If they were to deliberate [thus], O Dimākhela, it would not be possible for all the teachers—who possess minds intent on dharma—to accept what is inauspicious and contrary to power; for from the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), a Smṛti text in the form of censure is inferred, and from that Smṛti, a Śruti is inferred, stating:
"A rite prescribed by the revealed scripture must necessarily be completed. Furthermore, there is a statement of the Taittirīyas that has no other purpose:
Having proceeded, he prescribes a prayer for the purpose of non-completion: "He who is in a state of non-attainment is indeed abandoned by the deities.
[Page 717]
The section concerning the lack of a restrictive rule regarding the completion of worldly undertakings once they have been commenced.
In the world, actions are like the Vedas; from that comes the knowledge of the Supreme Person.
Bhāṣya-sūtra-bhāṣya (The Commentary on the Sūtras of the Bhāṣya)
(Pūrvapakṣa) ||

Someone has begun a house, or a cart, or a chariot; his desire for the fruit has ceased, or he obtains the fruit. In this regard, there is a doubt: must it necessarily be completed by him, or may it be abandoned according to his will?

What is established?—Actions of this kind in the world, having been commenced, must be brought to completion; just as those that are Vedic, so too must these necessarily be completed. Why? Because "therefrom arises knowledge of the person"; from that, knowledge of that person ought to arise. Why? From scripture (*śāstra*); for the practice of those [who follow the tradition] is handed down in scripture, and therein the activity of deities is accepted—namely, "these deities are in the eastern direction, and these in the others"—if the activity of the deities is indeed established by scripture.
Just as there is censure by the learned when one has begun a work but not completed it, so it should be here as well.
And even in the case of an offense, they [should act] according to the scripture. (Yukti 17)

And regarding the transgression of those worldly [practices], an expiation scripture is traditionally taught by them: "When the *āra* is broken, the arm of Indra [is injured]; one should give much milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and feed Brāhmaṇas. Now, if the expiation were for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), it would not apply outside of the specific branch [of the Veda].
However, since it is for the purpose of avoiding an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga-parihārārtha*), it is understood that this [expiation] applies even to what is unmanifested (*avyākṛta*).

Having said this, "If one does not sacrifice, one should sacrifice with the Trai-dhātavyā [offering]; for one does not turn away from the deities," it is observed that even when the fruit is not attained, the completion of the rite must be performed, according to the rule: "If it should rain, one should offer only that much. This is to be kept in mind here from the *Tantraratna*.
"Just as Vedic rites must necessarily be brought to completion, so too is this [the case]"—this is the reading in the Cāṇḍāla-śoṣaka-puṇya manuscript;
thus, kaṃ saṃ...
In the manuscript of Kākī, the word "api" is not present.

[Page 718] But the attainment [of these practices] is without a scriptural basis; scripture would not be the originator [of them]. Therefore, since they are not already established, scripture must be understood as having purpose through its meaning. (Siddhānta Sūtra 18). The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position. We say that their "attainment" is "without a scriptural basis. You infer a scripture for this Smṛti.

"—there is no recollection (smṛti) without a scripture (śāstra), nor is the composition of those [texts] possible without recollection; therefore it is said: there is indeed a recollection here, namely, 'this sacrificial act, such as the *guhā* and so forth, becomes delightful'—but from this act, no visible result [is obtained]."
"Something"—that is to say: that beauty which exists can be known even without the *śāla* tree;
and having been known, it is remembered. Therefore, the *śāla* tree is not the object (*prakalpyam*) of this memory; for if it were not without the *śāla* tree, [the memory] would not arise.
The scripture would be rendered meaningful here; therefore, this [practice] is not what is taught in the scripture.
For the learned censure one who abandons that which has been half-performed according to the scriptural injunction, as well as that which relies upon a deity.
[Objection: But even here, deities have been accepted—such as "in this direction is this deity."

"It shall be requested from her"—so it is said. It is replied: the learned remember the deities as following the person, not the house; therefore, there is no fault. (6.2.4) Thus concludes the section. (6.2.4)
The section concerning the occurrence of an undesirable consequence when performing what is prohibited. (A certain principle).
In prohibitions, there should be an action because they lack an object; for those actions that have been prohibited are distinct from those that have no objects. (Pūrvapakṣa 18)
The Bhāṣya states:

For they teach this: "One should not eat garlic, nor leeks, nor onions. Regarding this, there is a doubt: should such things not be eaten by one who desires the fruit [of the ritual], while they may be eaten by one who is free from desire; or rather, are they forbidden by rule for everyone?

"Is it indeed to be avoided?"—this is the question. What is the prima facie conclusion? One who desires the fruit should not consume it; for one who does not desire it, there is no restriction. Why? Because this restriction is stated as "this must not be consumed," and when this is said, the following consequence arises:
[Page 719]
Adhyāya 2, Pāda 1.

645 Bhāṣya: Whether it be that "non-eating should be performed," or whether it be that "eating should not be performed," if it is accepted that "eating qualified by negation should be performed," then the suffix *tavya* enjoins eating by means of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), while the negative particle (*nañ*) negates it.

[The word "non-eating"] is a qualifier; and because of its function, the negative particle (*nañ*) is not connected with [the act of eating] as something to be performed. Now, if the meaning of the negative particle were what is to be performed, then it would be enjoined by means of a sentence (*vākya*); and while the verb "eats" (*bhakṣayati*) would be a qualifier for the negative particle, direct denotation (*śruti*) is more powerful than syntactical connection (*vākya*). Therefore, non-eating is what must be performed.
It is understood that non-eating is the absence of eating, and there is no obligation to perform that [absence].

Therefore, it is the mental activity involved therein that is taught here—namely, the means by which eating does not become qualified; first, there is a connection between the negative particle (*nañ*) and the verb "to eat" (*bhakṣayati*).

Next is the rule: just as in the case of the Prajāpati-vows, such as "One should not look at the rising sun," there is a fruit for one who performs them, but no fruit and no fault for one who does not perform them;
so it is here as well, because actions are distinct, action is not prohibited here.
Only non-action is being taught; for action is one thing—the eating that is being prohibited—while non-action is another, namely, a mental resolve.

But since their own scriptures possess purposefulness, the human goal is enjoined by them; because those two [the Veda and the Smṛti] do not share the same basis, there is a transgression of that injunction. (Siddhānta 20)

First, the rebuttal by way of description is stated: It is appropriate that in the case of the Prajāpati-vows, "by virtue of the meaningfulness of the scriptures, the human goal is enjoined"; for therein a restriction (*niyama*) is taught as something to be performed, and that which is to be performed results in auspiciousness, whereas that which is not...

That [act] which results in sin must be performed. But how is it that a restriction is enjoined as something to be performed regarding the Prajāpati-vows? It is said in reply: having introduced the subject with "his vow," the Prajāpati-vows are enumerated; and a "vow" is a mental act.

It is said: that resolve which is "I shall not do this"—what is that vow (*vrata*)? It is the mental activity that must be performed so that the looking [at the sun] does not occur, as in the injunction, "One should not look at the rising sun," and the maintenance thereof. In that regard:

Therefore, it must be understood that there exists a human purpose. And in this regard, with reference to these very [acts], the Bhāṣya says: "By this much one becomes joined with sin"—meaning, "by having performed this much, one remains unjoined with sin."

Now, in this case, "of those two" refers to their non-inherence; here, action is prohibited, but inaction is not being taught. For one who is eating a *kalaa* fruit does not [violate] the prohibitory injunction.

He does not transgress [the rule]; moreover, one who looks at the sun here does not transgress the injunction, for looking at it is not prohibited; rather, a restriction (niyama) is taught there, such that he who observes that restriction becomes connected with the fruit, whereas here it is prohibited.

[The prohibition of] *kalañja* and so forth. How is this understood? Because there is no statement here introduced by the phrase "his vow" (*tasya vratam*). Nor does the meaning of "it must not be eaten" consist of a mental operation; rather, by the word itself, "it must be eaten" (*bhakṣayitavyam*) signifies that eating is to be performed.

It is said: "No"—that is what is prohibited by the scripture itself. In this way, the well-known meaning is upheld; otherwise, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And when there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and figurative indication, the direct statement is the proper course, not the figurative indication. Therefore, in this case, there is a prohibition. It may be argued: "Granted that there is a prohibition, yet no fault is heard of here."

"Therefore, even that which is prohibited must be performed"—if this is argued, [we reply: no, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued, "Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is the authoritative evidence, because otherwise the instruction would result in being purposeless," we say: this is not so; for even a purposeless instruction is possible due to ignorance. Therefore, a fault need not be presumed. To this it is replied:
True, it need not be presumed, but it is already established. How? Immediately after this...

The learned (śiṣṭas) would avoid him, saying, "He is fallen from the fruits of ritual action"—and this is a great fault, that the learned avoid him. Therefore, one must not eat *kalañja* and such things as a matter of rule, just as one should not place a finger in the mouth of a serpent. In that regard:
Because one perceives a fault, one does not intentionally place a finger in a snake's mouth, nor does one step on a thorn with the foot; so it is with this case as well—thus [it is concluded]. (Ha.

Regarding the phrase "cāra pratiṣiddhaṃ nāma," the reading "na doṣo'tra śrūyate" is found in the *Kāśikā-vṛtti*. Furthermore, the view of the *Vārttika*— namely, "codanāyāṃ phalāśruteriti dve adhikaraṇe" (there are two sections [regarding the absence of mention of results] in the injunction)— should be considered here.
[Page 721] The section concerning the duties to be performed in the subsequent period for those who have not approached the Guru and so forth.
But when [certain rites] are enjoined with respect to that [initiation], they should proceed by virtue of birth. Sūtra 21.
Bhā. (touch) ||

In this context, the items prescribed by Smṛti serve as examples, as do the customary practices governed by established rules—such as, "The teacher is to be followed and saluted," and "One who has reached old age is to be met with rising and honored. Regarding these, there is a doubt: are these items for those who have merely been born, or for those who have been initiated (upanīta)? What is the prima facie view? They are for those who have merely been born, because the instruction is given without qualification. Why? Because they are enjoined upon the person (puruṣa).
And as soon as a person is born, these things [become his]. Therefore, regarding newborns, these are the objects—thus are the objects. This being the case, we reply:
Or rather, because they are equal to the Veda, they may proceed by means of an expedient. || 22 ||

Bhāṣya: "Or rather" (*api vā*) marks the rejection of the previous position. "They should proceed by means of [initiation]" (*upāyena pravarteran*); that is, they should proceed together with initiation (*upanayana*). This is because of their equality with the Veda; for the Smṛti is equal to the Veda, since it is stated (1.3.10) that the very same Vedic matters are what are remembered in the Smṛti. And those Vedic matters are prescribed as occurring after the time of initiation; these Smṛti matters are indeed Vedic, therefore they belong to the period following initiation. (6)

Thus, when there is a syntactical connection (*anvaya*) between the injunctive word and the word [denoting] meat, since the prohibition of the impulse toward eating—which is impelled by passion—is what is enjoined, that prohibition is not purposeless, as it serves to ward off falling into hell. This being the case, the heard [text] is not deficient; whereas in your position, an unmentioned mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) must be assumed, and for that purpose, even within the act of eating, an effort regarding a mere fragment of salt [would have to be postulated].

Therefore, one should also keep in mind the Nyāyamālā: "Consequently, the qualification for heaven belongs to one who desires it, but the qualification [for liberation] belongs to one who fears death."
[Page 722] The section concerning the obligation to perform the Agnihotra and other rites throughout one's entire life, even when the specific time for them has passed. (The case of the Agnihotra).
The practice [of meditation] is enjoined as a human goal because it is not subsidiary to ritual action. || 23 ||
(1 Ma Pū0) ||

The Bhāṣya states this: "As long as one lives, one should offer the Agnihotra; as long as one lives, one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—thus, a sacrifice for the sake of the person's purpose is enjoined, and it has been stated that this is not a repetition (abhyāsa) that is a subordinate part of the ritual action (karmaśeṣa). Now, a doubt arises here: what...?

Should the offering be performed continuously, or not continuously? What is the prima facie position? Because it is enjoined with reference to the person, it should be performed continuously; for this person [is enjoined]—thus it must be practiced continuously. [Objection: But it is heard in scripture that "the Agnihotra is to be offered at twilight" and "in the morning when dawn has broken," and "one should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsa on the full moon day, and with the Āmāvāsya on the new moon day. [Reply: This [scriptural statement] does not refer to the performance of all the constituent parts together.
The application [of this rule] is therefore that there is no fault when it is deficient by merely a matter of time.
In that case, since it is impossible [for the two to be simultaneous], it follows by implication [that they must occur sequentially]. (2nd Pūrvapakṣa)
Bhāṣya: This is not so, that one must offer [the oblation] thinking "offer, offer.
— Sūtra Bhāṣya.

It is said that one should offer the oblation in such a manner as one is able; yet it cannot be performed continuously, for one must necessarily attend to food and movement. Therefore, the oblation should be offered at times other than those incompatible with these activities.
They are not taught with respect to specific times. (Siddhānta) || 25 ||

This is not so; as for what was stated—that one must always offer during times not inconsistent with the purpose—this specific time is indeed heard in scripture: "The Agnihotra is to be offered at dusk, and in the morning when it has dawned. Likewise: "On the full moon day, [one should sacrifice] with the Paurṇamāsa [offering]."

"One should sacrifice; one should sacrifice with the New Moon [offering] on the night of the new moon"—thus it is said. Therefore, it is not the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) that is being expressed. (This is the reading found in the editions of A0, Ma0, Pu0, E0, Ka0, and Maṃ0 Pu0.)
"Even when it is merely the time," such is the reading in the Kāśmīra-Kośa manuscript.

[Page 723] Bhāṣya: "Continuity"—thus it is said. [Objection: "Well then, since the performance may take place even when the qualities are deficient, time need not be observed. To this, it is replied: Time is not a quality (*guṇa*), but rather the occasion (*nimitta*).

For this has been stated: "Therefore, because it is not prescribed at other times, even if performed, it would be as if unperformed. Consequently, the performance of that which depends on a specific time must continue for as long as one lives."
The determination of time is established by the observation of the characteristic signs of time. (Yukti) 26.

Furthermore, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*): "Verily, he who, being a performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, should let the full moon day or the new moon day pass by, is cut off from the heavenly world. If the oblation were to be performed at all times, then what would it mean for [the time] to pass by?
Therefore, for this reason also, there is no constant repetition. (6.2.7)
The section concerning the lapse [of the obligation] due to the omission of the Agnihotra and other rites at their proper time.
kha. Since those [words] are innate, one should proceed by means of traditional scripture (āgama). (Siddhānta) || 27 ||
Bhāṣya: "The Agnihotra is to be offered at nightfall; [it is] at dawn in the morning. Likewise:

"One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsa on the full moon day; one should sacrifice with the Amāvāsya on the new moon day. In this regard, there is a doubt: should it be offered at the very moment of nightfall, or...

"At every evening?"—or likewise, "once at dawn in the morning," or "at every dawn"? Likewise, "once on the full moon or new moon day," or "whenever the time arrives"? What is the prima facie view? Once.
The word "latā" (repetition) has been used in the sense of "having performed," and there is no restrictive rule regarding frequency.
This being the position reached, we reply: "One should proceed according to the traditional injunction," meaning "at each arrival of the [prescribed] time."
The application (prayoga) must be performed—why? Because "they are innate" (autpattika);
an action, as it arises, arises already connected with time. This has been stated: [the purpose is for the occasion (nimitta)].
In all manuscripts, having previously read, "The Agnihotra is to be offered at dusk," it is here said, "at dusk."
What has been recited does not cohere.
[Page 724] Bhāṣya:
Regarding the "declarations concerning time"—since when a specific occasion (nimitte) has arrived, the corresponding occasional duty (naimittika) must be performed;
therefore, the performance (prayoga) must be carried out when the time has arrived.
Sūtra: For there is also the observation of an indicative mark. (Yukti) || 28 ||

"He who, being a performer of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, should let the full moon or the new moon day pass by— verily he is cut off from this world and the heavenly world"— this [scriptural passage] shows that the performance must take place whenever the specific time arrives. (6.2.8)
Sūtra:
From the beginning up to the section on the division [of the sacrifice] starting with the Darśa, and ending with the section on the Homa.
Likewise, those performed internally are prescribed for the sacrifice. || 28 ||

Bhāṣya: It is heard in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices: "One offers when [the ladle] is broken; one offers when it has spilled. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the purpose of the offering fulfilled by performing the sacrifice once upon a broken or spilled vessel, or must one offer for every single instance of it being broken or spilled? In this regard, the principle of extension (*atideśa*) from the preceding section applies.

"The former part is that which has been completed, and the latter part is that which follows; thus, having performed it a hundred times, the purpose is accomplished"—this is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa). "Because it serves as the occasion (nimitta), there must be a repetition"—this is the final view (uttara-pakṣa). (6.2.9)
The section concerning the repetition of each individual cause for following after a fool and so forth.
In the case of those [rites] whose procedure is not specifically prescribed, it should be as [stated] above, because they serve a human purpose.

The Bhāṣya states: "An elder is to be followed and saluted; one of equal age is to be stood up for and greeted. In this regard, there is a doubt: when an elder or one of equal age arrives, must that which has been prescribed be performed each time they arrive, or is the purpose fulfilled by doing it once?
[The answer is: "In the case of those matters perceived through established custom (*ācāra*), it should be so [performed repeatedly], because they serve the purpose of human conduct (*puruṣārtha*)."

—Thus ends the extension of the legal topic (*adhikaraṇātideśa*). In this regard, whatever was the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) there, that is the prima facie view here; whatever was the final conclusion (*uttarapakṣa*) there, that is the final conclusion here; having applied it accordingly, the meaning of the suffix *lat* is established—thus is the prima facie view.
[Page 725]
The subsequent [view] is that there is a repetition of the performance because it serves as a cause for the result. (6.2.10)
Sra.
Bhā.
Section on the Necessity of the Removal of Impurity for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
But for the Brāhmaṇa, [the obligation to study] arises from the connection with the scriptural statement regarding the debts concerning Soma, Vedic knowledge, and progeny. || 31 ||

This is heard [in the scriptures]: "One should sacrifice with Soma," "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in his eighth year from conception," and "One should procreate offspring. In this regard, there is a doubt: are these obligatory (nitya) or non-obligatory (anitya)? What is the prima facie view? They are non-obligatory because of their connection with specific desires. This being the prima facie view, it is replied: for Brāhmaṇas and others, the Soma-sacrifice and the rest are obligatory. Why? Because they are connected with the statement regarding debts: "Being born..."

"One is born with three debts: through sacrifice to the gods, through the life of a student (*brahmacarya*) to the seers (*ṛṣi*), and through progeny to the ancestors"—thus it is said. "He indeed is free from debt when he has sacrificed, lived as a student, and had offspring. This praise of debts refers to those duties that must necessarily be performed.
"Therefore, they are eternal.
[Objection: "But surely an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not a proof; let the logical argument (*nyāya*) be stated, of which this is the indicator.
[Reply: It is said: their separate sentences are connected with the absence of desire (*akāma*).

There are such injunctions as: "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring," "One performs the Agnihotra as long as one lives," and "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa as long as one lives. Likewise: "One should study the Veda," and likewise: "Offspring must be produced. Thus, this is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the attainment of the state of being obligatory (*nityatā*).

Alternatively, there is another meaning: since the Soma-sacrifice, Vedic study, and procreation are connected for the Brāhmaṇa by means of the scriptural statement regarding debts (*ṛṇavākya*), are the Soma-sacrifices and so forth obligatory for the Brāhmaṇa alone?
• And in that very manuscript, the reading is *cahavā*; however, in other manuscripts, the reading *aruṣān* is observed.

[Page 726] Bhāṣya: Are these [observances] unrestricted for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, or are they restricted for all? What is the prima facie view? That they are restricted for the Brāhmaṇa alone, not for the other two. Why?
Thus it is heard: "The Brāhmaṇa indeed is one who is approaching [the sacrifice].

A restrictive rule (niyama) is observed for the Brāhmaṇa, but not for the other two [castes], because of the specific mention of the Brāhmaṇa. This being the position reached, we reply: the restriction applies to all. Why? Because the injunction of the restriction is made without distinction.
That statement which is not connected with desire and serves as a restrictive rule is common to all; therefore, the restriction applies to one's own [duties].
[Objection: But is it not the case that the mention of the Brāhmaṇa occurs in the passage, "Indeed, the Brāhmaṇa is born..."?

In this statement, there is a mention of the Brāhmaṇas, but this is not an injunction prescribing a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Rather, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the rule already established by these statements connected with the absence of desire, intended for the purpose of praising the *abhyavadāna* (the subsequent cutting). Therefore, there is no [restriction] here by virtue of the mention of the Brāhmaṇas.

For a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, no fixed rule is known [regarding the time of initiation]. However, the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is for the sake of illustration—namely, that "one being born is a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya"—and likewise, that "one being born and one already born. (6.2.11)
Thus ends the second quarter of the sixth chapter in the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya composed by the venerable Śabarasvāmin.
[Page 727] Now begins the section on the performance of what is possible regarding permanent [rites].
Sūtra: There would be activity toward every possible power, because the instruction is of such a nature. (1)
(Pūrvapakṣa)

In the *Bahvṛcabrāhmaṇa* it is heard: "One should perform the *Agnihotra* as long as one lives; one should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives. Thus, the *Agnihotra* is obligatory (*nitya*), and the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are also obligatory. In this regard, there arises a doubt concerning that second [set of injunctions] which, unlike the first, is heard without reference to a specific desire (*akāmaśravaṇa*): does one who intends to fulfill the injunction in its entirety [perform it], or...?

Is it that only one who is capable [of performing the rite] has the entitlement (*adhikāra*), or should it be performed even if it is deficient? This will be considered in the eleventh book regarding the first mention of a rite connected with a specific desire (*kāmayukta*) as being accompanied by its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*); here, however, it concerns the second mention in the context of a compulsory (*nitya*) rite. What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? "The performance should take place when there is capacity for everything, because the instruction is given in that manner."

He who is able to perform the procedure in its entirety should practice it, because of the instruction regarding such a state; for that which is heard as connected with desire in such a manner is taught as being eternal in that very same manner. Therefore, the performance must be carried out with the employment of all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). Furthermore, the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* denotes only that which possesses the auxiliaries. How so? Because the [sacrifice] together with its auxiliaries is enjoined on the full moon day and the new moon day; and that which is enjoined on the full moon day—
"From hearing about desire, [one attains] that which is conjoined with the absence of desire as the second"—this is the reading in the Kāṇva-Kṛṣṇa-Purāṇa (Kākrīpu).
"In the eleventh [book], however, the state of being a statement is accepted by all as belonging to none [of the others];

'by all' is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). When the eleventh [book] stands as the occasion for the performance of all auxiliary parts (*sarvāṅga-prahara*), [the rule] 'one offers the *agnihotra*' thus arises."

Because it is prescribed with respect to the sign and the fruit of one who is performing [the rite] in reverse order, this is neither a separate ritual (*karmāntara*) nor a separate preliminary application (*prayogāntara*), since the obligatory application (*nityaprayoga*) is included within the optional one (*kāmya*). Nevertheless, there is a great difference due to the scriptural statement (*śruti*); and relying on that very point, the author of the *Bhāṣya* said, "In the second hearing," as stated in the *Vārttika*.
[Page 728] Bhāṣya:

And that which is prescribed for the full moon is the full moon; and that which is prescribed for the new moon is the new moon—thus, that which is prescribed for the new moon along with its subsidiaries is [also] prescribed for the full moon. Therefore...
Jaimini held the view that the term "Darśapūrṇamāsa" refers to the sacrifice together with its constituent parts (aṅgas).
Or rather, it may apply even to a single part, for the accomplishment of the purpose resides in the principal; the rest is merely subsidiary, being for the sake of that. (Siddhānta) II.1.2.

Bhāṣya: "Or rather"—this marks the rejection of the previous position. There may indeed be the performance [of the rite] even when only a portion of the "limbs" (subsidiaries) is present; for whether it is performed with all its limbs or without them, this purpose is accomplished through the principal act alone, whereas the "mere accessory" [is fulfilled] by the performance of all the limbs.

It occurs. What is the benefit? The accomplishment of heaven [results] from the primary rite together with its auxiliary parts (*sāṅga*); this other result arises from the primary rite alone. Therefore, thinking, "I shall perform it with all its auxiliary parts for the sake of attaining heaven," one begins;
even if one is unable to perform some of the auxiliary parts, nevertheless, the result will arise from this primary rite when it is endowed with the qualities of even a portion of its auxiliaries.

Therefore, the application belongs only to the primary acts and not to the subsidiaries; for the words *darśapūrṇamāsa* and *agnihotra* denote the primary ritual entities, while the subsidiaries are subordinate to them.

And those [acts] which are not its [the primary act's] constituent parts are defects; therefore, there would be a distinction from that [primary act], because of its connection with the principal [act]. (Sūtra 3) (First Argument)

It is heard in scripture that "there is no fault in the omission of the primary [rite]," yet it is said: "He who, being a performer of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, should omit either the full moon or the new moon day, is indeed cut off from the heavenly world. By declaring this fault in the omission of the primary rite, the text demonstrates its obligatory (nitya) nature.
But Jaimini [holds] that this is one's own karma; for, because the injunction of performance is a single unit, there should be instruction regarding all [the priests]. (Sūtra 4) (Śrauta-sūtra).
Bhāṣya: As for what was stated— that there is no distinction between these being subsidiary members (*aṅga*) and these being primary elements (*pradhāna*)—
[this is addressed in] the first quarter of the third chapter.

Bhāṣya: Thus, because of the unity of the injunctive statement—so says Jaimini; here, he is the instructor of all [the rites], stating: "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day, and one should sacrifice with the Amāvāsyā on the new moon day."
Since the purpose is already accomplished, it would suffice even to employ a single [mantra], as is the case with other categories. (Ābhāsa-nirṇaya 5)

[Commentary: Even in the performance of a single constituent part, there would be a result; that is to say, even from what is deficient [in its subsidiaries], a fruit arises. Why? Because "the purpose is distinct" (*arthasya vyapavargitvāt*). The principal act is distinct from its constituents; the fruit arises here from that which is designated as the *Agnihotra* and that which is designated as the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*. For that is taught as something to be performed. That which is taught on the full moon day is the *Paurṇamāsī*.

That which occurs on the new moon day is the *Amāvāsyā* sacrifice, as it is said: "The cake for Agni (*āgneya*) on eight potsherds is offered on the new moon and the full moon days. Therefore, there is a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) for Agni, and another for Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomau*) on the full moon day; and for Agni, the *sānnāyya*, and so forth, on the new moon day.

As for what was stated—that because of the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Full Moon [offering] on the full moon day" and "one should sacrifice with the New Moon [offering] on the new moon day," the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* denotes the rite together with its subsidiaries—this is not so. For it is only when the meaning of *darśa* and the meaning of *paurṇamāsa* are already established that the result is enjoined along with the subsidiaries. Therefore, the term *agnihotra* does not denote the rite together with its subsidiaries, nor does the term *darśapūrṇamāsa*. Just as the *agnihotra* is enjoined elsewhere, so too is it enjoined here.

Because they are [prescribed] as things to be performed— namely, the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices— the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa must indeed be performed even when deficient in their constituent parts. Just as in other sacrifices, whether archetypal (prakṛti) or modified (vikṛti),
the ritual properties (dharma) of one do not belong to another, so too the properties of that which is connected with a specific desire do not apply [to others].
They ought to belong to that which is eternal.
And because completion is seen even when there is a defect in the injunction. (Sūtra 6, Second Yuktis)

The Bhāṣya shows the completion [of the rite] even when there are transgressions; by stating, "That very [rite], however it may be, is to be heard," it shows the completion of that which is deficient in its qualities.
Sphuṭārthā Bhāṣya [Page 730]
And because of the prescription of expiatory rites in the Mīmāṃsā system. (Sūtra 7, Third Yuga)

Furthermore, expiations are prescribed for the failure of an injunction as constituent parts of the rite when a specific occasion arises, such as: "One offers an oblation when [the ladle] is broken. If the rite were defective and thus fruitless, what purpose would there be for these constituent parts? Therefore, the performance must be carried out even when the rites are defective. (6.3.1)
Sūtra Bhāṣya: The section concerning the fruitlessness of optional rites when there is a deficiency [of accessories].
And likewise in the case of optional rites, because of the presence of desire [for their results]. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 8 ||

Regarding such injunctions as, "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni," "One desiring spiritual luster should offer a pap to Soma," and "One desiring a village should offer a *sāṅgrahaṇī* sacrifice to the Viśvedevas," a doubt arises: is [the rite] fruitful even when deficient in its constituent qualities?
Or is it that even a rite devoid of its constituent qualities (*guṇa*) is productive of fruit? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? "In the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), it should be so:
even one lacking qualities is productive of fruit. Why? "Because of the presence of the seeker (*arthitvāt*).
If even a rite lacking qualities were productive of fruit, then the mere presence of the seeker would be sufficient.
Otherwise, a general term will be restricted to a specific instance even without a specific [word].

If it is argued that "it is not entitled [to perform the action] because of incapacity," [we reply: it is incapable of performing [the action] along with its subsidiaries (sāṅga), but it is capable of performing the primary act alone; therefore, it will be entitled only to the primary act.
But because of the lack of connection with its own [context], it cannot be so; for an injunction has the Vedic word as its sole authority. (Siddhānta) || 8 ||

But [the author] says "tu" (but), by which the position is reversed: it would not be as stated—that even that which is deficient in its qualities (*viguṇa*) is fruitful—because there is no connection with the fruit for the principal act alone; rather, the cause [of the fruit] is [the act] together with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*). (*This reading is found in the Kāśīmudrita and Krītapustakapāṭha editions.*)
[Page 731] Chapter 6, Section 3.

For the fruit is heard in scripture as resulting from the principal act, not from the subsidiary alone; therefore, even if it is mentioned as being performed alone, one should not perform such an act in that manner, because it does not belong to the subsidiary alone.
"Conjunction with the fruit"—this is what is enjoined regarding the matter, for this is based on verbal authority;

and we shall explain that the word declares the fruit as resulting from the rite together with its auxiliary parts. Therefore, a ritual action of this kind must not be performed when it is deficient in its constituent factors.
Sūtra Bhāṣya Sthāna 3.2.11–16: *Sūtrabhāṣya* on the *Sūtras*.
Bhāṣya:
And because there is no transgression when [the rite] is not performed. (Yukti 10)

Furthermore, it is not the case that a transgression is declared here for the mere principal act alone, as is the case with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; therefore, an action characterized by such [deficiencies] must not be performed as something deficient. (6.3.2)
Even when there is a difference in substance, there is a locus for the non-difference of the cloth.
Because actions are dependent [on substances], there would be a division [of the substance] when another substance is present. (Pūrva-pakṣa 11)
The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice is prescribed with a *puroḍāśa* cake, and it is heard in the scripture: "That *puroḍāśa* must be made of *vrīhi* rice. In this regard, the following is considered:
if the sacrifice were performed with a *puroḍāśa* cake made of *nīvāra* rice, would it be that very same sacrifice?
[The question arises: "Is it the same [sacrifice], or is it another? What is the prima facie view? "There would be a division [of the sacrifice] with respect to a different substance;

[it would be] another sacrifice. Why? Because of its dependence: since the substratum differs, a distinction is understood—namely, that this one, which has *nīvāra* as its substratum, is different from the one which has *vrīhi* as its substratum.
The difference in the substratum is indeed quite clear; because of that difference, it is understood that the form (*rūpa*) is also different.
Therefore, the sacrifice is another, being a distinct substance.

Or rather, because there is no difference [in the action] and because the word for "form" is inseparable [from it], there should be a single action, just as in the case of "cowness"; and it is a name, just like "being-ness. (Siddhānta 12)
Bhāṣya:
"Or rather"—this marks the rejection of the alternative view. "There would be unity" regarding the substance...
[Page 732]
Also in another passage of the Mīmāṃsā-darśana-bhāṣya: "When there is an action, such as moving or falling, even then the object remains exactly that same;
there is no additional distinction or deficiency therein."
Indeed, it is not that the form is something else, nor is there another word as its denoter.

[Objection: "But surely the difference in substrata is perfectly clear. [Reply: We admit that the substratum is indeed distinct; however, the thing supported does not become distinct because of that difference in substrata, because they are different. For it is not so.
But when a jar or a garment is broken, a difference between persons is understood from that [destruction].
If it is argued, "That [person] is also distinct from his self," this is not so; for only those who perceive a distinction can speak in such a way, and no distinction is perceived in this case.

"Is it not indeed the very distinction that one has perished while the other still exists? As for what is said—that it has not perished—there is no proof of its existence because it was previously perceived; therefore, it has perished. Nor is it recognized as something distinct from that substance, since no difference is perceived. How then [is this so]?"

If it is asked, "What is the cognition [expressed by] 'it moves'?"—it is replied: because we observe the attainment of another location, that which goes to and comes from another location is said to "move";
in that case, the mover is perceived, as is the other location reached by him.
And it is said, "he has come," and it is said, "he has arrived. Truly, that which is spoken is the reading found in the Kāśikā-vṛtti on Pāṇini 8.2.96.

The proponent raises an objection regarding the distinction of action (*karmabheda*) with the words "na ca" (and not). Therefore, motion is not recognized as distinct from substance. Why? Because no difference is perceived; that is, because it is not known as a separate entity from the substance. The point is this:

action is certainly not a different entity from the substance, because its own nature is not perceived as something distinct from the form of the substance that arises and perishes. Consequently, it must be said that action is merely another state (*rūpāntara*) of the substance itself; and thus, when the substance is one, the non-difference of the action is established.

The opponent raises an objection regarding the preceding view: "How is this so?"—meaning that if action (*karman*) were essentially a substance (*dravyātmaka*), then the uniform cognition "it moves" would not occur, because substances are distinct. The response is: "In another location"—meaning that because the result, consisting of conjunction with and disjunction from a subsequent location, is one and the same, there is a uniform cognition applicable to various actions due to the commonality of their causal nature, but not because of the identity of the actions themselves. [Objection: But how can this uniform cognition be supported by an inferred result?

For one might suspect that reaching another location is merely inferential in the case of space because space is imperceptible; to address this doubt, [the author says] "there too, there is a mover. Since the mover is perceptible, and likewise the other location is perceptible, recognition occurs through the identity of the result (*phalaikya*), and not through the identity of the action (*kriyaikya*).
Because this appears clearly, the meaning is that space itself is indeed perceptible. He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "True—[even though] there is a difference in the actions..."

"Since the universal is one, recognition is logical; therefore, just as in the case of the application of rice and barley, the identity of the action is established among the *mīvara* [beans] as well—whether by way of its universal nature or its individual nature—this is the meaning. Thus says the Vārttika-ṭīkā of Śabarasvāmin.

[It is] not [the case that it is] other than the non-perished from the perished; for even that which is other, it is indeed denoted by the word *yajati*. The generality (*sāmānya*) of the sacrifice is not divided, nor is it not expressed by the word. Therefore, even one who performs a sacrifice with wild rice (*nīvāra*) has performed exactly what was enjoined; and for one performing what is enjoined, the desired result follows, not something unenjoined. This is a name (*nāmadheya*).

And it shows [this] by means of the terms "Darśa" or "Pūrṇamāsa," which belong to this very generality, just as the name belongs to the generality among individual beings and not to the individuals themselves.
What is the purpose of this inquiry? This will be deliberated upon in the subsequent section (adhikaraṇa).
(6|3|3 Śrauta Sūtra)
The section concerning the completion by means of a substitute when there is a deficiency of materials for both obligatory rites and those commenced as occasional rites.
Sūtra 13: (Pūrvapakṣa) Because the Veda is the authoritative means of knowledge, in the absence of cultured persons (śiṣṭas), there is no tradition from others, since they are not cultured.
The obligatory rites such as the *agnihotra* serve as the illustration. Regarding these, when there is a deficiency of the prescribed substance, a doubt arises:
"Should the performance be carried out by taking a substitute, or should the rite be abandoned at that point? What is the prima facie view?
Since there is no scriptural injunction for the introduction of another [substance] in the absence of the prescribed one, the rite should be abandoned at that very point.

Why? Because it would be improper (*aśiṣṭatvāt*). That which is prescribed as having rice or barley as its quality and is productive of fruit, becomes fruitless when performed with wild rice (*nīvāra*) as its quality; therefore, that [procedure] must be abandoned right there. Thus.
Sūtra:
And because there is an injunction in some cases. (Yukti 14)

In some cases, it is prescribed: "If one should not find Soma, one should press Pūtīka plants. If the performance were to be carried out by taking a substitute whenever [the original] was unavailable, this would not have been prescribed. Since it is indeed prescribed, therefore, where it is not prescribed, there is no substitute.
[Page 734] According to the Mīmāṃsā system: "Or rather, it is the Vedic scripture, because there is no difference in the meaning of the injunction. (Siddhānta Sūtra 15).
Bhāṣya-khaṇḍana-bhāṣya (The Commentary on the Refutation of the Commentary)
Śrī Bhāṣya Sūtra (1.1.4)

"Or there is the scriptural authority (āgama) for the substance to be substituted. Why? Because there is no difference in the meaning of the injunction; for the act enjoined by the injunction 'he sacrifices' (yajati) is not distinguished whether it is performed with rice grains or with wild rice (nīvāra), and the sacrifice must necessarily be performed in both obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites once they have been commenced."
In some cases, an injunction has the purpose of restriction. || 16 ||

Now, as for what was said—‘In some cases, because of an injunction’—the reply is: ‘In some cases, an injunction is for the purpose of restriction. When many similar substitutes for Soma are available in the absence of Soma, a restriction is made: ‘Only Pūtīka plants are to be pressed. Therefore, there is a substitute.
One should apply oneself with effort, having taken this as the basis.
"That is constant, for it is the desire to perform that [act].

(Śrauta Sūtra, Adhikaraṇa 17) How, then, is this understood—that the mention of that [substitute] is solely for the purpose of a restrictive rule? It is said: because the *pūtīka* plants are already obtained. And how are they obtained?

"For one who desires that [the substitute] is indeed one who desires similarity in that regard—this we shall explain—and by the desire for that, the *pūtīka* plants are obtained. Therefore, the statement 'that is constant' is understood to mean that this injunction is constant for the sake of restriction. (6.3.4a)
The section concerning the absence of substitutes when there is a failure in the performance of rites involving deities and mantras.
The word "devatā" does not denote the act of sharpening, because it is connected with a different meaning. || 18 ||

The deities are those such as "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" and so forth; [the deity] Agni is [defined by] the statement, "By that which one offers in the Āhavanīya fire, Soma becomes desired and pleased.
The words are those such as "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" and so forth; the actions are...
[Bhāṣya, Page 735]:

"He offers the *samidh* oblation," "He offers the *tanūnapāt* oblation"—such are the examples. In this regard, there is a doubt: when there is a deficiency (*apacāra*) regarding the deity, the fire, the word, or the action, should a substitute (*pratinidhi*) be adopted, or not? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It is that [a substitute should be used], according to the principle of the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*).
"Having substituted another [element], the performance should be carried out"—
this being the position reached, we reply: "No," in the case of the non-occurrence of the deity, the fire, the word, or the action.
"It must be a substitute. Why? "Because of the connection with another purpose";

that which is substituted is different from these [original materials], and something else would not be able to perform their purpose. And what is their purpose? First of all, it is the dedication to the deity.

It accomplishes the purpose; namely, that the cake on eight potsherds is offered with reference to Agni on the full moon and the new moon days. And as for what is prescribed regarding other oblations (*carus*), the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices do not consist of those; in that case, another [deity] being referred to would not effect the purpose of the deity mentioned in the Vedic text, for when another is being referred to, [the purpose of the original one is not achieved].

The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices exist; therefore, no substitute for the deity is permitted. Likewise, regarding the rule "that which one offers in the Āhavanīya fire," when the Āhavanīya fire is absent, neither another fire nor another substance should be substituted. Why? Because [the sacrifice is defined by its specific components].

"Because of its connection with a different purpose," that which is substituted does not perform the function of the *āhavanīya*. How so? The function of the *āhavanīya* is invisible (*adṛṣṭa*); that which occurs when an offering is cast upon the *āhavanīya* does not occur when it is cast upon something else; for it is not so.

By the word "yajati" (he sacrifices), that [place] is indicated by implication—that upon which one relinquishes [the offering]; for indeed, the location of that which is being relinquished does not provide any assistance.
Therefore, fire is not a substitute.
Likewise, when the Soma is omitted, no other mantra is substituted; for this is the purpose of the mantra: that it causes one to remember either the ritual action or its means.
If there is no remembrance, the ritual action would not be accomplished. Therefore, if the Soma is omitted, [another substance] should be used for its sake.
The reading is "anyatra" (elsewhere) according to Ka0;
the reading is "arpitam" (offered) according to So0.
This is not found in the Saṃyukta-puṇya, the Evaṃ-cāra, or the Soḍaśaka manuscripts.
Puṇya-pāṭhaḥ.
[Page 736] Bhāṣya:
He utters another word while uttering the word for the object previously understood; he does not [utter it] otherwise.

One should understand the meaning from the word itself! If, even after it has been understood, one were to understand it again by uttering a substitute word (i.e., produce understanding from that word), then the adherence to the utterance of the substitute word would be purposeless; for there is no authority whatsoever for the claim that "the meaning must be conveyed by a word. Whatever such authority exists applies specifically to this word, such as *barhis* and so forth—it is thus. In its absence, adherence to another word would be purposeless.
Therefore, there is no substitute for the word. Sūtra.

In the case of the omission of a ritual act, there is no substitute act, because it is connected with a different purpose. The Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices must be performed as possessing the *samidh* offerings; if another [act] were performed instead, they would not possess those [offerings]. And [the word denotes] the deity, because it has that as its purpose. (Yukti 18)
