"Now, it might be argued that because of its connection with the dual case-ending (*vibhakti*), the word 'both' (*ubhaya*) implies that the affliction is qualified by both. That is not so; for the connection with the case-ending is indeed a qualifier of the oblation (*havis*).

One would be able to apply the word "both" (*ubhaya*) because of its co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*), but it is not a qualifier of the pain (*śrarti*); for there is no co-occurrence of this [word] with the oblation (*havis*) as qualified by the pain.
(*Note: The reading "aśaśaśabdāt" is an additional one found in the Cāṅguṇya Soma-puṣpa manuscript.*)
pu0 pāṭhaḥ | + mī iti cā0 so0 [Page 764] The reading is "pu"; and "mī" according to Cāndra and Sārasvata.
[Page 764]

The Bhāṣya says: "Now it is replied: even in the absence of co-utterance (samabhivyāhāra), because the word *ārti* is mentioned, the affliction (*ārti*) qualified by that [word] will be understood. This is not so;
for in the absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), mere proximity (*sannidhāna*) is not a cause [of syntactic connection], just as in the case of the word "wife" (*bhāryā*).

[The opponent says: "In the case of 'the king's [servant]' or 'Devadatta's man'—as in the word *dūti*—because they occur within a single sentence, it is understood as qualified by that [other term]. [The author replies: This is not so; even within a single sentence, there is no connection for that which is an unrequired member of it. For example, in the expression "he goes on horseback, covered with a white cloth," the whiteness does not belong to the horse, which is [already] unrequired.

It becomes a qualifier. [If it is argued: "Now, it is said that there is a connection of both with the oblation (*havis*) as qualified by *ārtti* (decay/damage),"—that too is not tenable. For in the phrase "one should offer when [the oblation] has reached decay" (*ārtim ārcchat*), the oblation is not introduced as a qualifier; rather, what is it? It is introduced as the occasion (*nimitta*) for the five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*). If the connection of both with the five-platter offering were accepted simultaneously with the oblation having reached decay, the sentence would be split (*vākyabheda*).
[If it is argued: "The oblation is connected with that which is characterized by its generic form (*ākṛti*), while 'has reached decay' (*ārcchat')..."
The word "both" (*ubhaya*) would be connected with the term "oblation" (*havir*), which is qualified [by the number]. Even so, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, the occasioning condition (*nimitta*) is not an affliction (*ārti*) qualified by both.
Furthermore, just as when the meaning of the verb is primary, the offering is understood as qualified by both and not as qualified by only one, so it is in the other case as well.

Even in the alternative view, it is said that she is qualified by both qualifiers; yet, although she is qualified by her own self, nevertheless, being qualified by only one or the other, she cannot be the cause—what then is the distinction? To this, it is replied:
In my view, the two qualifiers are intended as things to be adopted (*upādeya*), whereas in your view, they are intended as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

[The opponent] asks: "What follows from this, that they are defining characteristics? It is replied: This follows from it; namely, that the substance is characterized by the form of the oblation (*haviḥ-ākṛti*), and something must be said regarding that.
If that were stated without being characterized, it would not be understood to whom it would belong;

or else, it might be understood as belonging to every substance whatsoever. Since both of these possibilities are indistinguishable, the form of the oblation (havirākṛti) is mentioned in order to characterize its substratum.
[Page 765] Chapter [X],
Section [X].
In this regard, two possibilities arise: either that which has the form of an oblation is spoiled, or that both [the substance and its form] are spoiled— provided, first of all,
that it is that which has the form of an oblation.

In that case, "that which is afflicted" (*tad-ārttam*) is expected; therefore, the occasion (*nimitta*) is understood as being either both or neither, characterized by the form of the oblation (*havir-ākṛtika*). Now, if that which has the form of the oblation is "both," then the affliction is not qualified by the oblation. [End of section on] the oblation.
If the *śruti* (the direct Vedic statement) were not qualified, the word "both" (*ubhaya*) would qualify the oblation (*havis*);
however, this is not tenable. Why? Because it would be qualified in this manner: "that which is both and has the form of an oblation. In that case, it must further be stated: what...

If both [the *ṛjīṣa* and the *pūtaṃnava*] were of the nature of *ṛvi*, and that were afflicted (*ārtam*), how could the affliction be connected with that qualified [substance]? Furthermore, the two words "oblation" (*havis*) and "both" (*ubhaya*) would not be uttered for the purpose of qualifying the affliction. Now, if they are not uttered again, then even if the word "oblation" is not uttered by way of indicating the characteristic of being the substratum of both, [the connection remains].

The characteristic of distress would be non-distinct; it would be non-distinct for both. If, however, a distinct [distress] is intended, a further recitation must be performed, and in that case there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Thus, if the word "both" (*ubhaya*) were connected with the verb "to suffer" (*ārcchati*), it would not qualify the sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
It might be so; in that case, the breaking [of the vessel] would be the cause for the re-offering of the undifferentiated oblation (*havis*).

Alternatively, if it were connected with the word *havis*, then for the sake of connecting it again with the re-offering, the word *havis* would have to be uttered together with it, or it would have to be indicated by a pronoun, such as "this"—in that case, that [would be the requirement].
In this way, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

On the other hand, if [the two terms] were to be taken as things to be enjoined (*upādeya*), there would be no purpose in qualifying one another; for even this [term] would be uttered merely to qualify the act of eating (*atti*), and thus it would not serve as the basis for the name (*nāmadheya*) by being qualified by the other. However, in the case of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), it is indeed qualified by the other.

— this is the distinction. Furthermore, when every word is connected with another word, if there is a possibility [of connection] with a third word, a connection with even an immediately adjacent [word] is not proper in the absence of a [grammatical] term; for it does not happen that "the king's wife, Devadatta's man."

—In this case, "king" is a qualifier of the person; for when there is no other way, even if there is a separation, the connection of several subordinate elements with the principal element is permissible, even if it is mediated by an interval.
[Page 766]

Because of the placement [of the word] in the heart, the purpose is more powerful; however, if it were a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa), then in the event of a conflict between two characteristics regarding that which must necessarily be given, either the remote factor or the subordinate quality would have to be abandoned.
The section concerning the fact that both the performer of the oblation and the performer of the consecration [are entitled to the fruit].
And likewise, the offering, the pressing, and the consumption [are to be performed] by him. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 24 ||

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "Having pressed [the Soma] with the stones at the *havirdhāna* shed and having offered it in the *āhavanīya* fire, they go back and consume the portions in the *sadas*. In that context, the pressing has been enjoined by another statement, and the offering by the root *yajati*; these two, however, are not [identical].

It is enjoined, yet there is no specific sequence for those two, for that sequence is obtained through the very nature of the matter; therefore, the consumption is enjoined as having a single agent in relation to both the offering and the pressing—meaning that once the pressing and the offering have been performed, the consumption must be carried out by their performers. In this regard, there is this doubt:

—Should only he who performs both [acts] consume [the remnant], or may it be consumed by either one as well? What is the prima facie view? "The offering, the pressing, and the consumption are like that; they should be exactly like that, just as in the case of the two-fold affliction. How so? It is not connected in this way.

"—having pressed [the Soma], then having offered it, then one should consume it"—by this, the sequence of the pressing and the offering is not being stated; rather, it means "those who offer after having pressed [the Soma] are the ones who consume it. For otherwise, the sentence would be split: "having pressed, they consume," [and "having offered, they consume"].

"Having offered, they consume"—thus it is said. Therefore, there is no mutual connection between the offering (*homa*) and the pressing (*abhiṣava*); consequently, the consumption could be connected with either one, as in "having pressed, they consume. Therefore, by whichever one of these two [acts] serves as the occasion...
There is eating—thus it is said.
Or rather, [the authority belongs] to both; for there is no Dharmaśāstra regarding those two. (Siddhānta) || 25 ||

Or rather, one should consume [the soma] by means of both causes; for there is an additional reading in the Cāndra-mohana-puṣpa manuscript: "They do not consume [it] without having performed the offering (homa) and the pressing (abhiṣava)."
[Page 767] No.
A property (dharma) is not being enjoined here; for what would happen if a property were enjoined for those two?
If the oblation (homa) and the pressing (abhiṣava) were the primary acts, then the consumption (bhakṣaṇa) would be a subordinate quality, and it would have to differ with each primary act!

Furthermore, if the eating is enjoined by both signs, then when that is enjoined, a single purpose is enjoined; therefore, it constitutes a single sentence. Thus, it culminates in this much: "Having pressed [the Soma] and having offered it, they eat. In that case—

This is a subordinate sentence, namely, "Having seen it, they eat"; and when there is a principal sentence, a subordinate sentence does not constitute an authority, because it is sublated by another word, just as from the principal sentence, "One should not look at the rising sun," a prohibition is understood.

From the intermediate sentence, there is an injunction for gazing. Therefore, eating based on either one of those two [conditions] is not what is heard; rather, from the great sentence (*mahāvākya*), this is understood: "There are two conditions for eating"—and one who performs the eating otherwise would abandon what is heard in scripture.
Therefore, the consumption [of the remnant] is by both. (Section 4.7a).
This is the section concerning the two types of following [the fire] as the cause for re-establishing the sacred fires.
The re-establishment of the sacred fires is like the preparation of cooked rice; thus [says] the Purvapakṣin. (26)

In the context of the Agnihotra, it is heard in scripture: "For one whose two fires have both gone out at sunset, or for one whose two fires rise at sunrise, the re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya) is indeed the expiation.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the re-establishment required upon the extinction of either one, or only upon the extinction of both? What is the prima facie view? It should be that the re-establishment is like the case of the cooked rice (odana).

Just as there is prosperity for one of two [persons] who share a single earthenware vessel of five measures, so too, when one of the two has passed away, the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*) ought to take place; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
Thus, the connection is exactly like this: "If I die here, I shall perform a meritorious deed here."

When both the Āhavanīya and Gārhapatya fires have gone out (*anugata*), if at that time there occurs either the setting or the rising of the sun, then one must perform the *punarādheya* (re-consecration); this is the meaning according to Mādhava.
↑ "In this very way they kindle me," such is the reading in the Kāṇva-Kṛṣṇa-Puṣpa manuscript.
Sūtra-bhāṣya [Page 768]
Or rather, because of the production of the substance, it would belong to both. (Siddhānta) || 27 ||
When that [fire] has been destroyed, the re-establishment of that very same substance is the expiation;
its visible purpose is: "How may the substance come to be?"—thus the re-consecration is performed.
And this is the rule: the two fires arise together, not separately; in that regard, [the following applies].
If one follows either [of the two fires], it is not possible to establish the other; it would be deficient.
"Now, one might establish the second as well. If that is the Āhavanīya, then since the Āhavanīya already exists for the purpose of oblations, it is not [needed] for the oblation."

It may be so. That which is produced for the purpose of the oblation is the *āhavanīya*, because this [term] denotes a consecration (*saṃskāra*); and that which denotes a consecration does not exist without even a single consecration, and this very consecration is the state of being for the purpose of the oblation, namely, "that which [is offered] in the *āhavanīya*."

It is heard in the scripture: "He offers. If one [fire] has gone out while the other is being kindled, there is a deficiency; for indeed, there is a deficiency in both cases. Therefore, when one [fire] has gone out, there is no re-establishment [of the fires], because it is impossible—so [it is said]. (6.4.1)
The section concerning the preference for the fifth oblation as a means of extinguishing the fire:
"But the animal and the earthenware vessel should be substitutes because of the direct scriptural mention of the substance. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 28 ||

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "If both sacrificial offerings (havir) of one should meet with ruin, he should offer five śarāvas of cooked rice to Indra. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the five-śarāva offering a substitute (pratinidhi) for the ruined offering, or is it a separate ritual occasion (karmāntara) triggered by that cause?

— thus [it is asked]: "How is there a substitute? How is there a different rite? If the connection is as follows—"One should offer (perform) the five-platter oblation"—then [the word] *tasyāḥ* [is used]. (Ka0 Saṃ0 Pu0).
[Page 769] Bhāṣya:

Therefore, the five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*) is a substitute for the *sānnāyya* (milk-offering). Now, it is not that one performs the five-platter offering with the act of pouring out (*nirvapati*), but rather that it is connected with the deity: "One should make the five-platter offering for Indra. Thus, the sacrifice is enjoined as having a specific occasion (*nimitta*).
Śrībhāṣyasūktiḥ (The Elegant Sayings from the Śrībhāṣya)
Bhāṣya: Why?
What, then, is the prima facie view?—The five-earthenware dish is a substitute because of the scriptural mention of the substance.
"The five-platter offering" is a substitute for the *sānnāyya* (curdled milk offering).
This is because of the mention of the substance; there is an injunction regarding the substance to be offered, not regarding its connection with Indra. Why?
Because in this way the injunction for the offering will be established, and in that case the Vedic text (*śruti*) is prescriptive; otherwise, [it would not be].

In the case of a connection between a substance and a deity, there would be a syntactical statement (vākya), and that is weaker than direct audition (śruti). Therefore, there is a substitute (pratinidhi) for it. Thus [the conclusion].
Or rather, it is an injunction [of the sacrifice], for there is an injunction regarding the substance and the deity where [the sacrifice] itself is not explicitly expressed. (Siddhānta 28)

Or rather, the sacrifice [performed] on the basis of the specific mark (*nimitta*) is a distinct ritual action, being an injunction regarding the material and the deity; for here the material and the deity are heard in the text: "One should prepare a five-portioned oblation for Indra.

Otherwise, the term "for Indra" (*aindram*) would have to be understood as a scribal error. Or else, the word "for Indra" would be an inaccurate restatement (*anuvāda*) of both Indra and Mahendra, for those two deities cannot be referred to by the single word "Indra. Indeed, they are not denoted by that term.

Or, if [the word] were a qualifier, there would be a split in the sentence. [Objection: "But was it not stated that direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is more powerful? [Reply: That is indeed true; however, in the other case, the direct statement is even more contradicted, because the word *aindra* possesses the status of a direct statement. (6.4.9)
The section concerning the occasional performance of the Darśa sacrifice at the fifth watch [of the night]:
"That [sacrifice] should be postponed because of its position. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 30 ||

This is that occasional sacrifice (*naimittika-yāga*). Should it be connected with the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*)? [The reading in the Kātyāyana-Śrautasūtra-Kośa-Pustaka is: "The fifth oblation (*pañcama-rāva*) is connected with the deity. [The reading in the Pāṇini-Siddhāntakaumudī-Pustaka is: "It is connected with the offering of the fifth oblation (*pañcama-rātra-nirvapa*)."
[Page 770] Bhāṣya:

Is it not so? What is the prima facie view? "He should substitute that [sacrifice], because of its position. That very sacrifice is entitled to be enjoined with respect to the New Moon (Amāvāsyā). Why? "Because of its position."

If the sacrifice has perished, then this sacrifice being heard [in the scripture] would not be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of that which has perished; consequently, it would be purposeless. Now, if it were an auxiliary performed for the sake of something that is itself purposeless, it must necessarily be purposeless as well;
and this [sacrifice], being defective, is indeed purposeless, since the *āmāvāsya* [new-moon sacrifice] has perished.
"—this is perception; 'this also is to be done'—this is verbal testimony;
'that which has perished is fruitless—therefore it is not to be done'; and 'this is to be done'—thus is the counter-injunction understood."
Or rather, it is a rule regarding its own constituent parts, because of the connection with the occasion. (Siddhānta)
Indeed, this is enjoined as an auxiliary; for when the occasion of the offering of the oblation has arisen, a sacrifice is heard of in scripture.

In that regard, the following alternatives present themselves: either the fruit is to be produced when the occasion arises, or whatever function belongs to the New Moon (Amāvāsyā) sacrifice is the function of this [sacrifice], or it is an auxiliary to that [New Moon sacrifice].

First of all, it is not independent, because the fruit is dependent on an instrument. It does not function as the effect of the new moon sacrifice (*darśa*). Why? Because it is not so heard; indeed, it is not heard that "it functions as its effect.
Nor is there a determination [of its status] among these three by means of an instruction regarding what is to be done (*kartavyopadeśa*).
In those various positions and in the positions intended to be stated, the instruction regarding what is to be performed is formulated.

[Objection: "But surely the connection will be as follows: for one whose two oblations have met with ruin, he should accomplish by means of this sacrifice whatever he desires to accomplish; and what is it that he desires to accomplish? It is the fruit of the New Moon sacrifice."

It is said in response: because there is no connection with the word denoting the fruit, the sentence that enjoins the connection is [set aside], and by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), the necessity of performing the sacrifice is enjoined; and that [direct statement] is more powerful than the syntactical connection (*vākya*). Therefore, it does not function toward that [fruit]. What then?

What is the purpose? It is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of that New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*). [Objection: But even this is not its auxiliary. [Reply: To this it is said: because it is mentioned in connection with it, it is grasped by the injunction of its performance (*prayogavacana*), [as part] of the Darśapūrṇamāsa for the sake of the fruit.
The reading in the Kāśī edition of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata Purāṇa is: *tatsannibhitasvānāt*.
[Page 771] Bhāṣya:
It should be accomplished together with all its constituent parts; and in this case of distress (*śrārtta*), this sacrifice constitutes the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

Therefore, it is understood thus: when the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) has perished, that which is the New Moon sacrifice (*āmāvāsya*) and is unable to perform its own function, that [function] is performed by means of this procedure.
"It is capable [of performing] together"—therefore, the rite is a subsidiary element of the occasion.
The section concerning the necessity of the Viśvajit sacrifice for one who has set out on a journey toward the sun.
Sūtra 32: In the case of one who has undertaken the Viśvajit sacrifice, there should be the performance of ritual acts. (The established conclusion.)
Bhāṣya:
This is recorded in the tradition: "He who pledges himself for a sacrificial session (sattra) pledges himself to all deities and to all *pṛṣṭha* chants; [therefore, he should perform] the Viśvajit."

"One should sacrifice with the Atirātra, which has all the *pṛṣṭha* chants and for which the gift of all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*) is the sacrificial fee; by this, one ransoms oneself from all the deities and from all the *pṛṣṭha* chants"—thus the Viśvajit is heard in the Veda as being occasioned by the undertaking (*āgoraṇa*) of a *satra*. In this regard, there is a doubt: does the Viśvajit belong to him who, having undertaken a *satra*, performs it, or [to someone else]?

Does one employ [the mantra] for that [act], or not? What, then, is the prima facie view? That one employs both that which is used and that which is not, because there is no distinction; or rather, it belongs to one who is employing it. Why?

Because it has been stated that such a thing is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the ritual action when its occasion (*nimitta*) arises; how then could it be a constituent part for one who does not employ it?

This being the case, we reply: the Viśvajit should take place when [the sacrifice] has not commenced; that is, the Viśvajit occurs in the absence of the performance of the Sattra. What is the reason? For it is heard in scripture thus: "He who pledges himself to a Sattra shall sacrifice with the Viśvajit Atirātra."

He who makes a formal resolve (āgurate), thinking "I shall perform a sacrificial session (satra)," should accomplish that by means of the Viśvajit sacrifice; it is understood that this is for the sake of whatever purpose he desires to perform the sacrificial session. How so? The meaning of the sentence is understood as: "He who resolves should sacrifice with that [Viśvajit], he should bring it about by means of that sacrifice," and not "he should bring about the sacrifice."
Why? Because the sacrifice is heard of as being subordinate (guṇatva). [Question: "In what way is it subordinate? [Answer:
Because of its designation by the third case-ending; for if it were primary, the result would have to be inferred. But in the other case...
The understanding of the result [arises] either from direct perception or from the sentence.
And because there is a statement regarding its redemption. (Yukti 33)

Bhāṣya: Thus it is heard there—“Verily, by this [Viśvajit], one ransoms oneself from all deities and from all *pṛṣṭha* chants. And praise by way of a ransom is not appropriate when [the sacrifice] has already commenced. Therefore, the Viśvajit applies when [the sacrifice] has not commenced. Now...

Why is the connection not made in this way: "Having resolved to perform a *sattra*, one should sacrifice with the *viśvajit*," whereby a relationship between the *viśvajit* and the *sattra* would be understood at the time of the resolution (*āgoraṇa*)? It is not so, for the *sattra* is indeed a qualification of the resolution.

In the context of the connection between the *satra* and the *viśvajit*, there would be the assumption of an intervention. Furthermore, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) connects the *viśvajit* with the person, saying, "A person should sacrifice with the *viśvajit*," and not with the *satra*; for it says, "The *viśvajit* sacrifice belongs to the *satra*," and also, "The *āgū*."

In this way, the hearing [of the text] becomes meaningful. However, if it were a subordinate element (*aṅga*), its meaning would already be established and need not be stated; nor can one enjoin immediate sequence after "buying" (*krītvā*) in the phrase "one should sacrifice after buying," for in that case, a non-verbal meaning would have to be resorted to, whereas the fact of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatā*) is indeed expressed by the word.
And because the existence at a prior time is already established by implication, it need not be explicitly stated.
Therefore...

The connection of the Viśvajit sacrifice is with the very act of "having resolved" (*śrāgūryya*); that is to say, if one does not sacrifice with the Soma after having resolved, for him there is the Viśvajit. (6.4.11)
The section concerning the purpose of the scriptural passage beginning with "barhir dīkṣita" as being intended to prescribe the time for the vow.
[The vow should be enjoined] upon the connection with the calf.

(Pūrvapakṣa) Bhāṣya: Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard [in the scripture]: "They undertake the vow with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) at the full moon, and with the calf at the new moon. In this regard, there is a doubt: what...?
And "ya cāmūryya" is the reading found in the Kāṭhaka, Krīta, and Puṣpasūtra recensions.
"At the full moon, they undertake the vow with the calves"—this is the reading in the Kātyāyana-Śrautasūtra (Kā° ŚrSū. and the Kṛtyakalpataru (Krī° Pu°);
thus says Mādhava.
In this regard, where there is a vow, there is eating.
(Chapter 4, Pāda 1) [Page 773]

Bhāṣya: Is a vow (vrata) that has a calf as its means being enjoined, or is it the time for the vow? Or rather, is the calf an auxiliary part (aṅga) of the vow? What is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)?—That the vow has a calf as its means.

Is it enjoined?—namely, "On the new moon day, one should perform the vow with the calves"—thus, the previously unestablished connection with the calf-vow is enjoined; and when that is enjoined, both are indeed enjoined: namely, the calf and the vow.
b. Or rather, it is time [that determines the order], because of the connection with what has arisen, as previously stated. (Siddhānta) || 35 ||

Bhāṣya: "The optionality of what has been stated" (i.e., that which is obtained through another statement) is enjoined. Why? "Because of the connection with what is already established"; there is a connection of the vow with what is already established, not a connection with its origination.
How so? "They observe the vow as one free from beans, free from meat, and containing abundant clarified butter."
The vow has been prescribed, but the time is not known; therefore, this is an injunction regarding the time.
Sūtra-bhāṣya:
And because the meaning is immeasurable. (Yukti)

And the meaning cannot be fully measured: regarding the statement, "They enter upon the vow with a calf," does it mean that the calf itself is to be consumed as the vow? (In this way, the vow would be entered upon by means of the calf);
or does it mean that one should consume [the food] while holding the calf in one's hand? (In this way...)

[The question arises: "Should one approach [the cow] while she is already with her calf, or should one first bring the calf near and then approach her? Thus, the meaning of the scripture is not definitively settled; for this is a clearly defined instrument (*karaṇa*), not a procedural detail (*itikartavyatā*). It has been stated merely that "one should perform the vow using the calf as the means. How?—this requirement remains unqualifiedly expectant; the purpose is not at all delimited.

"What is performed by the calf in relation to the vow?"— or rather, "Is it this or that? In that case, the calf, being connected with the vow, would be perceived as having its own independent purpose (aparārthatā),
whereas the third-case ending (*tṛtīyā*) indicates its subservience to another (parārthatā), for [the third case] is used in the sense of the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*).
That [conjunction] occurs; therefore, that conjunction also has time as its purpose.
kha. But the calf, because of its connection with the Vedic revelation, should be an auxiliary to that [rite]. (Sūtra 37; Second Pūrvapakṣa)
As for what was stated— that this is a restatement (anuvāda) because the vow has already been described— that is true.
[Page 774] Mīmāṃsā-Damana.

As for what was said—that it is for the purpose of prescribing a time—that is not so; rather, the calf (vatsa) is prescribed as an accessory (aṅga) to that [act]. Why? Because of its connection with the direct Vedic statement (śruti). The ritual acts of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are not being enjoined here;

rather, what is enjoined is that those ritual acts must have no other performer. And this is the syntactical structure: "the officiating priests" is the subject term (*uddeśapada*), and "they" is what is enjoined; those who are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*), they alone [are the officiating priests].

"The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are [the performers], not others"—thus, regarding the ritual acts belonging to the officiating priests, the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) are prescribed as the agents because of a direct substitution (*pratyāmnāna*); consequently, others are excluded. This being the case, the ritual acts belonging to the officiating priests serve their original purpose; no unseen refinement (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer is thereby prescribed. The *satras* themselves serve as the examples: "Those who, knowing thus, perform the *satra*; those who, knowing thus, enter upon the *satra*"—regarding these, there is a doubt: do they belong to both those who possess the sacred fires (*sāgnī*) and those who do not (*anagnī*), or only to those who possess the sacred fires? What is the prima facie view? They belong to both those who possess the sacred fires and those who do not. Why? Because of the capacity of the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*).
For even a monastery belonging to others is capable of benefiting everyone;
indeed, its purpose is accomplished by it—whether that purpose is achieved through what belongs to one person or through what belongs to another.
Therefore, it may rightly belong to those who do not maintain sacred fires as well.
And because it is seen in the case of the Sārasvata [sacrifice]. (Yukti 1) || 28 ||

And in the Sārakhata sacrifice, there is a scriptural statement: "Those who, having established the sacred fires, perform a sacrificial session (sattra), go to the heavenly world by means of another chariot. And because there is a prescription for expiation. (28) (02)

[The Bhāṣya says: "A sentence-meaning can be established only with that which is immediately perceived; however, when unrelated words are uttered, there is no immediate perception, and thus no syntactic unity [is achieved].

"Alternatively, having understood the meaning of the constituent parts (*pūrvapadārtha*) through another means such as meditation (*dhyāna*), one might produce the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*). That [resulting] sentence-meaning would be non-Vedic (*avaidika*) and preceded by human intellect (*puruṣabuddhipūrvaka*),
just as, for example, when one takes a verb (*ākhyātapada*) from one section (*anuvāka*) and [another word] from another...

That which is produced as the meaning of a sentence must be such that one can produce that sentential meaning after having understood the preceding word-meaning through another means, such as meditation; therefore,
it is determined that sentential unity does not exist when there is an intervention by an unrelated meaning.

Therefore, there is no syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the *sāmidhenī* verses and the *upavīta*. For it is by means of the direct statement that the optional variations of the *sāmidhenī* verses enter into a relationship [with the ritual], not by following the context; nor, moreover, do the *sāmidhenīs* become part of the primary rite through the statement of the variations. For there is no statement regarding them therein that "they are to be performed"; rather, what is it?

The *adhvara-kalpa* rites serve as the illustration; namely, those rituals characterized as the *Āgrayaṇeṣṭi*, the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), and so forth, in which there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses. Regarding these, a doubt arises:

do all three social classes (*varṇas*) have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform these rites, or is it for the Vaiśya alone? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? In this "modified rite" (*vikṛti*), the agent would be restricted by the "rule concerning the person. Why? Because the *adhvara-kalpa* and the others are suitable [for all], being characterized by this specific number [of verses].

And this [sacrifice] has been declared to belong to the Vaiśya; therefore, only the Vaiśya is capable of performing this ritual in its entirety. This ritual possesses seventeen constituent parts, and the state of having seventeen parts (sāptadaśya), when performed by one who is not a Vaiśya, is improper. For that [state] is not enjoined for others; thus, because of the incapacity [of non-Vaiśyas], the injunction "one should sacrifice" will not apply to Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas.
And because of the indicative mark, it is like a specific sacrifice. (31) (Yukti)

And there is an indicative mark (liṅga): "Just as for the Vaiśya there is the state of being seventeen-fold," namely, "The Vaiśya is indeed seventeen-fold. Therefore, the state of being seventeen-fold belongs to the Vaiśya; hence, such types of rites belong to the Vaiśya, just as the specific distinction of the *ilā* belongs to the Vaiśya in the injunction, "A Vaiśya should sacrifice with the Vaiśyastoma," because of its connection with the Vaiśya; in the same way, the state of being seventeen-fold belongs to him alone.

Sūtra 38: Or rather, it is not so, because of the distinctness of the conjunction; for the quality is subordinate to the sacrifice, since the injunction is indeed unconnected [to other rites]. (The Established Conclusion)
This is not the case; these two, conjunction and the single sentence, are distinct, as the reading in the Kātyāyana-krīta-pustaka states: "The entitlement of the Vaiśya here is sevenfold."

[Page 821] Bhāṣya: One should recite—thus it is stated; and in other passages such as the *Adhvarakalpa*, there is the injunction, "One should recite seventeen. This accessory (*guṇa*) has the sacrifice as its primary element (*pradhāna*), not the sacrifice for the sake of the accessory. What follows from this? If this is so, then wherever there is a sacrifice, there it must exist with that accessory, but not wherever there is an accessory, there must be a sacrifice. Even the sacrifice of a Vaiśya is in accordance with his specific accessory; the sacrifice belongs to the three castes, and thus it requires that accessory therein.

—so it is said. Furthermore, the injunction regarding the sacrifice (*ijyā*) is a secondary injunction for that which has become a subordinate factor; it is not connected with the Vaiśya, but rather it indicates a quality (*guṇa*) that is not restricted to the Vaiśya. If it is argued, "The first [injunction] is connected with the Vaiśya," we say no, because the Vaiśya is the primary subject there;
in that context, the Vaiśya is heard as the principal element. Therefore, there is entitlement for all.
In one's own sacrifice, it should be restricted by way of distinction because it is subordinate to that [sacrifice]. (Yukti 38)

Now, as for what was said—that "as it is in the Vaiśyastoma, so it is here too"—that is appropriate in that case, because the sacrifice is heard of for the Vaiśya; there, the rule would be determined by the specific injunction itself. Therefore, in that instance, there is no fault. (6.6.7)

The section concerning the non-giftability of fathers and others in the Viśvajit sacrifice.
In the case of one's own gift, everything [is equal] because there is no distinction. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 1 ||
Regarding the Viśvajit sacrifice, they prescribe: "He gives everything that is his own.

A doubt arises: should everything denoted by the word "own" (sva)—such as mother, father, and so forth—be given, or should only that which is denoted by the word "own" through the connection of ownership be given? What is the prima facie view? Because there is no distinction, [everything including] the mother...

The father—these and other such [names] should also be mentioned. Now, it is said that "giving" consists of the cessation of one's own ownership and the production of another's ownership; however, in the case of the father and others, it is impossible to cease their ownership, for in no way can a father cease to be a father.

It is said: "True, he does not cease to be the father; however, it is possible to make him subject to another's authority, and giving consists in transferring ownership to another, which involves the relinquishment of one's own ownership. Therefore, everything is to be given."
Or rather, it belongs to him who is its owner, because for anyone else it would be impossible [to perform]. (Siddhānta) || 2 ||

The word "bhā" (in the commentary) reverses the position. That which possesses ownership by virtue of its connection to sovereignty (*prabhutva*) is alone to be given, and not anything else. Why? Because that which is connected to sovereignty is possible [to give], whereas the other is impossible;
for it is not possible [to give away] the ownership of one's father and so forth.
"To renounce.

[Objection: "But was it not stated that making him subject to another's will is possible? [Reply: It is said that when one's own self, which possesses sovereignty, is being given away, its universality (*sarvatva*) is expressed, and not—
The giving away of the ether, which is characterized by sovereignty, is not impossible; nor is it impossible for one to serve as an attendant to one's father and others.
Even if this were logically possible, one might still not give it away.

Bhāṣya: Here he says, "But surely, when it is said 'this [belongs] to him' (*tad-iyam*) regarding that where the word *sva* (one's own) occurs, fathers and the rest are understood as those to whom [the property] should be given. Therefore, one should strive for mastery over them, even by setting aside the Smṛti. To this, it is replied: The word *sva* denotes each individual among one's own wealth and kinsmen, not the collection as a whole; therein, with respect to one's own [wealth]...

When the "universality" (sarvatā) has been established, once the purpose of the hall has been fulfilled, universality should not be applied to kinsmen who are incapable [of participating], nor should the traditional rule (smṛti) be set aside. Furthermore, when one's own cattle and other property are obtained through the extended application of the injunction (codaka), the universality pertaining to one's own property must necessarily be adopted;
and since that has been adopted, the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled—this is the case regarding kinsmen.
There is no cause whatsoever for ownership in the act of taking; therefore, fathers and others are not to be given away.
Consequently, only that which possesses ownership through the application of one's own authority is to be given. Thus it is said.

There would be no "ground" (bhūmi), because it would be indistinguishable with respect to all [beings]. || 3 ||

Bhāṣya: Here, regarding the gift of everything (*sarvadāna*), there is a doubt: should land (*bhūmi*) be given, or not? What, then, is intended here by "land"? It is that distinct substance composed of earth—the terrestrial globe (*pṛthivīgolaka*)—and not merely a field or soil. What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) on this point? That it should be given without distinction; for in that case, ownership (*prabhutva*) is connected to it.
The word "kha" (space/sky) occurs, and it is possible to remove the "sky-nature" of space through a mental operation—this being the position reached, we reply: "Land is not to be given.
Why? Because humans are seen to be the lords of fields, but not of the whole [universe].
Regarding the "earth-globe":

[the opponent says], "Well then, he who is currently the sovereign of the whole earth (sārvabhauma) will give it to you. We reply: even he cannot do so. Why? Because only to the extent that the sovereign possesses enjoyment does he rule over the earth.

To that extent, there is no distinction whatsoever between the two; however, for this [king], being a sovereign over all (sārvabhauma), there is this additional [duty]: namely, the protection of the rice and other crops produced upon the earth.

He has authority over some portion that has been enjoyed [by him], but not over the land itself; nor is there any distinction regarding his lordship over the support, movement, and so forth of all living beings—which are derived from the land—belonging to those men who have enjoyed it. Therefore, there is no gift of the land. (6.7.2)

Regarding the Viśvajit sacrifice itself, there is a doubt: "Are horses and other such things to be given as gifts, or not? What is the prima facie view? Since everything has been prescribed [as a gift], the horses are to be given. This being the position, we reply: that which is prohibited from being given should not be given, just as...
Regarding horses: for it is improper to give them away. This indeed is the distinction of horses from other objects, namely that their giving is prohibited, as in the text:
"One does not give maned animals (horses), nor does one accept those with teeth in both jaws."
It is recited in the context of the Viśvajit sacrifice itself: "Therefore, horses are not to be given. (6.7.3 Śrauta Sūtra)
The section concerning the giving of all existing [possessions] in the Viśvajit sacrifice.
And because it is eternal, there is no connection with things that are non-eternal. || 5 ||

Regarding the Viśvajit sacrifice itself, there is a doubt concerning the injunction, "He gives away his entire property" (*sarvasvaṃ dadāti*). Does this mean that one should give all those things—whether they are implements or whatever else a person is able to acquire—that are ready at hand, such as finished vessels and the like; or rather, that only all those things which he actually possesses are to be given, and he need not produce those which are not already in existence? Why is there this doubt? Because both modes of verbal expression are possible.

In the Mīmāṃsā view:

the meaning of a sentence can be established only with that which has been immediately cognized; however, when unrelated words are uttered, there is no immediate cognition, and thus no syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) occurs.
Therefore, [the opponent suggests]:

"Alternatively, by means of another method such as meditation (dhyāna) and so forth, one may first comprehend the meaning of the preceding word and then produce the meaning of the sentence. That [sentence-meaning] would be non-Vedic, being preceded by human intellect.

It would be like this: just as when one takes a verb from one section (anuvāka) and a noun from another, a sentence-meaning is produced; such would that [sentence] be, wherein one might produce a sentence-meaning by first understanding the meaning of the preceding word through some other means, such as meditation. Therefore...
It is determined that syntactic unity does not exist when there is an intervention by unrelated matters;

therefore, the upavīta does not form a single sentence with the *sāmidhenī* verses. [Objection: "But the upavīta is indeed prescribed in proximity to the various forms of the *sāmidhenī* verses, which are present in the immediate consciousness."

"Therefore, it shall be connected with the *sāmidhenī* verses"—to this we say: "No. For the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *sāmidhenīs* has indeed ceased, due to the intervention of the *nivid* formulas. Since it is clearly stated in another recension (śākhā) that "the goat is for Agni-Soma," this is a deliberation on the ritual portion (kalā).
